In the second part, we explore the problem of slicing and consider how dualities of monoidal structures interact with slice constructions. We end by providing a construction for both enriched slice model categories and enriched coslice model categories.

title: BlockAlign: Preference Optimization for Trajectory-Distilled Video Generation
abstract: Directly aligning trajectory-distilled video generators slashes rollout costs and optimizes the deployed few-step model without teacher fine-tuning or re-distillation. However, conventional flow-matching preference objectives assume single-head local velocity supervision, mismatching the finite-interval, block-average transition interface of trajectory-distilled generators such as Parallel Decoding Distillation (PDD) and Parametric Trajectory Distillation (PTD). Naively supervising individual unfused sub-interval velocity heads across all sub-steps rather than the fused block-average velocity at block starts (DirectAlign) induces a severe training--inference mismatch that degrades preference below the unaligned baseline. We introduce BlockAlign, an interface-consistent preference optimization framework that constructs states at valid block boundaries, queries the fused block-level velocity predictor, and supervises span-normalized transition residuals---seamlessly supporting DPO-, NFT-, and rollout-style objectives while preserving the native few-step sampler. We further build a unified post-training pipeline integrating offline pairs, reward-free semi-online continuations, and online rollouts with hierarchical preference selection and objective-aware block scheduling. Experiments on multi-reference video generation across MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA and an in-house model RefVid-V4 show that BlockAlign consistently outperforms unaligned distilled models and DirectAlign in structural plausibility, reference consistency, and visual quality. Notably, our approach unlocks PDD's 5x few-step rollout speedup for 3x faster end-to-end online training, achieving statistically significant human preference gains over PDD baselines (54.0% vs. 33.3% wins/losses, or 61.8% non-tie win rate on RefVid-V4; 51.3% vs. 34.7%, or 59.7% non-tie win rate on MiniMax-H3) and up to an 82.7% win rate against DirectAlign.

title: EPI-SST: Renewal-Structured State-Space Transformers for Epidemic Forecasting
abstract: Epidemic forecasting supports public health decisions ranging from capacity planning to intervention timing, for which both point accuracy and calibrated uncertainty are essential. Although neural models have advanced point forecasting, producing reliable probabilistic predictions over multiple future horizons remains challenging. Renewal models encode epidemic propagation, while neural forecasters learn flexible multi-horizon representations; integrating these strengths within a probabilistic future rollout remains underexplored. We propose EPI-SST (Epidemic State Space Transformer), a probabilistic forecaster centered on an evidence-driven renewal transition. At each horizon, neural evidence produces a bounded update to an internal multiplier and advances a finite-memory renewal state that generates the future mean trajectory. A separate heteroscedastic Gaussian head controls predictive scale using a validation-selected log-variance penalty. Across four epidemic surveillance benchmarks, EPI-SST achieves the lowest pooled RMSE on every dataset, reducing RMSE by up to 14.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline. It also achieves the lowest continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at horizons h = 4, 5, 6 on every dataset, with reductions of up to 43 percent relative to the strongest probabilistic baseline. During the abnormal 2019-2020 influenza season, EPI-SST reduces CRPS by 16.9 percent and calibration error by 78.9 percent; a three-seed replication preserves its distributional lead. Ablation studies and frozen-path interventions show that the renewal transition, attention conditioning, horizon coupling, and uncertainty-scale control make complementary contributions to predictive performance.

title: Finite generation of the second homology group of the genus three Torelli group
abstract: We prove that the group $H_2(\mathcal{I}_3;\mathbb{Z})$ is finitely generated, where $\mathcal{I}_3$ is the Torelli subgroup of the mapping class group of a closed genus-three surface $Σ_3$. A key role in the proof is played by establishing the following property: for each symplectic transvection $t_x\in\mathrm{Sp}_{6}(\mathbb{Z})$, we have $$ \bigl(t^{120}_x-1\bigr)^{57}\bigl(t_x^{24}-1\bigr)(t_x-1)^6H_2(\mathcal{I}_3;\mathbb{Z})=0. $$ The proof is based on the study of the spectral sequences associated with the action of $\mathcal{I}_3$ on the Bestvina-Bux-Margalit complex of minimizing cycles and with the actions on certain auxiliary complexes of the stabilizers of two- and three-component multicurves on $Σ_3$. The remaining ingredients are Tavgen's theorem, which asserts that $\mathrm{Sp}_{6}(\mathbb{Z})$ has bounded elementary generation, and the result of Kassabov and Putman, which asserts that $H_2(\mathcal{I}_3;\mathbb{Z})$ is finitely generated as a $\mathbb{Z}[\mathrm{Sp}_6(\mathbb{Z})]$-module.

title: Symmetric discrete Mikhailov models
abstract: The discrete Mikhailov model of [1] lacks conjugation symmetry, which prevents a direct reduction to the discrete Fokas--Lenells (dFL) equation and restricts the study of its solution structure. Revisiting the Cauchy matrix scheme, we construct four families of fully conjugation-symmetric discrete Mikhailov models by combining the equivalent relations of the auxiliary quantities pairwise. All of these models reduce to the symmetric semi-discrete and continuous Mikhailov models via a two-step continuum limit. The local reduction $ν=μ^{*}$ and the nonlocal reduction $ν=\mathrm{i}μ_{-}^{*}$ then give four families of local and of nonlocal dFL equations, for which exact Cauchy matrix solution schemes are established: the AKNS-type scheme for the local case, and both the AKNS- and KP-type schemes for the nonlocal case. We further characterize the dynamics of the obtained solutions in detail.

title: Adaptive Koopman Predictive Control without Persistent Excitation via Matrix Normal Invariant Priors
abstract: Finite-dimensional Koopman models are increasingly used in predictive control, but their accuracy remains limited by truncation errors and offline identification data. Adaptive Koopman predictive control promises to address this limitation, but typically requires closed-loop persistent excitation (PE). Since this is difficult to achieve in practice, in this paper we develop an adaptive generalized Koopman (GeKo) predictive controller that does not require PE. To this end, we formulate a recursive matrix regression in fixed lifted coordinates that extends the Kalman filter with back-to-the-prior forgetting to matrix-valued operators and uses a matrix normal invariant prior, centered at the operator identified offline. For any regressor sequence, and thus under any feedback law, we prove that the covariance remains between two multiples of the prior covariance and that the estimation error is input-to-state stable. On an academic example, a differential-drive robot and a power system with plant changes and little excitation, the invariant-prior estimator yields the lowest overall tracking error among the compared estimators and prevents covariance windup.

title: Triple Exchange at the Cosmological Collider in Closed Form
abstract: Particles with masses near the Hubble scale leave a characteristic pattern in the primordial bispectrum, turning inflation into a cosmological collider. For light fields, where this signal is largest, no closed form is known for the full shape of the quasi-single-field triple exchange. Using Feynman-integral methods, we obtain the first closed-form results, exact in the momenta, as expansions in terms of multiple polylogarithms around the massless and conformally coupled limits. We show that the template used in Planck analyses overestimates the amplitude by up to a factor of 1.8 and underestimates the mass, whereas our new template recovers both, as needed for current and upcoming CMB and galaxy surveys. We also compute the collapsed trispectrum and, combining it with the bispectrum, find that at weak mixing it bounds the self-coupling more tightly.

title: Demographic dynamics of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025
abstract: We investigate the demographic evolution of the Japanese astronomy and astrophysics publication community during 1996-2025 using bibliometric data from 23,274 publications in major journals in the field. The number of active Japan-affiliated authors increased from approximately 600 in the late 1990s to more than 2,000 by the early 2020s, while annual publication output reached approximately 1,400 by 2025. Participation was highly heterogeneous, with 46% of authors observed in only one publication year within the study period and a smaller core showing long observed participation periods. We define the Community Renewal Rate (CRR) as a community-level measure of renewal, calculated as the fraction of active authors not observed during a specified preceding interval. The 5-year CRR typically remained near one quarter of the active community, with annual values ranging from approximately 21% to 33%, indicating persistent renewal despite substantial community growth. An order-of-magnitude comparison suggests that newly entering students account for only part of the renewal-author population. The community therefore expanded while sustaining both continuity through authors with long observed participation periods and renewal through recurring changes in active membership.

title: Tracing the Luminosity Evolution of Globular Cluster Systems with JWST: MACS J1149.5+2223 at z=0.544
abstract: We present a study of the compact-source population associated with the massive galaxy cluster MACS J1149.5+2223 at z=0.544 using deep JWST/NIRCam imaging in F115W, F150W, and F200W. After photometric and morphological selection, we identify 1,202 unresolved compact-source candidates. The observed luminosity distribution samples only the bright side of the expected globular-cluster luminosity function (GCLF), remaining several magnitudes above the turnover. Based on published GCLF turnovers for Abell 2744 and MACS 0417, we adopt an expected turnover magnitude of m_0=33.66 mag for MACS 1149. A forward-modeled fit then yields sigma=1.71 mag, which characterizes the observed bright-side slope under the adopted turnover rather than the intrinsic width of the full GCLF. Comparison with PARSEC simple stellar population models shows that the elevated luminosities of the compact sources are consistent with the expected fading of younger stellar populations as they evolve toward the present epoch. The brightest sources reach luminosities comparable to those of ultra-compact dwarfs. However, stellar-population degeneracies and possible foreground contamination make it difficult to distinguish. Together with recent JWST studies of globular cluster systems across a range of redshifts, MACS 1149 extends the emerging observational sequence of compact stellar systems and supports stellar population fading as an important contributor to their luminosity evolution across cosmic time.

title: Minimum Sum-of-Radii Clustering with Strong and Weak Oracles
abstract: In the minimum sum of radii (MSR) problem, the input is a set of $n$ points in a metric space and a parameter $k$, and the goal is to cover the points by at most $k$ balls, each centered at an input point, while minimizing the sum of their radii. We study MSR in the weak-strong oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), where the metric is unknown and is accessed through two oracles. The answers of the weak oracle are given to us for free: for every pair of points, we receive a distance value that, with probability $δ$, is arbitrarily corrupted. Exact distances are available only through costly strong queries, where a strong query on a point reveals its exact distances to all previously strongly queried points, and the goal is to minimize the number of strong queries. For every constant $δ< 1/2$, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm that makes $O(k \log n \log\log n)$ strong point queries and, with high probability, returns an $O(1)$-approximation for MSR; the previously best algorithm required running time and a number of strong queries exponential in $k$. This is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of a lower bound that we prove: any constant-factor approximation that succeeds with high probability on every instance must make $Ω(k \log n)$ strong queries in expectation on some instance. The same $Ω(k \log n)$ lower bound holds for $k$-center, where it matches the known upper bound up to an $O(\log\log n)$ factor. An optimal MSR cluster can be small both in size and in radius, so a uniform sample of strongly queried points may miss it entirely. Instead, our algorithm uses a packing LP over the balls certified so far to decide which points to query next. The analysis holds against an adversary who knows which pairs are corrupted.

title: Flow Matching for Sampled-Data Control of Angular Distributions
abstract: Synchronization and clustering in oscillator networks depend on the joint distribution of the phases. Flow Matching can steer this distribution by learning an angular velocity field from shortest arcs between paired configurations. Each arc is traversed at constant speed, yet the resulting field can vary along its own trajectories. In this article, we study how to control angular transport on the circle and product torus when each controller evaluation selects a rate to hold until the next update. Using the same local velocity samples, Flow Matching learns the instantaneous angular rate and MeanFlow learns its average along the reference trajectory over the control interval. Under direct angular actuation, holding the exact average gives the reference displacement. We relate the displacement error of holding the instantaneous rate and the training residual of MeanFlow to the conditional covariance of the teacher velocities. Experiments with 100 phases show that endpoint pairing affects the comparison. MeanFlow gives smaller one-step errors under minibatch pairing, while permutation alignment reverses the ranking for exchangeable phase clusters.

title: Structure-Guided Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer for Efficient Monocular 3D Human Pose Estimation
abstract: Existing multi-granularity methods for monocular 3D human pose estimation emphasize spatial joint features while underusing skeletal structure, including global connectivity and temporal continuity. Moreover, modeling entire frame sequences incurs high computational costs. We propose a Structure-Aware Multi-Granularity Spatiotemporal Transformer that integrates structural priors across spatial and temporal representations for accurate and efficient pose estimation. A three-level feature extractor captures human topology at the joint, bone, and limb levels. Gated Adaptive Spatial Attention (GASA) embeds structural constraints into spatial attention, while Multi-Granularity Feature Enhancement (MGFE) uses hierarchical pooling and fusion to strengthen local details and global semantics. Temporal Segment Fusion (TSF) aligns temporal contexts across granularities to capture both short- and long-range motion patterns. Hierarchical Cross-Attention (HCA) promotes spatiotemporal interaction between granularities, and Keyframe Attention (KFA) selects informative motion segments to reduce redundancy and computational cost. Experiments demonstrate improved accuracy and efficiency over conventional Transformer-based approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of structure-aware multi-granularity modeling for monocular 3D human pose estimation.

title: Settling the Support Complexity of Correlated Equilibria
abstract: We study the support complexity of approximate correlated equilibria (CE) in two-player games, that is, the minimum number of pure action profiles that must be assigned positive probability to approximate a correlated equilibrium of a two-player matrix game. For $\varepsilon$-approximate coarse correlated equilibria, constant approximation is possible with support $O(\log N/\varepsilon^2)$ in $N\times N$ games. For correlated equilibria, the best known upper bound was $O(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ [Babichenko et al., 2014, 2017], but whether this bound was tight remained open. We establish a matching lower bound, resolving the open question of Ko and Schvartzman [2017]. Specifically, we show that, already for two-player zero-sum games, for every $1\leq k\leq N^{1/2}$ the worst-case correlated-equilibrium gap achievable by a distribution supported on at most $k$ pure profiles is $$ Θ\left( \min\left\{1,\frac{\sqrt{\log N}}{k^{1/4}}\right\} \right), $$ which implies a $Θ(\log^2 N/\varepsilon^4)$ worst-case support bound. The proof builds on a probabilistic-method construction based on random sign matrices.

title: EWMA Principal Eigenportfolios of Equity Returns: Market Representation and Beta-Hedging Performance
abstract: This study examines whether an adaptively estimated principal eigenportfolio improves equity beta hedging relative to capitalisation-weighted and equal-weighted market benchmarks. Using stock returns from a historically changing S&P 500 universe, it constructs a portfolio from the leading principal component of an exponentially weighted second-moment matrix of volatility-standardised returns. The resulting portfolio, EWMA-PC1, is compared with SPY and RSP under a common beta-hedging procedure across randomly generated portfolios of varying sizes and weighting schemes. Evaluation considers variance reduction and average pairwise residual correlation, with paired blockbootstrap inference. EWMA-PC1 exhibits broad market participation and achieves greater mean variance reduction and lower average residual correlation than SPY across all tested configurations. Its incremental advantage over RSP is smaller and mixed. For 50-stock Dirichlet portfolios, mean variance reduction is 92.17% under PC1, compared with 79.03% under SPY and 91.93% under RSP; RSP instead achieves greater mean variance reduction for multistock liquidity-tilted portfolios. Statistical evidence of improvement is more consistent against SPY than against RSP. These findings distinguish the extraction of a market-like component from incremental hedge effectiveness and highlight the importance of benchmark weighting and targetportfolio composition. The results concern gross statistical risk reduction and exclude additional trading, financing, and borrowing costs.

title: Multi-Library Feature Engineering and Statistically Validated Classification for Power Swing Detection and Stability Assessment
abstract: Faults occurring during power swings, and the evolution of a swing into an unstable condition, cause distance-relay maloperation and cascaded outages. This paper identifies faults, faults during power swings, and power swings, and distinguishes stable from unstable swings in a 9-bus WSCC system modeled in PSCAD/EMTDC. Three time-series feature libraries (tsfresh, TSFEL, and tsfeatures) are applied to the 3-phase relay voltages and currents, giving 3286 statistical, temporal, spectral, and fractal descriptors per event window. A two-step feature selection (Boruta all-relevant filtering followed by RFECV- and SHAP-guided minimal-optimal pruning) reduces the feature set to 18 compact, non-redundant features. 14 classifiers spanning linear, kernel/instance-based, probabilistic, neural, and tree-ensemble/boosting families are then benchmarked under repeated stratified cross-validation, with model differences assessed by a Friedman/Nemenyi omnibus-and-post-hoc test and a Nadeau--Bengio corrected paired t-test. Rotation Forest (ROF) identifies the three event types with 99.98% and SVM-RBF distinguishes stable from unstable swings with 97.97% balanced accuracy. The results show that automated, library-driven feature extraction combined with rigorous statistical model comparison achieves near-perfect discrimination while retaining feature-level interpretability through SHAP importance.

title: On Pairwise Independent and Strongly Correlated Random Variables
abstract: Characterizing joint distributions that maximize the centered third-order moment under prescribed marginal distributions and pairwise independence has various statistical applications. This problem can be formulated as a multistochastic optimal transport problem. In this work, we generalize the results on the $(3,2)$-multistochastic Monge-Kantorovich problem to cost functions of the form $c(x,y,z)=f(x)f(y)f(z)$, where $f$ is defined on $[0,1]$ through dyadic expansions: $f(x)=\sum_{i\geq 1} a_i x_i$, with $x_i\in\{0,1\}$. Under summability and domination conditions on the coefficients, we show that an optimal transport plan is concentrated on the Sierpinski tetrahedron. We also characterize mixtures of geometric coefficient sequences through Hausdorff moment sequences and construct a recursive dual solution with its integral representation for costs with geometric coefficients.

title: Lower bounds for testing the completely depolarizing channel
abstract: We study lower bounds to the query complexity of testing whether an unknown quantum channel mapping a $d_{\mathrm{in}}$-dimensional input to a $d_{\mathrm{out}}$-dimensional output is the completely depolarizing channel or is $\varepsilon$-far from it in diamond distance. We show that for this task (i) any ancilla-assisted, coherent, adaptive tester requires at least $Ω(d_{\mathrm{in}}d_{\mathrm{out}}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries; (ii) any ancilla-assisted, coherent, non-adaptive tester requires at least $\max\{Ω(d_{\mathrm{in}}^{1.5}d_{\mathrm{out}}/\varepsilon^2), Ω(d_{\mathrm{in}}^{2}/\varepsilon^2)\}$ queries. We also show that these lower bounds apply to the more general problem of determining whether an unknown channel belongs to the set of all state-replacement channels or is $\varepsilon$-far from the entire set in diamond distance.

title: "Can a Robot Really Care About Me?" How Perceiving a Tutor as Human or AI Affects Computer Science Students' Attitudes and Experiences
abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

title: HoloGene: Learning to Lift Sliced Spatial Transcriptomics to Holistic 3D Gene Fields
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) provides spatially resolved gene expression measurements, but most 3D ST datasets are acquired as independently processed 2D sections. Computational approaches span slice registration and integration, explicit or generative interpolation, and coordinate-field modeling. Within the last family, implicit neural representations (INRs) offer a continuous, coordinate-queryable parameterization, but standard isotropic coordinate encodings do not explicitly reflect that serial-section measurements are dense in-plane and sparse along the axial direction. We present HoloGene, an anisotropic conditional INR framework for estimating continuous 3D gene-expression fields from pre-registered ST sections. Its central contribution is an acquisition-aware factorization that couples dense in-plane synthesis with sparse axial evolution using established GAE, FiLM, pseudo-label supervision, and CORAL components. HoloGene compresses high-dimensional expression profiles into a graph-autoencoder latent manifold, uses pseudo-label-derived signature conditioning to provide coarse intra-section context, and applies depth-dependent FiLM modulation to model axial variation. A signature-stratified correlation-alignment regularizer encourages cross-slice covariance alignment in latent features. Using held-out measured sections as cross-sectional references, HoloGene improves reconstruction accuracy and biological preservation metrics compared with general-purpose INRs and adapted spatial-transcriptomics baselines. These results support anisotropic conditional modeling as a practical strategy for estimating 3D expression fields from discontinuous ST sections. Code is available at https://github.com/Szym29/HoloGene.

title: The Optimal Interface Method: A Modelling Paradigm for Two-Body Contact Problems via Optimal Control and $Γ$-convergence
abstract: This paper is concerned with the derivation of a model governing the equilibrium configuration of two linearly elastic bodies that may come into contact with each other. The contact zone, or coincidence set, is an \emph{a priori} unknown of the model, and the equilibrium configuration is governed by variational inequalities. We introduce a new modelling paradigm in which the contact interface between the two linearly elastic bodies under consideration is now regarded as the \emph{primary variable} of an optimal control problem whose states are the unique solutions of two \emph{independent} unilateral contact problems for which this very contact interface represents the obstacle itself. As a result, the free boundary emerges as the solution of a low-dimensional optimisation problem rather than as the active set of coupled variational inequalities. We establish the existence and uniqueness of optimal controls minimising the reduced cost functional arising from the modelling paradigm introduced beforehand, and we show that the family of marginal energy functionals associated with such model $Γ$-converges to the energy functional associated with the original variational inequalities as the positive \emph{cost parameter} $β$ in the reduced cost functional tends to zero. This $Γ$-convergence argument also yields a characterisation of the coincidence set of the limit problem in terms of the optimal interfaces. We further show that, after a suitable regularisation, the reduced cost functional is Gâteaux differentiable, and that its Gâteaux derivative can be explicitly computed \emph{without solving any adjoint system}. Finally, we corroborate the $Γ$-convergence result obtained beforehand with numerical experiments on a simplified and exactly solvable configuration.

title: Block Generalized Inverses in Skew Corner Pairs
abstract: We view generalized inverses from another perspective, through invertibility in the skew corner bimodules $eRf$ attached to a pair of distinct idempotents $e, f$ of a ring $R$. Many generalized inverses are defined by a system of equations together with conditions on ranges and kernels, which makes them harder to visualize as inverses in the traditional sense. In the language of invertible blocks, however, they become genuine one or two-sided inverses of a suitable compression of the element. We will systematically show how block invertibility in a skew corner $eRf$ can be used to visualize Drazin's $(b,c)$-inverse, which contains the Moore--Penrose, Bott-Duffin $(e,f)$ inverses amongst others. On this foundation we develop a way to produce units of the corner ring from complementary blocks, and transport stable range one across two-sided Peirce decompositions for distinct idempotents.

title: Pretty Linear Liars: Unregularized Probes Favor Intervention-Unfaithful Features
abstract: Linear probing is a common technique in mechanistic interpretability despite the fact that the decodability of a given feature does not necessarily imply the network uses that feature. Intervention faithfulness, not merely decodability, is the appropriate criterion for whether a feature serves a defined active role in the model. Meanwhile, probe regularization has been used for feature discovery, but the impact of regularization on feature causality remains unclear. We study probe regularization systematically, starting with unregularized ordinary least squares (OLS) regression and considering increasing amounts of regularization via ridge regression. We show theoretically that OLS probes amplify low-variance directions in activation space that have spurious correlations with the target feature, whereas regularization reduces influence from these directions. Empirically, we find in a toy transformer and Llama-2-7B that intervention faithfulness increases up to a point, and then decreases again, and that the optimal regularization strength leads to features bearing striking similarity (in both direction and variance) to those learned by optimizing for intervention outcomes directly. Together, these results provide mechanistic justification for regularizing regression probes.

title: VisDrone-ReID: A Unified Multi-Category Object Re-Identification Benchmark
abstract: Object re-identification (Re-ID) benchmarks remain predominantly confined to single-category evaluations, limiting the development of unified systems capable of operating across diverse object types. This paper presents VisDrone-ReID, a unified multi-category Re-ID benchmark derived from the VisDrone2019-MOT dataset through a principled conversion pipeline. The pipeline resolves structural incompatibilities between multi-object tracking annotations and Re-ID evaluation requirements, addressing sequence-scoped identity collision, temporal redundancy, and the absence of a principled identity-level train/test split. The resulting benchmark comprises 9,516 identities and 150,016 images across ten object categories - pedestrian, people, bicycle, car, van, truck, tricycle, awning-tricycle, bus, and motor, sourced from 80 unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sequences captured across urban environments. A leave-one-out (LOO) evaluation protocol is adopted to provide a comprehensive assessment. Baseline experiments across four representative Re-ID models spanning CNN and transformer architectures establish the first systematic performance reference on this benchmark. Results reveal a consistent Rank-1 to mAP gap across all models, suggesting that VisDrone-ReID presents a genuine retrieval challenge beyond nearest-neighbour matching. Per-category analysis identifies pedestrian as the most challenging category and reveals that vision-language pretraining provides a measurable advantage on semantically distinctive categories. VisDrone-ReID provides a consistent platform for studying multi-category object re-identification under the scale variation, viewpoint challenges, and category diversity characteristic of real-world surveillance scenarios.

title: Nazarov-Sklyanin Lax operators at higher rank
abstract: We construct a rank-$m$ Nazarov-Sklyanin Lax operator for generalized Macdonald functions. The operator acts on the horizontal Fock module of quantum toroidal $\mathfrak{gl}_1$, extended by an auxiliary polynomial space with $m$ components. A geometric realization is given by the tensor product with the dual tautological line on the equivariant $K$-theory of a Hecke correspondence studied by Negut. The eigenbasis is indexed by an $m$-tuple of partitions and an addable corner, whose content is the eigenvalue. We give an anti-normal factorization and prove that the Lax operator is self-adjoint for the transported Euler pairing. With unit framing weight, the rank-one specialization recovers the Nazarov-Sklyanin factorization. We then show that the Lax operator is conjugate to the companion matrix of a projected q-Miura operator of the deformed $W$-algebra of type $\mathfrak{gl}_m$. This also gives an explicit presentation of the $K$-theory of the Hecke correspondence.

title: Goldman's Ergodicity Conjecture and Branched Developing Maps
abstract: We prove that every representation $ρ:π_1(Σ_g)\rightarrow\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathrm{R})$ which sends every simple closed curve to a hyperbolic element admits a branched developing map. As a corollary, the mapping class group action on the Euler class zero component of the $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathrm{R})$-character variety of a genus $g$ surface is ergodic if $g\geq3$. (The action is not ergodic if $g=2$.) Moreover, almost every representation of nonzero Euler class admits a branched developing map.

title: Supporting Community Members Navigating Reentry with Revisable Future Envisioning
abstract: Future-planning tools often treat agency as individual and leave out the institutional conditions that shape how aspirations become action. We examine this tension in the context of reentry from incarceration and recovery from substance use disorder, through a partnership with a nonprofit organization. Building on participants' physical vision-board practices, we designed a digital future-envisioning tool that helps users represent current circumstances, desired futures, and pathways that connect goals to concrete resources. We draw on data from three workshops involving 18 participants and follow-up interviews with 10 participants to examine how they used future envisioning within a fragmented support system. Participants described reentry and recovery as ongoing processes in which the everyday work of staying stable was central to progress. Envisioning futures supported this work by surfacing constraints and interdependencies, by reframing personal strengths and institutional supports as assets, and by helping participants move from abstract hopes toward articulated goals and contingent plans. We theorize revision as maintenance work and conclude with design implications for community-embedded interactive systems that support revisable, dependency-aware planning.

title: Uniqueness and nondegeneracy of positive solutions for a class of fractional Schrödinger equations in $\mathbb R$
abstract: We study positive solutions $u\in H^s(\mathbb R)$ of the fractional Schrödinger equation $(-Δ)^su+λu=f(u)$ in $\mathbb R$, where $0<s<1$, $λ>0$, and $f$ is a general nonlinearity such that $f(t)/t$ is increasing. We prove that, under a single concavity condition on an auxiliary function, positive solutions are unique up to translations. The result applies to all positive solutions rather than only to ground states, and it allows $f'$ to be unbounded below at zero. It covers pure powers, sums of powers, logarithmic and saturable nonlinearities, for suitable ranges of the parameters. We further prove that every positive solution is nondegenerate, with the kernel of the linearized operator spanned by $u'$, and that it has Morse index one. If moreover $f(\sqrt h)/\sqrt h$ is concave, then for $1/2\le s<1$ a positive solution with prescribed $L^2$ norm is unique together with its Lagrange multiplier. The proofs are purely variational, using neither a continuation argument in $s$ nor the nondegeneracy of the linearized operator. Our method rests on the convexity of the action along an interpolation between symmetric decreasing functions that preserves a suitable integral quantity, and this convexity allows us to identify every positive solution as a constrained minimizer. For $1/2\le s<1$ we use the height interpolation of Delgadino, Yan and Yao, while for $0<s<1/2$ we introduce a new two-level interpolation.

title: Halting in Recurrent Sequence Models
abstract: Recurrent sequence models, such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and state space models (SSMs), are often trained to emit an end-of-sequence (EOS) token when their output sequence is complete. During training, EOS is treated as another token without a special loss term or incentive. Although this training paradigm is widely used, it is not understood how models decide to output EOS. We study a minimal version of the EOS halting problem in which networks are trained to emit a given input sequence an instructed number of times, followed by EOS. We train tanh RNNs and linear SSMs on this task, finding that the RNNs encode the number of tokens left to copy in a linear subspace, of which two principal components capture most of the variation. Hidden states with the same remaining count converge to a shared representation regardless of their instructed repeat count. By modulating the hidden state using an affine transformation at the boundary between copied sequences, we shift the RNN's state to the representation shared by states with one fewer copy remaining. The unchanged network emits EOS one copy earlier while reproducing the shortened target sequence in 94.4% of new sequences, revealing that this representation causally determines the stopping time. In the SSMs, the difference between trajectories with different repeat counts is separated across two-dimensional rotation planes whose contributions to the EOS comparison cancel during copying and align near the stopping time. Rotating the planes independently removes most of the intended stopping while preserving the copied content, which shows that the stopping time depends on the planes' relative phases. These results identify two candidate primitives of EOS halting in recurrent models: a shared encoding of the number of remaining tokens in tanh RNNs and phase alignment across fixed rotations in linear SSMs.

title: Straight to the Product: What Online Retailers Miss When Shoppers Ask AI First
abstract: When people ask an AI assistant what to buy, what happens next at the store? We link the same people's assistant conversations to their later browsing at twenty large online retailers. People go to the product the assistant named: among shoppers who had not visited the store in the past week, visits to the named product within a day rise from 0.02 to 2.07 per 100 answers (+2.0 points [1.7, 2.4]), and on days with a product-page visit at the store, 44% show a product from their own answer, against 1.5% for a matched answer given to someone else. The result replicates in a separate five-month period. Few arrive through the assistant's link: after recommending answers, 89% of visits carry no sign of it, and 54% follow a web search, the same share as their usual visits. When a search comes just before the first visit, it names the answer's product 28% of the time (1% in earlier weeks), as if the search box were an address bar. The chat names the product; the store logs a search. Once there, shoppers keep browsing. We propose product follow-through, the share of answers followed by a visit to the product they named, as a way to evaluate shopping assistants and agents by what people do next: it needs no referral data or provider logs and can be computed for each assistant.

title: Ionospheric bow waves during Starship Flight 14: coupling through vented propellant
abstract: Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations of Starship Flight 14 show clear bow-shaped waves in detrended total electron content (dTEC), including during motor-off coast. These observations raise a coupling problem because the spacecraft hull is small compared with the thermospheric molecular mean free path. Sustained visible release in flight video motivates the hypothesis that vented, unburned propellant supplies a much larger interaction region capable of producing a fluid response. We model gaseous methane and oxygen using the Stochastic Parallel Rarefied-gas Time-accurate Analyzer (SPARTA) for direct simulation Monte Carlo calculations at a combined release rate of 10 kg s$^{-1}$. The calculated collisional energy transfer extends over a region roughly 10 km across. We use this deposition pattern as a moving source of mass, momentum and total energy in a nonlinear neutral model coupled to a passive plasma response. The model produces a South American dTEC bow with broadly similar morphology and propagation speeds to the observations. Representative South American cuts have simulated root-mean-square (RMS) residuals of about 0.015 total electron content units (TECU), compared with observed values of 0.021--0.032 TECU; the North American response remains substantially weaker than observed. These results support collisional transfer of orbital momentum and energy by vented propellant as an explanation for the coast-phase waves. The release rate remains uncertain, and chemical contributions require further testing.

title: Strong Decays of the $2^-$ Heavy-Light Mesons in the Relativistic Bethe-Salpeter Approach
abstract: We present a relativistic study of the mass spectra, the $^1D_2$--$^3D_2$ mixing angles, and the OZI-allowed two-body strong decays of the heavy-light $J^P=2^-$ mesons $D_2$, $D'_2$, $D_{s2}$, $D'_{s2}$, $\bar{B}_2$, $\bar{B}'_2$, $\bar{B}_{s2}$, and $\bar{B}'_{s2}$. The mass spectrum and the meson wave functions are obtained by solving the full instantaneous Bethe--Salpeter (Salpeter) equation, in which the wave-function representations are constructed directly in terms of the $J^P$ quantum numbers rather than the non-relativistic spectroscopic notation ${}^{2S+1}L_J$. For the decay amplitudes we use the partial conservation of the axial-vector current (PCAC) together with the low-energy theorem for the $H\to H'P$ channels, so that the light pseudoscalar meson enters only through its decay constant, and the effective chiral Lagrangian for the $H\to H'V$ channels. The total widths of these mesons are estimated by summing over the partial widths of all OZI-allowed strong decay channels.

title: Trait Collapse in Text-to-Image Generation: Evaluating and Mitigating Personality Inconsistency in Visual Storytelling
abstract: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}. We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' $κ= 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.

title: Signs of Wear: Evaluating Intelligent Speed Assistance Under Synthetic Adverse Conditions
abstract: Intelligent Speed Assistance (ISA) systems rely on cameras to recognize speed-limit signs, yet existing benchmarks underrepresent the weathered, dirty, and overgrown signs commonly encountered on rural roads. We use generative image editing to introduce different forms of wear into real street-level images of speed-limit signs. The resulting ISA-Wear dataset contains paired original and edited images. Guided by text instructions, a multimodal image-editing model adds snow, rust, vegetation, faded paint, or mud to the speed-limit sign in a street-level frame at three severity levels. Where appropriate, the surrounding scene is adapted as well, and the viewpoint is kept. Every edited frame has an unedited counterpart, and we only evaluate frames whose original is recognized correctly, so any failure can be attributed to the wear. Since the model alters the sign's geometry in 21\% of the edits, all edits are filtered by a geometric check and a manual review. Severity is measured as the LPIPS distance between the original and the edited sign plate. On 716 worn frames, we find that in detect-then-read pipelines, wear breaks detection before it breaks reading. The detector finds only 62\% of the worn signs, even though it finds every one of them in the original frames. Missed detections account for 78--87\% of failed reads, a pattern that a zero-shot detector shares. Given the annotated sign box, as in the crop-based benchmarks, a classifier still reads 78\% of the worn signs, but only 56\% when it has to rely on the detector

title: The unitary group $U_3(4)$ as a Galois group over $\mathbb{Q}$
abstract: We prove that the simple unitary group $U_3(4)=\operatorname{PSU}_3(\mathbb{F}_4)$, of order $62400$, is the Galois group of a regular extension of $\mathbb{Q}(t)$, and hence of infinitely many extensions of $\mathbb{Q}$. The extension has four branch points, with inertia groups of orders $2$, $2$, $3$, $3$, and it is the only extension with these properties up to a rational change of the coordinate $t$. We give an explicit polynomial of degree $65$ for it.

title: JointQ: Joint Scale-and-Integer Quantization for Large Language Models
abstract: GPTQ is the de facto standard solver for layer-wise post-training quantization (PTQ) of large language models, yet the solver itself has received less attention than weight preprocessing and cross-layer objectives. We target a bottleneck of GPTQ: its greedy procedure optimizes continuous group scales separately from the assignment of discrete integers. Evaluating each integer candidate with its closed-form optimal scale has been used for per-channel quantization; JointQ extends it to group-wise quantization, where a row's scales are coupled through the Hessian, and applies it to refine the GPTQ solution. Each local-search move changes one integer and recomputes its group's optimal scale in closed form, accounting for the other groups through the full Hessian; all scales are periodically re-solved jointly. The search starts from a row-wise selection among scale-refitted candidates including the GPTQ solution, so unregularized JointQ never has a larger layer-wise calibration error than GPTQ. JointQ preserves the GPTQ output format and is thus a drop-in replacement. Across four models and four settings, JointQ improves six-task average zero-shot accuracy over vanilla GPTQ in 14 of 16 comparisons and perplexity in 12 of 16. The mean accuracy gain increases from 0.0044 in W4G128 to 0.1559 in W3 per-channel, and JointQ also improves average accuracy over GPTQ with MSE-based scale search and activation ordering in all eight per-channel comparisons, though rarely in G128. An ablation shows that JointQ's diagonal Tikhonov regularization mitigates severe W3 per-channel perplexity degradation, so the largest gains are not due to the local search alone. Overall, JointQ's primary empirical benefit is downstream accuracy preservation in challenging low-bit and large-group regimes. Code is available in the OneComp library at https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/OneCompression.

title: DominoBench: Evaluating Multi-Step Physical Reasoning from Still Images
abstract: Can a vision-language model look at a picture of a chain reaction and tell what will happen? Recent multimodal models describe scenes fluently and solve textbook physics problems, which suggests they should also predict how a scene of ramps, ledges, pendulums, seesaws and dominoes plays out once a ball is pushed. We tested this claim on 30 models from 10 families and reached a clear conclusion: unaided, no model predicts the outcome reliably. We built DominoBench, a benchmark of still images of 2D rigid-body scenes whose outcome a physics simulator computes. It holds 854 items in 427 minimal pairs, in which a change of one to three grid steps in one quantity decides whether one person survives, and every item comes with a four-rung hint ladder ending in the exact calculation that decides the outcome. Unaided, frontier models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI are right about the person whose fate flips in at most 75% of items and answer both twins of a pair correctly in at most 40%. Pointing at the deciding step helps little, and exact geometry given as text barely helps, yet once the deciding calculation and the quantities it needs, including speeds that a still image cannot show, are written out, the same models reach 80-92% on the deciding person, while small open-weight models stay near chance. Physical prediction from a still image therefore fails at the quantitative step: the strongest models use the deciding quantity when they are given it, but do not produce it on their own. For models that plan or act in the physical world, a fluent account of a scene is thus no evidence of a correct prediction: such models must find and compute the deciding quantity unprompted, and DominoBench tests whether they do.

title: Lean-Verified No-Go Theorems for $R$-Symmetries and Modular Symmetries in 4D GUTs
abstract: $R$-symmetries are instrumental in supersymmetric model building. However, a no-go theorem restricts us from using them in a large class of four-dimensional (4D) grand unified theories (GUTs). Specifically, it has been shown that a supersymmetric 4D GUT based on SU(5), with finitely many chiral multiplets, cannot be broken spontaneously to the exact minimal supersymmetric standard model (MSSM) while preserving a discrete $\mathbb{Z}_M^R$, with $M \geq 3$, or continuous U(1) $R$-symmetry. We use Lean 4 to formalize this proof. In the process, we identify and close a gap in the general case of the published argument. Further, we discuss the implications for GUT models with modular symmetries. We point out that modular symmetries are inevitably $R$-symmetries in a supersymmetric framework that also describes gravity. At certain critical points in moduli space, discrete $R$-symmetries are linearly realized. In the context of 4D GUTs, the no-go theorem then implies that exotic states become massless at these points, provided the GUT-breaking vacuum preserves these symmetries. In the vicinity of these critical points, these exotics are parametrically light, which may spoil gauge coupling unification.

title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
abstract: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

title: What Unlinked Aggregates Still Prove: Ranker Comparisons from Exact and Differentially Private Item Counts
abstract: Privacy controls can prevent an evaluator from linking purchases to the recommendations users received, while a merchant can still release complete item-level purchase counts for the evaluation cohort. We ask when these counts identify which recommender performs better. The counts constrain who could have bought each item. We bound the performance difference over all assignments consistent with the counts. A reduced transportation network handles full catalogs and can certify attainable endpoints. If the interval excludes zero, it identifies the better recommender for that cohort. With differentially private counts, one confidence guarantee applies jointly to all comparisons from the same release. In two e-commerce cohorts of about 20,000 and 100,000 users, exact counts narrowed every interval compared with bounds that ignored the counts. Most decisions involved a recommender that favors popular items. For NDCG@10, which rewards ranking purchased items higher, each setting combined one of three personalized pairs with a pattern and rate of missing links. Exact counts settled 14 of 168 settings in the smaller cohort and none of 81 in the larger cohort. In the smaller cohort, exact counts broken down by user group settled two personalized pairs when 90% of users remained linked, at the cost of revealing more about individual purchases. Whole-cohort private releases with one count per item retained much of the narrowing but settled no personalized pair in either cohort. Grouping less popular items into bins let private counts settle one personalized pair in the smaller cohort.

title: Where the Evidence Lives: Measuring Privacy and Diagnosability of Exported AI-Agent Traces
abstract: Execution traces help diagnose AI-agent failures, but sharing them can expose customer identities. For example, detecting that an agent handled the wrong customer's records requires knowing whether the records belong to the requested customer, but not necessarily knowing who that customer is. Our executable benchmark measures what a trace export reveals and whether a proposed repair restores the correct output in synthetic multi-tenant workflows. Conventional redaction can remove evidence needed for repair while leaving encoded identifiers recoverable. Two exports preserve ownership comparisons by reporting the match as a comparison fact or by using pseudonyms consistent within each execution. Both preserve the original diagnostic program's repairs. The tested identifier matchers identify no requested customer from either export. An independently written program produces correct outputs on 39 of 42 faulty cases with comparison facts and on all 42 with execution-scoped pseudonyms. Row counts still expose identities. With prior knowledge of customers' row counts, an attacker uniquely identifies the requested customer in 97 of 240 executions under each of the 15 export policies. Removing selected counters from the comparison-fact export stops this attack and preserves the original program's repairs. The benchmark lets engineers test what their diagnostic program can repair and what an attacker can still infer from the same export.

title: Architectural Principles for Parameter-Efficient Unitary Transformations in Coherent Optical Neural Networks
abstract: Coherent optical neural networks based on interferometric architectures offer a promising route toward high-throughput, energy-efficient computation by exploiting the multiple degrees of freedom of light, including spatial, temporal, and spectral modes. However, practical implementations are constrained by the number of tunable parameters due to fabrication complexity, device footprint, and control overhead. In such parameter-constrained settings, achieving high expressive power remains a central challenge. We identify two key architectural requirements for maintaining high expressive power under these constraints: (i) statistical uniformity in the implemented transformations and (ii) strong mixing capability per parameter, which enables rapid and unbiased redistribution of information across modes. To realize these requirements, we develop a logarithmic-depth butterfly-topology architecture whose fundamental building block is a single phase-shifter--beam-splitter pair, in contrast to conventional rectangular mesh architectures based on Mach-Zehnder interferometers. Computational evaluations show that, particularly at restricted parameter counts, the proposed architecture achieves lower matrix-reconstruction errors and higher classification accuracies than conventional meshes in both feedforward and recurrent networks. We further quantify these design principles using graph-theoretic measures, expected squared moduli of transformation-matrix entries, and matrix-reconstruction error. The resulting framework provides a quantitative and physically interpretable basis for parameter-efficient optical neural networks.

title: Phase-conjugate Gaussian encoding for continuous-variable quantum key distribution with a single phase-sensitive amplifier
abstract: Phase-conjugate encoding is naturally compatible with shared phase-sensitive amplification and joint detection, offering a compact optical receiver architecture for continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD). Here, we develop a unified encoding and security framework for two-mode Gaussian CVQKD with tunable phase-conjugate intermode correlations matched to a joint receiver comprising a single phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) and one balanced photodetector. We present both coherent-state and squeezed-state prepare-and-measure protocols that use the same transmitted ensemble. The two preparations can be implemented through classically precoded Gaussian displacements of coherent sidebands or a directly generated two-mode squeezed vacuum, respectively, without an actual optical mode converter. The encoding and detection scheme separates low-variance joint quadratures for key generation from high-variance joint quadratures carrying private random modulation. This complementary modulation can reduce Eve's Holevo information without changing the Alice--Bob mutual information. Numerical results show that optimized correlated coherent-state encoding achieves higher asymptotic key rates at long distances and extends the positive-key range compared with optimized single-mode coherent-state modulation. The optimal intermode correlation increases with transmission distance, and the range advantage persists under the symmetric correlated two-mode Gaussian attacks considered here. These results provide a theoretical basis for the design and implementation of PSA-enhanced two-mode CVQKD with phase-conjugate encoding.

title: Probabilistic Power Estimation and MPC-based Scheduling of Construction Electric Vehicles Supported by Mobile Charging Stations
abstract: The adoption of construction electric vehicles (CEVs) is held back by sparse on-site charging infrastructure, limited mobility, and insufficient knowledge of their power consumption. Mobile charging stations (MCSs) towed between grid connection points and construction sites address the first barrier, yet scheduling them optimally requires an accurate estimate of the CEV power consumption. In this paper, we address these gaps, first, by estimating the power of each subactivity of a representative CEV (a compact electric excavator) based on real-world construction demonstration data. We use Bayesian linear regression to obtain the subactivity power distributions, accounting for their operational uncertainty. Second, we formulate a mixed-integer program that jointly schedules CEV work and charging together with MCS routing, charging, and discharging, optimizing electricity costs, carbon emissions, work completion, and MCS travel. We embed the optimizer in a shrinking-horizon model predictive control (MPC) loop to perform real-time control on the CEV-MCS system. Two MPC variants, one a certainty-equivalent MPC (CE-MPC) controller, and the other a scenario-based MPC (SB-MPC) controller, are compared in closed-loop against an open-loop day-ahead schedule. Realistic simulations show that SB-MPC performs the best, lowering the operating costs by $60.2\%$ relative to the open-loop baseline, and by $23.3\%$ relative to CE-MPC, demonstrating the efficacy of incorporating predictive control with feedback. The code is available at https://github.com/Shubhanflash22/CEV-MCS-MPC-Joint-Scheduling

title: Collective coupling of over 100 individually trapped atoms to a single cavity mode
abstract: Coupling optical tweezer arrays to high-finesse cavities provides a shared optical interface for neutral-atom registers. Scaling this interface to large tweezer arrays requires placing many traps within the coupling region of a single cavity mode while maintaining uniform trapping and site-resolved detection. Here we match a two-dimensional array of 192 optical tweezers to the coupling profile of a millimeter-scale Fabry-Perot cavity. To improve trap uniformity in the array generated by crossed acousto-optic deflectors, we combine optimization with optical feedback and atomic fluorescence feedback, achieving a mean cesium loading probability of approximately 58%. In each trial, fluorescence imaging determines whether each individual tweezer site is occupied, allowing the cavity transmission spectra to be grouped by atom number. The grouped spectra exhibit resolved normal-mode doublets, and the group with 120 imaged atoms yields an effective collective coupling of $G_{\mathrm{eff}}/(2π) = 21.30 \pm 0.23$ MHz. A model based on the calculated coupling profile and measured site loading probabilities predicts that the mean squared coupling per occupied site changes little between 97 and 120 atoms. The fitted collective coupling is therefore consistent with square-root scaling with atom number despite the spatial variation in single-atom coupling. These results provide an experimental basis for studying photon-mediated many-body dynamics and developing cavity-assisted readout and optical links between neutral-atom registers.

title: On König's non-existence conjecture for the one-dimensional fractional Bianchi-Egnell inequality
abstract: König conjectured that the sharp stability constant in the Bianchi-Egnell inequality for the one-dimensional fractional Sobolev inequality equals the local stability constant and that the associated quotient has no minimizer outside the set of optimizers of the fractional Sobolev inequality. We prove both assertions for $s<1/2$ sufficiently close to $1/2$, with an explicitly computable threshold. The proof is based on a reinterpretation of the Frank-Lieb rigidity mechanism. Due to the lack of smooth variational structure of the Bianchi-Egnell quotient, we work with a refined limiting inequality of Beckner-Onofri-type on the circle with vanishing first-order moments, which we derive from Toeplitz determinants.

title: Lifting the local logarithmic Cartier transform modulo $p^n$
abstract: Let $p$ be a prime number and $n\ge 1$ an integer. We construct a local logarithmic Cartier transform modulo $p^n$, following an approach by Shiho. More precisely, consider the ring $W$ of Witt vectors of a perfect field of characteristic $p$. Let $f:\mathfrak{X}\rightarrow \mathfrak{S}$ be a log smooth morphism of fs logarithmic $p$-adic formal schemes, whose underlying formal schemes are flat and locally of finite type over $W$, and assume the exact relative Frobenius after reduction modulo $p$ admits a lift $F$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be Lorenzon's indexed algebra on the reduction modulo $p^n$ of $\mathfrak{X}.$ We define an indexed subalgebra $\mathcal{B}_F\subset\mathcal{A}$ and equip it with an integrable quasi-nilpotent $p$-connection. Our main result is an equivalence between the category of indexed $\mathcal{B}_F$-modules equipped with integrable quasi-nilpotent $p$-connections compatible with the $p$-connection on $\mathcal{B}_F$, and the category of indexed $\mathcal{A}$-modules equipped with integrable quasi-nilpotent connections compatible with the canonical connection on $\mathcal{A}$. This gives a local logarithmic version of the Cartier transform modulo $p^n$.

title: A singular minimizer of a uniformly convex Hessian-dependent functional
abstract: We construct a smooth, uniformly convex Hessian-dependent energy functional, which admits a singular $C^{1,1}$ minimizer on $\mathbb{R}^5$ that is a two-homogeneous normalization of Cartan's five-dimensional cubic. Our construction relies on constructing a quadratic null Lagrangian for the Hessian that is suitably non-degenerate on the image of the Hessian for the candidate minimizer. This complements a partial regularity result previously obtained by the authors in this setting, and demonstrates that one cannot hope for a fourth-order version of classical second-order elliptic regularity theory à la De Giorgi-Nash-Moser.

title: Capacitary Hardy inequalities, Dirichlet boundary conditions, and the limit as $p\downarrow1$
abstract: We use nonlinear Dirichlet resolvents to prove Hardy inequalities with capacity-based and resolvent-based weights for $1<p<\infty$ on arbitrary open sets. On bounded Sobolev extension domains, integrability against either weight characterizes Sobolev functions satisfying homogeneous Dirichlet conditions on arbitrary closed subsets of the boundary. On bounded Lipschitz domains, the resolvent-based weight $\bm{W}_{D,p}$ converges locally in $L^1$ to the negative of Barozzi's interior variational mean curvature as $p\downarrow1$.

title: Deploying a Control-Logic LLM Assistant in Air-Gapped Power Plants: Lessons in Source Authority and Bounded Retrieval
abstract: Deploying Large Language Model (LLM) assistants in industrial operational technology environments poses constraints largely absent from cloud applications: site policies restrict engineering and operational data from leaving the plant, on-premises compute is limited, and incorrect causal attribution can mislead incident response. We report lessons from deploying a control-logic evidence layer that underpins a broader on-premises operator assistance system at two gas power plants. Two prototypes revealed where generative models added avoidable uncertainty and cost. The first used a Vision Language Model (VLM) to reconstruct control topology from PDF printouts routinely exchanged by engineers. Across the full 6,979-page document, extraction reached 0.51 connection precision and required 3.1 hours on 4xH200 GPUs; consultation with controls engineers then revealed a native structured export from the authoring system. The second used an LLM tool-calling agent to plan repeatedly over eight predefined graph operations. In a controlled benchmark of 40 template-generated questions, replacing this agent with explicit execution plans reduced mean token use by 20x and median latency by 3x, with identical retrieved node sets across repeated runs. The deployed design ingests the authoritative export into a versioned knowledge graph, executes bounded graph operations in fixed software, and confines the local LLM to fallback intent classification and evidence-grounded explanation. At one site, the graph contains 221K nodes across seven controllers. Our experience suggests a practical division of labor for high-consequence AI: LLMs interpret natural-language requests and explain results, while deterministic software constructs and retrieves technical evidence grounded in authoritative sources. Abstention, entity disambiguation, graph versioning, and read-only integration provide additional safeguards.

title: Implicit-Reasoning-Enabled Elastic Semantic Communications for AI-Agent Networks
abstract: AI-agent networks introduce new communication demands driven by proactive interactions and autonomous task execution. Existing adaptive semantic communication schemes primarily adjust semantic representations and resource configurations within predefined processing scales and capability sets, which may be insufficient for evolving task requirements. To address this gap, we introduce elastic semantic communications (ESC), a task-driven framework that extends semantic adaptation to the runtime execution and participation of task-supporting capabilities. ESC comprises two complementary dimensions: vertical elasticity adjusts the execution intensity of existing capabilities, while horizontal elasticity reconfigures the participating capability set. The framework connects these dimensions through the expected marginal value of additional information and computation. To realize ESC, we propose an implicit-reasoning-enabled device--edge mechanism that supports variable-depth local inference through shared-parameter state updates and edge-side continuation through wireless transfer of intermediate reasoning states. Experiments on Sudoku-Extreme demonstrate that the benefits of additional inference depend on wireless conditions, while task-aware edge invocation can preserve task accuracy with substantially lower state-transfer overhead.

title: Observation of Strong Directed Flow for $ϕ$ Mesons in the High Baryon Density Region at RHIC
abstract: We report measurements of the rapidity-odd directed flow ($v_{1}$) of $ϕ$ mesons in 10--40\% Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{sNN}=3.0$--4.5 GeV from the STAR fixed-target program at RHIC, together with the collider-energy measurement at $\sqrt{sNN}=7.7$ GeV. Despite its mesonic nature, the $ϕ$-meson $v_{1}$ exhibits a magnitude comparable to that of protons and $Λ$ baryons and is significantly larger than that of $K^{0}_{S}$ mesons in the high-baryon-density region. Comparisons with UrQMD calculations indicate that the observed $ϕ$-meson directed flow is consistent with production through high-mass baryon resonances and the collective motion of baryons influenced by baryonic mean-field interactions. These results provide new experimental constraints on baryon-resonance production and strange-hadron transport dynamics in dense QCD matter.

title: Interlocking Tiling of 3D Finite Domains
abstract: A K-hedral tiling of a 3D finite domain is a covering of the domain with tiles without gaps or overlaps, where each tile is congruent to one of the K distinct shapes called prototiles. To use 3D K-hedral tilings in practice, they need to satisfy two requirements. First, K should be small to reduce the fabrication cost (e.g., through reusable molds) and simplify the (dis)assembly process. Second, a K-hedral tiling result should be structurally stable, in particular via interlocking, where all the tiles are immobilized by their geometric arrangement, except the key. Since these two requirements are often in conflict, existing approaches always trade one for the other. In this work, we formulate a new tiling problem called interlocking tiling, aiming to generate 3D K-hedral tilings that satisfy the above two requirements simultaneously. Given a 3D finite domain represented as a voxel grid, our goal is to compute a small prototile set whose instances exactly tile the input domain while ensuring that the tiling result forms an interlocking assembly. To solve this challenging problem, we propose a twolevel computational approach that hierarchically decomposes the input domain into interlocking parts (domain-level partitioning) and further partitions each part into interlocking tiles (part-level partitioning). To guide the part-level partitioning, we propose a new graph representation with regular structures to facilitate the generation of tiles with identical shapes while ensuring that they are interlocking. Our approach allows generating interlocking tilings that exactly cover 3D finite domains with diverse shapes while achieving high prototile reuse. We compared our approach with state-of-the-art methods to demonstrate its superiority, and validated the practicality of our interlocking tiling results via fabricating two of them.

title: Making Koopman Control Guarantees Hold on Robots
abstract: Koopman operator theory lets linear controllers handle nonlinear robots: an encoder lifts the state into a latent space with approximately linear dynamics, on which LQR or MPC is designed. A controller that stabilizes the latent model, however, may fail to stabilize the real nonlinear system. Stability is analyzed on latent rollouts, where the linear model propagates its own predictions, but on the robot the nonlinear dynamics produce each next state, which the controller re-encodes at every step. We prove that latent stability transfers to the robot when the latent model reproduces the true closed-loop dynamics to first order on the embedding's tangent space at the target. We also derive a margin for approximate matching and show that an open-loop stable latent model cannot match the plant's linearization at an unstable equilibrium. We propose Tangent-Invariant Koopman (TIK), which estimates a local plant linearization from offline transitions and builds first-order matching to it into the Koopman matrices. At the target, TIK's feedback gain equals the LQR gain of this linearization, and a bilinear input term models state-dependent actuation during large maneuvers. On four simulated open-loop unstable benchmarks, all 40 Standard Koopman controllers stabilize their latent models but are locally unstable on the real system, whereas all 40 TIK controllers stabilize it. An offline stability test with empirical curvature estimates identifies the stable TIK controllers on two cart-pole systems but is inconclusive under high noise. Given explicit model-error and curvature bounds, an invariant terminal set guarantees constraint satisfaction under local feedback after entry. TIK reaches 88% success in constrained cart-pole swing-up with a 0.25 ms planning budget and controls simulated seven-joint arms within 1~5 ms per step.

title: Attention Sinks as Spectral Spikes: A Mechanism Analysis of Gated Attention
abstract: Transformer attention exhibits attention sinks, where a small subset of source tokens absorbs disproportionate attention mass across layers. Recent work shows that post-SDPA output gating strongly reduces attention-sink behavior, while separate studies link attention sinks to gradient sinks and massive activations through backward training dynamics. Yet how the same gate affects forward sink structure, backward gradient concentration, and training-time representation signatures remains unclear. We address this gap by formulating attention sinks as sink-induced low-rank modes in token-space covariance, with directions aligned to high-mass attention columns. Under this view, post-SDPA gating acts as a mode-dependent contraction: it attenuates sink-induced spectral energy in the forward pass and locally reduces value-path gradients routed through sink columns in the backward pass. Empirically, random-matrix diagnostics show that gating reduces outlier mass, weakens sink-subspace alignment, and increases effective rank, while backward analyses show active-gate attenuation of first-token value gradients. Training-time diagnostics further show that gating suppresses the co-emergence of attention concentration, value-gradient amplification, and representation dominance.

title: Latent Feedback Is a Compute and Data Amplifier
abstract: When high-quality data runs out, a common practice is to train on it for several epochs, but each repeat is worth less than the last. Latent feedback, which feeds each token's top-layer state into the next token's input, is another way to spend that compute, yet it has not been tested against a vanilla Transformer that spends the same compute on more epochs. We run this test across a ladder of model sizes, unique data and epochs, tuning both models at every size and amount of unique data. Latent feedback makes every FLOP and every token count for more except when unique data is scarce relative to model size, a regime that today's models are far from. We find that latent feedback serves as an amplifier: with unique data fixed, it reaches a Transformer's loss with less compute; with epochs fixed, it reaches that loss with less unique data. Furthermore, both savings grow with unique data per parameter and with repetition, and downstream tasks agree. To go beyond our grid, we fit one scaling law to both models, in which latent feedback enters as a Transformer with more parameters; it predicts that both savings keep growing with unique data and repetition. Fitted on models from 60M to 271M parameters, the law predicts the losses at a held-out 778M size to within 0.3% and the gap between the two models to within 0.05%. At most, latent feedback saves 48% of the compute and 47% of the unique data. When data, not compute, is the limit, latent feedback is the better use of a FLOP for a model of a given size.

title: Refusal Register is Causally Steerable: Decomposing the Refusal Direction into Category-Aligned Components in Gemma-2-9B-IT
abstract: Prior work shows that refusal in instruction-tuned language models can be ablated by intervening on a single residual-stream direction (Arditi et al., 2024), and more recent work finds multiple refusal-mediating directions and concept cones (Wollschläger et al., 2025). We ask a different question: do refusal-related directions carry information about the register of refusal language - how the model refuses - and not only whether it refuses? In Gemma-2-9B-IT we identify two SVM-derived linear directions (B1 for harmful-content vs. neutral, B2 for self-reference vs. neutral) at layer 20 with cos(B1, B2) = 0.252 (about 75 degrees, substantially non-parallel). Adding the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction (cosine 0.68 with B1) to the residual stream of self-reference prompts at alpha = 2.0 shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens, while a magnitude-matched random direction produces 1.13-2.16; the model continues to refuse but switches register from meta-style ("as a language model...") to content-style ("this would be harmful"). The same register-injection effect reproduces qualitatively in Gemma-2-2B-IT at layer 12 (content vocabulary 1.72 -> 6.37 at alpha = 1.0, vs. random control 1.35), with a narrower coherent-injection window than in 9B. The two directions are not symmetric: the B2 -> harmful intervention produces a much smaller register effect, and across ablation, sufficiency, and injection B1's causal effects are consistently larger than B2's. We frame this asymmetry as part of the finding: B1 appears to encode both category detection and refusal-vocabulary information, while B2 encodes primarily category detection. We frame the contribution as identifying category-aligned components related to the Arditi-style difference-of-means direction that play distinct functional roles in refusal register.

title: The numerical index with respect to a Lipschitz map
