These results demonstrate that exceptionally loud gravitational-wave events enable robust, high-dimensional tests of inspiral dynamics and provide direct access to the measurable subspace of post-Newtonian deformations.

title: On Sobolev spaces and Koksma-Hlawka-type inequalities of fractional order
abstract: Spaces of fractional smoothness in the sense of Riemann-Liouville of order $0<α<1$ were introduced in [J. Dick, Ann. Math. Pura Appl., 187, 385-403, 2008]. Dick also proved Koksma-Hlawka type inequalities for these spaces, using a notion of fractional discrepancy. In [M. Gnewuch et al., Constr. Approx., 63, 647-711, 2026] upper error-bounds for QMC-integration on these spaces were obtained using $(t,m,s)$-nets and it was proved that the above mentioned Koksma-Hlawka inequalities by Dick are sharp. One step in the proof of the upper bounds was the embedding of the spaces of fractional smoothness into Bessel potential spaces, also called fractional Sobolev spaces. We prove that, up to norm equivalence, spaces of fractional smoothness and Bessel potential spaces are equal. From this we deduce that the upper error bounds for QMC-integration from Gnewuch et al. are indeed optimal for spaces of fractional smoothness. Furthermore, we obtain two types of Koksma-Hlawka inequalities for Bessel potential spaces. The first type uses the fractional discrepancy as introduced by Dick. The second type adopts an approach by Triebel from [H. Triebel, EMS Press, 2010] by using the norm of the (local) discrepancy function in an adjoint Bessel potential space.

title: High-quality intrinsic circular dichroism in silicon-based bound states in the continuum metasurfaces via strong coupling
abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) can significantly enhance spin-selective light-matter interactions. However, current BIC metasurfaces generally rely on single or multiple chiral BIC modes to enhance circular dichroism (CD), limiting their application in functional integrated devices. This paper proposes a method that utilizes the strong coupling effect in BIC metasurfaces to achieve intrinsic CD with both a high quality factor (Q-factor) and high efficiency. The metasurface is designed as a silicon-based cross-shaped nanohole array, which can simultaneously support a TM-like BIC mode and a TE-like guided-mode resonance (GMR) mode. By introducing under-etching to break the out-of-plane symmetry and tuning the in-plane asymmetry parameter, strong coupling between the quasi-BIC (QBIC) mode and the GMR mode can be induced, thereby achieving near-perfect intrinsic CD with a high Q-factor. In the strong-coupling region, the resonant wavelengths of the QBIC and GMR modes exhibit anti-crossing behavior, while the imaginary parts of the eigenfrequency cross; the corresponding Rabi splitting energy reaches a minimum of 3.16 meV, and the induced intrinsic CD achieves a maximum of 0.995 at a wavelength of 1653.9 nm, with a high Q-factor of 1083. The evolution of far-field polarization singularities shows that, under strong coupling, the Γ point corresponds to a left-handed circular polarization singularity (C-point). Furthermore, the strong-coupling-induced CD exhibits good robustness. Even under considerable variations in structural parameters, the high-Q and high-efficiency CD response is maintained. This method offers a novel design strategy for integrated chiral photonic devices and holds promise for applications in areas such as chiral sensing, chiral lasers, and nonlinear chiral optics.

title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
abstract: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

title: Reduced Density Matrices from Renormalization-Group Flows
abstract: We reconstruct complete one- and two-body reduced density matrices (RDMs) by a single collective backward evolution along the in-medium similarity renormalization-group flow. Benchmarks show improved accuracy and physical consistency over conventional elementwise evolution. In neutron matter, two-body RDMs reveal spin-triplet dominance in interaction-dependent Fermi-sea depletion trends. Meanwhile, the forward-backward energy difference provides an internal diagnostic of many-body truncation errors, whose quantification remains challenging in nuclear $ab\ initio$ calculations.

title: An adaptive Gaussian splitting scheme for linear Fokker--Planck equations
abstract: We develop an adaptive numerical method for linear Fokker--Planck equations on $\mathbb R^d$, based on approximating the evolving probability density by linear combinations of Gaussian functions (LCGs). The method applies to polynomial-type drift fields, without requiring a gradient-flow structure or a stationary distribution. It relies on an operator splitting that separates diffusion and affine drift, for which Gaussian functions can be propagated exactly, from higher-order transport, whose evolution is approximated adaptively by LCGs. Both the number of Gaussian components and their means and covariances are adjusted to meet the prescribed accuracy tolerances. The adaptivity is driven by computable error indicators involving polynomial moments of Gaussians that can be evaluated analytically. We provide a rigorous error analysis that relates the approximation error to the indicators driving adaptivity and illustrate the performance of the scheme in several test cases.

title: Linear Dynamics of Composition Operators on Zygmund Spaces of Rooted Trees
abstract: We conjugate composition operators on the Zygmund and little Zygmund spaces of an infinite, locally finite rooted tree $T$ by the second-difference isometries. A path Green kernel gives row-finite matrices that characterize boundedness and yield exact operator norms. A rigidity result holds on the chain $\mathbb{N}_0$. Boundedness on $\mathcal{Z}_0(\mathbb{N}_0)$ is equivalent to $φ(n)=qn+b$ for all sufficiently large $n$, with $q\in\mathbb{N}_0$ and $b\in\mathbb{Z}$. For these symbols, $φ(n)>n$ eventually characterizes Li-Yorke chaos of $C_φ$ on either Zygmund space, allowing noninjectivity and periodic vertices. If $C_φ$ is bounded on $\mathcal{Z}_0(T)$ and $φ^k(T)$ eventually avoids every finite set, then for each $λ\ne0$, $λC_φ$ is Li-Yorke chaotic on either space exactly when the norms of its powers are unbounded. For $φ_q(n)=q(n+1)-1$ with integer $q\ge2$, the corresponding conditions are $|λ|q^2>1$ on both Zygmund spaces and $|λ|q>1$ on the little Lipschitz space. For bounded $C_φ$ on $\mathcal{Z}_0(\mathbb{N}_0)$, topological mixing and Devaney chaos each hold exactly for injective symbols with no periodic vertices and eventual slope $q\ge2$. For such bounded operators with strictly increasing $φ$ and $φ(0)>0$, $q\ge2$ also characterizes hypercyclicity and frequent hypercyclicity.

title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

title: European derivatives pricing via constrained Gaussian process regressions
abstract: This article develops a Gaussian process method for pricing European derivatives when the underlyings, and the risk factors driving them, follow a multivariate jump-diffusion. A Gaussian process prior on the pricing function is conditioned on the Feynman-Kac partial integro-differential equation at a set of collocation points. The price is returned as a closed-form and differentiable function, allowing the Greeks to be obtained without simulation or finite differences. The jump terms are handled iteratively: the price is computed as the limit of a sequence of boundary value problems. Our main theoretical contribution is a convergence result for this iteration: using Weissinger's fixed-point theorem in the supremum norm, we show that it converges from any starting point, and provide a worst-case number of iterations for a given precision. The method is illustrated with derivatives of two underlyings under the Heston model with Kou double-exponential jumps, a five-dimensional problem, and benchmarked against Monte Carlo simulation.

title: Dimension-seven spectator effects in charm-hadron lifetimes at NLO
abstract: We compute the next-to-leading-order (NLO) QCD corrections to the connected current-current part of the dimension-seven spectator coefficients in the heavy-quark expansion of charm-hadron widths. The finite terms are fixed in NDR-$\overline{\rm MS}$, with the evanescent operators defined by the standard Greek projection and averaged over Hermitian-conjugate pairs, and with a finite subtraction that sets the finite mixing of the dimension-seven operators into the dimension-six ones to zero. In several channels the one-loop term is comparable to the LO coefficient, and two operator families absent at LO are generated. Since the NLO matrix elements of the dimension-seven operators are not known, we estimate the effect of the coefficients on the widths with tree-level matrix elements from vacuum insertion for $D$ mesons and from the bag model for charmed baryons. The $1/m_c$ corrections to the matrix elements of the dimension-six QCD operators are treated by a naive expansion. Without their $O(α_s)$ part the semileptonic width of the $D_s^+$ would be negative. The NLO dimension-seven correction raises the $D^+$ width by 0.78 ps$^{-1}$, so that its central value, slightly negative as published, becomes positive. At central inputs, it is about 1% of the $D^0$ width, 10% of the $D_s^+$ width and at most 2% of the widths of the singly charmed baryons. Added to the published pole-scheme width, the $D^+$ correction gives $τ(D^+)=1.41^{+\infty}_{-0.76}$ ps. The NLO term reduces the scale dependence of the nonleptonic dimension-seven contribution severalfold for the singly charmed baryons, whose matrix elements are evolved, but not uniformly for the $D$ mesons.

title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

title: Kinetic and Thermodynamic Limits of Sodium Pore Filling in Hard Carbon
abstract: The low-voltage plateau-like capacity of hard carbon anodes is widely regarded as a key signature of sodium storage in closed pores, often defining the performance of Na-ion batteries. Here, we combine first-principles calculations with a grand canonical Monte Carlo pore-filling model to show that Na storage in closed pores is not governed by a single equilibrium-plateau mechanism but by a distribution of pore-specific thermodynamic and kinetic activation processes. Thermodynamically, the voltage at which Na pore filling becomes favorable decreases with increasing pore size. Kinetically, pore filling involves Na nucleation, coalescence, growth, and bulk diffusion. While small pores fill rapidly, large pores exhibit both a smaller thermodynamic stimulus and significant kinetic limitations. Nucleation can be accelerated by introducing defects at the pore walls, although an excessively high defect concentration slows bulk diffusion. This work shows that not all closed pores contribute equally to Na storage: some may be thermodynamically favorable but kinetically inactive under realistic charge/discharge rates. Because of this, the inverse design of hard carbon electrodes should target a kinetically accessible pore-size and defect-density window that balances high plateau-like capacity with fast-charging performance.

title: Scintillator-Based Event-Mode Neutron Imaging with Timepix4 Readout
abstract: Scintillator-based event-mode neutron imaging is emerging as a powerful approach to neutron radiography. Unlike conventional integrating-mode neutron imaging, which accumulates scintillation light during an exposure, event reconstruction estimates neutron-event positions and arrival times from time-stamped optical responses. We investigated this approach using a self-developed Timepix4-based optical readout system, image-formation analysis, and beam experiments at the China Spallation Neutron Source under different scintillator and optical configurations. The analysis explains how event localization can reduce image blur associated with the spatial extent of individual scintillation responses. Under the same 0.35$\times$ optical configuration, event reconstruction improved the spatial resolution from 164.2 to 91.9 $μ$m at 10% modulation transfer function (MTF), while a 2.1$\times$ configuration with a $\mathrm{Gd_2O_2S:Tb}$ scintillator achieved 26.1 $μ$m at the same MTF threshold. Following event reconstruction and rejection of single-photon reconstructed events, the mean peak-normalized spectral response in the 6-8 angstrom out-of-band interval decreased by 85.4% relative to the raw-pixel wavelength-count spectrum, indicating reduced afterglow-related spectral background. Under the tested pulsed-beam conditions, the maximum instantaneous pixel-hit rate per pixel was approximately four times its time-averaged value, providing an experimental basis for assessing readout requirements at higher neutron flux. Conventional radiography resolved structural details, while energy-selective imaging enhanced the contrast between materials with similar broadband transmission and Bragg-edge imaging revealed crystallographic features in steel. These results demonstrate the imaging-quality benefits and capabilities of scintillator-based event-mode neutron imaging.

title: Cavity Control of Emission Dynamics from Spin Defects in Hexagonal Boron Nitride
abstract: Optically addressable negatively charged boron vacancy ($\mathrm{V_B^-}$) defects in hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) are promising for quantum sensing at room temperature. The two-dimensional structure of hBN allows direct access to the local environment, enabling proximal sensing of target materials. However, its broadband emission and low quantum yield hinder efficient light-matter interaction, and the coupling of $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ optical dipoles to confined cavity fields remains poorly understood. In this study, we integrate $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defects with a tunable plano-concave microcavity, achieving three-dimensional optical confinement. This approach yields photoluminescence (PL) enhancement and cavity-modified optical decay dynamics, providing insights into the orientation of the $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect dipole. Time-resolved PL measurements identify a distinct fast decay component, suggesting a complex dipole geometry for the defects. Therefore, a tilted optical dipole model is considered to attribute the fast and slow decay components to in-plane and out-of-plane dipole contributions, respectively. Additionally, optically detected magnetic resonance and excitation-polarisation-dependent PL measurements provide further insights into local symmetry breaking and potential optical dipole configurations. These results highlight the role of optical dipole orientation in $\mathrm{V_B^-}$ defect-cavity coupling.

title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
abstract: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.

title: UIAnchor: Anchoring UI Perception and Action Execution for Reliable Service-Composed Mobile Task Automation with GUI Agents
abstract: Mobile task automation aims to streamline multi-step, cross-app interactions on smartphones and in-vehicle systems. Recent LLM-based GUI agents have advanced rapidly, yet reliability remains limited because modern mobile workflows are increasingly service-composed (app switching, forms, pop-ups/permissions, copy-paste), requiring fine-grained operations on dense, dynamic, and heterogeneous UIs, often in distraction-sensitive contexts (e.g., hands-busy or attention-limited use). Through an in-the-wild failure analysis of deployable GUI agents, we identify two dominant bottlenecks: agents often miss or misread actionable UI elements, and they execute actions without verifying target correctness or outcomes. We present UIAnchor, a modular multi-agent system that improves mobile GUI automation by anchoring both perception and execution. UIAnchor combines a two-stage UI parser for high-recall element capture and context-aware semantics with a meta-controller that performs pre-action verification, post-action outcome perception, per-step state tracking, and targeted recovery. We further introduce an L1-L5 task taxonomy based on step length, cross-app scope, and UI granularity, showing that L5 remains beyond today's practical frontier. On the hardest practical tier, L4 tasks (20-30 steps, multi-app, targets < 100 x 100 px, ~5 mm on typical phones), UIAnchor improves success by 31.5% over GPT-4o and 16.6% over Mobile-Agent-v3. With edge/cloud assistance, UIAnchor runs at ~2 s per step, comparable to human operation, while reducing per-step latency by up to 75.5% and energy by 52.4%. It also generalizes to unseen apps and cross-platform GUIs.

title: Directionality of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO experiment
abstract: Electron-recoil directionality can help distinguish solar-neutrino interactions from backgrounds and, together with recoil-energy measurements and three-dimensional tracking, enable neutrino-energy spectroscopy. We study the reconstruction of the initial direction of low-energy electron recoils in the CYGNO optical time-projection chamber, focusing on the 50 L LIME prototype and its high-granularity scientific CMOS (sCMOS) readout. A dedicated algorithm identifies the interaction point from the asymmetry of the track light distribution and estimates the recoil direction from the early portion of the ionization trail, before multiple scattering erases most of the directional information. The method is characterized with a detailed Monte Carlo simulation of electron recoils and detector response. Samples spanning 15 keV to 70 keV are used to optimize the algorithm parameters by minimizing the width of the reconstructed-minus-true projected-angle distribution. The projected angular response is modeled by two Gaussian components that account for its dependence on track inclination. The narrower component, associated with favorable projections approximately parallel to the Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) plane, has a width that improves from about $20^\circ$ near 20 keV to about $12^\circ$ at 60 keV. We also quantify the fraction of events in the correctly reconstructed angular core and discuss the dominant limitations of a camera-only two-dimensional measurement.

title: GPRM: Global Perspective Process Reward Model
abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) are widely used for step-level evaluation of multi-step reasoning in large language models, but existing methods are often limited by weak historical dependency modeling and insufficient global awareness. They typically fail to leverage prior step evaluations for coherent judgment and lack visibility into subsequent reasoning, leading to suboptimal assessment of intermediate steps. To address this issue, we propose the Global Perspective Process Reward Model (GPRM), which jointly models the problem, previous reasoning steps and their evaluations, the current step, and future steps to enable history-aware and globally informed process evaluation. We further introduce a structured evaluation framework along four dimensions---look back, look ahead, self-check, and goal alignment---to assess prior consistency, future plausibility, step validity, and task alignment. Based on this framework, we construct datasets for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (GRPO). Experiments show that, despite using less training data and smaller model sizes, GPRM outperforms strong baseline models by 7.8 and 5.4 points on PRMBench and ProcessBench, respectively. GPRM also generalizes well across tasks, surpassing the GPT-4.1 baseline on Agent Error Bench, improving strong baselines by around 4 points under test-time scaling (TTS), and achieving competitive performance on PPE.

title: Genuine multipartite entanglement in ring-shaped Hubbard models
abstract: Spin states can be extracted from many-electron systems by detecting electrons at a set of lattice sites, which act as particle labels. Here we quantify the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) of such spin states, which are generally mixed, in standard and extended Hubbard rings, together with the corresponding detection probability. We show that the on-site repulsion, by suppressing charge fluctuations, enhances the GME, and that in the strongly interacting regime at half filling the detection probability decreases only weakly with the number of spins. The GME is robust at temperatures below the singlet--triplet gap, and can even be enhanced by doping, in spite of the induced charge fluctuations. The transition from spin- to charge-density waves in the extended Hubbard model is signaled by an abrupt suppression of both the GME and the detection probability.

title: A Lifted Hessian-Riemannian Gradient Flow for LQR Synthesis under Passivity Constraints
abstract: The static state-feedback gain that renders a linear system passive at an external port and minimizes a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost cannot be computed by convex optimization, since the passivity certificate and the LQR cost are coupled bilinearly through the common gain. A previous indirect approach restricts the gain to a convex inner approximation of the passivity region, which is conservative and whose construction scales exponentially with the number of gain entries. This paper proposes a direct approach. The set of strictly passivating gains is the image of a convex lifted set of inverse storage matrices and transformed gains. We describe this set by a strict linear matrix inequality and an affine equality for every feedthrough matrix with positive semidefinite symmetric part, including feedthrough matrices with a singular symmetric part, and minimize the LQR cost over it by a gradient flow whose metric is the Hessian of a logarithmic barrier. For multi-input systems, this Hessian is singular along gain changes that preserve the storage function, and we complete the metric along these directions by the metric of the gain space. We prove that the flow exists for all times, that every gain along the flow is strictly passivating with an explicit storage function, and that the cost decreases monotonically while the gains remain in a compact set of stabilizing gains. Numerical examples show that the flow attains a lower cost than the indirect approach, that the completion is required for multi-input systems, and that the flow can converge to a local minimizer on nonconvex passivity regions.

title: UniGraph: A Unified Graph-based Index for Dynamic Hybrid Dense-Sparse Vector Retrieval
abstract: Hybrid dense-sparse vector retrieval combines semantic signals from dense representations with lexical signals from sparse representations, typically ranking items by a query-dependent weighted sum of dense and sparse vector distances. Existing systems commonly search separate dense and sparse vector indexes and rerank the union of their candidates, incurring two retrieval passes and potentially discarding items that rank highly only after the semantic and lexical signals are combined. Constructing a graph-based index directly under a hybrid distance can mitigate this premature candidate loss. However, because varying the hybrid weight alters the underlying neighborhood relationships, a single static graph built at a fixed weight cannot accommodate dynamic query-specific weights. Therefore, we propose a Unified Hybrid Graph (UniGraph), which merges neighbor sets computed at multiple hybrid weights into a single bounded-degree graph index, enabling hybrid vector retrieval with different query-specific weights without index reconstruction. We further develop an adaptive weight-guided search framework that chooses between sparse- and dense-guided entry points according to the query weight, together with a dense-first hybrid distance pruning strategy that avoids unnecessary exact sparse distance computations. Extensive experiments show that UniGraph provides a favorable Recall-QPS trade-off across different query weights. In the mixed-weight setting, UniGraph delivers 27.6%~52.3% higher QPS than the fastest baseline on each dataset at Recall@100 greater than or equal to 0.95. UniGraph has been deployed at scale in Ant Group's production environment, where hybrid retrieval with query-dependent weights is in strong demand.

title: Instant Weight-Space Consolidation for Long-Term Memory in LLMs
abstract: Agentic memory systems give LLMs persistent memory by extracting experience into text and retrieving it at query time, but the model itself does not evolve: however many interactions it has had, it starts each query the same. Extraction errors compound, implicit cross-session patterns that no single fragment states cannot be surfaced, and the construction cost grows with every conversation. Fine-tuning on past interactions does change the weights, but requires backpropagation at serving time and degrades on long histories. We introduce CLAM (Carried Latent Adapter Memory), which combines the strengths of both: a recurrent hypernetwork performs parametric consolidation, compiling a stream of session activations into a low-rank adapter in a single forward pass with no gradient steps and no language-model generation calls, while a complementary episodic buffer supplies verbatim detail at inference. A gated latent state carries knowledge across sessions in fixed size, so the parametric memory accumulates without growing. On LoCoMo and LongMemEval-S across three open models (2-7B parameters), CLAM leads all agentic baselines by 1-45 points and all gradient-based parametric methods by 10-45 points, while requiring zero generative LLM calls, zero gradient steps, and 3-151x less wall-clock time than extraction systems to build its memory. The two channels are complementary: the consolidated adapter adds 12-15 accuracy points when the episodic buffer misses the gold evidence, and still adds 4-5 points even with an oracle buffer.

title: Deformation Quantization of Coisotropic A-branes
abstract: Motivated by the Gukov--Witten proposal that the endomorphism algebra of a coisotropic A-brane should be described by a deformation quantization of its transverse holomorphic symplectic geometry at the perturbative level, we study deformation quantization on transverse holomorphic symplectic manifolds $(M,Ω)$. Extending the approach of Nest--Tsygan to this setting, we show that, under an admissibility condition, equivalence classes of deformation quantizations are in bijection with \[ \hbar H^2\bigl(\operatorname{F}_1Ω^\bullet(M,\mathbb C),d\bigr) [[\hbar]], \] where $\operatorname{F}_1Ω^\bullet(M,\mathbb C)$ is the differential ideal generated by transverse $(1,0)$-forms. We further illustrate this framework through examples arising from mapping tori, $T$-duality, and coisotropic lifts in cotangent bundles. These examples clarify the roles of admissibility and the transverse Atiyah class, as well as the distinction between deformation quantizations and global star products. Finally, for a coisotropic A-brane $M$ induced from a transverse complex manifold $Q$, we use transverse jets and the Fock representation to construct a perturbative level action $End(M)\curvearrowright Hom(M,Q)$ under suitable compatibility assumptions, providing a geometric realization of the brane quantization philosophy.

title: Large deviations and the asymptotic geometry of Lorentz balls
abstract: We study the uniform distribution on finite-dimensional Lorentz balls $B_{q,p}^n$ in the range $1<p<q<\infty$. We prove a Sanov-type large deviation principle for the empirical measures of the absolute coordinates of a random vector uniformly distributed on $n^{1/q}B_{q,p}^n$. The rate function is given by an entropy deficit under a weighted quantile constraint. We show that the entropy maximizer is unique and characterize its distribution function as the unique increasing solution of a nonlinear boundary-value problem. The limiting distribution has compact support, for which we obtain an explicit bound. These results establish the conjectured empirical limit of Kabluchko, Prochno and Sonnleitner [Journal of Functional Analysis, 288(1):110682, 2025] in the range $1<p<q<\infty$. As consequences, we determine the exponential volume asymptotics of Lorentz balls and obtain asymptotic independence of any fixed number of coordinates. We also prove a law of large numbers for Lorentz norms with finite parameters and use it, together with the volume asymptotics, to obtain a Schechtman--Schmuckenschläger type theorem for intersections of volume-normalized Lorentz balls. We further derive a variational formula for the logarithmic intersection asymptotics. The proof combines an exponential change of measure with quantile interpolation and a variational argument that does not assume regularity of the maximizing quantile in advance.

title: Muon and Tau Anomalies and $Δα_{had}^{(5)} (M_Z^2)$ in the Standard Model
abstract: I review the present status of the Standard Model (SM) determination of the muon anomaly by emphasizing the estimate of the lowest hadronic vacuum polarization contributions using recent $e^+e^-$ data on $2π$ and $3π$ and the inclusive ratio $R^{ee}$ of total cross-sections compiled by PDG to which we add the QCD continuum including HO PT QCD up to $α_s^5$, quark mass $m_q^2$ up to $α_s^3$, $m_s^4$ up to $α_s^2$ and QCD condensates. Adding the $e^+e^-\to π^0γ+ ηγ$ contributions to the CMD3 data, one obtains\,: $a_μ\vert^{hvp}_{lo}=(7094\pm 37)\times 10^{-11}$. Combining this LO result with the HO estimate of the hadronic, QED and EW contributions, one obtains\,: $Δa_μ^{sm} \equiv (a_μ^{exp}-a_μ^{sm})= (86\pm 38_{th}\pm 14.5_{exp})\times 10^{-11} $. The average of the recent estimates quoted in Table\,3 [$\oplus$ attempt to fit all $\,e^+e^-$ data] gives\,: $Δa_μ^{sm} = (84.9[90.0]\pm 21.3_{th}\pm 14.5_{exp})\times 10^{-11}$\,. These results agree with the precise BMW20 lattice one and still suggest a window for new physics beyond the SM of $(2.1\sim 3.5)\,σ$. Besides some future projects for improving the $e^+e^-$ data, the MUonE for extracting directly $a_μ^{tot}\vert^{hvp}_{lo}$ and J-PARC (E34) for an independent measurement of $a_μ$, it is important to improve the Lattice results shown in Fig.\,9 which (at first sight) disagree each others despite the large errors and may question the reliability of the {\it averages of different averages} used in the White Paper (WP25) Our analysis is completed by updating the estimate of the hadronic contribution to the tau anomaly\,: $a_τ\vert^{hvp}_{lo}=(3516\pm 25)\times 10^{-9}$ and to $α(M_Z)\,: \,Δα_{had}^{(5)} (M_Z^2)= (2770.7\pm 4.5)\times 10^{-5}. $

title: Rigidity and classification of complete translating solitons and self-expanders with constant curvature in $\mathbb{R}^{4}$
abstract: For complete immersed surfaces in Euclidean four-space whose mean curvature vector has constant length, translators are affine planes parallel to their fixed nonzero velocity, and self-expanders are planes through their centre. This rigidity requires no Lagrangian assumption, properness, volume growth control, or bound on the second fundamental form. Complete Lagrangian translators and self-expanders in $\mathbb{C}^{2}$ with constant Gaussian curvature are flat and, up to unitary equivalence, are properly embedded products of two complete planar curves. Translating factors are lines or grim reapers. Expanding factors are lines through the origin or nonstraight self-expanders. The proofs use moving frames, a transnormal function, a cubic tensor identity, and analytic continuation.

title: Tunneling effect in some singular wells
abstract: The Schrödinger operator in one dimension is considered. When the electric potential has a linear/V-shaped well, an approximation of the ground-state is established at fixed distance from the well. In this situation, the classical WKB analysis and the localization techniques à la Agmon near a non-degenerate minimum do not work. We propose an alternative to the WKB analysis better suited to the shape of the well and we prove that our Ansatz is an exponentially good approximation by means of revisited (and simplified) Agmon estimates.

title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

title: Design Rules for Low-Latency Multipath Congestion Control
abstract: We first study optimal congestion control from a theoretical perspective. Concretely, we consider a system that optimizes the sum of the utilities of all the users, in which the users are allowed to send their traffic over different paths over the network and derive design rules that optimal (low-latency) multipath congestion control needs to follow. Because, as it turns out that optimal congestion control requires coordination between the network nodes, and hence, is hard to implement, we investigate how to approximate its performance with algorithms in which (i) the network nodes make independent decisions and (ii) coordination is only allowed between the subflows that belong to the same user. Therefore, these design rules need to be slightly relaxed. We compare the performance of these realistic algorithms with the optimal algorithm. We also investigate to what extent the algorithms that are currently defined and are being defined in the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF), in particular, (i) Prague congestion control (i.e., congestion control based on Accurate Explicit Congestion Notification (AccECN) marks) and (ii) a variant of a loss-based multipath congestion control algorithm, adhere to these rules.

title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
abstract: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

title: Hemispheric asymmetry and up/down anisotropy of Jupiter's auroral electron precipitation: Juno/JEDI statistics
abstract: Energetic electron precipitation shapes Jupiter's auroral emissions, thermal structure, and atmospheric chemistry. Whether its intensity differs between hemispheres, and whether that difference is consistent across auroral sub-regions, remains statistically unexplored over a large perijove sample. We statistically characterize the precipitating electron energy flux in Jupiter's auroral sub-regions, polar emission (PE) and main emission (ME), separating downward and upward fluxes and comparing hemispheres, using Juno/JEDI data from PJ3 to PJ66. Juno footprints from JRM33 and a current sheet model assign each spectrum to an auroral sub-region, where the downward and upward energy flux are integrated over the corresponding loss cone. The median energy flux differs between hemispheres by a factor of about two in the PE and the ME, for both flux directions, but the dominant hemisphere is reversed, the north dominating in the PE (N/S of 2.5 downward, 2.0 upward) and the south in the ME (0.65 and 0.5). The mean electron energy is nearly identical in both hemispheres in every sub-region, so the asymmetry lies in the number flux rather than the local acceleration efficiency. The PE also shows a systematic upward excess over downward flux in both hemispheres, maximal at the magnetic pole. The PE/ME reversal shows that the two hemispheres partition precipitated energy differently between the polar cap and the main oval. The PE anisotropy, qualitatively identical in both hemispheres, indicates that this partition is not driven by a hemispheric contrast in field-aligned acceleration efficiency.

title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
abstract: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.

title: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
abstract: Non-imaging optical tactile sensors encode contact through changes in optical intensity, wavelength, spectra, or photon counts, offering diverse architectures for robotic touch. Their usefulness depends on whether contact variables can be reliably distinguished from coupled mechanical and environmental effects, and whether the resulting information can be delivered in time to guide action. This review develops a unified framework linking mechanical load transmission, optical encoding, readout, and tactile inference to robotic task requirements. It examines reflective and waveguide-based devices, micro/nanofibers, fiber gratings, interferometric and resonant structures, and mechanoluminescent composites. Three considerations emerge across these approaches. First, high optical sensitivity supports accurate tactile estimation only when target variables remain identifiable under the relevant contact and calibration conditions. Second, spatial coverage and feedback timing must be assessed at the system level, accounting for multiplexing, acquisition, demodulation, and inference. Third, device characterization, offline recognition, and closed-loop robotic performance provide distinct levels of evidence and require different evaluation criteria. Representative studies illustrate how these considerations shape force estimation, contact localization, slip correction and distributed interaction. This review concludes with priorities for calibration transfer, reliable interfaces, scalable readout, and task-based validation, providing a basis for selecting and developing non-imaging optical tactile architectures for robotics.

title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
abstract: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

title: Building Fully On-Device GUI Agents with Mobile NPUs
abstract: Mobile GUI agents are increasingly used to automate everyday smartphone tasks, but most existing systems still rely on cloud-hosted models or remote inference, introducing repeated communication latency, privacy exposure, and dependence on network availability. Modern smartphones integrate neural processing units (NPUs) that provide an attractive substrate for fully on-device LLM inference. However, directly deploying conventional GUI-agent pipelines on mobile NPUs is inefficient. GUI-agent inference is fundamentally a long-input, short-output workload, yet conventional agents spend substantial time on autoregressive reasoning and action generation, while mobile NPUs provide much higher throughput for prompt prefill than token-by-token decoding. Meanwhile, dynamically varying GUI-agent contexts conflict with the fixed context profiles required by statically compiled NPU runtimes. We present DroidPrefill, a prefill-centric inference architecture that reshapes the GUI-agent workload around mobile-NPU execution. DroidPrefill combines Prefill-Centric Inference to reduce unnecessary autoregressive decoding with Efficient Context Management to preserve decision-critical information within a fixed compiled context budget. Experiments on commercial smartphones show that, in controlled comparisons with the autoregressive T3A+ baseline, DroidPrefill reduces per-step inference latency by up to 85.0%, while improving task success rate by up to 24.6%.

title: When Does Interaction Help? Toward a Reynolds Number for Collective Intelligence
abstract: Multi-agent systems combine distributed information through interaction, which can improve performance but also spread errors or suppress useful differences. Predicting when interaction helps is central to understanding and designing collective intelligence. We investigate whether a few dimensionless parameters can predict gains over explicitly defined non-communicating baselines across group sizes, network structures, and tasks, toward a Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence. Using distributed classification tasks, stochastic tracking networks, and neural cellular automata, we combine analytical and empirical evidence to examine information sufficiency, dynamical applicability, and finite-sample prediction. We construct inference systems with bounded random variables and matching specified joint moments up to total degree three, yet opposite interaction gains under a fixed readout. These moments alone cannot generally determine the gain sign. Tracking networks likewise exhibit gain reversals despite matched candidate parameters when task power occupies different spectral modes. Under concentrated task spectra and aligned observation noise, however, we derive a low-dimensional similarity relation with an explicit zero-delay error bound and test it across network sizes and topologies under frozen protocols. The relation does not directly apply to the neural cellular systems, where a separate moment-based predictor underperforms direct gain measurement at matched calibration sample budgets. These results establish conditions and limits for low-dimensional gain prediction, providing a restricted similarity law while leaving a general Reynolds-number-like description of collective intelligence open.

title: Flat and very flat pro-quasi-coherent pro-sheaves on ind-schemes
abstract: This is a paper about homological algebra of flat pro-quasi-coherent pro-sheaves. We recall and collect various techniques such as accessibility and deconstructibility, and adopt them to ind-schemes under various assumptions. We also discuss the foundations of the notion of an ind-scheme.

title: Co-simulation-Based Safety-Assessment of Black-Box Maritime Cyber-Physical Systems
abstract: Modern maritime cyber-physical systems consist of tightly interconnected subsystems ranging from multiple engineering domains, making exhaustive safety verification impractical. Simulation-based testing offers a scalable alternative, while co-simulation enables heterogeneous subsystem models, potentially developed by different stakeholders, to be integrated without requiring access to their internal implementations. Adaptive Stress-Testing further improves testing efficiency by formulating failure discovery as a sequential decision-making problem, guiding the search toward the most likely failure scenarios, and giving the counter safety examples using reinforcement learning. However, black-box co-simulation may provide only partial access to the system state required by conventional Markov decision process formulations. To address this limitation, we proposed Event-Based Adaptive Stress-Testing version 2, a co-simulation-based safety-assessment method formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process. This method employs Recurrent Proximal Policy Optimization to exploit observation histories when selecting adversarial actions. The method is evaluated on a ship-in-transit operation in which a collision-avoidance system is stress-tested against multi-adversarial target ships. An extended Intermediate Waypoint Sampling mechanism enables independent multi-adversary trajectory control and supports the generation of realistic collision-inducing scenarios. The experiment demonstrate that the learned stress-testing policy generalizes across different encounter cases, can be further improved through continued training, and can be made effective when the collision- avoidance system under test is replaced by another version. These results demonstrate the method's potential for scalable black-box safety assessment of complex maritime cyber-physical systems.

title: Extensions of $q$-supercongruences arising from a quadratic summation of Gasper and Rahman
abstract: In this paper, inspired by recent work of Guo and Zhao, and of Guo and Zudilin, we establish two parametric extensions of their $q$-supercongruences using Gasper and Rahman's quadratic summation, the Chinese remainder theorem, and the creative microscoping method. These extensions yield two one-parameter generalizations of the $q$-supercongruences considered by Guo and Zhao and by Guo and Zudilin.

title: Treewidth and Separation Number: An Optimal Linear Bound
abstract: The \emph{separation number} $\sn(G)$ of a graph $G$ is the smallest integer $a$ such that every subgraph $H$ of $G$ admits a separation $(A,B)$ of {\em order} $|A\cap B|\le a$ whose two sides $A\setminus B$ and $B\setminus A$ each contain at most $2|V(H)|/3$ vertices. Dvořák and Norin proved that $\tw(G)\le 15\sn(G)$ for every nonempty graph $G$. We improve the constant to its optimal value: every nonempty graph satisfies $\tw(G)\le 4\sn(G)-2$. This is best possible: for every $k\ge 2$, there is a graph $G_k$ with $\tw(G_k)=4k+2$ and $\sn(G_k)=k+1$.

title: Longitudinal Parton Correlations in MRW-Type Unintegrated Double Parton Distributions
abstract: Double parton scattering offers a way to investigate correlations between partons inside the proton that are absent from the usual product approximation for double parton distributions. In this contribution, we discuss how these correlations enter unintegrated double parton distributions when transverse momentum is generated using MRW-type prescriptions. Starting from non-factorized GS09 distributions evolved to unequal scales, we examine the double LO-MRW, virtuality-ordered MRW, and modified KMRW constructions, focusing on their transverse-momentum dependence and flavor structure.

title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

title: Top-Level Operational Equilibrium: When is the response of a distributed system predictable from its own telemetry?
abstract: Distributed systems deployed across the edge-cloud continuum are adapted continuously: scaled, re-routed, given more or less capacity. Each adaptation rests on an expectation of how the system will respond, yet operators cannot tell from the telemetry they already collect whether that response is predictable. We define top-level operational equilibrium (TLOE), a notion of equilibrium for a running system, stated relative to the controls its operator declares. TLOE has three conditions: stationarity with time-scale separation, sufficiency of a top-level aggregate for the controls, and time-reversibility of that aggregate. We prove that an aggregate satisfying the last two exists if and only if the minimal sufficient statistic of the controls is time-reversible, so the coarsest admissible aggregate is derived rather than chosen. Under the first two conditions, the response to a small control change follows from passive telemetry through the steady-state fluctuation-response identity, with a conjugate observable fixed by the type of control: the total work in progress for a change of load, the occupancy of a stage for a change of its capacity. For chains of exponential single-server stages with Poisson input, TLOE holds exactly for load control at every stable throughput, but never for a control on the capacity of the first or last stage. On reference models, a per-stage conjugate overestimates the early response about threefold, blocking between stages breaks both conditions weakly, and a hysteretic autoscaler leaves no admissible aggregate at any reaction time computed. We specify a test for each condition, show that a static sufficiency test with an estimated top-level conjugate has no power, and quantify on simulated telemetry the window lengths the prediction and the reversibility test need. The evidence is on reference models; real telemetry is left to future work.

title: Verification-Guided Safety-Repair of Learned Controllers
abstract: Formal verification can certify that a learned controller is safe. But what should be done when verification fails? Simply suppressing actions that lead to unsafe next states is insufficient because the dangerous action that ultimately caused the safety violation might have occurred many steps earlier. Retraining modifies the policy globally, thereby potentially introducing new failures. Instead, we introduce ReachECO, a verification-guided repair procedure that exploits the information of failed multi-step reachability analysis for synthesizing explicit constraints on controller behavior. For Differentiable Weightless Controllers, the repairs compile into exact circuit patches that leave the controller unchanged everywhere outside the targeted policy cells. We prove soundness and termination of the repair procedure for ReachECO, as well as, assuming exhaustive continuation search, completeness relative to the reachability abstraction. Empirically, we demonstrate \method's ability to successfully repair otherwise unsafe controllers in three continuous-control benchmarks: ACC, Docking2D and Car2D.

title: Baryonic Keys and the Inheritance of Crypto-Assets: Revisiting the Tales From the Crypt Protocol
abstract: The inheritance of crypto-assets faces a structural obstacle: ownership is the knowledge of a key, so the key either disappears with its owner or has to be shared beforehand. The Tales From the Crypt Protocol (TFCP) addressed one part of the problem, the distributed and privacy-preserving acknowledgment of a death by a blockchain. We revisit it with a new primitive. A \emph{baryonic key} is a physical object from which bits are obtained only through a measurement, are never stored digitally, and which exists in exactly $n$ copies, where $n$ is neither zero nor unbounded. We define the primitive, outline a candidate instantiation based on a replicated micro-fractured relief, and state its limits: digitising a copy is slow and tamper-evident, not impossible. We also outline other uses of the primitive, from post-quantum pre-shared keys to common coins for Byzantine agreement. We then give a threat model for TFCP, review the attack models of the literature that apply to it, and show where it resists and where it does not. We propose TFCP-B, in which decrypting the will requires both a secret shared among registrars and the response of a baryonic key, and in which heirs claim their share through hash commitments, without any prior key or wallet. We detail each change from TFCP to TFCP-B, with its rationale and its price. TFCP-B removes the anonymity loss caused by colluding registrars and blocks several false-alarm attacks. It does not remove the shallow-account attack, remains exposed to transaction censorship during the deliberation period, and introduces new assumptions on custodians and reading devices. The security arguments are informal and the physical figures are design estimates.

title: On Erdős' last equation
abstract: For a positive integer $n\ge 2$, we look at the number of solutions of the Diophantine equation $$ n(x_1+\cdots+x_n)=x_1\cdots x_n. $$ Denoting by $f(n)$ this number we show that $\liminf_{n\to\infty} \log f(n)/\log n=0$.

title: On homogeneous hypertournaments
abstract: Sullivan recently constructed continuum many countable homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for every $n\ge3$ by forbidding configurations he calls pair-cancelling. We show that, for every family $\mathcal F$ of pair-cancelling $n$-hypertournaments, the class of all linearly ordered finite $\mathcal F$-free $n$-hypertournaments is Ramsey and has the ordering property. In particular, freely ordered $\mathbf{H}_4$-free $3$-hypertournaments are Ramsey, answering a question of Cherlin, Hubička, Nešetřil, and the author from 2021. For every odd $n\ge3$, we give a simple Ramsey expansion with the expansion property for even $n$-hypertournaments by naming an $(n-1)$-hypertournament and a free linear order. We also show that, for $n\ge6$, no unbounded hereditary strong amalgamation class of finite $n$-hypertournaments has EPPA. Moreover, we prove the failure of EPPA for all Sullivan's classes with $n\ge4$, and for the even $5$-hypertournaments. We conjecture that even hypertournaments and classes omitting a family of pair-cancelling hypertournaments, together with the homogeneous cyclic order in arity three, are the only countably infinite homogeneous $n$-hypertournaments for $n\ge3$. We give some supporting evidence.

title: Validation of Ariel candidates orbiting K-M stars
abstract: One of the key goals of planetary population studies is to achieve broad coverage of the parameter space, which is not yet fully represented by confirmed planets. This limitation can be mitigated by including planets that have been statistically validated through a vetting procedure, even if they are not fully confirmed. In preparation for the Ariel mission, a Mission Candidate Sample has been assembled, comprising both confirmed planets and several unvalidated candidates. In this context, we apply a vetting analysis to a selected subsample of these candidates. Our methodology is based on the TRICERATOPS tool, aimed at confirming the presence of transiting planets or ruling out false-positive scenarios. We applied TRICERATOPS to a sample of 318 targets drawn from the last three Ariel TESS Planet Candidates catalogues. The analysis includes evaluation of statistical probabilities, as well as checks on stellar binarity indicators such as the Renormalized Unit Weight Error (RUWE) and the IPD_frac_multi_peak values from Gaia Data Release 3. Our analysis validated 56 candidates as planets, identified 29 false positives, and classified 35 as likely planets. These results are intended to support the Ariel mission by providing a probabilistic priority ranking to guide follow-up observations and optimise targets for atmospheric characterisation studies.

title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
abstract: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

title: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
abstract: Remote-sensing (RS) image scene classification aims to assign a semantic category to an overhead image, and in practice must often do so from only a handful of labelled examples, since annotation requires expert interpretation and the resulting labels transfer poorly across sensors and regions. Recent progress has come from adapting vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, through learned prompts or feature adapters. Although effective, these methods construct their representation entirely in the spatial domain. RS scenes are dominated by periodic texture and regular geometry, which the Fourier spectrum describes compactly through an amplitude component, carrying texture and contrast statistics, and a phase component, carrying spatial structure. Existing frequency-domain adaptation of VLMs either exploits amplitude alone or does not separate amplitude from phase, leaving the structural component unused. In this article, we propose PhaseCLIP, which inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder and trains only 1.30% of its parameters. Because the amplitude and phase pathways share an identical parameter layout, a single weight set is learned on phase and transferred exactly to amplitude, giving a two-stage scheme that adds no parameters. Experiments on five public RS datasets, EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS and RSSCN7, against eight baselines under a matched protocol, show that PhaseCLIP attains 84.28% mean accuracy and is the best method in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot cells, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the most difficult dataset. Because the modules act on the spectrum of image patches and transformer tokens and leave the text encoder untouched, the approach can be extended to other RS sensors and tasks, and to other domains in which class evidence lies in spatial structure.

title: VA-Assembly: View-Aligned Score Guidance for Training-Free 3D Part Assembly
abstract: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.

title: Detecting False Self-Consistency in Density-Functional Calculations
abstract: Density-functional calculations feed materials databases and machine-learning models, and are declared converged when energy changes and residuals fall below thresholds. We show that these criteria, and even the agreement of independent optimizers, can accept a state from which the energy still descends or whose Hamiltonian is inconsistent with the energy. A variational formulation of self-consistency in the space of Kohn-Sham Hamiltonians yields a descent probe that exposes lower states accessible from a returned solution, and a frozen-orbital Janak test detects such an inconsistency. Both apply to any code without modification. In VASP, a UO$_2$ PBE+$U$ calculation converges 1.46 eV above a lower state, and CoO and FeO converge as metals 0.8-0.9 eV above insulating states. In a census of 339 converged calculations on tungsten-free Materials Project structures, recomputed with a modified static protocol, 57 (16.8%) show energy decreases above the threshold, 49 without an initial energy rise exceeding the tolerance.

title: Relationship between generic Hecke algebra modules and $0$-Hecke algebra modules
abstract: Let $H_{R,a}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ be the Hecke algebra over a principal ideal domain $R$ with parameter $a\in R$. The representation theories of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ differ substantially and have largely been studied independently. In this paper, we relate the categories of finitely generated modules of these two algebras through specialization functors from the category of finitely generated $H_{\mathbb{C}[v^{1/2}];v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules. We first investigate the fundamental properties of these functors concerning dimensions, essential surjectivity, and characters. We then construct $H_{\mathbb{C}[v^{1/2}];v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules which, through these functors, provide connections between skew Specht modules of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and $0$-Hecke skew Specht modules of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$, and between Kazhdan--Lusztig cell modules of $H_{\mathbb{C}(v^{1/2});v}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$ and dual plactic class modules of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$. Both families of $H_{\mathbb{C};0}(\mathfrak{S}_n)$-modules are closely related to regular Schur labeled skew shape posets. We further explore how specialization functors relate the Frobenius characteristic to the quasisymmetric characteristic and connects the branching rules for skew Specht modules with those for $0$-Hecke skew Specht modules. Finally, we use the established connection with Kazhdan--Lusztig cell modules to obtain a result on the classification of dual plactic class modules up to isomorphism.

title: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.

title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
abstract: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

title: Multiple moiré polarization textures in twisted trilayers
abstract: Twisted van der Waals layers exhibit nontrivial polarization textures from moiré-modulated stacking and the inherited sliding ferroelectricity. However, in any twisted bilayer, the topology of polarization texture is essentially fixed due to the inherent twist-stacking landscape for a given material. Here, this constraint is overcome in some twisted trilayers, where the relative moiré phase emerges as an additional structural degree of freedom. Using CrI$_3$ and BN as representative sliding ferroelectrics with distinct symmetries, it is clarified how the relative moiré phases reshape the trilayer stacking landscapes and tune the net polarization texture by layer sliding.
