This yields Lipschitz regularity of stationary controls and second-order conditions without gap for polyhedral constraints. For the SAA scheme with sample size $M$, we prove almost sure uniform consistency of the empirical minimizers, convergence rates of order $M^{-1/2}$ for the optimal values, independent of the dimension of the parameter space. We then derive the asymptotic distributions. The optimal values satisfy a central limit theorem, obtained from a functional central limit theorem for the SAA objective. The empirical minimizers are asymptotically Gaussian when the constraints are inactive; under polyhedral constraints, their limit solves a quadratic problem on the critical cone with a Gaussian linear term. We also derive confidence intervals for linear functionals of the optimal control and illustrate the results on two numerical examples.

title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models likely outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification), while weaker models score near or below them. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

title: Pinned simplex volumes from thin sets in Euclidean spaces
abstract: Let $E\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a Borel set, with $d\geq2$. We prove that if $\dim_{\mathrm H}(E)>d/2$, then there exist distinct points $a,b\in E$ such that the set of triangle areas with fixed base $a,b$ and third vertex varying in $E$ has positive Lebesgue measure. More generally, for $2\leq r\leq d$, if \[ \dim_{\mathrm H}(E)> \max\left\{r-1,\frac{d-r+2}{2}\right\}, \] then there are $r$ affinely independent points in $E$ for which the corresponding base-pinned $r$-simplex volume set has positive Lebesgue measure. The geometric input is a thin-plane estimate of Bright, Ortiz, and Zakharov \cite{BrightOrtizZakharov}. For a suitable $(r-2)$-dimensional anchor spanned by $E$, this estimate yields simultaneous Frostman bounds for a projected vertex measure in the normal space of the anchor and for the distribution of directions determining bases that share the anchor. The Peres--Schlag machinery \cite{PeresSchlag}, applied to a local family of distance-to-line maps in this $(d-r+2)$-dimensional normal space, then produces the desired base. Finally, we establish an exact correspondence between fixed-base simplex volumes and pinned distances in the normal space of the base, prove a converse for matched bases in layered lifts, and obtain the lower obstruction $\max\{r-1,d/(2r)\}$ for any universal dimension threshold.

title: D/H and 12C/13C ratios of benzonitrile and indene in TMC-1 support bottom-up formation of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon-like molecules
abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) have recently been detected in cold dark clouds through their rotational spectra, but it is currently a matter of debate whether they form through a bottom-up process from small hydrocarbons or through a top-down scenario involving the fragmentation of large PAHs inherited from a previous evolutionary stage of diffuse cloud. Isotopic ratios can shed light on the origin of PAHs in cold dark clouds. Large aromatic molecules observed in the infrared are enriched in deuterium and may also be enriched in 13C because they likely formed in the ejecta of evolved stars. We synthesized indene deuterated at the aliphatic position in the laboratory and measured its rotational spectrum, together with those of the nine 13C singly substituted isotopomers of indene. We used the measured spectra of the D and 13C isotopic species of indene, together with previously measured spectra of D and 13C isotopic benzonitrile, to search for these species in the cold dark cloud TMC-1 using QUIJOTE data obtained with the Yebes 40m telescope. We used a line stack method to tentatively detect deuterated benzonitrile and detect 13C-substituted benzonitrile, but find no evidence of either the D or 13C isotopic species of indene. We derive an aromatic D/H ratio of 0.53 % from benzonitrile, an aliphatic D/H ratio <3.3 % from indene, and 12C/13C ratios of 126 and >55 for benzonitrile and indene, respectively. These values are consistent with isotopic ratios derived for other molecules in TMC-1 and show no enrichment in either D or 13C that could be ascribed to inheritance from large PAHs in a top-down scenario; a bottom-up scenario is therefore the most likely.

title: Revisiting Index Performance under High Cache-Miss Penalties
abstract: Modern data-intensive applications often query very large datasets, making index performance critical. Recent index structures exploit the fine-grained access capabilities of emerging storage devices such as DCPMM and CXL. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate indexes in isolation using saturated, closed-loop workloads that emphasize maximum throughput. Such workloads favor highly concurrent designs while overlooking the application work that follows an index lookup and competes for cache, memory bandwidth, and CPU resources. We present AuxBench - a microbenchmark that evaluates indexes as auxiliary access paths within larger application workloads. Using AuxBench, we evaluate four byte-addressable indexes under controlled post-lookup memory activity, concurrency, and request arrival patterns. Our experiments show that post-lookup memory activity can change the relative performance of competing indexes, that concurrency-oriented designs may lose their advantages when substantial application work is introduced, and that time-varying request arrivals can produce severe tail latency near saturation. These findings demonstrate why index-only benchmarks may not adequately predict performance in larger application workloads

title: Forests of Omnitrees: Analysis and Applications to Anisotropic Space--Time Finite Elements
abstract: We prove output-optimal work bounds for omnitree forests, which bisect cells along selected axes. A canonical descriptor characterizes representable partitions independently of split order. Complete one-level cycles, including coarsening, face balance and selected coarse meshes, take sequential work proportional to stored input and output at fixed dimension and key width, with polynomial depth dependence even for unbalanced input. From balanced input, refinement-only balance stays within each request's coordinate slab; this bound is attained. Polynomial trace equations characterize conforming high-order spaces across crossed face partitions. Reconstruction moments bound interpolation errors and capture the logarithmic loss that bilinear nodal interpolation can suffer on balanced meshes. Elements of degree up to four resolve moving heat layers on unstructured 4D space-time and 5D space-time-parameter meshes. Multigrid uses the generated hierarchies.

title: Primal--Dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox for Dynamic Mean Field Games
abstract: We compute finite-horizon dynamic mean field equilibria using a primal--dual Kullback--Leibler Mirror-Prox algorithm. Each iteration updates occupation measures by exponential tilting and computes the dual correction by solving a linear PDE, without solving a nonlinear Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or a best-response control problem. Under assumptions and Lasry--Lions monotonicity, we prove an $O(K^{-1})$ ergodic Minty bound after $K$ iterations and an $O(K^{-1/2})$ approximate-equilibrium bound for the corrected average. We obtain convergence rates for the population flow under strong monotonicity, and for smooth diffusions with uniformly convex control costs under ordinary monotonicity. We also prove convergence of continuous-time Markov chain approximations to diffusion equilibria and, under additional smoothness and convexity assumptions, bound the error in terms of the spatial mesh size and the number of iterations. Galerkin approximations preserve the $O(K^{-1})$ estimates under suitable bounds on the correction errors. Numerical experiments illustrate the method and its convergence.

title: Super-Eddington Accretion onto Compact Objects: Theory Meets Observation
abstract: We review candidate super-Eddington populations together with semi-analytic models and radiation magnetohydrodynamic simulations, with the following conclusions: $\bullet$ Likely super-Eddington sources over a range of black hole mass show similar properties, including outflow on a range of scales, hard X-ray weakness, decreased emission from jets, and suppressed optical/UV variability. $\bullet$ Theoretical treatment of super-Eddington accretion predicts similar behavior across a range of methods and initial conditions, although interesting differences remain, particularly in the importance of magnetic fields. Numerical simulations produce a puffed-up inner disk with a funnel that grows narrower at higher mass accretion rate. Radiative efficiency declines with accretion rate in thermal-pressure--supported disks. $\bullet$ Ubiquitous outflow is likely an important ingredient in galaxy feedback at high Eddington ratios, as wind mechanical power increases with accretion rate and can rival jet power. Wind kinetic power depends far less on uncertain black hole spin and magnetic fields. $\bullet$ Observational classes of objects can be sorted in a two-dimensional parameter space of Eddington ratio and orientation. Observations down the funnel observe rapid X-ray variability, while observations through the wind will see suppressed X-ray emission. At the highest Eddington ratios, we envision a regime where the photosphere extends to $r > 10^6 \, r_g$, and the observer sees only thermalized emission covering most of the sky, speculatively corresponding to super-soft sources and Little Red Dots.

title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.

title: Quantum-Classical Separation in Probability Distribution Transport via Nonlocal Games
abstract: In many-body physics and generative artificial intelligence, locality provides a natural notion of phase equivalence: two quantum states or classical probability distributions are regarded as in the same phase when local dynamics can reversibly transform one into the other. This raises a fundamental question: can local quantum dynamics transport classical probability distributions in ways that local classical dynamics cannot? We establish a quantum-classical separation in distribution transport: two classical distributions can be connected exactly and reversibly by a constant-depth local quantum circuit, whereas classical stochastic transport requires a substantially larger spatial range. We demonstrate this separation explicitly on a one-dimensional chain and develop a general construction principle on graphs, based on nonlocal games. Moreover, the source distribution can itself be generated by a simple local classical process, establishing a quantum advantage in distribution generation as well. Our results reveal a fundamental distinction between classical and quantum local reversibility, even when both the initial and final states are entirely classical.

title: Three Dimensional Structure of Jovian Polar Cyclones Revealed by Juno Microwave Radiometer
abstract: Jupiter's circumpolar cyclones (CPCs) represent one of the most extreme dynamical regimes of the Solar System, where rotation, stratification, and convection interact to organize a stable polygonal cyclone lattice at each pole. Yet the depth and vertical structure of these cyclones remain unresolved. Here, using Juno Microwave Radiometer observations acquired between May 2023 and May 2024, we retrieve the 3-D thermal/compositional structure of Jupiter's northern CPCs at depths beyond those detectable by Earth-based telescopes and spacecraft that have ever visited. The eight CPCs, appearing with enhanced microwave brightness, show as modest ammonia depletion near the water lifting-condensation level ($\sim$5 bar) and/or, equivalently, warm-core structures analogous to terrestrial tropical cyclones. Five of them show substantially stronger and deeper anomalies than the remaining three, with approximately twice the inferred ammonia depletion and localized heating. In contrast, the central polar cyclone exhibits little microwave brightness contrast relative to its surroundings, despite its substantially cloudier and visually distinct appearance in visible and infrared observations. Previous dynamical models have treated the CPCs and the central polar cyclone as dynamically similar structures arising from the self-organization of turbulent flows. The new observations, however, suggest that the CPCs and the central polar cyclone may have distinct origins and operate under different dynamical regimes.

title: Simple Models of Thermal Order in $2+1$ Dimensions
abstract: Heating need not destroy order. We show that it persists to arbitrarily high temperatures in simple quantum field theories in $2+1$ spacetime dimensions. In a $\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$ model of two real scalar fields, a sufficiently negative mixed quartic coupling drives one field to condense, spontaneously breaking its $\mathbb Z_2$ symmetry. When coupled to massless Dirac fermions through a Yukawa interaction, this condensate generates a fermion mass, thereby spontaneously breaking parity and time-reversal symmetries. We extend this construction to a $\mathbb Z_2\times O(n)$ scalar model, in which the Mermin-Wagner theorem precludes spontaneous breaking of the continuous $O(n)$ symmetry at finite temperatures. Nevertheless, for $n=2$, a Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless superfluid phase persists to arbitrarily high temperatures. In this phase, spatial correlations decay algebraically, with an exponent that approaches zero as the temperature increases. For $n\geq 3$, we uncover a further unexpected feature of these models: the characteristic size of ordered domains grows asymptotically with temperature, revealing an unusual enhancement of spatial correlations upon heating. We establish our results using a controlled high-temperature expansion, with selected findings corroborated by numerical functional renormalization group analysis. The simplicity of the field content in these models provides a promising starting point for exploring experimental realizations of persistent thermal order in thin-film materials.

title: Structure Constants of Planar N=4 SYM at Any Coupling
abstract: We recast a recent conjecture for structure constants in planar N=4 supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory in a separation-of-variables-inspired form suitable for non-perturbative analysis. All state-dependent information enters through the quantum spectral curve. As a showcase, we compute at finite coupling the three-point functions of two half-BPS operators and the spin-two member of the Konishi multiplet. Our results span weak to strong coupling, reproduce the known perturbative and string-theory limits, and are consistent with conformal-bootstrap bounds. We also obtain new six- and seven-loop perturbative coefficients and extract new strong-coupling data from high-precision numerical fits.

title: Bias-Reduced and Parallel Heavy-Tailed Stochastic Convex Optimization in $\ell_p$ Geometries
abstract: We consider the fundamental problem of parallel stochastic convex optimization (SCO), whose aim is to approximately minimize a convex objective when given the ability to query a moment-bounded stochastic gradient oracle multiple times in parallel per round. Whereas most previous results have focused on the variance-bounded Euclidean ($\ell_2$-norm) setting, meaning the objective is Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell_2$-norm over an $\ell_2$-bounded feasible set in $\mathbb{R}^d$, in this work we study parallel SCO in $\ell_p$ settings for $2 \le p < \infty$ under a heavy-tailed noise model. We begin by introducing a new class of $\ell_p$-optimal-distance-convergence (ODC$_p$) algorithms, drawing on prior stochastic bias-reduced techniques [ACJ+21], which combine with multilevel Monte Carlo methods to efficiently estimate the optimum of uniformly convex objectives. As a consequence of our ODC$_p$ algorithms, we first establish rates for projection-efficient $\ell_p$-Lipschitz optimization, composite convex minimization, and efficient $\ell_p$-proximal point estimation. Combining our ODC$_p$ algorithms with a new $\ell_p$-generalized Gaussian-based stochastic gradient estimator ($p$-GREG), we provide two efficient $\ell_p$ parallel algorithms, EpochDA and $\ell_p$-AC-SA, which achieve optimization error $ε> 0$ with at most $\tilde{O}(d^{\frac{p}{2p + 2}} ε^{-\frac{p}{p + 1}})$ query depth, improving upon the sequential heavy-tailed stochastic query depth of $O(ε^{-p})$ for $ε\leq \tilde{O}(d^{-1/(2p)})$. We also establish dimension-dependent lower bounds of $Ω\bigl(\min\{ε^{-p},d^{p/(3p-2)}\}\bigr)$ adaptive rounds for nonsmooth convex optimization over a subset of the unit $\ell_p$ ball. Our results improve upon the $Ω(\min\{ε^{-p},ε^{2/3}d^{1/3}\})$ bounds of [DG19], when adapted to the same feasible set.

title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

title: Can a World Model Predict a Deepfake Video? A Consistency Margin Prior for Deepfake Detection
abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.

title: Inventa: Decentralized Self-Improving Agents for Autonomous Scientific Discovery
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can generate research ideas and improve scientific discovery through iterative experimentation. However, increasing the number of agents or iterations does not automatically translate to producing more diverse or feasible ideas. Agents may converge on similar candidates, propagate unsupported claims through shared memory components and repeatedly apply search strategies that no longer yield any improvements. We introduce Inventa, a framework for automated scientific discovery that employs autonomous research units and verified shared knowledge. Each unit creates a lineage of candidate ideas using a mutator agent. A local orchestrator agent periodically adapts the mutator's harness. When progress stalls, the orchestrator agent replaces its model or restarts the idea evolution process. Verifiers evaluate each candidate idea and record verified improvements, useful components and constraint violations in a shared knowledge, the only channel between units. We evaluate Inventa on five benchmarks spanning the research cycle, covering retrieval (ScholarCatalyst), ideation (IdeaBench), proposal writing (IdeaScientist), and scientific law discovery (EurekaBench, SciLaws-Bench). It leads all five, achieving 73.6% on EurekaBench versus 56.2% for CORAL. On IdeaBench, it discovers 26.0 novel ideas per paper, compared with 18.6 for ResearchAgent, with 82% fewer model calls.

title: High-resolution top-down nanopatterning of NbN thin films for superconducting metamaterials
abstract: Periodic nanopatterning offers a route to tailoring vortex motion and the electromagnetic response of superconducting films, providing a basis for superconducting metamaterials. Here, we report a high-resolution top-down nanopatterning process for ultrathin epitaxial NbN films on sapphire substrates. Electron-beam lithography using hydrogen silsesquioxane (HSQ) and ZEP 530A resists was optimized through proximity-effect correction and adhesion-layer integration. Dense superconducting nanowire grids with pitches down to 70 nm were fabricated, alongside millimeter-square areas patterned with 100-nm-pitch hole arrays with high pattern fidelity. A thin Si capping layer was found to significantly improve HSQ adhesion on epitaxial NbN. The nanopatterns were successfully transferred into 5-nm-thick NbN films by reactive ion etching (RIE). Structural and dimensional characterization was performed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and atomic force microscopy (AFM), enabling cross-validation of nanoscale feature dimensions and etch quality. Electrical transport measurements reveal periodic resistance minima and switching-current oscillations at magnetic fields set by the hole-array pitch, consistent with enhanced vortex pinning when the vortex configuration matches the patterned lattice. Cryogenic THz time-domain spectroscopy further reveals a reduced superfluid density in the nanopatterned region relative to pristine NbN, while both regions have a spectroscopic superconducting transition near 14 K. These results establish a robust fabrication platform for superconducting nanopatterns targeting vortex pinning, metamaterials, and quantum-device applications.

title: When Does Discrete Ricci Curvature Help? An Edge-Level Analysis of Curvature-Enhanced GCNs for PPI Prediction
abstract: Curvature-enhanced graph convolutional networks (CGCN) incorporate Ollivier-Ricci curvature (ORC), grounded in optimal transport theory, into message passing, motivated by the claim that curvature-weighted edges alleviate "over-squashing" at structural bottlenecks. But does CGCN's improvement actually come from mitigating over-squashing? We investigate this on four real-world protein-protein interaction (PPI) datasets, comparing CGCN against a standard GCN at the level of individual edges rather than aggregate metrics alone. While CGCN improves aggregate AUC, AUPR, and F1 across all four datasets, this gain is concentrated almost entirely on low-degree edges, while performance on low-curvature (bottleneck) edges systematically degrades in three of four datasets, the opposite of what the over-squashing motivation predicts. Examining the learned edge-weight function directly, together with clustering-validity metrics, edge-distance ratios, and a layer-depth ablation across four depths, we find evidence for an alternative account: curvature-weighting sharpens the separation between clusters, which improves intra-cluster predictions at the cost of inter-cluster (bottleneck) ones. We test this account against topologically defined communities rather than the classification labels used elsewhere. Additionally, we offer practical guidance on when to prefer CGCN over standard GCN, depending on whether intra- or inter-cluster predictions matter most.

title: Improved accuracy of the reference photon calibration standards in the network of gravitational-wave observatories during the O4 observing run
abstract: The global network of gravitational wave observatories uses systems known as Photon Calibrators to provide absolute calibration via laser radiation pressure. Successive detector improvements are increasing sensitivity, enabling not only increase the detection rate but also detections with high signal to noise ratios. To optimally extract information from these detected signals, continual effort is directed at pushing the state of the art of the interferometer calibration accuracy. To improve the accuracy of the locally-maintained laser power standards for photon calibration, a new global calibration scheme was implemented by using transfer standards calibrated at both the National Institute of Standards and Tech- nology (NIST) in the US and the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Germany during the recently completed fourth observing run. We report the results of a long-duration NIST-PTB bilateral comparison conducted over almost three years and the results of propagation of transfer standard calibrations to the reference power sensors maintained at each observatory.

title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

title: The Hidden Cost of MoE Diffusion Decoding: Profiling and Fixing the Sampler
abstract: Masked diffusion language models (dLLMs) decode by iteratively denoising a full canvas of tokens, so every forward pass runs a per-token sampling and stopping pipeline over the entire canvas-by-vocabulary logits tensor. We profile single-user decoding of a 26B-parameter diffusion Mixture-of-Experts model on a bandwidth-bound edge accelerator (NVIDIA GB10) and report a result that is easy to miss: after weight quantisation, this logits pipeline, not the expert GEMMs, is the single largest consumer of decode time. Unlike autoregressive decoding, where sampling touches one position's logits per committed token, diffusion decoding processes S times as many logit entries per output token, where S is the number of denoising steps. We show this pipeline is largely redundant or fusable and remove it in two lossless tiers: a bit-exact tier whose output is byte-identical to the reference decoder, and an accuracy-parity tier using a fused single-pass entropy kernel and Gumbel-max sampling. Combined with a W4A16 expert kernel, the full stack reaches 2.4-2.7 times end-to-end speedup over bf16 at unchanged benchmark accuracy on GSM8K, HumanEval, and MATH, on a single 273 GB/s device. We confirm the finding on a second, independently built diffusion MoE (LLaDA2.0-mini: pipeline 28.8% of decode, fused W4A16 3.3 times at accuracy parity) and show it disappears on a dense diffusion model (3.6%). The cost is specific to MoE diffusion, where quantisation makes the backbone cheap. Code and quantised weights are released.

title: Translation surfaces with logarithmically growing systole
abstract: We exhibit a sequence of translation surfaces $T_1, T_2,...$ with $T_g$ of genus $g$ and area $g$, such that the systole grows logarithmically with $g$. They are produced by starting with a fixed translation surface, taking covers with the same topology as those discovered by Brooks, and then adding handles by gluing along slits.

title: Kernel Tuning for the HSIC-Based Global Sensitivity Analysis of High-Dimensional Models
abstract: We consider global sensitivity analysis of models with high-dimensional input parameters using HSIC-based indices. The numerical estimation of these kernel-based indices is known to be challenging for such models. Without proper kernel tuning, the standard estimator for the HSIC can become unstable and break down. Focusing on models with independent parameters, we introduce a dimension-aware bandwidth formula and provide theoretical analysis justifying the proposed approach. In particular, we show that unless kernel bandwidth parameters explicitly scale with the input dimension, the corresponding sensitivity indices return uninformative rankings of parameter influence. Further, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed scaling strategy on linear and nonlinear test problems, including models with correlated inputs.

title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks
abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erdős-Rényi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.

title: Optimal Network Design under Node Failures
abstract: Networks are frequently constructed before it is determined which nodes will persist. We address the design problem in scenarios where nodes fail independently, links are costly and must be established in advance, and the benefits to surviving nodes diminish with distance. Examples include supplier, interbank, and infrastructure networks. Among all possible networks, the complete, star, and empty configurations are each welfare-optimal within specific ranges of link costs. However, with four or more nodes, failures introduce a range of costs in which every optimal network contains more links than the star but fewer than the complete network. At the lower end of this range, we show that the optimal networks are exactly those obtained by removing a matching from the complete network. We develop an exact algorithm for complete multipartite networks. It finds an optimal network by dynamic programming in a number of operations that grows with the fourth power of the number of nodes, although the class itself grows superpolynomially. For networks with up to six nodes, restricting the design to this class results in no loss under explicit conditions. We also characterize pairwise-stable networks within this class and establish their existence for every level of link cost. Finally, we quantify the cost of misjudging failure risk. Overestimating node survival leads to overbuilding and can yield lower welfare than building nothing, whereas underestimating it never does. Under uncertain failure risk, design should therefore favor conservative reliability estimates.

title: tmol: a GPU-accelerated implementation of the Rosetta energy function for machine learning
abstract: Physics-inspired forcefields complement generative machine learning models, showing better generalization beyond the training distribution. However, these forcefields are typically slow to evaluate, and their derivatives are difficult to integrate into ML frameworks. We introduce tmol, a GPU-native PyTorch library implementing the state-of-the-art RosettaGenFF forcefield. tmol supports efficient batched differentiable scoring and whole-structure refinement with up to 362-fold throughput increase (batched). Used as a reward in generative protein design, tmol increases hydrogen bonds and water bridges at designed interfaces.

title: Tie-Line Scheduling Using Real-Time Contraction Metrics: Hierarchical Reachable Sets for Multi-Area Inverter-Dominated Grids
abstract: Managing transmission congestion in multi-area power grids dominated by inverter-based resources (IBRs) requires bridging a severe timescale and modeling divide. Supervisory congestion optimizers -- such as Online Feedback Optimization (OFO) and two-tiered differentiable Model Predictive Control (MPC) -- rely on linearized, convex algebraic grid approximations that cannot guarantee dynamic stability during sub-second converter transients. Conversely, fast distributed consensus schemes like Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) depend on convex plant assumptions and iterative message exchanges that lag behind rapid tie-line surges. This paper replaces convex ADMM emergency consensus with a Distributed Nonlinear Separable Control Contraction Metric (SCCM) architecture spanning three nested tiers: the Device layer, the Area layer, and the Grid tie-line layer. By pairing online Prediction Error Method and Moving Horizon Estimation (PEM-MHE) parameter tracking with offline convex Linear Matrix Inequality (LMI) synthesis, the controller executes a closed-form nonlinear feedback law online without solving real-time optimization problems. We derive the Pontryagin attainable (reachable) ellipsoids for each layer, prove hierarchical tube containment via Schur-complement matrix inequalities, and project the certified Grid reachable tube through Power Transfer Distribution Factors (PTDFs) to supply guaranteed safe thermal limits to the supervisory coordinator. Validation on modified IEEE 39-bus (100% IBR, zero synchronous generators) and 3-area IEEE 118-bus systems demonstrates an 82.8% reduction in cumulative tie-line thermal overload while maintaining strict exponential contraction ($λ_{\max} \le -2.43$) even under a 3 s communication blackout.

title: Diversity Preservation Recovers Transcription Factor Motifs Across Challenging Confounder Landscapes
abstract: Motif discovery is a process where DNA sequences are searched for the short patterns, called motifs, that transcription factor (TF) proteins bind. However, the motif lengths are often unknown and motif attribution often competes with a near-identical motif of a related protein. In this work, we pair a motif genotype whose length emerges from an evolvable gate with MAP-Elites archives organized by three descriptor pairs, and validate every motif against the full HOCOMOCO database. On five liver ChIP-seq datasets spanning distinct confounder landscapes, a $(μ + λ)$ baseline differing only in survivor selection collapses onto a single motif and never ranks the target first across three datasets, while every MAP-Elites archive does so in at least 13 of 30 seeds on every dataset. Against the motif discovery tool MEME, run on the same sequences and validated identically, the archives recover the target signal as reliably on four datasets and more robustly when motif width is constrained. Neither method ranks the target above its closest relatives on HNF4A and JUND over the full width range, but narrow archive motifs rank HNF4A first in up to 43% of seeds, where MEME misses the motif in all settings. Diversity preservation improves our ability to recover consistent motif signal, although motif annotation remains a challenging problem for all methods we tested.

title: Anomaly inflow for simplicial Kähler fermions
abstract: We study massive Kähler Dirac fermions propagating on finite triangulations of various three dimensional manifolds with one or more boundaries. To probe the anomaly structure of these models we decompose the Kähler field into two reduced Kähler fields and choose boundary conditions that ensure that any edge modes are necessarily massless. We then show how to factorize the Pfaffian of this system into a product of bulk and boundary sectors each of which can separately pick up a phase under a global $Z_4$ transformation of the fermions that simultaneously changes the sign of the mass. These phases are topological, depending only on the index of the lattice Kähler operator in that sector. For the boundary sector a non-trivial phase signals the presence of a 't Hooft anomaly. We study cases where the boundary is anomalous but an inflow from the bulk cancels its phase. Canceling this anomaly for a non-orientable boundary in the absence of the bulk recovers the known classification of topological superconductors. We also give a continuum interpretation of these results in terms of inflow from a gravitational Chern Simons theory which is induced by integrating out massive bulk Kähler Dirac fermions. In the presence of a boundary the latter gives rise to Wen-Zee terms that mediate the anomaly inflow mechanism.

title: A search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst in the M81 globular cluster, FRB 20200120E
abstract: We present a search for optical bursts from the repeating fast radio burst FRB 20200120E, which is located in a globular cluster of M81 and is the closest known extragalactic FRB. We observed FRB 20200120E simultaneously with the high-speed, quintuple-beam optical camera HiPERCAM on the 10.4-m Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Effelsberg 100-m Radio Telescope. We detected one radio burst of fluence $\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} = 0.14\pm0.01$ Jy ms during our observations, but found no evidence for corresponding optical bursts in the 11.98 ms frames. We find 5$σ$ upper limits on the optical burst fluence of $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O} < 1.8\times10^{-3}$ Jy ms (combined $u_s g_s r_s i_s z_s$-bands) and the optical burst energy of $E_{\rm O} < 5.4\times10^{36}$ erg ($r_s$-band), corrected for interstellar extinction. We compare our upper limit on the optical-to-radio fluence ratio $\mathcal{F}_{\rm O}/\mathcal{F}_{\rm R} < 0.013$ to various emission models involving inverse-Compton scattering in the magnetosphere or nebula of a highly-magnetised neutron~star.

title: Avalanche Sharpness and the Stationary State of the Bak--Sneppen Model on $\mathbb Z^d$
abstract: We establish the stationary picture for the nearest-neighbour Bak--Sneppen model on $\mathbb Z^d$, for every $d\ge1$. There exists a critical level $t_c$ such that, as $N\to\infty$, every fixed family of stationary fitnesses on the torus $(\mathbb Z/N\mathbb Z)^d$ converges, in exponential coordinates, to independent random variables with law $t_c+\operatorname{Exp}(1)$. The proof relies on three estimates for avalanches. For $d\ge2$, these replace the interval structure available in dimension one. We show that the threshold at which the mean avalanche range diverges coincides with the threshold for the appearance of an infinite avalanche, using the hierarchical structure of avalanches and an estimate on the creation of new sites under translation. We then prove that an avalanche reaching a macroscopic distance on the torus can, after any fixed positive increase of the level, be amplified into one covering the whole torus. Finally, below criticality, we obtain exponential integrability of the avalanche range and give a finite--infinite volume comparison. These three ingredients allow us to implement the Meester and Znamenski program that connects these avalanche estimates to the stationary law of the finite-volume process.

title: When Is Membership Graded? Identifiability and Resolution Limits of a Graded Gaussian Mixture Model
abstract: Mixed-membership models describe each unit as a graded blend of latent types. Before the blend is interpreted, the data should be able to rule out the simpler story in which every unit belongs to a single type. We ask when they can, in a scalar graded Gaussian mixture model, in which each observation is a Beta-weighted convex combination of independent Gaussian draws from two types, the mechanism behind functional mixed-membership models and the normal compositional model. The model is identifiable, unequal variances included, but the identifying information sits in the far tails of the marginal. For the symmetric model we give a closed-form hard-membership mixture that matches the graded marginal in five cumulants, and a Le Cam bound turns it into a certified sample size below which no test separates graded from hard membership with summed error under one half. The threshold is governed by the concentration $c$ relative to $c_0\approx d^2$, where $d$ is the type half-separation in within-type standard deviations. At $d=3$ it is about 2,600 observations at $c=3$ and 77,000 at $c=6$. Most of the difficulty comes from learning $c$. On 100 simulated datasets with graded membership, a correctly specified posterior under the default priors of a published Bayesian sampler for this model class reports hard membership every time, a weak prior gives intervals for the concentration spanning orders of magnitude, and the sampler's own answers depend on where it starts.

title: Inverse Design for Nonplanar Conformal Layers
abstract: Conformal layering, where a deposited layer follows the nonplanar topography beneath it, arises from both deliberate passivation overlays and imperfect planarization between depositions. However, inverse design methods typically model planar, vertically extruded layers, resulting in geometric discrepancies between the modeled and fabricated structure. To address these discrepancies, we present differentiable mapping functions that incorporate both uniform conformal overlays and partially conformal interlayer dips into a standard inverse design paradigm, requiring no additional design parameters over planar structures. Using these mappings, we design (1) mode-selective GaAs grating reflectors with uniform conformal SiN passivation for high-aspect-ratio VCSELs, reaching differential modal reflectivities of 33.1% (single-etch) and 63.4% (dual-etch), and (2) a dual-layer silicon grating coupler whose upper layer dips up to 40 nm into the lower layer, reaching -0.75 dB coupling efficiency. Modeling conformal layering during optimization, rather than treating it as post-hoc fabrication error, permits direct exploitation of the conformal layering, yielding inherently fabricable and performant designs.

title: PromptPack: Training-Free Augmentation of Diffusion Editors for Intent-Aligned Spatial and Semantic Control
abstract: Many image-editing tasks require confining changes to intended spatial regions while exactly preserving user-designated source content. Instruction-driven editing pipelines often leave such user-intent underspecified, while inpainting editors condition generation on explicitly defined edit support but not on the spatial assignment of individual edit concepts. PromptPack addresses both limitations by equipping diffusion editors with two explicit 'Edit Guides': an edit-role partition that labels each pixel as 'Keep,' 'Permit,' or 'Modify' to specify where edits may occur, and a regional-prompt assignment that maps spatial regions to text prompts to specify which concepts apply where. These guides may be manually specified or, for source-object edits, automatically derived from a text-grounded SAM 3 mask. Without retraining, PromptPack injects independently embedded regional prompts into the editor's fixed-length text sequence and uses the Edit Guides to spatially mask attention, gate flow updates, and restore protected source pixels. We integrate PromptPack into FlowEdit FLUX, FlowEdit SD3, and FLUX Kontext and demonstrate improved requested-concept placement and protected-content preservation across all three integrations on PIE-Bench++. In a pairwise user study, PromptPack achieves an 87% preference rate over FlowEdit FLUX, establishing PromptPack as a practical, training-free interface for intent-aligned diffusion editing.

title: Topology of some smooth real Fano threefolds arising from blow-ups along rational curves
abstract: We describe the topological blow-up of a fibre of a Seifert fibration. We then apply this result to determine the diffeomorphism types of the real loci of smooth real Fano threefolds obtained by blowing up either $\mathbb{P}^3_{\mathbb{R}}$ or a smooth real quadric threefold along a smooth real rational curve. As an application, we also determine the topology of the real loci of the two real forms of the quintic del Pezzo threefold $V_5$, completing the topological classification of smooth real rational del Pezzo threefolds.

title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
abstract: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

title: The Conic Tverberg plus minus
abstract: We prove a Tverberg type theorems: Given a set $A\subset \mathbb{R}^d$ and an affine subspaces $L_1,...,L_m\subset \mathbb{R}^d$. In some conditions there is a partition $A_1, ..., A_m, B_1, ..., B_m$ of $A$ such that the sets $L_i\cup A_i\cup B_i$ for $i=1,...,m$ have common barycentre with negative masses in $B_i$ and positive masses in $A_i$. The case $B_1=...=B_m=L_1=...=L_m=\varnothing$ is Tverberg's classical theorem. The case $L_1=...=L_m=\varnothing$ gives a partial answer to the question of Barany-Soberon about the possible number of negative masses.

title: Magnon-Phonon-Polariton Optomechanics in a van der Waals Magnet
abstract: The layered anti-ferromagnet CrSBr hosts self-hybridized exciton-polaritons that couple parametrically to coherent magnons and phonons. In this work, we explore the tripartite optomechanical interaction between these quasiparticles in suspended CrSBr membranes supporting high-$Q$ breathing-type acoustic phonon modes. Using resonant pump-probe spectroscopy on the polariton state, we resolve the coupled dynamics in the $\simeq 20$ GHz range while sweeping the magnon mode across the phonon resonance with an external magnetic field. We observe an attractive magnon-phonon interaction of strength $V/2π= -43$ MHz, which primarily leads to phonon amplification. At the magnon-phonon resonance, we find predominantly unidirectional energy flow from magnons to phonons while the possible back-action is limited by kinetic losses of coherent magnons. Our study enables direct interfacing of collective magnetic excitations with sound and light in layered van der Waals materials, paving the way for quantum-coherent transduction in the GHz range with optical readout.

title: A local-local principle for quadratic forms over semiglobal fields
abstract: Given a quadratic form over a semiglobal field, the set of discrete valuations on the field for which the form is anisotropic over the completion is either empty, or it contains a valuation extending that of the base field with a transcendental residue field extension. In dimension at least $3$, this gives a refinement of the local-global principle for isotropy. In dimension $2$, the result yields a description of the set of elements that are locally squares everywhere.

title: Obstructions to Hadamard Deformations of Fourier Matrices
abstract: We study deformations of the Fourier spin model commuting square in the space of commuting squares, or equivalently deformations of the matrix $\sqrt nF_n$, where $F_n$ denotes the Fourier matrix, by complex Hadamard matrices. If $n$ is neither a prime power nor twice a prime, we show that there exist unit vectors in the enveloping tangent space that cannot be realized as directions of convergence of sequential deformations. Consequently, the derivative of any differentiable Hadamard family through $\sqrt nF_n$ has rank strictly smaller than the dimension of the enveloping tangent space at $\sqrt nF_n$ (i.e., the defect of $F_n$). This is particularly surprising because for every $n$ there exist enough one-parameter analytic families to provide a basis of directions in the enveloping tangent space. We obtain cubic obstructions when $n$ has at least three distinct prime divisors, quartic obstructions when it has exactly two and a repeated factor, and quintic obstructions when it is the product of two distinct odd primes. These results extend our order $30$ result from \cite{HN}.

title: Linearization of nonlocal elasticity based on nonlocal gradients via Γ-convergence
abstract: We provide a rigorous variational derivation of linear nonlocal elasticity from a general nonlinear elastic model based on nonlocal gradients. Under standard assumptions of nonlinear elasticity, we prove that the rescaled nonlinear energies Γ-converge, in the small-strain limit, to the corresponding quadratic linearized energy. The proof relies on a nonlocal geometric rigidity estimate and does not require any global upper growth condition on the stored-energy density.

title: A general theorem on the analytic spread and associated primes of divisorial filtrations
abstract: We prove that a classical theorem of McAdam about the analytic spread of an ideal in a Noetherian local ring $R$ is true for rational divisorial filtrations on an arbitrary Noetherian local ring. We deduce McAdam's original theorem from our result. This generalizes earlier work by the author, showing that this theorem is true for rational divisorial filtrations, with the restriction that $R$ is an equidimensional local ring which is essentially of finite type over an excellent local ring of dimension $\le 3$.

title: Quantitative unique continuation for semiclassical Witten-Schrödinger type operator with low regular coefficients
abstract: In this note we study eigenfunctions localization of the semiclassical selfadjoint Schrödinger operator with low regular coefficients on domains of $\mathbb{R}^2$. We show a unique continuation result on the local decay of the eigenfunction: local supremum on open sets can't vanish faster than global supremum on these same sets times an exponential term that decrease in the semiclassical limit $h\to 0$ as $\exp(-c\log(1/h)/h)$ in the worst case. We deduce from this result a control on the eigenfunctions of the semiclassical Schrödinger operator on a $W^{2,\infty}$ compact Riemann surface with Lipschitz positive metric and with Robin boundary condition. This last part leads us to study the Schrödinger operator with a Witten Laplacian.

title: Virtually solvable groups with balanced presentations
abstract: We show that if $G$ is a virtually solvable group with finite Hirsch length and such that $β_2(G;\mathbb{Q})\leqβ=β_1(G;\mathbb{Q})$ then $β\leq3$. This sharpens bounds on the Betti numbers of 3-manifolds which embed in $S^4$ with the fundamental groups of each complementary region virtually solvable and of finite Hirsch length.

title: Magnetic tuning of odd elastic instabilities in chiral active crystals
abstract: We investigate the dynamical properties of an odd active crystal whose elementary units follow an inertial dynamics and experience a Lorentz force induced by an external magnetic field. The continuous injection of energy associated with active chirality gives rise to odd elasticity, manifested through transverse forces between the crystal constituents. We show that the interplay between the magnetic field and these transverse forces produces a distinctive long-wavelength instability at vanishing wavevector, which is absent in both non-magnetic elastic crystals and passive crystals subjected to a magnetic field. Moreover, the magnetic field provides a means of tuning the collective oscillations of the crystal, enabling the emergence of exceptional points and tuning the dynamical instability induced by odd elasticity at finite wavevectors. Our analytical results yield explicit predictions for the displacement spectrum, static structure factor, and intermediate scattering function. These findings suggest that magnetic fields could provide a powerful tool for controlling collective phenomena in high-density systems of granular or colloidal spinners.

title: Simultaneous analysis of approximate leave-one-out cross-validation and mean-field inference II: General convex penalties
abstract: For smooth penalties and group Lasso, Part I (https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.02624) analyzed approximate leave-one-out (ALO) cross-validation by comparing its weights with the trace correction used in mean-field inference. For a $C^2$ penalty $R$, the matrix entering these corrections is $A=[\nabla^2R(\widehat b)+X^TDX]^{-1}$, where $\widehat b$ is the full-data estimator and $D$ is the diagonal matrix of fitted loss curvatures; for group Lasso, the penalty and loss curvatures are first restricted to the active support before taking the pseudoinverse. The obstacle to extending this argument to general convex penalties was the lack of an explicit formula for the matrix $A$ entering these corrections. For every finite-valued strongly convex penalty, we construct such a matrix from ordinary derivatives of the penalty response at the observed subgradient. Its projection--pseudoinverse formula separates the response space and penalty curvature, fixed by conditioning, from the explicit design dependence. This supplies the missing ingredient to extend the probabilistic argument of Part~I. The construction recovers the inverse Hessian for smooth penalties and the active-group inverse for group Lasso, including inactive boundary groups. In the proportional regime, for Gaussian designs with general positive-definite covariance and covariance-scaled strong convexity, we obtain unconditional bounds comparing both ALO and mean-field predictions with exact leave-one-out predictions in regression and single-index models. The expected average squared prediction error is $O(n^{-1})$, and the expected absolute criterion error is $O(n^{-1/2})$, under bounded, 1-Lipschitz loss scores and suitable test functions. The matrix and ALO weights use only observed data; the mean-field correction additionally uses the design covariance. The proofs are formalized in Lean~4.

title: Knowing Which, Not How Much: Language Models Order Party Positions They Cannot Place
abstract: Language models are increasingly asked where real actors stand: what a party's platform prioritises, what an institution has committed to. Such judgments are gradable, carrying both an order and a magnitude. Nearly every benchmark that tests them asks about one entity at a time, then reads that score as the model's knowledge of the domain. Order and magnitude, however, need not be acquired together. Text about social entities carries far more comparison than measurement, so a model may hold a dependable ordering with no anchored scale beneath it. We ask whether a model can place a documented social position on a scale or only order the actors it compares, and what that means for how such knowledge is measured. We test this on party positions in Japan and South Korea, where the Comparative Manifesto Project's coded data supplies a rare external answer key. Asked to order four parties, models beat the strongest fixed-answer baseline by more than a factor of two; asked to place one party on the same scale, they fall below it. The ordering survives inside those failed placements, and supplying the coded values lifts placement to near ceiling. Comparative and absolute questions about the same fact therefore measure different things here, and for party issue salience a benchmark built from one cannot speak for the other.

title: Adaptive Memory for Online Reinforcement Learning under Sparse Model Changes
abstract: We study the discounted reinforcement learning (RL) problem in a setting where the underlying environment changes between deployments. Each deployment provides $H$ observations from a fixed MDP. The reward function and transition kernel are fixed within each deployment. Across deployments, at most an $ε>0$ fraction of the reward and transition kernel entries may change. In this setting, learning each model to deploy from scratch may discard useful observations from past deployments, whereas pooling all past observations can bias the estimates of entries that have already changed. We then propose an algorithm that for each state and action pair, selects how much history to reuse to estimate the reward and probabilities of the next state. We start with observations from the current deployment and add earlier deployment observations one at a time, the most recent first. After each addition, we check whether a single average reward agrees with the estimates from all histories considered until that point. We apply the same check to the distribution of next states. For each estimate, we leverage the last history that passes these aforementioned checks. The optimal control policy is then computed on top of the fitted MDP. We characterize the average gap between the optimal return and the return of the learner's policies over a finite number of deployments. We demonstrate that when $0< |S|ε\leq 2$, with $|S|$ being the cardinality of the state space, our algorithm needs only the observations from the most recent $O(1/ε)$ deployments, and achieves a long-run average gap of at most $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{ε/H})$.

title: Cancellation-Free Constrained SquareCB for Safe Controller Selection
abstract: We study constrained contextual bandits, in which a learner chooses one of $K$ actions in each round to minimize loss while keeping the expected cost of its play below a budget. Existing reductions to online regression weight the cost by a Lagrange multiplier learned from past constraint residuals, so slack in some rounds can offset violations in others. We instead run SquareCB proposed in \citep{foster2020beyond} with a rectified weight on the cost: it is zero when the estimated cost is within the budget, and otherwise just large enough to bring it back to the budget. Under realizability and Slater's condition with margin $δ$, the algorithm attains regret $O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)}/δ)$ and cancellation-free violation $\sum_t(V_c^{p_t}-b)^+=O(\sqrt{KT\,\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}(T)})$, where $\mathrm{Reg}_{\mathsf{Sq}}$ is the error of the regression oracle. The same bounds hold when the budget must be met in every context, potentially adversarially chosen contexts. In controller selection for a safe-control-gym quadrotor and a BOPTEST building, the violation is 6 to 9 times lower than that of primal-dual and virtual-queue baselines, with a lower or comparable regret.

title: Stochastic differential delay equations with random delay driven by fractional Brownian motion
abstract: We prove an existence and uniqueness result for stochastic differential delay equations driven by a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H > \tfrac{1}{2}$, where the delay is a random process. Extending the pathwise Riemann--Stieltjes approach of Ferrante and Rovira \cite{FR2010}, we show that if the random delay $τ(\cdot,ω)$ has almost surely $γ$-Hölder continuous trajectories with $γδ> (1-H)/H$, where $δ\in(0,1]$ is the Hölder exponent of the gradient of the diffusion coefficient, then the equation has a unique solution with paths in $C^{1-α}(-r_0,T;R^d)\subset W_0^{α,\infty}(-r_0,T;R^d)$ for appropriate $α\in(1-H,\tfrac12)$. We also prove that the solution has moments of all orders when $γ>1/(2H)$ and the Hölder constant of the delay is bounded.

title: WM-Quant: Rollout-Aware Post-Training Quantization for JEPA-Style World Models
abstract: We present WM-Quant, to our knowledge, the first post-training quantization (PTQ) framework designed specifically for JEPA-style world models. Although world models typically feature relatively few parameters, action planning algorithms often require thousands of inferences, which can quickly become computationally expensive. PTQ is a natural way to reduce this cost. However, we show that in world models using autoregressive model predictive control (MPC) rollouts, quantization error can compound with each predictor step, resulting in action rankings from the quantized model becoming near-random. WM-Quant addresses this with three components that build on existing PTQ methods: early-encoder precision, control-path preservation, and rollout-aware scaling. Early-encoder precision protects accurate latent state and goal information to mitigate long-term error propagation. Control-path preservation allows the world model predictor to distinguish between fine-grained actions, significantly improving action rankings and execution. Rollout-aware scaling jointly calibrates encoder and per-step predictor activation ranges with respect to an entire rollout rather than a single prediction, reducing the cumulative rollout error. Across multiple world models, environments, and PTQ methods, WM-Quant substantially improves planning success at low bit-widths, approaching full-precision performance at W4A4.

title: Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

title: Rapid Protoplanetary Disk Evolution and Debris Disk Formation in Taurus-Auriga
abstract: We present a Submillimeter Array (SMA) 1.3mm (225GHz) continuum emission survey of Young Stellar Objects (YSOs) in the Taurus-Auriga star-forming region, comprising 69 class III and 5 class I/II YSOs with spectral types B9-M3, as part of a total sample of 149 class II and 82 class III YSOs. This represents a complete sample (100%) of class II and III YSOs with spectral types earlier than K3, and a near-complete sample (85%) for spectral types earlier than M2. The survey has a median $3σ$ sensitivity of 1.4mJy. We did not find any emission from circumstellar dust around class III YSOs, but present three detections that can be attributed to variable stellar activity, and one from an unresolved companion. We compile and model spectral energy distributions (SEDs) for the sample, and report 27 class III YSOs with excess thermal emission. We demonstrate that the class III YSOs in Taurus are typically older than their class II counterparts. We produce millimeter luminosity and dust disk mass distributions, and present evidence for a bifurcation between the class II and III populations, implying that ${\gtrsim}99.5\%$ of the dust mass is dispersed or transformed as YSOs transition from the class II to III stage. The combined infrared and millimeter properties demonstrate that warm (inner) and cold (outer) dust reservoirs evolve on comparable timescales: there is a rapid evolution across the radial extent of disks. We demonstrate that the survey properties are broadly consistent with a belt population that formed planetesimals from class II disks with an efficiency of a few tenths to a few tens of percent.

title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

title: Finitely generated groups with arbitrarily fast MIF growth
abstract: A group $G$ is mixed identity free, or MIF, if for each nontrivial $w(x)\in G\star (\mathbb{Z}=\langle x\rangle)$ there is some $g\in G$ such that $w(g)\neq 1$. Associated to MIF groups is a natural growth function that measures how far in the Cayley graph one witnesses such inequations. We adapt a recent construction of the author with Hyde to show that for each function $f:\mathbf{N}\to \mathbf{N}$ there is a finitely generated group $G$ whose MIF growth function grows faster than $f$. This answers a question first considered by Henry Bradford. As a consequence, we also provide the first examples of finitely generated MIF groups that are not selfless, answering a question of Bradford and Sisto.

title: Finite time blow-up for the Willmore flow of symmetric figure-eight tori
abstract: We show that the Willmore flow of symmetric figure-eight tori of revolution produces a finite time singularity, provided the initial energy is below $12π$. Our approach relies on the connection with elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane and a fine analysis of Palais--Smale sequences in the relevant energy regime.

title: A polynomial-time decoding algorithm up to half the square-root bound for quadratic residue and generalized quadratic residue codes
abstract: Binary quadratic residue (QR) codes, introduced by Prange in 1958, are cyclic codes of prime length $p\equiv\pm1\pmod 8$ and dimension $(p+1)/2$ whose minimum distance satisfies the square-root bound $d\ge\sqrt p$. They include the Hamming code $[7,4,3]$ and the Golay code $[23,12,7]$, and were generalized by van Lint and MacWilliams to generalized quadratic residue (GQR) codes of prime-power length $q$, for which the bound $d\ge\sqrt q$ still holds and is attained when $q$ is a square. In coding theory, one usually first finds a lower bound on the minimum distance of a family of codes, and then a polynomial-time algorithm decoding up to half of this bound, as for BCH, Reed--Muller or Gabidulin codes. Until now, GQR codes had resisted this approach: no such algorithm was known, apart from individual short lengths. We give a deterministic algorithm which, for every odd prime power $q\equiv\pm1\pmod 8$, corrects every error pattern of weight at most $\lfloor(\sqrt q-1)/2\rfloor$ in the binary GQR code of length $q$, in $O(q^{9/2})$ operations in $\F_q$. We start from a description of QR codes due to Helleseth, which we extend to GQR codes, and in which the syndrome gives the values of the quadratic character of the error-locator polynomial. We then recover this polynomial by adapting to GQR codes the tools that Kopparty developed for recovering polynomials from noisy character values, with the decoding of dual BCH codes as an application. Since the square-root bound is attained when $q$ is a square, this radius is the largest that can be guaranteed uniformly on the class of GQR codes.

title: Quantum Fisher information matrices for time-evolved bosonic Gaussian thermal states
abstract: Quantum Fisher information (QFI) is a fundamental quantum metrological quantity arising from the second order term in a Taylor expansion of a smooth divergence evaluated at nearby quantum states. The $α$-$z$ information matrix is a QFI measure arising from the $α$-$z$ Rényi relative entropy, and QFI measures corresponding to various underlying smooth divergences may be recovered from the $α$-$z$ information matrix, including the standard symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD) QFI. Bosonic Gaussian states are common probe states for quantum metrological tasks and admit a complete characterization in terms of their first and second moments. In this work, we consider the quantum metrological task of estimating parameters that characterize a Gaussian unitary time evolution of a faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal state. We establish a formula for the $α$-$z$ information matrix of faithful bosonic Gaussian thermal states that have undergone a Gaussian unitary time evolution. As an example, we calculate entries of the $α$-$z$ information matrix for a two-mode Gaussian thermal state that has undergone a beam splitting operation. For a parametrized family of time-evolved bosonic Gaussian states, we also derive a formula for the SLD operator, which is known to provide a measurement scheme that saturates the quantum Crámer-Rao bound and thus achieves the ultimate precision for single parameter estimation.

title: Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps
abstract: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x (1024 to 4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.

title: Call-Efficient ICD-10 Code Prediction via Supervised Candidate Generation and Selective LLM Invocation
abstract: Automatic assignment of ICD-10 codes from short clinical diagnosis text is a practical medical text classification and normalization task. The task is difficult because diagnosis phrases are short and noisy, the ICD-10 label space is hierarchical, and the class distribution is strongly imbalanced. This paper presents a call-efficient ICD-10 code prediction pipeline that combines transformer embeddings, tree-based supervised candidate generation, candidate-level reranking, and a gated LLM assistance.
