At Re = 20000 on a 20482 grid, the hybrid V/W-cycle reduces solution time by 14% compared with the W-cycle.

title: Data-Efficient Algal Bloom Segmentation in Freshwater Bodies Using a Three-Stage Transfer Learning Pipeline with Attention-Enhanced Decoding
abstract: Harmful algal blooms threaten water quality and public health, yet automated segmentation of bloom regions in freshwater imagery is limited by scarce pixel-level annotations. We present a transfer-learning pipeline that adapts a Swin Transformer U-Net with SCSE decoder attention from ImageNet-1K to water-body segmentation (RIWA, LaRS) and then to algal blooms, together with a model-assisted annotation protocol that expands the labelled algae corpus from 145 to 655 images. In a single-seed ablation on a 41-image validation split (checkpoint S2-A4 and its variants), corpus expansion is the dominant factor (+11 mIoU points); water-body pretraining helps only on the expanded corpus (+1.1 points over ImageNet initialization); SCSE attention adds 0.3 points; and a learnable positional encoding lowers mIoU by 0.6 points and is omitted. Adding 476 images, 188 of them algae-free, reduces false-positive area on non-water scenes from 22.6% to 4.9%. Against nine baselines on a 256-image test split, a separately trained checkpoint of the same architecture (S2-A13) reaches mIoU 0.919 and the highest algae IoU (0.902); a near-duplicate audit indicates train/test overlap in this split, so these scores are likely optimistic.

title: Two Counterexamples for e-means
abstract: e-means (Bessa et al., 2026) combines exponential averaging and cluster revival. We give two counterexamples to its published recipe with higher final loss than standard k-means (Lloyd, 1982) from identical initial centers. Mass-based revival can destroy a global optimum and make the ratio of expected losses unbounded even with k-means++ seeding.

title: Finite volume neural networks for singularly perturbed boundary value problems
abstract: We develop a singular-layer enhanced Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) methodology for solving singularly perturbed boundary value problems. The proposed framework combines flux-conserving finite volume residuals with analytically derived boundary layer correctors, enabling stable and efficient approximation of sharp boundary variations induced by small perturbation parameters. Numerical experiments over a broad range of small perturbation parameters ($10^{-4}$ to $10^{-12}$), demonstrate that the sl-FVNN yields uniformly accurate predicted solutions and significantly improved convergence behavior compared to conventional FVNN methods. Further comparisons with sl-PINNs from (Gie, Hong, Jung, Appl. Anal. 2024) show that our sl-FVNNs attain comparable accuracy for reaction--diffusion and Burgers equations, while achieving significantly improved convergence for convection-dominated nonlinear problems. These results highlight the effectiveness of incorporating asymptotic layer structures into finite volume based neural networks, offering a practical and scalable framework for multiscale PDE learning in stiff regimes.

title: Addressing Exogenous Variability in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) often fails under exogenous variability such as shifts in opponents or environment regimes that cannot be controlled by the team but alter the transition dynamics. We formalize this challenge as Exogenous Dec-POMDP (ED-POMDP), in which an episode-level exogenous regime, selected independently of the team, indexes the dynamics, and the global state is partitioned into components that are directly responsive to the current team action and components that are not directly action-responsive at the current step. This formulation exposes mediated influence: while team actions do not directly update the latter at the current step, they can shape their later evolution through induced changes in the former. Based on this, we propose LEICA, a CTDE-compatible algorithm that learns history-conditioned context representations for both components and shapes policy updates using agent-wise, influence-weighted counterfactual intrinsic rewards. Across SMAX benchmarks with opponent strategy shifts, LEICA consistently improves both training performance and generalization to unseen opponents' strategies over existing baselines, supporting the usefulness of influence-weighted shaping under exogenous train-test regime shifts.

title: Analog-Memory-Based Waveform Generation for Qubit Control
abstract: We propose an analog-memory-based arbitrary waveform generator for cryogenic qubit control that separates low-speed waveform programming from high-speed waveform generation. Waveform samples are stored as capacitor voltages and sequentially accessed through buffered switching networks, enabling repeated, non-destructive readout without high-speed digital-to-analog conversion. A cryogenic prototype demonstrated Gaussian-shaped waveform generation at 14 K with a sampling rate of 40 Msps using a programming rate of 50 ksps. No measurable voltage decay was observed over 2 s at cryogenic temperatures. A complementary room-temperature prototype achieved 160 Msps. The architecture offers a potential route toward lower-power cryogenic waveform generation.

title: MedGuardBench: A Patient-Oriented Benchmark for Personalized Guardrail Development
abstract: Safety is personal: the same action can be safe for one person but unsafe for another. Yet current guardrails judge content without considering who is affected. Using medication safety, we introduce \textit{patient-conditioned medication guarding}, which predicts a safety verdict and 17 risk categories from a patient profile and prescription. We release \textbf{MedGuardBench}, a drug-disjoint benchmark of 5{,}001 scenarios across 87 medications. We find that standard guardrails rely on surface cues, such as wording and profile presence, rather than patient facts. To address this, we develop \textit{personalized reasoning guardrails} with three components. \textbf{Personalized Reasoning Distillation} links risks to relevant patient fields. \textbf{Context Unrolling (CU)} makes models check each field themselves, reducing false alarms on most backbones; controls show that providing the check does not yield the same benefit. A \textbf{rule-based reward (guided GRPO)} improves unsafe recall and complex-risk detection, including allergies and adverse reactions, on some backbones, but increases false alarms on others. Our models outperform base models and matched no-profile controls in accuracy, while reducing false alarms relative to no-profile controls. Profile removal and swapping confirm that gains come from patient information, not fine-tuning alone.

title: Why do continual physical learners need sleep?
abstract: Sleep is widespread across the animal kingdom, including in organisms without a centralized nervous system. Does learning create a need for sleep, even without biology? To explore this question, we study a disordered spring network trained to perform a sequence of mechanical allosteric tasks through local changes in bond stiffness. We find that continual learning progressively reduces the network's ability to acquire new tasks as individual bonds become increasingly specialized. We identify an exact algebraic relationship between the polarization of bond dominance and the network's remaining learning capacity, providing a quantitative measure of this loss of adaptability. We then demonstrate that random internal perturbations allow individual bonds to estimate their mechanical dominance and locally adjust their stiffnesses to restore learning capacity. However, the forces associated with active learning bias these local measurements and interfere with restoration. Separating learning and repair into wake-like and sleep-like phases removes this interference and improves continual-learning performance. Our results suggest that the need for offline restorative phases can emerge from the mechanics of physical learning, even in systems without biological components.

title: Gradient estimates and monotonicity formulae for the $p$-filtration equation on Riemannian manifolds
abstract: We derive Li--Yau type estimates on closed Riemannian manifolds and local Hamilton-type gradient estimates on complete manifolds for the $p$-filtration equation $u_t=Δ_pF(u)$. Under nonnegative Ricci curvature and a structural condition on $F$, we establish a $\mathcal W$-entropy formula, entropy-power concavity and local entropy rigidity. We also prove a parabolic frequency monotonicity formula without curvature assumptions. The results include homogeneous doubly nonlinear diffusion and extend to nonhomogeneous power sums and the arctangent law.

title: Singular layer neural networks for the Navier-Stokes equations at small viscosity
abstract: We develop neural network methods for the two-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations at a small viscosity $\varepsilon > 0$, whose accuracy is uniform in $\varepsilon$ and whose residual is evaluated on a grid that does not resolve the vorticity boundary layer. In the vorticity-stream function formulation with the slip boundary conditions, a vorticity layer of width $\sqrt{\varepsilon}$ forms along the walls. The trial function of the singular layer Physics-Informed Neural Network (sl-PINN) contains the corrector of the asymptotic analysis, together with the law that fixes its amplitude at the wall. The amplitude is tied to the wall trace of the network itself, so that the method requires no a priori knowledge of the limit solution. The sl-PINN keeps the error uniform in $\varepsilon$ over six decades, for the Stokes and the Navier-Stokes equations alike, although in the latter the wall trace travels with the flow and is not known in advance. An enrichment that uses the thin scale but leaves the profile and the amplitude of the layer free deteriorates as $\varepsilon\to0$. Since the corrector carries the layer analytically, the Laplacian in the residual can be discretized by a finite volume flux difference on a coarse grid. The resulting singular layer Finite Volume Neural Network (sl-FVNN) attains the same uniform accuracy as the sl-PINN, to within the scatter of the random seed, at about half the cost of a training step. The combination of the asymptotic corrector with the coarse-grid finite volume discretization is the main result of this article.

title: Apparent contact angle equation for a dielectric droplet on a conductive hydrophilic surface in an electric field
abstract: A dielectric droplet resting on a conductive substrate elongates when a voltage is applied across the surrounding gap without touching the upper electrode. We construct a closed form theory of the equilibrium shapes by approximating the interface as a truncated spheroid with a single shape parameter and obtain the dimensionless electrostatic prefactor that corrects the free-space depolarization, based on the mirror symmetry across the substrate. Minimizing the resulting free energy along voltage ramps reproduces the boundary-element-method (BEM) equilibria, both the droplet height and the contact-line radius, with and without gravity, at negligible computational cost. An explicit apparent contact angle equation is found that collapses all the numerical calculation data. The configuration shows a behavior of fixed contact angle and an increasing apparent angle with the applied voltage, which is completely different from that of the Young--Lippmann equation.

title: Electrostatic screening and nitrogen-vacancy charge states in boron-doped/nitrogen-doped diamond junctions
abstract: Boron-doped diamond (BDD) enables the integration of electrical functionality with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers, but the influence of junction electrostatics on NV charge-state stability remains unclear. In this study, we investigate the equilibrium electrostatics of BDD/nitrogen-doped diamond junctions using self-consistent Poisson-Fermi calculations. The results reveal two distinct electrostatic length scales in the nitrogen-doped substrate: a near-interface region of ionized donors that produces dominant band bending and determines the NV$^{0/-}$ charge-state boundary, and a much longer screening tail associated with weak donor ionization in the neutral bulk. The resulting NV$^-$ depletion depth depends strongly on the nitrogen concentration but exhibits a more moderate dependence on boron doping. At $N_B = 10^{21}$ cm$^{-3}$, varying the interface grading scale $w$ from 0.5 to 8 nm changes the depletion depth by approximately 22 nm, whereas variations in the modeled bulk BDD charge response produce a shift of only 1.27 nm. These results indicate that, under the conditions studied, the nitrogen donor concentration and local interface structure primarily govern the equilibrium NV charge-state profile, rather than the bulk electronic response of BDD alone.

title: Can You Undo It? Reversibility Classes for AI Agent Actions
abstract: Tool-using AI agents change files, databases, access rights and public information, yet permission to call a tool does not establish whether a mistake can be undone. We present Reversibility Classes, a declared five-level vocabulary with argument-sensitive rules, conservative defaults and an explicit prior-state capture contract. The pinned implementation and evidence-linked registry cover 536 tools across 20 MCP servers. All 738 rule-case checks conform to declared expectations, while native annotation mapping differs from draft registry labels for 118 of 481 comparable tools. One AI-assisted reviewer approves 148 ratings, 75 matching the registry; this is not independent agreement. On 2,158 recorded runs, the implemented session guard gates the associated action in all 29 attributable attack-positive runs, compared with 18 for a read/write proxy, while adding nine approval points across 1,209 benign runs. Controlled file, Git, SQLite and three-browser experiments show that recovery depends on captured state, later changes, editor storage and recovery route, and expose a Git merge-state exception. The evidence supports making recovery assumptions explicit and testable. It does not establish registry-wide accuracy, reduced production harm or general recovery reliability.

title: Segmentation-Guided Direct Capacity Estimation of Rooftop Photovoltaics from Aerial Imagery
abstract: Distribution planners need installation-level inventories of rooftop photovoltaic (PV) capacity, but interconnection records may be incomplete or spatially aggregated. Conventional image-based estimators segment PV arrays, convert the mask to physical area, and multiply by an estimated power density, coupling capacity prediction to mask-derived area. We propose Direct Head, a segmentation-guided architecture that retains U-Net segmentation and soft-mask pooling while directly regressing nonnegative capacity from PV-region features and area descriptors. We evaluate three independent runs on 7,590 French rooftop installations under the original split and a department-based holdout. Relative to a parameter-matched area-density neural model, Direct Head reduces mean absolute error by 8.7% and 12.5%, and symmetric mean absolute percentage error by 14.0% and 20.7%, respectively. Comparisons with conventional estimators, controlled architecture variants, auxiliary-loss ablations, and representative cases show that segmentation provides useful spatial evidence without requiring capacity to be determined by an area-density product.

title: ReLAP: Latent Action Pretraining through Recurrent Video Prediction in JEPA Space
abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.

title: Residual-driven lattice Boltzmann equation. Part I: framework and nonlinear solution methods
abstract: We developed a residual-driven framework of the lattice Boltzmann equation (LBE) to integrate general nonlinear iterative methods. The nonlinear residual is constructed directly from the complete LBE collision-streaming update, allowing general nonlinear solvers to be integrated without modifying the original LBE algorithmic structure, i.e., the kernel consisting of collision-streaming, boundary conditions, and various forcing and interaction effects. Sophisticated techniques, such as weighted fixed-point iteration, full approximation scheme (FAS) multigrid, and Jacobian-free Newton-Krylov methods are integrated into the LBE via this framework, and preconditioned LBE is further incorporated as a nonlinear smoother to demonstrate solver composability. Numerical tests validate that FAS and Newton methods do converge to the same discrete steady fixed-point obtained with the primitive LBE iteration. For the 2D lid-driven cavity flow, the FAS scheme reduces the measured solution time by a factor of approximately 44 at Re = 1000 and more than 224 at Re = 5000. Accurate results are also obtained for the steady flows past a cylinder at Re = 20 and the NACA0012 airfoil at Re = 1000. The low Mach-number tests for the flow past a NACA0012 airfoil further show that both the FAS scheme and preconditioning can not only substantially reduce the work required to reach steady solutions, but also mitigate the zero Mach-number crisis.

title: SIMQ: A Single Graph-based Index for Multi-Vector Query
abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness by representing documents as sets of token-level vectors and scoring via MaxSim, but their high computational cost limits scalability to large corpora. Existing approximate methods face fundamental bottlenecks: centroid interaction matrix approaches require computing a full matrix at every query and rely on GPU-accelerated clustering, while data-oblivious compression methods yield unstable recall that requires repeated compensation. We propose SIMQ (Single graph Index for Multi-vector Query), a framework that bridges single-vector graph indices and multi-vector retrieval through data-aware sampling-based clustering and per-token graph navigation, simultaneously bypassing all aforementioned bottlenecks. SIMQ organizes all token vectors into fine-grained clusters via data-aware sampling, builds a single graph index over cluster centroids independently of PLAID's residual representation, and approximates the MaxSim score through per-token graph search without materializing any interaction matrix or relying on GPU acceleration. We provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a manifold assumption and successful cell retrieval, data-aware partitioning has a smaller expected approximation error than a data-oblivious partition. Building on this foundation, SIMQ+ further introduces count-based scoring and a dynamic candidate set to improve robustness across varying query conditions. Experiments on five benchmarks compare recall, throughput, and construction time against several baselines, primarily on CPU; large-scale PLAID k-means centroids are built on a separate GPU machine. SIMQ has been integrated into VSAG, an Ant Group's open-source vector search library.

title: CRA: Continuous Risk Assessment for Safety-critical Visual Navigation
abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods often rely on predefined constraints that separate states into safe and unsafe regions. While recent studies have extended geometric safety toward semantic safety, real-world safety is rarely purely binary. The risk associated with an object or human can vary continuously with its physical properties, like motion, and interaction context; for example, a person carrying a heavy object or a hot object moving at high speed may require a different safety response from an ordinary static obstacle. In this paper, we propose a vision-based continuous risk assessment framework for safety-critical visual navigation. Our method uses RGB and LiDAR observations to estimate four risk factors (kinetic, potential, contact-severity, and thermal) and combines them into a continuous risk score for each assessed object or person. These estimates are integrated into a Poisson safety function with a Laplace guidance field as a safety filter, enabling online monitoring and intervention in open-world robot navigation. We demonstrate the proposed method in a simulated restaurant scene.

title: Facet-offset Polytope Expansion for Dynamic Operating Envelopes of Aggregated Distribution Grid Resources
abstract: This paper presented a facet-offset polytope expansion framework with sensitivity-informed directions (FOPE-sen) for constructing DOEs in three-phase unbalanced distribution systems. The facet directions are selected from DGR coordinate directions and sensitivity-informed network-critical directions, while the facet locations are determined through a two-step bisection procedure guided by a power-flow feasibility oracle. Numerical results demonstrate that FOPE-sen captures at least 106% more flexibility per dimension than box-shaped and random-direction expansion methods. Moreover, FOPE-sen constructs DOEs comparable to or larger than those of VBPE while using fewer than 1/40 as many facets in dimensions greater than four. Future work will focus on stronger safety verification for nonconvex AC feasible regions, scalability in high-dimensional spaces, and extensions to multi-aggregator allocation and market-participation applications.

title: Enumerating orbits of finite classical groups on their Lie algebras
abstract: We enumerate the orbits of a finite classical group in the adjoint action on its Lie algebra, giving exact generating functions and very good upper bounds. We treat the general linear, unitary, symplectic and orthogonal groups, in both odd and even characteristic. In even characteristic, we get very nice formulas for the number of orbits on nilpotent classes both in the finite and algebraically closed case. We discuss the connection with commuting varieties.

title: BernBRS: Certified Backward Reachability for Deep Bernstein Neural Networks
abstract: Ensuring the safety of complex neural network systems requires mathematically rigorous verification. While backward reachability analysis is a critical tool for identifying safe initial states, computing tight, formal bounds remains notoriously difficult to scale. Recent advancements have demonstrated that DeepBern-Nets neural networks utilizing Bernstein polynomial activation functions possess advantageous mathematical properties that enable exceptionally fast and tight forward reachability analysis. Building upon this efficiency, this paper introduces BernBRS, a highly accurate and scalable framework for the backward reachability analysis of DeepBern-Nets. BernBRS simultaneously computes certified inner and outer approximations of the Backward Reachable Set (BRS). Rather than relying on single convex bounding, our method intelligently refines a cover of the input space by analyzing activation patterns, splitting the input domain precisely where an exact decomposition of the relaxation gap predicts the most significant reduction in error. This targeted refinement enables high levels of scalability to highly complex and massive architectures that remain intractable for existing certified methods. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on high-dimensional models, including a linearized closed-loop approximation of the Half-Cheetah controller and a distilled Bernstein student of a Transformer block and we empirically study how these model-level guarantees relate to the original Half-Cheetah and TinyBERT classifier, respectively.

title: When Lower Harm Misleads: Auditing Concept Corrections
abstract: An expert who corrects a concept prediction, such as a BI-RADS descriptor in breast ultrasound, expects the diagnosis to improve. Objectives that reduce the harm of such corrections are judged by harm and accuracy, yet harm also falls when a model responds less to every correction or starts from a worse uncorrected prediction, the reference for harm. We propose a correction audit, a reproducible evaluation protocol that separates these explanations: it splits each correction into harm and useful gain on identical events, separates the starting prediction from the correction response, and compares objectives with amplitude baselines matched in source harm. On three breast-ultrasound sources, worst-case correction training, evaluated from the mean-case model's start, lowers harm but gives up more useful gain in all 21 source comparisons pooled over six seeds, raising the corrected negative log-likelihood (NLL); from the same start, selecting between the objectives by harm picks the less helpful model on all three sources. On CUB, a monotonic harm penalty at its reported weight lowers path-level harm in all 80 concept sets while raising the NLL in all 80, almost entirely before any correction. At a fixed start, rescaling both responses to the same source harm reproduces the penalty's mean harm, useful gain and NLL on single-concept corrections within a prespecified margin of 0.0005 nat, although the two responses point in different directions. Lower harm therefore signals better corrections only when it is read together with useful gain, absolute risk and the start it is measured from.

title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

title: HyCoInfer: Cloud-Edge Collaborative Inference for Large Language Models on Heterogeneous GPU-FPGA Architectures
abstract: Large language model (LLM) serving relies predominantly on cloud GPUs, yet autoregressive decoding is memory-bound and often leaves their arithmetic units underutilized. Edge FPGAs offer attractive decoding efficiency, but are ill suited to sustaining a high-concurrency serving workload alone. This paper presents HyCoInfer, a heterogeneous cloud-edge serving system that assigns prefill to cloud GPUs and distributes decoding across cloud GPUs and edge FPGAs. The design addresses three barriers to practical offloading: capacity balancing across heterogeneous accelerators, the large KV cache crossing a constrained wide-area link, and the latency added by heterogeneous execution. HyCoInfer incorporates FPGA decode capacity into GPU prefill/decode role partitioning and places requests according to queue load, prompt length, and network state. It further combines layer-wise pipelined transfer, decoder-side precomputation, and bandwidth-adaptive KV cache compression based on residual vector quantization. We implement HyCoInfer using two NVIDIA V100 GPUs and an AMD Xilinx Alveo U280 and evaluate it over 100-1000 Mbps links. At 500 Mbps, HyCoInfer delivers up to 4.11 times the request goodput of cloud-only vLLM and reduces mean end-to-end latency by up to 61.1%. Across different network conditions and workloads, the system improves overall serving capacity, with the largest gains on communication-intensive tasks, and reduces per-request energy.

title: Commutator-guided repair and classical-accessibility boundaries for shallow quantum circuits
abstract: Trainability does not guarantee low-energy arrival: a shallow quantum circuit can be optimizable yet fail, under fixed depth and evaluation budgets, to reach Hamiltonian-selected states. We introduce a commutator-guided repair for this operational failure mode. Low-order host--Hamiltonian commutators and fixed same-support companion axes define a restricted pool of local Pauli rotations, from which a compact completion layer is selected before full reoptimization. Across 189 paired six-qubit trials, unrepaired circuits achieve 0/189 strict successes, a non-deployable per-trial control envelope achieves 109/189, and two predeclared selectors achieve 133/189 and 127/189. The repair loses to matched controls for transverse-field Ising, is weak for pure-ZZ MaxCut, and remains size-limited for weighted MIS. Under fixed-depth geometric locality, repaired losses and gradients are classically computable, while corresponding ground-state targets admit low-bond-dimension tensor-network approximations through the tested sizes. The method reveals a trainability--arrival--classical-accessibility tradeoff rather than quantum advantage.

title: Second Harmonic Flexoelectricity
abstract: Flexoelectricity (polarization induced by strain gradients) is assumed to be insensitive to space inversion in all materials: flexoelectric polarization should not depend on whether a crystal is bent upwards or downwards. In this work, we show that this assumption is wrong for ferroelectrics of all thickness and at all curvatures, owing to an intrinsic quadratic contribution that persists down to strain gradients of 1 m-1 or less, which is millions of times smaller than conventional expectations for nonlinear flexoelectricity. As a consequence, ferroelectric crystals can generate second-harmonic voltage at twice the oscillation frequency of the bending.

title: Toroidal Obstructions with No K_5 Minor
abstract: Finding the complete set of forbidden minors for the torus remains an open problem. We determine the complete list of toroidal minor obstructions with no $K_5$ minor and prove that there are exactly $74$, each with between $10$ and $14$ vertices. Combined with the known classification of toroidal obstructions with no $K_{3,3}$ minor, this determines every toroidal obstruction that excludes one of the forbidden minors for planarity. The proof uses three-vertex cuts to show that, apart from $K_{3,7}$, every three-connected obstruction in this class has two distinct independent triples, each the common neighborhood of at least two degree-three vertices. The classification proceeds by considering the possible intersections of these triples and reduces each case by planarity tests and enumeration of the possible graph forms. From the $74$ minor obstructions we also obtain a complete list of $381$ topological obstructions for the torus with no $K_5$ minor.

title: On the Morse index of some Riemannian homogeneous fibrations
abstract: In this paper, we use the technique developed by the first named author in arXiv:2610.07815 to compute the Morse-index of some Riemannian homogeneous fibrations. For the quaternionic (resp. octonionic) Hopf fibration, we compute the index and nullity, where the metric on the $\mathbb{S}^7$ (resp. $\mathbb{S}^{15}$) is the quaternionic (resp. octonionic) Hopf--Berger metric. In particular, for the round metric on the domain, the Morse-index is $45$ (resp. $153$). We also give a spectral formula for the Aloff--Wallach projections. In particular, we obtain that the Konishi $\mathbb{R} P^3$-fibration $N_{1,1}\to\mathbb{C} P^2$ is stable throughout the two-parameter metric family, while the unit tangent sphere bundle $T^1(\mathbb{C} P^2)\to \mathbb{C} P^2$ is stable under some conditions on the metric. We also compute the index and nullity of the Clifford hypersurface in the fiber-squashing range of the quaternionic Berger family. Finally, for the identity map on the quaternionic Hopf--Berger spheres, we determine its Morse--index by an explicit sequence of transition parameters.

title: Non-monotonic Age-metallicity Relations Across the Galactic Disk Revealed by APOGEE Red Clump Stars
abstract: Using APOGEE red clump stars and open clusters with precise ages, we investigate the age--metallicity relation (AMR) across the Galactic disk as a function of Galactocentric radius $R$ and vertical height $|Z|$. For stars older than $\sim$6--8 Gyr, the AMR shows little dependence on either $R$ or $|Z|$ within the uncertainties, suggesting rapid and well-mixed chemical evolution in the early disk. In contrast, younger populations exhibit a clear negative radial metallicity gradient, with the inner disk being more metal-rich than the outer disk, consistent with inside-out disk growth since $\sim$6--8 Gyr ago. Most importantly, at fixed location, the AMR for ages $\lesssim6$--8 Gyr is non-monotonic: [Fe/H] decreases toward younger ages, reaches a minimum at intermediate ages, and then rises again. Beyond $R\sim11$\,kpc, the relation becomes even more complex, exhibiting an additional reversal and a distinct metallicity peak at an age of $\sim2$\,Gyr. Such complex behavior cannot be explained by continuous local enrichment alone, but instead points to the combined effects of a multi-phase gas-accretion history and radial migration. Episodes of metal-poor gas inflow can dilute the interstellar medium and reset its chemical evolution, while subsequent enrichment raises the metallicity again; radial migration further reshapes the observed AMR by mixing stellar populations formed at different radii and metallicities. A toy model incorporating inside-out growth, two gas-inflow episodes, and radial migration qualitatively reproduces the observed trends, highlighting the combined roles of episodic gas accretion and radial migration in shaping the chemical evolution of the Galactic disk.

title: Search for the low-mass isotropic signature of QCD instantons in $pp$ collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV using the ATLAS detector
abstract: This Letter presents the first search for QCD instanton-induced events at the LHC. Instantons are semi-classical solutions of the Yang-Mills equations of QCD and correspond to non-perturbative tunneling between topologically distinct vacuum sectors. The search is performed in 1.6 $\text{nb}^{-1}$ of very low instantaneous luminosity proton-proton collision data collected by the ATLAS detector at 13 TeV. Angular variables based on reconstructed charged-particle tracks are used to discriminate the expected rest-frame isotropy of low-mass instanton events from the minimum-bias background. The minimum-bias event background is predicted using a data-driven technique and reweighted Monte Carlo models. A profile-likelihood fit is performed in a two-dimensional classifier variable to extract a possible signal contribution, yielding an excess of low-mass isotropic events with an observed significance of $3.5σ$.

title: Projected Route Cues for Bouldering: Effects of Circular, Linear, and Combined Highlighting on Route Observation and Climbing
abstract: Before attempting a bouldering problem, climbers inspect the route to find its holds and plan their moves, which novices find difficult on walls where many routes overlap. We built a projector-camera system that projects route cues onto the wall and compared three cues: circles on the route holds, limb-colored lines connecting the holds, and both combined. Ninety-six participants, 61 of them first-time climbers, each climbed four routes, one per cue and one without projection, in a Latin-square order. In mixed-effects models, all three cues shortened the time before the first attempt; with circles, its geometric mean fell from 83 s to 39 s. Circles also increased the number of moves made within each trial. Lines led to more use of off-route holds than circles, mainly on routes where such holds lay under the projected lines. Participants preferred the combined cue, although no behavioral advantage of it over circles was detected.

title: When AUC Meets Generative Reconstruction: A Unified Principle for Balanced Visual Representation Learning
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) require visual encoders that extract fine-grained visual features while constructing semantically disentangled and discriminative representations. Conventional methodologies encounter a fundamental trade-off: contrastive learning enhances inter-class discrimination by suppressing intra-class variability, whereas generative reconstruction emphasizes perceptual fidelity but lacks explicit comparative supervision. The naive aggregation of these objectives via composite loss functions often induces optimization conflicts and instability due to gradient interference within the shared latent space. To resolve this, we introduce a unified representation-learning paradigm that reformulates generative reconstruction as a discriminative ranking problem within the generative output manifold. Our approach maintains perceptual reconstruction as a supervisory signal and integrates a ranking-based discriminative constraint by systematically ordering matched and mismatched reconstruction outputs. This formulation embeds discriminative information seamlessly into the generative process, alleviating the risk of loss competition. Specifically, we propose AUC Generative Reconstruction (AUCGR), which optimizes the area under the ROC curve (AUC) by ensuring higher scores for matched pairs than for mismatched pairs, and Partial AUC Generative Reconstruction (pAUCGR), which addresses supervision bias by focusing on mismatched comparisons within reliable feature subspaces. The proposed objectives are designed to be plug-and-play, requiring no architectural modifications to existing generative reconstruction frameworks. Theoretical analysis establishes rigorous connections to AUC/pAUC optimization and provides generalization guarantees. Extensive experiments validate that our method advances both discriminative accuracy and fine-grained perceptual representation.

title: CueSplat: Learning to Schedule Sparse Deformation for Dynamic Gaussian Splatting on Edge Devices
abstract: Deformation-based 4D Gaussian splatting (4DGS) enables dynamic scene rendering. However, evaluating deformation networks for all Gaussians at every frame is compute-intensive on edge devices. We find that Gaussian trajectories are often locally predictable, yet prediction reliability varies across Gaussians and time. Thus, we propose CueSplat, a post-training framework that exploits local temporal regularity while keeping the pretrained backbone frozen and retaining its Gaussian set. Specifically, CueSplat predicts Gaussian attributes from recent history and uses a lightweight learned router to select exact deformation updates within a scene-specific budget calibrated offline. Selection accounts for prediction reliability and rendering contribution. Selected indices are reused across nearby frames to reduce routing overhead, while selected Gaussians still receive exact updates each frame. To control accumulated prediction error, we use drift signals to schedule three consecutive full-deformation frames that rebuild the prediction history. Evaluated across four mainstream 4DGS algorithms, CueSplat achieves up to $6.74\times$ and $8.15\times$ speedups on Jetson AGX Orin and Orin NX, respectively, with a negligible quality drop (at most $0.16$ dB in dataset-average PSNR).

title: COSI: A Framework for Robustly Valid Inference
abstract: We introduce COSI (COnfidence from Scale Invariance), a framework for constructing confidence sets for statistical functionals. COSI builds on the HulC (Hull-based Confidence), which uses median unbiasedness to construct confidence sets from batch estimates. COSI uses scale-invariance properties shared by many common estimators. We divide the data into batches, compute an estimate in each batch, and retain each candidate parameter value for which the batch estimates pass a test of scale invariance. The resulting confidence sets are asymptotically valid under weaker assumptions than classical Wald and bootstrap procedures require, and their coverage can be closer to the nominal level in small samples. Applications include robust inference for the mean, regression coefficients in misspecified linear models, tensor norms, and Fréchet means.

title: A counterexample to the one-supremum conjecture and sharp logarithmic weighted bounds for Calderón--Zygmund operators
abstract: We give a negative answer to the one-supremum conjecture of Hytönen and Lacey~\cite[Remark~1.3]{HL}, in the strong-type form stated by Lerner and Moen~\cite[Conjecture~1.3, formula~(9)]{LM}. The conjecture asks whether the mixed $A_p$--$A_\infty$ characteristics $K_p(w)$ and $K_{p'}(σ)$, with both factors evaluated on the same cube, control Calderón--Zygmund operators without a logarithmic loss. For every $1<p<\infty$, we construct explicit weights for which $K_p(w)+K_{p'}(σ)\eqsim_p m$, but one fixed Hilbert transform has weighted norm at least $m(1+\log m)^{γ_p}$, where $γ_p=\max\{1/p,1/p'\}$. Thus the proposed bound fails even for a fixed singular integral. The counterexample also extends to a fixed Riesz transform in each dimension $n\ge2$. We further establish a logarithmically corrected bound for Calderón--Zygmund operators, with powers $1/p'$ and $1/p$ on the respective one-supremum terms. Together, the lower and upper bounds identify $γ_p$ as the optimal common logarithmic exponent and give the sharp worst-case growth $(1+\log A)^{γ_p}$ under the constraint $[w]_{A_p}\le A$. The results show why information from any one cube cannot fully capture the accumulation of a singular integral across many scales.

title: Every Measurement, Every Direction, All at Once: Multimodal Flow Matching for Molecules and Spectra
abstract: Generative modeling in science is often data-limited, where experiments are expensive. However, each experiment may yield several coupled measurements of the same physical entity. Standard generative models often train only on a single direction, discarding supervision from the rest. We argue that each experiment contains more training signal than this asymmetry allows the model to exploit: random masking enables measurements to serve as either conditioning inputs or prediction targets, yielding multiple supervised denoising tasks from a single experiment. We investigate this premise with MOSAIC, a multimodal flow matching transformer over molecular 3D structure and UV, IR, and Raman spectra. MOSAIC is a single model that is capable of any-to-any generation: generating any subset of modalities from any disjoint subset of the others. On QM9S, MOSAIC achieves 88.8% molecular graph recovery, outperforming the strongest spectra-to-structure baseline by 23.2% in structure generation, while simultaneously outperforming a structure-to-spectra specialist model in spectral generation. Ablations show that the any-to-any objective improves structure generation over structure-only training across model sizes. Furthermore, MOSAIC supports arbitrary subsets of available measurements and enables molecular identification by matching generated spectra to experimental references.

title: Differentiable High-Order Mesh $r$-Adaptivity
abstract: High-order mesh r-adaptivity typically entails minimizing a nonlinear functional using its gradients and, for Newton-based methods, its Hessian. These derivatives can be expensive to derive, must be updated with any changes to the functional, and errors in the derivatives directly impact the convergence of r-adaptivity. Additionally, derivatives of the r-adaptivity operator are required for consistent sensitivity analysis for inverse problems. This work develops a framework for differentiable r-adaptivity based on the Target-Matrix Optimization Paradigm. Given a pointwise functional defining the local mesh-adaptation objective, the proposed framework uses $\partial$FEM to automatically generate pointwise first- and second-order derivatives. These local derivatives are then assembled into a global gradient vector and a Hessian operator through the finite element operator decomposition. The derivative kernels support portable CPU and GPU execution, with partial assembly and tensor sum factorization enabling matrix-free application of the Hessian operator. The framework also provides consistent sensitivities of the r-adaptivity operator through automatically generated mixed derivatives and implicit differentiation of the mesh stationarity equations. Numerical experiments show GPU solve times comparable to those of hand-derived TMOP implementations on a benchmark problem, improvement in r-adaptivity convergence due to accurate computation of the derivatives, and demonstrate the use of mesh sensitivities for material-interface identification in an inverse heat-conduction problem.

title: Semantic Communication via Analog RF Computing: When the Radio Computes the Meaning
abstract: Semantic communication (SC) systems transmit continuous latent representations of meaning, but computing the semantic encoder at resource-constrained edge devices incurs substantial energy and memory costs. To address this challenge, we propose an end-to-end SC framework that executes the semantic encoder in the client's RF receiver front end using analog RF computing. A base station (BS) broadcasts encoder weights as RF waveforms, while each edge device reuses its receiver's passive mixer to compute semantic latents at ultra-low energy. These latents are transmitted over the uplink for network-side task inference. We show that analog computing noise across encoder layers and channel noise affecting transmitted latents admit a unified mathematical model. We define a task-posterior semantic distortion metric and derive its second-order decomposition into per-client, per-stage semantic sensitivities. Using this decomposition, we obtain a closed-form semantic-aware water-filling allocation of the total client energy budget across clients, encoder layers, and uplinks, assigning tighter accuracy targets to semantically sensitive stages. This allocation induces a broadcast beamforming problem that accounts for client-specific, per-layer accuracy requirements. We further refine the allocation through stochastic optimization and jointly design it with multi-task noise-aware training of the shared semantic model. MNIST simulations show that, at matched total client energy, the proposed allocation reduces network semantic distortion by 9.2\%-19.2\% compared with uniform precision and 5.1\%-13.1\% compared with client-blind allocation. Noise-aware co-design yields a further 46\% reduction.

title: An Omnidirectional WECT: Closed-Form Computation of the Directionally Integrated Weighted Euler Characteristic Transform
abstract: The weighted Euler characteristic transform (WECT) and related directional descriptors have become popular, efficiently computable tools for shape analysis across a variety of domains. In practice, however, they are approximated over a finite set of filtration directions, and thus the vectorized descriptor depends on this choice of directions and the rotational orientation of the data. In this manuscript, we formally introduce the directionally integrated weighted Euler characteristic transform (DIWECT), which averages the WECT over all directions $s \in \mathbb{S}^n$ for a weighted simplicial complex immersed in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. A framework for computing the DIWECT exactly, without sampling directions, is outlined: for each simplex, we partition $\mathbb{S}^n$ into the sets of directions in which a given vertex enters the filtration last, and then the DIWECT at height $t$ reduces to measuring intersections of these regions with a set of directions in which the simplex has entered the filtration by height~$t$. We provide implementations for complexes immersed in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and $\mathbb{R}^3$, in which case the problem reduces to computing arc lengths and spherical areas. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that the DIWECT, while resulting in more compact vectorizations, also successfully encodes shape information and discards noise from data orientation. On a barley seed classification task, it outperforms the WECT in every pose except a hand-curated frame, whose advantage disappears under a two-degree rotation error. Compared with averaging the WECT over sampled directions, the DIWECT is often faster at matched accuracy. In one instance, this is upwards of a $50 \times$ speedup on a one-million-cell image with an error of $10^{-3}$.

title: EvoDisco: Strategy Discovery for Evolving Agent Memory
abstract: Large language model agents accumulate experience in memory, and how that memory evolves during interaction is as important as what it stores. Recent methods update memory online, yet both the operators that transform memory and the rules that select them remain fixed by design. We propose EvoDisco, which formulates agent memory evolution as evolutionary strategy discovery: the agent must discover which operator to apply, when to apply it, and how to instantiate it, rather than rewriting memory under a static operator schedule. A learnable policy conditions on the current memory state and recent task history, then selects and instantiates one of four semantic operators---Abstract, Refine, Bridge, and Reframe---which respectively compress related memories, decompose overloaded entries, connect weakly linked experiences, and reorganize retrieved reasoning chains. The policy is updated with a bi-level fitness. An inner signal scores each transformation using a retrieval-quality improvement regularized by memory complexity. An outer signal scores strategic efficacy over a window of past decisions, combining historical operator-utility regret, utility-prediction error, and selection diversity. Under a one-pass online plus frozen-transfer protocol on ALFWorld, WebShop, and LifelongAgentBench (OS and DB), EvoDisco improves over strong memory baselines including MemP and MemRL. The largest gains are on ALFWorld ($+8.8$ online / $+12.9$ frozen-transfer points over MemP; $+16.4$ / $+17.9$ over MemRL). Ablations attribute these gains to both fitness levels and the operator library.

title: From Sorry to QED: Refining LLM Math Proofs via Angelic Execution
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can now generate Lean proof scripts that capture the high-level structure of many mathematical arguments. However, these scripts frequently fail on complex theorems: a single missing side condition or misapplied lemma can cause the prover to abort early and discard an otherwise viable proof outline. This paper presents MathEye, a framework that converts imperfect LLM-generated proof scripts into fully verified Lean proofs by combining symbolic reasoning with minimal human interaction. At the core of MathEye is angelic proof checking, an optimistic execution model that replaces failing proof fragments with placeholders while preserving the overall structure of the argument. This optimistic check produces an angelic proof that isolates the exact proof obligations that the LLM fails to discharge. Because these unresolved obligations are often logically interdependent, asking a mathematician to address every placeholder directly is inefficient. To minimize human effort, MathEye performs residual analysis over a proof dependence graph that captures symbol-level data flow in the angelic proof. By formulating obligation selection as a MaxSAT optimization problem, MathEye selects a minimal-cost set of essential obligations whose resolution suffices to complete the entire proof. MathEye presents these essential obligations to the mathematician in ordinary mathematical language and uses the mathematician's answers to automatically reconstruct the complete Lean proof. Experiments on 30 real-world benchmarks across analysis and algebra show that MathEye solves 93.3% of the problems while reducing the number of required user interactions by 55%.

title: Directed triangles in oriented graphs without a directed cycle of length $3t$
abstract: For integers $k,\ell\ge 3$, let $\operatorname{ex}(n,\Cdir_k,\Cdir_\ell)$ denote the maximum number of directed cycles of length $k$ in an $n$-vertex oriented graph containing no directed cycles of length $\ell$. Grzesik, Jaworska, Kielak, Kuc and Ślusarczyk~\cite{GJ} systematically studied the generalized Turán problem for directed cycles and conjectured that, for every fixed integer $t\ge 2$, $\operatorname{ex}(n,\Cdir_3,\Cdir_{3t})=\frac{t-1}{4}n^2+o(n^2)$. They proved this asymptotic formula for $t=2$. In this paper, we prove it for every fixed integer $t\ge 3$, thereby confirming the conjecture.

title: Uniqueness of tangent flows in mean curvature flow (I): smooth minimal cone
abstract: We prove uniqueness of multiplicity-one minimal-cone tangent flows in mean curvature flow when the cone has a smooth embedded two-sided link and satisfies strict Hardy stability, radial Gaussian nonresonance, and weighted stationary rigidity. We also establish a discrete Lojasiewicz inequality, polynomial convergence rates, and rigidity among smooth self-shrinkers. In particular, these conclusions hold for all Simons cones $\mathcal C_{p,q}$ with $p,q \geq 1, p+q\geq 6$.

title: Diagnosing and Correcting Skin-Tone Color Casts in Ultra-Lightweight Photo Retouching Networks
abstract: Color casts are expected to come from the scene or camera, and a retouching model removes them. We report a case where the model leaves one: an ultra-lightweight retouching network renders human skin greener than the original because it under-restores the skin chroma that a degradation removes and, even on clean inputs, adds a small hue shift of its own. A common paired-data-free recipe, synthetic self-supervision (degrade high-quality images, learn to restore them), silently produces this cast while whole-frame PSNR/SSIM stay essentially unchanged. In a representative 6,825-parameter histogram-conditioned network, the cast appears in 52 of 70 portraits under a ground-truth-anchored, white-balance-free protocol. Both a histogram-conditioned and a CNN-conditioned network develop the cast under synthetic self-supervision, yet both are near-neutral in-domain when trained on MIT-Adobe FiveK expert pairs. Image-level objectives miss it: a global-mean green loss worsens the cast (52/70 to 57/70). With zero added parameters, our per-pixel, skin-masked, asymmetric green-excess loss reduces the cast to 1/70 across stratified skin tones (68.1% to 2.2% over the 70,000-image FFHQ corpus; 64.4% to 0.8% on held-out CelebA-HQ photos). In-domain FiveK PSNR/SSIM are unchanged (+0.13 dB, +0.004), at the cost of a small whole-frame CIEDE2000 increase (8.77 to 9.69) and a magenta over-correction where skin is nearly neutral (skin Delta a* -1.5 to +4.4 and CIEDE2000 5.6 to 6.4 on clean inputs): the loss targets the signed green-magenta axis, not total skin-color fidelity. The same loss suppresses the cast across three ultra-light architectures. A whole-frame green metric correlates with skin-region CIEDE2000 at the method level (Spearman rho = 0.89). The final network exports to a 35 KB TFLite model.

title: Regular/Singular Black Hole Thermodynamics from Renormalised Volume/Area
abstract: We study the finite mismatch between the holographically and topologically renormalised Euclidean actions of the four-dimensional AdS C-metric. Starting from the relation between Renormalised Volume and the Einstein sector of Conformal Gravity, we separate the regular curvature contribution from the contributions supported on the two conical axes. After introducing the usual Euler normalisation for smooth manifolds, the residual difference between the regular action evaluations is determined by the tension-weighted Euler terms of the renormalised worldsheet area. We identify this difference with the Gauss--Bonnet entropy contribution at the polar conical points of the horizon. The ordinary Euler characteristic remains fixed, while the deficits determine how its curvature representation is divided between regular and singular contributions. At fixed total string tension, the difference of the renormalised worldsheet areas per unit Euclidean time determines the relative tension work, giving a geometric interpretation of the relative thermodynamic length.

title: Perturbative Recovery of Stabilizer-Subspace Correlations for Quantum Computational Chemistry
abstract: Stabilizer-based subspace methods can substantially reduce the quantum resources required for electronic structure calculations, but the resulting projection neglects Hamiltonian couplings to configurations outside the retained subspace. In this work, we introduce Stabilizer-Subspace Perturbation Theory (SSPT) to recover the associated correlation contributions, using the Contextual Subspace Variational Quantum Eigensolver (CS-VQE) as a representative application. The central idea is to exploit the Pauli terms eliminated by stabilizer projection as perturbative operators that generate an external manifold from the optimized reference state. Their energetic contributions are evaluated using an Epstein-Nesbet-type second-order correction or a resolvent-based formulation that retains couplings within the external space. By exploiting the factorized structure of the stabilizer-constrained reference state, the required matrix elements can be evaluated through Pauli expectation values on the reduced contextual register without explicitly reconstructing the full-space wave function. Molecular benchmarks demonstrate substantial reductions in projection-induced energy errors, allowing chemical precision to be achieved with fewer contextual qubits in several cases. These results establish stabilizer-guided perturbation theory as a promising strategy for improving the accuracy of resource-efficient quantum chemistry calculations.

title: VTT: Reading Vehicle Size and Powertrain Type from Motion Trajectory Across Unseen Car Models
abstract: Vehicle size and powertrain information can enrich trajectory data for traffic analysis and simulation. We present VTT, a dataset and benchmark for identifying these attributes from motion and controller area network (CAN) signals across unseen car models. The dataset contains 9,062 drives, about 3,950 h, from 1,431 vehicles and 174 car models. It provides three footprint-based size classes, powertrain labels, and evaluation on unseen car models and unseen drivers. Using 60-s windows, we compare four sequence architectures, statistical features and physical features proposed by large language models. Training with auxiliary physical targets, data augmentation and task-specific weighting raises drive-level macro-F1 to 92.6-93.0% for battery-electric versus combustion vehicles and from 62.9% to 67.1% for size classification. On public logs from 4,061 additional drivers, the full-input model identifies powertrain correctly for 86 of 88 car models; size accuracy is 63.2%, close to the internal vehicle-level result of 63.5%. Physical-feature analysis links powertrain recognition to deceleration behaviour and size recognition to steering response. Errors near size-class boundaries and limited gains from longer observations highlight the importance of label resolution and training-fleet coverage for cross-model generalisation.

title: Real-Rootedness and Log-Concavity of Zigzag Eulerian Polynomials
abstract: We prove that the zigzag Eulerian polynomials have only real, negative, simple zeros, and hence strictly log-concave coefficients, settling the first two parts of a conjecture of Petersen and Zhuang. Real-rootedness in combinatorics is usually proved inside a single algebraic framework, such as interlacing or stability. Our proof rests on a different premise: different parts of a zero set become visible in different representations of the same polynomial, and classical tools suffice once each part is viewed in the right one. The bridge between representations is a local rule. Forgetting the order in which a bounded-jump path visits positions leaves only a nearest-neighbor condition on sorted gaps, which makes an encoding via a transfer matrix much simpler to see. From there the argument passes to complex analysis. The sizes of the matrix's eigenmodes locate the zeros at the two ends of the negative axis, through Rouché's theorem. In a logarithmic coordinate the generating function becomes a combination of derivatives of the hyperbolic secant, akin to the classical derivative polynomials, and the arguments of its nearest poles produce a sine that fixes the signs between consecutive central zeros. The zeros are thus read off from the poles of an associated kernel. More broadly, the proof suggests that combinatorial polynomials defined by local constraints carry analytic structure, in their spectra and in the poles of their kernels, that is complementary to the usual algebraic methods and that classical complex analysis can exploit directly.

title: Boundedness of a Schur multiplier on the Schatten p-class, $1 < p \neq 2 < \infty$, does not imply complete boundedness
abstract: We prove the existence of a bounded Schur multiplier on the Schatten class $S_p(\ell_2)$ which is not completely bounded when $1<p\ne 2<\infty$, which confirms Pisier's conjecture (1998).

title: Weak error estimates of a spectral Galerkin approximation to the stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough white noise
abstract: In this paper, we investigate weak error estimates for a spectral Galerkin approximation to a stochastic Burgers equation driven by rough space-time white noise. The roughness of the driving noise results that the mild solution possesses only $L^\infty$-regularity rather than any positive-order differentiability order regularity. The theory of classical numerical analysis reveals that the convergence rate of numerical solution is determined by the smoothness of the exact solution, and hence $L^\infty$-regularity is insufficient to yield any positive convergence rate. Indeed, De Vecchi et al.\ \cite{DeVecchi2026} studied a spectral Galerkin approximation to such equation and only proved pathwise convergence. However, we aim to derive positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation, which is determined by the roughness order of noise. To overcome the difficulty caused by the absence of smoothness of the exact solution, we turn to study the differentiability regularity of the first and second order Fréchet derivatives of the solution to a Kolmogorov equation associated with the spectral Galerkin approximation. We manage to prove that they possess nearly second order smoothness, enabling us to derive a positive weak convergence rate for the spectral Galerkin approximation. Finally, we conduct a numerical experiment to illustrate the theortical analysis.

title: RegimeCouncil: Paired-Evidence Routing For Memory Conflict Governance In LLM Agents
abstract: Alongside memory storage and retrieval, a fundamental challenge in long-term LLM agent systems is how the agent should act when stored memories conflict with an evolving world. Facts often go stale without explicit deletion, so the conflict surfaces before the store is refreshed: delayed feedback shows that acting on one outdated record hurt, but not whether suppression should stay on that fact (a local policy) or extend to other stored facts (a global policy). Existing systems hard-code one of these scopes at design time. We formulate this online choice, under hidden validity and delayed feedback, as memory conflict governance, and propose RegimeCouncil, a lightweight router that keeps both scopes as advisors and arbitrates between them without retraining the LLM. Each memory-assisted response is scored against a no-memory anchor, by off-path paired comparison or by inverse-propensity estimation from the executed action alone. A Local Advisor tracks only the queried fact, a Global Advisor pools recent outcomes across the store, and an asymmetric Meta Governor follows Local by default, switching to Global only when pooling yields a strictly positive recent utility margin. We prove that using delayed outcomes escapes the prompt-only regret floor, that neither fixed scope suffices alone, and that this margin gate switches within bounded time. On LongMemEval streams, historical drift in TempLAMA and TAQA, delays $τ\in [1, 96]$, and sparse or bandit feedback, with Qwen3-30B-A3B and GPT-4o, RegimeCouncil outperforms the better fixed scope in all 30 held-out settings, by 5.2-7.3 points on disagreement episodes and +27.9 points over standalone cold-start fallback under clustered shifts, while cutting harmful stale-memory use at microsecond overhead.

title: Backward-scattering photoelectron holography of a polar molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse
abstract: We investigate photoelectron holographic interference in the polar CO molecule driven by a sub-cycle laser pulse using time-dependent Schrödinger equation simulations and a classical-trajectory-based analysis. The sub-cycle temporal confinement of the driving field enables the forward-scattering holographic (FSH) and backward-scattering holographic (BSH) interference structures in the photoelectron momentum distributions (PMDs) to be clearly distinguished. The FSH fringes exhibit a strong dependence on molecular orientation, which is associated with the orientation-dependent transverse displacement of the ionizing electron wave packet (EWP). Furthermore, the heteronuclear nature of CO results in different FSH fringe shifts for ionization occurring predominantly from the C and O sides of the molecule. In contrast, the curved interference structures in the negative parallel-momentum region are identified as BSH interference arising from the coherent superposition of direct and backward-scattered EWPs. The BSH fringe positions show weak dependence on molecular orientation and remain clearly visible after orientation averaging. We further show that BSH visibility depends on the carrier-envelope phase (CEP) and that the fringes remain discernible after CEP averaging. Moreover, the BSH interference pattern exhibits a systematic dependence on the internuclear separation, demonstrating its sensitivity to molecular geometry. These results highlight the potential of sub-cycle pulse enabled backward-scattering photoelectron holography for probing molecular structure and demonstrate its robustness against molecularorientation and CEP averaging

title: TeleChat to Xing4: Advancing Frontier Agentic Models on Domestic Chips and Frameworks
abstract: We present Xing 4, a series of large language models that extends the TeleChat lineage through coordinated advances in model architecture and training infrastructure on Ascend. This report describes the design principles and systems engineering behind the series, spanning architecture selection, large-scale pretraining, and reasoning and agentic post-training. We study how sparse activation, attention design, model depth and width, and speculative decoding balance model capacity with computation, memory access, and execution overhead. Our pretraining infrastructure builds on MindSpore HyperParallel, combining topology-aware hybrid sharding, efficient distributed optimizer execution, and coordinated management of long-sequence workloads and activation memory. CPU affinity and core isolation further reduce host scheduling interference. Together, these mechanisms support the pretraining of a 285B-parameter model on 8,192 Ascend 910C cards, providing a concrete setting for the architectural and systems studies. For post-training, we introduce TeleGym, a unified agent execution platform that connects execution, evaluation, and trajectory construction to policy optimization. Disaggregated asynchronous execution, bounded oversampling, and partial rollout accommodate heterogeneous task durations while preserving trajectory continuity across policy updates. Together, these advances establish an Ascend-oriented training foundation for the continued development of Xing 4 across model scales and increasingly demanding reasoning and agent workloads.

title: Reserve Systems in Dynamic Settings: Account Design and Inherited Rights
abstract: Research on reserve systems mainly considers static settings, formulating and studying choice rules for a given allocation problem. Dynamic settings are different in that the problem is not given. Over time, more positions become available, and each time the institution must build the current problem from its past. We distinguish the ledger, which stores information about earlier allocations, the account, which transforms these data into the current problem, and the choice rule, which selects an outcome for that problem. The same choice rule can implement very different policies under different accounts. If each new batch is assigned while holding earlier recipients and their categories fixed, then as batches shrink, over-and-above, the most generous reserve policy we study, can select nearly the same recipients as minimum guarantee, the most conservative one. Cumulative implementation uses a different account, which reconsiders the categories of earlier recipients, and prevents this compression. We characterize it by resource-release invariance. With arrivals or changes in priorities, the ordinary choice rule might reject an earlier recipient whose appointment has to be honored. We introduce and characterize retain, reassign, and boost (RRB) choice rules, under which every incumbent retains her appointment and can have her category changed. Combining RRB with individual-proposing deferred acceptance gives a strategy-proof mechanism under which each incumbent keeps her appointment or receives one she prefers. Applications include waiting lists in school and university admissions, public recruitment, and court-ordered corrections.

title: RetiDual-Select: Reliability-Aware Specialist-Generalist Routing for Retinal OCT under Image-Quality Shift
abstract: Adaptive fusion can repair a static ensemble's errors, but can also overturn correct decisions. RetiDual-Select combines retinal specialist RETFound with the image encoder of the medical vision-language model MedSigLIP, separating candidate fusion, routing safety and predictive review. Calibrated product-of-experts (PoE) fusion is the static reference, a small gate proposes an alternative for each image, a validation-frozen harm guard decides whether that candidate may replace the reference, and a separate score prioritizes review. Static PoE reached the highest or joint-highest clean accuracy on all three datasets. At a clean 2% accepted-error target the review policy accepted 94.3% of Kermany-4 images at 99.89% selective accuracy, and 92.4% of OCT-C8 at 98.65%. Both branches were correct on 95.0% and 91.8% of clean images; only 4.4% and 6.2% had exactly one correct branch. Across 15 prespecified synthetic conditions, adaptive gains were concentrated in severe contrast reduction, where this routing opportunity widened roughly ninefold; percentile rescaling largely removed the effect, linking it to compressed dynamic range. In post-hoc validation-only analyses, gain was higher when the gate followed the more reliable branch, and a frozen guard cut the worst-condition OCT-C8 loss from 1.39 to 0.36 percentage points. Adaptive routing was useful when image quality created a reliability opportunity and the gate followed it; otherwise the system retained Static PoE or deferred for review. The findings are bounded by the synthetic perturbations evaluated and do not establish robustness to natural acquisition or scanner shift.

title: Variational Relevance-Informed Sparsification of Term Measurements for Variational Quantum Algorithms
abstract: Repeated measurements are a major bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms (VQAs). We uncover and characterize parameter-specific sparsity in the matrix of qubit-wise commuting (QWC) group contributions to parameter-shift gradients: most absolute contribution mass concentrates in a subset of groups whose relevance varies across parameters and optimization states. Building on this structure, we introduce a learned controller that predicts group relevance from Hamiltonian, circuit, light-cone, and current-state features, then selects measurements through a tunable coverage threshold. Exact contributions provide offline supervision without being required at deployment. Across 15 molecular VQE settings, our method saves 49.6% of nominal gradient-measurement shots with a mean absolute energy gap of 5.67 mHa to Full-QWC. We then ask whether large language models (LLMs) can solve the same selection problem without fine-tuning. The results reveal both promise and a clear limitation: LLMs can identify useful measurement groups, yet without guidance, local models do not consistently prioritize the physical information that matters most. Our learned controller uses these cues more effectively. This contrast points toward a broader direction for AI-assisted science: combining the flexibility of general-purpose models with explicit physical representations, task-specific objectives, and domain-grounded validation.

title: An axiomatic foundation for optimized certainty equivalents
abstract: Optimized Certainty Equivalents (OCEs) are an important class of risk measures for optimization and risk management that includes the Mean--Variance criterion, Expected Shortfall, the Entropic Risk Measure, and expectation. Despite their importance, economic axioms have not characterized OCEs. We propose a new axiom called Fair-Coin Compensation, which characterizes OCEs together with Strong Risk Aversion and Normalization. We interpret Fair-Coin Compensation through the fair assignment of two losses by a coin toss: transfers between two participants can remove the additional risk created by the random assignment. Adding further axioms yields sharper characterizations. Monotonicity yields standard OCEs; Positive Homogeneity, together with Prudence, yields Expected Shortfall; and Fair-Coin Independence yields the Entropic Risk Measure. We also axiomatize the Mean--Variance criterion using our novel axiom of Equal-Mean Randomization, which states that random assignment of two losses with the same expected value does not produce a risk measure above the average of their risk measures.

title: What MoE Routing Controls: Causal Interventions on Expert Trajectories
abstract: In mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models, a token is routed to a sequence of experts across layers. We investigate how forcing tokens onto chosen expert paths influences model behavior. We build a target path from the experts that a concept's or role's tokens most often use, and we add a fixed bias to each target expert's router logit during generation to steer the token toward this expert path. We study two kinds of targets. Format targets concern the form of the output, and concept targets concern its topic. In Qwen3-30B-A3B, we show that steering a format path changes the text the model writes. We also show that steering a concept path shifts the model's next-token probabilities toward the concept, even when the path is built in another language, yet this shift has little effect on the generated text. We investigate why formats reach the text but concepts do not by steering only part of the generation, and find evidence that a format, once started, reinforces itself. We show that the concepts religion and money steer most strongly, and that the effect is concentrated in the middle layers. We attempt to explain why the strength of the effect varies by concept through an analysis of embedding distinctiveness and word frequency.

title: Three Circles in a Unit Disk: Three Solutions to an Extremal Problem
abstract: We place two disks inside the unit disk so that they touch each other and the unit circle. We then insert a disk of the largest possible radius, requiring it to touch both original disks. We show that the smallest possible sum of the three areas is $11π/18$, and find all equality cases. We give three solutions, using Descartes' circle theorem, inversion, and contact-point coordinates. The main difficulty is checking that the third disk is largest among all disks that fit, not only among disks touching the first two.

title: Low-speed Limit Cycle Walking of Planar X-shaped Bipedal Robot with Special Properties
abstract: This paper proposes a novel planar semicircular-footed X-shaped bipedal robot in which the center of mass of each leg link is at the same position as the hip joint, and discusses a method for generating a stable limit cycle gait on level ground. First, we outline the assumptions of the robot model with four degrees of freedom, and develop the mathematical equations of motion and collision. Second, we set the relative hip-joint angle as a control output and design a control system to follow it to the desired trajectory specified as a fifth-order function of time. Third, we mathematically show that there are special properties: the angular velocity of the swing leg does not change before and after the collision, and the time-integral of the control input becomes zero in a steady gait. We also mathematically show that the model has the feature that approximate linearization is effective and the antigravity effect of semicircular feet can be utilized. Through numerical simulations, we verify the validity of the theoretical results, and analyze some fundamental gait properties such as convergence speed and mechanical energy restoration.

title: Two-Qutrit Quantum Battery Charging through Ising Model and Anisotropic XZ Heisenberg Interactions
abstract: In this paper, we propose a model of a two-qutrit quantum battery composed of two spin-1 systems coupled to an external field via anisotropic Heisenberg interactions.
