Having expanded to 100 times larger than their main-sequence sizes, they occupy the cool, luminous extreme of the Hertzsprung--Russell diagram. Characterised by extended convective envelopes, complex and dynamic atmospheres, and, sometimes, substantial mass loss, RSGs play a critical role in shaping both their own evolutionary outcomes and the circumstellar environments into which they ultimately explode. Despite decades of study, fundamental aspects of RSG physics remain poorly constrained, including the mechanisms driving mass loss and the connection between observed RSG populations and the properties of Type II supernovae. Recent observational advances have transformed the field, revealing episodic mass-loss events, asymmetric circumstellar structures, and signs of rapid evolutionary change in individual objects. Alongside these advances, studies of Type II supernovae and their progenitors have raised important new questions about the final stages of massive star evolution, including the possibility of rapid changes in the years immediately preceding core collapse. Motivated by these developments, this review aims to describe our current understanding of how RSGs live and die, from their observed properties through to their role as supernova progenitors, and where that understanding remains incomplete.

title: The Fragility of Reasoning-Importance Attribution for Pruning Language Models
abstract: Attribution-guided pruning scores components by their causal contribution and protects the important ones, and it is increasingly applied to compress reasoning language models without destroying their chain of thought. Its reliability rests on an unexamined assumption: that reasoning importance can be faithfully measured. Across four small reasoning models, we show this measurement is fragile in three ways, each of which changes pruning decisions. First, scoring final-answer tokens, the natural choice, saturates in every chain-of-thought model we test (answer-token negative log-likelihood, NLL, of $10^{-4}$--$10^{-3}$) because the model states its answer inside its own reasoning; guiding head pruning with this target costs 27.6 and 32.2 accuracy points relative to scoring reasoning tokens on the two models we power with five seeds, while perplexity barely moves and even reverses sign at 7B. Second, causal importance is not localizable to single units: single-neuron effects sit at the measurement floor, their cross-split ranking is noise, and they cancel: a group's ablation effect disagrees in sign with the summed effects of its members in 90\% of groups. Reproducible importance emerges only at groups of $\sim 100$ neurons. Third, contrastively isolated ``reasoning-specific'' importance is not separable from generic importance, and protecting it is worse than protecting raw importance. We additionally pre-registered the hypothesis that distillation-induced concentration of importance predicts the pruning cost; it is not supported, and since our grid confounds concentration with scale, we report it as unresolved rather than reversed. The result is a short set of measurement rules: score reasoning tokens, attribute at coarse granularity, and evaluate with accuracy rather than perplexity.

title: CoSphere-SLAM: Multi-Agent Panoramic Gaussian Splatting SLAM with Spherical Loop Closure
abstract: Dense collaborative mapping is essential for search and rescue, building inspection, and warehouse automation, where panoramic cameras capture the entire surroundings in a single frame. Unlike pinhole agents that share views only at similar headings, panoramic agents observe overlapping scenes at any 3D orientation, yet searching full rotations also produces mutually consistent false loop closures across distinct symmetric rooms. Moreover, continuous monocular scale drift splits rigidly merged maps at revisited surfaces, while depth noise at short baselines distorts loop translation directions. To address these challenges, we propose CoSphere-SLAM, the first multi-agent Gaussian splatting SLAM framework for panoramic cameras, whose spherical loop closure aligns spherical features over $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ via fast Fourier correlation across arbitrary orientations and rejects symmetric false closures through global $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ consensus. Building on these closures, directional global optimization solves a per-keyframe $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ pose graph with log-scale regularization to correct scale drift while separating optical-flow translation directions from depth-based magnitudes. Finally, omnidirectional Gaussian fusion transforms each Gaussian with its keyframe similarity and renders Gaussians at their maximum ray response to jointly refine poses and maps. Experiments on indoor and cross-session multi-agent panoramic benchmarks demonstrate that CoSphere-SLAM achieves state-of-the-art trajectory accuracy and rendering quality among single-agent and multi-agent methods. Project website: https://cosphere-slam.github.io.

title: Spatially local mini-batching for implicit neural representations
abstract: Neural surrogates based on implicit neural representations (INRs) are typically trained on mini-batches spread over the whole domain, since a generic INR loses accuracy when every point of a batch lies in one small region. We show that low-rank neural representations (LRNRs), INRs whose weight matrices are products of shared bases with coefficients emitted by a small hypernetwork, can be trained with spatially local mini-batches. Each step uses the points of one time snapshot of an adaptive-mesh numerical solution inside one small cell, with snapshots and cells drawn according to the refinement of the mesh. We posit that such training is enabled by the structural property of LRNRs, as a local step reaches the shared bases only through the $r$ coefficients of each layer, and keeps one cell from rewriting the network. By a Kolmogorov-width argument, we show that when restricted to a small cell, the hidden states of LRNRs lie close to a low-dimensional subspace, which suggests the local steps only affect low-rank subspaces of the shared bases. On six hyperbolic-conservation-law problems with solutions computed using adaptive mesh refinement, one local training recipe reaches 1.1-2.3% relative $L^2$ error with a tenth of the parameters of a dense network of the same width. Finally, we provide a comparison by training a hypernetwork-SIREN, a DeepONet, and a Fourier neural operator (FNO) of the same size with the same local batches and training budget. We observe that these baselines reach 16-78% where the LRNR reaches 4.9%. Interestingly, we also observe that local training has a significant effect on the per-cell low-dimensional structure even in a wide generic hypernetwork-SIREN.

title: Flavor Entanglement as a CPT Violation Witness in Neutrino Oscillations
abstract: We present a comprehensive study linking the single-particle flavor entanglement of a \(ν_{e} \rightarrow ν_μ\) oscillation to CPT violation using the concurrence. In a two-flavor vacuum with CP-conserving mixing, CPT invariance strictly demands \(\mathcal{C}_ν(L) = \mathcal{C}_{\barν}(L)\), meaning any measured difference \(Δ\mathcal{C}_{\mathrm{CPT}} \equiv \mathcal{C}_ν - \mathcal{C}_{\barν}\) serves as a clean, background-free witness of CPT violation. We derive exact, first-order analytical relations connecting this entanglement asymmetry to the standard probability asymmetry, the baseline reflection sums, and the long-baseline decoherence floor. To rigorously test the experimental viability of this framework, we perform extensive numerical simulations. We demonstrate that the framework projects stringent sensitivity limits on Standard-Model Extension (SME) parameters at DUNE-like densities, isolate a coordinate-independent CPT invariant, and show that the signal remains robust across realistic, variable Earth matter density profiles. Crucially, we identify a distinct 24-hour sidereal modulation of the entanglement asymmetry, providing a definitive temporal "smoking gun" to disentangle CPT violation from matter effects. Finally, we show that at PeV astrophysical energies, the reflection-sum mismatch scales up to \(10^{13}\) meters, opening a novel frontier for CPT tests beyond terrestrial experiments.

title: Context Has a Price: Adding and Removing Context for LLM Coding Agents under Prefix Caching
abstract: Coding agents repeatedly send their conversation history to a language model. Adding useful code may reduce search, while removing old tool outputs may shorten later prompts. But do these changes reduce the cost of solving a task? We study this as a measurement problem in more than 20,000 runs of open models on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench and Loc-Bench. We account separately for uncached input, cached input and output tokens. Three findings emerge. First, in our main evidence-package experiments, retrieved code reduces read and search commands by 18--34%, but increases cost by 33--42% when cached input costs one tenth of uncached input, without a measurable improvement in resolution. Second, removing old observations can either save money or increase cost: the same approach saves 19--36% without a cache discount but increases cost by 38--116% with a tenth-price cache. Third, shorter prompts do not guarantee cheaper runs because agents may respond by taking more steps. We also find that concurrent experiments can share cached prefixes and distort cost comparisons. These results show why context-management methods should be evaluated using both token prices and the agent's subsequent behavior.

title: Solver-Free and Cost-Aware Online Scheduling of AI Data Center Tasks
abstract: AI data centers receive computing tasks continuously, whereas solver-based optimization takes time to run and electricity is priced per settlement period. This paper bridges this timing gap through a solver-free online optimization rule inspired by dual decomposition. The rule assigns each task a start period upon arrival to optimize energy cost subject to operational constraints, shifting flexible tasks toward low-price periods while keeping high-priority tasks on schedule. Simulations on the A100 GPU trace (3,456 GPUs, 1,343 tasks) show that the proposed rule keeps GPU and CPU use within capacity while scheduling tasks at low cost. Compared with a multi-timescale optimization benchmark, it achieves a lower cost and, because it needs no solver, much less computation time.

title: Cross3DGS: Unified Vulkan-Based 3D Gaussian Splatting Training from Workstations to Mobile Devices
abstract: Scenes captured with handheld and wearable cameras are still shipped to a CUDA workstation for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) training. Training on the device that captured them, or on its companion phone or laptop, requires more than translating kernels: GPUs and drivers differ in parallel features, memory limits, and command submission, and these differences decide whether a training schedule executes and returns the correct update. We present Cross3DGS, a cross-vendor, cross-platform Vulkan trainer that keeps one optimizer and chooses its execution schedule per device in two steps: rules on device limits, workload size, and observed driver failures exclude the schedules known not to run correctly, and a fixed preference order selects one of the remaining feasible schedules. The same core completes standard-quality training (30k updates, one million Gaussians) on every configuration we measured, spanning NVIDIA, Intel, Arm, Qualcomm, AMD, and Apple GPUs and including Android devices and an iPhone, whereas the existing portable trainers VkSplat and Brush do not run on some of the mobile GPUs. Averaged over 11 scenes on a workstation, Cross3DGS has higher quality than VkSplat with no significant difference in training time, and Brush reports about three times the training time at comparable quality. The final quality of Cross3DGS is nearly identical across devices. A mobile application turns a handheld capture into a viewable model entirely on the device.

title: Where Does Hindsight Enter Clinical Agent Benchmarks? An Audit of Simulators and Case Construction
abstract: Benchmarks for LLM diagnostic agents are built from retrospective records: the case an agent reads is rewritten from discharge summaries, and unrecorded test results are generated by a simulator that often sees the final diagnosis. HindAudit separates three hindsight channels (the diagnosis given to the simulator, the retrospective context it conditions on, and the agent-facing case text) and measures each with judges trained only on real data. On 27,489 emergency admissions from MIMIC-IV, five registered tests found no leakage into simulated laboratory results: providing the diagnosis to five simulators had a negligible effect, and prompted gatekeepers diluted the diagnostic signal, although exploratory results suggest they can raise agent scores. The largest effect lay in the case text. Against a presentation-time reconstruction from triage records, benchmark-style summaries raised the zero-shot accuracy of four LLMs from 25.4% to 39.7% and discharge histories to 45.3%, and raised six interactive agents' scores while barely changing their ranking. The exploratory gap was reproduced in a registered replication on held-out patients. Masking diagnosis names left it unchanged. Because MIMIC lacks a contemporaneous bedside history, the gap is an upper bound on hindsight. We report all registered outcomes and recommend construction practices.

title: Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for Multiple Cloud Data Centers
abstract: This paper studies coordinated Large Language Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The central question is how two scheduling flexibilities - cross-CDC task transfer and task reordering - affect service and economic outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute, bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formulate a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing, pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility operation. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103. The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone temperatures within 24°C-27°C. These fixed-instance results indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes under the studied conditions.

title: From Token Changes to Task Failures: Bit Flips in a Shared KV-Cache Block
abstract: In LLM serving systems with prefix caching, each KV block of a shared system prompt is held in GPU memory as a single physical copy, which every request with that prompt reads. Our earlier work measured change and showed that one bit flip in such a block changes many later responses without making them visibly degenerate. This paper extends that work by measuring how often the changed responses are wrong. Using software fault injection into vLLM serving Qwen3-8B, we flip the most significant mantissa bit or the sign bit of a value in such a block. We score responses on four tasks: code generation, short-answer questions, multiple-choice reasoning, and refusal under a policy. The fraction of changes that turned a correct response wrong depended strongly on the task: 0.023 on MBPP+ and 0.59 on held-out TriviaQA at the mantissa bit, and 0.019 and 0.60 at the sign bit. Harm fell on requests whose sampled answers are sometimes wrong, so the damage of a flip depends on how common such requests are. Harmed responses looked like ordinary errors, so a flip should be detected by checking cached blocks rather than by monitoring outputs.

title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Project page: https://phyvggt.github.io.

title: Multi-Agent Memory Inconsistency: Where Factual Conflicts Disappear in LLM Agents
abstract: Multi-agent delegation lets LLM systems distribute evidence collection across workers with separate contexts. This creates a consistency challenge: facts retrieved by workers may be missing from the evidence available to the lead for a joint conclusion. We introduce a benchmark and evidence-flow profiler for studying multi-agent memory inconsistency through controlled factual conflicts in Harvey LAB document-review tasks. Pooled across three models with comparable generation spending, requiring delegation increases retrieval of both conflicting claims from 50.2% to 68.7% relative to single-agent execution, yet conflict detection falls from 16.2% to 13.2%. Within this setting, workers report both claims for only 35.2% of retrieved pairs, and pooled matched comparisons show higher detection than single-agent execution when one worker reads both claims but lower detection when the claims are split across workers. Worker-to-lead handoffs are a central target for improving conflict detection in multi-agent LLMs.

title: Multispectral-Polarization-Infrared Multi-Aperture Camouflaged Vehicle Detection
abstract: Camouflaged vehicle detection is challenging because camouflage suppresses discriminative cues across sensing modalities. Existing multimodal methods often require precise pixel-level registration and feature-level fusion, creating a trade-off between accuracy and latency. We propose a spectral-polarization-infrared tri-modal detection framework co-designed with a multi-aperture imaging setup to exploit complementary imaging physics. A consensus-guided decision-level fusion strategy combines cross-modal detections within bounded registration tolerances, reducing dependence on precise alignment while maintaining accuracy and real-time performance. We construct a tri-modal camouflaged vehicle dataset containing infrared, polarization, and spectral data. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves 82.7% mean Average Precision (mAP) with an end-to-end latency of 16 ms, outperforming representative feature-level fusion approaches. On the public MID-1K dataset, the framework generalizes to RGB-Depth-Infrared modalities without architectural modification and improves mAP@0.5 by 5.7% over state-of-the-art methods. These results demonstrate the potential of decision-level consensus fusion and multi-aperture sensing for robust and deployable camouflaged vehicle detection.

title: CHEQ: A Concurrent Hardware Evaluation Platform for QEC Decoders via Batch-Invariant Circuit-Level Noise Sampling
abstract: Hardware quantum error correction (QEC) decoders require validation of logical error suppression and timing compliance before deployment. Rare logical failures and deadline violations demand extensive sampling, while algorithm-level software evaluation does not directly measure hardware response times. Circuit-level noise models contain many error mechanisms but few firings per shot at low physical error rates, making exhaustive per-shot scanning inefficient. We present CHEQ, an FPGA platform integrating on-chip sampling, concurrent decoder evaluation, scoring, and RISC-V control. Its Sampling Units use geometric skipping to sample firing locations from detector error models and amortize mechanism traversal across shots within each batch. Under independent random draws and exact geometric sampling, the shot distribution is invariant to batch size, enabling a memory-throughput tradeoff. A throughput model guides joint selection of the Sampling Unit count, batch size, and decoder count under FPGA resource constraints. Across evaluated conditions, the pooled one-sided 95% upper bound on the weighted root-mean-square relative firing-rate difference from Stim is 0.16%. At a batch size of 4,096, a Sampling Unit uses only 4.8%-11.2% of a Helios decoder's LUTs for code distances 7, 9, 11, and 13. On an AMD VCU118 FPGA at code distance 7 and physical error rate 10^-3, two Sampling Units supply 20 Helios decoders at 49.2 million shots/s, completing 10^10 shots in 3.4 minutes without host-side shot generation.

title: OAK-Mind: Zero-Training Mental Health Change Inference from Passive Sensing via Knowledge-Grounded Multi-Agent LLMs
abstract: Wearable and smartphone sensors capture behavioral signals associated with mental health, yet inferring mental health outcomes from these signals has traditionally relied on supervised models requiring labeled data and offering limited insight into their predictions. Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities to reason over behavioral evidence, but existing LLM-based approaches to passive sensing have largely continued to rely on task-specific fine-tuning or sensor-specific pretraining. In this paper, we introduce OAK-Mind, a zerO-training, multi-Agent, Knowledge-grounded LLM pipeline for inferring mental health changes from passive sensing data. The pipeline organizes sensing data into behavioral dimensions including sleep, physical activity, location mobility, and smartphone use, and orchestrates specialized agents grounded in mental health literature to interpret longitudinal behavioral changes. It synthesizes their assessments and applies questionnaire-based symptom rating to infer changes relative to an individual's baseline assessment with human-readable rationale grounded in observed behavioral patterns and domain knowledge. Across datasets and prediction tasks, while without task-specific training, OAK-Mind achieves comparable or better performance than the most predictive supervised baselines trained on additional labeled samples. It also demonstrate consistent improvement upon direct prompting across four tested LLM backbones. Ablation analyses support the benefits of combining behavioral interpretation with symptom rating, distributing analysis across domain-specific agents, and incorporating domain knowledge. Our findings highlight the potential of knowledge-grounded, multi-agent LLMs for training-free inference of mental health changes from passive sensing data.

title: $H_2$-optimal riblet profiles for turbulence suppression in channel flows
abstract: The drag-reducing properties of streamwise-elongated surface corrugations, commonly referred to as riblets, have been extensively studied through experiments, simulations, and reduced-order modeling. Notably, the linearized Navier-Stokes framework introduced by Ran, Zare, and Jovanovic (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 906, 2021) employs volume penalization to model riblet-induced boundary conditions and predict drag reduction. These approaches typically quantify drag reduction as a function of a single geometric parameter, such as spanwise spacing or groove cross-sectional area, evaluated over fixed riblet shapes. As a result, identifying optimal riblet geometries across a broader design space often necessitates exhaustive parametric studies. To address this problem, we propose an optimization framework for the systematic design of optimal riblet shapes. Accordingly, we reformulate the volume penalization term in the linearized dynamics as a structured state-feedback operator. Targeting maximal suppression of turbulence, we pose a composite optimization problem that minimizes the steady-state variance of velocity fluctuations and riblet-induced dynamical augmentations while maintaining a constant bulk-flux. For a fixed spanwise wavelength (riblet spacing), this framework yields optimal wall-normal profiles that achieve maximal turbulence attenuation.

title: PCGRL for Complex Platformers: Synthesizing Playable and Diverse Levels via Inflated Envelopes and Forward Curricula
abstract: Procedural Content Generation via Reinforcement Learning (PCGRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for automated game development. However, existing PCGRL frameworks still suffer from severe exploration bottlenecks and scaling limitations when faced with long-sequence generation tasks governed by strict rigid-body rules and non-linear kinematic boundaries (e.g., platformer constraints). Consequently, traditional approaches frequently fail to maintain reliable level solvability on large-scale canvases. To address these challenges, we present a physics-aware, curriculum-guided PCGRL framework. First, we construct an "Inflated Volume Envelope" mechanism, which provides a physics-constrained representation that incorporates continuous kinematic feasibility into the discrete state space of the MDP. Second, to alleviate the sparse reward challenge induced by extremely long decision sequences, we introduce intermediate state-transition feedback and a multi-stage forward extension curriculum learning framework, enabling informative value estimation and stable credit assignment over long-horizon trajectories. Finally, to resolve the issue where deterministic policies after convergence generate highly monotonous map paths with a lack of diversity, we activate high-entropy stochastic inference during the synthesis phase, regularized by a post-hoc parallel rejection filtering mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances structural diversity while maintaining high physical playability across multi-scale environments. Comparative evaluations across multi-scale canvases demonstrate that our framework maintains superior convergence stability and dimensional scalability, reliably synthesizing solvable levels where traditional PCGRL baselines degrade.

title: Recovering hysteresis in reduced models of plasma turbulence: a Mori--Zwanzig-inspired closure
abstract: Hysteretic transitions between turbulent and strongly zonal-flow-dominated states provide an important test for reduced models of plasma turbulence and a minimal setting for studying dynamics relevant to L-H transitions. The 12-mode truncation of the modified Hasegawa-Wakatani system developed by Guillon and Gürcan retains this transition but underestimates the hysteresis observed in direct numerical simulations (DNS). Guided by the Mori-Zwanzig framework, we construct a phenomenological closure for the influence of discarded modes. The discarded spectrum is coarse-grained into a reservoir, whose feedback on the retained modes is modeled together with a separate drift-wave damping term. Without increasing the number of retained modes, the closure recovers nearly all of the hysteresis width missing from the unclosed truncation and places both transition thresholds close to their DNS values. To test the model beyond hysteresis, we also examine particle flux. The closed model improves upon the unclosed truncation, agreeing more closely with DNS at low adiabaticity but underestimating transport at high adiabaticity. These results show that a low-dimensional representation of discarded-mode feedback can improve predictions of hysteretic turbulence-flow transitions.

title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only. Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings. Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types. Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

title: OCP: a greedy projection method for row-sparse representations of minimum-norm solutions
abstract: In this paper, we propose a greedy projection method, termed orthogonal constraint pursuit (OCP), for identifying a small set of rows of a consistent linear system $Ax=b$ whose span contains the minimum-norm solution $x^*$, along with the coefficients of that representation. The method successively activates the most violated constraint, and then projects the iterate onto the intersection of all activated constraints. We prove that OCP is equivalent to OMP applied to the dictionary $A^T$ and the signal $x^*$, and that it terminates in at most rank(A) iterations. When $x^*$ is a linear combination of $s$ rows of a matrix whose rows are independent and uniformly distributed on the unit sphere, OCP identifies those rows in exactly $s$ iterations with probability $1-O(m^{-1})$, provided that $n\ge Cs\ln m$ for a sufficiently large constant $C$. We also derive a variant of OCP with constraint removal for hard-margin support vector machines with regularized bias, which returns the support vectors, along with the multipliers that satisfy the KKT conditions. Numerical results on both real and synthetic problems demonstrate the identification of representing rows and the regime in which it is competitive with Krylov subspace methods.

title: Between proper and strong edge-colorings of graphs with maximum degree at most four
abstract: A $(1^j,2^k)$-packing edge-coloring of a graph $G$ is a partition of its edge set $E(G)$ into $j$ matchings and $k$ induced matchings. It can be viewed as intermediate colorings between proper and strong edge-coloring. The study of this topic on subcubic graphs has drawn considerable attention recently, with many conjectures and open problems proposed and resolved. However, very few results are known for graphs with maximum degree four or more. Henderson, Kennedy, and Santana showed that every graph with degree at most four has a $(1,2^{19})$-packing edge-coloring and a $(1^2,2^{17})$-packing edge-coloring. In this paper, we improve the results of Henderson, Kennedy, and Santana by showing every graph with degree at most four has a $(1,2^{17})$-packing edge-coloring. As a corollary of our result, every graph with degree at most four has a $(1^2,2^{16})$-packing edge-coloring.

title: Global existence and emergent dynamics of singular Cucker-Smale model on general digraphs
abstract: We investigate the global-in-time dynamics of the Cucker--Smale model under general network topologies with a singular communication weight function $ψ(r) = r^{-α}$, $α>0$. For $α\ge 1$, we establish the global-in-time existence of smooth solutions when network topologies belong to one of several classes of directed graphs. In particular, in one dimension, we present a necessary condition on the network topology for global existence by constructing finite-time blow-up solutions from non-collisional initial configurations. Moreover, we provide a sufficient framework for the emergence of mono-cluster flocking. For certain classes of network topologies, we further show that mono-cluster flocking occurs unconditionally for non-collisional initial configuration when $α=1$.

title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

title: The Online LSTM Prediction Models and The Term Structure of Predictions
abstract: We examine and illustrate the properties of the Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) prediction models applied online to stationary inputs. We discuss the effects of: a) the network architecture that defines the admissible prediction functions, b) the objective function used to measure the prediction accuracy, and c) the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. We also study the prediction optimality, the term structure of predictions, the filtered memory dynamics. We also introduce a set of diagnostic tools for memory-based prediction models that focus on the estimated dynamics of the hidden states.

title: ALERT: Extending Humanoid Motion Trackers with a General and Lightweight Human Avoidance Pipeline
abstract: Whole-body motion tracking has enabled humanoid dancing, athletic motions, and teleoperation, providing a foundation for capability demonstrations and manipulation data collection. However, existing tracking policies lack awareness of nearby humans and proactive avoidance capabilities, while motion substitution and local constraint-based corrections may compromise reference motion integrity and tracking continuity. We propose ALERT, a general lightweight pipeline for extending motion tracking to shared human-robot environments. Through lightweight adaptation, it integrates human perception and proactive avoidance into pretrained tracking policies, balancing avoidance demands with reference motion tracking while preserving existing motion capabilities. Simulation and real-world experiments across tracking backbones demonstrate reliable collision-free execution through localized human avoidance, preserving whole-body coordination and enabling rapid recovery of reference tracking, while retaining the ability of pretrained policies to track unseen motions.

title: Multi-Gaussian Model for Intrabeam Scattering
abstract: Conventional analytical models of intrabeam scattering (IBS), such as the Piwinski model and Bjorken-Mtingwa model, generally rely on the assumption of a Gaussian beam distribution, limiting their applicability to non-Gaussian cases. In this work, we develop a multi-Gaussian model to extend analytical IBS calculations to a broader class of non-Gaussian phase-space distributions. The proposed approach represents a non-Gaussian distribution as a superposition of Gaussian components sharing a common covariance matrix but having different mean values. We derived a generalized model for evaluating the momentum second-moment evolution rate and the IBS growth rate. Furthermore, for equally spaced Gaussian components, we developed an infinite bunch train model and introduce a practical truncation rule to reduce computational costs. The model is applied to a representative steady-state microbunching (SSMB) storage ring, where longitudinal overlap between neighboring microbunches is shown to enhance IBS growth rates in all three directions. The proposed framework provides a practical approach to evaluating IBS in non-Gaussian beam distributions and offers a basis for further development toward a more general non-Gaussian IBS theory.

title: Logical error prediction and geometry selection for rectangular surface codes under biased circuit-level noise
abstract: Realistic quantum hardware often exhibits biased noise, but at the circuit level this bias may affect only a subset of operations and need not be transferred uniformly to logical errors. The logical response to a given physical bias is therefore central to selecting resource-efficient surface code geometries. Here, we study unrotated rectangular surface codes under standard depolarizing and superconducting-inspired circuit-level noise models. We first construct geometry-dependent logical error rate models from unbiased circuit-level simulations. We then use logical sensitivities to compare the responses to localized idle-bias and global physical error perturbations, defining logical-error-type-dependent response coefficients from an unbiased reference circuit without fitting to finite-bias data. These coefficients are incorporated through effective error parameters, yielding a median fold error of 1.09 over the evaluated finite-bias conditions. Geometries selected by the model are validated through direct biased circuit-level simulations. At a physical error rate of 0.004 and a target logical error rate of 10^{-3}, the validated rectangular codes reduce physical qubit overhead by up to 42.4% and 26.2% under the two noise models, respectively, relative to unrotated square codes. These results provide a practical link between circuit-level bias response and resource-efficient surface code design.

title: Manufactured Authenticity: How Behavioral Signals Are Produced and Misread in Online Markets
abstract: Online platforms increasingly ask users to infer credibility from behavioral signals whose production conditions are opaque. We introduce manufactured authenticity: the platform-mediated production of observable activity that interfaces invite users to read as organic participation. Using 996,834 cryptocurrency tokens and 50,895 creator wallets from Pump.fun, a Solana-based token launchpad, we examine how legitimacy signals are produced in an automation-enabled online market. We identify four production strategies (high-velocity launching, passive launching, template-content creation, and organic-style creation) that generate distinct but interface-similar cues of activity, narrative plausibility, and participation. High-velocity and template-content strategies emerge as alternatives rather than cumulative layers: the former produces activity at scale, while the latter produces descriptions associated with higher reply engagement. Yet visible engagement does not imply broader diffusion: template-like content attracts replies without greater ownership dispersion, and tokens associated with non-organic production strategies exhibit more concentrated investor holdings than organic-style tokens. We argue that platform governance should move beyond detecting manipulation toward making signal provenance legible. We propose authenticity disclosure as a design approach for surfacing production conditions without requiring definitive claims about automation, AI authorship, or actor intent.

title: OfficePrism: Benchmarking Agents on Single-Domain Operations Across Enterprise Business Functions
abstract: Broad workplace scores can mix competence within one business function with the extra cost of coordinating across functions and systems, making failures hard to localize. OfficePrism evaluates this prerequisite through 420 single-domain enterprise tasks spanning seven business functions under shared, benchmark-defined L1--L3 task-structure levels. Each task runs in a fresh environment combining a shared synthetic organization with one function-specific domain and yped state access. Our pipeline uses grounded records, business rules, and tool schemas to jointly construct a Chinese-language ticket, a hidden executable reference witness, and an expected response, followed by automated filtering and human curation. The same task set is evaluated through full-schema and search-and-dispatch packages. Across 124 model--harness--package configurations, the per-case joint natural-language-and-database pass rate ranges from 22.6% to 76.4%, with a median of 67.9%. L1 is highest in all 124 configurations, and L2 exceeds L3 in 122. Among 50 configurations sharing the same harness and model labels across both packages, search scores higher in 30, ties in one, and scores lower in 19.

title: Fidelity Regret: Measuring Simulator Misspecification in Verifiable Design
abstract: RLVF assumes the verifier evaluates the quantity of interest. In genetic-circuit design, a topological verifier can establish that a program is a valid circuit computing the target function, whereas ranking its physical performance requires a simulator. We measure fidelity regret, the reference simple regret incurred when a cheap simulator selects the design, over a 21,362-design combination subspace spanning 5 measured gate libraries and 3 organisms. Exact ordered-assignment checks retain positive regret in every tested cell while shifting magnitudes in both directions. Mean normalized regret is 0.369 over 72 cells and only 6 have zero regret. The discrepancy depends strongly on the reference axis: the yeast library SC1C1G1T1 has mean regret 0.113 for cytometry quality and 0.801 for growth burden, and every evaluated library--circuit-size pair has positive burden regret. Topological verification ties all valid gate assignments, while an oracle whitelist subject to retaining at least 25% of the design space leaves positive regret in 30 of 52 cells. Design-space optimization and feedback-guided search with frozen language models reach the high-regret regions; on a matched zero-regret control, additional optimization instead reduces regret. At a matched modeled-cost budget, mitigation is budget- and library-dependent. An in-sample fixed rule spending $α{=}0.34$ of the budget re-scoring top cheap-simulator designs achieves mean excess regret 0.016, compared with 0.305 for cheap-only and 0.034 for reference-only selection, improving on cheap-only in 330 of 360 cells. More broadly, any workflow optimized through a simulator or digital twin can satisfy its verifier yet perform poorly on the intended physical objective. Fidelity regret provides a transferable template for detecting this gap before optimization and comparing budget-aware remedies across scientific domains.

title: Doing Well by Doing Good: Alignment of Revenue and Welfare in Robust Product Line Design through Data-Driven Optimization
abstract: Product line design (PLD) selects product variants for a firm to maximize expected revenue. Candidate assortments are usually evaluated under random utility maximization (RUM), in which choice probabilities stem from the joint distribution of latent consumer utilities. As this utility distribution cannot be directly observed and is estimated from choice data, distributional uncertainty inevitably arises. This paper studies how to hedge PLD decisions against such ambiguity. We construct a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) model that maximizes worst-case expected revenue over an l1-Wasserstein ball around a nominal utility distribution. We derive a dual reformulation for general nominal distributions and then specialize to two cases. With independent Gumbel utility shocks, the dual simplifies to a closed-form robust multinomial logit. We derive revenue gap bounds for parameters estimated from finite full-assortment choice data. When the true model structure is unknown beforehand, we adopt a data-driven scheme using the empirical distribution of sampled utility vectors and extend optimality-gap analysis to a general RUM oracle. For the NP-hard empirical problem, we propose Adaptive Parametric Search (APS), an algorithm with certified relative optimality guarantees. Numerical experiments show fast computation and better out-of-sample performance.Dual analysis shows that robustness to preference uncertainty endogenously encourages the firm to raise buyer welfare. This incentive takes distinct forms: robustness supports larger assortments in the unconstrained logit setting, whereas under the empirical nominal, it favors products with lower prices and higher utility relative to the outside option. Numerically, we identify a "doing well by doing good" effect: product lines with higher in-sample buyer welfare attain higher out-of-sample revenue and buyer welfare.

title: Algebraic Vector Fields on Compact Homogeneous Spaces are 2-generated
abstract: Let $M$ be a compact, connected manifold on which a compact Lie group $K$ acts smoothly and transitively. We show that the Lie algebra of algebraic vector fields on $M$, i.e., of smooth vector fields whose translates under $K$ span finite-dimensional spaces, is generated by two vector fields. Consequently, the subgroup generated by the flows of these two vector fields is dense in the identity component of the diffeomorphism group of $M$. For spheres, explicit generators are obtained from earlier results on spherical vector fields.

title: Gravitational waves from cosmological first-order phase transitions with fluctuation-induced friction
abstract: We study gravitational-wave production in a cosmological first-order phase transition with fluctuation-induced friction using three-dimensional lattice simulations of two coupled scalar fields. Kinetic and gradient energy in the additional field $s$ accumulates near the expanding bubble walls of $ϕ$ and affects their motion. The contribution from $s$ exceeds that from $ϕ$ at the spectral peak and has a slope similar to that of the bulk flow model over a finite interval above the peak. In the high-wave-number (UV) direction, $ϕ$ dominates and the total spectrum develops a broad feature. For the larger coupling, slowly contracting false vacuum remnants persist long after bubble merger.

title: Virtual EMI Receiver Generation (VERGE) for Improved EMI Removal in MRI
abstract: MRI is not designed to operate in the presence of EMI emitting electronic devices. To accomodate this, we propose VERGE which improves on previous EMI removal methods and can operate without external EMI sensors. VERGE estimates a reference coil non-linearly from all imaging and non-imaging coils by training a small per-scan convolutional neural net to generate a virtual coil. The virtual coil is then used with STRIDE, a reference-based EMI removal method. For single-source EMI contamination, VERGE performed similarly to the reference method. For multi-source dynamic EMI contamination, VERGE outperformed the comparison methods. Notably, VERGE with zero physical EMI sensors outperformed the comparison methods even with two physical EMI sensors. A non-linearly estimated virtual EMI coil improves reference-coil-based EMI removal under dynamic multi-source EMI, and enables effective EMI removal without physical EMI sensors or training data.

title: Anticipating or Speculating? Making Futures Pay in AI Ethics
abstract: Philosophers have recently been trying to develop uniform decision rules for instances in which physicians' judgments diverge from the recommendations of medical artificial intelligence (AI) systems. I argue that this effort is fatally flawed because the performance and appropriate use of algorithmic recommendation systems by physicians are highly context-specific, empirical medical matters rather than epistemological ones. In such instances, general decision rules can be stipulated only to the extent that they abstract away from relevant, indeed determinative, contextual circumstances. The alleged problem of physician-AI disagreement, and others like it, play into longstanding disputes in technology ethics about the viability and utility of envisioning possible futures: is this useful "anticipation" or wasteful "speculation"? I suggest that the two may be distinguished. Anticipation explores plausible futures to help inform present actions under irreducible uncertainty. Speculation abstracts away uncertainty, developing formal solutions to stipulated circumstances whose relationship to the real present is often quite unclear. Efforts to develop crisp philosophical solutions to physician-AI disagreement, among other problems, fall into the latter category. Technology ethics should remember that fruitful futures thinking must both begin from and return to the messy, uncertain present.

title: Precise Eigenvalue Asymptotics for Electrostatic Layer Potential Operators
abstract: We investigate the eigenvalue asymptotics of electrostatic layer potential operators associated with the Laplace equation on smooth bounded domains in two and three dimensions. In two dimensions, we establish precise eigenvalue asymptotics for the single-layer potential operator, up to a remainder of order $O(j^{-\infty})$. In three dimensions, we obtain refined eigenvalue asymptotics for the single-layer potential operator on arbitrary smooth surfaces and for the Neumann--Poincaré operator on smooth surfaces with everywhere positive Gaussian curvature. Under suitable nonperiodicity assumptions on the associated Hamiltonian flows, the remainder estimates in three dimensions improve to $o(j^{-1})$.

title: Teaching Language Models to Narrow Boolean Patent Searches from Search Feedback
abstract: Patent prior-art searchers issue Boolean queries line by line, broadening to find relevant documents and narrowing until candidates can be screened. We distill 38,397 Japan Patent Office search reports into executable expert strategies, re-execute them, and evaluate generated strategies by citation recall and the smallest set containing each citation. Prompted models write valid, high-recall strategies but leave citations in sets too large to screen. We adapt a generator offline from scored rollouts in two forms: strategy-level learning from a screening-aware strategy score, and line-level learning from citation-preserving narrowing credit, which upweights the query lines keeping a found citation in a smaller set. On shared rollouts, line-level credit outperforms strategy-level scores on screening measures; iterated, it cuts the median citation-containing set from 768 to under 50 and places more citations in sets under 100 documents than experts, at lower recall. Strategy-level preference learning reaches near-complete recall; the two forms are complementary.

title: Approximation numbers of Hankel Operators on Weighted Fock Spaces and the Berger--Coburn Phenomenon
abstract: Let $φ\in C^2(\mathbb{C}^n)$ be a real-valued weight whose real Hessian is uniformly positive definite and bounded. For $0<p<\infty$, $1\le q<\infty$, and possibly unbounded symbols $f$, we give necessary and sufficient conditions for prescribed decay of the approximation numbers of Hankel operators $H_f$ from weighted Fock spaces $F^p(φ)$ to weighted Lebesgue spaces $L^q(φ)$ in terms of the non-increasing rearrangement of the IDA function of $f$. We also characterize membership in the approximation ideals $\mathfrak A_s(F^p(φ),L^q(φ))$ and their weak counterparts $\mathfrak A_{s,\infty}(F^p(φ),L^q(φ))$ for $0<s<\infty$. The symbol criteria involve Lorentz, Lorentz--Zygmund, and Copson--Lorentz spaces. Our approach also yields the converse to the sufficient condition in [15], thereby completing the characterization of prescribed singular value decay for Hankel operators on a broad class of weighted Bergman spaces. For the pair $H_f$ and $H_{\bar f}$ on weighted Fock spaces, we characterize simultaneous decay of their approximation numbers and simultaneous membership in these ideals in terms of the mean oscillation function of $f$. For bounded symbols, we establish the Berger--Coburn phenomenon for both ideals in sharp exponent ranges. A new feature in the case $p<2<q$ is that the Berger--Coburn equivalence holds for $s_0(p,q)<s\le1$, where the sharp threshold $s_0(p,q)$ is strictly less than $1$.

title: Neural Network Path Optimization for Finding Transition States on a Machine Learned Potential
abstract: Transition states govern chemical reaction rates and outcomes, yet locating them remains a central challenge in computational chemistry. Double-ended search methods find transition states given reactant and product structures, but generally rely on discretized path representations developed for density functional theory, where potential energy surface evaluations are expensive. Machine learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) dramatically reduce this cost and leverage automatic differentiation to access higher-order derivatives efficiently. We introduce Popcornn, a framework to find transition states by optimizing continuous neural network paths atop an MLIP with a parallelized adaptive numerical integrator. This combination eliminates path discretization artifacts, reduces hyperparameter sensitivity, and enables non-local optimization to overcome local features using second-order potential-energy-surface information. Popcornn consistently recovers more correct transition states than standard methods such as nudged elastic band and growing string, across MLIPs on thousands of organic reactions, establishing it as a robust, automation-ready method for high-throughput transition state search. Popcornn's infrastructure is flexible in path objective, integration strategy, and optimization algorithm, making it a practical tool and platform for investigating open questions in MLIP-based path optimization.

title: SARVIA: Fast-Adapting the Strong SAR Foundation Models That Are Already in Your MLLMs
abstract: Synthetic aperture radar (SAR) foundation models provide transferable representations for diverse perception tasks in all-weather Earth observation. However, their development often relies on costly large-scale SAR pretraining, raising the question of whether such extensive domain-specific pretraining is necessary. We find that modern multimodal large language models (MLLMs) already provide visual encoders that can outperform dedicated SAR foundation models as downstream initializations. This motivates a new paradigm: reuse general visual capabilities and devote domain training to brief specialization. We therefore introduce SARVIA, an adaptive post-pretraining method that specializes modern MLLMs using self-supervised visual questions with computable answers. These questions are constructed from unlabeled observations through general image tasks that capture spatial relations and SAR-specific tasks that exploit native measurements and SAR--optical correspondence. A shared answer-prediction objective jointly trains low-rank adapters across visual and language components, with loss-driven task sampling. We then export the adapted visual encoder as a standalone backbone. With 600 adaptation steps and 2 GPU-hours, SARVIA outperforms the compared foundation models on all six SAR detection and segmentation benchmarks. Compared with dedicated SAR pretraining, SARVIA reduces domain-training costs by orders of magnitude while improving visual transfer across architectures and scales. This new paradigm shifts the emphasis from repeated, costly pretraining to a reusable specialization process that can benefit from advances in open MLLMs. Dataset and code: https://github.com/zcablii/SARVIA.

title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.

title: Heave-Ho: Decentralized Long-Horizon Multi-Humanoid Collaboration
abstract: Collaboration promises to extend humanoid capabilities beyond what individual robots can achieve. However, realizing this potential requires coordinated whole-body interactions, coherent long-horizon planning, and precise synchronization across robots. We introduce Heave-Ho, a decentralized framework for long-horizon collaborative multi-humanoid loco-manipulation. At the low level, we develop a multi-agent post-training framework that adapts a humanoid foundation tracking model to physically coupled interactions between humanoids, enabling coordinated decentralized control from local observations alone. At the high level, we train a vision-language planner and design a speech-based leader-follower coordination mechanism to synchronize decentralized execution without network communication. Trained with two identical humanoids, our system scales to teams of up to ten robots and generalizes to heterogeneous teams without retraining. To benchmark these capabilities, we introduce HH-Bench, comprising 12 tasks involving teams of 2 to 10 humanoids, including heterogeneous teams. Systematic evaluations show that Heave-Ho consistently outperforms baseline methods, while real-world experiments demonstrate robust decentralized collaboration across challenging tasks.

title: Residual Curvature and Wald Calibration in Autocorrelation-Based Timescale Estimation
abstract: Autocorrelation-based timescale estimation often fits a single exponential to a finite sample autocorrelation vector, even when the underlying process is not autoregressive of order one. We examine the first-order uncertainty of this fixed-lag projection under model misspecification. Standard extremum-estimation arguments yield a sandwich variance whose denominator is the full population curvature, including a residual-second-derivative term omitted by a Gauss-Newton approximation. A conditional sign rule and two stationary Gaussian examples with exact standard-error ratios 14/13 and 13/15 show that omission can underestimate or overestimate uncertainty. Full-to-Gauss-Newton population standard-error ratios are 1.34 and 1.45 in two K=36 noise-mixture models and range from 0.38 to 1.37 across an evaluated published-process parameter grid. In a follow-up experiment with 24,000 synthetic series, empirical standard deviations in four Gaussian models are consistent with the full-curvature scale at the main sample length, whereas the Gauss-Newton scale is substantially too small in the two noise-mixture models. In all 4,000 observed replicates of the primary condition, full-curvature intervals contained their Gauss-Newton counterparts, constraining the observed coverage gain to be nonnegative. Fixed-bandwidth HAC targets a smoothed long-run variance, and full sample curvature can worsen finite-sample coverage in an exactly specified model. Bandwidth-specific results, directional coverage errors, and oracle comparisons separate curvature effects from long-run variance estimation and transformation effects. These findings identify an application-specific discrepancy in a published autocorrelation-domain variance formula and characterize its asymptotic and finite-sample consequences.

title: Explaining Realized Returns: Roll's $R^2$ 40 Years Later
abstract: Can we explain asset price movements even with hindsight? Reinterpreting Roll's (1988) AFA Presidential Address, "$R^2$," as a modern empirical exercise, we show that conventional macroeconomic, cash-flow, expectations, and flow variables explain less than 10% (often with negative $R^2$) of monthly U.S. equity return variation out of sample and lack daily observations. We use generative AI to extract reasons stated in Wall Street Journal market summaries while filtering out price-related language. These reasons explain around 30-40% of daily and monthly return variation out of sample. Their content spans interpretable themes, including corporate news, macroeconomic conditions, monetary policy, sentiment, and geopolitics.

title: DACE: Diversity-Driven Adversarial Co-Evolution for Robust LLM Safety Alignment
abstract: Ensuring robust safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly difficult as adversarial attacks evolve and outpace alignment pipelines built on pre-collected data. Existing co-evolutionary frameworks let the defender chase a moving attacker, yet their training dynamics expose two compounding pathologies: \emph{attack strategy collapse}, where the attacker overfits to a narrow set of high-reward rewrites, and \emph{defense adversarial forgetting}, where the defender loses competence against earlier attacks as the attack distribution drifts. Existing remedies are partial: attacker-side diversity rewards score textual novelty rather than strategy novelty, and defender-side replay relies on discrete judge scores that ignore estimation uncertainty, response stochasticity, and defender non-stationarity. We introduce \textbf{\method}, a diversity-driven adversarial co-evolution framework that targets both pathologies jointly. On the attacker side, \method couples an explicit two-dimensional strategy space (risk category $\times$ attack style) with a \emph{normalized marginal coverage gain} reward, providing a bounded, non-vanishing exploration signal at the strategy layer. On the defender side, \method maintains a unified \emph{Bayesian adversarial replay pool} whose Beta--Bernoulli threat posteriors are refreshed by time decay and sampled via Thompson sampling, anchoring defender training to an evolving threat landscape. Across standard safety, automated-attacker, and general-capability benchmarks, \method improves robustness to out-of-distribution attacks while preserving general capabilities, and yields broader attacker strategy coverage.

title: Critical Times for Local Controllability and Steady-State Transfer of a Water Tank
abstract: We determine the critical times for a water tank governed by the one-dimensional Saint-Venant equations with horizontal acceleration as the control. Time is measured in units of the linear wave crossing time. For $C^1$ fluid trajectories and continuous controls, local exact controllability holds exactly for $T>T_c=2+d_c\approx 2.43674$, where $d_c$ is determined by two transcendental equations. In the same trajectory class, the system is locally controllable between still-water equilibria if and only if $T>2$. These thresholds confirm Coron's conjecture for steady-state transfer and give a larger value for local exact controllability. The same quadratic endpoint formula and nonlinear correction yield the positive results for both problems. At $T_c$, comparison with a critical plane curve gives the obstruction to local exact controllability. At $T=2$, the nonlinear flux forces small trajectories between still-water equilibria to be stationary.

title: XM-Sparse: High-Throughput Sparse-Attention LLM Serving over Scale-up Memory Pools
abstract: Sparse attention has been increasingly adopted by production LLMs for long-context inference, yet serving systems must still retain the full KV history, making GPU HBM capacity a key limit on serving concurrency. Existing systems offload the KV cache to host memory, but suffer from the limited bandwidth of PCIe and the limited capacity of host memory. Emerging scale-up memory pools (e.g., X-Mem) relieve both limits and open new opportunities for sparse-attention offloading. In this paper, we first conduct an in-depth analysis and reveal that, even with scale-up memory pools, decode throughput remains bounded by HBM capacity, as hot KV buffers and the fully resident indexer key (K-index) cache occupy substantial HBM. Moreover, the two caches exhibit distinct access patterns. Based on these insights, we present XM-Sparse, the first sparse-attention offloading system over scale-up memory expansion. The core idea of XM-Sparse is to offload both caches aggressively while matching each with an I/O mechanism tailored to its access pattern. Specifically, for dynamically selected KV entries, XM-Sparse fuses TMA-based retrieval with attention in a tile-level pipeline to hide on-demand retrieval latency. For predictable K-index accesses, it prefetches pages via SM-efficient GPU-initiated DMA and coordinates prefetching with latency-critical operations to avoid interfering with decoding. We have implemented XM-Sparse atop SGLang, and our experiments on DeepSeek-V3.2 and GLM-5.3 with an emulated scale-up memory pool show that XM-Sparse delivers up to 4.98$\times$ and 4.52$\times$ higher decode throughput than PCIe-based ECHO and HiSparse, respectively, and up to 1.34$\times$ over a naive integration on the same platform, across 16K-1M contexts.

title: SeasonRainBench: Global Seasonal Precipitation
abstract: Accurate seasonal precipitation forecasts help societies prepare for drought, flooding, and crop failure months in advance. While data-driven methods have made rapid progress in weather and subseasonal forecasting, operational seasonal precipitation prediction still relies on numerical ensemble systems. These systems are computationally expensive and exhibit biases and drift that increase with lead time, motivating more efficient data-driven alternatives. Yet this transition faces three linked challenges: comparing data-driven forecasts with operational ones requires (1) a global benchmark that does not exist, scoring them requires (2) metrics that capture operational priorities beyond anomaly correlation (ACC) and RMSE, and training them must (3) rely on a single, short observational record. To address the first two challenges, we introduce \BenchName, the first such benchmark, covering monthly precipitation forecasts 1--5 months ahead. It pairs global $1^\circ$ satellite precipitation with oceanic and atmospheric predictors, includes seven operational centers, and provides 310,944 simulated months from 52 climate models for training. Beyond standard scores, we introduce two operationally motivated metrics for anomaly strength and monthly rain-belt position. To address the third challenge, we develop \MODEL, which learns from simulations what the record lacks and transfers it to Earth through three modules: SimForced aligns the climate background, SimMemory transfers a history encoder pretrained on simulations, and SimAnalog supplements Earth labels with simulated analog outcomes. Extensive experiments show that \MODEL{} improves ACC, CRPS, anomaly strength, and rain-belt position by 12.0\%, 3.6\%, 2.9\%, and 0.3\% over the strongest operational or data-driven model, opening a path from simulated worlds to Earth system prediction.

title: Approximating Itô Processes in Adapted Wasserstein Distance with Finite Support Laws
abstract: Motivated by finite-scenario surrogates in stopping and control problems, we study the approximation of Itô diffusion laws by laws supported on $M$ paths in an adapted Wasserstein distance, which we term adapted functional quantization. Under the strict adapted Wasserstein distance, no finite-support approximation can achieve vanishing error, while even under its relaxed counterpart, naive empirical measures still fail to converge. To resolve this, we develop a recursive conditional sampling algorithm and derive constructive upper bounds on the adapted quantization error. In one dimension, this yields the Brownian rate $(\log M)^{-1/2}$ for every diffusion with continuous coefficients of linear growth and pathwise uniqueness. In several dimensions, a quantitative Osgood stability condition with exponent $β$ yields the rate $(\log M)^{-η_p}$, where $η_p=\min\{1/2,β/(β+4p-2)\}$. Without the Osgood condition, we construct a two-dimensional diffusion with smooth bounded coefficients whose adapted quantization error decays more slowly than $(\log M)^{-γ}$ for any $γ>0$.

title: Towards Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow for Climate Downscaling: What Projections Can Certify?
abstract: Statistical downscaling restores the regional detail behind flooding and crop stress, but diffusion and flow-matching generators can produce sharp fields that break the conservation laws of their coarse input. Physics-Constrained Rectified Flow (PC-RF) is a conditional flow-matching downscaler. Its training penalties target wind divergence, negative precipitation, and mass drift from the coarse total, and a projection after sampling removes the last two exactly. On one corrupted synthetic field with no trained network, the projection drives the Non-negativity Violation Rate (NVR) from 0.236 and the Mass-Conservation Error (MCE) from 0.184 to zero, and the penalties lower the Divergence Error (DE) by about 30%. On ERA5 the projection gives PC-RF and RF-base, the penalty-free rectified-flow baseline, an NVR of exactly zero and an MCE of zero up to float32 rounding. The penalties add no perceptual gain that we can separate from training budget or run-to-run variation. At a matched budget on 2019-2021, PC-RF has no edge over RF-base (SSIM 0.939 vs. 0.942, PSNR 31.81 vs. 31.79, CRPS 0.771 vs. 0.772). Our unprojected CorrDiff reimplementation beats both flow models on PSNR (28.38) and CRPS (1.092) on 2020, yet 45% of its ensemble-mean precipitation cells are negative. On ERA5 a sign error in the divergence operator made that penalty and DE act on a deformation-like term. The fine reference is interpolated from ERA5 and accumulates precipitation over a longer window, so the perceptual scores cannot establish downscaling skill. NVR and MCE need one pass and no fine reference, so we argue they should run first as pass-or-fail checks, with DE as a diagnostic.

title: Nonlocal regularization of sharp-crack energetics: a variational bridge from Griffith geometry to emergent constitutive degradation
abstract: We develop a variational diffuse-crack model based on nonlocal averaging of tensile strain energy. A bounded potential acts on the scaled average, while the compressive energy remains local. The initial slope preserves the averaged tensile strain-energy density to leading order. The first variation yields a constitutive stress in which the tensile contribution is multiplied by the adjoint average of the derivative of the saturation potential. The resulting degradation is therefore determined by the stored-energy functional, without introducing an independent fracture field or prescribing a separate degradation law. For fixed smooth displacement fields with bounded strain, the energy density converges to the classical elastic strain-energy density as the averaging radius tends to zero. The Griffith surface-energy coefficient is recovered for planar opening transitions. A structure-preserving scalar auxiliary variable (SAV) scheme satisfies an exact discrete balance between the modified-energy increment and external work. We compare SAV and velocity-Verlet solutions for dynamic crack branching and Kalthoff--Winkler impact.

title: Uniform spatial Schauder estimates for backward stochastic partial differential equations with random coefficients
abstract: We prove spatial Schauder estimates for super-parabolic backward stochastic partial differential equations. All coefficients can be random and depend on time and space, and the estimates are uniform in probability and time. The key ingredient is a weighted conditional energy norm adapted to the parabolic scale of each frequency block. Together with heat-kernel bounds and coefficient freezing, it controls the gradient-martingale coupling without assuming a bounded martingale integrand. As an application, we establish Schauder solvability for semilinear stochastic Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equations.

title: Learning Regions of Attraction for Transverse Feedback Linearization under Controller Singularities
abstract: Transverse feedback linearization (TFL) achieves path following by exactly linearizing the error dynamics, but its controller is undefined on a singular set, such as zero speed for a unicycle or zero thrust for a quadrotor. The constrained region of attraction, the set of initial states from which the closed loop converges to the path without violating state or regularity constraints, determines where the controller can be safely activated. Exploiting the exact linear error dynamics, we show that this region is the largest forward invariant subset of the admissible set. We then decompose its state-constrained Zubov value function into an analytically known quadratic cost-to-go and a safety value function. We learn only the latter, by fitted value iteration without infinite-horizon trajectory labels. The resulting estimate combines an inner layer verified by interval branch and bound with a learned outer layer tested on samples. On a unicycle following a circle and a sinusoid and on a planar quadrotor, it covers on average 72.0%, 83.4% and 19.1% of the simulated region of attraction. In comparison, the quadratic cost-to-go and two physics-informed neural network (PINN) solvers of Zubov's equation cover at most 11.3%, 4.0% and 0.0% on average. Code and animations are available at https://gradslab.github.io/roa_tfl

title: Decoding Without a Decoder: Direct Pixel Prediction from Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.

title: ConfGuard: a physics-grounded reference monitor for predictive-maintenance large-language-model agents
abstract: Large-language-model agents now close the industrial predictive-maintenance loop, reading sensor windows, retrieving procedures and dispatching work orders. Two attack channels meet there: injected text in a retrieved document can hijack the decision, and a bounded sensor perturbation can corrupt the remaining-useful-life estimate behind it. Recent agent defenses police data provenance and tool privilege but cannot tell whether a prognostic quantity is physically plausible. ConfGuard is a reference monitor with a physics-grounded policy. Its conformal monitor tests each prediction, anchored to the asset's admitted history, against degradation physics: capped remaining life never rises and falls at most one cycle per cycle. Calibrating its threshold over whole asset trajectories lets the operator set the expected share of a clean asset's windows the running monitor escalates. A physics-policy validator checks the agent's maintenance-urgency decision against the decision a deterministic policy derives from the same interval. On all 10,196 C-MAPSS test windows the monitor cuts a covert attacker's reach on healthy assets from 0.529 to 0.046 and closes suppression of failing assets (0.151 to 0), escalating 0.027 of clean windows against a 0.05 target, while the fixed physical range it replaces leaves both attacks open. Behind a Qwen3-14B planner the composed monitors hold urgency-class injection to 0.00 and the universal sensor attack to 0.12, against 0.29 and 0.54 for a defended prompt.
