However, this scheme relies on an additional Short Integer Solution (SIS) assumption and SIS-based commitments, which only support relaxed range proofs. Consequently, these schemes are forced to adopt significantly weaker parameter choices, resulting in additional online overhead. In this paper, we propose a novel vPIR protocol that employs a newly designed error-correcting code-based commitment scheme as the database digest. This approach (i)supports efficient proofs of linear relations, (ii) achieves precise range proofs and (iii) eliminates the reliance on the SIS assumption. Thus, our scheme successfully adopts parameter choices identical to those of SimplePIR. As a result, our vPIR protocol is the first to achieve exactly the same online communication and server computation costs as SimplePIR, while keeping online client computation nearly identical. Additionally, compared to VeriSimplePIR,our protocol reduces online communication and client-side computation by approximately 20%, and decreases online server-side computation by over 35%.

title: Electrical addressing of compensated magnetic order in artificial spin ice
abstract: Compensated magnetic systems, such as antiferromagnets, hold immense potential for spintronic devices thanks to vanishing stray fields, robustness to perturbations, and ultrafast dynamics. Yet, electrical writing and reading of their order remains a major challenge. Here we use artificial spin ice as a mesoscale platform in which compensated order can be engineered, directly imaged, and electrically controlled. Specifically, we demonstrate combined electrical writing and reading of a compensated state in a triangular artificial spin ice. Exploiting the orientation dependence of the spin-orbit torque switching current, we independently switch three nanomagnet sublattices through a single current channel, with the planar Hall effect providing sublattice-resolved readout. This grants access to all eight magnetization states of the triangular plaquette, including its fully compensated state, yielding a nonlinear, history-dependent electrical response. Our results establish an approach to electrically programmable compensated magnetic systems and provide an important foundation for reconfigurable magnetic devices and unconventional computing.

title: A novel method for dust evolution in protoplanetary disks and a new criterion for gap opening
abstract: We present the Grain Residence-Time Method (GRTM), a computationally efficient particle-tracking approach for studying dust evolution and trapping in protoplanetary disks. By reconstructing steady-state dust distributions from particle residence times, this method provides a way to obtain radial dust surface density profiles without directly evolving the dust as a fluid. We compare the GRTM with dust profiles computed via standard methods using the $\texttt{FARGO3D}$ code, which models the dust as a pressureless fluid, and find very good agreement over a wide range of parameter space. Finally, we investigate how dust gap formation depends on the planet-to-star mass ratio ($q$) and Stokes number ($\mathrm{St}$), through a parameter study, establishing an empirical criterion for dust gap opening. In doing so, we have discovered a new regime of gap opening for small grains with $St \lesssim 10^{-2}$ and for planet mass well below Jupiter's, which is likely very relevant for gaps seen in ALMA images.

title: FastSpecFit: Spectrophotometric Modeling of 38 Million Extragalactic Targets from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Second Data Release
abstract: Optical spectrophotometry provides a direct window into the physical conditions, kinematics, and formation histories of galaxies and quasars. FastSpecFit is an open-source Python software package that forward-models each Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) spectrum jointly with its broadband photometry, convolving stellar-population synthesis and emission-line templates with each fiber's native spectral resolution. This forward-modeling approach preserves DESI's uncorrelated pixel statistics, fits a typical spectrum in ~0.1 s of single-core time, and scales to tens of millions of objects, with uncertainties estimated via Monte Carlo resampling. FastSpecFit measures stellar velocity dispersions, non-parametric star-formation histories, stellar masses, star-formation rates, dust attenuation, K-corrections, rest-frame magnitudes, and fluxes and equivalent widths for 46 emission lines, including separate narrow and broad components for the Balmer lines. We describe these algorithms in detail, validate the measurements against independent codes, and present the resulting value-added catalog for DESI Data Release 2, which provides spectrophotometric and physical properties for 38 million extragalactic targets at 0<z<4. We also release a companion photometry-only catalog and document the catalogs previously released for the DESI Early Data Release and Data Release 1.

title: Entanglement cost and classical capacity of multimode Gaussian states and channels
abstract: Gaussian states and operations are central to continuous-variable quantum information and communication. For systems with any finite number of modes, we prove that entanglement of formation, Gaussian entanglement of formation, and entanglement cost coincide for every finite-energy bipartite Gaussian state. Their common value is strongly superadditive and lower-bounds entanglement of formation and entanglement cost for arbitrary non-Gaussian states with the same covariance matrix. We then determine the entanglement cost of every multimode Gaussian channel as well as its classical capacity under a mean energy constraint. These quantities reduce to Gaussian covariance optimizations, and the capacity is attained by pure Gaussian signals with Gaussian displacement modulation, independently across channel uses. The proof combines geodesic convexity of entanglement for pure Gaussian states with a relative-entropy inequality for arbitrary states. We also obtain a closed formula for the entanglement cost of a family of four-mode bound entangled states.

title: Problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates for improved QAOA
abstract: We show that the use of problem-adjusted excited eigenstates of the $X$-mixer Hamiltonian can be beneficial for the performance of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) when applied to problems with degenerate ground states. We show that this advantage persists in the presence of quantum gate and readout noise, with the problem-adjusted excited initial states achieving better optimal performance than the standard ground state initialization. The realized advantage depends on the number of QAOA layers and whether or not the initial state has a reasonable time evolution path into the ground space of the problem Hamiltonian. We also explain how to prepare these problem-adjusted $X$-mixer eigenstates exactly, as well as how to approximate them using a linear combination of ladder operators. Finally, we discuss how the power of these initial states can be applied to any problem Hamiltonian regardless of the degeneracy of its ground state by making use of a Grover-style mixer Hamiltonian.

title: Exact Inversion of Relaxation from Rheometer Measurement Data
abstract: A rheometer is commonly used to measure the input-output relation for analyzing the relaxation of stress for rheological materials. Here, the input is a time-harmonic torque and the output is the angular displacement. This paper aims to propose an exact inversion scheme of the relaxation function from two input-output relations only having different moments of inertia. The relaxation function is represented by a Prony's series of known number of terms, with a positive constant term and terms with distinct relaxation times. The augmented system relates the material parameters to its characteristic roots. These roots are the poles of the transfer function. Here the transfer function is the Laplace transform of the output divided by that of the input, and it is a rational function in the Laplace variable. The poles of the transfer function are recovered using Pade's approximation. By measuring two input-output relations only having different moments of inertia, we can rigorously recover the relaxation function. Thus, we note a clear link between the characteristic roots and the poles. Numerical experiments reconstruct the relaxation function from synthetic angular displacements corresponding to two given moments of inertia based on our inversion method. The results show the effect of measurement noise on the recovered characteristic roots and relaxation function.

title: Reconstructing hidden attractors with reservoir computing
abstract: Hidden attractors are difficult to locate as their basins of attraction do not intersect with any small neighborhood of an equilibrium point. We examine the possibility of reconstructing the hidden chaotic attractor from time series via reservoir computing, where the reservoir is built by a network of driven Kuramoto oscillators. We compare all-to-all coupling, nearest-neighbour ring coupling, and a ring with one modified oscillator equation which ensures that any attractor will be hidden. The numerical results suggest that ring coupling supports accurate reconstruction over a wider range of coupling and forcing strengths than all-to-all coupling. Searches near reservoir equilibria nevertheless show why agreement in short-term prediction and long-term statistics does not establish preservation of hiddenness. Numerics for the modified ring show that it has the highest performance which coincides with our intuition that reconstructing the global dynamics would yield a more faithful attractor reconstruction. We also show that this construction precludes global forgetting of initial conditions for constant inputs, although local conditional contraction along a nonconstant signal remains possible. The distinction between reconstructing attractor dynamics and preserving basin structure provides a basis for evaluating and designing reservoir models of hidden attractors.

title: Tannaka groups of holonomic D-modules on semi-abelian varieties are almost connected
abstract: In this short note we prove that Tannaka groups arising from convolutions of D-modules on complex semi-abelian varieties are almost connected. This generalizes results known for tori on the one hand and abelian varieties on the other.

title: Round hyperspheres uniquely minimize most tangent-point energies
abstract: We show that round hyperspheres uniquely minimize a broad class of generalized tangent-point energies among all boundaries of bounded Caccioppoli sets sharing the same perimeter or enclosed volume. This includes closed $C^1$-hypersurfaces. Equivalently, we establish sharp lower bounds for the associated scale-invariant ratios of energy to surface measure and energy to volume, respectively, with equality precisely for round spheres.

title: Action-outcome coupling: a pre-investment feasibility audit for offline reinforcement learning in supply chain operations
abstract: Prescriptive analytics initiatives in logistics, such as offline reinforcement learning and next-best-action systems, are often funded before anyone verifies that the available historical logs can support an improved decision policy. We formalise this pre-investment feasibility question via action-outcome coupling: a total-effect variance index measuring how much expected outcomes change with the logged action. Coupling provides an algorithm-independent upper bound on any policy's achievable value, expressed in monetary units per decision for both single-step and discounted sequential objectives. We also analyse the asymptotic false-licensing risk of an invalid workflow: fitting a value model and evaluating the model's greedy policy on the same data. The false-licence rate is driven mainly by the number of state cells over which selection is performed, rising from the nominal test level with one cell to near certainty with a few dozen, while overlap has a smaller effect. We then propose an audit that assigns logs to four tiers of decision support, separately for fixed and contextual policies, and returns an explicit stopping rationale. On a randomised e-commerce log, the audit endorses a fixed recommendation policy, certifying gains equal to 30 per cent of the theoretical ceiling; the remaining gap reflects bound looseness under an 80-action design. Two public logistics logs fail at different checkpoints: one because the target is an accounting identity of the action, and another because, with 27 clusters, estimated coupling stays below the design's detectability threshold even though a conservative offline learner certifies an improvement in 29 of 30 seeds.

title: SWIR-cGAN: Synthesizing SWIR Bands Using VNIR Imagery from CBERS and AMAZONIA-1
abstract: Spectral band synthesis is an important research topic in remote sensing. The Brazilian satellites CBERS-4, CBERS-4A, and AMAZONIA-1 provide high temporal resolution (1-3 days) visible and near-infrared (VNIR) imagery through the Wide-Field Imager (WFI), but lack short-wave infrared (SWIR) bands. Recent deep learning methods have shown promising results for spectral synthesis, but challenges remain for cross-satellite generalization and spectrally distant bands. This paper presents a conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cGAN) with an attention-enhanced U-net generator and a multi-loss objective to synthesize Sentinel-2/MSI SWIR bands 11 (SWIR-1) and 12 (SWIR-2) from WFI VNIR inputs. Experiments used 4,125 patches for training and cross-validation and 1,026 unseen patches for testing, with hyperparameters optimized using a subset of the training data. On SWIR-1, the model achieved SSIM of 0.900, PSNR of 31.44 dB, and MAE of 0.019 in TOA reflectance. On SWIR-2, it achieved SSIM of 0.917, PSNR of 33.35 dB, and MAE of 0.015. Benchmarking was performed on the test dataset, with each model optimized separately prior to evaluation. SWIR-cGAN outperformed the baselines, particularly for SWIR-2. The ablation study identified the multi-loss as the main performance contributor, while the attention and residual modules provided additional improvements. Our results demonstrate the feasibility of synthesizing SWIR bands from WFI imagery. The SWIR-cGAN is available at https://github.com/marujore/swir-cgan.

title: A short proof of the 1-1/e performance of RANKING on the complete upper triangular instance
abstract: The randomized online bipartite matching algorithm RANKING of Karp, Vazirani and Vazirani (1990) matches, asymptotically, a fraction $1-1/e$ of the vertices of the complete upper triangular (CUT) instance. We give a short proof of this fact that looks at the final matching from the offline side. A single observation drives the argument: the first $k$ arrivals can distinguish the offline vertices $v_k,\ldots,v_n$ only through their ranks. As a consequence, whether $v_k$ is matched is decided by a uniform draw among the remaining ranks, and the number of matched vertices among $v_1,\ldots,v_k$ is a Markov chain with explicit transition probabilities. A linear differential equation, solved by hand, gives the limiting profile of this chain, and the constant $1/e$ appears where the matching probability reaches one.

title: Non-local Transport Geometry for Papangelou Point Processes
abstract: We develop new analytical tools for the analysis of interacting point processes and their associated dynamics by introducing a non-local Benamou-Brenier-type transport distance tailored to (stationary) Papangelou point processes. Under a suitable Dobrushin-type condition, quantified by a constant $ζ$, we show that the natural spatial birth-and-death dynamics associated with a Papangelou point process is the EVI$(ζ)$-gradient flow of the (specific) relative entropy. Moreover, we establish $ζ$-geodesic convexity of the (specific) relative entropy and derive new functional inequalities, including HWI, Log-Sobolev, and Talagrand inequalities.

title: Code World Model 2.0: Towards Infinite Controllable Video Generation
abstract: Visual proxies decouple explicit world-state simulation from photorealistic video synthesis, offering a controllable interface for both offline clip creation and real-time interactive streaming. Yet a practical renderer must address two challenges. Upstream proxies vary from coarse layouts to fine articulated geometry depending on the interaction, and streaming inference must operate in a few causal steps without accumulating drift across self-generated history. We present Invoker-Render, pairing a bidirectional creation model with a causal four-step streaming model under a shared conditioning interface over structural proxies, an appearance reference, and language. Trained on an aligned approximately 200-hour multi-granularity corpus, Invoker-Render honors fine geometric constraints when supplied while synthesizing plausible local motion under coarse proxies, enabling runtime selection of input detail. To bridge bidirectional creation and real-time streaming without compounding step compression and rollout drift, we introduce Progressive Forcing (ProForcing). ProForcing first trains a causal predictor and distills it into a four-step renderer using histories derived from training videos. Training then shifts to continuous self-generated rollouts. A pipelined serving stack supports efficient streaming inference. Experiments show versatile control across proxy families, granularities, and camera paths, consistent gains over recent streaming baselines, and stable 30-minute racing rollouts that preserve scene and subject appearance.

title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

title: Sideslip-Conditioned Drift Trajectory Planning with Flow Matching and Control Barrier Functions
abstract: Drifting, the deliberate control of a vehicle at large sideslip angles, is relevant to both motorsport and recovery from unexpected oversteer. Existing autonomous drifting methods typically determine drift intensity through predefined reference trajectories, optimization objectives, or learned policy rewards, rather than accepting a desired sideslip angle as an explicit input. We propose, to the best of our knowledge, the first generative drift trajectory planner explicitly conditioned on a requested peak sideslip angle. A conditional flow matching model is trained on demonstrated drift laps with hindsight-derived sideslip labels and refined through reinforcement fine-tuning. A control barrier function (CBF) correction is then applied to satisfy model-based road, tire friction, and actuator constraints at the planning waypoints. In closed-loop experiments in the racing simulator Assetto Corsa, a nonlinear model predictive controller tracks the generated plans for six requested sideslip angles from 20 deg to 45 deg, with 30 laps (approximately 75 km) per request. The median peak sideslip angle measured across drift-corner passes follows the requested angle, with a mean absolute error of 1.2 deg across the six conditions. Ablation experiments show that reinforcement fine-tuning improves conditioning accuracy, while CBF correction substantially reduces off-road and spin events.

title: Non-Invertible Quantum Cellular Automata I: Microscopic Definition of Non-Invertible Symmetries
abstract: We introduce non-invertible quantum cellular automata (QCAs), defined as locality-preserving quantum channels that are dualizable and pure. This provides an operator-algebraic definition of non-invertible symmetries of quantum lattice systems, formulated in terms of their action on local operators. Focusing on quantum spin chains, we motivate these defining conditions and conjecture that every such quantum channel admits a realization by dualizable topological defects or, equivalently, by dualizable sequential quantum circuits. We construct a broad class of examples, including on-site non-invertible symmetries that are anomalous, as well as higher-dimensional examples. In Part II of this work, we reconstruct topological defects whose boundary algebras yield an index theory that classifies non-invertible QCAs up to blend equivalence.

title: Projected Penalty-Gradient Tracking for Communication-Efficient Byzantine-Resilient Federated Learning
abstract: We investigate communication-efficient federated learning over heterogeneous datasets in the presence of Byzantine adversaries capable of uploading arbitrary information. Penalty-based methods bound the influence of each worker through the bounded gradient of a penalty function; however, the bound is lost once the uploads are compressed, since a Byzantine worker can accumulate an unbounded state at the server. To retain the Byzantine resilience under compressed uploads, we propose a projected penalty-gradient tracking framework, where each honest worker uploads a compressed residual of its penalty gradient and the server projects each reconstructed state onto the known penalty-gradient ball. The framework accommodates any contractive compressor and yields two algorithms: fault-resilient proximal gradient with consistent sparsification (FRPG-CS), whose shared mask is protected by freshly drawn reserve rows, and lazily aggregated FRPG (LAG-FRPG), whose uploads are event-triggered. For smooth and strongly convex losses, we establish a finite-time bound on the expected objective gap, where the Byzantine error floor is independent of the compressor and the compression error decays faster than the optimization error. We also bound the expected number of lazy uploads and derive certificates that separate the finite-penalty model bias from the optimization error. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST show that the proposed algorithms attain the highest accuracy among twelve methods under the Min-Max attack, whereas a compressed-momentum benchmark and a local-update benchmark remain preferable in attack-free accuracy and total traffic, respectively.

title: Global solvability, regularity and exponential convergence in a quasilinear chemotaxis-haptotaxis system with mostly repulsive signal production
abstract: Motivated by biological and mathematical viewpoints, we systematically investigate the global dynamics of a quasilinear chemotaxis haptotaxis system with mostly repulsive signal production. We show unconditional 2D boundedness, blow up prevention for parabolic-elliptic-ODE case in nD, small data boundedness and exponential convergence under endpoint Lebesgue smallness, and 3D weak-solution eventual regularity. Our findings extend the corresponding repulsive chemotaxis only theory to the chemotaxis haptotaxis setting and demonstrate a positive effect of chemo-repulsion on global dynamics.

title: Pluricanonical locally conformally almost Kähler metrics, circle-invariant $G_2$ structures, and Laplacian flows
abstract: We study explicit Hodge evolutions of pluricanonical locally conformally almost Kähler metrics and their relation to locally conformal parallel $G_2$ structures. A compact locally conformal parallel $7$-manifold with a parallel non-zero Lee form, carrying a structure-preserving free circle action of constant orbit length orthogonal to the Lee field, has a $6$-dimensional quotient which is pluricanonical with a parallel Lee form and a non-integrable almost complex structure. The fundamental forms upstairs and downstairs are Laplacian eigenforms with an explicit eigenvalue ratio. Conversely, for a fixed normalized $SU(3)$ completion, we characterize the curvature of a circle-invariant locally conformal parallel lift. The lift equations force a pluricanonical base to have parallel Lee form, even locally, and exclude strict integrable pluricanonical bases. Independently, the pluricanonical eigenform identity gives a shrinking solution of He's full Hodge equation and an immortal $d^*d$ solution contracting the Lee plane.

title: Testing the Pareto law through a Stein-Laplace characterization
abstract: A Stein--Laplace characterization yields two closed-form goodness-of-fit statistics for the Pareto type-I family with unknown shape and known lower endpoint. The signed integral statistic $T_n$ has a standard normal limit after studentization, but explicit non-Pareto alternatives show that it is not omnibus consistent. The integrated squared discrepancy $S_n$ yields a consistent test against every fixed non-Pareto alternative on the specified support with a finite, positive logarithmic moment. We derive the weighted chi-square null limit of $nS_n$ and give conditions for an asymptotically valid parametric-bootstrap and plug-in covariance-operator method. The latter uses Nyström eigenvalue approximation to avoid repeated sample generation and parameter estimation. A large Monte Carlo comparison study shows competitive performance relative to existing procedures in the literature. In the paired study, the two calibrations have similar empirical power, with slightly higher small-sample rejection rates for the bootstrap in some settings. In the timing experiment, covariance-operator calibration is approximately $28$--$37$ times faster at $n=200$. An exploratory threshold-sensitivity analysis of Danish fire-insurance losses illustrates the dependence of Pareto goodness-of-fit conclusions on the specified tail region.

title: Dynamical Decoupling via Continuous Unitary Design
abstract: Dynamical decoupling is a cornerstone of quantum control for protecting and engineering quantum systems. However, conventional schemes rely on idealized instantaneous pulses, limiting their performance under realistic finite-duration and imperfect controls. To overcome this limitation, we establish a dynamical decoupling framework based on continuous unitary designs, which intrinsically suppresses arbitrary static noise during continuous control. We further derive closed-form phase conditions to suppress Rabi-amplitude errors, unifying universal decoupling, finite-pulse compatibility, and control-error robustness within a single analytical framework. We experimentally validate our approach on a superconducting quantum cloud platform, demonstrating significantly extended coherence times and the highest robustness against Rabi-amplitude errors and detuning among the tested sequences.

title: JALE: A new Python toolbox for coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation
abstract: Coordinate-based neuroimaging meta-analysis using activation likelihood estimation (ALE) is commonly used to synthesize reported results of functional or structural magnetic resonance imaging studies. We here present JALE, a new, open-source Python package for conducting ALE meta-analyses. Besides computing standard ALE main effects and contrast analyses, this toolbox implements several novel analytical approaches including new options for thresholding (threshold-free cluster enhancement statistics, significance threshold prediction) as well as sensitivity and cluster analyses that were only available as in-house scripts in the past. The purpose of this paper is to provide an integrated conceptual foundation of recent developments in the ALE meta-analysis framework, with a particular focus on novel methodological implementations that can be executed in a straightforward and standardized manner using the new JALE toolbox.

title: The Shared Word: Evaluating Language Models on Dutch Word Puzzles
abstract: Many LLM benchmarks for languages other than English are translated, multiple-choice, or difficult to score automatically. We introduce The Shared Word (TSW-NL), a Dutch benchmark built around four core principles: it is language-specific, open-vocabulary, human-curated, and deterministically scored. Each puzzle gives three clues that describe different senses or uses of the same Dutch word. The clues are individually ambiguous, requiring the solver to combine evidence across multiple clues. We construct the benchmark from Dutch Wikipedia disambiguation pages, followed by automatic filtering and extensive manual curation. The final dataset contains 222 instances, with three independent human answers per test item. The task is clearly challenging: scores in our human study range from 49.5% to 61.0% and the highest-scoring open-weight model we tested reaches only 39.3%. Many others even score below 20%. At the same time, closed-source models show great progress: GPT-4.1 (April 2025) scores 59.2%, whereas GPT-5.6 Sol with max reasoning scores 88.8%. We believe this task provides a useful addition to Dutch model evaluation, plus a clear recipe that can be applied to construct a similar benchmark for other languages.

title: Probing the Macroscopic Imprints of Singularity Resolution: Polarization Diagnostics of Rotating ABG Black Holes
abstract: Recent observations by the Event Horizon Telescope have revealed important electromagnetic information around the supermassive black holes $\text{M87}^*$ and $\text{Sgr A}^*$, providing experimental supports for investigating physics near the event horizon. In the absence of a complete quantum gravity theory, exploring the observational appearances and polarized images of accretion flows in regularized geometries, and seeking specific observational differences from Kerr black holes, is of value for understanding the singularity problem. Based on backward ray tracing method, this work investigates both the optical and polarimetric observational features of rotating Ayón-Beato-García spacetime with regularization parameter $Q$. It is found that, compared with the Kerr case, the parameter $Q$ leads to a significant contraction of the size of the inner shadow in the observed optical images. This contraction remains visible even after an illustrative Gaussian filter for images observed at a low inclination angle (e.g. $17^\circ$). In the polarized images, we focus on two observables, the electric vector position angles (EVPAs) and the depolarization regions, on the observer's screen. It is found that depolarization regions do not necessarily reside in the vicinity of the bright photon ring in images at high inclination angles (e.g. $83^\circ$), and a multi-branch structure can be observed. Furthermore, the distribution of EVPAs is insensitive to the regularization parameter $Q$ while the morphology of the depolarization regions can be impacted remarkably by $Q$. The results provide possible optical observable characteristics for the rotating regular spacetime.

title: LASH-PAT: Deadlock-Free Adaptive Shortest-Path Routing for Inter-Chiplet Interconnects
abstract: With the slowdown of transistor scaling, chipletbased systems, and in particular chiplet-based wafer-scale integration, have emerged as a promising approach to sustain growth in computing capability per cost for modern processors and accelerators. In recent years, many specialized inter-chiplet interconnect topologies have been proposed. In these topologies, the simple, well-established, and deadlock-free dimension-order routing scheme is not applicable due to its reliance on regular mesh structures. In this work, we study routing in these recently proposed inter-chiplet interconnect topologies by categorizing and evaluating nine deadlock-free routing functions for irregular topologies known from data center networking in this new context. This reveals a trade-off between turn-based routing, which enables path diversity, and layered routing, which ensures shortest-path delivery. To resolve this trade-off, we propose LASH-PAT, a routing function that extends layered shortestpath routing with adaptive path diversity. LASH-PAT supports multiple shortest paths and dynamically selects among them based on local congestion while preserving deadlock freedom. When compared to the best-performing baseline routing function for each combination of topology, traffic pattern, and evaluated metric, LASH-PAT improves throughput by 21.15% and reduces energy per packet by 12.77%, while providing latency comparable to the lowest-latency baseline routing function.

title: From quasiperiodic three-colour order on a triangular lattice to covalent carbon sheets
abstract: Can the quasiperiodic colouring of a lattice be encoded in the bonds of a single carbon sheet? We construct golden-, silver- and bronze-mean three-colour patterns on a triangular lattice. The positions of one colour determine the other two through a nearest-neighbour rule. The three patterns have eight, nine and seven first-shell environments, respectively. A triangle of three identical motifs frustrates the alternating bond ports of each of the three molecular alphabets in the golden and silver patterns. The bronze pattern admits four designs with direct or ethynylene connections. Three periodic structures reproduce its infinite environment frequencies in a local-energy model. For a 708-atom sheet with independently matched environment counts, the predicted energy lies 0.295 meV per carbon below the density-functional result. Across four periodic cells initialized from two smaller donors, relaxation changes the bond lengths by at most 0.00113 angstroms in root-mean-square terms. Fitting one 60-degree sector to relaxed periodic geometries gives complete sixfold-symmetric fragments with up to 22,140 carbon atoms. In the 13,950-atom directly linked sheet, a $π$ doublet places 79.05% of its weight in a boundary shell comprising 7.96% of the atoms, whereas the lowest unoccupied doublet places only 0.124% there. These calculations connect a testable motif-selection rule to the energetics and finite-patch spectra of candidate quasiperiodic carbon sheets.

title: Hadamard inverse mapping theorem for certain continuously Gateaux differentiable mappings
abstract: Hadamard inverse mapping theorem concerns global inversion of continuously differentiable mappings between Banach spaces. Here we consider a weaker notion of smoothness and work with continuously Gateaux differentiable mappings. We prove that a continuously Gateaux differentiable mapping with invertible derivatives such that the inverses are uniformly bounded, possesses a continuous right inverse on every compact set. We also provide sufficient conditions for global invertibility of certain continuously Gateaux differentiable mappings between Banach spaces.

title: KL-Guided Support Selection and Subspace Cubic Newton Methods for Sparse Optimization
abstract: We study sparse composite optimization with a smooth loss and a possibly nonconvex, nonsmooth regularizer. The objective is locally smooth on each fixed support. Our method combines full-space proximal-gradient steps with inexact cubic-regularized Newton steps on a subspace selected by thresholding. If the iterates are bounded and the objective satisfies the Kurdyka--Łojasiewicz (KL) property, the entire sequence converges to a first-order stationary point. A threshold based on the KL exponent ensures that the selected coordinate set coincides with the support of the limit after finitely many iterations, without requiring a nondegeneracy assumption. We also provide a residual-based threshold when such an exponent exists and its value is unknown. Under an additional continuity assumption on the restricted Hessian, the line search eventually accepts full cubic steps. With bounded cubic regularization parameters and damping parameters chosen to meet the target tolerances, we bound the number of outer iterations needed to reach restricted approximate second-order stationarity after support identification and entry into the full-step regime. We conduct numerical experiments in two settings: when the KL exponent is known and when it is unknown. In the former case, we use a degenerate problem to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. In the latter case, we compare the proposed method and its adaptive variant with existing solvers on sparse recovery and logistic regression problems.

title: A Transformer-Derived Iterative Preconditioner
abstract: Transformers trained on in-context prediction problems can learn known numerical algorithms, e.g., gradient descent. We go further, showing that their internal computations can reveal new algorithms with provable guarantees. A softmax-attention transformer trained to solve linear systems $Xw=y$ implicitly improves matrix conditioning. Tracing $XX^\top$ reveals an iterative preconditioning primitive, which we develop into RAPID, a standalone algorithm requiring no learned components. RAPID is an anytime preconditioner for symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrices, using randomized mixing and sparse local corrections to improve conditioning. Proof-of-concept experiments on synthetic and real-world problems consistently improve conditioning and reduce conjugate gradient iterations needed to reach a target accuracy. For a Haar-mixing idealization, we prove convergence to any fixed target condition number regardless of spectral distribution, with only logarithmic dependence on initial conditioning. Together, these results show how a transformer can discover a broadly applicable numerical algorithm.

title: Sobolev theory for the inverse problem of time-dependent density functional theory on the torus
abstract: We show that, given a sufficiently regular time-dependent density, there exists a unique potential such that the Schrödinger equation with this external potential has the prescribed one-particle density. We treat densities that are twice differentiable in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space; the resulting potentials are continuous in time and of finite Sobolev regularity in space. Our method of proof is to rewrite the problem as a nonlinear Schrödinger equation with a loss of derivatives, which we in turn handle with a completion-of-the-square argument. This is a refinement of our recent work [Lauritsen, Lewin, and Oldenburg, arXiv:2609.08984], which handled this loss of derivatives using the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem and treated analytic-in-space densities and potentials.

title: Generation of Sample Complex Wishart Distributed Matrices and Change Detection in Polarimetric SAR Data
abstract: The complex Wishart distribution is used to describe synthetic aperture radar (SAR) data in the so-called covariance matrix representation. We give a test statistic for detection of differences between two instances in this distribution and an associated probability measure. Generated complex Wishart distributed covariance matrices are used to show that this test statistic and the probability measure in situations with no differences follow the expected distributions.

title: Binary Affine Optimization with Nearly-Graphic Constraint Matrices
abstract: We present a polynomial-time algorithm for binary affine optimization with a linear objective when every column of the constraint matrix has Hamming weight at most 2, and prove that the problem is NP-hard when every column of the constraint matrix has Hamming weight exactly 3. We obtain fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) algorithms for the unrestricted problem provided that a nearly-graphic certificate is given, where the certificate roughly measures how far the constraint matrix is from having columns of Hamming weight at most 2. We apply our FPT algorithm to Max-Lin$_2$ on graphs and obtain FPT algorithms parameterized by the contraction distance and contraction rank of the graph, utilizing the concept of Eulerian-spanning set. In the case of contraction distance, another FPT algorithm can be used to find the corresponding certificate; that is, we obtain an FPT algorithm that requires no information beyond the problem instance itself.

title: Universal Mass Equation for Equal-Quantum Excited-States Sets~III
abstract: Using our simple logarithmic Universal Mass Equation, we considered heavy non-$q\bar{q}$ meson states. PDG2026 reported a series of mesons with quantum numbers not allowed for standard $q\bar{q}$ states. Using LQCD predictions, we evaluated a scalar $0^{++}$ and tensor $2^{++}$ glueball series for which predictions are available. This approach allows us to predict heavy states that require future experimental studies. Additionally, we consider the possible misidentification of some meson states.

title: Pair distribution function oscillations at electrostatically stabilized nanocrystal surfaces reflect nanocrystal lattice periodicity
abstract: Nanocrystals (NCs) stabilized electrostatically by short, multivalent inorganic ligands exhibit rich interactions and phase behavior believed to hinge on the configuration of ions at the NC surface, yet these molecular details have not previously been measured. Here we use double-difference pair distribution functions (ddPDFs) of total X-ray scattering to determine the configuration of Sn$_2$S$_6^{4-}$ ligands on PbS NCs suspended in multivalent electrolyte. The measured ddPDFs exhibit a $\sim$3-$\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ wavelength oscillation that extends $\sim$10 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$. Comparison with a PbS NC model decorated with Sn$_2$S$_6^{4-}$ ligands indicates ligands are aligned $\sim$radially, suggesting bidentate binding. Calculated partial PDFs show that the oscillatory signal is dominated by nanocrystal-Pb to ligand-Sn correlations. A simplified model that replaces the ligand with a strongly scattering Pt atom near the NC surface confirms the oscillation period in the ddPDF originates from the NC lattice constant. Nanocrystal lattice periodicity therefore merits consideration when interpreting ddPDFs of colloidal NCs.

title: The Kernel Reality Check: Benchmarking and Distilling Efficient Attention at Scale
abstract: Kernelized attention methods, which aim to replace the $O(N^2)$ complexity of softmax attention with $O(N)$ alternatives, have been the focus of intense research in the last five years. Despite growing interest, systematic evaluations and fair comparisons across approaches and scales are still missing. We analyze kernelized attention in two halves and highlight prominent limitations on each. On efficiency, FlashAttention achieves lower memory consumption and faster wall-clock time than SOTA kernelized methods during training and in vision transformers across most sequence lengths (with inference-time memory in causal language models the only clear exception), contradicting the core assumption for pure kernelized attention used as a drop-in replacement for softmax. We also discover that reported efficiency gains often fail to reproduce against modern baselines. On quality, current kernelized methods leave gaps of 2-10 points relative to softmax under a unified distillation protocol, and model scala alone does not close these gaps. We show this gap is not intrinsic to kernelization: LARA++, a principled extension of LARA that approximates softmax via importance sampling with adaptive proposal distributions, recovers up to 99% of softmax accuracy. We establish that the gap is closable; however, the computational overhead remains substantial, leaving the efficiency wall intact. Code is available at https://github.com/firatoncel/KernelRealityCheckNeurIPS2026

title: Symmetries of Counterfactuals: Identification and Testability of Counterfactual Maps from Covariate Heterogeneity
abstract: In general, counterfactuals are not identified from data alone, because many causal models produce the same observed distributions but different counterfactuals. A common approach to circumvent this problem is to restrict the mechanism to a class in which it becomes unique, such as triangular monotone maps or optimal transport maps. However, whether the assumed class is correct is usually not examined. In this work, we study what the data can tell us when covariates are available that influence the outcome only through its latent cause. First, we characterise all counterfactual maps that are consistent with the data. They differ from the true map by a group of symmetries that preserve the conditional outcome distributions given the covariates. The more these distributions vary across covariate values, the smaller the group. Second, we show that for the classes above, consistency with the data is equivalent to a single conditional independence, which yields a test of the assumed class. We illustrate both results on synthetic data and on the ACTG 175 HIV trial.

title: Can Decision Models Replace LLMs in Real-World Contact Center Classification and Judging Tasks?
abstract: Contact center systems often need to make bounded decisions, such as identifying a caller's intent, retrieving the knowledge-base article that answers a query, assessing agent compliance, or judging the output of AI models used in production. Decision models return a typed answer and its probability directly, making them a promising cost-effective alternative to generative Large Language Models (LLMs) in such bounded conversational tasks. However, their effectiveness in real-world contact center applications remains unclear. In this paper, we compare nine decision models against thirteen generative LLMs in zero-shot settings across eight contact center use cases: six classification tasks and two judging tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that many decision models can match the performance of frontier LLMs on contact center classification, and API-based closed decision models achieve this at the lowest per-request cost among the API models we evaluate. We further observe that their confident predictions are more accurate, enabling selective routing in real-world production scenarios. Across classification tasks, the main weakness of most decision models is abstention: they rarely choose the no-answer option, which accounts for most of their gap to the strongest LLMs (although Gemini-Decision-1 is the notable exception in this regard). We also find that the judging quality of decision models drops sharply for smaller models, and they are also more prone to position bias. In short, our findings provide practical guidance for selecting decision models based on abstention behavior, confidence, and deployment cost, rather than overall accuracy alone.

title: Mean Field Games: Large Sparse Network Limits and Laplexion Dynamics
abstract: Dynamic games are considered with large subpopulations distributed over large sparse graphs, where each agent has mean field coupling with all agents within the same cluster and meanwhile receives impact from neighboring clusters. Tractable limit models are obtained via the network limits of graph Laplacian operators modelling second order interactions. The resulting mean field game (MFG) has what is called Laplexion dynamics. For ring and torus topology cases, solutions for linear quadratic Laplexion MFG systems with infinite populations on infinite node networks are obtained via a second order linear partial differential equation system. This work focusses on the relationship between the finite population model and the sparse network limit model. We prove an $ε$-Nash equilibrium property for the obtained decentralized strategies.

title: A high-dimensional spatial-physical coupling operator for generalizable super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulent flows
abstract: Accurate representation of turbulent flows requires simultaneously capturing multi-scale spatial structures and the complex, nonlinear coupling between distinct physical quantities (\textit{e.g.}, velocity components and density). In practice, however, turbulent data are often constrained by low spatial resolution due to hardware limitations and computational costs. While current data-driven super-resolution methods have shown promise by learning mappings via convolutional neural networks (CNNs), they typically treat physical variables as independent channels. This simplified approach neglects intrinsic cross-variable correlations, causing models to struggle with high-fidelity reconstruction, particularly under extremely sparse conditions or in out-of-distribution regimes. To bridge this gap, we propose an architecture-agnostic spatial-physical coupling operator that extends the standard convolution into a joint spatial-variable dimension. Unlike conventional linear channel mixing, our framework constructs a unified spatial-physical representation within CNNs to explicitly capture local inter-variable interactions. By lifting features into a higher-dimensional manifold, this operator significantly enhances the model's representation capacity. Experiments demonstrate that this approach enables strong reconstruction performance and zero-shot generalization, offering a physics-aware inductive bias for super-resolution of three-dimensional turbulence. More broadly, this work suggests that high-dimensional operators offer a promising avenue for modeling intricate multi-scale turbulent flows.

title: Observational diagnostics of external photoevaporation at millimetre wavelengths
abstract: External photoevaporation is increasingly recognised as an important influence on protoplanetary disk evolution. However, there are no established molecular line diagnostics that can reliably distinguish external irradiation from variations in intrinsic stellar and disk properties. We use a large grid of thermochemical models to predict the fluxes of 48 transitions from eight species observable with ALMA, spanning a wide range of system properties and external FUV fields of 100 to 100,000 G0. At fixed stellar and disk properties, all transitions generally brighten with increasing FUV field strength. HCO+ and CO fluxes increase monotonically in virtually all disks, whereas lower-excitation lines, particularly those of C2H and N2H+, respond weakly and non-monotonically. However, variations in stellar mass and disk size introduce substantial degeneracies, limiting the usefulness of individual line fluxes as tracers of external irradiation. We therefore assess all pairwise line flux ratios, which can significantly reduce these degeneracies, evaluating their correlation with the external field, the magnitude of their change across the FUV range, and predicted ALMA detectability. We identify 135 promising ratios, including several combining strong FUV sensitivity and high detectability with efficient single-tuning ALMA observations. The strongest diagnostics either contrast high- and low-excitation lines of the same or co-spatial species (e.g. CO J=8-7/J=1-0), probing different regions of the photoevaporative wind, or pair an FUV-sensitive wind tracer with comparatively insensitive emission arising closer to the disk (e.g. HCO+ J=3-2/C2H N=3-2). Our results provide a framework for identifying externally photoevaporating systems from spatially unresolved emission and constraining their incident FUV field strengths.

title: Fiberpose: state-of-the-art fiber morphometry and instance segmentation with a distance-transform neural network
abstract: Analysis of fibrous structures in SEM images is a routine task in biomedical engineering and materials science. However, most available methods for fiber quantification still rely on classical image binarization followed by simple post-processing. These approaches often produce unreliable results in images with weak boundaries, heterogeneous contrast, and densely packed fibers. Here, we introduce Fiberpose, a framework that reformulates fiber analysis as direct regression of a smooth distance-transform (DT) field, together with a novel set of geometry-based algorithms specifically adapted to this representation. The predicted field directly encodes fiber geometry, while the accompanying algorithms enable instance reconstruction and measurement of diameter and orientation within a unified workflow. The framework is implemented as a standalone Python desktop application and a web tool https://fiberpose.org. On an independent dataset of fibrous SEM images, Fiberpose achieved state-of-the-art instance-segmentation accuracy in comparison with SAM2 and Cellpose-SAM, and more accurate diameter measurements than DiameterJ, Fibar and GIFT. The method remains effective in dense and weakly contrasted regions and shows qualitative generalization across microscopy modalities not represented in the training data. Fiberpose therefore provides an interpretable geometric representation and an automated pipeline for reproducible quantitative characterization of fibrous materials.

title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives
abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.

title: ResoLUT: Distilling Residual Networks into Lookup-Table Networks
abstract: Logic networks built from Boolean gates or lookup tables (LUTs) promise efficient hardware inference, but training them at depth and learning their connectivity remain difficult. We do not train logic as logic. Instead, ResoLUT distills a trained residual network (ResNet) layer by layer into LUT trees, preserving its multi-bit residual stream and BatchNorm while extracting connectivity from the teacher rather than learning it. To our knowledge, ResoLUT is the first convolutional logic network in computer vision to retain a ResNet-style multi-bit residual stream. Hard LUT decisions are used throughout training and inference, avoiding a discretization gap in the logic. ResoLUT-20 reaches 95.66% on CIFAR-10 with twice the trees, and ResoLUT-56 reaches 78.87% on CIFAR-100 and 53.69% on ImageNet at 64px, the best results of logic and lookup-table networks on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, showing that LUT networks can scale in depth. We explore and quantify the role of the residuals and the tree budget and shape. The most optimized model, a ResoLUT-8 with one eighth of the trees and further optimizations, fits on an FPGA and reaches 90.04% at 189k images per second, the highest throughput among the compared models above 85% on CIFAR-10.

title: Is model self-assessment enough for diverse LVLM ensembles?
abstract: Ensembles of diverse Large Vision Language Models have demonstrated performance beyond that of single models across multiple datasets and tasks. However, the necessary aggregation process usually relies on training, parameter fitting, or complex task-specific pipelines. Furthermore, evaluation is limited, making a fair comparison difficult. We create a unified pipeline where we perform candidate response selection: we build an ensemble by selecting the best answer from a set provided by different models. We comprehensively evaluate across 34 different means of confidence estimation, 24 ensemble configurations, 20 datasets, and two prompt specifications. We show that simple training and parameter-free approaches can be sufficient, even for ensembles of different architectures. These simple self-assessment approaches rely solely on each constituent model's confidence, without explicit calibration, yet are able to perform better than said constituent models. They are also competitive with more involved alternatives on standard metrics such as accuracy, including on open-ended problems. However, we also discover that dataset, ensemble composition, and prompt wording are key confounding variables insufficiently explored by prior work that significantly affect ensemble performance, such that the ensemble can perform worse than its best constituent model. These must be optimized for to get the most out of ensembles, at the cost of limiting their generalizability. We recommend that practitioners consider training-free ensembles only if deployment conditions can be precisely characterized, with Best-of-N configurations of strong models being a good starting point.

title: Sums and Products in Dynamically Central Syndetic Sets
abstract: Glasscock and Le introduced the notion \textit{dynamically central syndetic sets} in a minimal topological dynamical system under the minimal action of the semigroup $(\mathbb{N}, +).$ In this short note, we introduce these large sets in the semigroup $(\mathbb{N}, \cdot)$ and establish that dynamically central syndetic sets contain the Hindman configuration $\{x,y,x+y,xy\}$. Furthermore, we show that there are dynamically central piecewise syndetic sets that do not contain such configurations.

title: DDSL: Iterative Self-Labeling for Financial Market States
abstract: Financial market states lack a unique ground truth and must therefore be constructed from price data. Conventional labeling methods typically define states independently of the downstream classifier, leaving unresolved whether the resulting labels can be recovered from information available at prediction time. We propose DDSL, an iterative self-labeling framework that couples a price- and grammar-guided Viterbi labeler with a Transformer classifier through model feedback. DDSL constructs a nine-state representation that jointly encodes current and future market trends while retaining structured price emissions and temporal constraints throughout refinement. Experiments on SSE50, CSI300, CSI500, and NASDAQ100 show that DDSL increases held-out joint-state macro F1 by 78%-96% over single-pass dynamic-programming labeling. An independent GRU classifier that never participates in the labeling loop reproduces the same trend, while label entropy and class coverage remain stable, indicating that the gain transfers across architectures and is not caused by label collapse. We further show that learnability is controlled by both iteration and the model-feedback weight $β_{\mathrm{model}}$. Iterative gains diminish as successive label systems converge, whereas stronger feedback increasingly widens the performance gap between the feedback Transformer and the independent GRU. Increased learnability is accompanied by declining segment-level price-feature separation after an initial improvement. Finally, a non-anticipative event study provides partial external validation: refinement strengthens a conditional BEAR$\rightarrow$BULL reversal signal on the three A-share datasets, while the corresponding effect has the opposite sign on NASDAQ100. These results position DDSL as a structured framework for constructing market-state labels whose learnability can be explicitly controlled and evaluated.

title: Exact factorizations of countable groups into discrete and thin subsets
abstract: For every countably infinite Hausdorff topological group $G$, we construct an exact factorization $G=AB$, where $A,B\subseteq G$ and every element of $G$ has a unique representation as $ab$ with $a\in A$ and $b\in B$. Both factors are infinite, closed, discrete, and thin. A subset $C\subseteq G$ is thin if the intersections $hC\cap C$ and $Ch\cap C$ are finite for every nonidentity element $h\in G$. In any countably infinite group, an exact factorization into two infinite thin subsets can be constructed starting from any partial exact factorization with finite nonempty factors. Given a finite or countably infinite family of infinite subsets of the group, we can choose the extension so that each factor meets every member of the family in infinitely many points. If the topology on the group has a countable base and every nonempty open set is infinite, taking the nonempty members of the base as this family yields dense thin factors.

title: A Predictive Nuclear Effective Field Theory from Wilsonian Renormalization Group Principles I: Medium-mass nuclei and nuclear matter
abstract: The predictive power of nuclear effective field theory (EFT) from few- to many-body systems is substantially restricted by regulator dependence. Wilsonian momentum-shell renormalization group (RG) offers a natural framework for cutoff-independent predictions, but its many-body implementation requires regulating single-particle momentum modes, which breaks Galilean invariance. RG scaling analysis shows that this symmetry breaking is encoded in irrelevant operators whose effects can be included explicitly or absorbed into higher-body interactions. Guided by Wilsonian RG, we construct a regularization scheme for chiral EFT contact interactions and predict binding energies of nuclei up to $^{40}$Ca using interactions calibrated only to $A\leq3$ systems. The predicted energies vary at the percent level and agree with experiment for $300\leqΛ\leq450$~MeV. The same scheme reduces the overbinding of symmetric nuclear matter obtained with conventional relative-momentum regulators. Our results suggest that some model dependence observed in nonrelativistic many-body calculations originates from treating EFT vertices as static, Galilean-invariant potentials rather than as field operators regulated consistently across particle-number sectors.

title: On Ext-groups between Arthur-type modules of the graded Hecke algebras of type A
abstract: Let $\mathbb H_n$ be the graded Hecke algebra of type $A_{n-1}$. This article establishes a formula for Ext-groups between a Speh $\mathbb H_n$-module and a $W$-type $\mathbb H_n$-module in terms of Littlewood-Richardson coefficients. As a consequence, we obtain an explicit and efficient method to compute Ext-groups between a Speh $\mathbb H_n$-module and an Arthur-type module of $\mathbb H_n$. In particular, this proves new instances of a conjecture of Chan and Prasad on Ext non-vanishing between Arthur-type representations. We also discuss some other non-Ext vanishing results for calibrated modules.

title: Hierarchical Diffusion Transformer for End-to-End Image Generation
abstract: Pixel-space diffusion learns visual representations and image generation jointly in a single end-to-end training stage, without a separately pretrained visual encoder. However, plain pixel-space Transformers still trail leading two-stage latent diffusion models in generation quality and training efficiency. We hypothesize that part of this gap arises from retaining one token per patch throughout the backbone, which does not explicitly encourage a visual hierarchy that summarizes related content at progressively coarser levels. To address this, we introduce Hierarchical Diffusion Transformers (HiT), which progressively group related tokens and represent each group with a single token. The main Transformer bottleneck processes these compact group tokens, and ungrouping restores features to their original image positions. A compression budget regulates the average compression ratio across the batch, allowing group memberships and counts to vary across images and diffusion timesteps during both training and generation. The model exhibits emergent semantic structure, learning to group coherent objects and object parts without segmentation labels. In text-to-image generation, HiT further learns to group caption words with image patches depicting the same concepts, without region annotations. HiT achieves 1.48 FID on ImageNet $256\times256$ and reaches comparable generation quality to JiT using approximately 40\% of its cumulative training FLOPs. For text-to-image generation, HiT exceeds UniLiP's average score across five benchmarks with roughly $6\times$ fewer denoiser parameters and $3\times$ fewer forward FLOPs. These results suggest that learning a visual hierarchy within the generator breaks down the barrier to stronger image generation without external visual pretraining.

title: Smoothing Bias and Direction Recovery at Boundary Minima of the Nuclear Norm along Matrix Lines
abstract: We study optimal matrix directions associated with minimizing $\|G+λΘ\|_*$, the nuclear norm along a fixed affine line of real matrices with scalar multiplier $λ$. At a rank-deficient minimum, the compact polar factor can violate the tangency constraint even at the minimizing multiplier. Spectral smoothing gives a continuous scalar equation for tangency. We quantify its bias at a unique boundary minimum, where exactly one one-sided derivative vanishes. An orthogonal block decomposition shows that pseudo-Huber smoothing with scale $δ$ shifts the multiplier by exact order $δ^{2/3}$ as $δ\to0$. The Frobenius error relative to the minimum-Frobenius-norm optimal direction has exact order $δ^{1/3}$ when some singular values vanish at exactly second order in the multiplier displacement, and $δ^{2/3}$ otherwise. A sharp rank bound rules out the slower rate when $Θ$ has rank at most two. Huber smoothing gives an error of exact order $δ$ for the same limiting direction. Convergent expansions in powers of $δ^{1/3}$ also yield a three-scale extrapolation with $O(δ)$ error after restoring feasibility.

title: Training-Free Building Change Detection with Example-Induced Discriminants
abstract: Building change detection (BCD) relies on dense annotations that are costly to collect across regions. A few annotated examples offer a more economical way to specify the target, but change maps provide incomplete building supervision: they label only changed buildings and leave the building-containing date unspecified. Our key observation is that these annotations nevertheless reveal features that recognize buildings in other images, including unchanged ones. We present Linear INduced Discriminants (LIND), a training-free framework that turns regional feature contrasts into a reusable linear building classifier. Using a single frozen vision transformer, it unifies building recognition and temporal comparison in the same feature space. This approach requires neither text prompts nor an auxiliary segmentation model. Only one parameter is tuned on a single validation dataset and then kept fixed across datasets and shot settings. Extensive experiments demonstrate strong detection accuracy, cross-dataset transfer, and efficient inference, with extensions to other semantic classes and broader land-cover changes. Change annotations thus provide a compact visual specification for detection in new scenes. Code: https://github.com/lzcn/lind

title: High-Dimensional Black-Box Optimization via Guidance Sampling of Diffusion Models
abstract: Many real-world optimization problems involve optimizing black-box objectives for which only a limited number of evaluations are available. Bayesian optimization (BO) is a powerful framework for such problems, but its effectiveness often deteriorates in high-dimensional spaces. Recent work leverages diffusion models for black-box optimization, often through pre-training a reward-conditioned score network to steer generation towards high-reward samples. Alternatively, gradient-based guidance methods assume access to a differentiable reward function from which guidance gradients are queried. However, these approaches either require large amounts of labeled data for offline training or access to exact reward gradients, limiting their applicability in black-box settings. We propose BReaD (Black-box Reward-guided Sampling of Diffusion Model), a guidance sampling framework for optimizing black-box rewards without assuming access to a labeled dataset or reward gradients. The proposed method uses a Gaussian process (GP) as a differentiable surrogate for the unknown objective and actively queries labels for the generated samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the total-variation distance between the generated distribution and the target distribution. Using Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) as guidance signals, our method balances exploration and exploitation during generation and enables the discovery of high-reward regions in the data space. Numerical experiments on scientific discovery and image generation tasks demonstrate that our framework can effectively optimize black-box rewards in low-data scenarios.

title: Polymer adsorption on vicinal surfaces
abstract: While polymer adsorption is theoretically well established on flat surfaces --- and somewhat understood on rough surfaces --- the common and practically relevant case of nearly flat stepped surfaces remains poorly studied. Here, we address this gap via extensive simulations of flexible polymer chains grafted at the step edge of vicinal surfaces. For wide terraces, the polymer-step interaction yields a stable step-attached (SA) phase, alongside the desorbed and terrace-adsorbed (TA) phases, all of them separated by continuous transition lines that meet at a multicritical point previously unanticipated in polymer thermodynamics. This scenario is observed for terrace widths $\mathcal{W} \gtrsim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, being $R_g^{(2D)}$ the radius of gyration of TA polymers. Simpler phase diagrams, absent this multicriticality, are found for $\mathcal{W} \lesssim 3 R_g^{(2D)}$, where a simple crossover exists between the SA and TA phases. The presence of kinks at the steps does not alter these behaviors. Besides their theoretical relevance, these findings unveil an interesting route to produce polymer nanowires and control polymer conformation via step attachment-detachment on designed stepped surfaces.

title: CodeReel: Accelerating Code-to-Video Agents with Exact Frame Reuse and Blocking-Aware Scheduling
abstract: Coding agents make videos by writing and refining programs in a build--inspect--edit loop. A finished film costs a median of $2.85 in model calls and 11 minutes, over a third of that time in builds that block the agent. We find that much of this time is avoidable, for two reasons. First, 37.5% of the frames of a session's later films were drawn before, many shifted in time or inside an edited scene. Second, half of the builds stop at a check, where the agent needs only the verdict, but which builds stop is unknown until the checks finish. We present CodeReel, a training-free execution layer behind agents' existing commands. Exact frame reuse keys each frame by its drawing commands, regardless of its position in time, and reuses each frame whose key recurs. Blocking-aware scheduling runs the checks first and starts the render alongside them, at idle priority, unless the session's recent builds make a pass unlikely. Scheduling spends CPU to answer sooner and reuse returns it; exact keys let later versions use frames rendered for a failed one as the agent thinks. We introduce EditLoop, a benchmark of replayable agent sessions whose films are checked against renders from scratch. On it, CodeReel cuts the agent's wait by 36.3% against Rebuild, a warm pipeline with parallel rendering, and by 57.9% against Sequential, today's step-by-step pipeline. On time-shifting edits its reuse renders 43.9%, close to the 43.0% whose pixels are new, while Manim-style caching renders 99.8%. With real agents, the median wait per build is 0.62x Rebuild's in Claude Code, on topics never used in development, and 0.67x in Codex CLI. The gain holds for five models and two frameworks.

title: MI-Hyper: Generating Multiple Instance Models for Weight Space Transfer Learning in Histopathology via Mixed Tasks Pretrained HyperNetwork
abstract: Zero-shot whole-slide image (WSI) prediction aims to generalize to new pathology tasks without parameter updates at deployment. MI-Zero makes these predictions by pooling patch-text similarities. Conditional weight generation, combined with supervision from diverse pathology tasks, offers an alternative: learning to construct predictive rules from task descriptions. We introduce MI-Hyper, a hypernetwork pretrained across mixed tasks to generate the aggregation and classification weights of multiple instance learning (MIL) models. We first train the generator and a shared MIL basis jointly using source labels. We then freeze the basis and refine the generator. The generated task weights are reused across cases. Across 308 tasks from 52 pathology datasets, MI-Hyper improves mean AUC, balanced accuracy and macro-F1 over MI-Zero by 1.85, 1.17 and 0.57 percentage points, respectively. On some molecular prediction tasks, both AUC and balanced accuracy improve by more than 20 points. These results support task-conditioned weight generation as a promising approach to weight-space transfer for long-sequence modeling.

title: Rescaling OLS-Merged Adapters To Improve Personalized Image Generation
abstract: Merging multiple adapters into a single image generation model reduces deployment costs while preserving diverse task capabilities or personalization modes. State-of-the-art methods such as RegMean, Mix-of-Show, and Subspace Routing fit the outputs of the merged model to those of the individual adapters using ordinary least squares (OLS). We show that this reconstruction objective systematically shrinks task-specific signals whenever the activation distributions of different tasks overlap, producing a merged adapter that is too weak for downstream use. We derive a decomposition that quantifies this shrinkage and propose rescaling the merged update to restore signal strength. On multi-subject personalization with up to 30 merged adapters, rescaling substantially improves subject fidelity over unscaled baselines. Our approach also improves results on style transfer, concept erasure, image classification, and LLM-based text classification.

title: Shell crossing and the dynamical formation of thin shells in the collapse of self-gravitating relativistic dust
abstract: In this paper, we show that shell crossing in the collapse of self-gravitating relativistic dust in spherical symmetry can be understood as dynamical formation of a thin shell of dust. More precisely, we consider the spherically symmetric Einstein-dust system in double null coordinates (E-d), for which first singularities with area radius bounded away from zero are known as 'shell crossing' singularities. We show that there exists a weak solution of (E-d), in which a thin shell of dust forms, extending beyond any 'non-degenerate' first shell crossing singularity of a smooth 'collapsing' solution of (E-d). This local extension is unique in the class of piecewise smooth solutions of (E-d) satisfying a 'determinism condition'. We then consider the physical problem of smooth data for (E-d) on an initial hypersurface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^3$, containing a collapsing dust cloud. We show that, for generic such initial data, there exists a maximal globally hyperbolic piecewise smooth development satisfying a 'propagation condition' (stronger than the determinism condition). The development may contain an arbitrary (finite) number of thin shells which can moreover merge. All shell crossing singularities are 'resolved' and the area radius extends continuously to zero at any first singularity of the maximal development. We note that, for an open set of initial data in the smooth topology, as shown by Christodoulou, a Cauchy horizon emanates from a central 'shell-focussing' singularity.

title: SEAM: Computer-Use Agents Know the Harm Between Screens, and Commit It Anyway
abstract: Safety benchmarks for computer-use agents (CUAs) place the harm either in the intent of the task or on a single screen: a malicious instruction, an injected command, a phishing page. An agent that checks the task and each screen in isolation can pass them, so they do not test whether it combines facts seen on different screens. Yet in delegated work, harm often arises exactly this way: a fact about a person on one screen, a fact about an item on another, and a legitimate task that binds them. We introduce SEAM (Safety Execution Across Multiple screens), a benchmark of such cross-screen compositional harm: 600 multi-step, cross-application OSWorld tasks in which the instruction and every single observation are benign and only their combination is harmful. Minimal-pair variants that differ in one place, scored from the server log rather than by an LLM judge, locate where an agent fails. General-purpose open-weight and flagship agents carry out the harm in up to 92% of runs, yet decline when the user states it in one sentence. Agents open the decisive pages, so exposure is not the primary bottleneck. Asked about those pages, they flag the harm, and with thinking they often write the conflict into their reasoning and confirm anyway. Safety recognition thus does not reliably translate into safe execution, and the translation depends on the information channel: the same warning stops agents far more often in the user's instruction than on screen. Proprietary models are markedly more cautious. We release SEAM with its generator and quality gates at https://yuxuan2003.github.io/SEAM/ .

title: Hypersurfaces that are far from ruled
abstract: We show that a very general complex hypersurface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb P^{n+1}$ is not ruled whenever $n\geq3$ and $d\geq2\lceil(n+2)/3\rceil$. This improves Kollár's original degree bound to the bound subsequently obtained by Totaro for stable irrationality and, in particular, includes very general quartic fourfolds. More precisely, we find new bounds for the minimal degree of a dominant rational map from a very general hypersurface to a ruled variety or a conic bundle, improving on previous bounds of Chen--Stapleton. The proofs combine Kollár's reduction to positive characteristic with the Jacobson correspondence for inseparable extensions.
