The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

title: Faster polynomial-space algorithms for poset problems
abstract: We give a polynomial-space, deterministic, exact algorithm for counting linear extensions of partial orders over $n$ elements, with running time $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n}) \subseteq O(2.829^n)$. This improves upon the long-standing bound of $O^*(4^{n})$ attainable by standard divide and conquer (Savitch 1970, Gurevich and Shelah 1987). Our algorithm uses a similar balanced splitting approach as the classical algorithm, but applies it only to the elements outside a largest antichain. For the elements of the antichain itself we develop a formula based on inclusion-exclusion that accounts for the ways in which they can appear in a linear extension. The technique is also applicable to other problems on posets, which we illustrate by solving the well-studied jump number problem in a similar running time of $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n})$ and polynomial space. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with a running time below $4^n$ for both problems.

title: Radar-Native Control Barrier Functions: Doppler Range Rate as a Measured Barrier Derivative
abstract: Safe control around dynamic obstacles requires information about both distance and relative motion. Range-based filters commonly reconstruct the required range rate from successive range measurements or from obstacle-state estimators, which can introduce estimator delay or sensitivity to range noise when obstacle motion changes. A frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) radar measures radial relative velocity directly through Doppler. We use this measurement as the derivative of an ego-centered range control barrier function (CBF) and obtain a closed-form filter on the robot's forward velocity. A measurement margin constructed from sensor error bounds accounts for errors in range, Doppler, ego velocity, and bearing. In 508 paired encounters within the platform's retreat capability, direct Doppler produces two buffer incursions, compared with 15 for a constant-acceleration and 25 for a constant-velocity Kalman filter. On a Unitree Go1, the controller stops at $0.777 \pm 0.015$ m against the predicted $0.758$ m and reacts to a farther approaching object while a nearer static return remains. The guarantee covers the longitudinal range channel under bounded measurement errors and continuously available detections. Direct Doppler removes the need to reconstruct range rate in the safety loop, reducing the delay between a change in obstacle motion and its effect on the safety command.

title: Benchmarking Linux CGroup and Schedule Idle
abstract: cgroups are a Linux kernel primitive that limits, accounts for, and isolates the resource usage (CPU, memory, disk I/O) of a collection of processes. Many provider-side serverless systems (Mitosis, gVisor, Havest VM, FAASM) leverage linux containers based around cgroups/namespaces for their performance isolation. However, how well does this primitive map to the needs of serverless platforms? How does the linux CFS scheduler deal with cgroups and SCHED IDLE and what are the core sources of high tail latency? Would a new primitive design fit the needs of serverless isolation better? In this work we take the first step to answering these questions by profiling the current behavior of cgroups and a sched idle policy via a thorough benchmarking study. We emulate the setting of Performance-Critical (LC) server in the presence of an intensive background (BE) process and note the impact of each primitive on the performance of the server. We show it is non-trivial to balance the potential tail-latency impact on a LC server with the throughput of BE tasks. Furthermore, there are many variables to adjust for the developer between hard maximum bandwidth limits, weighted cpu shares, the presence of the sched idle policy, or additionally "niceness" priority in the scheduling policy.

title: Theorems of the Alternative and Nonnegativity Certificates for Systems of Jensen-type Polynomials with Universal Quantifiers
abstract: We introduce Jensen-type polynomials, a class of possibly nonconvex polynomials that extends the Jensen inequality for SOS-convex polynomials while retaining natural sums of squares (SOS) certificates for nonnegativity. We show that polynomials with essentially nonpositive coefficients belong to this class and establish a composition principle that yields further examples, including componentwise univariate compositions and compositions with structured quadratic maps motivated by source-localization loss functions. We then derive theorems of the alternative that provide SOS certificates for infeasibility of systems of strict inequalities involving Jensen-type polynomials and universally quantified variables. We illustrate our results through two applications, with numerical examples. First, we show that source-localization problems admit an exact SOS reformulation under a simple dimension condition, and that an optimal solution can be recovered by solving a semidefinite program (SDP) and applying the explicit Jensen map. Second, our SOS certificates yield two {\it convergent} SDP hierarchies for semi-infinite optimization with Jensen-type polynomials, providing upper and lower bounds on the optimal value. We also establish finite-convergence and solution-extraction results, under flat truncation rank condition and the associated Jensen maps.

title: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits
abstract: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.

title: Gumbel Fluctuations of the Maximum of the Airy$_1$ Process
abstract: We establish the Gumbel limit for the maximum of the Airy$_1$ process over $[0,N]$ as $N\to\infty$, with explicit centering of order $(\log N)^{2/3}$ and scale $(\log N)^{-1/3}$. The proof starts with a two-term expansion for the tail of the maximum over a fixed interval. Its leading term determines the centering, while the second term gives the joint-exceedance asymptotic for touching intervals. We then bound joint exceedances in separated unit intervals, uniformly over gaps up to a fixed multiple of the square root of the threshold. Covariance and mixing estimates control the larger gaps and complete the blocking argument.

title: From Persistent Cohomology to Maps into Arbitrary Eilenberg-MacLane Spaces
abstract: In this paper, we address the construction of Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates (functions from datasets to Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $K(G,n)$) that encode nontrivial persistent cohomology classes in arbitrary dimensions $n$ and coefficient group $G$. The construction leverages the connecting homomorphism in the long exact sequence in Čech cohomology, from the short exact sequence of sheaves of continuous maps with values in $G$, $EG$ and $BG$. Crucially, the derivation is constructive: we give an explicit, recursive formula for preimages under the connecting homomorphism, which yields a constructive version of a classical cohomology vanishing theorem and, in turn, an algorithm for general Eilenberg-MacLane coordinates. We validate our approach through experiments on synthetic datasets, and present novel examples of $K(\mathbb{Z}/2, 2)$-coordinates not addressed in prior work.

title: Protecting Web Applications using a Multimodal AI-based System for Classifying Web Injection Attacks
abstract: Web applications have been essential to accessing and managing online services. Made available with weaknesses, much due to their rapid development and human error, they are exposed to frequent web injection attacks, leaving security analysts overwhelmed with threats and alerts that often lack critical details for proper risk assessment. Detecting these attacks requires inspecting the payload of network traffic packets, which becomes inaccessible when traffic is encrypted via HTTPS, as encryption hides the content of the traffic. This paper introduces a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI) system to protect online services that rely on web application security by detecting and classifying web injection attacks, and provides security analysts with information to support attack prevention and incident response. The system employs unsupervised Machine Learning (ML) to flag potentially anomalous Network Flows (NetFlows). The corresponding data recorded in Web Server Logs (WebLogs) is then analysed using a heuristic framework based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and supervised ML to detect and classify web injection attacks. Finally, the resulting classifications are scrutinised using a Similarity Search Engine (SSE) based on Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to validate them. The solution handles encrypted traffic by analysing NetFlows and WebLogs, the latter in their natural, unencrypted form, by leveraging NetFlow-level metadata for anomaly detection and analysing web server logs after TLS termination, thereby avoiding any additional in-network traffic decryption. It was evaluated in the classification of eight web injection attack classes. The results demonstrated its ability to accurately identify attacks and their classes, achieving an F_1 score of 91% and an accuracy of 95%, and offering valuable insights for alert prioritisation.

title: LightSEAD: Lightweight SE(3)-Aware Keypoint Detector through Selective Knowledge Distillation
abstract: The pursuit of improved performance in deep learning has often been accompanied by increasing architectural complexity and computational demands. We explore an alternative direction: achieving more with less through structured supervision. We introduce LightSEAD, a lightweight SE(3)-aware keypoint detector initialised with calibrated Harris pseudo-labels and enriched through viewpoint-aware and appearance-aware supervision and selective knowledge distillation. LightSEAD comprises only six convolutional layers and 84,289 learnable parameters, achieving competitive repeatability across HPatches, KITTI 06 and 4Seasons while demonstrating its downstream applicability to relative pose estimation on MegaDepth-1500. Further optimised for mixed-precision inference, LightSEAD Coarse achieves approximately 909 FPS on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 and 139 FPS on a Jetson Orin Nano Super.

title: Conditional limit theorems in dynamical systems
abstract: This paper develops a comprehensive theory of conditional limit theorems for open dynamical systems. We study the statistical properties of the dynamics within transient regimes by establishing a suite of limit theorems describing the behavior of trajectories under the condition that they remain outside a ``hole'', or region of no return. Under a spectral gap assumption for the associated open transfer operator, we first establish conditioning and Yaglom limits and identify the corresponding conditionally invariant and conditionally ergodic measures. We then establish conditional exponential decay of correlations and the Strong Law of Large Numbers for both deterministic and quenched random systems. We also obtain a conditional Central Limit Theorem, Large Deviation Principle, and Berry--Esseen theorem, with additional assumptions in the quenched random case. We also derive standard (non-conditional) limit theorems on the surviving set of points that never enter the hole.

title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

title: CratesBump: A Version-Bump Dataset for the Rust Ecosystem
abstract: We release CratesBump, the first public dataset for predicting version bumps in the Rust ecosystem, together with semver-extract, the tool that builds it. CratesBump is built from every crate on crates$.$io with at least two releases before 14 September 2026 (about 220,000 crates), giving over two million consecutive release pairs. Each pair has 41 features (code changes from AST diffs, dependency changes, complexity, release cadence, GitHub commit and issue activity), its source repository where listed, and two labels: the literal reading of MAJOR$.$MINOR$.$PATCH, and Cargo's rule, under which a 0.y bump is a breaking change. semver-extract regenerates the dataset from public crates$.$io data and the GitHub API. To illustrate its use we (i) benchmark bump predictors on held-out repositories, finding the task learnable but far from solved, with lower scores on later releases; (ii) measure which feature groups carry the signal; (iii) check, against declared dependency ranges, how often Cargo's rule shields dependents from pre-1.0 breaking releases; and (iv) audit a sample of releases with cargo-semver-checks, finding minor and patch releases that break the public API despite their version number. Dataset and tool are released under open licenses.

title: Wei-Norman Factorization of Frenet-Serret equations and the Cardan Lock
abstract: Frenet-Serret equations for particles moving along differentiable curves, in the case of non-constant curvature and torsion, are considered in the framework of the Wei-Norman factorization of the propagator using the Lie algebra of the rotation group. It leads to a system of coupled linear equations that are highly coupled if Euler or Cardan angles are used, but that can be uncoupled if the Cartan basis in the Lie algebra is used, resulting essentially in a Ricatti equation. However, since the rotations algebra is not a solvable algebra, the global Wei-Norman Theorem does not apply and singularities in the solutions of the system of equations appear at certain points, related to the \text{gimbal o Cardan lock}. Notwidthstanding, a detailed study of the limit at these points shows that in most of the cases the propagator is well defined and gimbal lock is avoided.

title: Rented Oscillations: Multi-Tenant Data Center Workload Synchronization Attacks and Mitigation
abstract: Multi-tenant data center (DC) facilities rent computing capacity on demand, placing controllable load within reach of anyone willing to pay for it. This paper considers a stealthy adversary who rents workstations and runs deliberately unoptimized large language model (LLM) training, synchronizing their consumption into large periodic oscillations while each workload remains individually indistinguishable from benign training. The periodicity of such workloads is characterized experimentally and used to model facility consumption, showing that oscillations emerge from the interaction of concurrent workloads, whether aligned by an adversary or arising naturally. A combined small- and large-signal assessment, under a hardware-grounded threat model whose feasibility is supported by experiments on a supercomputer, locates the oscillatory weak points of the network. MW-scale oscillations are shown to saturate the generators' control limiters, amplifying their effect, while Floquet analysis reveals a lightly damped mode emerging near the forcing frequency. To counter both origins, signal-energy-based detection and mitigation are proposed, the latter re-timing the workloads to minimize the facility's oscillatory energy. The approach is validated through power hardware-in-the-loop (PHIL) experiments and real-time simulations on a surrogate model of the Saudi Arabian transmission network.

title: Simultaneous spectral measurement and programmable filtering on a universal silicon photonic chip
abstract: Spectral measurement and spectral filtering are two fundamental operations in optics, yet they are conventionally implemented using separate optical systems, hindering their simultaneous and programmable operation on a common platform. Here, we demonstrate a universal silicon photonic chip that unifies spectral measurement and programmable filtering within a single integrated architecture. The chip comprises two 8 * 8 programmable unitary transformation circuits interconnected through optical intensity modulators, forming a universal linear optical circuit. In contrast to conventional universal circuits employing equal-length interconnections, we deliberately introduce different optical path lengths between the two unitary circuits. The resulting wavelength-dependent phase evolution provides spectral diversity while preserving the programmability of the universal circuit, enabling parallel spectral measurement and programmable filtering. The fabricated chip achieves a spectral resolution of 0.05 nm over a bandwidth exceeding 100 nm, simultaneously measures eight independent laser sources, and generates multiple programmable spectral filter functions. We further demonstrate simultaneous spectral measurement and filtering during dynamic reconfiguration of the filter functions. These results establish universal photonic circuits as a versatile platform for integrating spectral sensing and programmable optical processing on a single chip.

title: Circular decompositions for hyperbolic genus one knots
abstract: We consider hyperbolic genus one knots having two or more non-isotopic, disjoint, genus one Seifert surfaces, with the property that the complementary regiones are handlebody pairs. We determine whether or not these knots have circular width equal to $(3)$. Moreover we give bounds on their circular widths. We also give explicit examples of such knots having three or five non-isotopic genus one Seifert surfaces and compute their circular widths. In particular this shows that many of these knots are non-almost fibered.

title: FlowSH: Detecting Web Attacks by Correlating Anomalous Network Flows and Endpoint Logs
abstract: Web applications compose the core of internet services, rendering them prominent targets for audacious attackers. Among web attacks, SQL injection (SQLi) remains a persistent, damaging web applications connected to databases. The widespread adoption of HTTPS has been a critical advancement for online security, ensuring the confidentiality and integrity of communications by encrypting network payloads. However, it also renders traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) less effective, as these typically rely on packet inspection of plaintext traffic. To access encrypted payloads, some NIDS resort to TLS-interception proxies, which leads to data leaks and security risks. This paper presents FlowSH, a system for detecting web attacks that is agnostic to whether the traffic is encrypted (HTTPS) or not (HTTP). Rather than decrypting packets in transit, FlowSH correlates flow-level metadata (NetFlows) with endpoint logs, which inherently contain decrypted payloads after reaching the web server. The system combines unsupervised machine learning to flag anomalous NetFlows and similarity search over server-side logs using Locality Sensitive Hashing (LSH) to confirm attacks. We implemented and evaluated FlowSH in a testbed with multiple web scanners and demonstrated its detection effectiveness, detecting 70% of SQLi attacks missed by ModSecurity, a leading web application firewall.

title: EyeDiT: Anatomy-Grounded Multi-Modal Eye Generation and Simulation
abstract: Synthetic eye data are critical for rapid development of eye tracking (ET) in AR/VR applications. However, existing synthetic eye generators are largely image-centric and lack a high-quality underlying 3D anatomy of the eye, which limits their control mainly to the gaze and provides no anatomical labels. To address this problem, we propose EyeDiT, an anatomy-grounded, multi-modal 3D eye generation and simulation model trained with optical coherence tomography (OCT), labeled anatomy point clouds and near-eye images. Our pipeline first trains a Multi-Modal Anatomy Variational Autoencoder (VAE), which encodes an anatomy-aware latent representation from all input modalities. Then, our Eye Latent DiT is trained to generate latent samples conditioned on the optical axis, the pupil position and radius, and the subject identity. Together with Gaussian decoders for novel-view simulation, our model enables control over the pupil, subject identity and viewpoint for data synthesis. We show that our model outperforms previous eye image synthesis models in novel-view synthesis (24.9 against 21.8 dB PSNR from a single view), and that a public ET neural network trained on our synthetic data shows a smaller sim-to-real gap than when trained on data from other generators (3.5$^\circ$ vs. 8.4$^\circ$ gaze error), approaches a network trained on real data, and further improves ET performance when combined with real data (2.3$^\circ$ vs. 2.6$^\circ$). More information is available on the project page: https://lyhan12.github.io/eyedit

title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
abstract: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

title: Image-Condition-Controlled Diffusion Network with Large-Scale CT Pretraining for CT-Free Attenuation Correction in Dynamic Cardiac PET
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) provides quantitative information on myocardial perfusion. In dynamic PET, tracer kinetics are tracked through a series of reconstructed time frames. Reliable attenuation correction is essential for accurate measurements. Clinical attenuation maps ($μ$-maps) are typically derived from computed tomography (CT), which adds radiation exposure and may introduce PET-CT misregistration due to respiratory and cardiac motion. Moreover, supervised CT-free methods rely on paired non-attenuation-corrected (NAC) PET and CT data, which are scarce, whereas large-scale unpaired CT data are more readily available. To address these challenges, we propose Large-scale Unpaired CT-Informed Diffusion (LUCID), a framework that transfers anatomical priors learned from 10,000 chest CT volumes in the public CT-RATE dataset to $μ$-map synthesis for dynamic cardiac $^{82}$Rb PET. First, a convolutional neural network (CNN) predicts an initial $μ$-map from each NAC PET frame. Second, the CT-pretrained diffusion backbone refines a low-noise perturbation of the CNN prediction through a single denoising step, conditioned on the corresponding NAC PET frame via ControlNet. Finally, frame-wise predictions are averaged voxel-wise to obtain the final $μ$-map. We further introduce the voxel-wise temporal standard deviation (TSD) to quantify inter-frame variability without requiring a reference $μ$-map. We evaluated LUCID on an in-house dataset of 102 patients and found that it achieved the best quantitative accuracy while maintaining competitive inter-frame consistency. Ablation studies showed that refinement with a diffusion backbone pretrained on in-house CT data from the training patients was less accurate than the CNN prediction alone, highlighting the importance of large-scale CT pretraining.

title: Communicative On-Policy Distillation: Distilling Black-Box Teacher Capabilities through Communication for Long-Horizon Tasks
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a powerful paradigm for improving language-model agents on long-horizon tasks, yet its conventional formulation relies on teacher logits that text-only black- box models do not expose. To address this limitation, we introduce Communicative On-Policy Distillation (COPD), which uses natural-language communication as a medium for distilling a stronger model's capabilities into a smaller student. During task execution, the student au- tonomously decides when to consult a black-box teacher and formulates open-ended natural- language requests without predefined question templates or intervention schedules. Successful student-teacher interactions are retained as privileged references to supervise fresh adviser-free student rollouts through on-policy self-distillation, jointly with task-reward reinforcement learning. On CAMG-II, COPD achieves 2.46 times the gain of the strongest black-box OPD baseline. The capabilities it learns through communication generalize to Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, improving task success without adviser access.

title: Learning What to Degrade: A Recoverability-Aware Curriculum for Reliable Smart-Glasses Super-Resolution
abstract: Degradations in smart-glasses images obscure small text and fine-grained structures needed by vision-language models (VLMs) for visual assistance. We introduce an high-resolution (HR)-referenced semantic evaluation protocol that compares VLM outputs on restored images with those on corresponding HR references. Our evaluation reveals two failure modes: generative SR can synthesize misleading details, whereas restoration-oriented SR can leave critical evidence blurred or ambiguous. These findings motivate improving faithful detail recovery in restoration-oriented SR, where a key training challenge is to provide sufficiently difficult inputs while retaining recoverable visual information. We propose ReDiC (Recoverability-Difficulty Curriculum), which combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to adapt training degradation severity. ReDiC increases severity when inputs are recoverable and restoration is easy, maintains challenging but recoverable conditions, and reduces severity when estimated recoverability is low. It modifies only training degradation generation, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction objective unchanged. Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by approximately 2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by about 3 points over the corresponding baselines on synthetic benchmarks, with further gains confirmed by LLM-based and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.

title: A Multisite Super Learner for Survival Prediction with Limited Target-Site Data
abstract: Survival prediction models developed in multi-site studies may transport poorly to a new site because of between-site heterogeneity in covariate effects and baseline hazards. Pooled models may fail to capture site-specific risk patterns, while site-specific models can be unstable in small cohorts. We propose a Multi-Site Super Learner (MSSL), a domain-adaptive ensemble for survival prediction that combines diverse pooled and site-specific base learners. A meta-learner optimizes the ensemble weights using source data alone or, if available, a small target-site calibration sample. In simulations, when even a small target-site sample was available, MSSL substantially reduced prediction error relative to a pooled super learner under moderate to large between-site heterogeneity and generally matched or improved upon models fit to the target-site data alone. It did so by downweighting dissimilar or noisy models and upweighting models from structurally similar sites. Without target-site data, MSSL did not improve upon the pooled super learner. In an application to predicting dementia progression using the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center (NACC) Uniform Data Set across 10 sites, MSSL matched or outperformed standard super learning using pooled data in 9 of 10 sites. MSSL offers a practical framework for adapting multi-site survival prediction models to a new site when a small calibration sample is available.

title: Finetuning VLAs for Dexterous Manipulation: The Right Checkpoint Is All You Need
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities. A limitation of VLA models is that most manipulation datasets focus on parallel-jaw gripper systems, making transfer to multi-finger hands challenging, particularly as teleoperation datasets are harder to collect with multi-fingered robots. In this work, we study how to best adapt VLAs to dexterous hands by pairing supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with diffusion-steering reinforcement learning (DSRL). Using $π_{0.5}$ and a LEAP hand, we evaluate five fine-tuning recipes across two simulation tasks using only a handful of demonstrations. Our empirical analysis yields three key insights: (1) SFT success is poorly correlated with post-DSRL success, meaning the best SFT checkpoint is rarely the most effective to steer; (2) freezing the vision-language model (VLM) and tuning only the action expert produces the most steerable policy for both training and out-of-distribution placements; and (3) low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the least steerable approach. Consequently, we recommend an adaptation recipe that freezes the VLM, fully trains the action expert, and eschews SFT rollout success as a checkpoint selection metric.

title: Simpler Tiny Recursive Models
abstract: Small models that execute deep looped computational graphs have shown great experimental results on puzzle-like problems like Sudoku, finding shortest paths through mazes, etc. The most well-known one is TRM (tiny recursive model), a simplification of HRM (hierarchical reasoning model). However, the underlying recursion is complicated and involves a high-level and a low-level state, a nested loop recursion, and the network calls with different input and output signatures depending on where we are in the loops. These mechanisms are needed to avoid memorization and overfitting. We propose STRM, a simplified design with a single state and a uniform update. STRM does not sacrifice generalization, improves training speed and final performance. Our key architectural choices that allow our simpler recursion to work are exponential moving updates on the states with varying rates that are jittered during training and readout of the solution on slow-updating channels only. We test STRM on Sudoku-Extreme, PPBench and Maze-Hard with the same data, parameters and compute as TRM: we improve over TRM by $3.8$ points on Sudoku-Extreme and $8.4$ points on PPBench and match it on Maze-Hard. On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, STRM improves over the published TRM results by $5.4$ and $0.5$ points. We will release our code upon acceptance of the paper.

title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

title: The Kazdan-Warner equation on a finite graph with a Neumann boundary condition
abstract: We study the Kazdan-Warner equation $Δu = c - h \mathrm{e}^u$ on a finite connected domain $Ω$ of a locally finite graph, with Neumann boundary data $\partial u / \partialν= g$. We reduce the boundary condition to homogeneous form and use variational methods and upper and lower solutions to study solvability. Let $c_g \mathrel{:=} |Ω|^{-1}\int_{\partialΩ} g\, \mathrm{d}μ$, and let $ψ$ solve $Δψ= c_g$ with boundary data $\partialψ/ \partialν= g$ and zero mean on $Ω$. When $c = c_g$ and $h \not\equiv 0$, a solution exists if and only if $h$ changes sign and $\int_Ωh \mathrm{e}^ψ\, \mathrm{d}μ< 0$. When $c > c_g$, a solution exists if and only if $h$ is positive somewhere in $Ω$. When $c < c_g$, solvability requires $\int_Ωh \mathrm{e}^ψ\, \mathrm{d}μ< 0$. Under this condition there is a threshold $-\infty \le c_-(h) < c_g$ such that a solution exists for $c_-(h) < c < c_g$ and no solution exists for $c < c_-(h)$. If $h \le 0$ and $h \not\equiv 0$, a solution exists for every $c < c_g$.

title: Structured Extraction of Diffraction Data from Covalent Organic Frameworks
abstract: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) is the primary structural evidence for covalent organic frameworks (COFs) and many other materials. Yet decades of measured patterns exist only as images in published figures. Automatic recovery is difficult, because PXRD figures vary widely in format, from a single curve to crowded stacks with labels, insets, and neighboring plots that challenge traditional computer vision. This work presents a pipeline in which a vision large language model (LLM) interprets the layout of each figure, locating the diffraction plot and its curves and sketching a coarse trace of each, while classical computer vision (CV) refines every trace to pixel-level accuracy. Applied to 3,954 COF articles, the pipeline produces 11,445 calibrated diffraction curves, released in the open database COF-PEAK. Compared with a hand digitization of 60 panels, extracted peak positions differ by a median of only 0.07 degrees. Whereas papers usually report only a few peak angles, which limits further analysis, the digitized curves enable tracking how peak prominence, a possible marker of crystallinity, changes with synthesis conditions. Vision LLMs and classical CV can thus turn such figures into reusable experimental data.

title: Geography of Klein bottle Luttinger surgery
abstract: We propose and study a modification of Auroux's uniqueness question on Luttinger surgery by replacing Lagrangian tori with Klein bottles. In Kodaira dimension $-\infty$, we introduce two simple graphs whose connected components give bounds and, in several cases, exact counts of Klein bottle Luttinger equivalence classes. In Kodaira dimension zero, we provide examples of numerical invariants supporting infinitely many equivalence classes and prove a homological non-triviality theorem for Lagrangian Klein bottles in all symplectic Calabi--Yau surfaces with positive Euler characteristic. In positive Kodaira dimensions, we construct examples in which Klein bottle Luttinger surgery changes the symplectic Kodaira dimension.

title: Axion: A differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework,demonstrated on phase-field fracture
abstract: We introduce Axion (Autodifferentiable, XLA-compiled, Implicit, On-device Numerics), a differentiable, GPU-native finite element framework written in JAX. The element kernels, Newton and Krylov iterations, bound-constrained updates, staggered coupling of fields, and the loop over load increments are expressed as a single program that is just-in-time compiled and executed on the GPU without host intervention. Consistent tangent operators are obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation of the element residual, and derivatives of the discrete solution with respect to model parameters are obtained by differentiating the same program. Global operators are applied element by element without assembling a sparse matrix, octree mesh refinement is performed within fixed-size arrays, and a cell-based domain decomposition runs the same program on several GPUs. Phase-field fracture is implemented as the first module because it combines fine mesh resolution, bound-constrained damage, and repeated nonlinear solves over a loading history, which together make it computationally expensive. On two- and three-dimensional single-edge-notched tension benchmarks, a uniformly refined Axion computation completes faster than the corresponding adaptive FEniCSx computation. At identical discretization, the two-dimensional benchmark runs 37.9 times faster on one GPU than a FEniCSx implementation on one CPU. Strong and weak scaling efficiencies on four GPUs are 92% and 96%, respectively. Large-scale demonstrations include hydraulic fracture in a poroelastic medium (0.38M degrees of freedom), fracture of a multi-material premolar under contact loading (0.69M degrees of freedom), and a concrete gravity dam (96M degrees of freedom) on a single GPU. The implementation is available as open-source software.

title: JEV vs. LLMs: A Comparative Analysis for Phishing Email Detection
abstract: Phishing remains a major source of credential theft and fraudulent payments, and email security systems must classify large message volumes reliably, quickly, and at manageable cost. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer flexible text understanding, but their token-based generation increases response time and API cost, and the reliability of their confidence values requires measurement. Jev 1.13, a typed decision model from TypeSafe AI, instead returns a structured outcome with a confidence value. This paper compares Jev 1.13 with Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite, NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra, and Meta Llama 4 Maverick on a labelled dataset of 1500 emails, covering classification performance, decision latency, token consumption, API cost, and probability calibration. Jev achieves the highest accuracy (79.67%), precision (71.43%), recall (97.97%), and F1 score (82.62%). It also records the shortest batch time (173.88 seconds), the lowest token count (597,895), the lowest cost (USD 0.015103 per 1000 decisions), and the lowest Brier score (0.1698) and ECE (0.1594). These results suggest that Jev is a promising option for fast, structured, high-volume triage. LLMs retain the advantage of generating explanations, which we do not evaluate, and all four systems require further validation before standalone deployment.

title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Measuring the Conservatism of Latent Safety Filters for World Models
abstract: A latent safety filter decides from the latent of a world model whether a planned action is safe. Conformal calibration sets the threshold of the filter so that it accepts an unsafe action only with a small probability. However, the filter can still be conservative and refuse many safe actions, depending on the latent. To measure the conservatism that a latent forces on the filter, we group similar latents and actions into cells. A filter that gives one decision per cell can refuse the unsafe transitions of a cell only by refusing the safe ones in it as well. We call the share of safe transitions that lie in such cells the overlap. We prove that the overlap is the minimum share of safe transitions that such a filter has to refuse in order to accept no unsafe transition in the data. Both the overlap and the conformal calibration can be applied to any latent. We use this to compare three existing designs, in which the safety labels train a classifier on top of the world model, the world model itself, or a separate encoder beside it. In a visual navigation task, the separate encoder has the lowest overlap, and at the same conformal level its filter refuses the fewest safe actions and lets the planner reach the most goals of the three.

title: Connectivity of Matroids with Breadth-Critical Tangles
abstract: We construct an explicit infinite sequence of nonnegative integers $(s_0,s_1,\ldots)$ such that, for every $k\ge2$, every finite matroid with a breadth-critical tangle of order at least $k$ is $(s_0,s_1,\ldots,s_{k-2})$-connected. The constants $s_i$ depend only on $i$. This proves a conjecture of Brettell, Jowett, Oxley, Semple, and Whittle.

title: Extremal Projectors and the Virasoro Algebra
abstract: Extremal projectors are universal operators projecting onto the highest weight space in a representation. Their existence and uniqueness (as formal series) are known for a broad range of Lie superalgebras and quantum groups. We consider a class of Lie superalgebras that contains reductive finite-dimensional Lie algebras as well as the Virasoro algebra. We prove the existence and uniqueness of an extremal projector for this class. The existence proof is given in terms of a recursive algorithm which can be used to compute the coefficients. To illustrate the method, we compute the terms for the Virasoro extremal projector up to order 6. Furthermore, we formulate a conjecture for the denominators of the truncated extremal projector of the Virasoro algebra. We provide symbolic computational evidence up to order 6 and prove a weaker version of the conjecture.

title: Two-Dimensional Ferromagnetic Weyl Half-Semimetal
abstract: Two-dimensional (2D) ferromagnetic topological materials provide appealing platforms for realizing spin-polarized topological states, yet the coexistence of Weyl fermions and robust high-temperature ferromagnetism remains elusive. Here, based on first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations, we predict monolayer BaMn$_4$O$_8$ to be a dynamically, thermally, and mechanically stable ferromagnetic Weyl half-semimetal. \textcolor{blue}{An anisotropic Monte Carlo simulation on a $20\times20\times1$ lattice yields a finite-size transition estimate of approximately 1446~K.} The spin-resolved electronic structure reveals a fully spin-polarized state, in which the spin-up channel hosts linear Weyl band crossings near the Fermi level, whereas the spin-down channel remains insulating. Corresponding Fermi-arc edge states connecting the projected Weyl points (WPs) are clearly observed along the (100) boundary, confirming the nontrivial topology. Importantly, both the Weyl points and their associated Fermi arcs remain robust in the presence of spin--orbit coupling (SOC). \textcolor{blue}{These results identify monolayer BaMn$_4$O$_8$ as a candidate for fully spin-polarized topological transport.

title: Stars and gas in the most metal-poor galaxies -- II. Search for VMS and determination of stellar population and nebular properties at $Z\lesssim0.1\,Z_\odot$
abstract: Constraining the properties of OB-star populations and ionized gas at low metallicity is essential for understanding a broad range of astrophysical objects, from stellar black holes to the first galaxies. Rest-frame UV spectra of nearby metal-poor galaxies provide crucial constraints on theoretical predictions of low-metallicity stars and gas. However, such spectra are scarce at $Z\lesssim0.1Z\,\odot$, and candidate Very Massive Stars (VMS) remain elusive. We analyse optical and new UV spectra of nearby star-forming galaxies with $Z\lesssim0.1Z\,\odot$, selected for their nebular He II $\lambda4686$ emission and lack of Wolf-Rayet blue and red bumps, making them promising targets for VMS searches. Some galaxies exhibit stellar wind features (group 1), while others do not (group 2). For group 1, we compare STARBURST99, GALAXEV, and BPASS predictions with observed stellar lines to constrain OB-population ages and masses. The inferred ages are too old for VMS to be present. We also use pySTARBURST99 and GALAXEV photoionization models to investigate the ionized gas in a subsample, finding no evidence for VMS-dominated ionization. The absence of detected VMS may reflect their rarity, our limited sample size, or shortcomings in current models. Moreover, reproducing the extreme optical and UV line ratios simultaneously requires unrealistic N/O, ionization parameters, or Lyman continuum escape fractions, suggesting that multiple ionizing-source populations may be needed.

title: A Probabilistic Behavioral RTL Simulation Framework for Probabilistic Compute Fabrics
abstract: Coupled oscillator Ising hardware can produce different solution qualities across repeated runs of the same problem, while a deterministic behavioral model used for the design yields a single outcome under fixed conditions. Capturing this stochastic variability during design time is essential for evaluating how closely simulation reflects silicon behavior. This work presents a probabilistic behavioral RTL simulation framework that introduces Gaussian timing variation into coupling delays. This variation changes oscillator timing during evolution, producing different outcomes across runs while retaining the existing chip control and readout blocks. The framework is evaluated against measurements from two chips: a 28-nm CMOS chip with 66 spins and a 16-nm FinFET chip with 49 spins, using 250 problems run 100 times repetitively. Compared with deterministic simulation, the model reduces the average absolute gap between sorted simulation and silicon outcomes by 14.0% and 28.4% on the two chips, respectively. These results demonstrate that a simple behavioral timing variation model can be a useful tool for designing and verifying probabilistic computing chips.

title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

title: Linear Connectivity of Boundaries of Right-Angled Coxeter Groups
abstract: To every right-angled Coxeter group one can canonically associate a hyperbolic metric space, called its maximized hyperbolic space. This space is Morse recognizing and is obtained from the Davis complex by coning off its standard product regions. We characterize, purely in terms of the defining graph, when the Gromov boundary of a maximized hyperbolic space is nonempty and linearly connected. As an application, we prove that among one-ended right-angled Coxeter groups, splitting over a subgroup of an unbounded product subgroup is a quasi-isometry invariant. We also establish several features shared by maximized hyperbolic spaces and curve graphs, including the existence of dead ends and visibility of boundaries. Moreover, when the boundary is nonempty, it is non-compact if and only if the defining graph contains an induced 4-cycle.

title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
abstract: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.

title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $π$. We show that $π^2 = p\,α_*$ for a unique automorphism $α$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $ζ_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $π^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,χ))$, where $χ$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.

title: MoMoVL: Modality-Aware Adaptive Compression for On-Device Sparsely-Activated Vision-Language Models
abstract: The rise of the agentic web has been accompanied by growing demand for on-device Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that perform diverse cross-modal web tasks with enhanced privacy and reduced latency. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.

title: 2-Walk-regular graphs with $k_2$ at most twice the valency
abstract: In this paper, we characterize $2$-walk-regular graphs with valency $k$, diameter at least four and $k_2\leq 2k$, generalizing a result of Koolen and Park, and classify the distance-regular graphs satisfying these conditions. We also classify $2$-walk-regular graphs with valency $k$, diameter at least four and at most $4k+4$ vertices.

title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.

title: Fast closed-loop STEM navigation using vision-language models with typed decisions
abstract: Closed-loop scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), in which each acquired image determines the next field of view and magnification, offers a route to autonomous atomic-scale materials analysis. Such a loop would automate navigation to defects and grain boundaries, a task that has long relied on operator judgment, and would enable systematic analysis of diverse local structures at scale. Realizing it hinges on the decision step, which must translate each acquired image into the next operation both quickly and correctly; yet which decision method can deliver both remains unclear. Here, we isolate this decision step. Using simulated atomic-resolution STEM images of a substitutional W dopant and a grain boundary in monolayer MoS$_2$, where the true target position is known and every method starts from identical conditions, we compared four vision-language models (VLMs) and three decision methods. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of Typed Decision, which directly obtains the probabilities of candidate labels from a pretrained VLM, for closed-loop STEM navigation. Typed Decision showed the shortest decision latency for all models (0.13-0.21 s) and generally achieved the highest navigation success rate among the three methods: it was the best for all models in W dopant navigation (66-91%) and for the best-performing model, Cosmos-Reason2 32B, in grain boundary navigation (43%). Furthermore, navigation to the different targets, the W dopant and the grain boundary, was possible by natural-language specification alone, without task-specific training of the VLM. These results indicate that Typed Decision is an effective decision method for realizing fast, accurate, and flexible closed-loop STEM.

title: Optimal Production Scheduling for Multi-Product Mineral Manufacturing
abstract: Short-term scheduling in multi-product mineral manufacturing requires coordinating material movement and production across interconnected processing stages while addressing confirmed customer orders and longer-term production requirements. This work develops a generalized network-based, lexicographic multi-objective optimization (MOO) scheduling framework for these systems. The formulation represents the progression of material from raw-material supply through production and inventory to customer fulfillment. A sequential objective hierarchy first prioritizes fulfillment of confirmed customer orders and then progressively directs feasible production capacity toward cumulative targets supplied by the facility's demand-planning process. This approach ensures that the performance achieved for each higher-priority objective is preserved before subsequent targets are considered. Selected product-line activation decisions are represented using generalized disjunctive programming (GDP). An industrial mineral-manufacturing case study demonstrates the proposed framework's ability to generate feasible shift-level schedules and preserve the intended operational priorities with practical computational performance.

title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
abstract: Emergency care requires auditable decisions, but a language-model agent just outputs text. We introduce Decision2Care, a decision agent that generates a probability for every option at each step. It diagnosed 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases with 86.5% accuracy in a median of 2.2 s; language-model agents reached 86.1 to 91.7% but took more than 90 s. Its drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than documented first-day care and with about half as many records, it predicted death as well as three ICU clinicians. In the four cases where it was confident but wrong, we traced each decision to one imaging report. Our study suggests that an agent's work-up can be reviewed like a clinician's, motivating prospective trials.

title: Data Poisoning Attacks to Locally Differentially Private Triangle Counting Protocols
abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) has become a crucial paradigm for privacy-preserving graph analytics, enabling graph analytics tasks such as subgraph counting without requiring a trusted curator. However, while LDP provides strong privacy guarantees, the integrity and robustness of LDP subgraph counting protocols in the presence of malicious participants remain poorly understood. In particular, since data are randomized locally before collection, it is inherently difficult to distinguish malicious users from honest ones based solely on their submitted reports, and small, protocol-compliant local manipulations can be systematically amplified through reconstruction and calibration into large global estimation bias. In this paper, we use LDP triangle counting as a representative task to characterize the vulnerability of LDP subgraph counting to data poisoning attacks. For both non-interactive and interactive LDP triangle counting protocols, we analyze their attack surfaces and develop a unified gain-driven framework that captures how adversarial users can manipulate calibrated subgraph count estimates, which we instantiate on representative protocols of both types. Extensive experiments on four real-world graph datasets demonstrate that these attacks can significantly distort triangle count estimates across different protocols and adversarial settings. Moreover, we show that existing and straightforward defenses are insufficient to mitigate these attacks, underscoring the need for robustness mechanisms tailored to LDP subgraph counting.

title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are pushing research toward semi-automation: ideas turn into preprints ever faster, and autoresearch pipelines add papers of uneven rigor. When a technique can be overtaken within months, citations arrive too late to tell which new papers deserve reading, so strong work goes unnoticed and newcomers lose their bearings. Yet from the day it appears, a preprint carries the track records of the people and institutions behind it. Established researchers guard their reputations and choose problems and collaborators with research taste, so their involvement tends to raise a paper's quality floor. Building on this signal, we present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight arXiv discovery tool that weights each paper's topical relevance by the reputation its authors and institutions stake on it. Author credit also diffuses by message passing along collaborations to surface rising stars, and institutions are profiled through the researchers they hold in each direction rather than by headcount. In a sealed test on 10,386 new papers, author credit doubled the chance of reaching the top tenth of early citations. As its library grows into a scholarly knowledge graph that research agents can query through a command-line interface (CLI), KnowMe also offers a promising literature entry point for future autoresearch and recursive self-improvement (RSI).

title: Degree-three Euclidean spanning trees within a factor of 1.514 of the minimum
abstract: For every finite point set $X$ in a Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension, we prove that there is a spanning tree of maximum degree three and total length at most $(757/500)\MST(X)=1.514\MST(X)$, where $\MST(X)$ denotes the unrestricted minimum spanning-tree length. More strongly, for any root and any finite list of other points, there is a Hamiltonian path starting at the root whose length is at most $1.514$ times the sum of the root-to-point distances. The proof follows the rooted-path and variable-block framework used in earlier work, and applies Young's weighted-distance inequality to explicit rational mixtures of paths. Eight ordered radius regions cover the normalized domain. Their local estimates require only 29 vertex comparisons, all certified by rational arithmetic. The cover uses the three thresholds $1/4$, $3/8$, and $1/2$; its largest block has nine vertices. We give complete proofs of the normalization transfer, the global induction, and the terminal cases with zero or one actual tail point. We also give a fixed-dimensional cross-polytope lower bound, present Zbarsky's orthogonal simplex-cluster construction in explicit coordinates, and compare their finite-dimension bounds. The base cases complete the upper-bound argument before the lower-bound constructions are presented.

title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

title: A Hardware-Aware Comprehensive Study of Edge Vision Deployment with A Unified Hardware-Model-Runtime Mapping Framework
abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

title: Helicity-squared scaling of post-eikonal phases for electromagnetic and gravitational waves in Ricci-flat spacetimes
abstract: Spin-optical descriptions of electromagnetic and gravitational waves isolate finite-frequency corrections that are odd in the helicity. We study the complementary, helicity-even part of the first post-eikonal correction for scalar, electromagnetic, and linearized gravitational waves on Ricci-flat backgrounds. In a parallel-propagated null tetrad, the direct Weyl coupling of the gravitational field projects onto the circular transverse-traceless states as the multiple $2C_{\bar m m\bar m m}$ of the identity. The Ricci identity for the spin coefficient $μ$ then rewrites this projection as a total derivative plus optical terms. The helicity-even phase of a spin-$s$ wave, measured relative to the scalar wave, then obeys a helicity-squared law, $Δ_2=4Δ_1$, up to endpoint terms. The Weyl coupling is what completes the $h^2$ scaling in the gravitational case. For weak-deflection scattering by a Schwarzschild black hole we evaluate the relevant integrals along the ray and obtain $Δ_s=-3πs^2/(8Mωρ^3)$, with $ρ=b/M$. The same coefficient follows independently, and without reference to any frame or gauge, from the Regge--Wheeler phase shifts combined with the asymptotics of the rotation functions $d^l_{ss}$. Direct numerical integration of the radial equations confirms it. At first order in $M$ the helicity-even phase difference vanishes, as required by the Born amplitudes. The helicity-odd spin-optical sector and the helicity-even post-eikonal sector are therefore organized by the first and second powers of the helicity, respectively.

title: Functorial height and Orlov's rationality conjecture
abstract: An exceptional collection in the derived category of a smooth projective variety may fail to generate the whole category, and this failure cannot be detected by K-theory or by Hochschild homology. Kuznetsov's height detects it through Hochschild cohomology, that is, through natural transformations from the identity functor to its shifts. We replace the identity functor by an arbitrary endofunctor $F$ and define the height of a collection with coefficient $F$. It controls, in a range of degrees, the restriction of natural transformations $\mathrm{id}\to F$ to the orthogonal complement of the collection, and it is computed from the collection by a finite complex. For collections of line bundles on surfaces whose Hom divisors have nonnegative canonical degree, the tensor product with a skyscraper sheaf has height exactly two, and the projections of skyscraper sheaves form a two-dimensional family of point-like objects in the orthogonal complement. We apply these tools to Orlov's rationality conjecture. A smooth projective complex surface is rational if its derived category has a full exceptional collection in which all members except possibly one are line bundles, or one that consists of at most three completely orthogonal blocks of arbitrary objects; we also obtain rationality in several cases with four blocks or with a hereditary component. If $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of the form $(M_i\boxtimes\mathcal O(a_i))$, then the $M_i$ with relative degrees of a fixed parity form a full exceptional collection on $S$; consequently $S$ is rational whenever $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of line bundles. Finally, we show that the general case of the conjecture for surfaces is equivalent to the surjectivity and injectivity of two maps in Hochschild cohomology.

title: Rational Ensemble Logic for Cohort Discovery with Real-World Electrophysiology Data
abstract: Biomedical knowledge representation should make the passage from observations to conclusions transparent, rigorous, understandable, explainable, and reproducible (TRUER). We introduce Rational Ensemble Logic (QEL) for specifying temporal phenotypes in real-world electrophysiology data (RWED), with a meaning independent of the implementation software. QEL combines three parameterized modal operators (exact displacement, bounded existence, and bounded universality) over rational time with Boolean connectives and first-order quantification. Its Labeled Interval Ensemble (LINE) semantics represents annotated records as finite interval ensembles. We relate the operators to morphological operations and develop endpoint-array algorithms and finite rational evidence sets for model checking. We prove closure and semantic correctness of the interval operations, obtain finite evidence sets by quantifier elimination, and establish polynomial data complexity for fixed formulas. On 54 manually constructed records, a prototype agreed with the assigned outcomes for base and strict post-ictal generalized EEG suppression (PGES) queries. A separate feasibility experiment over 1,976 patients identified 37 qualifying patients and 45 annotation patterns in 16 seconds. The released prototype uses endpoint candidates and numerical tolerances. QEL supports the TRUER principle through explicit phenotype definitions, precise semantics, and provably correct evaluation procedures, with rational witnesses for existential queries. These provide a logical foundation for formal specification and correctness of algorithms that are independent of specific clinical interpretation, data annotation quality, and software implementation.

title: Fisher Information Characterization in GNSS DPE under Multipath-Induced Channel Uncertainty
abstract: The availability and utilization of Fisher information in global navigation satellite system (GNSS) direct position estimation (DPE) under multipath-induced channel uncertainty are investigated. First, a unified estimation-theoretic framework is developed to characterize information mapping and utilization across direct and two-step receivers. Next, a scalar-equivalent statistical channel model for short-delay multipath is established via least-squares (LS) projection.
