We determine all almost simple groups whose prime graph has a vertex $r$ not adjacent to $2$ and find the $2$-independence numbers of all almost simple groups.

title: A Lower Bound for the Chromatic Number of Ball-Packing Graphs
abstract: For every odd prime power $q$, we construct a finite packing of congruent balls in dimension $d=q^2-q+1$ whose contact graph requires at least $2d$ colors. Consequently, the ball-packing chromatic number satisfies $\chiball(q^2-q+1)\ge2(q^2-q+1)$, and the same lower bound holds for congruent-ball packings. The construction starts from the complements of Hubaut's $C_{20}$ graphs and uses their Taylor extensions. We give an explicit finite-field adjacency rule for the $q^3$-vertex graph $H_q$, prove its strong regularity, determine its spectrum and projection matrix, establish $α(H_q)=q$, and construct a two-distance embedding in $\R^{q(q-1)}$. Its Taylor extension $T_q$ has $2(q^3+1)$ vertices. We prove its distance-regularity, compute its intersection array, construct a three-distance embedding in $\R^{d}$, and prove $α(T_q)=q+1$. The chromatic lower bound follows by realizing $T_q$ as the contact graph of equal-radius balls and bounding the size of every color class. All coordinates, distances, and independence bounds are derived explicitly. The case $q=3$ uses the Schläfli and Gosset graphs and gives a packing of 56 congruent balls in $\R^7$ requiring at least 14 colors.

title: Beyond Intelligibility: Fine-Grained Perceptual Assessment of Dysarthric Speech with Auditory Large Language Models
abstract: Accurate assessment of dysarthric speech is vital for clinical diagnosis and rehabilitation, yet existing automated methods rely heavily on isolated, single-task models or generic speech quality metrics that fail to disentangle heterogeneous neuromotor deficits. This work presents the first systematic investigation into adapting auditory large language models (ALLMs) for multi-dimensional dysarthric speech assessment under a unified, prompt-conditioned framework. Four representative ALLMs are benchmarked across five clinical perceptual dimensions from the Speech Accessibility Project (SAP): naturalness, monopitch, intelligibility, imprecise consonants, and inappropriate silences. To bridge generic perceptual quality and clinical evaluation, a two-stage training paradigm is explored, leveraging out-of-domain pre-training followed by in-domain clinical adaptation. Experimental results demonstrate that leading ALLMs reliably capture fine-grained pathological variations, exhibiting distinct and complementary strengths across prosodic and articulatory attributes. These findings establish ALLMs as a scalable foundation for clinical speech evaluation and provide practical insights into model selection and multi-task transfer potential.

title: Keep the Reasoning, Read the Image: On-Demand Visual KV for Multi-Turn Reasoning VLMs
abstract: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) think for thousands of tokens before they answer, and retention policies keep the KV cache affordable by pruning it as the reasoning grows. We find that this pruning sacrifices the image in multi-turn conversations: the image and the reasoning share one budget, so the growing reasoning crowds the visual entries out. A chart question that loses 8 points to the full cache when asked first loses 24 points when asked after a round of reasoning. Protecting a small visual reserve from eviction recovers most of this loss, while adding the same slots to the shared budget recovers considerably less. The image therefore lacks protection, not capacity. Based on this finding, we propose ShelfKV, a training-free method that works on top of existing retention policies. It keeps every visual entry in CPU memory and, at each decoding step, swaps the visual entries that the current query scores highest into the attention slots of the text entries it scores lowest. The image is never evicted, yet it occupies attention slots only while it is read. We evaluate ShelfKV on four benchmarks, three of them conversational, with two retention policies and two reasoning VLMs. In conversations, it improves the strongest existing policy, DBTrimKV, by up to 20.3 points at matched GPU memory, and still leads by 8.7 points when DBTrimKV uses twice the memory. It also consistently outperforms a fixed visual reserve of matched GPU memory in these settings, without hurting accuracy on standalone questions. These results show that the image should be protected from the reasoning but read only on demand.

title: DetectViT: Test-time Backdoor Detection for Vision Transformers via Inter-Head Attention Discrepancy
abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) now underpin the visual encoders of most multimodal models, but this success comes at a cost: relying on third-party pretrained checkpoints leaves these systems open to backdoor attacks. Existing test-time detection methods rely on either the predicted label or intermediate embeddings, limiting their applicability across diverse tasks and incurring substantial computational overhead. In this work, we study how backdoor triggers affect the multi-head attention mechanism of ViTs and identify two distinct anomalous patterns: $\textit{complete attention hijacking}$, causing the attention to exhibit abnormally high inter-head spatial overlap, and $\textit{partial attention hijacking}$, causing an abnormally large variance in the concentration of the attention distribution. Motivated by these findings, we propose $\textbf{DetectViT}$, a test-time backdoor detection method that requires neither training data, model outputs, nor any prior knowledge of the trigger. DetectViT quantifies the two hijacking phenomena via an inter-head consistency score and an inter-head entropy variance score, with thresholds estimated from a small out-of-distribution (OOD) calibration set drawn from an arbitrary source. Across four representative attacks, diverse architectures (DeiT, CLIP, and LLaVA), and downstream tasks (image classification and captioning), DetectViT substantially outperforms all baselines with as few as 64--128 OOD calibration samples, achieving a true positive rate of $100\%$ and a false positive rate of $0.17\%$ on BadCLIP. Notably, it introduces negligible additional overhead by relying solely on attention weights already computed during inference. Code is available at: https://github.com/siquanhuang/DetectViT.

title: Mitigating the Grid Impact of Gigawatt-Scale AI Data Centers via High-Fidelity Model Flexibility
abstract: Gigawatt-scale artificial intelligence data centers (AIDCs) are being connected at a single point of interconnection (POI) faster than transmission can be reinforced, yet studies of their flexibility rely on DC power flow and simplified load envelopes that omit voltage, cooling dynamics, and workload deadlines. This paper addresses this gap by embedding a high-fidelity AIDC model, with separate inference and training pools, hall thermal mass, PV, a battery energy storage system (BESS) with reactive capability, and a STATCOM, in a five-minute multi-period AC optimal power flow. Simulations on the RTS-GMLC test system show that active-power flexibility mitigates local price spikes and relieves congestion, whereas reactive support from the BESS inverter or a STATCOM is needed to keep the POI voltage away from sagging around its 0.95~pu limit. Sensitivity analyses show that cost-driven charging of large batteries can induce new morning congestion and that storage largely substitutes for wider workload deferral.

title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
abstract: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.

title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
abstract: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. Yet subspaces defined by Hessian eigenvalue magnitude, such as the dominant/bulk decomposition underlying Dom-SGD and Bulk-SGD, have repeatedly failed to capture where optimization takes place, and adaptive Krylov-based alternatives built on energy-fraction thresholds show promise but still struggle at lower eigenmodes. We argue this failure is structural: the directions of highest curvature are not, in general, the directions along which training moves. We introduce the dominant aligned subspace (DAS), constructed from a full eigendecomposition of the Hessian but selected by gradient alignment rather than eigenvalue magnitude, as a tool for understanding optimization dynamics and a foundation for designing methods that exploit them. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. Across Poisson, heat, wave, and viscous Burgers benchmarks DAS-restricted training with a line search matches full-space training even where the projected Hessian remains ill-conditioned, showing empirically that convergence does not require all Hessian eigendirections but only a low-dimensional, gradient-aligned subset. We extend the analysis to Gauss-Newton within the DAS and discuss what this structure implies for future subspace-aware optimizers.

title: Improve How You Improve: Recursive Policy Self-Improvement for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Multi-Object Navigation
abstract: To advance the development of embodied general navigation, zero-shot open-vocabulary multi-object navigation has attracted increasing attention, aiming to enable robots to efficiently search multiple objects in unseen environments without training. For this task, the key lies in improving navigation policies from earlier searches to locate subsequent goals more efficiently. Recent methods automate this process through trajectory reflection and rule revision, enabling policy self-improvement. However, the mechanisms for diagnosing problems and generating revisions are typically designed by humans and remain fixed across iterations. Consequently, the system's capacity for continued self-improvement remains constrained, even as its navigation policy evolves. To this end, we propose RPSI-Nav, a Recursive Policy Self-Improvement framework for zero-shot multi-object navigation that revises both the navigation program and its revision mechanism. RPSI-Nav diagnoses search behavior, requests diagnostic views when existing observations cannot distinguish competing causes, and generates targeted navigation revisions. Feedback from subsequent goal searches is linked to the rules that produced these revisions, guiding changes to diagnosis, observation acquisition, and revision planning. The updated improver governs subsequent navigation improvements, forming a recursive loop in which RPSI-Nav revises its own improvement process. Across goals, the robot conditionally inherits accepted program updates and spatial memory, enabling search experience to improve both future navigation and adaptation. Benchmark experiments and qualitative real-robot evaluations validate RPSI-Nav's effectiveness.

title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
abstract: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based \(e\)-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based \(e\)-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed \(e\)-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal \(e\)-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the \(1/k\) fraction of the largest \(m\)th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.

title: Residual diffusion for fine-structure enhancement in low-count accelerator-based muon imaging
abstract: Accelerator-based muon imaging combines the penetrating power of high-energy muons with selectable momentum and a controlled beam direction, offering a powerful means of probing internal structures in large, dense and heavily shielded objects. Within a fixed beam-time budget, realizing this potential requires reliable recovery of fine structures from limited muon statistics. We propose an observation-conditioned residual diffusion method with decoupled linear schedules to enhance low-count muon images through iterative restoration guided by the observed image. We evaluate a simplified VSC-24 fuel cask under an idealized 5 GeV parallel muon beam, using 500,000 accepted events per low-count image and 40 million per reference image. Simulation results show improved recovery of structural boundaries and fine details, with the mean peak signal-to-noise ratio increasing from 11.4239 to 22.1719 dB. These findings highlight the potential of diffusion models to make more effective use of limited muon data and broaden the application of accelerator-based muon imaging across scientific and industrial settings.

title: STORM: A Lightweight Structure-Free Model for Binding Affinity Prediction
abstract: Accurately predicting a small molecule's binding affinity to a protein, a critical task in drug discovery, remains challenging. Physics-based approaches like free-energy perturbation (FEP) have very high computational costs and require expert setup. Recent machine learning--based cofolding models have reported accuracy approaching that of FEP---and at least one of them, Boltz-2, has already been widely adopted for affinity prediction---but they remain expensive for large computational screens and even more expensive for retraining on newly collected experimental data. To address these challenges, we introduce STORM: Similarity Transfer from Observed Reference Molecules. STORM is a fast, simple machine learning model that ensembles many small model fusions of diverse protein and molecule representations for binding affinity prediction. Trained on the same data, STORM matches or exceeds the accuracy of Boltz-2 on multiple evaluation datasets, while delivering a speed improvement of over five orders of magnitude for both inference and training. Our results also suggest opportunities to substantially improve affinity prediction accuracy by integrating historical experimental affinity data with structural and biophysical information.

title: Cumulant Generating Function of the Hill-Lane-Sudderth urn model
abstract: We consider the Hill, Lane and Sudderth urn, in which a black or white ball is added at each step with probabilities depending on the current proportion of black balls. We solve the equation for the limiting normalized cumulant generating function when the urn function is invertible on the outer branches beyond the fixed points and the corresponding inverses are Lipschitz. The solution has a parametric representation through three quadratures of the urn function and a limit of compositions of radicals, with no derivatives or inverses of the urn function in the final formula. We prove an error bound that does not accumulate along the partition and remains valid when starting from the initial singularity. Four examples with exact solutions illustrate the two orientations of the construction, the non-affine case and the presence of zeros.

title: TabBioMed: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Biomedical Tabular Learning
abstract: Recent advances in machine learning have accelerated biomedical prediction, but evaluation on structured biomedical data remains fragmented, especially for datasets with high dimensionality, large sample size, missingness, and class imbalance. We introduce TabBioMed, a large-scale benchmark of 94 curated public biomedical tabular datasets spanning electronic health records, drug discovery, genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, single-cell omics, and systems biology. TabBioMed unifies these datasets through a standardized, dataset-aware preprocessing and evaluation framework, enabling reproducible comparison across classification, regression, and multi-target tasks. We benchmark 23 models across classical baselines, gradient-boosted trees, neural tabular architectures, and tabular foundation models. Foundation models deliver the strongest family-level predictive performance. However, their gains are regime-dependent: tree-based models and tuned multilayer perceptrons remain highly competitive, often dominating under inference-time or training-cost constraints. Overall, TabBioMed shows that biomedical tabular learning is strongly context-dependent, with optimal model choice depending on data regime, task type, and computational budget. We release TabBioMed with curated datasets and splits, preprocessing code, baselines, and results, providing a reproducible benchmark for practical model selection and future methods development in biomedical machine learning, available at https://github.com/AI-sandbox/TabBioMed.

title: Subsequent Dust-Fading Events of the Wolf-Rayet Star WR 59: A Continuous Visual Record
abstract: This paper presents long-term visual and space-based monitoring of the WC9d Wolf-Rayet star WR 59 from 2017 to 2026, documenting a profound physical transition from a stable baseline to an ongoing phase of continuous dust production. Visual observations using a 22-inch telescope initially established a four-year quiescent baseline at magnitude 13.9. Following the historic May 2021 discovery fade to magnitude 15.2, long-term nightly visual monitoring documented an accelerating sequence of twelve distinct fading episodes over subsequent years, characterised by progressively shorter inter-fade recovery intervals. Due to severe pixel crowding and flux contamination from a close 11.7 V companion star 11 arcseconds away, automated large-pixel survey pipelines remain completely blind to these high-amplitude fading events. Direct comparisons with NASA's TESS satellite photometry during quiet phases show that targeted visual magnitude estimates measure systemic baseline micro-variations with professional accuracy while bridging space mission coverage gaps. High-density observation blocks during the minimum floor reveal a highly dynamic, rapid, minute-by-minute bimodal oscillation and sub-minute flickering between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2. At the time of writing, the system remains locked in an unprecedented deep minimum, varying between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2 for a sustained period exceeding 102 consecutive days. Intensive visual monitoring is ongoing to record the eventual egress recovery profile.

title: When accuracy hides risk: risk-controlled confirmation of the critical view of safety under expert disagreement
abstract: Automated assessment of the critical view of safety (CVS) in laparoscopic cholecystectomy has advanced rapidly, but a deployed check must decide, before the first clip, whether to confirm CVS. The standard rule calibrates a threshold so that false confirmations are rare on average. We show that this rule concentrates its errors on disputed videos, which one of three expert raters judged sufficient, and that the failure is structural. When reference labels are votes of a panel sampled from a larger expert pool, the rule that maximizes sensitivity at a fixed average false-confirmation rate also maximizes false confirmation of disputed videos, and for recognizers that recover expert judgement with less noise this rate rises with accuracy. We propose certified confirmation, a risk-controlled monitoring rule whose threshold is selected by multiple testing so that, with probability at least 1 - δ, false confirmation is at most α overall, among disputed videos, within vendor and country groups, and before CVS is visible, using disputed labels only to calibrate. In a pre-specified, hash-locked evaluation on the 300 test videos (18 countries) of the SAGES CVS Challenge, standard calibration falsely confirmed 8 of 39 disputed videos (0.21; one-sided p = 0.037 against α = 0.10), whereas certified confirmation confirmed 2 (one-sided 95% upper bound 0.15). On development data, protection held for vendor and country groups left out of calibration. The cost was confirming 10% rather than 35% of sufficient videos on time. Average accuracy hides this risk; disputed cases must be protected explicitly.

title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $β\ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $β$-TEF1 allocation.

title: The Population of Radio Hypernebulae from Mass-Transferring Massive Binaries
abstract: Massive binary evolution is punctuated by brief phases of highly super-Eddington mass transfer (MT) onto neutron stars and black holes, presaging luminous transients such as supernovae, common envelope events, and gravitational wave sources. These hyper-accreting phases power relativistic jets and slower mass-loaded outflows, inflating extended nebulae of relativistic particles. Though observed in the local universe as ultra-luminous X-ray binaries and micro-quasars, the present census is biased against shorter-lived and hence rarer but potentially even more extreme MT systems: so-called ``hypernebulae'' (HNbe). We use the binary population synthesis code (\textsc{COMPAS}) to estimate the MT population, which spans a wide range of MT rates $\dot{M} \sim 10^{2-7}\,\dot{M}_{\rm Edd}$ and source lifetimes $t_{\rm acc} \sim 10^{0-6}$ years. Combining this synthetic population with a semi-analytic model for their time-dependent radio emission, we predict the observable properties of HNbe over cosmic time. HNbe exhibit a broad GHz luminosity range extending to $L_{ν, \rm peak} \sim 10^{28-30}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}\,Hz^{-1}}$, and up to $\sim 10^{2}$ ($\sim 10^{5}$) HNbe are detectable by the wide-field radio surveys VLASS (DSA-2000) in our conservative model. A fraction of these systems should possess angular sizes and spatial offsets from star-forming regions (due to the first supernova kick) resolvable by VLBI. The most luminous donors, helium Hertzsprung-gap stars, may be detectable coincident with radio HNbe with Roman imaging out to distances $\sim 30$\,Mpc. Our findings suggest HNbe as promising probes of the pathways linking massive binaries to energetic transients.

title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
abstract: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.

title: Partial flags of tropical linear spaces may not complete
abstract: We construct two valuated matroids of ranks 2 and 4 on eight elements that form a valuated quotient, such that no rank 3 valuated matroid forms a valuated quotient with both simultaneously. In other words, a partial flag of tropical linear spaces need not extend to a complete flag containing every intermediate dimension.

title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
abstract: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.

title: Interface Weyl electrons in the kagome-bilayers
abstract: What makes a topological character prominent is whether its characteristic electronic states are located near the Fermi energy. While the kagome-metals possess unique topological characteristics owing to their distinctive electronic band structures, i.e. flat and Dirac bands, the control of Fermi energy to accentuate these characteristics has scarcely been studied in these materials. Here, we propose a new concept for activating the topological characteristics of Weyl electrons specifically near the interface of kagome-bilayers, namely interface Weyl electrons. The kagome-bilayers prepared by a sputtering technique surprisingly exhibit atomically abrupt interfaces thanks to the suppression of interdiffusion for maintaining the crystal symmetry of the hexagonal-type D0$_{19}$ and cubic-type L1$_{2}$ structures. Much higher electrical conductivity of the kagome-bilayers compared to single-layer films indicates the emergent contribution of a highly conductive electronic state at the interfaces. The enhanced electrical conductivity and the exceptionally large anomalous Hall conductivity about 2000 $Ω$$^{-1}$cm$^{-1}$ in the intrinsic mechanism indicates that the emergent interface electronic states comprise Weyl nodes in the D0$_{19}$ structure identified in our theoretical band calculations, triggered by nontrivial charge transfer. These results demonstrate that topological transport can be engineered at the interface of intermetallic compounds, leading further design principles towards development of device functionality.

title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
abstract: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
abstract: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.

title: Finite-time stochastic resetting in bounded domains: competing targets, energetic cost, and optimal search strategies
abstract: We investigate the first-passage dynamics and energetic cost of a Brownian particle subject to finite-time stochastic resetting in a bounded one-dimensional domain with two absorbing boundaries. Unlike conventional instantaneous resetting, the particle is returned to a prescribed resetting position through a finite-duration process driven by a linear trapping potential. By solving the corresponding backward equations, we derive analytical expressions for the mean global first-passage time and the splitting probabilities. Our results show that the finite duration of the return process can substantially modify the dependence of the mean global first-passage time on the resetting rate. In particular, we identify a critical trapping strength above which resetting can accelerate the search process, and characterize how the range of favorable resetting positions depends on the trapping strength. We further characterize the energetic cost of resetting by deriving the generating function of the total work and obtaining an analytical expression for its mean value. For the linear trapping potential considered here, we establish an exact relation between the mean total work and the mean cumulative return time. This relation allows us to establish a quantitative trade-off between the mean global first-passage time and the energetic expenditure, revealing how the finite duration of the return process affects search efficiency. Brownian dynamics simulations confirm our theoretical predictions.

title: A State-Level Assessment of Space Weather Impact on the Virginia Power Grid: From Vulnerability to Mitigation Strategies
abstract: Contemporary methodologies exist for assessing the nationwide impacts of geomagnetically induced currents (GICs), such as the Coupled Space Weather Impact Model (C-SWIM), which links power grid vulnerability with economic losses. Yet regional mitigation requires adapting the national model to the local transmission network so operators and planners can identify substations at risk and evaluate economic and population consequences and protective actions. We present the first adaptation of C-SWIM to Virginia, modeling the Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland (PJM) Interconnection, which includes Dominion Energy Virginia and Appalachian Power. Its extra high voltage network was assessed under the May 2024 Gannon, October 2003 Halloween, and March 2015 St. Patrick's Day storms in addition to nine return period scenarios derived from statistical fits to 92 historical events. Using the Leontief consumption and production input-output model, we estimated daily losses of USD 145.5M for a 100-year storm and USD 230.6M for a 250-year storm, with 339,000-535,000 people and up to 12,000 businesses at risk of power outage. The Ghosh input-output model was used to evaluate three island selection algorithms for protective islanding, which temporarily disconnects parts of the grid to reduce transformer damage. Only one algorithm yielded benefits exceeding costs across all twelve scenarios, with avoided losses up to USD 9.69M per day and a cost of USD 0.204M per intervention. However, these islanding benefits assume disconnection for 6 hours and transformer replacement after 365 days. Moreover, the analysis uses national economic relationships and models only transformer thermal failure, excluding voltage collapse, cascading failures, and restoration. Transmission operators and state energy policymakers can use this statewide assessment to prioritize regional monitoring and appraise protective islanding.

title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation (Extended Version)
abstract: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.

title: ROBIN++: Unified Copyright Protection and Tamper Localization for Diffusion Models via Dual-Domain Synergistic Watermarking
abstract: Digital watermarking provides a promising solution for verifying the provenance and integrity of generated content. However, existing methods often suffer from an inherent trade-off between copyright robustness and localization sensitivity due to the entanglement of conflicting signals within a single domain. In this paper, we propose ROBIN++, a paradigm that shifts from single-domain entanglement to a Dual-Domain Synergistic design. Our key insight is to explicitly decouple robustness and fragility during injection by assigning them to distinct domains, while re-coupling them for mutual reinforcement during verification. Specifically, we introduce an Adversarial Optimization Algorithm to inject a frequency-domain copyright watermark during generation, maximizing extraction robustness without visual artifacts. Complementarily, a Content-Aware Perturbation generator is integrated into the latent space to inject the spatial-domain localization watermark, ensuring sensitivity to spatial tampering with minimal interference to the copyright watermark. During verification, we propose a dual-branch synergistic detector that facilitates Frequency-to-Spatial Synergy, where robust spectral priors act as global anchors for local anomaly detection. Conversely, a Spatial-to-Frequency Refinement strategy is employed to rectify corrupted latent features using predicted tamper masks. Extensive experiments show that ROBIN++ significantly outperforms existing approaches in both copyright recovery and tamper localization accuracy, effectively mitigating the long-standing trade-off between the two tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Hannah1102/ROBIN.

title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

title: A Dual-SOM Learner Model of Instructional Efficiency within Cognitive Load Theory
abstract: This paper presents a novel methodological framework, integrating a dual self-organising map (SOM) neural network architecture with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), for assessing instructional efficiency within learning environments. By representing curriculum content as a directed acyclic graph of topic dependencies, the proposed model captures collective learning behaviour across two core dimensions: academic performance and subjective/introspective mental effort. During SOM training, representative data sets of successful learner trajectories are compressed into two topologically ordered, identically structured neural networks: PSOM (performance space) and ESOM (mental effort space). By pairing these behavioural maps, the model serves as a decision-support tool that enables instructors to simultaneously pinpoint structural instructional design defects, such as hidden topic prerequisites, and evaluate collective cognitive load profiles. The implementation and performance of the PSOM component (and, by extension, its symmetrical twin, ESOM) is linked to an earlier modelling study employing a SOM with identical structure and encoding semantics situated in the same domain (i.e., a learning environment). This paper combines the study of behavioural phenomena with theoretical work on human cognitive architecture via SOM neurocomputational cognitive behavioural modelling.

title: Critical--localized reentry under periodic spacer control
abstract: Tracking a fixed fraction of a quasiperiodic spectrum tests whether repeated critical--localized alternation extends over a nonzero spectral weight. We find such alternation in a matched-dimer chain by varying only the spacer on-site energies and following a fixed interval of integrated-density-of-states (IDS) labels. An exact Bloch-determinant identity links the physical transfer discriminant to the bands of a periodic reference operator. For the golden cell frequency, we prove that, on a common full-measure set of phases and for every finite value of the spacer control, the physical spectrum in the open reference bands is critical, with purely singular-continuous spectrum and zero Lyapunov exponent, while the spectrum strictly outside the bands is pure point, with exponentially decaying eigenfunctions. Validated IDS bounds certify repeated critical--localized alternation of the same fixed spectral fraction at successive spacer controls. Spacer shifts move the physical levels and reference-band edges at different rates, allowing us to reshape finite-chain return windows and place their endpoints at prescribed controls. An affine recalibration relocates the control family exactly.

title: Sharp orthonormal Strichartz estimates for the Schrödinger equation in all remaining cases
abstract: We study orthonormal Strichartz estimates for the free Schrödinger equation in homogeneous Sobolev spaces $\dot H^s$. We resolve the remaining open cases concerning the optimal summability of the coefficients. Together with earlier results and counterexamples, our theorems complete the classification for nonnegative Sobolev regularity $0\le s<d/2$.

title: Developing a Subdistrict-Level Economic Progress Index Using Geospatial Data
abstract: This paper develops an Economic Progress Index (EPI), a composite measure built from Earth Observation (EO) and open geospatial data with unsupervised Principal Component Analysis (PCA) weighting. The index captures the observable productive and enabling capacity of local economies and the intensity with which economic space is used. Sub-national monitoring in developing economies is held back by sparse data: district GDP estimates arrive with multi-year lags, rely on price deflators and top-down allocation, and do not exist at the subdistrict (taluka/tehsil) scale where place-based policy is targeted. The EPI fuses multi-sensor satellite data, gridded population and OpenStreetMap road and amenity networks across 357 subdistricts of Maharashtra, India, over 46 quarters (2015 Q1 - 2026 Q2). Seasonal-Trend decomposition using LOESS (STL) separates long-run trends from monsoon and crop-cycle seasonality. A non-negative PCA gives sign-consistent, interpretable weights and rankings nearly identical to standard PCA ($ρ$ = 0.998). Across districts, the index explains 74% of the variation in the NFHS-5 wealth index, 52% in household consumption (HCES 2023-24) and about 78% in real district GDP levels (65% in logs), but does not track short-run output growth. Because it measures structural capacity rather than annual output, the index kept rising through the FY2020-21 COVID-19 contraction. Across Maharashtra's six revenue divisions, relative inequality fell by 44% even as the absolute gap between leading and lagging divisions widened by 32%; district-level $β$-convergence implies a half-life of about 14 years. The framework offers a scalable, deflator-free basis for structural monitoring in data-sparse economies.

title: Character codegrees in $π$-separable groups
abstract: In this paper, we study the set $\operatorname{C}_π(G)$ of irreducible characters of a finite $π$-separable group $G$ whose codegrees (defined by Qian as $\operatorname{cod}(χ)=|G:\kerχ|/χ(1)$) are $π$-numbers, in relation to the Isaacs--Gajendragadkar classes of $π$-special characters $\operatorname{X}_π(G)$ and $\operatorname{B}_π$-characters $\operatorname{B}_π(G)$.

title: On pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian metrics
abstract: In our previous work, we studied the squared $L^2$-norm functionals $\mathcal G$ of Gauduchon's torsion $1$-form and $\mathcal F$ of the Chern torsion over the space of all Hermitian metrics with unit volume on a compact complex manifold. We introduced torsion-critical metrics as critical points of $\mathcal F$. In this paper, We prove that a pluriclosed and astheno-Kähler metric is torsion-critical if and only if it is Kähler. In particular, every compact pluriclosed torsion-critical Hermitian threefold is Kähler. We also give explicit examples and derive geometric consequences under additional curvature assumptions.

title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

title: SFiD: Self-Supervised Fitness-Driven Optimization for Next-Generation Networking
abstract: Next-generation (NG) wireless networks face increasingly complex and dynamic optimization challenges driven by data-intensive applications and massive device connectivity. Existing methods suffer from one or more limitations, including high computational complexity, poor scalability and adaptability, reliance on large labeled datasets, or weak generalization in dynamic and non-convex wireless environments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a self-supervised fitness-driven diffusion (SFiD) method that autonomously generates its own training data and iteratively learns from it. It also exhibits strong generalization capabilities and the ability to effectively tackle challenging optimization problems. We validate the convergence of our proposed method to the global optimum on both analytical convex and non-convex optimization problems. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, we consider reconfigurable intelligent surface (RIS) phaseshift optimization in cell-free massive multiple-input multipleoutput (CF-mMIMO) systems with imperfect channel state information and spatial correlation at the RIS as a case study. Specifically, we develop SFiD-C for continuous variable optimization and apply it to optimize continuous RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. We also develop SFiD-D for discrete variable optimization and apply it to optimize discrete RIS phase shifts in CF-mMIMO systems. Furthermore, we develop a binary neural network (BNN) based version of SFiDD for reducing its computational complexity, referred to as SFiD-D (BNN). Finally, our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods markedly improve computational efficiency and achieve comparable or superior performance compared to meta-heuristic and DRL benchmarks for both continuous and discrete RIS phase-shift optimization.

title: CoT-WAM: Collaborative Training of Vision-Language Models and World-Action Models via Plan Latents
abstract: General robot manipulation requires both semantic competence and physical foresight. World action models (WAMs) acquire an understanding of and predictive capability over the physical world by jointly modeling visual foresight and action distributions. However, existing WAMs still lack semantic competence: they have limited ability to perform open-world scene understanding, semantic reasoning, and long-horizon planning. Although vision-language models (VLMs) provide these capabilities, effectively integrating their semantic priors into WAM prediction and control remains challenging. To address this challenge, we propose CoT-WAM, a jointly trained WAM-VLM framework. CoT-WAM uses a learnable embedding to exchange information between the VLM and the WAM, which is supervised by textual and goal-image signals during training to encode rich intent information. A tailored two-stage training strategy enables joint optimization and more effective collaboration between the VLM and WAM. We evaluate CoT-WAM on six benchmarks covering control performance, zero-shot generalization, and long-horizon planning. CoT-WAM achieves SOTA performance on LIBERO, CALVIN, and RoboCasa-Kitchen, and demonstrates stronger zero-shot generalization on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-Pro without fine-tuning. On RoboCasa365, it further improves long-horizon planning over baselines with and without external planners. Real-world experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in practical deployments. Code is available at: https://github.com/jhz1192/CoT-WAM.git

title: TacPilot: Does Touch Need to Be Everywhere?
abstract: Tactile feedback helps visual manipulation policies respond to local contact, but changes in tactile observations do not always require corrective motion, and sustained corrections do not always require new tactile features. We introduce TacPilot, a tactile residual framework that separates representation updates from action intervention around a frozen visual policy. TacPilot uses a perception gate to determine when tactile features need refreshing and updates only affected regions while reusing unchanged features. A separate intervention gate determines whether bounded Cartesian and gripper residuals modify the nominal visual action. This separation allows tactile perception and action correction to follow different spatial and temporal demands during manipulation. In offline expert-trajectory replay, local feature reuse reduces encoded regions by 56.4% relative to periodic full encoding, with essentially unchanged action predictions. In an exploratory simulation evaluation spanning two cylinder sizes, TacPilot succeeds in 26 of 30 trials (86.7%). We further validate TacPilot on OpenArm v2 equipped with Paxini tactile sensors across four contact-rich manipulation tasks.

title: Hydrodynamic limit of the Toda lattice
abstract: In this paper we consider the Toda lattice under random, spatially inhomogeneous initial data, meaning that its initial momenta and interparticle spacings are independent and their laws may slowly vary in space. When the density is strictly positive (but sufficiently small), we identify the model's hydrodynamic limit under Euler scaling. More precisely, we prove that spatial averages of each of the model's local conserved quantities converge to moments of a density $m_τ(λ,q)$ solving the generalized hydrodynamic equation predicted by Doyon arXiv:1902.07624 and Spohn arXiv:1902.07751. To do so, we justify the notion that the Toda lattice can be thought of as a dense collection of many "quasiparticles" that interact through scattering. As in Aggarwal arXiv:2503.08018, we define these quasiparticles through spectral properties of the Toda Lax matrix, but in our inhomogeneous setting we must now show that the eigenvectors of this Lax matrix remain localized throughout the dynamics. The core of our work is to show that, with high probability, the quasiparticle trajectories converge to the characteristic curves of the generalized hydrodynamic equation.

title: Breaking the Myth of Four-Tier Stacked Transistors for Logic: an Investigation from Process to Device and Block-Level PPA
abstract: For the first time, this work evaluated whether 4-tier stacked transistors can translate the straightforward density gains into realistic chip-level scaling benefits. A practical dual-sided 4-tier transistor-stacking CFFET (Flipped CFET-to-CFET) process was proposed, on which a DTCO framework spanning standard-cell design, local interconnects, RO analysis, and physical implementation was built under 2A node design rules. The CFFET was also benchmarked with its 2-tier transistor-stacking counterparts FFET. Among CFFET configurations, the best-performing Symmetric Power still lags FFET by 11.2% in RO frequency due to the complex MOL parasitics. At the block level, CFFET reduces the Ibex RISC-V core area by only 12.8% (far below the 40% nominal cell-height reduction), while running 10.9% slower at iso-power. We further introduced a novel Tetris-like cell stitching to minimize the area overhead, which allows non-rectangular cell design and recovers 7.4% area in a 1-bit ALU design. An optimized NanoStack CFFET was finally proposed, inspired by previous work. This work indicates that straightforward vertical 4-tier stacking proves insufficient to guarantee enough PPA benefits, though the resulting design insights may guide future advanced architectures.

title: Sightline: Long-Window Speculative Decoding for Fast SVG Generation
abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation models write a graphic as code with one forward pass per token, so drawing is slow. Speculative decoding speeds them up losslessly, and block drafters guess many tokens per pass. On SVG, many of their rounds accept the whole draft and end only at the verification window. We find that their misses are rare and clumped, and that they stay accurate far deeper into a block than on natural language. A run-length identity and three propositions show that a longer window pays once the candidates are wide, up to the drafter's horizon. We propose Sightline, which pairs a window as long as the drafter's horizon with a draft tree wide enough to fill it. Experiments cover text-to-SVG and image-to-SVG with three models on six benchmarks from MMSVG, MMSVG-2M and SArena. In every setting, Sightline is the fastest of the compared lossless decoders. On SArena, it stays the fastest when every decoder shares one loop control. It also leads in almost every setting of six models from four other families, which write SVG code, compressed SVG tokens or Lottie JSON. Analyses trace the lead to rounds that shorter windows cut off, both in loop-free content and in loops. Speculative decoding also saves time for choosing samples by rendering, which beats choosing by likelihood. These results suggest that speculative decoding on vector graphics should verify as far as the drafter sees. Code and data are available at https://github.com/LiZaiyuan0619/Sightline.

title: PReMind: When Personal Memory Meets Visual Hazards
abstract: Personalized vision-language assistants use visual observations and personal memories to provide advice tailored to the user. When the observed scene contains a physical hazard, personal context, such as allergies, medical conditions, or mobility constraints, can change what help is appropriate. Responding appropriately therefore requires recognizing the visible hazard and applying the relevant person's information. We introduce PReMind-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark that evaluates this combination across diverse hazards and personal-memory conditions. It separately measures memory access, grounding, abstention, and hazard response, and assesses joint success on interdependency cases. Existing models often satisfy one requirement while failing the other, and training only for safety or personalization leaves a gap in joint success. We therefore propose PReMind, a two-phase reinforcement learning framework that combines on-demand and forced-call interactions (memory always retrieved) to jointly train grounded memory use and hazard response. At 4B, PReMind raises joint success from 12.9% to 28.6% over its base on the interdependency set and improves hazard adequacy and correct abstention on the main test. Joint-success gains persist under forced-call evaluation and under a second LLM judge across three Phase II seeds; averaged over these seeds, joint success also improves on unseen hazard groups. These findings highlight the need to evaluate and train personal assistants to connect visual evidence with the relevant person's context.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
abstract: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

title: Continual Tool-Space Extension Learning for Multimodal Agents
abstract: Multimodal agents largely rely on generic tools such as cropping, search, and code execution, leaving specialist vision models outside their tool space. However, bringing such a model into an already trained agent is not straightforward. The challenge is to learn each new tool efficiently while retaining the ability to use existing ones. This work proposes COTEX, continual tool-space extension learning, that adds new tools at efficient adapter-level cost. COTEX locates two sets of parameter directions; one triggers a tool call and thereby opens a multi-turn reasoning trajectory, while the other determines which tool is chosen. The adapter of a new tool is restricted to the calling directions that leave earlier tool choices unaffected by orthogonal constraint. We further introduce a protocol that converts specialist models' existing task-specific annotations into verified tool-use trajectories. Experiments on two representative agents and three specialist tools show gains on ten vision-language benchmarks, with at most a 0.3-point drop on existing tools.

title: Stephen: Verifying Sequencer-Aided Coordination Systems with Cross-View Prophecy
abstract: Many distributed systems achieve high performance by relying on dedicated sequencers to order requests, leaving replicas to commit them in that order. Despite more than a decade of such sequencer-aided coordination (SAC) systems, from Corfu and NOPaxos to LazyLog and SwitchBFT, their correctness has been argued only with pen-and-paper proofs or bounded model checking at the protocol level. In this paper, we formally verify implementations of SAC protocols. The sequencer seems to make this easy: it decides the order of all requests, so the proof can place each request's linearization point at the sequencer using a well-known technique, prophecy variables. Yet a linearization point placed at the sequencer is not durable, because the sequencer orders a request before any replica commits it. Crashes and other rare events may trigger a view change that discards the request, nullifying the earlier decision and the proof that rests on it. Our framework, Stephen, extends prophecy variables to handle view changes, and we make three contributions. (1) We develop cross-view prophecy peek, which lets the proof follow a request across view changes until it is either committed or permanently discarded. (2) Our verification uncovered bugs in existing SAC implementations, including one that can lose committed requests. We fix them and prove the fixes correct. (3) We apply Stephen to NOPaxos, Corfu and LazyLog. We build verified implementations with machine-checked proofs of linearizability. They perform within 17% of their open-source, unverified counterparts. The verified implementations and proofs will be open-sourced.

title: Fixed and periodic points of bi-dual intersection operators
abstract: We classify the fixed and periodic points, up to positive dilation, of the operators $\mathbb I_m=\mathbb I_{m,m+1}$ in the indexed bi-dual intersection family associated with centro-section integrals. For $n\ge3$ and $1\le m\le n-2$, a star body satisfies $\mathbb I_m^{\,r}K=cK$ for some $c>0$ and an integer $r\ge1$ if and only if it is an origin-centered Euclidean ball. No convexity, origin symmetry, or initial differentiability is assumed. An exact Grassmannian graph representation gives a decreasing weight and yields a strictly positive linear increment under continuous Steiner symmetrization unless the body is already symmetric. At a fixed point, a uniform radial Taylor estimate makes the same volume-preserving increment quadratic. Sobolev estimates for the spherical Radon transform and its adjoint supply the required regularity. Independently, a strict Lyapunov inequality reduces every periodic point up to dilation to a fixed point. We also prove automatic positivity and smoothness for bounded nonnegative solutions and local geometric convergence of normalized iterates near the ball.

title: SWIFT: Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely Action for Asynchronous Autonomous Driving
abstract: Driving scenes keep changing during model computation, making both observation freshness and action-delivery time central to world-action planning. To retain rich generative world priors in autonomous driving without stalling real-time control, we present SWIFT (Slow World, Instant Freshness, and Timely action), a deployment-oriented asynchronous world-action system that moves world updates off the observation-to-action critical path. On a background GPU, a slow Video DiT streams surround-view history into read-only predictive world context, trained with a predictive span that covers both the update interval and background world computation. On a foreground GPU, a lightweight freshness carrier encodes current surround-view images into a gated key/value bank at every step, letting a fast Action DiT combine live visual feedback with the latest completed world context without waiting. On open-loop NAVSIM, SWIFT reaches 94.2 PDMS at 198.4 ms per decision with a trajectory scorer; on closed-loop Bench2Drive, it achieves an 80.30 Driving Score at 109.9 ms foreground latency. SWIFT further transfers to the Waymo E2E hidden test (8.0050 Rater Feedback Score) and nuScenes (0.54 m mean endpoint error, 0.03% mean collision rate). Across all four benchmarks, SWIFT achieves the best results among compared world-action methods, establishing a favorable accuracy-latency trade-off.

title: From Powers--Stormer to Loewner Inertia: Weighted Trace Functionals and Orthogonal Perturbations
abstract: We study the weighted trace functional $\TT_{f,h}(A,B)=\Tr h^\circ(A-B)[f(A)-f(B)]$, where $h^\circ(H)=h(H_+)-h(H_-)$. The Jordan decomposition of $A-B$ yields exact common-roof decompositions for operator monotone and operator convex functions, including the Powers--Størmer and Ricard trace comparisons. The orthogonal cross term gives a finite rank-one realization of the classical conditional Löwner-matrix criterion for operator convexity. For powers, resolvent squares yield a coupling-dependent Mellin strip, endpoint identities, and quantitative bounds on off-sector spectral interactions. Linearization produces positive and inverse moment subspaces of power Löwner matrices. A confluent determinant calculation provides the remaining sign data in the known inertia classification. We give explicit equality conditions and a finite-copy application of the Powers--Størmer equality case.

title: CAFE-AQI: Coverage-Aware Day-Ahead AQI Forecasting with Early Warning and Conformal Uncertainty in Bangladesh
abstract: Next-day air quality forecasting often assumes city records are equally complete and independent. However, an audit of a large Bangladesh dataset revealed a sharp coverage expansion after August 2022 and showed that 103 city labels correspond to only 61 unique AQI trajectories. To address these issues, this paper presents CAFE-AQI, a coverage-aware framework for forecasting next-day maximum AQI. It also estimates the probability of Unhealthy-or-worse conditions (AQI >= 151). Data were divided chronologically into training (2022-2023), calibration (2024), and testing (2025). To prevent duplicate records from dominating training and evaluation, identical trajectories were weighted. The framework combines temporal and pollutant features with a five-neighbor spatial context. It also includes a class-balanced warning head and risk-conditional conformal calibration aimed at providing early warnings and prediction intervals. Evaluation on the duplicate-balanced 2025 data gave an MAE of 9.76, an RMSE of 15.04, and an R-squared value of 0.910 for CAFE-AQI. Its MAE was 3.63 AQI lower than persistence (95% CI: 3.49-3.76), with lower errors in each of the 61 trajectory groups. For unhealthy-air warnings, the F1-score was 0.908 and the AUROC was 0.982. The nominal 90% intervals covered 92.09% of observations. When an entire spatial block was excluded from training, the MAE remained 10.66, showing that the lightweight model transferred reasonably well to unseen locations.

title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
abstract: A patch to a robot's navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path. Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches. It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong. We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits. Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task's documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them. The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks. They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis. Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.

title: Metrics-in-the-Loop: Complexity Feedback Reshapes Agent-Written Code
abstract: Coding agents now write whole codebases in long autonomous runs, guided mainly by whether their tests pass. Yet passing tests alone does not reveal accumulating complexity or gaps in test coverage, which then persist as agents extend their own code. We introduce metrics-in-the-loop, an inference-time intervention that gives agents in-flight feedback: cheap, automatically computed code metrics injected into the agent's context during the trajectory. After each code-changing agent turn, we insert short feedback messages naming changed functions whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds a limit (complexity feedback) or changed lines that are skipped by tests (coverage feedback), giving the agent the opportunity to refactor code or strengthen tests before continuing. We run extensive experiments and ablations comparing several interventions across three long-horizon coding benchmarks and four strong models. We find that complexity feedback significantly reduces erosion, a measure of complexity concentration of code, without affecting held-out correctness of the code. Broadly, our experiments investigate a practical form of agent "re-railing", where timely, actionable measurements redirect agents before weaknesses become the foundation they keep building on. As agents scale to codebases with millions of lines, such interventions become critical to sustaining effective development and long-term code maintainability.

title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

title: Chromatic heights of homotopy fixed points of iterated topological Hochschild homology of connective spectra
abstract: Let $R$ be an $\mathbb{E}_{\infty}$-ring spectrum of height $m$. The chromatic redshift theorem implies that its $n$-fold iterated algebraic $K$-theory $K^{(n)}(R)$ has height $m+n$. Moreover, there is a natural map $K^{(n)}(R)\to (T^n\otimes R)^{hT^n}$, where $T^n\otimes R$ denotes the $n$-fold iterated topological Hochschild homology. Hence it is natural to ask whether the target also has height $m+n$. Although this fails in general, we prove that it holds whenever $R$ is connective and $m\geq1$. Our proof is based on an iterative calculation using Wilson spaces and relative topological Hochschild homology. As an application, we determine the support of the $T^n$-homotopy fixed points of $n$-fold iterated topological Hochschild homology of $\mathrm{BP}\langle m\rangle$ for $n=2,3$ with $\mathrm{BP}\langle m\rangle$ equipped with any $\mathbb{E}_3$-$\mathrm{MU}$-form.

title: Sensor Monitoring Towards Industry 4.0: Bridging Concepts on the $C_n$ Multivariate Control Chart
abstract: The main challenge in monitoring multiple sensors is the high dimensionality that a process can easily reach. From a decision-making perspective, converting these multivariate dynamics into an informative visualization is also not trivial. Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques detect changes in quality characteristics, but they are difficult to apply beyond the normality (Gaussian) assumption. For instance, the most well-known SPC multivariate control chart is based on Hotelling's $T^2$ statistic, which assumes that the process data follow a multivariate normal distribution (which rarely occurs in practice) and that the observations are serially independent. This study focuses on the multivariate case (dimension $d \geq 2$), regardless of the data dependence or marginal asymmetry. We propose a new control chart for change detection in copula-based multivariate processes, called the $C_n$-chart, which is based on a density level-set tolerance region built from a copula function, and we derive its run-length properties. The methodology also quantifies the (not necessarily linear) dependence among the variables. Two case studies are presented, one on water quality control and the other on monitoring brass-steel thermostats, complemented by a simulation study of run-length performance and computational cost. The results show that the proposed methodology captures both the association among variables and the anomalies, and that it accommodates variable selection through conditional (regression) modeling of the margins.

title: Hurwitz equivalence in quandles of order at most four
abstract: Let $X$ be a quandle and let $m\geq 2$ be an integer. The $m$-braid group acts on the $m$-fold Cartesian power $X^m$ by the Hurwitz action. For an $m$-tuple $\boldsymbol{x}\in X^m$, we introduce two invariants of the Hurwitz action: the product $Π(\boldsymbol{x})$ of its entries in the associated group $\operatorname{As}(X)$ and the orbit multiplicities $μ_w(\boldsymbol{x})$ $(w\in X)$. We prove that these two invariants completely classify Hurwitz equivalence classes for all quandles of order at most four. We also establish a complete classification of Hurwitz equivalence classes for a class of amalgamated sums of trivial quandles and a reduction theorem for disjoint sums with trivial quandles. Finally, we study the corresponding action of the virtual braid group. For this action, the orbit multiplicities alone give a complete classification for every quandle of order at most four.

title: Mapping the Design Space of Feature Sampling for Optical Flow
abstract: The computation of correlation features is crucial for optical flow estimation. Existing methods (e.g., RAFT) perform fixed-radius lookups on a cost volume, yielding a set of correlation features for each position; alternatively, WAFT performs single-point feature indexing, yielding one correlation feature vector per position. None of them designs a suitable correlation feature sampling scheme for each position according to regional characteristics. Our insight is that not every position requires the same sampling scheme.
