To resolve this representation dilemma, we propose GRODE-RTL, an anchor-centric representation that extracts the single-clock-stage fan-in cone of a suspect register from the netlist, maps netlist nodes back to editable source lines, and organizes them into a compact hop-partitioned dependency view. By prioritizing direct drivers and folding distant hops, GRODE-RTL guides standard tool-using agents without exposing ground-truth hints or oracle feedback. We evaluate GRODE-RTL across 30 formally validated non-local faults using three LLMs (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3) alongside a controlled six-configuration ablation study. GRODE-RTL improves pass@1 over source-level exploration by 16.7% on DeepSeek, by 26.7% on GLM-5.2, and by 20.0% on MiniMax-M3, with consistent gains on the hard-to-retrieve far-distance and indirect-anchor subsets of all three models. Our controls isolate structural relevance from generic context expansion, proving that selective dependency organization rather than full graph exposure is key to effective RTL repair.

title: Positive semidefiniteness of random submatrices
abstract: Given a symmetric matrix $A \in [-1,1]^{n \times n}$, we estimate the probability that a random principal submatrix, obtained by taking each index independently with probability $p$, is positive semidefinite. As a corollary, we show that $O(\varepsilon^{-1})$ indices chosen uniformly at random suffice for testing positive semidefiniteness with squared Frobenius distance threshold $\varepsilon n^2$, thus nearly matching the lower bound of Bakshi, Chepurko, and Jayaram (``Testing Positive Semi-Definiteness via Random Submatrices'', FOCS 2020). The key ingredient is a dense model lemma for positive semidefinite matrices, proved using the hyperplane separation theorem and a contraction inequality for Rademacher random variables.

title: Correctable Enrollment and One-Transaction Seed Proofs for Ethereum's Post-Quantum Migration
abstract: A quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can extract the private key of every Ethereum account whose public key is published, and accounts exposed by their own transactions hold 54.6% of execution-layer ETH. As the first such machine may stay secret, a migration cannot wait for visible thefts, and once keys are extractable, legacy signatures no longer tell owners from attackers. We design a migration in which owners enroll post-quantum keys cheaply with their existing signatures before ECDSA is retired at a scheduled time, while a zero-knowledge proof of the wallet's BIP-39 seed can correct any such enrollment until a common deadline afterward; an account nobody enrolled stays frozen and recoverable by seed proof without a deadline. Each proof binds the new key, a nonce and a fee cap, so neither a paying sponsor nor a reordering block builder can redirect or replay it. Validators switch to hash-based keys first, at a finalized checkpoint and under a stated bound on the attacker's voting power. We prove the account guarantees under explicit assumptions, model-check the rules, and implement the design in go-ethereum and a Lean consensus client. A three-layer recursive hash-based STARK yields a seed proof of about 190 KB that fits one transaction, verifies in 38 ms and takes a median of 111 s to generate on a laptop; four proofs aggregate into one. In a ten-node simulation with mainnet-derived accounts and fee demand, block space rather than proving sets the duration: the 4.45 million accounts with at least 0.1 ETH would migrate in 29.4 days if all enroll before ECDSA is retired and in 235 days if all recover after it in batches of four. In a mass enrollment, an enrollment waits a median of 19.1 minutes in the public mempool, longer than published estimates for a fast quantum computer to extract its key, so owners with a seed and an unexposed key should migrate by seed proof.

title: GPU-Accelerated Secure Inference for Drug--Target Interaction Prediction
abstract: Deep learning models that predict drug--target interactions (DTI) can speed up drug discovery, but the candidate drugs they score are valuable intellectual property that their owners cannot reveal. Secure multiparty computation (MPC) lets two servers compute a prediction on a secret-shared drug, without either server learning the drug. However, secure inference of deep models is slow. Non-linear operations require communication between the servers, and MPC arithmetic does not map naturally to GPUs. In this paper, we present our solution to Track~III of the iDASH 2026 privacy and security competition, which asked for fast two-party secure DTI inference on GPUs. Our solution is built on the co-design of MPC-friendly models and MPC protocols. On the model side, we design SlimDTA, a DTI model that reduces the operations on the secret drug, and in particular the non-linear operations that require communication. On the protocol side, we build a GPU framework that evaluates the linear layers with additive secret sharing and the non-linear layers with function secret sharing, including a custom CUDA kernel for the comparisons. Our solution won first place in the competition, at under 10,ms per prediction on average, and its secure predictions match the plaintext model to within 0.02%.

title: GNetSS: Towards Learning GNSS Corrections without Ground Truth
abstract: We present GNetSS, a self-supervised GNSS position correction framework that improves the robustness of single point positioning (SPP) without requiring ground-truth locations for training. GNetSS combines a transformer-based network with a deterministic differentiable positioning solver. The network predicts satellite-wise pseudorange corrections by modelling inter-satellite geometry and temporal context, while the solver converts these corrected measurements into receiver position corrections under GNSS geometry and optional motion constraints. Unlike supervised GNSS correction methods that rely on ground-truth, GNetSS derives its training signal directly from GNSS measurement consistency. Experimental results show that GNetSS improves robustness across open-sky, urban, and forested environments. The method is particularly effective at suppressing large-error outliers, reducing the maximum 3D positioning error by over 50% compared with SPP. These results demonstrate the potential of self-supervised pseudorange correction for scalable and robust GNSS positioning in real-world autonomy applications. Code and the in-house dataset will be released upon acceptance.

title: Impact of Effective Nucleon Mass and Symmetry Energy on Nuclear Pasta Phases and the Unified Equation of State of Neutron Stars
abstract: We investigate how the effective nucleon mass and symmetry energy affect pasta phase properties and the unified equation of state (EOS) of neutron stars. The nonuniform pasta structure is described within the self-consistent Thomas-Fermi approximation, while nucleonic interactions are treated in the relativistic mean-field framework with several typical parameter sets adopted. Our results indicate that the symmetry energy and its slope are crucial in determining the onset of pasta phases and their geometric configurations. In the high-density region where matter becomes uniform, the effective nucleon mass plays a dominant role. A larger effective nucleon mass tends to soften the EOS, which yields a smaller radius for a canonical $1.4 M_{\odot}$ neutron star and reduces the corresponding tidal deformability.

title: CauSyncVLA: Causal Latent World Modeling for Asynchronous Robot Control
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies must react while visual inference is still running. Overlapping computation and execution reduces waiting, yet leaves perceptual memory stale and successive action chunks disconnected. We present CauSyncVLA, an asynchronous dual-system controller that aligns perceptual-memory prediction and trajectory correction with actual robot execution. Rather than forecasting pixels or physical states, a Causal Latent World Model predicts current perceptual memory from delayed visual anchors and executed state-action history, supervised through action-sensitive distillation to retain the frozen expert's control response. Conditioned on this updated memory, Predictive Flow Warm-Starting (PFWS) aligns the unexecuted action horizon for single-step flow correction without extra training. On LIBERO-10, CauSyncVLA reaches 93.8% success at 5.04$\times$ inference throughput, improving closed-loop robustness and robot motion smoothness.

title: Norm-equation methods for structured group-penalized regression
abstract: Group-penalized regression with correlated predictors requires block updates for which familiar group soft thresholding formulas are generally inapplicable. Although proximal-gradient methods can solve such updates directly, their computational cost depends on the penalty and the design. We develop a norm-equation framework for a Euclidean group penalty combined with a finite, closed, convex, positively homogeneous within-group penalty. Each nonzero block minimizer is characterized by a unique scalar root, evaluated through strongly convex inner problems without enumerating sparsity or fusion patterns. Valid inner subgradients provide computable bounds on the scalar function and the block Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) error. These bounds allow scalar-search decisions and acceptance of approximate updates without solving every inner problem to high accuracy. Accounting for gradient changes during a cyclic sweep then gives a computable global KKT bound. Combined with standard stochastic-score and restricted-curvature conditions, this bound leads to a regularization-scaled stopping rule under which approximate estimators retain the usual estimation and prediction rates. Experiments with sparse-group and fused sparse-group regression show that computational performance depends strongly on the inner solver, with coordinate-descent and dual implementations offering advantages over direct proximal methods in some highly correlated settings.

title: Ask in the Crowd: Differentially Private LLM Inference via Dummy-Augmented Shuffling
abstract: Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

title: Efficient Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language Model via Dynamics-Aware Quantization and Distillation
abstract: Efficient chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning in vision-language models (VLMs) requires reducing both intermediate reasoning steps and their execution cost. Latent CoT methods compress textual rationales into continuous thoughts, yet their full-precision (FP) models retain substantial storage and computation costs. Lowering numerical precision could reduce these remaining costs, yet direct quantization severely degrades reasoning accuracy, particularly with 4-bit weights and activations. Operator and perturbation analyses reveal key sensitivity and direction-dependent predictive effects of continuous-thought errors, motivating preservation of information retrieval and subsequent reasoning beyond reconstruction accuracy. We therefore introduce QL-VLM, a dynamics-aware Quantization framework for efficient Latent reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs). First, Dynamics-Guided Quantization (DGQ) uses nonuniform codebooks that preserve rotary-key structure, mitigating quantization-induced distortion in vision-language information retrieval. Second, Dynamics-Preserving Distillation (DPD) aligns continuous thoughts, latent-query readouts, and predictions with a full-precision teacher, maintaining predictive consistency through subsequent low-precision reasoning. On ScienceQA-IMG with Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct, 4-bit QL-VLM achieves 90.43% accuracy and improves baseline by 40.33%, with 16.64x fewer bit-operations and 6.40x lower measured latency than explicit CoT.

title: LATER: Learning Action-Conditioned Temporal Evidence Retrieval for Predictive World Models
abstract: Early interactions can reveal physical properties that later observations no longer show. These properties can still gov- ern the effects of future actions. Inspired by the distinction between retention and selective readout in working mem- ory and cognitive science, we introduce LATER, an action- conditioned world model built on CF-JEPA. LATER stores completed real transitions in partitioned memories that remain fixed during candidate rollouts. A response bridge queries these memories using the current state and candidate action, while multi-cut auxiliary supervision trains the memory writ- ers. On distracted Two-Stage PushT, LATER raises terminal success from 15.5% to 25.0% over reconstructed CF-JEPA. In a separate comparison across six models and two scratch- training seeds, LATER achieves the lowest mean physical readout error in both clean and distracted views, reducing along-push mean absolute error (MAE) under distractors by 20.2% relative to CF-JEPA. Controlled history interventions show that later predictions depend on earlier physical evi- dence even when query observations and actions are fixed, with larger effects during pushing than waiting.

title: SEAF: Selective Semantic Enrichment and Visual Evidence Fusion for Multimodal Sarcasm Detection
abstract: Multimodal sarcasm detection requires textual, visual, and contextual evidence, particularly when multiple images provide complementary cues. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate auxiliary information from a post's text and images, but their outputs may mix useful background knowledge with redundant visual descriptions. We propose SEAF, a dual-branch framework for selective semantic enrichment and visual evidence fusion. SEAF assigns generated fields to distinct roles: entity background enriches semantic input, while image descriptions supply alignment statistics. The semantic branch combines the original post text, background from a frozen MLLM, and optical character recognition (OCR) text. The aligned visual branch combines global and local visual features with statistics of cross-modal and inter-image similarity. Text-Anchored Smoothed Aggregation (TASA) weights images by their similarity to the original post text while preserving contributions from images with low literal similarity. Summing the branch classification scores integrates contextual semantics with visual evidence. Experiments on the multi-image MMSD3.0 benchmark show that SEAF outperforms all compared methods.

title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks
abstract: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.

title: Solving the puzzle of tropical cyclone track bifurcation
abstract: Tropical cyclones whose predicted tracks bifurcate are among the most dreaded storms in disaster planning. Understanding when and why these bifurcations occur has been a long-standing puzzle in track forecasting. We address this issue by introducing the concept of "fate boundaries" hidden in the steering flow. Storms located on opposite sides of these boundaries follow dramatically different tracks. By analyzing 1,179 Northern Hemisphere storms over 2011-2025, we identified 61 with a strong signature of bifurcation. In every instance, fate boundaries explained why the ensemble tracks split. Additionally, they can reveal bifurcations days before they appear in any operational ensemble. Because fate boundaries often separate devastating from nearby benign tracks, they mark when and where minimal interventions could, in principle, redirect a storm.

title: Minimal Memory for Correctable Visual Continuation
abstract: Given past images and known actions, visual continuation generates future frames from one evolving scene state. Keeping this state revisable matters when an object reappears or a later view changes an earlier interpretation. Once past images cannot be replayed, a summary sufficient for current rendering can lose candidates needed after correction. We establish matching sparse and dense bounds on the bits needed for later correction under stable observations and bounded disagreement. For static streams at the stated smoothness and margin scales, correction incurs at least logarithmic overhead in one dimension and polynomial overhead in higher dimensions. Coherent Archive Memory (CAM) stores geometric summaries with exact updates under clipped expansion and coordinate assignments, then uses historical existence constraints to select one state for all requested frames. Exhaustive photographic tests show strict worst-truth image-risk gains from joint witnesses, while controlled neural continuations recover positions hidden in the current view.

title: On quasi-triangular Hopf algebras of square-free dimensions
abstract: Let $H$ be a quasi-triangular Hopf algebra of sqaure-free dimension over $\mathbb{C}$. In this note, we show that $H$ is semisimple and cocommutative. Equivalently, a braided finite tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ of square-free Frobenius--Perron dimension with a fiber functor is tensor equivalent to the representation category of a finite group.

title: Proportional Representation for Almost-Solid Coalitions and the Proportional Veto Core for Rankings
abstract: A proportional ranking should give groups of voters representation commensurate with their size at every prefix. Proportionality for solid coalitions (PSC) provides this guarantee to groups whose members rank the same set of candidates above all others. How much representation should a group receive when a few outside candidates disrupt that agreement? We extend the proportional veto core to rankings through candidatewise and setwise guarantees. We show that setwise veto protection is equivalent to robust Rank-PSC under reversal of both the voters' preferences and the collective ranking. Robust Rank-PSC extends representation guarantees to almost-solid coalitions at every prefix. Each distinct outside candidate that disrupts a coalition's agreement reduces its guaranteed representation by at most one, and this bound is tight. Using reverse-sequential variants of Ordered Phragmén and STV, we construct rankings satisfying robust Rank-PSC$+$ in polynomial time. This stronger axiom preserves the guarantee after deleting any suffix of the collective ranking and restricting voters' preferences to the remaining candidates. Verifying robust Rank-PSC is coNP-complete, whereas verifying robust Rank-PSC$+$ takes polynomial time. We also introduce Rank-Aligned PJR$+$, which requires the first $r$ candidates of the collective ranking to satisfy PJR$+$ when each voter approves their top $r$ candidates. We give a polynomial-time algorithm that meets this requirement simultaneously for every $r$. For fixed-size committees, the Expanding Approvals Rule guarantees Rank-PJR$+$ but can violate robust PSC regardless of how ties are broken or payments are assigned. We give a modification that satisfies both guarantees for any prescribed committee size.

title: Lightweight Low-Frequency Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring via Karhunen-Loève Feature Distillation and Temporal Convolutional Networks
abstract: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) is a critical enabler for demand-side management which allows for smart grid optimization. A deployment-ready NILM solution necessitates three key features: accurate disaggregation, low-frequency sampling, and low computational cost. This paper proposes a lightweight, edge-oriented NILM framework that combines activity-boundary-aware synthetic data augmentation with Karhunen-Loève Transform (KLT) feature extraction and a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). The augmentation stage extracts and recombines complete or near-complete appliance activation segments so that the model can be trained without new fully labeled household aggregates. The KLT filter bank extracts decorrelated, appliance-informed temporal features which are then fed into a compact TCN along with the original aggregate for energy disaggregation. Evaluations on two standard NILM datasets, UK-DALE and REDD, at 10-s sampling and with leave-one-house-out testing, demonstrate that the proposed architecture achieves comparable or superior disaggregation accuracy relative to NILMFormer, BERT4NILM, BiLSTM, and BiGRU. The computational footprint of the framework is 31,009 parameters, the fewest of the five models compared, and on a single CPU thread it needs 2.78 ms per 1000 samples, 84-95% less than the baselines. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency tradeoff for low-frequency smart-meter NILM.

title: LeCompass: Task-Level Execution through State-Indexed Interfaces
abstract: Action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) offer a foundation for predictive decision-making by modeling the consequences of actions in representation space. Yet evaluating local reachability in latent space does not by itself provide a task-level execution interface: intermediate targets must be generated, local inference has finite budgets, and execution requires spatial feedback and persistent interaction state. We introduce LeCompass, a state-indexed execution framework built around a frozen LeWorldModel (LeWM). A proposer supplies intermediate latent targets, while CompassFlow searches the source space of a learned trajectory prior to obtain effective action candidates under limited predictive-evaluation budgets. Patch-token readouts provide spatial feedback, while observation-based memory supports phase transitions and bounded recovery. State-indexed targets support cross-episode context-goal composition. On 1,000 official TEST full-episode Cube trials, the complete LeCompass execution system achieves 86.9% native 4-cm reach. Separate matched analyses show that predictive ranking raises success from 4.7% to 44.9% on TEST PushT and from 33.8% to 77.7% on TEST TwoRoom. These results demonstrate task-level execution with task-dependent roles for latent target proposal, predictive search, and observation-grounded control.

title: Beyond Entity Recognition: Vision-Centric Knowledge Visual Question Answering
abstract: We propose VC-VQA, a large-scale benchmark for vision-centric knowledge reasoning, aiming to systematically evaluate the capabilities of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition and complex multi-stage reasoning. Unlike existing benchmarks that primarily treat visual information as entity recognition and rely on text-based external knowledge, VC-VQA explicitly models the role of visual information by considering both its source (internal vs. external images) and stage of involvement (pre-retrieval vs. post-retrieval). Specifically, VC-VQA requires models to retrieve external visual evidence, identify visual clues before retrieval, and localize, verify, or match retrieved knowledge against the internal image. We further construct a controlled multimodal knowledge base with traceable textual and visual evidence for each sample. We evaluate 21 representative MLLMs under four settings: no external knowledge, with provided evidence, knowledge base retrieval, and open-web search. Experimental results lead to three key findings: current models still struggle with vision-centric knowledge reasoning; fine-grained visual knowledge acquisition remains the primary bottleneck; and agentic retrieval highlights the value of multi-step planning and cross-modal knowledge integration. Overall, VC-VQA provides a more challenging benchmark for evaluating vision-centric knowledge reasoning in MLLMs. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/CASIA-IVA-Lab/VC-VQA.

title: Explainability of genotype embedding models through observed cohort paths
abstract: Deep learning models that combine genotypes with neuroimaging predict neurological diseases more accurately than either modality alone. Their clinical use, however, requires identifying which genetic variants a prediction is based on. Path-based attribution methods like Integrated Gradients address this by integrating the model's gradient from a baseline to the input. These methods assume the model accepts any point along that path as a valid input. Genotype models violate this assumption. They map the three discrete allele dosages \{0,1,2\} to vectors through a learned embedding defined only at those values, so a straight line passes through fractional genotypes at which no embedding, and therefore no gradient, exists. Attribution must therefore proceed in embedding space where the choice of path can affect the resulting attribution. We show that the commonly used per-variant estimator does not generally satisfy completeness. Additive separability guarantees completeness for this estimator, but interactions between variants generally break that property. Instead, we integrate along piecewise-linear embedding-space paths connecting genotype waypoints observed in the training cohort. Each path satisfies completeness in the continuum although the interiors of its segments are not necessarily observed. Our method improves faithfulness over Integrated Gradients and discretized Integrated Gradients under both perturbation protocols, achieves the strongest results for Parkinson's disease classification under support-preserving perturbations, and is competitive with a support-background Shapley baseline under per-variant perturbations. It also shows higher seed stability and better recovery of planted non-additive effects in a synthetic benchmark.

title: FoodReact-AR: Learning Audience Reactions that Zero-Shot LLMs Miss in Arabic Food-Insecurity Discourse
abstract: Facebook reactions record how an audience received a post, a signal absent from the post's text. We treat the six differentiated reactions on 74,241 Arabic food-insecurity posts from public Facebook pages (2020-2024) as compositions, apply a centered log-ratio transformation, and cluster them into four audience profiles: Solidarity (Love-dominant), Dismissal (Haha-dominant), Grief (Sad-dominant), and a flat Ambivalent profile. Dismissal peaks in 2022 (22.3%), the year of the wheat price shock, and grief in 2024 (14.0%), during the Gaza food emergency; a page-clustered GEE confirms both shifts (odds ratios 2.18 and 1.34), and they survive minimum-reaction filtering, alternative zero replacements and clustering methods, and bootstrap resampling. We then test whether the profiles can be predicted without reactions. A zero-shot Arabic LLM recovers Grief for 83.8% of posts but Dismissal for only 3.4%, and in a matched ablation, it shows the reaction percentages do not help. A simple classifier trained on the reaction-derived labels and tested on unseen pages recovers dismissal for 60.0% (macro-F1 0.56 against 0.43), mainly from mentions of officials and institutions. Derisive audience responses are thus learnable from text, yet a zero-shot LLM misses them. We release the corpus, LLM, and human annotation layers, and an evaluation protocol as FoodReact-AR.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning to Refine Actions with Visual Reliability and Tactile Feedback for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce \textbf{TipDex-VTLA}, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

title: A sharp bounded bijection for tight cylindric partitions
abstract: Fix a cyclic profile of coprime rank $r$ and level $\ell$, both at least three, and an entry bound $n\ge1$. Let $d$ be the deficit from the maximum volume of a tight cylindric partition. For $d\le n\min(r,\ell)$, the one-row combinatorial $R$ matches the tight cylinders whose last slice lies inside the maximizer's last slice with the partitions of $d$ in which each part occurs fewer than $r$ times. The inverse preserves the profile and entry bound. We identify every partition missed at the next deficit. A prefix test decides whether any cylinder lies outside this sector and, if so, identifies the unique one of least deficit. This explains the leading coefficient gap in Warnaar's $Q_{n,c}$. We also determine the first correction to the vertex terms of the published bounded determinant.

title: Extremal spectral results of outerplanar graphs without starlike trees
abstract: A graph $G$ is $F$-free if it does not contain $F$ as a subgraph. Let $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,F)$ denote the set of $n$-vertex $F$-free outerplanar graphs with maximum spectral radius. Define $S(l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t)$ as the starlike tree obtained from $t$ vertex-disjoint paths of lengths $l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t$ by identifying one endpoint of each path, and $C_{l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t}$ as the graph obtained from $t$ vertex-disjoint cycles of lengths $l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t$ by identifying one vertex from each cycle. When $l_1=l_2=\cdots=l_t=l$, we abbreviate these graphs as $S(t\cdot l)$ and $C_{t\cdot l}$, respectively. Previous results determined $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,S(t\cdot l))$ for $t\ge4$ [Graphs Combin. 42 (2026) 80] and for $t=3$, in each case for sufficiently large $n$. For $C_{l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t}$, the corresponding extremal graphs are known for $t=2$ and sufficiently large $n$. The sets $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,C_{t\cdot l})$ were also determined for sufficiently large $n$ [Discrete Math. 349 (2026) 114673]. In this paper, we determine $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,S(l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t))$ for sufficiently large $n$ when the branch lengths are not all equal. Our result for $t\ge4$ also includes equal branch lengths. As applications, we determine $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,C_{l_1,l_2,\ldots,l_t})$ for arbitrary cycle lengths and sufficiently large $n$. We also determine $\operatorname{SPEX}_{\mathcal{OP}}(n,F)$ for certain linear forests $F=\bigcup_{i=1}^tP_{l_i}$ and sufficiently large $n$. Finally, we apply our main theorems to obtain the known results on outerplanar graphs forbidding matchings or theta graphs for sufficiently large $n$.

title: Energy transfers in decaying three-dimensional Hall-magnetohydrodynamics turbulence: Dependence on the Ion-Inertial Length and the Magnetic Prandtl Number
abstract: We present a systematic study of energy transfers in three-dimensional (3D) decaying Hall-magnetohydrodynamics (HMHD) turbulence. Our study has been designed to investigate the dependence of these transfers on initial energy spectra, the ion-inertial length $d_{i}$, and the magnetic Prandtl number $Pr_{m}$. Using shell-to-shell decomposition, we compute the energy transfer rates for (a) kinetic-to-kinetic, (b) magnetic-to-magnetic, (c) kinetic-to-magnetic, and (d) magnetic-to-kinetic interactions by carrying out extensive pseudospectral direct numerical simulations (DNSs) of 3D HMHD and its MHD counterpart. Furthermore, we examine the magnetic-to-magnetic and current-density-to-magnetic energy transfers arising from the Hall term in this framework. Energy transfers between like fields -- namely, kinetic-to-kinetic and magnetic-to-magnetic -- are predominantly local and forward in direction, cascading energy from large to small length scales. This behavior is consistent with a self-similar flow structure in the inertial range. Cross-field transfers, between kinetic and magnetic energy, are found to be forward but non-local in character. At low and high $Pr_{m}$, the transfers become local, and the nonlinear energy transfer is significantly suppressed. Moreover, we observe that the Hall term drives both inverse and forward transfers of magnetic energy, associated with local and non-local transfer, respectively.

title: Propagation of chaos with singular potentials: A weighted duality approach
abstract: We establish the propagation of chaos and derive the Vlasov equation from a many-body $N$-particle system in the mean-field regime with singular interaction forces bounded by $|x|^{-α-1}$ for $0\le α<(d-1)/2$ in dimensions $d\ge 2$, which in particular include the full range of sub-Coulomb interactions in three dimensions as well as the Coulomb interaction in two dimensions. Our proof is based on an energy-based framework for deriving weighted uniform bounds on cumulants that builds upon the recent duality method developed by Bresch--Duerinckx--Jabin in combination with a new Morawetz-type estimate, allowing us to remove the restriction to locally square-integrable interaction force kernels and handle more singular regimes.

title: Anisotropic Coulomb Interaction in Strongly Magnetized Electron Gas at Zero Temperature in Relativistic Quantum Framework
abstract: We present a microscopic derivation of Debye screening in a Landau-quantized electron gas subject to a strong magnetic field. By calculating the photon self-energy within the RPA framework, we explore how Landau levels influence the screening properties of the electron gas. Due to the quantum periodicity of Landau levels, the screening behavior is relatively insensitive to variations in the carrier density within each occupation cycle compared to the drastic changes induced by the magnetic field strength. Within a single occupation cycle, the Kohn anomaly dominates the low-density regime; at higher densities, its characteristic momentum shifts into the asymptotic high-momentum regime, rendering its singular contribution less prominent over the active screening domain and allowinga smooth orientation-dependent anisotropy to govern the system. Furthermore, a subtle competition in directional screening is observed between the parallel and perpendicular directions to the field depending on the density domain. At lower field strengths, multiple quantum oscillations emerge from the simultaneous participation of various Landau levels, marking a qualitative transition toward the isotropic three-dimensional limit. Our findings reveal anisotropic screening effects and provide insights into the behavior of charged impurities in such systems.

title: D3-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Models with Dynamic Mode Decomposition
abstract: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images and videos, but every sampling step requires a full network evaluation. Training-free caching reduces this cost by reusing or forecasting network outputs across steps, but common approaches use per-model calibrated skip criteria or maintain per-layer prediction histories. We present D3-Cache, which applies Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) to Diffusion sampling: it fits DMD to a short history of exact velocities and forecasts only the velocity that the scheduler consumes. A horizon-aware gate decides when to skip: whenever the network is evaluated, its output is compared with the forecast for that step, and the larger the error, the sooner the network is evaluated again, up to a cap on consecutive skipped steps. D3-Cache requires no training or per-model offline calibration curve and adds negligible memory. It shares one history length and risk tolerance across the four evaluated models. On four state-of-the-art image and video models, D3-Cache achieves speedups of 2.6-3.8x with high fidelity to the base model output.

title: Determinant Massey products
abstract: We introduce the determinant Massey product, a secondary operation on the cohomology of commutative dg algebras which is reminiscent of the classical Massey product. We prove some of the elementary properties of this product, compute several examples, and relate them to classical and matric Massey products. When 2 is invertible, a determinant Massey product is a matric Massey product, but over $\mathbb F_2$, it is not. In this case, we produce a finite-dimensional cdga whose Harrison cohomology does not inject into its Hochschild cohomology, and a divided powers algebra which is formal as an associative dg algebra, but not as a commutative one, with an explicit determinant Massey product witnessing the failure. Over $\mathbb Q$, we use determinant Massey products to construct a simply-connected coformal space with Koszul cohomology ring and vanishing ordinary Massey products of all orders, which is not formal.

title: Exploring Semantic Table Search in Data Lakes
abstract: Discovery of relevant datasets within data lakes remains a key challenge. Union and join search are effective techniques for discovering data when augmenting an existing table. In exploratory search, instead, keyword search is commonly adopted to find a relatively small set of highly relevant tables matching some search terms. In this context, semantic search is a new technique that exploits the presence of named entities in exemplar tuples used as queries and in target tables. Hence, keyword search and entity search are able to find a diverse set of tables. In this work, we propose \texttt{Thetis++}, which combines keyword and semantic table search to discover relevant tables that combine the semantic signal with the presence of exact keyword matches. Incorporating multiple paradigms and sources of information allow us to combine the best of multiple worlds. Therefore, we study many alternative techniques for combining rankings and evaluate these for the table search task in data lakes. We explore both unsupervised and supervised techniques, including TOPSIS. Finally, alternative to Thetis++ combining keyword and semantic relevance signals, we study a variant of learning-to-rank for the table search task in data lakes. Our evaluation highlights both the limitations of many standard approaches along with some promising directions offered by learned approaches. Furthermore, while indexes for keyword search are quite efficient, here we provide insights into how to improve the scalability of prefiltering techniques for semantic search, comparing LSH indexes with Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds. Our experiments show that HNSW drastically improves the runtime of semantic table search by 4.7X on average whilst retaining the high-quality tables. Together, our findings plot the line for effective and efficient data discovery techniques for semantic data lakes.

title: Measurable Does Not Imply Transportable: A Prospective Audit of Model Explanations in Multi-Year Field Trials
abstract: Model explanations are increasingly used as scientific evidence, yet it remains unclear what they license scientists to conclude beyond the data on which they were constructed. When a fine-grained explanation fails to replicate, the failure may be attributed to noisy measurement of its target, raising a fundamental question: does reliable measurement imply a reproducible explanation? We test this directly. We formalize prospective explanation transportability: the extent to which an explanation learned from past data is recovered in a genuinely future context. This property is distinct from feature importance and measurement reliability. Using multi-year Genomes-to-Fields maize trials, where each new year is a real future context rather than a random resample, we evaluate 16 agronomically interpretable environmental concepts across five forward splits and one prospectively locked test year. Coarse environment-level explanations transport reliably (median cosine 0.83); their locked 2024 value, 0.811, fell within a prespecified 80% bootstrap percentile interval. For grain yield, genotype-conditioned explanations have a historical median cosine of 0.30 and range from 0.006 to 0.822 across years. Reliability does not order these outcomes: the year with the highest split-half reliability had the lowest explanation transport. Within-context resampling showed that GxE explanations were reproducible within a fixed context (0.77-0.95) while exhibiting lower prospective alignment across the 2020-2023 transitions (0.01-0.36). A second phenotype transports strongly at both resolutions, and non-temporal validation inflates apparent interaction-level transport by +0.22. These results show that target reliability and within-context explanation reproducibility do not by themselves establish when a model explanation can support a reproducible scientific claim.

title: Constructible properties of minimal models
abstract: We prove that, given a projective minimal model and a projective family of good minimal models, the subset of the base parametrizing fibers isomorphic (or birationally equivalent) to the given minimal model is constructible in the Zariski topology. Together with recent boundedness results for polarized log Calabi--Yau fibrations, this constructibility theorem provides new finiteness results predicted by the relative Kawamata--Morrison--Totaro cone conjecture.

title: A weakly singular Volterra integral equation and the fractional Lyapunov asymptotic stability theorem
abstract: We study the weakly singular Volterra integral equation V(t) = A - (1/Gamma(alpha)) int_0^t (t-s)^{alpha-1} h(|V(s)|) ds, t >= 0, where alpha in (0,1), A > 0 and h is a class-K function. This equation arises as the scalar reduction of fractional-order Lyapunov inequalities through the fractional variation-of-constants formula. We prove that it admits a unique global solution V with 0 < V(t) <= A, that V is non-increasing, and that V(t) tends to 0 as t goes to infinity, under the pure class-K hypothesis on h. If, in addition, h is locally Holder continuous on (0,infinity) with exponent beta > 1 - alpha, then the rescaled function W(t) := V(t^{1/alpha}) is of class C^1 on [0,infinity) and satisfies W'(t) <= 0. We determine the optimal regularity of the solution, which is alpha-Holder continuous with the sharp expansion V(t) = A - h(A) t^alpha / Gamma(alpha+1) + o(t^alpha) at the origin, and its sharp decay rate h(V(t)) ~ A t^{-alpha} / Gamma(1-alpha) as t goes to infinity. In the power case h(x) ~ kappa x^p one has V(t) ~ (A/(kappa Gamma(1-alpha)))^{1/p} t^{-alpha/p}. As an application, we give a complete proof of the fractional-order Lyapunov asymptotic stability theorem of Li, Chen and Podlubny (Theorem 11, Automatica 45 (2009), 1965-1969) under the general class-K hypothesis, a case not covered by the linear, power-law and convex arguments available in the literature. This theorem plays for fractional-order stability theory the role of Lyapunov's classical theorem for ODEs, and its proof closes a gap that has been open since the theorem first appeared. We further show that the Caputo inequality C_0D_t^alpha V(t) <= -c V^p(t) with 0 < p < 1 implies Mittag-Leffler stability of V, yet neither entails nor precludes finite-time decay to zero, in contrast with the integer-order criterion V'(t) <= -c V^p(t), which entails finite-time decay to zero.

title: DMT-Attack: Diffusion-Prior Texture Search for Closed-Loop Vision-Language-Action Policies
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely on visual feedback throughout manipulation, making them vulnerable to persistent texture attacks. However, optimized patterns can stand out from their surroundings, making an attack easier to notice and its carrier more likely to be inspected or removed. To address this limitation, our key insight is to search the structured image distribution of a diffusion model for natural-looking textures while using closed-loop feedback to identify task-disruptive candidates. Based on this idea, we propose DMT-Attack, a gradient-free gray-box attack that generates textures for ordinary scene objects such as tablecloths. A frozen text-conditioned diffusion model defines the search space, and an eight-expert latent proposal network is initialized from evaluated teacher latents and refined using rollout feedback. We evaluate DMT-Attack against pi_0.5 and OpenVLA-OFT across four LIBERO suites. DMT-Attack achieves a macro clean-conditioned attack success rate (cASR) of 57.9%, compared with 44.7% for UPA-RFAS and 19.7% for random natural textures. It also attains higher scene similarity and a lower clean-calibrated detector flag rate (45% versus 97.5-100% for optimized patch baselines). These results demonstrate that natural-looking textures can disrupt VLA visual feedback and closed-loop decision-making, motivating defenses that jointly assess visual appearance and task behavior.

title: LIFT: Lifting Language-Controlled Image Fusion to Free-Viewpoint 3D Scenes
abstract: Multimodal image fusion traditionally generates a single fused image from paired observations at a specific viewpoint, limiting comprehensive scene perception and adaptability to diverse perceptual objectives. To overcome these limitations, we present LIFT, a novel framework for our proposed language-controlled 3D image fusion (L3D-IF) paradigm that extends multimodal image fusion from 2D images to free-viewpoint 3D scenes, enabling language-guided fusion tailored to diverse perceptual objectives. First, LIFT formulates Semantic Modality Binding (SMB), which interprets language instructions to identify semantic targets and their associated modality preferences and grounds these targets in corresponding regions of a shared Gaussian scene, establishing persistent semantic-to-spatial correspondences for consistent fusion control across viewpoints. Second, Language-Conditioned Gaussian Appearance (LCGA) is developed to achieve scene-wide multimodal appearance modeling by combining adaptive multimodal blending with language- and viewpoint-conditioned appearance refinement, enabling spatially adaptive realization of diverse fusion appearances while preserving source fidelity at pure-modality endpoints. Finally, we construct a Multi-View Language-Supervision (MVLS) dataset that associates language instructions and calibrated viewpoints with modulated fused images, providing effective supervision for learning instruction-dependent fusion from finite multi-view observations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LIFT achieves coherent multimodal fusion across continuous viewpoints, accurate semantic target localization, and consistent regional fusion control under diverse language instructions.

title: Controlling the mixing efficiency in a rotating arc-wall mixer
abstract: In the rotating arc-wall mixer, the flow through a plane channel is stirred by three segments of its walls, which rotate back and forth periodically, two in phase and the third in anti-phase. Using two-dimensional simulations of a Newtonian fluid, I study how the Strouhal number $St$ (0.25-8), the forcing ratio $Λ$ of the wall speed to the mean flow velocity (6.75-54), the Reynolds number $Re$ (0.1-20) and the Peclet number $Pe$ ($10^2$ up to the grid-limited regime) set the mixing efficiency and the chaotic transport that produces it. Throughout this range the fluid crosses a chaotic saddle without regular islands, so that mixing is limited not by a lack of chaos but by the fluid that crosses the mixer without being stretched much. The contrast of the stretching field, i.e., how unevenly the stretching is distributed, correlates with the efficiency better than the properties of the saddle ($r=-0.90$). The efficient periods lie in a window bounded by two kinematic conditions: every fluid parcel must see at least one reversal of the walls, and the fluid at mid-channel must be displaced by about one channel width per half period. Below the window, fluid escapes in pulses through the cells of an almost steady flow; above it, fluid is held near the arcs without being folded. The window closes below $Λ\approx7$ and moves to faster forcing as $Λ$ increases. Inertia strengthens the stretching but opens a weakly stirred wake, so that the efficiency is highest at moderate inertia ($Re\approx8$) and decreases beyond. The efficiency decreases only slowly with $Pe$, and a lamellar model based on the measured stretching extends the results to the Peclet numbers of applications. The energy cost grows as $Λ^2$ and does not depend on the period, which should therefore always be chosen inside the window.

title: Rigidity of ordinal spaces
abstract: A Hausdorff space $Y$ is called rigid if, for every positive integer $k$, every continuous open $k$-to-one map $p:X\to Y$ from a Hausdorff space $X$ admits a partition of $X$ into $k$ open sets, each mapped homeomorphically onto $Y$. We show that the Sorgenfrey plane is not rigid, giving negative answers in $\mathsf{ZFC}$ to Velichko's questions on finite products of rigid spaces and on strongly zero-dimensional spaces. For ordinal spaces, we prove in $\mathsf{ZF}$ that every regular uncountable cardinal with the tree property is rigid. In $\mathsf{ZFC}$, we obtain a characterization for arbitrary limit ordinals: a limit ordinal $α$ is rigid if and only if every coherent family $\langle f_ξ:ξ<α\rangle$, where $f_ξ:ξ\to\{0,1\}$, admits a uniformization. As a consequence, a limit ordinal is rigid if and only if its cofinality is rigid. The characterization also implies that $ω_1$ is not rigid in $\mathsf{ZFC}$, answering a question of Velichko.

title: Displaceability of monotone Lagrangians in $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$
abstract: We show that the generalized Polterovich submanifold $L_{0, 2}^P$ in $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and the Chekanov-Oakley-Usher Lagrangian $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ in the quadric $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$ are displaceable. Since $L_{0, 2}^P$ and $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ are in the zero level set of the moment maps of the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-actions on $\mathbb{C}P^3(\sqrt{2})$ and $Q^4(\sqrt{2})$, the main idea is to construct Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms mapping $L_{0, 2}^P$ and $L_{1, 2}^{Q, \mathrm{Ch}}$ to nonzero level sets of the moment maps.

title: Real-Time Single-Pixel Imaging via Exploiting Temporal Mixing: A Unified Calibration and Composite Readout Framework
abstract: In high-speed optical measurements and computational imaging such as in single-pixel imaging temporal mixing arising from the mismatch between modulation and the electro-optical acquisition chain is conventionally treated as an unmitigated distortion that corrupts measurement orthogonality, breaks compressive sensing priors, fundamentally limits imaging speed, and induces catastrophic reconstruction failure. Here, we establish a transferable, unified calibration and composite-readout framework for single-pixel imaging that systematically repurposes temporal memory from a readout limitation into a powerful measurement resource. Beyond achieving robust high-fidelity recovery, this engineered approach enables cost effective, lower bandwidth configurations to consistently deliver superior image quality compared to higher bandwidth reference setups across diverse operating conditions turning a historical hardware bottleneck into an active imaging advantage. Specifically, target scenes are reconstructed directly from mixed observations without the need to recover individual pattern projections, thereby significantly advancing high-speed and video-rate single-pixel imaging capabilities. Crucially, the transferability of our framework allows calibration routines established on one hardware platform (such as digital micromirror device-based setups) to be readily transferred across different optical systems (such as rotating coding disks), paving the way for calibrated temporal memory as a versatile and generalized measurement paradigm for broader computational imaging.

title: A Unified Unfolding and Slide-Vector Model for Asymmetric Dissimilarities via Clustered Lasso
abstract: Asymmetric multidimensional scaling (AMDS) methods represent asymmetric dissimilarity data in a low-dimensional space. Existing approaches include the highly flexible unfolding model and the parsimonious slide-vector model. However, a highly flexible model is not necessarily optimal for adequately representing asymmetric relationships, and a model with an intermediate level of complexity may be more effective. In this study, we propose a new AMDS model that integrates the unfolding and slide-vector models by incorporating a clustered Lasso penalty. By fusing similar slide vectors, the proposed method can represent intermediate model structures and adjust model complexity according to the observed data. In numerical simulations, we compared the proposed method with existing methods by varying the number of groups, the number of objects, and the number of dimensions. The results demonstrated that the proposed method achieved high estimation accuracy across various asymmetric structures. Furthermore, in an application to cola brand-switching data, the proposed method achieved the highest accuracy in reproducing asymmetric relationships among the three methods compared and yielded a lower stress value than the slide-vector model. These findings suggest that adaptively adjusting model complexity may be effective for representing asymmetric relationships more accurately.

title: The Statistical Cost of Second-Order Orthogonality
abstract: Debiased machine learning removes the first-order effect of nuisance estimation, but the remaining quadratic bias can invalidate inference when nuisance functions are hard to learn. Second-order orthogonal moments remove this bias at the cost of additional variance. We characterize this cost as the minimum variance of a correction that offsets the quadratic sensitivity of the moment to nuisance errors, and show that exact correction is possible only when this cost is finite. Because the cost varies across moments, the first-order efficient moment need not minimize total variance. We therefore choose the moment and its correction jointly, and derive the resulting minimum variance, a second-order analogue of the semiparametric efficiency bound. The optimal moment may trade first-order efficiency for a lower correction cost. In a binary choice logit model, it uses information beyond the conditional likelihood only in well-populated covariate cells; in difference-in-differences with continuous covariates, exact correction forgoes the efficiency gains from exclusion restrictions. In the partially linear model with continuous controls, the cost is infinite for every moment, so that only part of the bias can be removed. For such cases, we propose a data-driven adaptive rule that chooses how much bias to remove within a bound on variance inflation, and we show that inference remains valid after selection. In simulations for the partially linear model, the coverage of nominal 95\% intervals rises from 32--80\% to 94--97\% in all designs but a stress test.

title: From Geographic Memory to Spatial Generalization in Large Language Models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can associate places with geographic descriptions, but recovering an observed association does not establish an ability to generalize across geographic space. We distinguish geospatial memory, the recovery of location--description associations observed during training, from spatial generalization, the prediction of descriptions for locations in unobserved regions. We investigate whether continuous location representations improve this generalization and encourage geographic knowledge to become spatially organized within an LLM. We frame this organization as a latent spatial field: a learned mapping from locations to descriptions connected through spatial dependencies. Building on a continuous spatial encoder, we project location representations into the model's embedding space and supply them as spatial tokens. We evaluate the resulting models on two newly curated geo-text benchmarks for Los Angeles and London using two complementary assessments. Geospatial captioning tests both memory and spatial generalization by generating descriptions at observed locations and at locations beyond the spatial coverage of the training observations. A separate geospatial grounding model tests whether generated location--description pairs provide useful additional supervision for mapping text to geographic space. Across multiple LLM families, continuous location representations improve captioning at unobserved locations relative to textual coordinates, while their generated descriptions yield modest but consistent improvements in downstream grounding. Layer-wise probing and representation clustering provide additional evidence consistent with spatially organized geographic representations. Together, these findings show the value of evaluating spatial generalization separately from memory and of incorporating continuous spatial representations into language models.

title: False Periodicities in Repeating Fast Radio Bursts Caused by Burst Clustering
abstract: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) are millisecond-duration radio transients with high brightness temperatures, but their physical origin remains uncertain. The association of FRB 200428 with a Galactic magnetar provides compelling evidence that at least some FRBs originate from magnetar-like systems. Nevertheless, periodic modulation associated with neutron-star rotation has not been robustly detected in extragalactic FRBs. Motivated by the reported 1.7 s periodicity in the active repeater FRB 20201124A, we conduct a systematic search for short-timescale periodicity in four highly active repeating FRB sources. We employ a sliding-window method that analyzes temporally adjacent bursts within restricted time intervals, allowing transient or intermittent periodic signals to be identified. The search yields apparent period candidates with nominal Poisson-calibrated significances comparable to that reported for the 1.7 s signal, although the inferred periods vary substantially among sources and observing windows. We then perform a nonparametric waiting-time randomization test, in which the observed waiting-time distribution is preserved while the temporal ordering is destroyed. The randomized sequences reproduce the main candidate-period structures seen in the data, demonstrating that these apparent periodicities can arise from the non-Poissonian waiting-time statistics rather than from a coherent periodic process. Rotation-modulated epidemic-type aftershock sequence simulations provide a complementary parametric illustration of the same effect. We therefore find no robust evidence for a short intrinsic periodicity in these data, and the reported 1.7 s signal is not uniquely distinguished from clustering-induced candidates. Robust periodicity searches must evaluate significance against null models that account for the observed waiting-time statistics and the full search procedure.

title: STARK: Moving towards Personalized Agents That Truly Learn and Remember
abstract: Long-term memory is essential for personalized agentic systems that interact with users over long time periods, yet current architectures only capture what happened while leaving the reasoning of why it happened to be derived later by underlying LLMs. These events can, however, convey not only what a user experienced but also how that experience shaped their behavioral patterns. We introduce STARK, a dual-graph memory architecture which treats these events not just as nodes but also as edges between behavioral insights. STARK maintains an Episodic Graph which records interactions as temporally, causally, and semantically linked episodes; and an Insight Graph which represents LLM-extracted behavioral signals scored by how many events support them, connected by the very events that led to them. At inference, behavioral knowledge is retrieved directly from insight nodes grounded by event-as-edges, eliminating repeated episodic traversal. The event-as-edge structure also naturally enables projecting the knowledge graph into a relational embedding space where cross-user transfer becomes possible under shared contextual circumstances, allowing the system to infer missing insights for cold-start users. Evaluations show that STARK improves by 1.48 judge score on LongMemEval information extraction and 0.93 on LoCoMo open domain questions over state of the art. On the public LongLaMP abstract-generation benchmark, cross-user transfer improves open-ended judge scores by 0.7 points and ROUGE-L by 3 at 5% graph sparsity.

title: Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya inequalities on the lattice graph \(\mathbb Z^N\)
abstract: In this paper, we study the following Hardy--Sobolev--Maz'ya inequality on the lattice graph \(\mathbb Z^N\): \[ \sum_{j=1}^N\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^N}|u(z)-u(z-e_j)|^2 -C_H(n,m)\sum_{z\in\mathbb Z^N\setminusΣ} \frac{|u(z)|^2}{d_Σ(z)^2} \geq\overlineκ_{m,n}\|u\|_{\ell^{2^*}(\mathbb Z^N)}^2, \quad u\in C_c(\mathbb Z^N\setminusΣ), \] where \(n,m\geq1\), \(N=n+m\geq3\), \(Σ=\mathbb Z^n\times\{0\}\), \(2^*=2N/(N-2)\), \(e_j\) is the \(j\)-th coordinate vector, \(d_Σ(z):=\inf_{ζ\inΣ}|z-ζ|\), and \(C_H(n,m)\) is the best constant for the Hardy inequality on \(\mathbb Z^N\setminusΣ\). Using the supersolution method and multilinear interpolation, we first prove that the best constant \(\overlineκ_{m,n}\) is positive if and only if either \(1\leq m\leq8\) and \(n\geq1\), or \(m=9\) and \(n\geq14\). Then, we show that \[ \overlineκ_{m,n}=\overline S_N \quad\text{if }m=2\text{ or }(m,n)=(1,2), \] where \(\overline S_N\) is the best constant in the critical Sobolev inequality on \(D^{1,2}(\mathbb Z^N)\). Moreover, for \(m\neq2\) and \(N\geq4\), we prove \(0\leq\overlineκ_{m,n}<\overline S_N\). Finally, using the equality \(\overlineκ_{2,n}=\overline S_{n+2}\), we prove that \(\overlineκ_{2,n}\) is not attained, while for \((m,n)=(1,2)\), we establish nonattainment of \(\overlineκ_{1,2}\) by developing a duality argument based on a comparison of Green functions.

title: Safeguarded Learning-Assisted Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient Methods
abstract: A learning-assisted framework for Nonlinear Conjugate Gradient (NCG) methods is developed in which lightweight online prediction is used to support, rather than replace, the classical optimization process. The proposed approach retains the standard two-term NCG structure and introduces two independent online extreme learning machine models. The first model predicts an NCG coefficient during restart recovery or when persistent stagnation is detected, whereas the second model is used only after a line-search failure in finite precision arithmetic to propose a bounded correction to the deterministic fallback step size. Neural predictions are accepted only when they satisfy deterministic numerical safeguards, including descent, scale, and out-of-distribution requirements; otherwise, the corresponding deterministic recovery or fallback mechanism is retained. Both learning models are updated online using quantities already generated along the optimization trajectory and therefore require no additional function or gradient evaluations for training. These learning frameworks are applied to six well-known classical NCG methods, producing corresponding low-storage learning-assisted variants with deterministic safeguards. Numerical experiments on 480 CUTEst test problems show improved robustness for all six variants at broadly comparable evaluation costs. A PDE-constrained conductivity-identification example further illustrates the potential of the proposed approach to reduce evaluation costs and computational time for problems with expensive function and gradient evaluations. These findings suggest that restricted online learning can improve the robustness and computational performance of classical NCG methods while preserving their low-storage structure and deterministic optimization safeguards, and is particularly promising when function or gradient evaluations are expensive.

title: Slide2PPT: Native PowerPoint Reconstruction with Localization-Guided Refinement
abstract: Image-to-slide reconstruction must recover both visual appearance and native object structure for subsequent editing. Yet visually faithful charts and tables may lack editable series and cells, and direct code generation couples content prediction to rendering implementation. We present Slide2PPT, a model-agnostic, training-free framework that equips both open- and closed-source vision-language models with native PowerPoint reconstruction capabilities. Through a unified typed interface, the model predicts object records while a fixed renderer materializes their native properties, enabling integration with different backbones without task-specific training or architectural changes. Localization-guided refinement then connects visual discrepancies to object records for correction. Regional updates preserve unselected records, while whole-slide updates address cross-region relationships. Record refinement and targeted object editing support structural and attribute-level changes, with rendered feedback governing iterative acceptance. To evaluate this framework across diverse reconstruction demands, we introduce Slide2PPT-Bench, covering controlled elements, real slides, and scientific figures. Evaluation separately measures file production, rendered agreement, and native-object availability. Experiments across open- and closed-source backbones demonstrate substantially more reliable PPTX generation than direct code generation, improved layout and text recovery on scientific figures, and native chart and table interfaces beyond geometric primitives.

title: Distortion in Online Voting
abstract: We initiate the study of distortion in online voting, a framework that bridges computational social choice and online algorithms. In contrast to the classical offline setting, where the full election instance is known in advance, we consider a dynamic environment where a fixed set of voters is present from the beginning, but alternatives arrive sequentially over time. Upon each arrival, a mechanism must immediately and irrevocably decide whether to retain the currently selected candidate or switch to the newly arriving one, operating solely on the partial ordinal rankings induced by the underlying cardinal preferences. We provide upper and lower bounds for deterministic and randomized mechanisms under two standard cardinal preference frameworks. Utilitarian framework: For deterministic mechanisms under adversarial arrival order, we establish an $Ω(mn)$ lower bound and give an matching online algorithm with distortion at most $\frac{2}{3}m(n+\frac{1}{4})$. For randomized rules, we introduce regularity, which allows any regular, order-independent offline randomized rule to be converted into an online rule with the same expected distortion. The Harmonic voting rule satisfies this property, yielding online distortion $O(\sqrt{m\log m})$. Metric framework: For deterministic mechanisms, maintaining an alternative within a $φ$-weighted uncovered set guarantees distortion $2+\sqrt{5}$. We show that matching-based offline rules achieving distortion $3$ cannot be directly implemented online. We establish a lower bound of $\sqrt{13}$, even with three alternatives, and a matching upper bound for three alternatives and any number of voters. For randomized mechanisms, regularity gives an online distortion of $3-\frac{2}{n}$ via Random Dictatorship.

title: A Sharp Nodal Measure Bound for the Mixed Clamped--Navier Biharmonic Eigenvalue Problem in Dimensions $n\ge 2$
abstract: We estimate the interior nodal set of real eigenfunctions of $Δ^2u=λu$ on a bounded connected Euclidean domain. Each boundary component is either of class $C^\infty$ with clamped conditions or of class $C^{2,α}$ and subject to Navier conditions. We obtain $\mathcal H^{n-1}(\{u=0\}\capΩ)\le C_Ωλ^{1/4}$ for $n\ge2$. A spectral inequality on auxiliary clamped collars supplies fixed-scale interior mass. On clamped patches we localize the Carleman estimates of Liu, Tian and Yang. On Navier patches a single harmonic function with trace $u$ controls the two boundary data required for subdivision at every spatial scale. Summing an index linear in local doubling and frequency gives the stated bound. An annulus with one component of each type realizes its order of growth.

title: Calibrate in Context: Efficient Data-Free Quantization from Small Synthetic Pools
abstract: We enable accurate low-bit recovery from small synthetic pools by improving both image synthesis and student preparation. A grid with lower local response error can incur greater error in the student's block context. Functional Grid Calibration (FGC) selects activation scales and integer offsets against full-precision responses constructed from the student's current block input. With weights fixed during calibration, FGC evaluates candidates only at their consuming operators, bringing block context to calibration at nearly local-scoring cost. For DeiT and ViT, progressive inversion updates the same images through increasingly deep teacher prefixes. With 1,000 images, the complete pipeline exceeds MimiQ's reported accuracy in all 18 W4A4/W5A5 settings across nine backbones. With 256 images, DeiT-S and ViT-S reach 68.20% and 66.90% ImageNet top-1 accuracy at W4A4 in 26-27 minutes on one RTX 5090. The pipeline outperforms strengthened 1K-image MimiQ by 13.03 and 24.36 percentage points at lower preparation cost and the same recovery-update count. The same low-budget checkpoints retain their advantage on ImageNetV2.

title: SkillLens: Action-Guided Dense Visual Dynamics for Proficiency Estimation
abstract: Human proficiency estimation is challenging because skill is a high-level and often subjective property that is not captured by action identity alone. Existing approaches leverage multimodal observations such as ego-exo video, gaze, pose, and inertial signals, but the gap between sensor-level evidence and abstract proficiency labels remains difficult to bridge. We present SkillLens, a proficiency estimation framework that uses atomic action descriptions as temporal guidance, rather than direct semantic supervision, to localize proficiency-relevant windows for dense visual-dynamics extraction. Each window is summarized into an action-dynamics feature and scored by a high-low prototype margin against higher- and lower-proficiency executions from the same activity-action category. Fusing these ego/exo PDM cues with a global ego-exo-gaze baseline through CORAL ordinal calibration, our method achieves 0.542 accuracy on Ego-Exo4D. Our project page is available at https://skill-lens.net/

title: Interpreting DeepStack-Style Vision-Language Models: Do Input or Deeper-Layer Visual Tokens Drive Answers?
abstract: DeepStack-style vision-language models feed visual tokens to the language model at its input, and again at deeper layers. We call these the main entry and the later entries. What do the later entries add when the model already has the image? We give the entries versions that differ in one object's color and see which one the answer follows. On photographs, the original DeepStack follows the later entries, while Qwen3-VL-8B/32B follow the main entry. Does weakening the main entry give the later features more influence? On synthetic images, we keep this conflict and reduce color saturation at the main entry only. The unchanged later features gain a stronger effect on the relative scores of the two colors, in all four models, including Granite Vision. This holds even under mild desaturation, when accuracy without the conflict stays at 100%. To test whether later features can also correct errors, we degrade both entries and restore only the later ones. The same blur costs both Qwen models 50 percentage points of accuracy on stripe orientation. The 32B model recovers 48 points and the 8B model only 8. Accuracy with one clean entry predicted which entry each model can lose, and five of six tested predictions held on new GQA attribute questions. With the other entry zeroed, Qwen3-VL-8B loses only 0.3 points on its main entry alone, and DeepStack at most 3.45 points on either entry alone. In split inference on these questions, DeepStack can then send only its main-entry features at higher precision. This takes 49% fewer bytes than all entries at a shared precision, at similar accuracy.

title: Mitigating Row Buffer Contention Through Multiple Row Buffer (MRB) DRAM
abstract: DRAM chips contain multiple banks to handle sev- eral memory requests in parallel. However, requests to different rows of the same bank (e.g., from different cores or workload access patterns) interfere with each other by contending for a single shared row buffer. This introduces row buffer conflicts, which incur performance and energy overheads. In this work, we reduce row buffer conflicts caused by interference by introducing multiple row buffers in each bank. We propose multiple row buffer (MRB) DRAM, which employs a primary global row buffer along with multiple secondary SRAM row buffers in the DRAM chip. These secondary SRAM row buffers act as a cache that enables each bank to serve requests to multiple rows in parallel, thereby improving performance and reducing row buffer conflicts. Our evaluation shows that MRB-DRAM with four SRBs per bank improves performance by an average of 29.7%, 24% in singlecore, multicore systems, respectively, compared to a conventional DDR4 baseline with a modest area overhead of 2%.

title: Real Principal-Minor Detectors: Normal Forms and Regular Parity Lifts
abstract: Let $A$ be a symmetric matrix over $\mathbb{F}_2$ on a finite index set, and let $t$ be the column of diagonal entries of $A$, viewed over $\mathbb{R}$. A real detector of $A$ is a real matrix whose principal minors equal the integer $0/1$ representatives of the corresponding principal minors of $A$. We prove that $A$ has a real detector if and only if it has one of the form $K+tt^T$, with $K$ skew-symmetric and $\{0,\pm1\}$-valued. These conditions are equivalent to the existence of a principally unimodular skew-symmetric signing of the bordered lift matrix of $A$, and to regularity of the parity lift of its delta-matroid. If the graph on the nonempty index set of $A$, with edges given by its nonzero off-diagonal entries, is connected, every real detector of $A$ is diagonally similar to a detector of this form. The proof uses cut-transposes to preserve the prescribed symmetric part up to diagonal similarity, then applies feasible singleton pivots to a minimal counterexample. For ribbon bouquets, the characterization proves Whistler's conjecture. For every $A$ with a real detector, the feasible-set generating polynomial is Hurwitz stable, and the polynomial counting feasible sets of sizes $2i-1$ or $2i$ by $i$ has only strictly negative real zeros and ultra-log-concave coefficients.

title: Noncompactifiable Kähler threefolds with positive Ricci curvature
abstract: We construct a complete Kähler threefold $(M,ω)$ with positive Ricci curvature and infinite-dimensional third rational homology. It admits no analytic compactification, answering Yau's compactification question negatively (see \cite{Yau1992}, Problem~71, p.~304). The metric is obtained by solving a complex Monge--Ampère equation on an affine threefold and lifting the solution to an infinite cyclic cover. Its Ricci form $ρ_ω$ satisfies $\int_Mρ_ω^3=\infty$, disproving the top Yang--Yau conjecture.

title: VR-SparseQuant: Accurate FP4 Quantization with 2:4 Sparsity on Vera Rubin
abstract: In recent years, GPUs have incorporated increasingly specialized support for low-precision computation, from Hopper's FP8 to Blackwell's FP4 Tensor Cores. Precision formats have evolved alongside this hardware, from MXFP4 and NVFP4 on Blackwell to E2M1 FP4 with direct UE5M3 block scaling on Vera Rubin, which we term as $\boldsymbol{VRFP4}$. These advances help serve larger language models at lower cost, but four-bit activation quantization can substantially degrade model quality. We introduce VR-SparseQuant, which uses Vera Rubin's elementwise 2:4 sparsity to recover accuracy while retaining native FP4 execution. By allowing two sparse streams to overlap, we use the same FP4 value budget as dense quantization to refine activations with larger errors.
