title: Avoiding squares over words with lists of size three
abstract: We prove that every sequence of lists of size three admits an infinite square-free word, establishing that the Thue choice number of the path is three. More precisely, the number of compatible square-free words of length $n$ is at least $c(5/4)^n$, where $c>0$ is an absolute constant. The proof combines a computer-assisted construction of weights with the weighted counting method previously introduced by the author. We first consider words avoiding only squares of bounded period and use a finite state model to certify a uniform lower bound on their growth. The counting argument then controls the loss caused by excluding longer squares. The main new ingredient is a coarser description of the states, which makes the computation feasible without restricting the union of the lists. The same computation yields a deterministic polynomial-time strategy for constructing an infinite square-free word when each list is chosen adversarially after the preceding letters have been fixed.

title: A rigorous Abel-summed Hardy-type identity for $p$-circle domains via regularized Poisson summation
abstract: In our previous work, a generalized Hardy-type identity (GHI) for astroid-type $p$-circle domains was formally derived in terms of generalized $p$-Bessel functions. However, the direct application of the Poisson summation formula to the indicator functions of these domains leaves the convergence and rigorous justification of the resulting oscillatory series unresolved. In the present paper, we address this difficulty by introducing an anisotropic regularization based on convolution kernels with Fourier multipliers $e^{-t(|ξ_{1}|^p+|ξ_{2}|^{p})}$. We establish the corresponding regularized Poisson summation identity and rigorously justify the limiting process through uniform estimates for lattice-point sums. A key feature of our analysis is the determination of boundary contributions: smooth boundary points carry weight $1/2$, whereas the contributions from axial cusps vanish for $0<p<1$. These results lead to an Abel-summed GHI, expressed in terms of the distorted-angle-dependent $p$-Bessel functions introduced in our previous work, with explicit boundary corrections. In particular, for $p=2$, the identity recovers the Abel-summed form of the classical Hardy--Voronoï Bessel series. Our result provides a rigorous regularized counterpart of the previously proposed identity, while the convergence of the corresponding unregularized series remains a separate problem.

title: Who Should Verify? Reviewer Selection with Partial Information and Outcome Audits
abstract: Selecting an AI reviewer requires evidence about what it does after reading a draft. On a fixed batch of items, a team can keep the original answers or adopt one reviewer's answers throughout. We ask how much it costs to certify that the chosen procedure falls at most a specified number of correct answers short of the best available procedure, for every completion of the unobserved evidence. When all reviews are available and only verified answer keys cost money, we give an exact stopping rule and an integer program for the cheapest certificate in hindsight. When reviews and keys both have prices, a polynomial-time algorithm using the completed record approximates the minimum certificate cost within a factor logarithmic in the number of procedures. This dependence is tight to leading order unless P equals NP. Finding a certificate can be much more expensive. We exhibit a two-procedure family with $n$ unresolved items where one purchase suffices in hindsight but the exact minimax expected search cost is $(n+1)/2$. For two binary procedures under a known independent and identically distributed item law, five counts suffice to compute an optimal search policy. We replay reviews on 2,000 MMLU questions, 896 numerical reports, and 48 Singapore electricity forecast reports. With reviews available, a targeted audit used 6.9% fewer keys on MMLU and 1.2% fewer on numerical reports than a fixed order selected on development data. Compared with selection by stand-alone accuracy, the chosen procedures gained 2.94 percentage points on held-out MMLU questions and zero on numerical reports. On electricity reports, five checks certified a tie across all 48, yet each procedure was correct only eight times.

title: Suffused NV-FETs for Reconfigurable Hardware
abstract: We define a new category of programmable device, the non-volatile (NV) suffused FET, in response to recent advances in photo- [1]-[3] and e-beam doping [4] We demonstrate that the writing mechanism of suffused NV FETs largely reduces the required access circuitry compared with other NV switches, and that with available configurations as a closed switch, open switch, NFET, or PFET, the suffused NV FET is ideal for configuration storage in reconfigurable arrays, reducing FET count in one case by 84.5%.

title: Finite-Time Singularity Formation for the Three-Dimensional Euler Equations
abstract: We construct smooth periodic initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations whose solution blows up in finite time. The velocity remains bounded, while the vorticity magnitude at the origin tends to infinity. Away from the origin, the velocity and its time derivative have smooth spatial limits at the singular time. The construction uses localized Craik--Criminale waves as building blocks of a multi-scale construction.

title: FACET: A Data-Efficient Regional Parametric Head Model
abstract: Production face pipelines need parametric head models that are expressive, FACS-controllable, and buildable on a small, fixed pool of identities. More training identities would always help, but high-quality registered head scans are expensive to capture; when scaling the data is not an option, the remaining lever is architecture. We present FACET, a parametric head model that makes the most of a fixed identity pool through architectural locality rather than more scans, and makes three contributions, each isolated against a matched global-PCA ablation on our own topology, training set, and normalization. (1) A regional identity decomposition into 16 anatomical regions bypasses the N-1 rank ceiling of a global PCA, driving held-out neutral-fit error from a 1.95 mm floor down to 0.23 mm on the same training identities. (2) A learned FACS action-unit expression model with per-identity neural personalization not only stays FACS-controllable but beats a properly-regularized global expression PCA at every component count -- refuting the argument that FACS is too overcomplete to fit. (3) A dedicated neck/shoulder region reduces pose leakage into the pose-invariant upper face during unposing. Together, these show that architectural locality is the effective lever for a production head model under a fixed identity budget.

title: Searching for substellar companion candidates with Gaia IV. New planetary-mass companions found in debris disks
abstract: When spatially resolved, debris disks often exhibit structures (gaps, rings, and spirals) that may indicate the presence of unseen planetary-mass companions. However, such planets have not been detected in most cases. Gaia opens a new mass-separation parameter space for detecting unseen planets. A tool named GaiaPMEX has been developed to detect and characterize companions to stars. It is based on two binarity indicators derived from DR3: the Gaia astrometric signature and, when the sources were also observed by Hipparcos, the Gaia-Hipparcos proper motion anomaly. We used GaiaPMEX on 94 stars hosting resolved debris disks to search for companions. When companions were identified, we combined GaiaPMEX results with high-contrast imaging and radial velocity data to further constrain their mass and orbital properties. We found stellar or substellar companions around five targets (HD 54341, HD 146897, HD 206893, HD 107146, and HD 106906) and indications (2 sigma) for companions around three additional targets (BD+45 598, TWA 7, and HD 120326). The companion to the 150 Myr star HD 107146, which harbors a ring-like dust disk, is found to be a 2-6 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting between 2-10 au. A massive 3-20 Jupiter-mass companion is found 3-10 au from the close binary HD 106906, which already hosts a remote planet orbiting at more than 700 au, and an edge-on disk. The tentative companions to TWA 7 and HD 120326 are planetary-mass companions at 1-3 au. Both stars host a multiple-ring system. We finally provide meaningful upper limits on the possible presence of companions in the range of 0-100 au around a few emblematic stars (49 Cet, AU Mic, beta Pic, and epsilon Eri) and stars hosting well-defined ring-like structures.

title: Know Your Context Bank: Repairing Inconsistency and Measuring Generalization in Context-Aware Text-to-SQL
abstract: Text-to-SQL systems increasingly rely on context banks: curated collections of example queries, metric definitions, and domain knowledge that tell a model how an organization writes its queries. In the enterprise, a bank grows over years as many analysts add entries, checked one at a time for correctness (does the SQL answer its own question?) and rarely for consistency with one another. Yet correctness is often loosely defined: a question seldom fixes how an entity is counted or which table defines it, so two entries can each pass review yet resolve the same decision in opposite ways. We call this condition context bank rot. A second question follows: does a system that uses a bank generalize from it, or only reproduce it? Existing benchmarks cannot tell, as they do not control how far a test question sits from the context. We answer both questions by comparing queries decision by decision, with a fast scorer distilled from human-calibrated LLM judges. Turned inward, the comparison diagnoses and repairs a bank. Fine-tuning on a cleaned BIRD-train bank beats a same-size random subset at every epoch (+2.6 points on average), and 92.4% of our removals had their SQL corrected by an independent expert audit, against 45.6% of audited entries. In-context examples that follow one convention beat those following the opposite one by 13.3 points, while a mix is barely better than none. Turned outward, the comparison generates test questions at a controlled distance from a bank, a pipeline we call CAT (Context-Aware Testing). On CAT-BIRD, for retrieval and fine-tuning alike, the benefit of a bank falls step by step with distance and is largely gone once about three quarters of a question's logic is new, and on CAT-Spider the benefit of retrieval likewise shrinks with distance.

title: What Helps Language-Model Agents Review Violent Video? A Controlled Comparison with a Human Evidence Reference
abstract: Systems that flag violent video for a human operator can now be built from language models without training, by combining perception models and letting a language model decide. We ask how the observations of the perception models should reach the decision, and which evidence matters. On the XD-Violence test set (799 clips) we fix one set of perception agents (video description, object detection, sound tagging, speech recognition and speech tagging) and one reasoning model, and compare three interfaces: messages between agents, a typed evidence graph explored with tools, and flat text read in one pass; and a single audio-visual model given the raw clip. Two annotators provide a human reference that records the decision, the incident segments and whether they relied on sight, sound or speech. Flat text matches the single model (F1 0.967 against 0.968), while the graph agent and message passing are less accurate; a variant of the graph agent developed on a separate set did not close the gap, and both graph summaries and multi-turn tool use lowered accuracy. These results hold with reworded prompts and with a larger reasoning model, except that the larger model weakens message passing enough for the graph agent to beat it. Sound events improve F1 by +0.012 [+0.004, +0.021], in line with the annotators, who used sound or speech on most violent clips. Citations of stored observations are faithful, changing about half of the decisions when removed, but no more so with the graph than with flat text, and the agent pipeline costs about 3 times the GPU time of the single model. We also report two artefacts of vision-language describers that mislead pipelines built on them.

title: The Bell Experiment, Monadically
abstract: Bell's theorem says that no classical model satisfying certain independence assumptions can reproduce the correlations that quantum mechanics predicts and experiments observe. In this paper we write the two-party Bell experiment as a small Haskell program, and find those assumptions in its structure: in what each part of the program can see, and in how the parts are composed. The boxes of the two parties compute in one monad, and the experiment that schedules and repeats their trials computes in another; a \emph{membrane} runs the first inside the second. A run keeps the record of its trials, and both of its verdicts, the CHSH value and whether the boxes signal, are read off one table: the empirical model of that run. In this setting, a model is classical when it has three properties. It is \emph{blind}: the hidden strategy of the boxes is drawn without seeing the measurement settings. It is \emph{local}: given that strategy, neither box's outcome depends on the other party's setting. It is \emph{factored}: given the strategy and the settings, the two outcomes are independent. Together, they give the classical bound of $2$. We give them up one at a time and run what results. Without blindness, we get experimental loopholes and superdeterminism. Without factoring, we get quantum boxes, which reach $2\sqrt2$, and the hypothetical PR boxes, which reach $4$, both without signaling. Without locality, we get boxes that rewrite a shared hidden state; whether they signal depends on how that state is sampled. We also compare two ways to check no-signaling: reading it off the run's own table, and estimating it in separate experiments at fixed settings.

title: Source Conditions and Sharp Transition Asymptotics for the Factorization Method with Far-Field Data
abstract: The factorization method characterizes an obstacle through a range test, but practical implementations replace the associated Picard series by a regularized approximation. This paper studies the resulting regularization bias for inverse acoustic scattering by impedance obstacles. For a disc, we show that every positive-order Hölder source condition fails at each noncentral interior sampling point, whereas logarithmic source conditions hold uniformly on compact interior subsets for every exponent, with explicit constants. At the center, the bias decays linearly with the regularization parameter. We then derive sharp spectral transition asymptotics through the Lambert W function. These asymptotics determine the stabilization rate inside the obstacle, the iterated-logarithmic growth at the boundary, and the divergence outside. They also yield a threshold rule for which the reconstructed disc converges in measure, together with quantitative boundary-location estimates. For general impedance obstacles, we reduce the spectral decay of the symmetrized far-field operator to that of the data-to-pattern operator and obtain two-sided transition bounds in terms of the inradius and any radius larger than the circumradius. For a simply connected obstacle with analytic boundary, positive analytic impedance, and conformal center inside the obstacle, a Faber--Vekua normal form gives the sharp spectral law in terms of logarithmic capacity, with the same leading constant as for the disc. This class includes every convex analytic obstacle. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted spectral transition and illustrate its use in choosing the regularization level. The analytic normal-form result is proved only for a single boundary component.

title: Tracktail: Multi-View 3D Point Tracking without Depth Input
abstract: We introduce Tracktail, a novel architecture designed to efficiently track query points in 3D from multiple calibrated views without any depth input. Our architecture separates the task as a per-camera video encoding of features and a per-query decoder. Notably, camera cross-attention is only performed across queries in the decoder, allowing for efficient inference (7 FPS and less than 4 GB memory for 10 views and 100 query points). We further introduce a per-camera scene scale computed from camera geometry, which allows us to normalize inputs and predictions appropriately across a vast variety of dataset scales. We train on a synthetic Multi-View Kubric dataset as well as a novel Multi-View Point Odyssey benchmark dataset, which consists of synthetic renders of humans and animals across 499 frames. Tracktail achieves state-of-the-art results on the Panoptic Studio, DexYCB, and Multi-View Kubric benchmarks, outperforming methods that rely on estimated depth. Tracktail also demonstrates a strong ability to maintain accurate tracking over longer ranges compared to existing methods. Our code, data, and weights are publicly available: https://ai-hhmi.github.io/tracktail/

title: Higgs Fluctuation Solver in Four Dimensions: Part II-Toward Finite Lattice-to-MS bar Matching in the SU(2) Higgs Extension
abstract: We present a lattice-to-MS_bar matching framework for the $SU(2)$-Higgs theory, including Wilson-plaquette and fundamental scalar-link actions, a counter term basis through $ρ^{12}$, audited momentum-dependent lattice vertices, and fixed routings and projectors. At the benchmark $a=0.8$, $m_0^2=μ_R^2=0.4$, $g_0=0.65$, and $(λ,γ,δ)=(-2,0.8,0.08)$, the potential is $V_0(ρ)=\frac{1}{5}ρ^2-\frac{1}{2}ρ^4+\frac{2}{15}ρ^6+\frac{1}{100}ρ^8$. The scalar-only radial matching shifts, ordered as $(δm^2,δλ,δγ,δδ,δc_{10},δc_{12})$, are $(2.75293, -1.45119, -2.85120, 0.356724, 1.07432, 6.20492)$ in solver units, with the continuum-renormalized-minus-lattice convention. The Higgs two-point slope gives $δZ_H = 0.0329117974 \pm 0.00000036$ (QMC error). We also evaluate gauge-linked four-, six-, and eight-Higgs projections and derive the continuum one-loop gauge two-point tensor. The tensor passes 29 internal checks; at $p^2=0.4$, its total transverse projection is $Π_T=-0.01847$ at zero regulator and $-0.01716$ at $λ_{\mathrm{IR}}/μ_R=1/8$, while the regulator-induced longitudinal projection is $Π_L=1.04\times 10^{-5}$ at $λ_{\mathrm{IR}}/μ_R=1/32$. These results establish a tested foundation and quantitative benchmarks for the matching program. The gauge-linked projections remain preliminary, and full gauge-sector matching and Ward-Slavnov-Taylor closure are needed before a matched $SU(2)$ decay prefactor can be claimed.

title: Isolation in Random Graphs
abstract: We study isolation in the binomial random graph $G(n,p)$. When $p=o(1)$ and $np\to\infty$, allowing an $F$-free graph on the undominated vertices gives the same first-order asymptotics for every fixed forest $F$ as the domination number $γ(G)$ in $G(n,p)$. For the ordinary isolation number $ι(G)$ ($F$ is an edge) we prove two-point concentration when $p$ is bounded away from $1$ and $np^2/(\log n)^3\to\infty$. We also identify a transition in the gap $γ(G)-ι(G)$ when $\log(1/p)=o(\log n)$. This gap tends to infinity in probability when $p$ is well below $(\log\log n/\log n)^2$ and is at most one with high probability when $p$ is well above this scale. Finally, for every fixed graph $F$, we show that the classical minimum degree bound for domination is asymptotically sharp for $F$-isolation, even for regular host graphs.

title: ChatAtom: A Multi-Agent LLM System for Molecular Dynamics Simulation and Visualization
abstract: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulation resolves atomic-scale motion and predicts the structural, mechanical, and dynamic properties of materials, making it cen- tral to materials design and discovery. Yet an MD study requires an expert-driven workflow: designing the simulation, writing reliable input scripts, executing them, and analyzing the results with separate tools. Here we present ChatAtom, a multi-agent large language model system that translates a natural-language request into a complete MD workflow without the user writing input scripts or analysis code. Each agent has a defined responsibility within the workflow. An orchestrator plans the study; the LAMMPS and OVITO agents each use a generator-reviewer pair to prepare and review simulation and visualization scripts before execution; a high-performance computing agent dispatches jobs to remote resources; and an analysis agent interprets the completed run. The work- flow is accessible through a browser interface that streams thermodynamic data and rendered frames during local execution, allowing users to follow the simu- lation as it progresses. The architecture also supports new capabilities through loadable skills without modifying the agents, enabling autonomous hypothesis generation and testing. We evaluate ChatAtom through script-generation bench- marks, an end-to-end study of crack propagation, and a closed-loop campaign. By bringing script generation, execution, visualization, and analysis into one reviewed and observable pipeline, ChatAtom lowers the barrier to conducting MD studies and broadens access to advanced simulation workflows.

title: CADENCE:Temporally Coherent Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery that Preserves Expressive Hand Motion
abstract: Whole-body SMPL-X estimators recover body, hand, and face meshes from single images, but applied frame by frame to video they produce jittery motion. Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame's estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.

title: Parity-violating optical rotation in the Th-229 nuclear clock transition
abstract: The exceptionally low-energy nuclear transition in $^{229}$Th provides a new opportunity to study hadronic parity violation (PV) by optical methods. The PV nucleon--nucleus interaction admixes opposite-parity nuclear states into the $5/2^+$ ground state and the $3/2^+$ isomer, thereby inducing an electric-dipole amplitude $E1_{\rm PV}$ that interferes with the magnetic-dipole clock transition amplitude $M1$. In a single-valence-neutron Nilsson model, we find $|E1_{\rm PV}/M1| \sim 2\times10^{-5}$. This interference can be detected as a parity-violating nuclear optical rotation (PVNOR) of resonant laser light transmitted through a $^{229}$Th-doped crystal. For a highly-doped CaF$_2$ crystal fiber, the estimated rotation is of order $10^{-6}\,{\rm rad}$. A crossed-polarizer measurement can reach this sensitivity with existing ultraviolet laser technology. We also analyze systematic effects in the form of optical birefringence, stray magnetic-field-induced Faraday rotation, and local crystal defects. Such a measurement would provide the first direct probe of the PV neutron-nucleus interaction constant, $g_n$.

title: SciPIC-lite: A flexible Halo Occupation Distribution pipeline aimed at clustering observables
abstract: The Halo Occupation Distribution (HOD) framework provides a flexible approach to modelling the galaxy--halo connection in cosmological simulations, encoding the statistical relationship between galaxies and their host dark matter haloes. We present SciPIC-lite, a new public Python library for fast, flexible, and user-friendly HOD modelling, designed to populate dark matter haloes extracted from cosmological simulations with galaxies and to provide a comprehensive suite of tools for their subsequent analysis. The library is built around a modular and extensible codebase that incorporates the full breadth of the HOD framework, from the core occupation functions to a wide range of physically motivated extensions, making it suitable for a broad spectrum of galaxy clustering applications. We validate and characterise the performance of SciPIC-lite by developing a pipeline to fit the two-point correlation functions of H$α$-selected galaxies from the Flagship~2 simulation across multiple redshift bins. To this end, we populate AbacusSummit dark matter haloes with galaxies according to a variety of HOD parametrisations. We assess the robustness of the fits with respect to the choice of HOD parametrisation and the inclusion of physically motivated extensions, including assembly bias, velocity bias, conformity, and halo profile rescaling. The best-fit models are found to be remarkably robust across different HOD parametrisations and fitting configurations, with reduced $χ^2$ values clustering tightly around a common value regardless of the model adopted. We exploit these results to generate new AbacusSummit-based galaxy mocks that accurately reproduce the clustering properties of the Flagship~2 H$α$ galaxy population.

title: Compression with wildcards: The maximum anticliques of König-Egarváry graphs
abstract: By definition a König-Egarváry graph is such that the cardinality of each maximum matching equals the cardinality of each minimum vertex-cover. Each bipartite graph has this property. We unravel the structure of the family MACL(G) of all maximum anticliques (independent sets) of a König-Egarváry graph G. This enables us to enumerate $MACL(G)$ not only in output polynomial time, but also in a compressed format (using wildcards). All of this can be viewed as an instance where ALL minimum solutions of a submodular function can be enumerated efficiently.

title: Spatial Query Execution as Verifiable Rewards for Multi-step Spatial Reasoning
abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) remain unreliable on spatial reasoning problems that require composing grounded relations across multiple objects. Yet, scaling reasoning supervision is challenging since human-annotated visual datasets often rely on fixed relational annotations and coarse object localization, making it difficult to obtain precise intermediate reasoning states across diverse spatial configurations and complexities. We introduce FARON (Fully Automated Reasoning Over spatial relatioNs), a framework that executes spatial queries to provide both execution-grounded reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards. Rather than relying on existing annotated data, FARON constructs synthetic 2D and 3D scenes with explicit geometries, enabling configurable object arrangements, spatial relations, and multi-step compositions. Deterministic query execution yields intermediate sets and final answers, providing precise supervision without manual relation annotation. Our pipeline converts intermediate states into natural-language reasoning traces for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), while the execution-derived answers provide verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Controlled experiments show that trace-based SFT improves multi-step spatial reasoning over final-answer supervision and that subsequent group relative policy optimization (GRPO) provides further gains. The resulting models also demonstrate transfer across external spatial reasoning benchmarks and multiple LVLM backbones without benchmark-specific fine-tuning. These results show the potential of using spatial query execution as a unified, flexible source of reasoning supervision and verifiable outcome rewards for multimodal spatial reasoning.

title: Prediction of lattice thermal conductivity of half-Heusler compounds by machine learning and transfer-function calibration
abstract: High-throughput searches for half-Heusler thermoelectrics increasingly rely on lattice thermal conductivity ($κ_L$) from first-principles calculations, or from machine-learning models trained on them. These calculations describe an ideal single crystal, whereas measurements are made on polycrystalline samples, in which grain boundaries and defects scatter heat as well. The resulting gap between calculated and measured $κ_L$ has been noted for individual compounds but not, to our knowledge, quantified across a materials class, so the values used for screening carry an unknown, systematic bias. Here we quantify and correct this bias for cubic half-Heusler compounds with 18 valence electrons. Using a curated literature corpus that keeps calculated and measured values apart, we show that calculations overestimate measured $κ_L$ in most bonding families, and that the excess shrinks with temperature. Scattering by defects, added to the intrinsic scattering between lattice vibrations, would give such a trend, but the data do not single out one cause. A simple transfer function with this temperature dependence removes the median offset, and refitting its magnitude within a bonding family lowers the median error further, though not consistently compound by compound. Combined with a machine-learning model that predicts the calculated value from crystal structure, and tested on chemistries withheld from all fitting, the method predicts measured $κ_L$ in this class about as closely as independent laboratories agree with one another, and provides testable predictions for compounds not yet measured.

title: Opposite filtrations on the parabolic compactified Jacobian
abstract: We show that the Hikita filtration on the cohomology of the parabolic compactified Jacobian of the plane curve singularity $x^m=y^n$, $(m,n)=1$, is opposite to the perverse filtration in a precise sense. This implies the parabolic Hilb-vs-Quot conjecture from https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.19633, and consequently the main conjecture from https://arxiv.org/abs/1201.2115 for these singularities. The new ingredient is an analysis of how the Bott-Mitchell filtration on the homology of the affine Grassmannian of $SL_n$ relates to both of the above filtrations.

title: The 1-Loop and Ohtsuki-Takata Invariants for Alternating Braids
abstract: In a step towards resolving the 1-loop conjecture, Ohtsuki and Takata defined their own eponymous invariant in terms of an open knot diagram, and showed that it is equal to the adjoint Reidemeister torsion for two-bridge knots. Garoufalidis and Yoon then showed that the 1-loop invariant is equal to the Ohtsuki-Takata invariant using a technique involving a collapsed octahedral decomposition. This paper expands those techniques to relate the matrix determinants of the 1-loop and Ohtsuki-Takata invariants for the case of reduced alternating braids.

title: A relativistic von Kármán relation for assessing applicability of hydrodynamics
abstract: Relativistic viscous hydrodynamics is a widely used theoretical framework for simulating quark-gluon plasma (QGP) dynamics in relativistic heavy-ion collisions. One open question is how to quantitatively assess the validity of a hydrodynamic description of such a system. In this work, we extract the poles of linear response functions from numerical simulations of hydrodynamics and Boltzmann transport. By comparing these responses as a function of the rescaled wavenumber $\bar{k}$, we identify the wavenumber range over which hydrodynamics captures the underlying microscopic dynamics. We show that the averaged Knudsen number, $\langle\mathrm{Kn}^{*}\rangle$, which we define using the von Kármán relation, serves as a measure of $\bar{k}$. We find that $\langle\mathrm{Kn}^{*}\rangle_{\rm max}\sim 1$ marks the approximate upper limit of agreement between the linear responses of second-order viscous hydrodynamics and Boltzmann transport.

title: Infection Spreading and Stochastic Extinction in Finite Spatially Inhomogeneous Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible and Susceptible-Infected-Recovered Systems
abstract: Demographic fluctuations can drive finite epidemic populations into an absorbing disease-free state even when the corresponding infinite system supports sustained activity. By means of Monte Carlo simulations, we investigate how spatial coupling of two distinct subsystems modifies stochastic extinction and epidemic spreading in susceptible-infectious-susceptible (SIS) and susceptible-infectious-recovered (SIR) models on inhomogeneous two-dimensional square lattices. For isolated SIS systems, extinction times exhibit approximate power-law scaling near the epidemic threshold even for small systems. Traversal times characterize the distinct propagation dynamics of SIS and SIR infection clusters. We consider diffusively coupled regions with different transmission characteristics in coupled SIS-SIS, SIR-SIS, and SIR-SIR configurations. Invading fronts can reactivate a vulnerable SIS region after its initial infection has disappeared and establish a long-lived active epidemic state. This stabilization can be induced by either a sustained SIS source or a single transient SIR epidemic wave. Spatial correlation measurements support a mechanism in which the invading activity generates an extended correlated infectious population, effectively providing favorable initial conditions for renewed epidemic spreading. Correlations develop particularly strongly parallel to the subsystem interfaces. Decoupling the regions after some elapsed period demonstrates that autonomous persistence requires sufficient coupling time beyond the first interface arrival for this correlated population to become established. Increasing system size delays invasion but enhances the probability of ultimate successful stabilization. In two coupled SIR regions, transmission can initiate a macroscopic secondary outbreak, while permanent immunity restricts both epidemics to transient activity.

title: A functional Breuer-Major theorem under finite variance, with application to the $R/S$ test for long memory
abstract: The Breuer-Major theorem (Breuer and Major, 1983) states that, for a function $G$ of Hermite rank $m$ such that $\mathbb{E}(G^{2}(X))<\infty$, and a stationary Gaussian sequence whose correlation function $r$ satisfies $\sum_{i}|r(i)|^{m}<\infty$, the finite dimensional distributions of the normalized partial sum process of $G(X_{i})$ converge to those of a Brownian motion. Whether the functional version of this result holds under these sole conditions has remained open for a long time, the tightness being known only under additional moment assumptions. In this paper we prove that the functional central limit theorem holds under finite variance only. More generally, we give a high order expansion of the partial sum process which covers both short and long-range dependence: the long-range dependent components converge to Hermite processes, while the remainder converges to a Brownian motion. As an application, we discuss the question of testing long-memory in observed data using the $R/S$ statistics. We derive the limiting distributions of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics, prove the consistency of the test and propose a data-driven choice of the truncation parameter. A Monte Carlo study compares the performances of the classical and modified $R/S$ statistics for both short-memory and long-memory sequences.

title: Beyond Final Answers: Interpretable Tumor Immune Microenvironment Reasoning from H&E and mIF
abstract: Readouts of the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), such as CD8+ T-cell density, intra-epithelial infiltration and the Ki67 index, combine tissue architecture from H&E with cell phenotypes from multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF). Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) could automate these readouts with an explanation, but two gaps remain. Pathology MLLMs read H&E alone, while these readouts need the cell phenotypes that mIF measures. And their reasoning has no step-level truth to be checked against, so R1-style reinforcement learning rewards only the final answer and leaves the reasoning unverified. Same-section H&E and mIF provide what both gaps lack: mIF measures every cell without manual annotation, which gives cell-level ground truth for each step that clinical guidelines prescribe, from delineating a tissue compartment to counting and normalizing the marker-positive cells within it. We therefore present HERMES (H&E-mIF Reasoning with Multimodal Evidence Supervision), an R1-style MLLM that reasons jointly over paired H&E and mIF in guideline steps and is trained with a process reward that checks every stated quantity against this truth. Across four field-level TIME tasks in colorectal cancer, HERMES (4B) reaches an average accuracy of 84.5%, compared with 74.7% for the strongest of twelve proprietary, general, medical and pathology MLLMs, and a higher share of its intermediate quantities is correct than for the strongest open-weight baseline. Without the process reward, reinforcement learning barely improves on supervised fine-tuning (80.0% vs. 78.8%) and fewer stated quantities are correct; editing a decisive stated quantity changes the answer as implied in all 885 test questions. Without retraining, it keeps the highest average accuracy on an external cohort imaged with CODEX (76.4% vs. 67.3%) and on head and neck cancer, a cancer type absent from training (76.7% vs. 72.5%).

title: A boundary integral equation solver for capsule suspensions
abstract: Deformable capsules serve as models for biological cells, such as red blood cells, as well as for synthetic capsules in biomedical and industrial applications. In this work, we introduce a framework for fast and robust simulation of deformable capsules in three-dimensional Stokes flow, both in unbounded domains and in pipe-confined geometries. We solve the Stokes equations using a boundary integral formulation, employing a partition-of-unity discretization for the capsule membrane and the trapezoidal rule with regularization to handle the singular quadrature. Dense periodic interactions are evaluated via a fast Ewald summation scheme, achieving $O(N \log N)$ complexity for $N$ grid points. The interfacial forces on the capsule membrane are modeled using the Skalak constitutive law. We carry out a spectral analysis of this model for small perturbations of a spherical capsule, which indicates that the relaxation dynamics are intrinsically stable. However, the nonlinear character of the Skalak model induces aliasing errors that can compromise numerical stability. To address this when needed, we perform de-aliasing through upsampling and spectral filtering, and we derive guidelines for choosing appropriate filter parameters, thereby stabilizing the method. We investigate the stability and convergence behavior of the resulting scheme and conduct simulations of long-time dynamics, focusing on the relaxation of unconfined capsules and the lateral migration of pipe-confined capsules under various flow conditions.

title: Efficient Conversational Multi-Talker ASR with Predicted Speaker-Agnostic Activity Streams
abstract: Multi-talker automatic speech recognition (ASR) can be performed by conditioning a single-speaker recognizer on frame-level speaker activity. However, this approach requires a complete diarization pass to obtain the conditioning signals and one ASR pass per speaker, making both the frontend and recognition costs dependent on the number of speakers. We reduce these costs by using Heuristic Error Assignment Training (HEAT) to merge the activities of an arbitrary number of speakers into two speaker-agnostic streams. Conditioning on these streams limits recognition to two ASR passes regardless of the number of participants. Through an analysis of the resulting encoder representations, we show that under a stream-assignment heuristic suited to conversational speech, the recognizer represents a stream target much as it does a speaker target. Because the streams do not encode persistent speaker identities, we further replace the conventional sliding-window diarization and clustering frontend with a model that predicts both activity streams directly from the audio in a single pass. A combination of arrival-order and permutation-invariant training objectives over the two-stream powerset labels prevents the predictor from collapsing to identical streams. We also investigate post-hoc speaker attribution by matching decoded utterances to speaker activities within their assigned streams. Experiments on corpora with diverse conversational dynamics demonstrate a favorable efficiency--accuracy tradeoff. On AMI and ICSI, two-stream conditioning is respectively 44\% and 87\% faster than per-speaker conditioning using the same diarization frontend, with less than 2\% relative WER degradation. Direct activity prediction increases these speedups to 79\% and 132\%, with relative WER degradations of 10\% and 21\%, respectively.

title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
abstract: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.

title: Thurston measure is stationary with exponential Teichmüller moment
abstract: In 1967, Furstenberg proved that every lattice in a connected semisimple Lie group with finite center admits a probability measure whose stationary measure on the associated Furstenberg boundary belongs to the Lebesgue measure class. We prove an analogue of this theorem for the action of the mapping class group on Teichmüller space. Every regular probability measure in the Thurston measure class on the space of projective measured foliations is the stationary measure of a non-elementary random walk with a finite exponential moment in the Teichmüller metric.

title: Trajectories Through Parsons Problems: Making Student Difficulty Patterns Visible to Instructors
abstract: Existing Parsons problem tools primarily focus on correctness, indicating whether a student solved a problem, but providing limited visibility into the underlying problem-solving process. Without that visibility, instructors cannot see which blocks caused repeated confusion or which distractors were consistently selected. We introduce Pulla, a Parsons problem tool that instruments programming assignments to capture fine-grained interaction data. We examine what these behavioral traces make visible to instructors, namely how long students take on a problem and how many moves they make, which recurring errors the distractors expose and how the class arrives at them, whether those errors follow a student from one problem to the next, and which students complete the whole assignment without a single error.

title: Incentive Compatible Mechanisms for Sequential Fair Resource Allocation with Private Demands
abstract: We study a strategic variant of the canonical online fair allocation problem, where a planner must sequentially allocate a divisible resource to agents with privately known demands. At each stage, the planner announces an allocation rule, the agent reports their demand, and the planner allocates resources according to the rule and the reported demand. Unlike the standard model, we allow agents to strategically misreport their needs, as can arise in nonprofit settings where demand is self-reported and monetary transfers are unavailable. We characterize the structure of incentive-compatible (IC) allocation rules in this model, and use this to identify conditions under which the optimal mechanism has a simple cap structure. We then develop an approximation method for the optimal IC mechanism through a careful reduction of the discretized dynamic program to a longest-path problem on a directed acyclic graph. Numerical experiments show that ignoring strategic reporting can be substantially more costly than imposing incentive compatibility.

title: Benchmark Ne-like Transitions of W, Re, Os, Ir, and Bi Measured by High-resolution TES x-ray Spectroscopy with Absolute Energy Calibration
abstract: We present high-resolution measurements of $n=2$-3 transitions in Ne-like tungsten, rhenium, osmium, iridium, and bismuth using a transition-edge sensor (TES) microcalorimeter. These measurements provide new benchmarks for Ne-like ions in the high-$Z$ regime ($Z > 74$), extending previous EBIT studies of the sequence. To achieve sub-eV accuracy, we developed a dedicated x-ray fluorescence source employing well-characterized K-shell emission lines from metallic elements. Our results offer stringent tests for relativistic atomic structure theories and demonstrate the advantage of TES spectroscopy for precision measurements in highly charged ions.

title: Nonholonomic Event-Triggered Source Seeking
abstract: This paper introduces an event-triggered source seeking control (ET-SSC) strategy for autonomous vehicles modeled as nonholonomic unicycles. The key feature of the proposed design is the separation between the continuous probing motion required for gradient extraction and the event-triggered update of the source-seeking correction. This separation enables aperiodic computation and transmission of the correction while the periodic probing signals remain continuously active. The triggering mechanism acts on a low-pass-filtered gradient estimate, obtained by high-pass (washout) filtering, demodulation, and low-pass filtering of the measured signal, and combines a relative and an absolute threshold. Stability is proved with a time-periodic Lyapunov function constructed along the exponentially stable periodic solution of the filtered closed loop, establishing practical exponential convergence of the vehicle to a neighborhood of the unknown source. The guaranteed minimum dwell time is strictly positive and independent of the probing frequency, which excludes Zeno behavior. Unlike available Lie-bracket analyses of the forward-velocity design, the proposed averaging-based analysis accommodates anisotropic quadratic source fields with distinct spatial curvatures. The resulting ET-SSC framework therefore provides a resource-aware implementation in which the source-seeking correction is updated aperiodically while the information-generating probing motion remains continuous.

title: Don't Discard Your Rollouts: Reusing Teacher RL Traces for Student Distillation
abstract: RL post-training methods such as PPO and GRPO are computationally expensive, with substantial resources devoted to sampling rollouts, which contain multiple completions per prompt along with their respective rewards. Canonical distillation, however, discards these traces and uses more compute to regenerate data from the final teacher. We ask if and how we can reuse the saved teacher RL rollouts to distil student models. Reusing rollouts is non-trivial: naive SFT on the rollouts underperforms canonical distillation, and naive DPO, while performant, is unstable, collapsing on weaker students. We show that treating rollout reuse as a data selection problem using metadata already recorded during GRPO substantially reduces this gap. We use prompt pass rates to order the data, using the easiest prompts for an SFT warm start prior to using mixed-success prompts for DPO. For each prompt, we use saved teacher log-likelihoods as a proxy for selecting student-compatible completions. Across mathematical reasoning and Python coding tasks, with students from multiple model families, our two-stage recipe achieves comparable average performance to canonical distillation, while incurring no additional inference cost for dataset construction.

title: The Effect of Dust Grain Growth and Stellar Metallicity on Gas Giant Planet Formation by Disk Instability
abstract: The formation of gas giant planets by the gas disk gravitational instability (GDGI) mechanism depends sensitively on the thermodynamics of the protoplanetary disk gas: disk gas must be able to cool on orbital timescales for dense clumps to become gravitationally unstable and contract to form protoplanets. Since disk cooling is regulated by the opacity of the dust grains embedded in the gas, the properties of these dust grains are critical for the GDGI mechanism. Grain growth to larger sizes than assumed in traditional opacity models for solar metallicity, as well as protostars with sub-solar metallicity, should have lower opacity disks that are more conducive to planet formation by GDGI. Here we use a three dimensional radiative hydrodynamics and gravitation code to compute the evolution of the GDGI in $0.091 M_\odot$ disks with varied initial minimum values (1.3 to 2.7) of the Toomre criterion orbiting solar-mass protostars. Three sets of eight models are computed: one with the standard opacity, and two more with the opacity reduced by arbitrary factors of 10 or 100. As expected, the reduced opacity models result in enhanced disk fragmentation by the GDGI and the production of more self-gravitating clumps than the standard opacity models. Nevertheless, all three opacities form similar self-gravitating clumps at this early phase of clump evolution, with masses of 0.2 to 0.7 $M_{Jup}$ and semimajor axes between 6 and 13 au. Significant dust grain growth should enhance the ability of the GDGI to form protoplanets around super-solar metallicity protostars.

title: LEAN: Library-Based Adaptation for Asynchronous, Federated Fine-Tuning
abstract: Federated fine-tuning of foundation models with low-rank adapters (LoRA) is typically reconciled by averaging locally trained adapters. In cross-device settings, where participants hold heterogeneous data and join or leave asynchronously, averaging is poorly suited: locally trained adapters are not identifiable up to permutation, and averages of adapters trained on dissimilar data can be uninformative or unstable. We propose a simple idea called federated library-based adaptation (LEAN), which replaces averaging altogether. The server maintains a library of rank-1 basis pairs; participants check out random subsets, fine-tune them locally as a LoRA adapter, and check them back in, so that each pair is shuffled across sites and trained on many participants' data. Because no aggregation step is required, LEAN operates fully asynchronously and communicates only low-rank parameters. We prove that, in a synchronous setting, LEAN converges to a neighborhood of a stationary point, with the shuffle canceling data heterogeneity at first order. Across image and text fine-tuning benchmarks, LEAN outperforms averaging-based baselines in most settings with substantially less communication, and remains effective under heavy data heterogeneity, where averaging-based methods fail to reach nontrivial accuracy, and under heavy asynchrony, where they degrade substantially.

title: MedicalRSI: Medical Recursive Self-Improving Agents via Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution
abstract: Medical agents built on large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, yet most stay fixed once deployed and do not keep using their experience to improve later attempts. As a result, the same kind of error can recur across patients. To address this, existing self-improvement methods update an agent's weights or its medical harness from its own experience, but their improving strategy stays fixed and never learns which changes actually help, which caps how much the agent can improve. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) instead improves both the agent and its improving strategy. However, achieving RSI for medical agents is challenging, because clinical workflows rarely come with a reference harness, and a change that fixes early errors may not fix the problems the agent meets later. We propose MedicalRSI, an RSI framework built on Clinical Model-Harness Co-Evolution, in which one model plays two roles. The Solver is the medical agent itself, and the Improver is its learnable improving strategy, which writes a medical harness from the agent's failures. Each harness is rewarded by its gain over acting without it, and both roles are trained together, so the Improver keeps adapting to the problems the Solver has not yet solved. On multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, MedicalRSI outperforms existing context-level and weight-level self-improvement methods and transfers well to unseen workflows, new LLMs and new databases, a step toward medical agents that keep improving.

title: NitroGen: Observations on the Action Dynamics, Visual Instruction Following, and Spatial Exploration
abstract: NitroGen is an open vision-action foundation model for game control. It is trained by behavior cloning on online gameplay videos. In this paper, we study the frozen controller in Hollow Knight and Trackmania as examples along three dimensions: action adaptation, visual instruction following, and spatial exploration. Our results indicate that NitroGen can adapt its actions to local context, but it lacks the planning, recovery, and exploration needed for longer-horizon game control.

title: Tuning the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction in CoFeB thin film heterostructures
abstract: The Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya Interaction (DMI) is essential for stabilizing chiral spin textures in spintronics, yet achieving consistent quantitative measurements across different techniques remains a significant challenge. Heterostructures consisting of magnetic thin films sandwiched between non-magnetic heavy metals have been shown to possess substantial DMI; however, these vary in both magnitude and handedness for supposedly identical samples, indicating the sensitivity of DMI to both interfacial properties and measurement techniques. Here, systematic tuning of the DMI in ultra-thin magnetic heterostructures of Pt/CoFeB/Ta/Pt is achieved by varying the thickness of a tantalum sub-monolayer with thicknesses ranging from $0.1\,\mathrm{nm}$ to $0.4\,\mathrm{nm}$. The magnitude and sign of the DMI are measured using three independent methods: the parallel stripe domain model, edge nucleation field analysis, and Brillouin light scattering. The three independent approaches reveal excellent agreement within the experimental error. This ability to controllably tune and reliably quantify DMI provides a viable route toward engineering chiral magnetic textures, including domain walls and skyrmions, for next-generation spintronic devices. The necessity for precise measurements of magnetic parameters and careful attention to detail are discussed because calculations of the DMI for each technique depend on different parameters.

title: Search From the Start: Search-Native Pretraining for Language Models
abstract: Modern language models (LMs) are increasingly deployed with access to search tools at inference. Yet pretraining remains predominantly focused on predicting static text, with search capabilities typically introduced during post-training. We propose Search-Native Pretraining as a practical route to teach search capability during pretraining from ordinary text corpora. Specifically, we augment pretraining corpus at scale with web-search queries and retrieve web response using a local index. Training on this augmented corpus teaches models to generate search calls and incorporate retrieved evidence during language modeling. Across Wikipedia and DCLM-Edu corpora and 360M to 3.3B parameter scales, search-pretrained models ("QueryLM") show improved performance on knowledge-intensive tasks and higher steerability toward the retrieved evidence. Crucially, their advantage persists after supervised fine-tuning of both search-pretrained and conventionally pretrained models, indicating that the tested post-training procedures do not fully recover the capabilities developed during pretraining. Throughout our experiments, we find that a 1.4B QueryLM consistently beats or matches the performance of a FLOP-matched 3.3B baseline model across all knowledge intensive tasks. These results establish search-pretraining as a practical way to develop foundational search capabilities during pretraining. We release the training artifacts, including model checkpoints and data.

title: Acoustic Markers of Engagement in Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder and Their Caregivers
abstract: Characterizing user engagement is essential for developing effective human-computer interaction (HCI) applications, particularly for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Because home-based HCI naturally involves caregivers as conversational facilitators, analyzing both child and caregiver vocalizations can provide critical insights into characterizing interaction dynamics. Using a dataset of home-based socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions, this work demonstrates how child and caregiver vocalization patterns can model engagement in HCI contexts. We employed linear mixed-effects models (LMMs) with child and caregiver acoustic data to identify acoustic features that significantly differentiated engagement from disengagement. The results demonstrated that children and caregivers share three significant acoustic markers of engagement: mean Alpha Ratio (AlphaRatio), mean Harmonics-to-Noise Ratio (HNR), and mean Spectral Slope 500-1500 (SlopeV500-1500). This reflects cleaner and smoother vocalizations during engagement across both groups. Furthermore, we evaluated a State x Group interaction model to compare the magnitudes of standardized state-dependent differences between children and caregivers. The results indicated that children exhibit significantly greater state-related variation than caregivers in three acoustic features: AlphaRatio, HNR, and SlopeV500-1500.

title: Connectivity-Constrained Linear System Realization: Feasibility and Realizable Sets
abstract: In this paper, we first study the problem of finding a state-space realization of a given transfer function that adheres to a given connectivity pattern (i.e., support). While variants of this problem have been studied in distributed and structured control, existing work typically focuses on connectivity patterns relating to some networked plant. In contrast, we are interested in arbitrary connectivity patterns, which are relevant to modeling problems in sensorimotor neuroscience. We show that this problem is equivalent to solving a system of multivariate polynomial equations, and can be solved exactly without relaxation or approximation. We then study the reverse problem: given a connectivity pattern, what transfer functions have a state-space realization that adheres to this pattern? In other words, what transfer functions can this pattern realize? A surprising finding is that any given pattern can realize nearly all transfer functions, or very few transfer functions. We provide rigorous results and algorithms for both problems, leveraging technical machinery from algebraic geometry. The efficacy of our approach is demonstrated in examples at the end of the paper.

title: Studies on a Relationship Between Tate Homology and Local Cohomology of Tensor Products of Modules
abstract: We study the local cohomology of finitely generated modules with respect to specialization-closed subsets over commutative Noetherian rings. Our main result establishes a relationship between the local cohomology of tensor products of modules and Tate homology over Gorenstein rings. We present several consequences of our main result, which are of independent interest. For example, we study various aspects of the cohomological rigidity property of tensor products of modules and generalize results of Huneke-Wiegand in this direction. We determine conditions under which the vanishing of a single local cohomology module of a tensor product implies the vanishing of all lower ones, establish bounds for the depth of tensor products of modules, and obtain criteria for freeness of modules over complete intersection rings. Along the way, we also provide a splitting criterion for vector bundles on smooth complete intersections.

title: Persistent Bass and Lyubeznik Numbers of Stanley Reisner Rings
abstract: We define persistent Lyubeznik numbers and persistent Bass numbers of Stanley--Reisner rings along a simplicial filtration. For Lyubeznik numbers we show that the complex of Àlvarez Montaner and Vahidi computing $λ_{p,q}(\kk[Δ])$ is natural for inclusions of simplicial complexes, so that persistent Lyubeznik numbers are ranks of maps on its cohomology. We give an equivalent costar complex, whose terms are reduced homology groups of links of faces and whose differentials are induced by quotient maps; it requires neither Alexander duals nor free resolutions. For Bass numbers at coordinate primes we prove that the Hochster-type formula is natural for inclusions, which identifies the persistent Bass numbers with the persistent graded Betti numbers of Suwayyid and Wei for filtered links. Both families have finite barcodes and satisfy bottleneck stability. Examples, including two isomers with the same persistent homology, exhibit Lyubeznik bars that persistent homology does not detect.

title: Simple Routes to Turing-Like Patterns
abstract: Spots, stripes, and networks recur in systems with very different microscopic dynamics, suggesting that the competing processes behind Turing-like patterns may be easy to realise. We ask whether local amplification coupled to suppression over a wider region can generate these geometries in simple systems beyond chemical reaction--diffusion models. We test this idea in two settings, a binary cellular automaton obtained by adding a distant neighbour count to Conway's Game of Life and a self-gravitating toy universe described by particle motion and two continuous fields. The automaton produces spots, stripes, and coexistence across its control plane, while a rule retaining only the two opposing counts produces islands, stripes, and holes. Directional correlations and intrinsic dimension identify the same region of orientational order. In the gravitational system, convergence increases local density while mass transport depletes the surroundings. The two-field and particle densities have a smoothed spatial correlation of $0.962$ at scale factor $a=1$ under the original force law, and strengthening its long-wavelength component drives both descriptions toward fewer dense condensations. Together, these results show how simple counting rules and redistribution of a conserved quantity can realise competing growth and suppression, providing two concrete routes by which Turing-like geometries can recur across different dynamics.

title: Specification-Grounded Adaptive Triage and Formal Invariant Exclusion Synthesis for Autonomous Silicon Coverage Closure
abstract: Closing the final 5%-15% of code and functional coverage remains a major schedule bottleneck in silicon tapeouts. Existing LLM-based coverage closure loops feed raw uncovered RTL lines or branches directly into iterative prompts, failing on industrial subsystems due to: (1) token and context explosion from querying thousands of correlated holes independently; (2) illegal stimulus that violates cross-signal invariants and yields dirty coverage; and (3) unsafe exclusion hallucination on structurally unreachable dead code. We present ARGUS (Autonomous Reachability & Guided Unified Stimulus), a specification-grounded, dual-regime coverage closure and formal exclusion synthesis engine. ARGUS mines microarchitectural specs and SystemVerilog Assertions into a formal Block Contract (C), then runs adaptive Macro-Clustering vs. Micro-Surgery triage gated by a per-module hole-density threshold (tau): dense modules collapse correlated holes into root-cause mode, FSM, and backpressure clusters, while sparse modules use AST and loop-domain reachability to separate reachable corners from provably unreachable invariants. Directed tests pair with bit-exact golden scoreboards, and unreachable invariants emit tool-native .el exclusions with formal proofs. Across five core benchmarks -- three open-source LowRISC OpenTitan IPs (uart_core, i2c_core, aes_cipher_core) and two commercial AI accelerator Tensor Layout Converter datapaths (53 SV modules, 376,127 coverage points) -- plus a 2,626-module industrial interconnect subsystem, ARGUS triages 2,626 modules in 0.265 s, cuts token usage by 27.2x to >180x, achieves zero dirty merges via 3-step sanity gating, and reaches 99.32%-100.0% effective coverage with 0 false exclusions across 21,071+ proven exclusions.

title: Frequency-bin-encoded quantum secret sharing with fast basis switching
abstract: Frequency-bin encoding offers unique opportunities for fiber-native quantum information processing, yet its full potential has been hampered by challenges in rapid state control and protocol scaling. Leveraging high-speed microwave processing, we overcome several extant hurdles and unlock new fundamental capabilities in frequency-based quantum communications. First, we demonstrate three-party quantum secret sharing, representing, to our knowledge, the first multiparty ($N\geq 3$ users) quantum communication protocol implemented entirely with frequency encoding. Second, we demonstrate active, pseudorandom switching of frequency-bin quantum states and measurement bases at 20 MHz symbol rates, enabling real-time protocol operation without relying on hardware-intensive passive basis-selection schemes. Even under fast switching, we preserve high-contrast three-party correlations ($\geq 0.91$) and low quantum bit error rates ($\leq 4.5\%$). Our work extends frequency-bin quantum communication beyond static, two-party protocols, opening a pathway toward scalable, reconfigurable, and real-time spectrally encoded quantum networking.

title: Study of Radiative Muon Capture Experimental Data and its Implications for Muon-Conversion Experiments
abstract: Radiative muon capture (RMC) is an important background in searches for the neutrinoless conversion of a muon into an electron in the field of a nucleus, and in particular in searches for the lepton flavor and lepton number violating process of muon-to-positron conversion. The high-energy tail of the RMC photon spectrum remains theoretically understudied, leading to large uncertainties in background predictions for upcoming muon-conversion experiments. In this work, we revisit previously published RMC data to investigate improved modeling of the high-energy tail. We develop a model characterized by distinct nucleon-knockout final states, each with its associated multibody phase space and kinematic endpoint. This framework is applied to photon data from TRIUMF and positron data from SINDRUM II, and the results are compared to the previously used closure approximation. We find that separately modeling the distinct nucleon-knockout final states provides an improved description of the available RMC data near the endpoint, and we discuss the implications for the COMET and Mu2e experiments.

title: Realistic Robustness Evaluation of Tabular Data Driven Models
abstract: The increasing adoption of Machine Learning (ML) models in high-stakes applications has raised critical concerns regarding their robustness against adversarial attacks. While extensive research has focused on adversarial example generation in image and text domains, the study of such examples in tabular data remains comparatively limited, despite its widespread use in real-world systems. This work introduces AURORA, a modular, open-source tool for evaluating the robustness of ML models on tabular data classification. It integrates multiple adversarial perturbation methods and evaluation metrics within a unified framework to systematically assess model behavior under adversarial conditions. Central to AURORA is its evaluation report, which focuses on robustness analysis by quantifying performance degradation, comparing the impact of different perturbation strategies, and identifying model vulnerabilities across features and input regions. The report is complemented by visual artifacts that facilitate the interpretability of robustness patterns. Additionally, AURORA incorporates a distance adjustment mechanism that penalizes implausible adversarial samples based on feature-level constraints, ensuring that the robustness assessment remains grounded in realistic perturbations and is therefore more reliable.

title: Recovering from Averages: An Inverse Problem Perspective on Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials
abstract: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) approximate the potential energy surface of atomistic systems from quantum-mechanical reference data and enable molecular simulation at near-ab-initio accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Since they are fitted to total energies and forces, it is not obvious what is estimated: the total energy or the many-body potentials from which it is assembled. Mathematically, this can be formulated as a question whether a function can be recovered from averages of its values over random clusters. We study it for a linear model of fixed correlation order in simplified statistical setting. We show that, in the population limit, the potential is identifiable in a natural weighted Sobolev space, and derive finite-sample recovery guarantees. Numerical experiments for pair, three-body, and four-body models support the theory.

title: Dynamical friction on an extended satellite revisited
abstract: The original formulation of Chandrasekhar dynamical friction (DF) was developed for a point-like particle moving in a infinite and homogeneous medium. However, despite very useful order of magnitude estimates of the slowing-down time scales of a test mass in more realistic finite-sized models, high resolution $N-$body simulations often hint at a breakdown of Chandrasekhar's formalism (typically overestimating the effect of DF) for massive satellites sinking in the host galaxy. More advanced semi-analytical treatment of the DF expression managed to partially reduce said discrepancy, even though an accurate comparison with numerical simulations still remains difficult, specifically due to the interplay between the DF force and the tidal stress effects on an extended stellar systems sinking in the gravitational potential of the parent galaxy or halo. In this study we perform ad hoc $N-$body simulations of a satellite orbiting in a simple spherical galaxy model, for different values of the initial orbital eccentricity, satellite mass, scale radius and velocity anisotropy profile of the host model. We adopt an $N-$body code where the self-consistent interaction among the particles representing the galaxy can be substituted by the effect of the static smooth potential of the system's continuum limit. Moreover, the satellite itself is either modeled with $N_{\rm sat}$ particles or represented by a single particle with an effective size parametrized in the form of the force exchanged with the other simulation particles representing the galaxy. We find that, at fixed galaxy model and satellite mass, the more extended the satellite, the weaker is the effect of DF. This trend, which is found for both isotropic and radially anisotropic host systems, is particularly evident for orbits with initial orbital eccentricity exceeding $\approx0.3$.

title: Feshbach Projection Formalism for Resonant Electrodynamics
abstract: Open resonant photonic systems are widely described by effective non-Hermitian formalisms, such as temporal coupled-mode theory, which capture radiative decay through complex eigenfrequencies. In conventional formulations, however, these effective models remain largely phenomenological, lacking a direct microscopic connection to the underlying Maxwell equations. To bridge this gap, we present an analytically tractable light-matter framework based on the Feshbach projection formalism applied to classical electrodynamics. Starting from a coupled system of mechanical oscillator and a one-dimensional electromagnetic field, we construct a strictly Hermitian first-order Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that rigorously eliminating the electromagnetic degrees of freedom via the outgoing Green's function automatically generates a non-Hermitian mechanical operator. Crucially, the resulting radiative damping is determined by the local electromagnetic response rather than introduced ad hoc. Furthermore, we extend this framework to two spatially separated dipoles and show how field retardation transforms a finite set of discrete modes into a countably infinite Fabry-Perot-like spectrum as the separation deviates from zero. The proposed framework provides an intuitive yet rigorous foundation for deriving effective non-Hermitian dynamics directly from conservative light-matter interactions.

title: Kinetic Sunyaev Zel'dovich Velocity Reconstruction Using Vision Transformers
abstract: Kinetic Sunyaev Zel'dovich (kSZ) velocity reconstruction uses correlations between maps of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and a tracer of large scale structure (LSS) to infer the large-scale peculiar velocity field. Standard approaches to kSZ velocity reconstruction use quadratic estimators that are Fisher optimal for purely Gaussian fields. Here, we develop a pipeline for kSZ velocity reconstruction based on Vision Transformers (ViT) and show that this approach can improve the fidelity of velocity reconstruction. This is consistent with the network utilizing non-Gaussian information in the inputs that the quadratic estimators do not, though with the single simulation realization we have access to, we cannot exclude overfitting. Our approach can be applied to full-resolution maps from existing and near-term CMB and LSS datasets.

title: Geometric Contribution to the Electron-Phonon Coupling Constant: Checkerboard and Hyper-diamond Models
abstract: Recent theoretical studies on electron-phonon coupling (EPC) - a key ingredient in the emergence of diverse quantum phases such as superconductivity and charge-density waves - have revealed a distinct contribution to its strength arising from the quantum geometry of electronic bands. Here we investigate the quantum geometric contribution, characterized by the quantum metric, to the dimensionless EPC constant in the checkerboard and hyper-diamond models, under the Gaussian approximation. We show that in the checkerboard model, the geometric contribution can be tuned independently while keeping the energetic part fixed, demonstrating the possibility of enhancing EPC strength through quantum geometry. In the hyper-diamond model, the geometric contribution accounts for roughly $50\%$ of the total EPC constant across all spatial dimensions, generalizing the $d=2$ result for graphene to higher dimensions.

title: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection and Alert Correlation
abstract: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.

title: Skill-JEPA: Learning Planner-Aligned Action Spaces for World Models
abstract: World models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn from pixels to predict the outcome of actions in a latent space. To reach a goal, a planner samples many candidate action sequences, uses the model to predict where each one leads, and executes the best one. However, standard planners draw their candidates from a Gaussian, while the model has only seen the structured, state-dependent actions of its training data. Its predictions for such candidates are unreliable, and planning fails more often as goals move farther away. We propose Skill-JEPA, which learns an action space aligned with the planner. A variational autoencoder conditioned on the current state encodes short action sequences into latent skills with a standard Gaussian prior, and decodes them back into actions. The world model predicts the effect of skills rather than raw actions, and the planner searches over skills starting from that same Gaussian, so its candidates resemble the model's training data. Skill-JEPA adds a single module, trained end-to-end with the world model, and leaves the planner untouched, with no subgoals, hierarchy, or hand-designed skills.
