Experiments on four privacy applications (geolocation, PII, facial, and medical) across five datasets and six VLMs show that SecretAgent preserves image quality substantially better than existing methods while achieving state-of-the-art privacy protection in every application, and that its protection transfers to other VLMs.

title: Looking Right Is Not Being Right: Evaluating the Geometry of Agent-Built 3D Scenes
abstract: Vision-language agents can reconstruct rooms from video as editable 3D scenes, but convincing renders do not establish geometric accuracy. We introduce a scan-referenced evaluation and use controlled experiments to study reconstruction accuracy, the role of geometric inputs, and agents' ability to verify and correct their scenes. Our geometric score measures surface, depth, and furniture placement agreement with laser scans of 30 real rooms on a 0-100 scale. The strongest tested agent, GPT-6 Astra, scores 51.4 from video alone, while a dense reconstruction from the same video scores 75.9. Given the point cloud used for that reconstruction, Astra produces an editable scene that scores within three points of it. Agents also inherit input errors: rescaling the supplied geometry changes scene scale almost proportionally. During revision, viewing renders improves appearance more consistently than geometry. Logs of their tool calls show that agents repeatedly measure their inputs but rarely compare them with the scenes they build. To provide this missing check, we introduce a geometric error report that compares each saved scene with the agent's input points and lists the largest discrepancies. Without new geometric evidence, the report raises the revision gains of GPT-6.1 Terra and Sol by 3.9 and 5.5 points over concurrent controls.

title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
abstract: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

title: Acceleration of Sparse and Irregular Workloads through Energy-Efficient Stream Extensions
abstract: The slowdown of Moore's law and Dennard scaling has motivated computer architects to uphold performance scaling through architectural specialization. So far, most efforts have focused on highly regular workloads, which exhibit good data locality, ample reuse, and a data-independent execution flow. As this specialization hits diminishing returns, attention shifts towards sparse and irregular workloads, which are essential to applications like sparse neural networks, multiphysics simulations, and graph analytics. However, they lack the convenient properties of highly regular compute that modern architectures are optimized for, resulting in very low (<10%) functional unit utilization on traditional CPUs and GPUs. The most promising approaches to their general hardware acceleration leverage memory streams, which decouple data movement from execution. In this thesis, we explore energy-efficient hardware stream extensions that significantly accelerate sparse and irregular workloads in general-purpose systems without specializing to specific application domains or compromising on regular-workload performance. We design a flexible, core-coupled stream extension supporting affine and indirect streams as well as intersection and union of sparse tensors. We integrate it into an energy-efficient RISC-V compute cluster, achieving significant performance and energy efficiency benefits on general sparse linear algebra, and further use it to accelerate stencil computations, spiking neural network inference, and model-predictive control. We evaluate it at scale in a 432-core 2.5D RISC-V system fabricated in 12nm FinFET, achieving leading compute utilization and energy efficiency on sparse and irregular workloads while remaining competitive on regular workloads. Finally, we extend chip-level interconnects with end-to-end irregular streams, improving performance, energy efficiency, and bus utilization.

title: CENTRY: A Probabilistic Latent-State Model for Continual AI Risk Estimation, Monitoring, and Regulation
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical applications, yet existing AI safety frameworks primarily define, categorize, or govern AI risk rather than proposing implementable models and methods for continually estimating, monitoring, and regulating risk throughout an AI system's operational lifetime. This paper proposes CENTRY, a probabilistic framework that enables continual risk estimation, monitoring, and regulation of a deployed AI system from its interactions with its environment. The framework models AI risk as arising from three intrinsic sources: datasets, hardware resources, and models/algorithms. A structured latent-variable model is developed in which the latent representation is decomposed into a fast interaction subspace that captures the evolving AI--environment dynamics and three slow latent subspaces that encode the long-term risk states associated with the dataset, hardware, and model components. Rather than requiring a ground-truth risk label at every time step, the component-risk states are treated as latent variables and are learned by maximizing a variational evidence lower bound, optionally informed during training and continual refinement by evidence-supported behavior--cause records. The resulting framework unifies continual probabilistic inference, online risk estimation, and adaptive risk regulation in an implementable architecture. Under the explicit assumptions stated for the corresponding results, we establish formal guarantees spanning safety, learning, inference, and operations, including finite-horizon and asymptotic risk-budget compliance, regret and convergence bounds for adaptive regulation, consistency and identifiability of component-risk ratings, and detection-delay, false-alarm, containment, and computational-complexity characterizations.

title: Extracting Next Generation Access Control Policies from Natural Language Using LLMs: An Intermediate-Representation Approach with Back-Translation Verification
abstract: Organizations write access-control rules in natural language, but NIST's Next Generation Access Control (NGAC) needs them as a formal policy graph. Large language models (LLMs) can automate this translation, but their output can break the format, add rules the text does not state, or drop conditions. We present NGAC-IR, which follows model-driven engineering (MDE). First, the LLM fills in an intermediate representation (IR), a JSON template that records who may, must or must not do what, on which resource and under which condition; a grammar keeps the output within this template. Second, a compiler that uses no LLM converts the IR into an NGAC policy graph and links each rule to its source sentence. Third, a back-translation check writes each rule in English and asks an LLM whether the source sentence states it. On four public datasets, all outputs could be compiled, compared with 95.5% without the grammar, and 95.7% were faithful to their sentence. NGAC-IR outperforms two published methods on all four datasets: the LLM-based Code4Policy in exact match and faithfulness, and the rule-based extractor of Abdelgawad et al. in rule type. The back-translation check sent 10.5% of sentences to human review and found 26 of the 31 errors. To test enforcement, we deployed the compiled policies in NIST's Policy Machine: they gave the expected decision for all 390 access requests, and the tested obligations were carried out. On one local server with open-weight models, all 714 sentences take about 20 minutes and 0.35 kWh, at zero API cost.

title: CodeReviewBench: An Automated Benchmark for Evaluating the Software Factory
abstract: As AI agents ship more code with minimal human oversight, code review becomes the critical quality-control checkpoint -- but one without a reliable, objective verifier: review quality is nuanced and ultimately a judgment call by the PR author. Existing benchmarks are structurally misaligned with this: annotators are third-party reviewers, like the bots they evaluate, not the PR authors who actually decide what to fix. They also rely on small, static issue sets that require full re-evaluation as tools update, limiting how frequently progress can be tracked. We introduce CodeReviewBench, built on a fundamentally different signal: revealed developer preferences -- if a developer acts on a bot's suggestion, we treat it as useful; if they ignore it, we do not. This signal is mined daily from the public GitHub event stream, yielding 500K+ judged PRs across 18 tools, and refreshes continuously as tools evolve. We validate the developer preference against an independent offline benchmark: the two agree on precision rankings and independently detect the same product updates within days of vendor releases. Together, these form the benchmark.

title: An Infinite Family of Overpartition Congruences Modulo 1944
abstract: Let $\overline p(n)$ denote the number of overpartitions of $n$. We prove that $\overline p(16^α(96n+76))\equiv0\pmod{1944}$ for all nonnegative integers $α$ and $n$, extending the congruence for $\overline p(96n+76)$ established by Smoot. The key step is a three-term congruence modulo $243$ relating $\overline p(m)$, $\overline p(16m)$, and $\overline p(256m)$ for $m\equiv4\pmod6$. We derive this relation and the two initial congruences using theta-function dissections. A separate theta-series argument establishes divisibility by $8$.

title: Analysis of Multi-Client Inference Techniques for Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) are a new class of machine learning model for generalizable robot control. While they enable robots to perform complex tasks in unseen environments, serving VLAs leaves hardware idle between inference passes and under-utilized during inference. Serving multiple clients at once can improve utilization, but fundamental multi-client techniques such as batching and co-execution have not been characterized for VLAs. We therefore characterize the trade-offs these known techniques impose across latency, throughput, power, and hardware utilization. Our findings inform trade-offs and challenges for future multi-VLA serving systems.

title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
abstract: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.

title: A Stochastic Tamed-Regularized Random Batch Method for Uncertain Particle Systems with Singularities
abstract: The coefficients of particle systems often exhibit uncertainties due to incomplete knowledge. For particle systems with uncertainties and singularities in the drift and diffusion terms, existing methods may encounter numerical blow-up. In this paper, we propose a novel stochastic tamed-regularized Random Batch (str-RB) method for such uncertain particle systems with singularities. Specifically, since singularities in the diffusion term are more challenging than those in the drift term, building on a tamed scheme, we design an exponential regularization strategy that more effectively mitigates singularities in the diffusion term. This strategy ensures that the stochastic Galerkin (sG) projection coefficients remain finite even when the corresponding integrals for the original singular diffusion coefficient diverge. The sG method is applied to handle the random coefficients, and a random batch approach is then employed to reduce the computational complexity of large-scale simulations. Several theoretical properties of the proposed algorithm are established. Numerical tests demonstrate that the str-RB algorithm exhibits weak convergence, achieves lower errors than major existing methods across singular tests, and remains stable in a wider range of singular regimes. This work provides a robust and accurate approach for uncertain particle systems with singularities, laying a foundation for high-performance solvers in uncertain many-body dynamics.

title: Tensor products of additive groups as reciprocity sheaves
abstract: We compute the Nisnevich reciprocity sheaves associated with tensor products of the cube-invariant objects for the additive and multiplicative groups, with at least one additive factor. Over a perfect field of characteristic different from two, these sheaves decompose into direct sums of absolute K$ä$hler differential sheaves with binomial multiplicities. As an application, we compute the associated reciprocity sheaves of the Hochschild homology of the additive object.

title: Bottlenecked: The Capital Cost of Protected DeFi Lending
abstract: Securing hundreds of billions of dollars in decentralized finance (DeFi) requires both cryptographically secured collateral and economic capital to absorb losses that collateral alone cannot cover. Composability makes both the amount and location of this protection matter: Kelp's nearly \$300 million April 2026 bridge exploit showed how an attacker could borrow against stolen assets across lending markets. We study how to allocate junior capital that absorbs losses before users incur losses in lending protocols. The main object we study is a tripartite graph that records user assets, their covered liabilities, and the junior capital permitted to pay them. Cuts in this graph determine what protection is missing, while a static security game on the graph defines how much such protection should cost. We call this cost the adversarial default premium (ADP), which can be viewed as the excess cost of insurance in composable financial systems. We then study the joint cost of funding loans and protecting their creditors via this insurance. In a tripartite graph with $N$ borrowers and $M$ lenders, we show that existing systems such as Aave and Morpho have an insurance cost that is $Θ(N)$. Under mild assumptions, we show that the optimal graph has an insurance cost that is $Θ(\sqrt{N})$ with small constants. We apply our model to numerous 2026 DeFi cyber attacks and estimate ADP and the performance of optimized graphs. We find practical capital cost savings of up to 34.5% for our optimized design versus designs that resemble Aave and Morpho. Our results suggest that new lending protocols can improve capital efficiency by treating junior capital as a first-class constraint in protocol design.

title: Serial Dependence Emerges from Optimizing Vision for Noise Robustness
abstract: Human visual perception is dynamically shaped by the recent past, a phenomenon known as serial dependence. Mechanistic models show that a residual memory trace can generate this dependency, yet its functional purpose (why the visual system should carry information forward in time at all) remains debated. We tested the hypothesis that serial dependence emerges as a normative consequence of optimizing vision for robustness against sensory noise. We trained recurrent autoencoders (a CNN encoder, a ConvGRU memory module, and a CNN decoder) to reconstruct natural videos corrupted by Gaussian noise, with no objective referring to perceptual history. Models that used their temporal memory achieved lower reconstruction error than memory-free counterparts, and this advantage widened as training noise increased, indicating that integrating past context is an adaptive denoising strategy. Probing the trained models with Gabor and dot sequences, we found that memory gave rise to serial dependence spontaneously: an attractive bias toward previous orientations and a spatial "continuity field" toward recently seen locations, both strengthening with training noise. Across temporal delays, the model's serial dependence was strongest for the immediately preceding stimulus and decayed monotonically. This profile quantitatively matched human orientation judgments, including an independent public dataset, once a known response-autocorrelation confound was controlled: an apparent non-monotonicity in one dataset reflected this measurement artifact rather than a genuine model-human mismatch. These findings suggest that serial dependence need not be an idiosyncratic quirk but can arise as a byproduct of optimizing for noise robustness, offering a normative account of perceptual history-dependence that complements existing mechanistic explanations and links behavior to an underlying computational objective.

title: Mechanistic Analysis of Unified Proximity-Tactile Observation by a Capacitive Fingertip Array Constrained by a Metal Phalanx
abstract: A capacitive fingertip array on a metal phalanx under thin silicone skin senses centimetre-scale conductive targets by fringing fields and contact force by dielectric compression. Electrode-to-body parasitics exceed the useful proximity increment by one to three orders of magnitude, and crosstalk and time-division-multiplexing (TDM) settling prevent identifying the capacitance-to-digital converter (CDC) reading with the electrode-target capacitance. The array is modelled as a multi-conductor system (sensing electrodes, driven-shield nodes, phalanx ground and an external target). The CDC measurand follows from the Maxwell capacitance matrix, with each inactive termination in the observation operator. Three mechanisms are examined: driven-shield hiding of shield-branch current and gain/phase-mismatch leakage; distinct far- and near-field operators; and TDM settling as a frame-rate limit set by shield load. A single layer used for both proximity and force reads Delta C = Delta C_force + Delta C_dielectric(epsilon_target), so its force map cannot be material-independent. A dual-array stack is analysed: the outer array is grounded as a Faraday screen during contact, and the inner array reads silicone-gap compression. FEM simulations give a monotonic, nonlinear contact response (4.6 fF at 0.05 mm to 370 fF at 0.5 mm on a 1.08 pF base), a nylon-versus-metal difference of at most 0.3 fF at exported-matrix resolution (not mesh-converged), mutual-term cancellation under driven-shield readout, and about 1 fF crosstalk on the coarse mesh. In proximity mode, electrode-shield coupling of 1.47 pF makes 10^{-3}-10^{-4} mismatch a quantitative gate: a 15.9 fF increment at 5 mm equals the leakage at |epsilon_A| ~ 10^{-2}. Force map, mechanical crosstalk and all bench quantities remain unvalidated; the equations and FEM evidence are a baseline for prototype calibration, not measured performance claims.

title: Verification of Statistical Properties: Redefining the Possible
abstract: We revisit the setting of Interactive Proof Systems for Distribution Testing, introduced by Chiesa and Gur (2018), showing that a simple twist on the task requirements may lead to dramatic improvements, allowing verifiers with constant sample complexity. We define and investigate the multi-prover and zero-knowledge versions of these interactive proof systems, using as flagship example the task of farness verification - the "dual" version of closeness testing. We hope our results will inspire others to investigate and analyze the power and limitations of multiple provers for distribution verification.

title: A High-Resolution Stellar Extinction Map of M31 from PHAT and PHAST Photometry
abstract: High-resolution extinction maps of resolved external galaxies, such as M31, are crucial not only for accurately correcting dust extinction and reddening toward individual sources within the galaxy, but also for characterizing the distribution and evolution of interstellar dust in external galactic environments. We aim to construct a high-resolution and large-coverage stellar-traced extinction map of M31, based on multi-band photometric data from the HST PHAT and PHAST surveys. Using a stellar template library built from the PARSEC stellar evolution models and adopting the average extinction law of M31, we apply a matching method analogous to the SPar algorithm to derive A_V values for approximately 65 million stars. The extinction map is then generated using a HEALPix adaptive-resolution scheme. The resulting map covers approximately two-thirds of the star-forming disk of M31, with a maximum spatial resolution of 1.61 arcsec. The median extinction across the map is A_V = 1.24 mag. Comparison with previously published stellar- and dust-emission-based extinction maps shows broadly similar large-scale morphology, while differences remain in the extinction values. The extinction map further reveals fine-scale features such as inter-arm filaments, supernova-driven cavities, and spur-like structures. The map has been publicly released through the NADC platform and is expected to serve as an important observational basis for extinction correction in subsequent astronomical observations and for related M31 scientific studies.

title: Counterexamples to a conjecture of Gao and Gu on weighted Catalan numbers
abstract: We construct infinitely many counterexamples to a conjecture of Gao and Gu on when the 2-adic valuations of weighted Catalan numbers equal those of Catalan numbers.

title: Learning Video Foresight Reasoning from Unlabeled Videos via On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: Video foresight reasoning requires vision-language models to anticipate future events or next actions from currently observed videos. Existing methods fit future captions, rationales, or full visual states, but face two limitations. First, they rely on annotations or external large models for supervision, limiting scalability. We address this with an on-policy self-distillation framework that turns past-future video pairs into a natural self-supervised signal without extra annotations or LLM supervision. Second, they treat the whole future clip as equally valuable, although most of it is irrelevant context information. We address this by defining a foresight score, from which we obtain a contrastive privilege advantage that drives the model to learn the most valuable future information. Since the score is intractable, we optimize a tractable lower-bound surrogate that interpolates this advantage, computed between the true and a random reference future, with a teacher-student distillation advantage; together, they amplify decision-relevant content information and suppress irrelevant context information. We call the resulting framework Future-OPSD. On open-ended prediction and closed-ended planning, Future-OPSD improves base models by up to 14.2 and 15.9 points without compromising general video understanding. Code will be available at https://jingchensun.github.io/future-opsd/

title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data
abstract: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on Pólya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

title: Strong numerical radius orthogonality on bounded linear operators
abstract: Orthogonality is an important tool for studying bounded linear operators. In this paper, we introduce the concept of strong numerical radius orthogonality of operators and then, discuss the properties about numerical radius orthogonality, strong numerical radius orthogonality of operators as well as relationship between them.

title: Tracking and Limiting Unsupported Claim Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems: A Provenance-Aware Framework
abstract: This research examines how unsupported claims change as they move through multi-agent pipelines. It also examines whether preserving provenance can reduce these changes. We test both homogeneous and heterogeneous pipelines. Homogeneous pipelines use the same model across agents, while heterogeneous pipelines use different models. We compare the baseline with a provenance-aware framework. The framework passes each claim with its support status, source, evidence and transmission history. No new evidence is introduced during transmission. We measure changes in claim meaning, unsupported detail accretion, semantic drift, and provenance preservation. These metrics show whether the framework limits unsupported changes as claims pass between agents.

title: A Novel Dataset and Framework for Schenkerian Optical Music Recognition
abstract: Music theory enables performers, composers, and listeners to engage more deeply with music. Schenkerian analysis (SchA) is a particularly illustrative and widely used approach for modeling tonal structure, organizing music into hierarchical layers of harmonic and voice-leading relationships. Despite its importance in pedagogy and scholarship, producing well-formatted Schenkerian graphs remains difficult. A typical workflow might involve writing the Schenkerian analysis on paper, and then manually, painstakingly, entering each symbol by hand into music software, exporting to vector graphics, and manually refining layouts in graphical editors. Existing optical music recognition (OMR) systems for handwritten common western music notation (CWMN) can be leveraged for their ability to recognize small-scale symbols common to those in SchA. However, CWMN OMR models generally fail to recognize large symbols such as phrase slurs, struggle with dense notation, and do not recognize Schenkerian analysis markings. Thus, these models do not extend well to digitizing SchA. This paper introduces a novel framework for optical music recognition of both CWMN and SchA. Our novel contributions include (1) an ensemble model in which each individual model follows a different image-cropping scheme for improved object detection, (2) a topological neural network architecture for notation assembly, where candidate hyperedges attend to one another and perform hierarchical message passing, (3) the first dataset of labeled handwritten SchAs, gathered with novel model integration to the OMR-annotation software, MuNG Studio, and (4) the first algorithm for converting semantic Schenkerian graphs into typeset format.

title: High-Sensitivity Magnetometry with Scalable Mixed SQUID Arrays
abstract: The utilisation of Superconducting Quantum Interference Devices (SQUIDs), a loop of superconducting material hosting two Josephson junctions, has long been at the forefront of quantum sensing. To enhance performance and signal power, modern architectures connect multiple SQUIDs into two-dimensional series-parallel arrays called Superconducting Quantum Interference Filters (SQIFs). A major recent advancement, called a mixed-SQUID array, integrates junction-free ``bare" loops alongside active SQUID loops, offering a promising strategy to engineer high-performance alternatives to traditional SQIF technology. However, a rigorous theoretical optimization and performance scaling analysis for this novel geometry remains lacking. In this work, an analytical framework, validated against full numerical simulations, is developed to establish fundamental design rules for this technology. This work systematically examines how key quantum sensing parameters evolve as a function of loop inductance, parasitic coupling, and overall array dimensions. Crucially, it is demonstrated that these mixed SQUID arrays circumvent the severe inductive screening losses inherent to conventional SQIF designs, achieving a performance boost in flux sensitivity in the range of $2-4\:\times$ under realistic device parameters.

title: Resonance-controlled post-selected mode entanglement in one-dimensional quantum scattering
abstract: We study resonance-controlled post-selected mode entanglement in a one-dimensional quantum-scattering model. Two incoming electrons scatter independently from a symmetric double-barrier structure and the sector with one reflected and one transmitted electron is selected. The idealised delta-function barriers used in earlier work are replaced by exponentially localised cusp barriers, $U(x)=U_0\exp(-|x\mp d/2|/a)$, for which the single-barrier scattering problem is exactly solvable in terms of modified Bessel functions of imaginary order. We derive the corresponding reflection and transmission amplitudes, verify their current normalisation and validate them independently by direct numerical integration. Two separated cusp barriers are then combined through a Fabry-Pérot composition, whose accuracy is quantified by solving the full two-centre Schrödinger equation. In the well-separated regime the approximation reproduces the full resonance positions to high accuracy. The concurrence zeros are controlled by the resonance phase condition $δ(κ)+κd=nπ$, with a continuously unwrapped single-barrier reflection phase $δ$. We also calculate the post-selection probability $P_{RT}$, showing explicitly that large conditional concurrence can occur in a low-probability sector. Systematic scans in barrier width, integrated strength and reference momentum show that finite width can shift off-resonant concurrence maxima and, depending on the reference momentum, reduce their attainable height. The results identify resonance-controlled conditional entanglement as a robust feature of the well-separated double-barrier geometry rather than an artefact of the zero-range idealisation.

title: High-precision proper motions toward the Galactic bulge Baade's window from a decade of DECam observations
abstract: A complete characterization of the Galactic bulge stellar populations could offer important clues on the formation and evolution of our Galaxy. However, most bulge fields are hampered by high stellar crowding, strong interstellar extinction, and by heavy contamination from foreground disk stars. We aim to derive proper motions (PMs) towards the Baade's window by using DECam observations, extending kinematic studies of the Galactic bulge below the turn-off to a much larger field of view. We combined three datasets observed with DECam in the $r$-band spanning a ${\sim}$ 10-year baseline. As a pilot study, we only analyzed the field covered by a single detector. We developed an astrometric calibration pipeline that corrects for the DECam tree-ring pattern and residual distortions, tying all positions to the Gaia DR3 reference frame, and used them to derive PMs. We isolated the bulge population through a strict cut in $μ_{\ell^\ast}$, refined with a Gaia DR3 parallax selection. We measured PMs for $48\,239$ stars in the pilot field, with a median uncertainty of $0.65$ mas yr$^{-1}$ at $r_0<18$ mag. Our PMs agree closely with Gaia DR3, and reaches ${\sim}1.5$ magnitudes deeper than Gaia and a comparable depth to VIRAC2 in terms of relative completeness. We found velocity dispersions along Galactic longitude and latitude of $σ_{μ_{\ell^\ast}}=2.76\pm0.03$ mas yr$^{-1}$ and $σ_{μ_b}=2.49\pm0.02$ mas yr$^{-1}$ for the Galactic bulge, consistent with HST studies. We estimated a foreground contamination of ${\sim}14\%$ before any kinematic selection. The cleaned color-magnitude diagram reaches below the main-sequence turnoff, and shows no evidence for a large population younger than ${\sim}4$-$5$ Gyr in this field. Moreover, since the LSST camera shares the same CCD technology as DECam, this work offers a valuable precursor for crowded-field astrometry in the Rubin era.

title: Stability of independence polynomials of well-covered Ferrers graphs
abstract: We prove that every root of the independence polynomial of a well-covered Ferrers graph lies in the open unit disk centered at $-1$, that is, $|x+1|<1$. Consequently, the polynomial is strictly stable. We also exhibit a general Ferrers graph whose independence polynomial is not stable.

title: Causal Diffusion for Extreme Super-Resolution in Interactive Games
abstract: Existing game super-resolution methods typically operate at moderate upscaling factors, struggling to recover fine visual details from extremely low-resolution inputs (e.g., 120p). At such resolutions, super-resolution shifts from reconstructing existing information toward synthesizing missing visual details. While video diffusion models offer powerful generative priors for this challenging task, their dependence on future frames limits their applicability to interactive games. We present CIDER, a causal diffusion framework for extreme game super-resolution that synthesizes high-frequency details from current and past low-resolution frames, guided by G-buffers (depth and motion vectors) to preserve scene structure and temporal consistency. We collect data from two AAA games (Cyberpunk 2077 and Black Myth: Wukong). To reduce inference load, we develop a lightweight latent projection encoder tailored to ultra-low-resolution inputs, fine-tune a decoder (TAE) on our high-resolution outputs, and distill the diffusion model to reach interactive frame rates. Our experiments demonstrate high-fidelity 8$\times$ upscaling from 120p to 960p at around 13 FPS, outperforming state-of-the-art game upscalers in visual quality and showing potential for 16$\times$ magnification.

title: The Dirichlet problem for sum Hessian quotient equations on Riemannian manifolds
abstract: In this paper, we consider the Dirichlet problem for a class of sum Hessian quotient equations involving a gradient term on the right-hand side on Riemannian manifolds. Under the assumption of the existence of a subsolution, based on the a priori estimates for the solutions, we prove the existence and the uniqueness of $(k-1)$-admissible solutions for the Dirichlet problem on compact Riemannian manifolds with smooth boundary. Our existence results cover the case $0\le l<k<n$ with $k\ge 2$, where the subsolution is assumed to be $(k-1)$-admissible, and the case $k=n$ with $0\le l\le n-2$, where the subsolution is assumed to be $n$-admissible.

title: Beyond Prompt Heuristics: Assessing Child Safety Alignment in LLMs
abstract: Child-safety taxonomies typically characterize safety risks through a predefined set of harm categories, and existing evaluations largely operationalize these categories using prompts that explicitly invoke them. However, child-safety considerations can also arise in seemingly benign requests that lack recognizable harm-category cues. We therefore investigate how child-safety alignment generalizes to such settings. Across six models, we find considerably higher misalignment rates on requests without recognizable harm-category cues than on those containing such cues (80.0, 54.0, and 48.4 percentage-point gaps for Qwen3.5-27B, GPT-5.4-mini, and Claude-Haiku-4.5, respectively). Through controlled behavioral and mechanistic analyses, we find that introducing a single harm-associated word reduces misalignment across most models, with mechanistic evidence suggesting that child-safety reasoning may rely in part on lexical and semantic associations with words in the prompt. Our findings motivate evaluations that treat child safety as context-dependent, and not reducible to a fixed set of harm categories.

title: Keep the Process, Change the Supplier: Runtime Governance for Tool-Using AI Agents
abstract: Tool-using AI agents propose actions whose authorization and external effects cannot be inferred from generated text alone. We study an execution boundary that separates agent proposals from business-controlled authority, context disclosure, and supplier selection. The Open Process Control Plane (OPCP) mediates capability calls and records uncertain outcomes when a supplier may have acted without returning an acceptable reply. We evaluate this runtime with scripted requests and synthetic suppliers: 2,400 fault episodes across four policies, 60 process-termination/restart episodes, 19,000 timed calls across 19 configurations, five targeted mutations over 43 fixtures, and 160 substitution records. No language model or autonomous agent is evaluated. OPCP and a conservative composition agree on all measured fault outcomes. Both recover after definite refusal without cross-supplier duplication; retry-all duplicates effects in every tested lost-reply-after-commit case. Persistent runtime state prevents cross-supplier replay in the restart experiments, while same-supplier duplicate prevention also requires supplier idempotency. At 128 suppliers, best-score routing has a median latency of 1.411 ms versus 0.261 ms for pinned routing. All five selected mutations are detected, and record enumeration exposes acceptance of an empty regression set. These results characterize an execution mechanism relevant to agent governance, including its costs and assumption boundaries. They do not establish improved agent task success, prompt-injection resistance, or real-vendor model portability.

title: Data-Driven Detection of Volatility Regimes and Sector-Level Asymmetry During Sovereign Default
abstract: We present a data-driven framework for detecting changes in stock-market volatility and characterising their effects across industry sectors. The framework identifies volatility regimes directly from historical returns using dynamic programming, validated with a sup-F test and a Markov-switching model. We apply it to 1,559 trading days of the Sri Lankan All Share Price Index (ASPI) and 13 sector indices, covering pre-COVID, COVID-19, sovereign-default, and recovery periods. Within each regime, Student-$t$ EGARCH models quantify volatility response, persistence, and asymmetry between positive and negative shocks. The results reveal a distinct regime-specific pattern: significant negative-shock asymmetry occurs in 9 of 14 series during the sovereign default, compared with none during COVID-19 despite 2.6 times higher volatility than pre-COVID. For the ASPI, volatility persistence decreases from 0.936 during COVID-19 to 0.647 during the default. Cross-sector correlations increase during the default but largely disappear after adjusting for increased variance, providing little evidence of stronger shock propagation. Macroeconomic variables explain less than 4% of ASPI forecast-error variance at a 30-day horizon. These findings demonstrate how combining automated regime detection with interpretable time-series models can uncover structural changes hidden by aggregate analysis.

title: Right Numbers, Wrong Story: When LLMs Narrate Financial Changes Beyond Their Inputs
abstract: A financial report drafted by an LLM can state every number correctly but still go beyond its input, adding judgments and causes that no one supplied. We call these additions unsupported framing and find them far more often in LLM drafts than in reports written by proInput facts Revenue +3% Higher prices 10-K filings Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. 10-K writer Revenue surged 3% on higher prices, due to strong demand. LLM Fits the size? Surged: Unusual for 3% In the input? In the input? Strong demand: Not in input Higher prices: Kept fessionals, and attempts to fix them by prompting with how each word is used instead make such judgments more frequent. We therefore propose FrameCheck, a plug-in that sits beFrameCheck Revenue increased 3% on higher prices. No extra model call Judgment word Unsupported cause Supported cause tween the LLM and human review to keep each draft within its input. Specifically, FrameCheck 1) guides the draft with professional examples that report a change of similar magnitude, 2) flags judgments that professionals would not use and causes the input does not give, and 3) removes them by rule, without a model call. In experiments on 17 open LLMs and 3M drafts, FrameCheck removes almost all unsupported framing from drafts and brings the judgment rate close to that of the writers of 10-K filings, the annual reports that US firms file with regulators. Code is available at github.com/seunghan96/framecheck.

title: RoboDyna: A Benchmark for Evaluating Robotic Manipulation under Physically Grounded Dynamics
abstract: Object manipulation in the dynamic real world requires understanding how the environment functions and evolves, and acting accordingly. Existing benchmarks, however, do not adequately address these needs. Physics-oriented benchmarks evaluate predictive fidelity but not closed-loop action. Dynamic robotic manipulation benchmarks often use simplified, physically implausible object motions, limiting evaluation of reasoning and action under realistic dynamics. Evaluation is also typically synchronized, freezing the environment during inference and making computation time irrelevant to task outcomes. To this end, we propose RoboDyna, a benchmark for evaluating the physical understanding and action capabilities of manipulation policies in dynamic scenes. RoboDyna comprises 20 conceptual dynamic tasks spanning five capability categories, with simple objects and minimal scene clutter, under a two-factor difficulty design, and 10 household tasks that instantiate the same capabilities in visually and semantically richer simulated real-world environments. RoboDyna provides 3,500 expert demonstrations, paired synchronous and asynchronous evaluation protocols, metrics for task success and partial completion, and interactive tools for human baseline evaluation. Evaluating vision-language-action models and a world-action model across 5.4K episodes, we find that all policies achieve success rates below 20%, revealing substantial limitations in dynamic manipulation. The world-action model captures simple physical dynamics but struggles with complex interactions, and its prediction fidelity does not consistently align with task success. Sync-async comparisons show that inference latency flips 5-12% of episode outcomes while changing average success rates by at most 3%. Human baselines substantially outperform all policies under matched conditions. Project page: https://robodyna.github.io/robodyna/

title: Unveiling plastic rearrangements in silica glass through persistent homology
abstract: Plastic deformation of amorphous solids proceeds through localised atomic rearrangements. While much effort has been devoted to identifying where such rearrangements occur, how the local structure changes during a rearrangement is less well understood. In silica glass, a rearrangement can involve both distortion within SiO4 tetrahedra and deformation of the network connecting them, but the contributions of these two modes have rarely been quantified. Here, we characterise plastic rearrangements in silica glass under athermal quasistatic shear using persistent homology, which extracts rings from atomic configurations, and link the changes in the persistence diagrams to individual rings in real space. We classify rearrangement events into two types according to bond-coordination changes. By performing inverse analysis, we reveal that Si-centred triangles within tetrahedra, hinge triangles spanning two corner-sharing tetrahedra, and the other (non-hinge) O3 triangles are the dominant sources of topological changes upon rearrangements. The birth-time changes of Si-centred and hinge triangles closely follow the change in the angle opposite the longest edge, whereas that of non-hinge triangles also reflects changes in inter-tetrahedral O--O distances. Further, we clarify that triangles with large birth-time changes are localised in the rearrangement region. Comparing the two types of triangles, we find that the ratio of their birth-time changes is larger for coordination-changing events than for coordination-preserving events, indicating that such events involve relatively more intra-tetrahedral deformation compared with network deformation. These results demonstrate that persistent homology separates intra-tetrahedral and network deformation and quantifies each as a continuous quantity within a single framework.

title: RoboPRO: A Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-Aware Benchmark for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Object manipulation in the real world requires robotic policies to be robust to contextual perturbations and capable of safe planning in cluttered scenes. However, the majority of existing robotics benchmarks contain clean tabletop environments with success rate as the sole metric, leaving two critical deployment questions unanswered: does the policy manipulate safely under real conditions and what does lead to its failure? To this end, we present RoboPRO, a Robotics benchmark for Perturbation-Resilient and Obstacle-aware planning, which unifies various axes of robustness in manipulation. RoboPRO comprises 80 diverse bimanual atomic and compositional tasks across four furnished indoor environments, with a total of 16,000 demonstrations and 5.6K diverse language instructions. The scenes are populated with different numbers of distractors (non-targets), ranging from clean, involving only target objects, to densely populated to impose both visual and operational clutter. Moreover, we propose two safety-aware event metrics to determine unsafe contact between the robot and the environment or distractors. Our evaluation protocol consists of a per-factor analysis of three key perturbations, namely visual, linguistic, and object-level, with different levels of distractor densities. We conduct extensive experiments on RoboPRO using state-of-the-art manipulation policies to analyze the impact of visual and operational clutter, perturbations, and instructional diversity. Our findings indicate clutter can drastically reduce success and increase non-target collision, different perturbations have different effects on the performance, and that training data composition affects overall performance. Our findings highlight the key challenges for manipulation in real-world conditions and motivate future research in this domain. Project page: https://robopro-bench.github.io/RoboPRO/

title: When Perception Collides with Priors: Diagnosing Modal Polarization in Video Understanding Models
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved strong video comprehension, largely benefiting from extensive training on realistic video data. However, when video perception severely conflicts with internal priors or common sense, we identify a critical failure pattern termed Modal Polarization, where models fail to integrate modalities and instead bifurcate into two distinct extremes: Cognitive Inertia, where models rigidly adhere to priors despite contradictory visual evidence, and Perceptual Inertia, where they blindly trust video perception while ignoring logical inconsistencies. To investigate this, we introduce TheaterBench, a benchmark designed to expose Modal Polarization using counter-intuitive scenarios that violate physical laws or common sense - situations rarely encountered in standard training distributions. Extensive experiments reveal that current state-of-the-art (SOTA) models exhibit severe Modal Polarization, and many de-hallucination methods merely rebalance the trade-off between Perceptual and Cognitive Inertia rather than fundamentally resolving the conflict. This work serves as a foundational step for evaluating and enhancing the perceptual-cognitive equilibrium of future video understanding models.

title: Accretor Luminosity as Probe of Orbital Evolution and Magnetic Braking in AM CVn Binaries
abstract: AM CVn binaries are ultracompact systems with orbital periods $P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 70$ min, where a white dwarf accretes from a He-rich semidegenerate donor. At short orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \lesssim 20$ min), rapid accretion reheats the accretor. As the system widens and the mass transfer rate decreases, the accretor follows standard white dwarf cooling at longer orbital periods ($P_{\rm orb} \gtrsim 30$ min). The accretor cooling luminosity then acts as a powerful probe into the orbital evolution of the binary. Recent observations show that the accretor appears brighter (younger) at long orbital periods, compared to models where orbital angular momentum loss is solely set by gravitational wave emission. We show that additional angular momentum loss, which we ascribe to magnetic braking of the donor, can better reproduce observations of accretor luminosity. We test and constrain various proposed magnetic braking formalisms, for the white dwarf, helium star, and evolved cataclysmic variable (CV) channels for AM CVn formation. None of the magnetic braking formalisms in their original form can reproduce the observations, but the widely popular magnetic braking proposed by Rappaport et al. 1983 boosted by a factor $\approx 5$, or the saturated magnetic braking proposed by Matt et al. 2015 boosted by a factor of $\approx 150$, yields satisfactory results. We also find that the CARB formalism, recently applied to the evolved CV channel, is strongly in tension with observations of accretor luminosity. Our models motivate UV spectroscopy observations, and dedicated WD atmosphere models for AM CVn accretors.

title: Calabi-Yau at 50: mathematical discovery in the age of AI
abstract: Using the golden jubilee of Yau's proof of the Calabi conjecture as a spring-board, we discuss how the dataset of Calabi-Yau manifolds brought together mathematicians and physicists since the 1980s, and then further brought in the world of machine-learning and AI since 2017. We give a historical account on the growth of the field of ``AI-assisted mathematics'' in the last decade, and comment on what culminated in 2026 as perhaps the most dramatic year in the history of mathematics since Euclid.

title: Run One, Get Two: Near-Free Streaming Safety Checks for Local LLMs
abstract: Local LLM assistants decode for one user at a time, so decoding is bound by memory bandwidth and leaves compute idle. Streaming safety checks today trade accuracy against cost. A dedicated guard model is accurate but nearly doubles the latency per token, while a hidden-state probe is cheap but less accurate. We present ToRA, an adapter that runs a second model as an extra row in the generator's decode step, sharing its weights and KV cache. Dual-row kernels read each weight once for both rows. On Qwen3-0.6B, ToRA matches or beats a dedicated streaming guard, with higher F1 on 12 of 17 benchmarks. It detects 11.8 points more unsafe responses than the probe at a similar cost, under 4% added latency per token.

title: MixFold: Sub-4-Bit Mixed-Precision LLM Inference via Output-Channel Grouping on Mobile NPUs
abstract: Sub-4-bit quantization allows mobile devices to run larger LLMs, but its memory savings do not always translate into faster decoding on mobile NPUs. Their matrix units support only a few native integer datatypes, and converting unsupported weight formats on the vector unit can erase the gains from fewer bits. Mixed precision faces an additional constraint: each matrix-unit tile uses one datatype. MixFold executes 3-bit and perfectly symmetric 2-bit weights using native integer operations without expanding the weights to wider datatypes during decoding. MixFold then assigns datatypes to output-channel groups aligned with the matrix-unit tiles, enabling finer-than-layer assignment without disrupting matrix-unit execution. We compare MixFold with $\mathtt{llama.cpp}$ Hexagon backend on the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU of a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5. Across the Qwen3 model family, MixFold achieves comparable or higher accuracy than $\mathtt{llama.cpp}$'s sub-4-bit formats at matched bits per weight, while decoding 1.16-1.41 times faster and generating 1.5-4.3 times more tokens per joule.

title: $n$-absorbing ideals of rings of continuous functions I: minimal primes, common zero sets, and non-$z$ ideals
abstract: Let $C(X)$ be the ring of real-valued continuous functions on a Tychonoff space $X$, and for an ideal $I$ let $\K(I)$ be the set of common zeros of its members. We show that a proper $z$-ideal of $C(X)$ is $n$-absorbing if and only if it has at most $n$ minimal primes, if and only if it is an intersection of at most $n$ pairwise incomparable primes, if and only if its filter of zero sets is $n$-absorbing; the algebraic part of this equivalence is valid for radical ideals of any commutative ring. We prove that $|\K(I)|\le n$ for every $n$-absorbing ideal $I$ and that this bound is sharp. We further prove that the $z$-closure of every $n$-absorbing ideal is an $n$-absorbing $z$-ideal and has the same common zero set. Finally, every $n$-absorbing ideal of $C(X)$ is a $z$-ideal if and only if $X$ is a $P$-space. Moreover, for every non-unit $f\in C(X)$, the principal ideal $(f)$ is $n$-absorbing if and only if $\Z(f)$ is clopen and $(f)$ has at most $n$ minimal prime ideals.

title: Affine-Image Propagation for Tight and Scalable Neural Network Verification
abstract: While bound propagation methods are highly effective for certifying neural networks against $\ell_{\infty}$ adversaries, tight and scalable verification for $\ell_{2}$ adversaries remains a significant open challenge. Existing methods incur geometric loss by enclosing preactivation sets in elementwise intervals or axis-aligned ellipsoids, and functional loss by restricting the linear bounds constructed over those domains. Consequently, tight $\ell_{2}$ verification is currently restricted to Lipschitz-regularized networks where these approximations are accurate. In this paper, we introduce affine-image SDP-CROWN, a novel bound propagation method that better approximates preactivation domains using affine-image constraints and jointly optimizes the linear bound to adapt to the resulting domain. To bypass the prohibitive computational cost of dense semidefinite constraints required by the affine-image representation, we replace them with scaled diagonal-dominance conditions, allowing a GPU-accelerated implementation. Our method preserves the bound propagation recursion and can be integrated with branch-and-bound. On five MNIST and CIFAR-10 non-Lipschitz-regularized networks, our method improves verified accuracy over state-of-the-art methods by 17% to 57.5%. With branch-and-bound, these improvements increase to between 27% and 63.5%.

title: Droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction via pulsed electrohydrodynamics
abstract: Numerical simulations based on the phase-field lattice Boltzmann method are employed to investigate droplet formation dynamics in a T-junction microchannel under pulsed electrohydrodynamics. The applied electric field modulates the interfacial morphology, thereby altering the hydrodynamic stress distribution acting on the liquid-liquid interface. Three configurations are examined: no electric field, top-biased electrode, and bottom-biased electrode. The results show that the top-biased electrode promotes rapid transverse migration of the dispersed phase towards the upper wall, thereby accelerating the transition to the channel-blocking stage. By contrast, under the bottom-biased electrode, the dispersed phase first adheres to the lower wall and subsequently deforms upward under the electric force. As a result, the droplet formation dynamics are strongly affected by the spatial distribution of the electric field. The droplet generation process is further divided into a filling stage and a squeezing stage based on theoretical analysis. During the filling stage, the electric force modifies the filling duration but has little influence on the filling flux. During the squeezing stage, the necking rate and breakup time are governed by the pinning of the dispersed-phase contact line on the channel wall. Compared with constant electric forcing, pulsed electric forcing introduces an additional temporal degree of freedom, enabling stage-dependent modulation of interfacial evolution and breakup dynamics. Finally, droplet sequence diagrams and regime maps are presented for different pulse parameters. The results demonstrate that pulsed electrohydrodynamics in a T-junction enables active and programmable control of consecutive droplet generation.

title: Contexture: Runtime Context Eviction for High-Throughput Agent Serving
abstract: LLM agents such as Hermes, OpenClaw, and Codex repeatedly resend growing execution histories, increasing shared GPU key-value (KV) cache demand in high-bandwidth memory (HBM). We show that shared KV capacity limits agent-serving throughput. Existing context-reduction methods lack global cache-state visibility, while runtime KV managers lack tool-execution information. Tracing tokens to their originating tool operations reveals that later operations supersede earlier outputs and associated turns, identifying 64% of recorded final-history tokens as removal candidates. We present Contexture, a harness- and model-agnostic architecture for runtime context eviction. Contexture separates the harness's full conversation history from the model's execution context, reducing subsequent requests' KV demand without modifying harness logic or model execution. It combines tool-execution information with global visibility into shared KV pressure and prefix residency: supersession identifies removal candidates, while runtime state determines when removal justifies sacrificing cached computation. This coordination reduces memory demand and decode KV traffic while limiting re-prefill interference with concurrent decoding, without additional model calls or training. Across two models, two harnesses, and two benchmarks, Contexture improves throughput under SLO by 20-73% over the best of no eviction, harness compaction, AgentDiet, and Continuum, and by 7-63% over observation masking in five of eight configurations, and reduces GPU energy per completed session by up to 11%. It also raises throughput under SLO by 23% over LMCache alone on H100. Live-agent experiments show a mean accuracy improvement of 1.4 percentage points over unloaded no eviction, with a worst-case loss of 3.7 points, while observation masking loses 3-28 points.

title: ViewDreamer: A Robot World Model beyond Fixed Camera Setups
abstract: Video generation models are increasingly important for robot learning, yet most generate each camera view separately or tile all views in a fixed layout. Robot demonstrations, however, are captured by synchronized cameras whose number, placement, and order vary across embodiments. We present ViewDreamer, a single world model that handles variable sets of cameras by disentangling per-view generation from cross-view interaction. Each view follows the generation path of a pretrained single-view model, and views interact only through shared slot tokens. We stabilize multi-view training with a curriculum that gradually increases the number of views. Cross-View Slot Agreement uses visual foundation models to group geometrically and semantically similar regions across views into shared slots. On RoboView-Bench, which covers one to four cameras, ViewDreamer achieves the best generation quality among the models evaluated and improves cross-view consistency over independent per-view generation. These gains carry over to our world-action model (WAM) and action-conditioned world model (AC-WM). Our WAM outperforms the FastWAM-Joint baseline on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboDojo, and on a real Franka robot. Both variants improve out-of-domain generalization to various camera settings and scenes.

title: Persistent Mayer Path Homology and Mayer Path Laplacian
abstract: In topological data analysis, path homology accounts for directed graph while combinatorial Laplacian extends homology groups to spectral theory. However, these approaches are built on a boundary operator with condition $\partial^2=0$. Mayer homology replaces this condition with $N$-nilpotent boundary map $\partial^N=0$. By using the primitive $N$-th root of unity in the boundary operator, it relates each degree $n$ to the degrees $n-q$ and $n+N-q$. This work introduces persistent Mayer path homology. We show that Mayer path homology is functorial for strict digraph maps, which gives persistent Mayer path homology for filtered digraphs, and prove that its barcodes are stable under perturbations. For $N=3$ we derive formulas that reduce $β_0^{3,1}$ and $β_2^{3,2}$ to the classes of vertices identified by squares and the rank of a small matrix indexed by triangles. We also introduce the Mayer path Laplacian and its persistence theory, prove that their kernels recover (persistent) Mayer path homology, show that they distinguish digraphs with the same Mayer path Betti numbers, and prove a stability bound for the eigenvalues of the persistent up-Laplacian. We demonstrate that persistent Mayer path homology detects the formation of feed-forward loops, whose formation is not detected by ordinary path homology. In an application to cucurbit[7]uril, filtered by an interatomic distance normalized by van der Waals radii, Mayer path homology separates contacts that only close cycles from contacts that close feed-forward triangles, and changes at almost four times as many filtration values as path homology after the bonded framework is formed.

title: Privacy Protection in Self-Evolving Personal Agents: Persistent Memory and Cross-Carrier Transfer
abstract: Personal agents carry private experience into later decisions through persistent memory. This thematic survey compares memory admission, maintenance, release, and withdrawal by protected change, observer, and validation setting. Direct evidence in the screened corpus comes from controlled memory workflows. Three worked scenarios follow one private fact through booking, feedback-driven learning, and withdrawal. We show when prompt revision and memory reads compose, when skills inherit a private head's bound, and why reader non-use does not establish cleanup of learned state. Diagnostic experiments measure the utility costs of wider label protection and broad memory deletion, and test how missing lineage obscures descendants.

title: Comparing Visual Motion Patterns for Pedestrian Guidance with Multi-Display Signage: Two Field Studies
abstract: Public multi-display signage (MDS) has the potential to provide subtle pedestrian guidance through visual motion while retaining its conventional role in advertising and information delivery. However, it remains unclear how different visual motion patterns relate to pedestrian spatial distributions and how these relationships vary across deployment settings. We conducted two exploratory field studies in a museum, involving 18,402 pedestrian passages over 25 experimental days, to examine lateral positions in relation to stripe-motion contrast and coverage patterns. In Test Case 1 (TC1), involving predominantly one-way pedestrian flow, partial stripe presentation was associated with more leftward lateral positions than wider-coverage patterns in some comparisons, and lower contrast in full-screen stripes was not associated with a detectable reduction in the observed lateral bias. In Test Case 2 (TC2), conducted in a different spatial configuration permitting bidirectional walking, lateral positions differed by stripe-motion direction during one-way flow, but coverage effects on lateral position and stripe-advertisement differences in lateral position or passing-side choice were not significant. In both test cases, partial stripes received lower self-reported sickness ratings than full-screen stripes. These findings suggest that lower-contrast and reduced-motion-coverage designs hold practical potential for pedestrian guidance, with spatially restricted cues potentially allowing such guidance to coexist with existing advertising while reducing discomfort. At the same time, the contrasting patterns in TC1 and TC2 suggest that spatial context may shape how pedestrians respond to stripe coverage, highlighting the context-dependent suitability of visual-motion-based guidance and the need for further investigation.

title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator
abstract: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
abstract: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $μ$ on $Ω=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $ϕ_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(μ)=\mathbb{E}_{X\simμ}[ϕ_m(X)ϕ_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(μ)c=\mathbb{E}_μ[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $μ$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $μ\mapsto G_m(μ)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.

title: GeoCloak: Defending Against Geolocation Reasoning in Multimodal Language Models via Perceptual Image Editing
abstract: Multimodal large language models can infer sensitive geographic information from ordinary images by combining visual, textual, architectural, and environmental cues. This capability creates a privacy risk: users may reveal fine-grained location information even when explicit metadata such as GPS tags has been removed. We study this problem as geolocation inference in multimodal language models and present GeoCloak, a cue-aware perceptual editing framework for reducing location leakage from shared images. GeoCloak uses an accessible multimodal model as a proxy to identify geolocation-relevant cues, localizes high-impact regions through object grounding, and applies localized semantic edits designed to disrupt downstream geolocation predictions while preserving the overall scene content. Experiments on street-level image datasets show that GeoCloak substantially reduces administrative-level geolocation accuracy across multiple multimodal models, while maintaining automatic perceptual-quality scores closer to those of the original images than pixel-level perturbation baselines. These results suggest that cue-level semantic editing is a promising direction for reasoning-based visual privacy, while also highlighting open challenges in deployment cost, semantic plausibility, and adaptive evaluation.

title: From Letter-of-Credit Requirements to Executable Specifications: Evaluating Verification Accuracy and Completeness
abstract: In letter-of-credit (LC) document examination, a correct final decision does not show that every requirement was examined. We therefore evaluate examination requirement by requirement and make each requirement executable. A language model converts the bill of lading (BL) and commercial invoice (IV) requirements of a credit into atomic conditions and logical structures, and a deterministic verifier retrieves the named evidence and computes each outcome, so every check can be compared with a gold encoding and traced to logged evidence. Because LC records are confidential, our on-premises 9B parser is fine-tuned only on synthetic pairs built from templates and human-reviewed public document values. On 345 real LC cases, final-decision accuracy proves misleading: a constant PASS rule has the highest raw accuracy while examining nothing. Although it never sees a real record during training, the fine-tuned parser detects 93% of the atomic requirements its ontology covers and reconstructs 86% of the covered requirements exactly. It verifies 82% of the evaluable requirements correctly, against 54% for a tool-using agent, and leads the agent on both satisfied requirements and discrepancies. It also completely examines 1.8 times as many cases as few-shot prompting of the same model, while direct prediction and the agent complete none. Executing the gold encodings with the same verifier shows that some of the remaining errors, missed discrepancies included, come from the operators and normalization, which a better parser alone cannot fix. Every rejection comes with a trace of the units and evidence behind it, which suits examiner-in-the-loop review.

title: A simple approach to ends of manifolds and the Freudenthal compactification
abstract: In this note we give an alternative definition of the Freudenthal end-compactification of a non-compact manifold by defining ends to be the filters of open subsets with compact boundaries that have a base of connected subsets. We start by defining these notions and proving that the resulting compactification is equivalent to the Freudenthal compactification. In particular, we explicitly discuss the equivalence between our definitions and those from two different approaches: maximal binding families and inverse limits. After that, we give an example of a non-metrizable manifold, showing how these new definitions make it easier to identify ends and understand the topology of the end-compactification. We also prove a well-known metrization theorem, showing an application of our definition. Finally, we also give an alternative proof of the topological characterization of the Freudenthal compactification.

title: Semi-regular admixed arrays: asymptotic enumeration and when information is additive
abstract: In genomic data analysis, admixed arrays are pairs of matrices recording the local ancestry and the allele at each position of the haplotypes of admixed individuals. We study two-way diploid admixed arrays with $N$ individuals and $P$ loci under two families of constraints: local ancestry tallies, which fix the number of ancestry assignments per individual, and ancestry-specific sums, which fix the allele count per locus and ancestry. These two constraint families correspond to summaries of admixed genetic data investigated in biomedical and genomic applications. In the semi-regular regime, where all tallies and sums are uniform, we use complex martingale techniques to derive asymptotic formulas for the number of doubly constrained arrays as $N$ and $P$ grow with bounded ratio, over the whole feasible region. The leading term is governed by the Shannon entropy of the frequencies of the four possible pairs of entries at a position of the two matrices; on the boundary one or two of them vanish, changing the Gaussian correction. We then ask whether the two families carry information additively, that is, whether an independence heuristic predicts the doubly constrained count up to a bounded factor. Measured against the smallest set of arrays defined by a constraint that each family implies on its own, additivity holds only on a set of measure zero. It includes an edge of the feasible region with correction factor $e^{-1/4}$, extending our earlier result at the symmetric point. Thus, how far the two summaries jointly narrow down individual-level ancestry and genotype configurations cannot generally be predicted from how far each does on its own.

title: Explicit Bases for the Second Integral Homology of Cactus Groups
abstract: In this paper, we determine the second integral homology $H_2(J_n;\mathbb{Z})$ of cactus groups $J_n$. We first use Hopf's formula and Pontryagin products to obtain a smaller generating set of $H_2(J_n;\mathbb{Z})$. We then construct a detecting homomorphism to prove that these generators are linearly independent and hence form an explicit basis.

title: Geo-Force: A Theory of Force Sensing from Object Geometry
abstract: Robots need contact forces to handle delicate objects, but tactile sensors are fragile and hard to integrate, whereas depth sensors, such as RGB-D cameras, are widely available. A virtual touch sensor that keeps the sensing surface of a tactile sensor but replaces its electronics with a touch signal predicted from the target object's geometry, as measured by a depth sensor, could close this gap, yet it is unclear what such a virtual sensor computes and when its output can be trusted. We give a formal answer. We define the Geometric Force as the force on each taxel of a virtual touch sensor, computed in three steps: rendering the surface to be touched as seen from the virtual sensor, predicting the touch signal with a touch map, learned or simulated, and estimating the force from that signal. We prove three properties of the Geometric Force. First, its force vectors only rotate under a change of coordinate frame. Second, it vanishes when the rendered surface does not touch the virtual sensor. Third, it is stable: its error grows at most linearly with the errors of the three steps for Lipschitz maps. The rendering error, in turn, depends on how well the surface is sampled or reconstructed and how accurately the sensor is placed. We then show a fundamental limit: geometry does not reveal the object's stiffness, so no touch map can predict touch exactly for objects of the same shape and different stiffness. Under an elastic contact model, all object-specific knowledge resides in the touch map. From these results, we derive requirements on the depth sensor and the objects, design rules, and the conditions under which such a virtual sensor fails.

title: The upward conformal limit
abstract: For a compact Riemann surface $X$, both the Higgs bundle moduli space and the de Rham moduli space have stratifications by holomorphic Lagrangian fibrations over the space of complex variations of Hodge structure. The $\hbar$-conformal limit gives a biholomorphic identification of the fibers of the two strata over a stable complex variation of Hodge structure. We introduce here the $\hbar$-upward conformal limit, which is the limit at infinity rather than at zero.
