abstract: Pushy random walks are minimal models of transport in deformable media, in which the walker displaces the obstacles it bumps into rather than being blocked by them. On the Bethe lattice, we show that the walkable structure dynamically created by a pushy walker can be generated a priori as an explicit multi-type Galton-Watson tree, so that the walker reduces to a simple random walk on a static random tree, and its escape to infinity coincides with the survival of the underlying branching process. Standard generating-function tools then give direct access to the escape properties of these walks. For the Sokoban walk, which pushes a single obstacle, we recover the known critical density $ρ_c = 1-(z-1)^{-2}$ and the behavior of the escape probability close to $ρ_c$, and derive its small-density asymptotics. For the second-order pushy walk, which can push trains of two obstacles, we establish the conjectured $ρ_c = 1-(z-1)^{-3}$, and compute the escape probability at all densities. Beyond escape, the same framework yields the statistics of the trace of trapped walkers: the distribution of the maximal depth follows from the extinction probabilities, while the distributions of the visited volume and of the number of dead ends are encoded in explicit functional equations for their generating functions, which we invert numerically. All predictions agree with Monte Carlo simulations.

title: Finite Angular Derivative Sets and Almost Isometries of the Hyperbolic Disc
abstract: We prove that a subset $E$ of the unit circle is the set of points at which an analytic self-map of the unit disc has a finite angular derivative if and only if $E$ is an $F_σ$ set. We also prove that, for every countable dense subset $E$ of the unit circle, there exists an almost isometry in the sense of Garnett--Papadimitrakis whose angular derivative is finite precisely on $E$.

title: What Stays in the Picture? From Redundant Instructions to Dependency-Aware Image Editing
abstract: We introduce complex redundant-instruction image editing, where a single request specifies multiple objects, their attributes, and spatial relations while revising or canceling earlier editing requirements. Direct editing can fail to recover this intent, while splitting the request into successive steps can preserve obsolete edits and visual errors. Our key insight is to resolve the revision history into a final editing target that jointly guides planning and verification, so that obsolete requests do not become visual edits. Based on this insight, CRIE-Agent learns to consolidate revisions into object-level final intent and executes the retained objects in reference-first blocks, establishing referenced objects before their dependents. Verification then guides complete re-execution from the source image, with conditional layout hints, preventing visual errors from failed attempts from being carried into subsequent ones. We also construct CRIE-S, a benchmark containing 10,000 complex and redundant editing instructions with exact final intent annotations. Across five image-editing backends on CRIE-S, CRIE-Agent raises complete editing success from 0% under direct editing to 27.5--50.0%.

title: Beyond What They Say: Cue Acknowledgment and Robustness in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Explanations are used to assess whether vision-language models rely on visual evidence or misleading suggestions. A response that explicitly names a cue can still follow it, making disclosure alone an incomplete basis for judging robustness. We ask whether greater cue acknowledgment accompanies greater resistance. We compare matched answers and explanations under helpful, misleading, and conflicting visual and textual cues while holding the underlying question and correct answer fixed. A paired comparison shows that a model can select the endorsed wrong answer more often while acknowledging the cues more often. Reduced silence therefore need not indicate improved resistance. Explanations may also mention a textual suggestion while omitting an accompanying visual cue. Requesting evidence and acknowledgment does not consistently improve resistance in the tested settings. Outcomes vary across models and settings, and these comparisons do not isolate a causal effect of acknowledgment. Evaluations should report cue following and acknowledgment on the same instances, distinguishing visual from textual cues.

title: Evidence sufficiency assessment enables cost-effective review allocation in on-premise clinical AI agents
abstract: On-premise clinical AI agents must auto-accept high-confidence diagnoses, deferring others to clinician review, yet token probabilities and self-reported confidence miss errors, while more reliable five-run consistency incurs fivefold compute. We propose training-free decision-point evidence sufficiency assessment and a three-tier sequential triage protocol. Masking reasoning and diagnosis, the same 4B model scores sufficiency from objective evidence via prior-debiased probabilities over five ordered levels. Calibration freezes a nominal top-50% threshold, selecting single-run, five-run consistency, or full-deferral tiers by whether the one-sided 95% Wilson lower confidence bound of pass rate among accepted cases meets the 95% clinical target line. Across 1,605 MIRA-v2, CDM, VivaBench, and in-hospital liver malignancy primary cohort cases, MIRA-v2 single-run top-50% pass rate reached 98.91%, matching five-run consistency, saving ~80% compute; CDM achieved 96.00% test attainment by escalating to the five-run consistency tier; cross-specialty, missing-imaging, and combined enriched cohorts entered the full-deferral tier, capping calibration false-certification rate at 0.00%-3.50%.

title: Pure Orbitronics: Hall Responses and Torques by Orbital Exchange in Spinless Transition-Metal Dichalcogenides
abstract: Recent studies have identified orbital exchange fields as a novel mechanism for controlling electronic and magnetic phenomena through the orbital degree of freedom. In contrast to conventional spin exchange fields, orbital exchange fields couple directly to orbital angular momentum and can emerge from purely orbital interactions or dynamically through couplings to chiral excitations such as phonons and magnons. Motivated by these developments, we investigate the transport and torque responses generated by orbital exchange fields in two-dimensional materials. Using monolayer H-phase MoS$_2$ as a prototypical transition-metal dichalcogenide, we introduce a Zeeman-like orbital exchange field that breaks time-reversal symmetry in orbital space while leaving the spin degree of freedom inactive. We demonstrate that this perturbation induces a sizable intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity even in the absence of spin magnetism and spin--orbit coupling driven mechanisms. Simultaneously, the orbital Hall response remains robust in the weak-field regime and undergoes substantial reconstruction at larger exchange strengths due to pronounced band modifications. In addition, we show that currents can generate sizable current-induced orbital torques on the orbital magnetization. Our results establish orbital exchange fields as an effective route toward Hall transport and nonequilibrium torque phenomena driven purely by orbital physics, opening new perspectives for orbitronics and orbitally engineered quantum functionalities.

title: Hall effect in electrolyte solutions: Self-consistent Debye-Huckel-Onsager theory
abstract: A self-consistent statistical-mechanical theory of the Hall effect in electrolyte solutions is developed by extending the self-consistent Debye-Huckel-Onsager (SCDHO) framework to crossed electric and magnetic fields. The theory incorporates non-local ionic charge distributions through Slater-type form factors and ion-specific coefficients describing the effective Lorentz response, with experimental input for protons and hydroxide ions. Within the random-phase approximation, the Hall conductivity is expressed as mean-field, correlation, and electrophoretic contributions. Both interaction channels include the Lorentz rotation of the complete electric-field-induced ionic velocity. In the point-charge limit with hydrodynamics suppressed, the relaxation correction agrees with independent odd stochastic density functional theory and the relaxation part of Friedman's classical result. For 22 dilute aqueous electrolytes, the mean absolute relative deviations from measured Hall constants and Hall numbers are about 17 percent. At finite concentrations, the theory predicts a nonmonotonic Hall number for NaBPh4 and sign changes of the electrophoretic correction for NaI and HCl. Correlation effects dominate for HCl and LiOH, whereas the two interaction channels become comparable for KOH and aqueous imidazolium salts. The results clarify how ionic mobilities, effective Hall coefficients, charge distributions, and solvent hydrodynamics determine electrolyte magnetotransport.

title: Structure-Preserving Model Reduction of Metriplectic Systems via Oblique Projections and Block Structure
abstract: Metriplectic systems combine conservative and dissipative dynamics and are characterized by energy conservation and entropy production. The degeneracy conditions underlying these properties are generally not preserved by standard projection-based model order reduction. We develop two structure-preserving reduction strategies. The first enforces degeneracy conditions through oblique projections and combines gradient-preserving and matrix empirical interpolation for hyper-reduction. The second constructs reduced bases adapted to available operator block structure, preserving degeneracy without online oblique corrections. We establish sufficient conditions for preserving the Jacobi identity and derive a priori error estimates. Numerical tests on benchmark problems demonstrate accuracy, thermodynamic consistency, and computational efficiency.

title: Boundary concentration and Pohozaev identity for the fractional p-Laplacian
abstract: We prove a Pohozaev-like identity for bounded weak solutions of the fractional p-Laplace equation with a locally Lipschitz nonlinearity on bounded C^2 domains, provided that s>max{1/2-1/p,0}. We compare the weak equations for the solution and its spatial deformation to show that the first-order contribution of the energy remainder is concentrated at the boundary. The boundary term involves the weighted trace, with a coefficient expressed by an integral of the one-dimensional boundary profile.

title: Real stable multivariate Delannoy polynomials and their Rayleigh differences
abstract: The univariate Delannoy polynomials are known to have only real zeros. We construct a real stable multivariate refinement of these polynomials using weighted lattice paths and give both algebraic and combinatorial proofs of stability. More strongly, we show that every Rayleigh difference of the multivariate Delannoy polynomials is a perfect square and give an explicit factorization.

title: ParaBMG: A Parallel Block Multigrid Framework for Large-Scale Evolving Sparse Systems on Unstructured Meshes
abstract: Solving large-scale, evolving sparse linear systems on unstructured meshes remains the primary performance bottleneck in many GPU-accelerated geometry processing pipelines. Although modern linear solvers like multigrid and multilevel additive Schwarz (MAS) methods offer fast convergence and strong parallelization potential, a unified benchmark and solver design tailored for geometry processing tasks have been lacking. Addressing this gap, we present ParaBMG, a parallel block multigrid preconditioning framework that combines fully parallel geometric hierarchy construction, fast block-Jacobi smoothing, and GPU-optimized operators. We develop CUDA implementations of four standard geometry processing pipelines to form a large-scale benchmark for GPU linear solvers, comprising more than 40K linear systems with up to 6.6M unknowns. Across comparisons in this dataset, ParaBMG achieves speedups of 3.7x-7.7x over strong general-purpose algebraic multigrid baselines, 6x-105x speedups over our custom GPU implementations of the state-of-the-art CPU multigrid solvers for Poisson problems, and 6x-96x speedups over MAS. Compared with open-sourced multigrid baselines, ParaBMG reduces repeated hierarchy construction costs through hierarchy reuse and improves convergence through MAS-inspired block-Jacobi smoothing. Compared with MAS, the complementary coarse corrections reduce iteration counts by an order of magnitude while maintaining low per-iteration costs. It enables three interactive geometry processing applications with order-of-magnitude speedups over their public implementations.

title: AnyBodyCodec: A Shared Native Interface for Body-Model Conversion, Extension, and Humanoid Control
abstract: Parametric body models expose incompatible pose and shape controls, tying humanoid policies to particular input formats. AnyBodyCodec learns a shared representation through native conversion, then reuses it for new body models and control with its core frozen. Encoders map MHR, SMPL-X, and SOMA to aligned slots; native decoders recover target controls. The 1.090M-parameter converter covers nine routes and reaches 16.801 mm input-reference MPJPE across six cross routes: the 2.887M Transformer bank reaches 16.390 mm and its parameter-matched version 18.866 mm. Three measured routes take 7.43-7.67 ms on an RTX 4090. Adding ANNY shows that comparable conversion accuracy can accompany different action consistency under one frozen controller. Under a matched PPO budget, aligned slots support 60.78% full-action success across three formats. Separate 160-hour training reaches 66.10% source-weighted validation success, and the controller is deployed qualitatively on a physical G1 through three visual front ends. Together, these results establish reuse through both native geometric fidelity and downstream policy compatibility.

title: Taking Apart and Putting Together: Tracking Objects Through Physical Transformations
abstract: We introduce Transformation Tracking and Understanding (TTU), extending video object tracking to environments where objects undergo physical assemblies and disassemblies. TTU requires continuously tracking objects through transformations, identifying new entities, maintaining a state graph of their relationships, and assigning semantic labels to transformations. While foundation models (e.g., SAM 2/3) maintain tracklets through appearance changes, they cannot update semantic identities as objects physically evolve. Prior work addresses only disassemblies, relying on expensive searches triggered only when tracking fails. We propose Tracking Instances via Proposals and Overlaps (TIPO), a training-free framework that continuously infers transformations via a generate-evaluate-judge pipeline. TIPO generates split and merge proposals from disjoint mask components, scores them against mask-decoder priors using inner and external overlap, and queries an MLLM on the top proposal for visual verification and semantic labeling. To benchmark TTU, we curate Video Instances, States, and Transformation Annotations (VISTA), a dataset including state graphs with 124 assembly and 132 disassembly events across 50 sequences and over 26,000 frames. TIPO achieves state-of-the-art tracking and state-graph accuracy on VISTA, while operating $6\times$ to $15\times$ faster than prior methods. Project page: https://davidegardenal.github.io/tipo-tracking

title: Adaptive Redescending Regression with $q$-Polynomial Losses
abstract: We introduce a family of smooth $q$-polynomial losses for robust joint regression--scale estimation. The family contains the Cauchy loss at $q=1$ and converges pointwise to the squared loss as $q$ increases. For every finite $q$, its regression score is bounded and redescending, while its scale score is bounded and permits explicit analysis of scale existence. We formulate simultaneous estimation through a surrogate likelihood with a common scale calibration $κ=1/2$ and select $q$ by maximizing the normalized surrogate likelihood over a finite candidate set. We investigate existence, large-sample behaviour, and the robustness implications of the loss family and discuss how optional modification of the scale score, for example by taking $κ=q/2$, can increase the threshold against scale explosion. This breakdown-oriented adjustment is distinct from the baseline estimator and requires its own joint breakdown analysis. An MM-type algorithm provides a practical implementation. Numerical investigations assess the resulting robustness--efficiency trade-off under different tail regimes.

title: Active Learning of Flows from Curve Observations using Gaussian Processes
abstract: The active learning of real control systems requires informative roll-outs of controls. In this paper, we present a local optimization algorithm that finds the trajectory that most reduces uncertainty about the flow of a control system modeled by a Gaussian process. Therefore, we derive an approximation scheme for the posterior kernel of the Gaussian process after observing it on an entire continuous-time trajectory and establish a Pontryagin-type necessary condition for the optimizer. As the flow is unknown, the actual trajectory can deviate from the planned trajectory. We propose a trajectory planner that searches for the most informative control within a maximal allowed deviation horizon instead of a fixed time horizon. We show by trajectory-wise time rescaling that the underlying optimal control problem is equivalent to a fixed end time optimal control problem. Finally, we study both the fixed end time planner and the fixed maximum deviation planner in a numerical example and compare them with benchmarks.

title: Beyond Linear Decodability: Understanding and Improving Instruction Following in World Action Models
abstract: World action models (WAMs) exhibit strong manipulation capabilities yet often fail to follow test-time language instructions. Prior work shows that non-following (NF) WAMs encode information about the instructed target, but this information does not control their behavior. By comparing NF WAM with its instruction-following (IF) counterpart, we find that target information is substantially more linearly decodable in IF WAMs, despite being encoded in both. Motivated by this observation, we introduce linear decodability supervision (LDS), a simple yet effective auxiliary training objective that promotes the linear decodability of the instructed target information. On LIBERO-CF, InternW0-$Δ$ with LDS achieves a success rate of 74.6% and a grounding rate of 89.2%, surpassing the strongest baseline by 26.8 and 42.9 percentage points, respectively. The effectiveness of LDS challenges the prevailing interpretation that encoded target information does not contribute to WAMs' behavior. To reconcile this apparent contradiction, we propose a prior-instruction competition mechanism, which explains NF and IF behavior as arising from the dominance of prior and instruction signals, respectively. We provide causal evidence for this mechanism by evaluating two training-free interventions derived from it. We reinterpret LDS through this mechanism, showing that it acts as a form of instruction signal enhancement. Finally, more comprehensive evaluations across diverse manipulation tasks and visual domains demonstrate the consistent effectiveness of LDS.

title: Quantum computing for gearing down complex many-fermion problems
abstract: Quantum computing unlocks exciting opportunities to extend first-principles calculations of quantum many-body systems beyond classical computing limits. Despite advances in algorithms and proof-of-principle experiments, large-scale {\it ab initio} calculations on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices remain challenging. We introduce a quantum-classical framework that identifies compact single-particle bases to bring otherwise intractable many-fermion problems within classical reach while preserving an accurate ground-state description. We develop an efficient adaptive search scheme driven by simulated annealing that jointly optimizes natural-orbital-guided transformations and active-space selections. A quantum-assisted ground-state estimator provides search guidance using low-depth circuits and relaxed accuracy requirements, making the framework promising for NISQ devices. We demonstrate the framework's applicability for the nuclear structure of the oxygen isotopes. Our framework opens a new route to tackling complex {\it ab initio} many-fermion problems across disciplines through quantum-assisted basis reduction.

title: Improved perimeter bounds for Hausdorff approximation by convex polygons
abstract: We investigate how closely a convex polygon with at most n vertices can approximate a plane convex body of given perimeter. For free approximation in the Euclidean Hausdorff metric we improve Popov's bound for every $n \geq 3$. We also improve his inscribed bound for every $n \geq 3$ and his circumscribed bound for $n = 3$. The common step is to join successive boundary contacts of the body and estimate the perimeter lost in passing to their convex hull.

title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
abstract: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of every word, and a statistical model that takes into account that the spread of difficulty between requests itself depends on the load restores, for each component, the laws of its dependence on every kind of load. These laws make up the passport of a model. The paper presents the method of the separation, the principles of constructing the laws and the passports of seven models built by this method; the separation opens the way to studying the fine structure of the behavior of a neural network.

title: Learning effective stochastic predator and prey dynamics across physical and biological systems from limited data
abstract: Constructing an effective low-dimensional stochastic model from sparse observations requires separating deterministic drift from state-dependent fluctuations when the governing interaction law is unknown. We formulate an adaptive neural stochastic differential equation with topology constraints (TC-AdaNSDE) for two-variable predator--prey dynamics. To regularize the inverse problem when data are scarce, the model combines flexible drift and correlated diffusion fields with density-adaptive local Kramers--Moyal moment estimates and soft phase-space constraints reflecting boundary saddle behavior near extinction and local stability near coexistence. Using a known nonlinear stochastic system, we first show that short-time trajectory error cannot assess diffusion accuracy on its own and must be paired with distributional measures of one-step transitions and long-time phase-space occupancy. We then apply this framework to macroscopic turbulence and zonal flow energies reduced from Hasegawa--Wakatani plasma simulations and to short ecological time series. In the sparse-data regime, TC-AdaNSDE reproduces both short-horizon evolution and long-time invariant energy distributions where deterministic reductions collapse and unconstrained stochastic fits diverge, while recovering physically interpretable drift and fluctuation fields across both physical and biological systems.

title: How many states does an exact relaxation model need? Sharp state complexity and geometric obstructions for reversible chains
abstract: How many states does a reversible Markov model need to reproduce two prescribed relaxation modes exactly? We maximize the smaller of the two stationary coordinate variances over all finite reversible chains whose states lie in a given convex region and whose coordinates relax at rates $1$ and $ρ$. Detailed balance turns this into the equilibrium of a tension-only cable network whose loads depend on the stationary masses. For the moment curve of the Wright-Fisher diffusion no finite chain is optimal: maximizing sequences converge to a unique beta law, and the best deficit with $N$ states is of order $N^{-2}$. We find the exact leading constant for states on the curve and for states in its convex hull, together with the optimal cube-root density of states. The hull constant is the curve constant times $c/(1+c)$, $c=(ρ-2)/ρ$; at $ρ=5/2$ the hull needs $\sqrt{6}$ times fewer states, although the limiting law is the same. For $ρ>8/3$ any upward enlargement of the hull lowers the constant again. All lower bounds hold for arbitrary transition graphs. At every fixed number of states an optimizer exists. On a seven-gon the smallest optimal chain jumps from three to four states while the optimal value stays constant, and a family of polygons forces the state count to grow linearly with the number of sides. Monotone vector fields give exact upper certificates, which solve an asymmetric quadrilateral at all rates and 381 polygon-rate instances in exact arithmetic. We formulate a finite-realizability problem and a finite-dictionary conjecture for polygons, and derive state budgets and exclusion tests for finite kinetic models.

title: BladeR: Scalable, Shape-Guided 3D Reconstruction of Wind Turbine Blades from UAV Imagery
abstract: The structural integrity of wind turbine blades is critical for safe, efficient energy production. Accurate 3D reconstruction allows precise localization and quantification of wear and early damage detection. While drone-based inspections are standard, their high-resolution imagery poses challenges such as weak texture, lighting variability, and high computational cost. We present BladeR, a scalable pipeline for high-quality 3D reconstruction from inspection imagery. A hierarchical sparse reconstruction strategy leverages GPS/IMU data and blade shape priors to guide advanced keypoint matchers on full-resolution images. For dense reconstruction, a tiled Gaussian Splatting framework processes 45 MP images at native resolution, isolates the blade from background, and adaptively enhances detail recovery along the leading edge. Validation against commercial and open-source baselines shows significant improvements in model completeness and detail.

title: Structure-preserving compression of Matrix Product States
abstract: Matrix product state time evolution relies on compression to control the growth of bond dimensions, but compression can break the conservation laws of the equation being solved. A truncation is not the flow of a Hermitian generator, so even a small truncation error can violate exact algebraic identities of the Schrödinger equation. For any matrix product state integrator that leaves the state in canonical form with an orthogonality center, a scalar correction restores an admissible global invariant after compression whenever the resulting scalar quadratic constraint equation admits a real root, without enlarging any bond dimension. Rank-preserving recovery searches other canonical centers when that correction fails. The geometry of the low-rank manifold provides sufficient conditions for conservation by the fixed-rank projected flow and bounds what corrections within a frozen center frame can achieve. Numerical experiments demonstrate that recovery can be required even along accurate truncated trajectories.

title: Obliquity of Mercury with a fluid core and a deformable mantle
abstract: In anticipation of BepiColombo's orbital insertion in 2026, this study revisits the rotation of Mercury, modelling it with a fluid core and a deformable mantle. For this well-established physical model, we provide an analytical solution based on a novel Lagrangian formalism. Our approach enables a comprehensive 3D solution for the mantle's orientation, including the phase in longitude at the perihelion. The model incorporates dissipative torques from core-mantle boundary friction and tidal deformations, conservative pressure torques, and the effect of the planet's apsidal precession. We validate the equilibrium positions obtained numerically in previous studies, but identify discrepancies in earlier analytical works. These inconsistencies overestimated the out-of-Cassini-plane offset induced by tidal deformation by a factor of 100. Additionally, we explore the parameter space to determine where the spin axis deviates most from the Cassini plane and identify a region exhibiting bifurcation in the spin axis equilibrium position. This region cannot be adequately analysed using a model linearised with respect to the obliquity angle.

title: Detecting Word-Substitution Poisoning of a RAG Knowledge Base with Relative Entropy and Runtime Verification
abstract: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers questions using passages it retrieves from a knowledge base, so users must trust that knowledge base. We study an attacker who quietly edits existing passages by swapping words for synonyms (PWWS, TextFooler) in a cybersecurity RAG system built from MITRE ATT&CK and CAPEC. Using a reviewed 44-question benchmark, repeated paired runs and a control corpus in which only the layout changes, we find that poisoning lowers judged answer correctness from 0.714 to 0.555. The damage comes mostly from lost evidence and refusals, not from false statements. To find the edited passages, we use relative entropy. Comparing a whole passage with normal text is a weak signal. Still, one term of the relative entropy, the log-ratio between a word and its most probable synonym, works well: with a small language model as the reference, it reaches an AUROC of 0.95 and stays near chance on the control. Used as a retrieval filter, it halves how often edited text reaches the generator, and an attacker who must keep each passage as probable under the language model fails on all 57 sections it tries. Filtering does not restore correctness, because the edited passage is usually the one that held the answer. We therefore add a runtime monitor that checks each answer against trusted MITRE STIX data and remembers the passages it rejects. On its own, it reduces exposure to edited text from 0.41 to 0.26; when it may add the trusted MITRE entry as a source, correctness rises to 0.786. We report the costs and failure cases of every defence alongside its gains.

title: Neural variational Skyrmions as a topological benchmark: emergent symmetry, precision energies and KAN--MLP comparison
abstract: We propose the three-dimensional Skyrme model as a topological benchmark for neural variational methods and construct fully three-dimensional Skyrmions with baryon number $B=1,\ldots,4$ without imposing a symmetry ansatz, with high precision. For $B=2,3,4$, the relaxation of these Skyrmions starts from $B$ unit-charge lumps with random positions and orientations, which carry no symmetry information. The known toroidal, tetrahedral, and cubic Skyrmions nevertheless emerge spontaneously. The resulting variational energies for $B=1,\ldots,4$ lie slightly below the published reference values. The neural method highlights the high accuracy for retaining the topological charge, differing from $B$ by at most $10^{-6}$ in the highest-precision solutions. Our numerical method goes through physical constraint tests such as the Derrick virial relation and the Faddeev--Bogomolny bound, together with evaluation / verification through independent quadratures and resolution sweeps. We then compare Kolmogorov--Arnold networks (KANs) with multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) in more than a thousand training runs, both with and without a rational-map ansatz. With default settings, KANs appear markedly superior, but most of the gap disappears once the MLP activation function and learning rate are tuned. KANs remain more parameter-efficient and more robust at fixed epoch budget, while MLPs with the tuned activation function perform at least as well at fixed wall-clock time. We also argue that continuous gradient descent cannot smoothly change the topological sector of our neural field, clarifying the origin of topological freezing observed in our neural variational solvers. Our results on the neural methods applied to Skyrmions pave a research ground for AI-agentic benchmarks for classical topological solitons, toward AI-assisted soliton physics.

title: Projector Time Map Calibration for Event-based Structured Light
abstract: Existing event-based structured light obtains a dense projector-camera correspondence from the timestamp of an event. It assumes that the projector scans a parallel raster and that the sensor timestamps each pixel independently, and we show that neither assumption holds. We obtain the correspondence from a temporal code that identifies the projector pixel directly and therefore needs no prior calibration, we calibrate the projector time map from the same recording, and we recover the geometry of the system and the offsets between its clocks by a spatio-temporal self-calibration in a preamble of a few seconds that needs no reference object and no second camera.

title: Explicit construction of the normal cone at every nonlocal extreme behaviour of $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$ and device-independent applications
abstract: The set of quantum correlations $\mathcal{Q}_{2222}$, in the simplest Bell scenario with two parties performing two binary measurements each, is an object of fundamental interest both in quantum foundations and for device-independent applications. A nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this set can maximize many different Bell expressions, yet these expressions are not all equally useful in a practical experiment. Here, firstly, we give an explicit characterization of every Bell expression maximized by any given nonlocal extremal quantum behaviour in this Bell scenario. This determines the full normal cone at every such behaviour and makes it possible to optimize over all Bell tests with the same ideal behavior. We then derive an exact variational formula for the quantum bound of an arbitrary Bell expression in this scenario. As an example illustrating the construction, we derive the normal cone for a family of extremal quantum behaviours of importance in device-independent randomness certification, from Phys. Rev. Lett. 129, 150403, 2022. Finally, we explore the consequences of this characterization for device-independent randomness generation in practical experiments. Specifically, for any given detection efficiency $η\in [0.75,0.98]$, we construct Bell tests and two-qubit experiments that certify more single-round min-entropy from one Bell score than any CHSH score can certify with the same detector efficiency, even when the quantum devices used for the CHSH test are optimized. The results provide a systematic way to choose Bell tests for a desired quantum behaviour and to improve their performance for device-independent applications under experimental imperfections.

title: Claw-free difference graphs of finite groups
abstract: Let $\D(G)$ be the difference graph of a finite group $G$: the graph on the non-isolated vertices of $\PE(G)-\Pg(G)$, where $x\sim_{\D} y$ if and only if $\gen{x,y}$ is cyclic and neither of $x,y$ lies in the cyclic group generated by the other. A claw is the graph $K_{1,3}$ and a graph is claw-free if it has no induced claw. We prove that for every finite group $G$, $\D(G)$ is claw-free if and only if it is a disjoint union of copies of the path $P_3$, if and only if the element orders of $G$ are prime powers or $6$, every element of order $3$ has at most one involution in its centralizer, and every involution has at most one subgroup of order $3$ in its centralizer (equivalently: $C_G(a)$ has a normal Sylow $2$-subgroup of order at most $2$ for every $a$ of order $3$, and $C_G(u)$ a normal Sylow $3$-subgroup of order at most $3$ for every involution $u$). Consequences: a nilpotent group that is not a $p$-group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if $G\cong C_6$; $\D(\Sym_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 5$; $\D(\Alt_n)$ is claw-free if and only if $n\le 6$; a non-abelian simple group has claw-free $\D$ if and only if it is EPPO or $\PSL_2(11)$ or $\PSL_2(13)$, proved family by family (this uses the classification of finite simple groups). For soluble groups we obtain a complete classification: the non-EPPO soluble groups with claw-free $\D$ are $C_6$, $D_{12}$, $C_3\rtimes C_4$ and the Frobenius groups $N\rtimes K$ with $N$ an abelian $r$-group, $r\ge 5$, and $K\cong C_6$ or $C_3\rtimes C_4$. For every group with claw-free non-empty $\D$ we show $|O_2(G)|\le 2$ and $|O_3(G)|\le 3$, and we give non-soluble examples ($\Sym_5$, $\PGL_2(7)$, $\PSL_2(11)$, $\PSL_2(13)$). We also prove that the full enhanced power graph is claw-free only for cyclic groups and clarify the relations between claw-freeness of $\D(G)$, $\Pg(G)$ and $\PE(G)$.

title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.

title: Linear Quadratic Control With Event-Based Control Actions: Performance Beyond Periodic Control
abstract: This paper investigates linear quadratic (LQ) control for discrete-time stochastic systems to balance control performance and actuation rate. In our framework, the control input is sparse in time, and the actuation timings are determined in an event-based manner. We examine two types of problems: A sparsity-promoting regularization problem and a hard-constraint problem with a prescribed average actuation rate. Due to the combinatorial nature of these problems, finding optimal solutions is generally hard. Inspired by rollout algorithms in the context of dynamic programming, we develop a rollout-based approach to obtain tractable suboptimal policies. We show closed-loop stability and establish theoretical performance guarantees with respect to classical periodic control. Moreover, under additional conditions, we quantify the performance improvement over periodic control and prove that this improvement is strictly positive. A numerical example demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed method in balancing control performance and actuation rate.

title: Reset Quantum Channels
abstract: We introduce Reset Quantum Channels (RQCs), a class of quantum channels acting on a Hilbert space structured as a direct sum of an arbitrary number of subspaces. Within each subspace, the state evolves unitarily; across subspaces, it is transferred by measure-and-prepare resets along given states. In this general setting, we show that the determination of their invariant states reduces to a stochastic eigenvalue problem, whose size is set by the number of reset states rather than by the dimension of the Hilbert space, and we discuss the uniqueness of these states. We further address the primitivity and the spectrum of these channels, which we compute explicitly when the reset states commute with the unitary evolutions. Applications include a small system coupled to several thermal reservoirs. We also consider random unitary evolutions and analyze the averages of the invariant states in this setup. Finally, we show that a suitable continuous-time limit yields Lindblad generators of reset type on the algebra of block-diagonal operators.

title: Beyond Future Views: Exploring Future-State World Models for Vision-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-Language Navigation(VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through unseen 3D environments, where the target spaces often lie beyond the current observation. Navigation world models address this challenge by predicting future views either as pixels or latent representations, providing valuable look-ahead information for action decision. Both paradigms define the future primarily through what the agent may observe, raising a fundamental question: is predicting future views the ultimate form to represent the future for VLN? Cognitive studies show that the human hippocampus prospectively represents both future goals and intervening locations along planned routes. Inspired by this predictive-map view, we organize the navigation-relevant future around goal-directed spatial states and route structure. We instantiate this perspective with two complementary abstractions: a short-horizon waypoint that specifies the next local state to reach, and a mid-horizon corridor that captures the spatial support of the upcoming route. Based on this design, we propose FS-Nav, a future-state world modeling framework that predicts waypoint-corridor states from spatial memory and language instructions, and communicates them to a VLM navigator through top-down and first-person interfaces. Experiments on standard VLN benchmarks demonstrate that FS-Nav achieves state-of-the-art performance. This highlights navigation-relevant future-state modeling as a promising direction for representing the future in VLN.

title: Predicting HCN, HCO$^{+}$, multi-transition CO, and dust emission of star-forming galaxies
abstract: We present an analytical model of a turbulent clumpy star-forming disk that reproduces the spatially resolved observations for 6 molecular lines and 3 continuum bands at 250-700~GHz in the central 30~pc of the Circinus Galaxy. Using the properties of the stellar disk as input, and when matched to the line and continuum emission, the model yields the Toomre $Q$ parameter, mass accretion rate $\dot{M}$, metallicity $Z$, and cosmic ray ionization rate $ζ_{CR}$. These in turn are used to infer the gas properties (surface density, velocity dispersion, and radial velocity) as well as the star formation rate. Our main findings from the model include a low CO-to-H$_2$ conversion factor that varies with radius in the range $α_{\rm CO}=0.5$--1.5 $M_{\odot}$pc$^{-2}/({\rm K\,km\,s}^{-1})$, close to the canonical value for such environments. It shows that CO(3-2) is a poor tracer of the gas mass surface density $Σ_{{\rm H}_2}$ on these small scales, which is better represented by molecules such as HCO$^+$(3-2) with higher critical density. The steep relation between $Σ_{{\rm H}_2}$ and star formation rate surface density $\dotΣ_*$ is typical of compact starburst systems, and the star formation rate (10~$M_{\odot}$kpc$^{-2}$yr$^{-1}$ averaged over the disk) is high enough to drive a wind. Despite this, and in contrast to typical large scale galactic disks, the energy injection rate into the ISM is dominated by gas inflow through the disk rather than the supernova rate. As such, the decreasing inflow rate at smaller radii could be caused by a wind, or indicate a recent increase of the mass inflow from larger scales. We suggest that such variations in the inflow rate could be associated with the nested spiral structures which have been observed in Circinus.

title: Ultrafast imaging of ring currents in atoms and condensed matter by electron scattering
abstract: Ring currents are well known to generate magnetic fields. Despite the rich phenomena and detection of the ring current, an experimental reconstruction of the ring current at the atomic scale is still unsolved. In this work, we propose a method of resolving the ring current in a sample at the atomic scale by ultrafast electron diffraction. Inspired by the Rosenbluth formula, we study the electron diffraction of a sample with a ring current and separate the scattering cross sections into three kinds of response functions, which stand for the electric part, the magnetic part and the cross term, respectively. The ring current in the sample can be reconstructed from measuring the response function in different scattering configurations. Also, following the Rosenbluth formula, we propose that the response functions can be measured by fitting over fixed momentum transfer with different incident energy and relative direction, which is similar to the $ψ$-scan in crystal diffraction. With high-precision ultrafast electron diffraction, the magnetic part will be resolved despite being much weaker than the electric part. We simulate three examples with ring currents -- an ideal hydrogen atom, a circularly polarized helium atom ensemble, and a lithium crystal. Our model offers a promising way to resolve the current structure at the atomic scale.

title: ORBIT: Offset-based Activation Steering for Cross-lingual Multimodal Fact Verification
abstract: Multimodal fact verification faces a fundamental accessibility bottleneck: while large proprietary models exhibit cross-lingual robustness, small vision-language models suffer a severe, disproportionate accuracy collapse on low-resource languages. Closing this gap traditionally requires prohibitive scale or extensive language-specific fine-tuning. In this work, we propose Offset Recovery via Bilingual Inference-time Technique (ORBIT), an algorithmic intervention that mitigates this collapse at inference time. ORBIT estimates span-specific offset vectors from parallel claim-evidence instances and applies them to claim and evidence representations, targeting the cross-lingual degradation induced by low-resource evidence. Experiments across 81 configurations reveal that ORBIT substantially recovers both accuracy and F1-score in low-resource settings, exposes calibration offset norms as a diagnostic proxy, and outperforms translation-based and steering baselines.

title: One-Step Self-Assembling Lipopolymer Coatings Enable Direct Longitudinal Biosensing in Native Biological Matrices
abstract: Sample-driven cross-reactivity remains a fundamental bottleneck for sensitive and selective biosensing in complex biological environments, particularly in microfluidic systems where high surface-to-volumes ratios amplify non-specific interactions. Here, we address this challenge with a one-step, biomimetic surface functionalization strategy based on engineered lipid-based nanocarriers that self-assemble within minutes into immunoassay-ready, antifouling interfaces that couple pegylated-lipid passivation with biorthogonal, site-specific probe conjugation. This approach enables rapid, tuneable, and reproducible surface functionalization, which suppresses sample-specific cross-reactivity even in undiluted serum, and supports direct, label-free digital biosensing assays directly in native biological environments. When integrated into an optofluidic platform combining digital in-line holography and microfluidics, this approach allows time-resolved quantification of tetraspanin-positive extracellular vesicle secretion dynamics from two-dimensional and three-dimensional lung cancer cell models using 50 μL of sample within 10 min, without isolation or purification. Because the presented surface functionalization proceeds via self-assembly rather than covalent surface modification, this one-step modular-approach is intrinsically decoupled from device fabrication and applies to both glass and PDMS, coating the entire microfluidic channel, thereby establishing a general route for integrating biomimetic nanostructures into robust, high-performance immunoassays, advancing biosensing beyond end-point measurements, and towards rapid and continuous real-time monitoring.

title: ADEPT: Adaptive Monocular Depth Estimation via Model-In-The-Loop Photometric Tuning with Capture Risk Prediction
abstract: Exposure and gain determine the visual evidence available to monocular depth estimation (MDE), particularly when robot motion creates a tradeoff between light collection and motion blur. We present ADEPT, a framework that adapts these settings using learned feedback from a frozen depth model. During training, ground-truth depth identifies the lowest-error reference within a group of physically evaluated camera settings. A compact predictor learns reference-relative disagreement (RRD) between each candidate's depth prediction and the reference prediction using regression and ranking losses. At deployment, it scores observed captures using frozen-model features and camera, motion, and illumination context, without ground truth or reference images. A contextual Gaussian-process controller uses recent scores to select subsequent exposure and gain settings under motion and photometric constraints. We evaluate offline camera selection with relative and metric Depth Anything v2 and demonstrate online control with the affine-invariant variant on a mobile robot. Across nine equally weighted scene-illumination conditions, ADEPT reduces mean scale-and-shift-aligned $\mathrm{Abs}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ by 14.6% relative to built-in auto-exposure and by 10.0% relative to the best-performing evaluated prior controller.

title: Jagged Robustness: Uneven Safety Transfer and Emerging Vulnerabilities under LLM Quantization
abstract: Quantization enables efficient inference in language models through model parameter compression. This work audits the impact of quantization on capability and safety domains including model safeguards, instruction-following, ethics and bias. Through benchmarks, we find that model safeguards and bias can degrade under quantization, while other capabilities such as truthfulness remain more stable in Qwen3-4B. We define this uneven transfer of LLM capabilities under quantization as Jagged Robustness. We find multiple factors driving Jagged Robustness: task complexity, evaluation method and generation coherence. Moreover, we verify the degradation of model safeguards by observing increased compliance with unsafe requests under quantization, and demonstrate universal adversarial suffix attacks that are benign for the full model but jailbreak quantized models. The findings indicate that it is risky to assume that the performance and robustness can transfer evenly across different capability domains from full models to quantized models.

title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

title: Cleave: Severing Guardrails and Auditing Spectral Coupling in Open-Weight LLMs
abstract: Open-weight Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely downloaded for their strong coding and reasoning capabilities and deployed locally beyond the provider's control. To prevent misuse, developers embed safety guardrails into these models before release. However, we find that these guardrails rely on the residual writing weights to trigger refusals. Based on this insight, we propose Cleave, a training-free attack that directly edits these weights to remove safety restrictions while preserving general capabilities. With Cleave, malicious users can either remove all guardrails or selectively lift only cybersecurity restrictions. Because this selective removal retains up to a 99% refusal rate on other harmful requests and avoids weight rank collapse, it evades both behavioral spot-checks and static weight audits. Across five open-weight LLMs from 7B to 320B parameters, Cleave achieves up to a 67.97% attack success rate on seven safety benchmarks, substantially outperforming existing white-box baselines. On 356 cybersecurity tasks and 15 live vulnerable services, it further boosts executable exploit generation by up to 24.0 times and compromises up to 66.7% of the targets. To counter this threat, we propose a dual-stage defense that combines pre-release subspace diagnostics with post-release weight-coupling audits, achieving 100% detection recall at a 1% false-positive rate.

title: Neurodegenerative Differential Diagnosis with Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning
abstract: Accurate differential diagnosis of neurodegenerative disorders remains challenging due to overlapping clinical manifestations and heterogeneous, often incomplete multimodal observations. Existing multimodal models can integrate imaging and clinical measurements but often overlook disease-specific evidence patterns and pairwise relations among competing diagnoses. We therefore propose Knowledge-enhanced Structural Reasoning (KnowSR), which aligns multimodal patient representations with a literature-grounded knowledge bank of disease prototypes, signed evidence directions, and pairwise diagnostic relations. Specifically, in KnowSR, patient-specific knowledge alignment and target-aware pooling inject structured disease evidence, while anchored relational reasoning reconciles pairwise diagnostic margins over a sparse differential graph, thereby collectively enhancing differential diagnostic capability. Across extensive experiments, KnowSR consistently outperforms 19 baselines on patient-level six-class diagnosis under patient-disjoint five-fold evaluation. This shows that grounding patient evidence in structured medical knowledge enables more effective differential diagnosis than naive multimodal fusion alone.

title: A Negative-U Double Quantum Dot in a LaAlO3/SrTiO3 Membrane on Silicon
abstract: The development of freestanding oxide membranes creates new opportunities to integrate oxide functionalities with silicon technology. A central question is whether local gates can control the correlated electronic states of transferred membranes at the scale required for hybrid mesoscopic quantum devices. Here, we demonstrate local electrostatic control of freestanding LaAlO3/SrTiO3 (LAO/STO) membranes transferred onto silicon. In a dual-gated constriction in the interfacial electron system, we observe an oxide-based double quantum dot (DQD) in the regime of attractive on-site interactions (U < 0). Low-temperature transport reveals the characteristic honeycomb charge stability diagram, and spectroscopy identifies a paired-electron ground state at low magnetic fields, with odd-occupancy states becoming accessible above the pairing field. The observed transport spectra are reproduced by simulations within an attractive two site Hubbard model, and we extract the relevant DQD parameters, including intradot and interdot interactions, interdot tunnel coupling, and spin-orbit-assisted tunnel coupling. These findings establish oxide membranes as hosts for DQDs and extend coupled quantum dot systems into the regime of attractive on-site interactions.

title: Non-local ergodic measures in symplectic dynamics
abstract: We consider the direct product of two symplectomorphisms, one of which exhibits a basic set and the other one acts on a compact surface and has a non-degenerate elliptic equilibrium. Under a local domination condition we show that a typical real-analytic perturbation of this system displays a large normally hyperbolic lamination on which the natural invariant measure is ergodic. The proof, which introduces a novel geometric source of semi-local ergodicity, combines tools ranging from KAM theory to geometric measure theory and is robust enough to be of interest in more general configurations.

title: Conductivity of electrolyte solutions: Self-consistent Debye-Hückel-Onsager theory
abstract: This study presents a novel approach to addressing the limitations in understanding the behavior of charged particles in solutions. The approach is based on the development of the Self-Consistent Debye-Hückel-Onsager (SCDHO) theory, which integrates the effects of non-local charge distributions using a Slater-type charge form factor model. This results in a modified Coulomb potential at short distances, unlike traditional approaches such as the classical Debye-Hückel-Onsager theory. The proposed method relies on explicit expressions derived from gradients of local chemical potentials rooted in classical Density Functional Theory (DFT) and the Ornstein-Zernike formalism for correlation functions. Our theoretical framework enables the derivation of analytic equations that describe both correlation (aka relaxation) and electrophoretic contributions to total electric conductivity. Within the established theoretical framework, the model of smeared charges with Slater-type charge form factors provides an accurate predictive tool that can be applied to a wide range of ion valences, concentrations, and temperatures, including both aqueous and non-aqueous electrolyte solutions.

title: Lower bounds for mixed moments of modular and Dirichlet $L$-functions
abstract: Let $f$ be a fixed holomorphic Hecke cusp form of level one. For every fixed positive integer $k$, we prove a lower bound of order $q(\log q)^{2k^2}$ for the $2k$-th moment of $L(1/2,f\otimesχ)L(1/2,χ)$ over primitive characters modulo a sufficiently large prime $q$.

title: Space-Efficient Text Indexing for Advanced Counting Queries
abstract: In the classical problem of text indexing, the objective is to preprocess a text $T=T[1..n]$ over an integer alphabet $[0..σ)$ into a data structure that supports efficient pattern matching queries. Given a pattern $P=P[1..m]$, a reporting query lists the set $\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)$ of occurrences of $P$ in $T$, whereas a counting query returns $|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|$. Space-efficient suffix-tree variants use only $\mathcal{O}(n\logσ)$ bits and support reporting queries in $\mathcal{O}(m+|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|\cdot\log_σ^ε n)$ time, where $ε>0$ is an arbitrarily small constant, and counting queries in $\mathcal{O}(m)$ time. Notably, space-efficient indexes for more advanced counting queries have largely resisted achieving the same optimal (or near-optimal) query times when using less than $Θ(n\log n)$ bits. We change this situation by proposing a general framework that supports advanced counting queries, denoted by $ϕ_T(P)$, provided that $ϕ_T$ satisfies two mild conditions: (1) $ϕ_T(P)$ is an integer in $[0..|\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)|]$ that can be computed from $\mathsf{Occ}_T(P)$ via sorting; and (2) $ϕ_T(Q)\geqϕ_T(P)$ for every prefix $Q$ of $P$. We show that our framework supports optimal $\mathcal{O}(m)$-time queries using $\mathcal{O}(n\logσ+n(\log\log n)^2)$ bits or near-optimal $\mathcal{O}(m\log_σ^ε n)$-time queries using $\mathcal{O}(n\logσ)$ bits. As an example, our trade-offs improve upon the classical MAST index for counting non-overlapping occurrences [Apostolico and Preparata, Algorithmica, 1996; Brodal et al., ICALP 2002], which uses $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ bits and supports $\mathcal{O}(m)$-time queries, and the recent compact index for the same problem [Bals et al., ESA 2026], which uses $\mathcal{O}(n\logσ)$ bits and supports $\mathcal{O}(m\log n\log_σ^ε n)$-time queries.

title: Consensus of Consensus: Decentralized Consensus-Based Optimization
abstract: We propose and analyze a decentralized variant of Consensus-Based Optimization (CBO) for the global minimization of continuous, possibly non-convex functions accessible only through a stochastic, possibly biased, zeroth-order oracle with bounded mean-squared error. The agents are split among $N$ units of an undirected communication network. Each unit evolves its swarm of $M$ agents towards a local tracking variable, which follows the network average of the local consensus points through one round of neighbour-to-neighbour communication via a doubly stochastic mixing matrix, without any central coordinator. We show that, under an explicit condition linking the drift and diffusion parameters to $M$, all agents reach consensus almost surely, at an exponential mean-square rate governed by the spectrum of the mixing matrix. Using a finite-agent quantitative Laplace principle, we prove that, for large $α$ and provided some agent visits a neighbourhood of the global minimizer with sufficient probability, the expected mean-squared distance of the swarm from the minimizer falls below any tolerance within an explicit number of iterations, at a rate that deteriorates for poorly connected networks. We verify this hitting assumption for a simplified dynamics. Experiments on benchmarks up to dimension $d=1000$, with stochastic objectives, and on a federated learning task demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

title: No Audio, No Transcripts, No Problem: LLM-based ASR Adaptation Using Only Domain Documents
abstract: Can a speech recognizer be adapted to a new domain with no target audio and no transcripts, using only written documentation? This is the realistic onboarding setting: a new customer hands over raw documentation, not the transcripts that text-only adaptation normally assumes. We turn a domain's documents into adaptation text in two ways, directly as written sentences or rendered by a large language model (LLM) into synthetic spoken dialogs, and feed them to a recently proposed denoising-based text-only adaptation method. We show that, across in-domain, out-of-domain, and cross-domain settings on two corpora, document-only adaptation can match or closely approach real transcriptions; whether written or conversational rendering is best depends on speaking style and the amount of text generated. To our knowledge, this is the first study of document-only adaptation of LLM-based ASR. As no existing corpus pairs audio, transcripts, and documents, we also built and released a document-grounded benchmark.

title: Learned Network Dynamics for Model Predictive Traffic Signal Control under Incidents
abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of urban traffic signals relies on a model of how queues respond to signal decisions, which is hard to specify and calibrate in heterogeneous networks, particularly when incidents change capacities and turning shares. Measurements add a second limitation: the controlled lanes at the stop line are often short, so queues extending upstream of them fall outside lane-level measurements. We propose GNN-MPC, a receding-horizon controller that plans with action-conditioned network dynamics learned by graph neural networks. Phase sequences are coordinated across intersections by approximate best responses, with an acceptance test that keeps the predicted cost no higher than that of the initial plan. In microscopic simulation under non-recurrent incidents, GNN-MPC reduces travel time and increases completed trips relative to all tested controllers, on a homogeneous grid and a heterogeneous 21-intersection network. Controlled comparisons on the heterogeneous network distinguish the roles of observation and prediction. With nearly as many vehicles entering the network, GNN-MPC reduces travel time by 13% relative to MaxPressure with the same upstream measurement, and GNN-MPC without the upstream representation does not reproduce its performance. Under the same traffic measurements, planner and objective, replacing the learned dynamics with calibrated store-and-forward predictors increases travel time by 31-34%. Observing hidden demand and predicting its response to control are thus complementary requirements of network-level predictive control.

title: THRIFTY: Cost-Constrained Reasoning-Data Synthesis for Small Language Models
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for efficient, specialized deployment, and are typically trained on reasoning trajectories distilled from a larger teacher LLM. Generating this synthetic data is a major cost of the pipeline, especially when the teacher is a frontier model. Existing collection methods, however, are largely cost-unaware, or at best spread a fixed sampling budget uniformly across queries. Such allocation ignores the wide variation in problem difficulty and the strategic over- or under-sampling it invites. Thus, we propose THRIFTY, a Thompson-sampling bandit controller that spends a fixed generation-token budget to collect diverse correct reasoning trajectories, casting the task as a bandits-with-knapsacks problem with a novel diversity-aware objective. It tracks each problem's success probability with an online Beta posterior and spends each token where it expects the most new distinct correct solutions. Because repeated solutions add progressively less value, THRIFTY adaptively stops resampling saturated problems, concentrates budget on under-covered ones, and retires the unsolvable at the budget's opportunity cost. On math (AIME, MATH-500) and code (LiveCodeBench) benchmarks, THRIFTY gathers up to 22% more diverse correct trajectories per generation token than both the standard uniform-sampling recipe and the strongest adaptive baseline, with the largest gains in the scarce-budget and hard-problem regimes.

title: Gauging background isometries of the ILST null string
abstract: We present a general gauging of a subalgebra, $\mathfrak h$, of the isometries $\mathfrak g$ of the background geometry for the ILST string (e-Print: hep-th/9307108 [hep-th]). We discuss which of the isometries in $\mathfrak g$ survive the gauging as symmetries. The gauged symmetry does not in general involve transformations of the vector density V. There is thus a corresponding contraction of the algebra of constraints as compared to the flat background and it no longer represent the full Carroll-Weyl algebra. This algebra of constraints is derived and discussed, partly in an appendix. The gauging of isometries sets the stage for a reduction, or quotient construction, leading to a new null string on the space of orbits of the gauge group. We illustrate this by deriving the ILST string in $AdS$ background as a quotient of a model in SO(d,2) background by a SO(d,1) isometry, in group space

title: The Complexity of Fair and Stable Data Exchange
abstract: Data exchange is a fundamental challenge for Web applications such as recommender systems, personalized search, and fraud detection, where combining data across participants can improve predictions. Sustaining such collaboration requires fair returns for contributions and protection against groups leaving for a more beneficial exchange. These requirements are captured by reciprocity, which equates each participant's received utility with its credited contribution to others, and core stability, which rules out any coalition exchanging its own data to make every member strictly better off. Akrami et al. prove that such exchanges exist under broad assumptions, but leave efficient computation open. Two fundamental cases are submodular utilities, capturing diminishing returns from overlapping datasets, and supermodular utilities, capturing complementarities. We settle the approximate computation of reciprocal and core-stable exchanges in both cases, establishing a computational separation under Shapley sharing. For cross-monotone shares, which include Shapley shares under monotone submodular utilities, we give a circulation algorithm that computes an exactly core-stable, $ε$-reciprocal exchange in time poly$(n,1/ε,L)$ given efficient access to approximate shares, where $n$ is the number of participants and $L$ bounds how fast each donor's credit changes with its own contribution. This yields an FPTAS when $L$ is polynomially bounded. In contrast, finding an $ε$-reciprocal, $ε$-core-stable exchange is PPAD-hard for monotone lattice-supermodular utilities, even at inverse-polynomial accuracy, with constant $L$ and exact polynomial-time evaluation of Shapley shares. Thus overlapping information permits efficient fair and stable exchange, while complementarities create a computational barrier even when contribution credits are easy to evaluate.

title: Single-shot holographic gradients for training wavefronts through disorder
abstract: Training optical systems in situ needs the gradient of their loss, yet a camera records only intensity and the medium is never exactly known. We show that one off-axis hologram gives this gradient, an approach we call holographic gradients. Light passes through the medium only forward; the hologram measures the error, and a compact adjoint, fitted to ten probes, is refreshed in seconds during train- ing. Each step costs one modulated pattern. Through a thin diffuser, it focuses light and forms images as well as a measured transmission matrix, without its thousands of patterns. Under controlled drift, refreshing the adjoint recovers a grating to 17.6 dB, against 9.1 dB for a frozen model and 19.5 dB without drift, and training succeeds through a thick diffuser. Trained offline, the reference beam becomes a computing layer that plays a video game. Holographic gradients let optical systems learn while they operate, from imaging through dynamic media to self-correcting processors.

title: Decoupling Exciton Energetics from Wavefunction Geometry in Imide-Based Defect Double Antiperovskites
abstract: The excited-state properties of imide-based defect double antiperovskites AE$_5$AsPn(NH)$_2$ (AE = Ca, Sr; Pn = Sb, Bi) are investigated using spin--orbit-coupled quasiparticle calculations, the model Bethe--Salpeter equation (mBSE), and analytical descriptions of lattice-polarization effects. Across five tetragonal ($P4/mmm$) and monoclinic ($Cm$) structural models, the calculated exciton binding energies range from 140 to 210 meV. Chemical substitution modifies both the binding energies and the hydrogenic estimates of exciton spatial extent. By contrast, the structural distortion from tetragonal $P4/mmm$ ($D_{4h}$) to monoclinic $Cm$ ($C_s$), which removes inversion and fourfold rotational symmetry, produces comparatively modest changes in binding energy but appreciably reshapes the real- and momentum-space exciton distributions. This contrast reveals a partial decoupling between exciton energetics and wavefunction geometry, and identifies a symmetry-associated sensitivity of exciton geometry to structural distortion. The changes are understood to occur together with modifications of local coordination and electronic dispersion, rather than as an isolated effect of symmetry alone. Lattice polarization provides an additional screening channel, reducing the estimated exciton binding energies by approximately 9--16\%. Complementary Fröhlich-polaron calculations yield moderate mass enhancement and model-estimated electron-polaron mobilities of 39--99 cm$^2$ V$^{-1}$ s$^{-1}$, with comparatively modest differences between the two polymorphs. These results highlight the distinct responses of exciton energetics, exciton wavefunction geometry, and carrier transport to chemical and structural modifications.

title: Ultra-diffuse Galaxies in the Kilo-Degree Survey: Globular Cluster Systems in Cluster and Field Environments
abstract: Ultra-diffuse galaxies (UDGs) are extreme low-surface-brightness systems whose formation pathways remain debated. Globular clusters (GCs) can trace their early assembly, but wide-area studies of UDG GC populations remain scarce. We study GC systems of 545 high-quality UDG candidates identified in the Kilo-Degree Survey (KiDS) with UDGnet, using a dedicated GC-detection pipeline. We identify 24 UDGs with $N_{\rm GC} \geq 3$ (14 associated with groups or clusters and 10 in the field), and use the globular cluster luminosity function to estimate their distances and physical sizes. At fixed luminosity or stellar mass, group- and cluster-associated UDGs tend to have higher GC counts and specific frequencies than field UDGs, although the distributions overlap substantially. Most systems with $S_N \gtrsim 40$ reside in groups or clusters, while field UDGs generally occupy the lower part of the distribution. Group- and cluster-associated UDGs also more often lie near the upper envelope of the $N_{\rm GC}$--$M_\star$ relation. Empirical GC--halo mass relations consequently imply higher halo masses at fixed stellar mass and lower stellar-to-halo mass ratios, although this environmental trend is mild. These findings are consistent with efficient early GC formation followed by suppressed or prematurely quenched field-star formation, suggesting that GC-rich UDGs may represent an extension of the dwarf-galaxy population. The environmental trends may reflect differences in early assembly, quenching, infall, and survival histories rather than a sharp field--cluster dichotomy.

title: A Relativistic Newton's Third Law for Binaries in Environments
abstract: We derive the relativistic form of Newton's Third Law governing the interaction between intermediate- and extreme-mass-ratio inspirals and surrounding relativistic matter fields. Working within a two-parameter expansion, we rewrite the evolution of the secondary's orbital elements in a form resembling the integrated forces acting on the environment, avoiding the need to calculate any gravitational perturbations sourced by the dynamical matter content. Using the retarded and advanced Green's functions, we obtain both instantaneous and orbit-averaged laws relating the rate of change of the secondary's orbital energy and angular momentum to that of the matter and the gravitational-wave fluxes at that order. Our results clarify and correct the mixture of ad hoc balance prescriptions currently employed in the literature, providing first-principles forcing functions for the secondary's orbital elements in two ready-to-use forms: a leading-order formulation suitable for fast evaluation with complex relativistic matter simulations, and a first-post-adiabatic formulation of the energy and angular-momentum evolution in environments that are stationary and axisymmetric at leading order.

title: Learning When to Ask: Advisor-Aware Post-Training for SLM Agents
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) are increasingly attractive for cheap, high-throughput agentic deployment, but they remain weak at multi-step reasoning and tool use that long-horizon tasks demand. We study how to post-train an SLM to seek advice from a stronger model and act on that advice itself, following an advisor-executor pattern. Out of the box, this pattern fails across open- and closed-source small-model families: wiring an SLM to an advisor is a harness-design matter that is not enough on its own. A post-training recipe is needed to teach the model when to ask, in a cost-aware fashion, and how to follow advice across steps. Our method, ADAPT (ADvisor-Aware Post-Training), is a multi-stage recipe that instills this behavior, learning entirely from the policy's own rollouts supervised by the environment's outcome, with no learned reward model or human annotation. Across three domains, compared to an untrained harness baseline, ADAPT improves success rate in embodied text reasoning (TextWorld) from 24.5% to 77.3%, code generation (LiveCodeBench) from 21.8% to 56.0%, and deep web search (GAIA) from 17.5% to 49.3%, while querying the advisor sparingly (~1.0-2.1 calls per task). On the two long-horizon domains it closes 70-85% of the gap to an oracle that perfectly times when to ask for advice, and on code generation it exceeds that oracle. The gains persist when the advisor is replaced by one unseen in training, showing that the learned help-seeking policy is robust to a changing advisor rather than tied to the one it was trained with.

title: Silent Arbitration: How Large Language Models Resolve Co-Authoritative Conflicting Instructions
abstract: Large language models increasingly receive high-level instructions about roles, values, interests, and communication style. Such instructions can conflict even when a prompt assigns them equal authority and provides no priority rule. We study co-authoritative persona conflict, in which a single prompt jointly assigns two opposing personas. Across eight conflict types grounded in published source material and five LLMs, we measure conflict acknowledgment, resolution strategy, and directional stance. Models acknowledge incompatibility in 72% of direct checks but explicitly surface it in only 22% of task responses, revealing silent arbitration. Dominance accounts for 45% of dual-persona responses, and 35% of compromise-labeled responses retain directional lean. Prompt framing further changes the visible form of arbitration substantially more than ordinary paraphrase variation. These findings show that evaluating instruction following should assess whether models disclose conflicts, how they resolve them, and which persona their responses favor.

title: Structurally Different, Functionally Persistent: Capability Regions Under Model Optimization
abstract: Large language model (LLM) capabilities have been associated with localized parameter regions, enabling targeted model editing and intervention. However, it remains unclear whether a region identified before model optimization remains an effective intervention target afterward. We evaluate the functional persistence and parameter overlap of coding capability regions across three instruction-tuned models under quantization, pruning, and LoRA-based adaptation. Although re-extracted regions exhibit substantial parameter reorganization, ablating the original region after optimization eliminates or nearly eliminates coding performance in almost all conditions, while magnitude-matched controls preserve performance. Partition analysis further shows that the shared subset of the original and re-extracted regions accounts for most of the observed ablation effect in the majority of conditions.
