These results expose a sharp latency-robustness trade-off: skipping reasoning for sub-second speed leaves fast decision models substantially more vulnerable to deceptive web content.

title: Characterisation of B-type stars in four young Galactic open clusters. II. Photometric variability with TESS and identification of pulsating stars
abstract: Pulsations and binarity are important properties of massive stars and influence their structure and evolution. Young open clusters are ideal laboratories to study massive stars, since they are mostly coeval and chemically homogeneous. We analyse 82 B-type stars in the Galactic open clusters $h$ and $χ$ Persei, NGC 457, NGC 581, and NGC 1960, which have ages between 15 and 30 Myr. We extract light curves using both simple aperture photometry and a point-spread-function-based method that minimises contamination from crowded fields in full-frame images from the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. We successfully extract light curves for 63 stars. The majority have photometric variability caused by pulsations, showing how pulsations are a common property of young B-type stars in clusters. We classify stars into different pulsator types based on their spectral type and frequency spectrum. The most common pulsator class are beta Cephei stars, with 29 stars in total, and we discover pulsation modes in almost all stars with a spectral type of B2 or earlier. All Be stars show pulsations, which supports the consensus of the ubiquity of pulsations in these stars. Finally, we confirm that the majority of early B-type stars are in binary systems, except for two pulsating Be stars and a star with rotational modulation. This indicates that pulsations do not significantly bias the spectroscopic detection of short-period binaries, except for Be stars where the spectroscopic radial velocity variability threshold should be higher than the typical value of 20 km s$^{-1}$.

title: Zeroing in on BSM at Colliders
abstract: Destructive interference between light and heavy dynamics can produce a zero in the amplitude which, for strongly coupled UV completions, lies parametrically below the heavy threshold. We identify under which assumptions this parametrically light zero exists, and when it admits an effective field theory description. We study how absorptive effects and helicity structure affect the existence of the zero and turn it into a dip. When the dip is kinematically accessible, we show how its position, depth, and curvature constrain the UV dynamics. Collider examples illustrate the importance of interference in indirect searches and the information available when the zero is kinematically accessible.

title: Large deviations and conditional laws for a time-integrated logarithm of averaged Gaussian squares
abstract: Systems with identical instantaneous power distributions can have very different probabilities of insufficient service over a fixed interval. We study the lower tail of the time-integrated logarithm of a weighted mean of $d$ independent squared Gaussian paths as $d\to\infty$. A global entropy inequality resolves the nonconvex service constraint, identifies the unique Gaussian minimizer and controls the nonlinear likelihood weight far from that minimizer. Combined with a joint local limit, it yields sharp probabilities at fixed internal thresholds and conditional path laws: a Fredholm determinant enters the leading factor, and tangential Gaussian fluctuations are independent of the exponential service deficit. The approximations extend through moderate deviations to the central scale. For stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck paths, cancellation in the radial likelihood expansion yields relative error $O(d^{-1})$ on compact positive parameter families with proportions and saddles separated from zero. Genuine temporal covariance attenuation by correlation kernels for a type of positive limiting proportion increases the lower-tail rate, yet the finite-sample outage distributions cross near typical service. Thus one-time power distributions alone do not determine reliability.

title: On the Role of Fisher Information, Variance and Asymptotics in Statistical Inference
abstract: Bahadur's \emph{Lectures on the Theory of Estimation} close with a chapter on asymptotics: asymptotic normality of the maximum likelihood estimator, Fisher's bound on its asymptotic variance with Hodges's counterexample, and local asymptotic normality. A companion paper read the earlier lectures with one modification, replacing the point estimator by a generalized estimator---Fisher's continuum of significance tests---assessed by information rather than variance. This paper reads Chapter 8 the same way. At each of its three parts the classical statement is an approximation about a point estimator, while the corresponding statement about the score is exact at every sample size. Superefficiency does not arise, because information is bounded by the Fisher information at every $n$; Hodges's estimator, computed exactly, is fully efficient at the origin and loses information only where its mean square error is worst. The information of a generalized estimator is argued to be Fisher information: the mean rate at which a continuum of tests responds to the parameter, standardized by its variance. The resulting Fisher upper bound differs geometrically, not merely algebraically, from the Cramér--Rao lower bound. The extension is not empty: the $t$-test continuum loses about half an observation's worth of the information in $\bar X$ at every $n$.

title: Exchange rights and vacancy priorities
abstract: Many institutions let incumbents exchange positions while allocating announced vacancies by priority, withdrawing positions released by vacancy recipients. A policy specifies permitted exchanges, vacancy eligibility, and priorities. A strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting exchange rights and vacancy priorities exists precisely for policies without conflict cycles. Restricting protection to first choices does not enlarge this class. We introduce the propose-and-trade rule, which satisfies these properties and selects the applicant-optimal core allocation under every conflict-free policy. We identify when propose-and-trade is the unique strategy-proof, individually rational rule protecting first choices. These axioms characterize deferred acceptance and top trading cycles in their classic settings. Under a policy with a conflict cycle, propose-and-trade is manipulable but protects exchange rights and first-choice claims. Replacing it with any strategy-proof rule makes some applicant worse off at some profile. We show when priority reform alone can eliminate conflict cycles and when eligibility or exchange permissions must change.

title: Proximity and Remoteness in Trees with given Segment Sequence
abstract: The average distance of a vertex $v$ of a connected graph $G$ is the arithmetic mean of the distances from $v$ to all other vertices of $G$. The proximity $π(G)$ and the remoteness $ρ(G)$ of $G$ are the minimum and the maximum of the average distances of the vertices of $G$, respectively. A segment $S$ of a tree is a path-subtree whose terminal vertices are either branching or pendant vertices, and all internal vertices have degree $2$. The segment sequence $(\ell_{S_1}, \ell_{S_2},\ldots,\ell_{S_m})$ of T is the non-increasing sequence of the lengths of all segments of T. In this paper, we characterise trees with a given segment sequence that minimise proximity and those that maximise remoteness. For trees that minimise remoteness, we establish sufficient conditions under which the tree is starlike and conjecture that a remoteness-minimising tree is always either starlike or a ($Δ,2$)-tree. For trees that maximise proximity, we derive a collection of necessary conditions that any tree maximising proximity must satisfy.

title: Learning in Symbiosis: Heterogeneous Federated Learning with ANNs and SNNs
abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), widely regarded as the third generation of neural networks, represent a promising neuromorphic computing paradigm with the potential to reduce the energy footprint of Artificial Intelligence (AI). Their en-ergy efficiency makes SNNs particularly attractive for resource-constrained Edge AI devices, motivating growing research interest in Federated Learning (FL) with SNNs. Despite these advantages, integrating SNNs into existing FL systems remains challenging, as replacing all conventional Artificial Neural Network (ANN) devices with SNN-based alternatives is impractical. Instead, we envision a gradual transition toward neuromorphic Edge AI, where ANN and SNN devices coexist and collaboratively participate in FL. To facilitate this transition, we propose Hybrid Neuromorphic Federated Learning (HNFL), a framework that enables joint training of heterogeneous ANN and SNN devices within an FL environment. Through experiments on CIFAR-10 using both VGG9 and ResNet architectures, we demonstrate the mutual benefits of collaborative ANN-SNN training. Specifically, HNFL achieves an average improvement of 16.85% when incorporating SNN devices into ANN-based FL and 8.02% when incorporating ANN devices into SNN-based FL. Furthermore, HNFL produces sparser spiking activity in the trained SNN models, with reductions of 12.4% for SResNet and 22.4% for SVGG9. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to demonstrate that ANNs and SNNs can coexist and mutually benefit from collaborative training in FL, providing a practical path toward the gradual integration of neuromorphic computing into existing Edge AI systems.

title: Random pullback attractors for evolution equations with nonlocal perturbations and fractional Brownian motion
abstract: We study semilinear evolution equations with time-nonlocal perturbations of \(μ\ge0\) and additive fractional Brownian noise with Hurst parameter \(H\in(1/2,1)\). Under the regularity assumptions and a globally Lipschitz nonlinearity, we establish global existence and uniqueness in the concept of pathwise mild solutions. We overcome the difficult in which the solution family lacks the cocycle property, by shifting the corresponding stochastic Volterra equation on a weighted space, and then the continuous random dynamical system follows. Based on a dissipativity condition, we establish the pullback random asymptotic compactness and the compact random pullback attractor \(\mathcal A_μ\). Finally, we prove that the family of random pullback attractors \(\mathcal A_μ\) is upper semicontinuous at \(μ=0\) almost surely.

title: Linear support bounds for supercuspidal matrix coefficients of p-adic groups
abstract: Let $\mathbf{G}$ be a connected reductive group over a non-archimedean local field $F$ of characteristic zero. For any standard congruence tower $K_{\bullet}=(K_n)$ in $\mathbf{G}(F)$, supercuspidal matrix coefficients between $K_n$-fixed vectors are supported in an adjoint ball of radius $an+b_{K_{\bullet}}$, compact modulo the center, with $a$ depending only on $F$ and $\mathbf{G}$. When $\mathbf{G}(F)$ is non-compact modulo its center, the linear dependence on $n$ is optimal. In algebraic families we obtain a uniform radius $An+Bk+C+\operatorname{val}_{F}(N)$, where $k$ bounds the logarithmic height of the parameter. We deduce a sharp linear bound for the exponent in Bernstein's stabilization theorem. For quasi-split classical groups, we also remove the dyadic level restriction in the limit multiplicity theorem.

title: Embodied-Harness: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Vision-language model (VLM)-based agents offer a promising approach to robotic manipulation, yet remain limited by inadequate memory organization, uncertain failure attribution, and limited reuse of execution experience. We propose Embodied-Harness, a dual-agent framework that improves manipulation by refining the execution harness without updating model parameters. The Actor interacts with the environment through a robot-control interface, while the Reflector converts execution evidence into reusable operational guidance. Hierarchical Memory Architecture maintains short-term execution context and long-term experiential knowledge to support execution and reflection. Evidence-based Experience Reflection grounds failure diagnosis in observed interactions, while Recursive Harness Self-Improvement refines operational guidance across successive attempts. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboSPA, and RMBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Embodied-Harness in generalization under environmental variations, spatial reasoning, long-horizon planning, and memory-dependent manipulation. Our method achieves success rates of 82.4%, 76.7%, and 94.4% on the three benchmarks, respectively. Real-world evaluation further yields an average success rate of 96.7% across three manipulation tasks. These results highlight the potential of Embodied-Harness to improve robotic manipulation through experience-driven harness self-improvement.

title: Dynamics of a spherical ferromagnet on a non-conducting incline in an external magnetic field
abstract: Magnetic particles of various shapes and sizes are used in biomedical applications, robotics, nanomagnetism, electrotechnology, and education. Yet despite years of study, a theoretical description of the rolling motion of a solid magnetic sphere still eludes us. One of the reasons is that coupling magnetic fields with mechanical degrees of freedom creates a highly non-linear motion with non-holonomic constraints, which makes modeling these systems analytically or by simulations non-trivial. The Lagrange-d'Alembertian approach to holonomic systems remains one of the most versatile methods to prove central theorems and solve problems in analytical mechanics and electrodynamics. While non-holonomic systems are not accessible by the original theory, recent developments generalize the principle to certain dissipative systems. Here, we present a successful application of these developments to a simple mechanical system comprising a magnetic solid sphere on an incline within an external magnetic field. Using numerical simulations, we characterized how the system depends on its initial parameters. Furthermore, our findings are in line with recent experiments, demonstrating that even very weak magnetic fields can cause unexpected motion of ferromagnetic objects. The simplicity of this example also makes it a promising candidate for undergraduate physics education where the treatment of non-holonomic variational principles is still widely uncommon.

title: To Own or Not to Own? Endogenous Ownership in Peer-to-Peer Sharing of Private Autonomous Vehicles
abstract: Autonomous driving allows private owners to release their vehicles to an on-demand platform and earn income when they do not need them. This possibility changes vehicle acquisition incentives, as rental income can encourage purchases, while access to shared vehicles can reduce the need for personal ownership. Understanding these competing effects is essential to assessing the ownership implications of private AVs sharing. While existing models of private AV sharing often take ownership as given, in this paper, we develop a stationary equilibrium model in which vehicle ownership and listing decisions determine service availability and operational frictions, which in turn shape individuals' incentives to own and share. Based on the model, we first characterize individual choices by comparing payoffs of being an owner and a non-owner. We then analyze the resulting potential population partitions, establish conditions for the existence of an active sharing market, and categorize them by owner types. The equilibrium is presented by a system of equations and solved through a tailored algorithm. An illustrative numerical study on calibrated U.S. travel and vehicle cost data shows that sharing can either increase or decrease ownership, depending on the balance between purchases encouraged by rental income and ownership displaced by shared vehicles. The balance is shaped by market parameters, including market density, AV cost, and platform operating conditions. Platform pricing and municipal regulation can also influence ownership through their effects on acquisition incentives and the shared service that makes nonownership attractive. These findings highlight the range of possible ownership outcomes in private AV sharing markets, and the model provides a framework for evaluating how market conditions, platform decisions, and regulation shape these outcomes.

title: Reconstructing risk preferences from data
abstract: We consider the problem of reconstructing risk preferences from data. Specifically, for a finite dataset consisting of contingent claims and their evaluations, we aim at reconstructing a risk measure that is finite-valued, cash-additive, convex, and Lipschitz continuous. Our first result establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for a dataset to be compatible with a risk measure, that is the evaluations are stemming from a risk measure applied to the contingent claims. Our second result provides a reconstruction formula for compatible datasets, which we term \emph{universal risk measure}. We further extend the reconstruction to monotone risk measures and establish sharp Lipschitz constants for both general and monotone reconstructions. We further show that we explicitly reconstruct linear preferences and evaluations by the Expected Shortfall. We conclude with a numerical application to European options.

title: Probing for relativistic outflows in the Ultraluminous X-ray pulsar RX J0209.6-7427
abstract: Context. Relativistic winds have been observed in Ultraluminous X-ray sources (ULXs), but their detection at large distances remains limited. Galactic neutron stars accreting matter from Be-star companions provide a valuable opportunity to improve our understanding of these outflows. Aims. RX J0209.6-7427 is a Be-XRB, powered by a neutron star with a spin period of 9.3 seconds, that underwent an outburst in 2019, exceeding a bolometric luminosity of $10^{39}$ erg s$^{-1}$ at its peak. Owing to its relatively low distance and a high-resolution XMM-Newton observation, this source is a strong candidate for investigating outflows associated with super-Eddington accretion. Methods. The RGS spectrum yields 105,000 counts, a factor of two higher than any other deep ULX RGS spectrum. RGS and EPIC-pn data sets were modelled with a phenomenological continuum accounting for emission from the accretion disc and accretion column. The emission and absorption features were fitted with the optically-thin plasma models available in SPEX, exploring the temperature-velocity parameter space. Results. The modelling of emission features suggests the presence of a multiphase photoionised plasma approximately at rest with respect to the source. The absorption features can be reproduced either by blueshifted photoionised absorbers moving at approximately $0.1c$ and $0.2c$, the latter being more tentative, or by an alternative collisionally ionised absorption model, which provides a comparably acceptable fit. The presence of ultrafast outflows therefore remains a plausible, but non-unique, interpretation of the data. If associated with outflows, the inferred column densities appear lower than those reported for some persistent ULXs, potentially reflecting differences in the accretion-flow properties or the shorter super-Eddington phase of RX J0209.6-7427.

title: Coding Length and Optimal Power Allocation in Correlated Block Fading
abstract: A codeword spans a fixed number of correlated Gaussian fading blocks. The receiver knows the gains and the transmitter knows only their law. At fixed average signal-to-noise ratio, we require the decoding error probability to decay exponentially with the number of receive antennas. When does outage predict the achievable rate? If block length grows faster than the number of antennas, outage gives the limiting optimal rate. If both grow to infinity at a fixed positive ratio of block length to array size, outage strictly overestimates the limiting rate. We determine the critical ratio above which positive rates are possible. For sufficiently large finite ratios, we find the exact limiting rate over all codes satisfying a total energy constraint on each codeword. The leading rate loss is inversely proportional to the ratio. Its coefficient depends on Gaussian channel dispersion at the most likely fade causing outage and on how quickly the outage rate decreases as the required error exponent increases. In the long-block limit, equal power loses rate on every window of three or more blocks under stationary first-order autoregressive fading with positive lag-one correlation. In a different three-block channel with identical marginal gains, tightening the reliability requirement first makes it optimal to leave the middle block unused and later to use it again.

title: Small noise limit for Entropic Variational Mean-Field Games
abstract: We study second order variational mean-field games with quadratic Hamiltonian. In analogy with entropic optimal transport, Benamou, Carlier, Di Marino and the second author recently proposed an entropy-minimization formulation of the problem, which could be interpreted as the Lagrangian counterpart of the classical Eulerian approach. We investigate the small-noise $Γ$-limit for the Lagrangian entropy-minimization formulation and establish $Γ$-convergence of second order mean-field games towards their deterministic first order counterpart. This also translates into another (dynamical) proof of the convergence of the Schrödinger problem to optimal transport. Moreover, we study the original Eulerian problem and prove a first order energy expansion, which establishes a selection principle for minimizers of the deterministic problem.

title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning Architectures for Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Chemical Processes
abstract: Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) is crucial for both maintenance and control in chemical industries, where early fault detection can prevent costly failures and optimize operations. This is particularly critical in pilot units like those at IFP Energies Nouvelles (IFPEN), which operate under short-term experimental conditions with frequently varying operational parameters. This study conducts an extensive benchmarking analysis using the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP), a widely used simulated chemical process dataset, to evaluate multiple approaches for fault detection and diagnosis, featuring numerous continuous operations with different sensors and faults. Several methods were implemented and compared including Multi Scale PCA (MS-PCA), AutoEncoder, Ensemble Learning, and LSTM models for fault detection, alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and BLSTM (Bidirectional LSTM) for fault diagnosis. Our results demonstrate that Ensemble Learning achieves detection rates ranging from 80% to 100% across various fault scenarios. For the fault diagnosis task, BLSTM achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 98.76%. The study reveals that ensemble-based approaches consistently outperform individual models in handling the complex, multivariate nature of chemical process data, due to its robustness in combining multiple perspectives, comprehensive data capture, and localized detection capabilities. Furthermore, the superior performance of the BLSTM is due to its ability to capture both past and future temporal dependencies in the sequential data, particularly important in chemical processes where fault patterns may manifest with complex temporal relationships. This research contributes to the field of Fault Detection and Diagnosis by providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of ensemble methods and Bidirectional LSTMs in order to address industrial FDD applications on chemical processes.

title: Ultrasensitive measurement of phase dynamics by time-holographic dark-port readout of a marginally imbalanced interferometer
abstract: Resolving displacements and surface irregularities far below a nanometer is now indispensable across fields, from precision manufacturing and biotechnology to nanoscience and fundamental metrology. High-precision optical interferometry reaches this $λ/1{,}000$ regime by reading out optical power, which provides a smooth response over the measurement range. Here we instead read out the complex dark-port field of a marginally imbalanced interferometer, whose phase response to small internal phase deviations $ϕ_{\textrm{in}}$ near destructive interference becomes extremely steep. For a small arm-amplitude imbalance $μ$, the tangent $T_{\textrm{out}}$ of the dark-port phase reduces to $μ^{-1}ϕ_{\textrm{in}}$, defining a phase magnification $M=μ^{-1}$. Crucially, this tangent estimator stays linear over a range $|ϕ_{\textrm{in}}|\lesssim\sqrt{|μ|}$---much larger than the imbalance $|μ|$ itself for $|μ|\ll1$---so that fine temporal substructure is resolved within much larger phase excursions. $T_{\textrm{out}}$ is synthesized from the dark-port complex field by optical time-domain holography and Fourier demodulation---a heterodyne readout that is intrinsically immune to laser relative-intensity noise at any magnification, and gives time-resolved access to phase dynamics. In a proof-of-principle Mach--Zehnder experiment, without optimization or environmental isolation, we demonstrate $|M|>10^3$ and optical-path resolution better than $λ/100{,}000$ ($\approx5~\textrm{pm}$), with a shot-noise floor orders of magnitude below this environment-limited value. The approach is compact, tunable, and compatible with existing interferometric platforms, offering a practical route to enhanced phase sensitivity in metrology, sensing, and optical instrumentation.

title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

title: Extremal problems for graphs with bounded $k$-th binding number
abstract: The binding number of a graph, introduced by Woodall [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B, 1973], is a central topic in structural and extremal graph theory. Recently, Chen et al. introduced the $k$-th binding number $β^k(G)$. Anderson [J. Combin. Theory, Ser. B, 1971] proved that every graph $G$ of even order with $β^1(G)\ge\frac43$ contains a perfect matching, and that the bound $\frac43$ is best possible. For $k\ge2$, Chen et al. proved that $β^k(G)\ge1$ guarantees a $k$-factor whenever $kn$ is even, and that the bound $1$ is best possible. The above facts reveal a fundamental distinction between the higher-order binding number and the classical binding number. This distinction makes extremal problems for graphs with bounded $k$-th binding number particularly intriguing. For positive integers $n,$ $k$ and $r$, we in this paper determine the maximum size and spectral radius among all graphs $G$ of order $n$ satisfying $β^k(G)<r$, and characterize the corresponding extremal graphs, respectively. In particular, when $k=1$, our results imply the corresponding extremal results of Fan and Lin [Electron. J. Combin., 2024] and Liu, Chen and Fan [Electron. J. Combin., 2026]. Our proofs develop a structural framework that relates higher-order neighborhood inequalities to the structure of the complements of graphs. This framework may provide an approach to Turán-type problem involving the $k$-th binding number, and the approach may be of independent interest.

title: Geometrically Constrained Learning II: Agnostic Proper Learning of Lipschitz Functions
abstract: We give a proper learner for Lipschitz functions over the Gaussian distribution on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Given random Gaussian examples labeled by a $λ$-Lipschitz function, $λ\ge 1$, the learner returns a function $h:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ that is globally $λ$-Lipschitz and has loss (absolute or squared) at most $\varepsilon$. The sample complexity, running time, and representation size are \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(λ/\varepsilon)}. \] The learning algorithm can be made \emph{agnostic}, given a known bound on the variance of the label marginal distribution. Some known control of label scale is information-theoretically necessary. For arbitrary labels with variance at most $V^2 \ge 1$, the complexity is \[ (d+1)^{\mathsf{poly}(Vλ/\varepsilon)}, \] and the error is $\mathsf{opt} + \varepsilon$, where $\mathsf{opt}$ is the minimal error among Lipschitz approximators. Our approach combines $L_1$ polynomial regression under a convex gradient constraint with local correction of the Lipschitz property. The learner finds a polynomial that, after smoothing and clipping its range, is very close to a canonical Lipschitz correction of itself, the lower Lipschitz envelope. Our local corrector modifies the lower envelope by replacing distances to sublevel sets with a Gaussian sampling proxy, allowing the construction to be locally and stably estimated from samples.

title: FOREST: Coordinating Tree-based HBF, RRAM, and HBM for Efficient Speculative LLM Inference
abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by combining lightweight drafting with parallel target-model verification. However, its stages impose distinct resource demands: target verification requires high-throughput access to large weight sets, sequential drafting executes a compact model under tight latency constraints, and long-context attention processes growing key-value (KV) caches. Conventional GPU-centric SD systems serve these workloads through shared HBM-centric memory and general-purpose compute, creating mismatches in capacity, bandwidth, and computation. These mismatches constrain deployable model-context configurations and limit the efficiency of bandwidth-bound and latency-sensitive operations. We propose FOREST, a heterogeneous memory-centric architecture coordinating HBF, 3D-stacked RRAM, and HBM memory-compute trees for efficient SD. It features: (1) compute-aligned 3D RRAM, combining ultra-wide, low-frequency reads with clock-decoupled interfaces and overlapped SRAM-DCIM weight refills for latency-sensitive drafting; (2) cross-tree numerical co-design, moving block-scaled Q/K/V preprocessing to HBF and RRAM root plates and enabling block-floating-point (BFP) attention with pipelined softmax reduction in the HBM tree; and (3) HBF-aware SD design-space exploration, revealing how bandwidth-compute provisioning and model scale determine performance, energy, and cost trade-offs. Evaluated across six SD configurations spanning 32B-405B target models, FOREST achieves up to 5.5x end-to-end speedup, 11.46x higher decode throughput, and 16.5x higher decode energy efficiency over NVIDIA A800 GPU-based SD baselines. Under a modeled total cost of ownership, FOREST delivers up to 6.73x higher token-generation cost efficiency.

title: Full-chip constrained quantum annealing via self-calibrating spin-susceptibility control
abstract: Discrete optimization in finance, power grids, and logistics requires minimizing Ising Hamiltonians under coupled linear constraints. However, quadratic-penalty formulations generate dense cliques that exhaust the minor-embedding capacity of sparse superconducting processors at 128-176 spins, and first-order dual subgradient schemes diverge or stall under constraint coupling. Accordingly, this study proposes a closed-loop primal-dual scheme, designated as Self-Calibrating Quantum Susceptibility Quasi-Newton (SelfCal-QSQN), in which linear constraints are encoded in longitudinal fields and dual curvature is reconstructed from single-shot spin-fluctuation covariances. This scheme requires no penalty couplers, slack qubits, or perturbation queries. Evaluated over 891 runs on D-Wave Advantage (5,612 qubits) and Advantage2 (4,560 qubits), SelfCal-QSQN achieves 83.3% full-chip exact feasibility, reduces high-constraint error by 6.1-20.1-fold over $K$-scaled first-order updates (138.4-323.3-fold over fixed-gain curvature), outperforms time-matched mixed-integer programming at 256 spins, and attains 95.0%-96.7% feasibility on non-native and inequality benchmarks. Moreover, the scheme is robust toward shot noise and freeze-out drift.

title: Single-realization Pauli twirling for suppressing coherent error accumulation in structured quantum circuits
abstract: Pauli twirling is conventionally understood as an ensemble-level noise-tailoring procedure which suppresses coherent components of the error channel by averaging over randomized compilations. This picture does not by itself determine whether a single realization of Pauli-dressed circuit can outperform its bare counterpart, nor does it predict when such an advantage should occur. In this work, we present single-realization based framework for the standard Pauli dressing of two-qubit Clifford gates in structured quantum circuits. This is afforded by the key insight that for weak coherent errors, the leading gate infidelity is governed by the variance of some accumulated error generator. Through both simulations and theoretical considerations, we verify that coherent errors accumulated at different entangling gates can produce $Θ(L^2)$ variance growth in a bare circuit, whereas independent Pauli dressing eliminates the cross-layer contribution on average and yields an $O(L)$ variance bound at any fixed confidence level for a single randomly sampled realization. We then develop a covariance diagnostic that predicts when this mechanism is effective in error mitigation. We find a strong Pauli twirling advantage for coherent errors whose transported generators have large off-diagonal covariance, and little advantage when the covariance matrix is nearly diagonal. Hardware experiments on IBM superconducting processors demonstrate fidelity improvements for GHZ-state preparation and reduced observable errors in Trotterized transverse-field Ising dynamics. These results indicate that single realizations of Pauli twirling without ensemble averaging is a useful coherent-error suppression technique for structured circuits containing repeated nontrivial two-qubit operations.

title: A pseudoscalar Higgs boson interfering with toponium: a QCD analysis of $\mathbf{gg\to A\to t\bar t}$ near threshold
abstract: The CMS and ATLAS collaborations have observed an excess of $t\bar t$ events near threshold that is consistent with the formation of the pseudoscalar toponium state $η_t$. A pseudoscalar Higgs boson $A$ with a large coupling to top quarks could contribute part of this excess and the presence of the $A$ boson could be concealed. We point out that, if such a state exists with $M_A$ close to $2m_t$, it necessarily interferes with toponium, since both live in the colour--singlet ${}^1S_0$ channel and share the same Coulomb final--state interaction. Using exact leading--order amplitudes, whose relative phase is fixed by unitarity, and Coulomb resummation applied coherently to the QCD background, the $A$ boson signal and their interference, we show that the line shape is controlled by a single complex number $κ$, the ratio of the resonant and non--resonant amplitudes at the peak. Unitarity fixes ${\rm Im}\,κ=-1$ exactly when $A$ decays into top quarks, so that the interference reduces the resonant rate by $2/|κ|^2$ and produces an exact zero of the ${}^1S_0$ amplitude just above $M_A$. The parameter $κ$ does not depend on the $A$ coupling to top quarks and, with the Coulomb--enhanced width we find $|κ|\approx1.5$--$1.7$ for $M_A=350$--$380$ GeV and, hence, the $A$ resonance is completely distorted. For an $A$ boson accounting for 50\% (25\%) of the observed excess, it enhances the toponium peak by about 10 to 70\% (5 to 35\%), and the threshold excess differs strongly from the sum of the toponium and $A$ contributions.

title: Stall-Triggered Newton-Krylov-Assisted DIIS and Its Machine-Learning-Accelerated Variant for CCSD Convergence
abstract: The iterative solution of the non-linear amplitude equations of coupled-cluster singles doubles (CCSD) theory can encounter convergence instabilities, asymptotic convergence or outright divergence. Direct Inversion in the Iterative Subspace (DIIS) is a widely used extrapolation technique but can also exhibit slow or oscillatory convergence in challenging regimes. In this work, we introduce a robust hybrid solver: Stall-Triggered Newton-Krylov Assisted DIIS (${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK-DIIS) alongside its machine-learning accelerated variant ${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK$^{\mathrm{ML}}$-DIIS which leverages the robust convergence of Newton-Krylov (NK) while avoiding the high computational cost of Krylov iterations. In our methods, DIIS remains the default accelerator and a matrix-free NK procedure is activated when sustained stagnation or divergence is detected with each NK step verified using the non-linear residual before acceptance. To alleviate the cost of Krylov iterations the ${}{\mathrm{st}}$NK$^{\mathrm{ML}}$-DIIS uses a gated recurrent unit (GRU) to predict a scalar logarithmic step-size ratio along the approximately computed Newton direction. When the ML-predicted step fails residual-based verification, the method falls back to a grid-based NK line search. Using CCSD as the underlying electronic-structure theory, we evaluate these methods against conventional DIIS and pure NK for stretched molecules exhibiting convergence difficulties in terms of residual convergence, iteration counts, and wall-time performance. These protocols may be generalizable to other non-linear equation solvers as well, as the ML model learns the convergence pattern of the variables and does not require system-specific knowledge such as atom identities or molecular orbital properties. This allows transferability across atom-type, bonding character and basis-sets.

title: Projectivized ASEP-Bethe system and counting solutions
abstract: This paper addresses the problem of counting solutions to the ASEP-Bethe ansatz equations. In an earlier preprint, Brattain, Do, and Saenz presented an algebro-geometric method for counting the number of such solutions. As their method relies on sophisticated machinery, it requires advanced knowledge of algebraic geometry and topology. In this paper, we provide an alternative and simpler method for counting solutions, based on a standard intersection theory on projective varieties. We take a conventional approach in algebraic geometry: ``Projectivize the problem and count degrees.'' We introduce a projectivized version of the ASEP-Bethe equations, whose solution set is realized as a subscheme of a certain projective variety. Varying the hopping-rate parameter $p$, we give a one-parameter family $S$ of the solution sets. We show that, for the ASEP with $n$ sites and $m$ particles, the fiber $S|_p$ with generic $p$ contains $\binom{n}{m}$ points with multiplicity, which equals the expected number of admissible Bethe roots to the ASEP-Bethe ansatz equation.

title: Comparing weakly interacting and free quantum dynamics locally
abstract: Lieb-Robinson bounds (LRBs) have become a standard tool for perturbative results in quantum many-body physics, including gap stability and many-body adiabatic theory. Here, we use LRBs to locally approximate weakly interacting many-body dynamics with one-body dynamics on large, perturbative time scales. This allows us to use one-body transport results to establish the expected many-body transport behavior on finite time scales in the following two illustrative settings: (i) We prove quantum diffusion, as quantified by a certain operator spreading diagnostic, in weakly interacting and weakly disordered Fermi systems in dimensions $D\geq2$ on large finite time scales based on the non-interacting diffusion result of Black, Drogin, and Hernández [arXiv:2506.06468]. (ii) We show for Fermi-Hubbard models with initially low spin-down density, that all local multi-time spin-up correlation functions are approximated by their free counterparts. In particular, we obtain an OTOC (out-of-time-ordered correlator) counterpart to the patterns of short-time entanglement related to lattice path counts observed numerically by Bippus et al. [Phys. Rev. B 113, 035152 (2026)].

title: Quark dipole operators in the gradient-flow scheme at NNLO QCD
abstract: Conversion factors for the dimension-five QCD operator basis from the $\overline{\textrm{MS}}$ to the gradient-flow scheme are presented through NNLO in the strong coupling. In the CP-even sector, the results are provided for general quark masses and arbitrary flavor content of the operators. Specifically, this concerns the quark CMDM operator and its mixing with lower-dimensional QCD operators. In the massless case, our results immediately apply to the quark chromoelectric dipole operator. As a by-product, we also determine missing entries in the $\overline{\textrm{MS}}$ anomalous dimension matrix of the CMDM operator to NNLO QCD.

title: Impulsive ejection of Worthington jets by flow focusing. Influence of a soluble surfactant
abstract: We experimentally investigate impulsive Worthington jet generation by flow focusing, considering the liquid meniscus location that maximizes the flow-focusing effect. This effect increases the jet velocity by up to two orders of magnitude over the bottom liquid velocity after impact. At sufficiently high liquid velocities, jet formation is governed primarily by inertia, making jet velocity largely independent of liquid viscosity, surface tension, and surfactant effects. Each liquid exhibits an optimum impact velocity that maximizes momentum transfer. Surfynol 465 lowers the impactvelocity threshold for water-jet emission and increases jet velocity by rapidly restoring equilibrium surface tension. In contrast, Triton X-100 has an almost negligible effect because of its slower adsorption kinetics. Importantly, both surfactants reduce jet diameter and, consequently, droplet size. This reduction is particularly significant with Surfynol 465 at high impact velocities, suggesting potential applications, for instance, in high-resolution printing technologies. The jet loaded with Surfynol 465 was even faster than that of the glycerine-water mixture with the same Ohnesorge and Weber numbers. This suggests that adding Surfynol 465 further accelerates jet emission, exceeding the speed attained by a clean interface with the same reduced equilibrium surface tension.

title: Abstract What Varies, Reuse Longer Patterns: Efficient Offline Chain-of-Thought Compression
abstract: Offline chain-of-thought (CoT) compression creates shorter supervision for efficient reasoning, but per-example compressors repeatedly process similar expressions across traces, wasting compressor budget. Methods that reuse identical text across examples miss longer shared expressions when names, numbers, or formulas change from one question to another. We introduce CRAFT, which abstracts problem-specific details into slots to uncover partially lexicalized expression templates (PLETs) and clusters wording variants into families. Compressing each family representative once yields shared deletion or rewriting edits, which are applied with each occurrence's own details to construct compact, ordinary-text training targets. Compared with per-example rewriting, CRAFT Rewrite reduces weighted compressor budgets by a median 90.7% with a median accuracy loss of 1.21 percentage points, while generating shorter reasoning. Against cross-sample encoding, it shortens reasoning across all eight model-dataset settings by 25.3% on average and improves accuracy in five.

title: Beyond the Ground State: Assessing the Machine-Learned Skala Functional in ΔSCF Calculations of Molecular Excitation Energies
abstract: We assess the transferability of the machine-learned Skala exchange-correlation (XC) functional beyond ground-state energetics using molecular vertical excitation energies and singlet-triplet gaps calculated with the $Δ$-self-consistent-field ($Δ$SCF) approach. We compare Skala with PBE, r$^2$SCAN, and PBE0 on subsets covering small-molecule excitations (QUEST1), inverted singlet-triplet gaps (ST-gap), and intramolecular charge-transfer excitations (QUEST6). Both spin-unrestricted Kohn-Sham (UKS) and restricted open-shell Kohn-Sham (ROKS) formalisms are considered. On QUEST1, Skala achieves the lowest mean absolute errors (MAEs) for singlet and triplet excitation energies with both formalisms, although PBE0 and r$^2$SCAN provide more accurate singlet-triplet gaps through error cancellation. For ST-gap, Skala yields the lowest gap MAEs with both UKS and ROKS. Evaluating the mixed-spin and triplet energy components on the same orbitals optimized for the ROKS open-shell singlet yields negative splittings for seven of eight ST-gap molecules with Skala. Separate triplet optimization increases the gaps, but six remain negative. All three conventional functionals give positive common-orbital splittings and optimized gaps for all eight molecules. For QUEST6, treated with UKS only, Skala yields more accurate singlet excitation energies than PBE and r$^2$SCAN but remains less accurate than PBE0. Across QUEST1 and ST-gap, Skala yields lower MAEs with UKS than ROKS. Overall, these results support Skala's transferability to molecular excited states while highlighting its dependence on the excitation class and open-shell treatment.

title: When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
abstract: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.

title: MetaRigor: From Agentic Automation to Verifiable End-to-End Meta-Analysis Through Scientific Decision Boundaries
abstract: Automated meta-analysis requires not only accurate numerical extraction but also the consistent preservation of result identity across stages, including the associated study, comparison, population, outcome, time point, and analysis conditions. We present MetaRigor, an LLM workflow framework for verifiable end-to-end evidence synthesis. MetaRigor organizes study results as Study x Target units and operationalizes scientific decision boundaries at the task level through Task Contracts, programmatic rules, and source binding. The model performs semantic interpretation that depends on study context, whereas programs execute formalizable rules, computations, validation, and source verification. We conducted controlled evaluations across five stages: evidence acquisition, data extraction, risk of bias assessment, certainty of evidence assessment, and manuscript generation. MetaRigor achieved an F1 score of 86.29% for complete result delivery and 80.20% agreement for domain-level certainty of evidence judgments. Generated manuscripts received scores of 86.00 under human evaluation, exceeding all three baselines. A seven-case downstream end-to-end evaluation further yielded an aggregate F1 score of 77.01%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.78 percentage points. Cross-system tracing of archived outputs from three systems further showed that local mismatches or omissions in result identity could alter statistical inputs and the objects subjected to risk of bias assessment, with these errors subsequently propagating into the final report. Ablation experiments showed that task constraints and programmatic rules played distinct roles across different stages. These findings indicate that, in LLM-driven evidence synthesis workflows, consistently maintaining explicit result identity, decision boundaries, and provenance relationships is critical to improving end-to-end verifiability.

title: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies
abstract: Adaptive decision systems in education and health choose interventions sequentially and are often required not to leave a protected group too far behind. We study the fairness-constrained optimal value: the largest population value attainable by a policy in a smooth parametric class subject to constraints that are smooth functions of group specific counterfactual functionals, such as value gaps, floors, max-min welfare and budgets. For multi-stage, non-Markov data under sequential ignorability, a sensitivity analysis of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system shows that this value is pathwise differentiable, with efficient influence function equal to the Lagrangian combination of the influence functions of the group values. The same analysis gives the influence functions of the optimal policy, the multiplier and the group values it delivers. A cross-fitted doubly robust estimator is efficient despite its data-dependent feasible set and yields confidence intervals for the constrained value and the price of fairness. When the constraint binds, any plug-in fair policy violates the population constraint, by a margin that vanishes as the sample grows, with probability tending to one half; tightening the estimated constraint by a one sided confidence margin certifies fairness at a small cost in value. Exact checks, simulations and a synthetic case study illustrate the theory.

title: Recoverable Symbols, Unstable Execution: Auditing Internal Pathways and Decision Identity in Visual State Tracking
abstract: Visual features can retain every symbol a task needs while a model built on them still changes its answer when irrelevant parts of the image change. We study this gap in visual state tracking, where a recurrent executor reads a sequence of symbol tiles through a frozen ViT encoder and decides whether a displayed candidate equals the final state. Our diagnostic pairs each input with a donor view that preserves every queried tile, checks with a symbol-supervised decoder that the full symbol chain is recoverable from both feature sequences, and swaps individual internal channels of the same fitted executor in both directions. On 3,526 pairs in which every symbol is recovered in both views, changing the surrounding context lowers the balanced accuracy of a rotary recurrent head by 17.13 points. The loss runs mainly through the input-dependent rotation phase: restoring the original phase repairs 351 of 391 new errors and brings accuracy back to 88.54%, yet 142 individual predictions still differ from the original ones. A locked test on 192 unseen program families reproduces the pathway (28 of 29 new errors repaired; 382 of 384 predictions unchanged), and the effect partly carries over to single-image canvases. Consistency objectives derived from this analysis reduce the internal discrepancy they target but do not outperform ordinary data augmentation.

title: Challenging the Körner-Pati-Woo Theorem in Charmed Baryon Decays
abstract: The Körner-Pati-Woo (KPW) theorem is a long-standing selection rule widely used in heavy-baryon decays. In this work, we argue that the conventional valence-color argument underlying the KPW theorem does not, by itself, establish an exact selection rule. The $\rm KPW$-$\rm SU(3)_F$ prediction for $\mathcal{B}(Ξ_c^0\to pK^-)$, inferred from $Λ_c^+\to Ξ^0K^+$, is $17.2\pm6.0$ times the measured value. A joint likelihood fit to five observables in $Ξ_c^0\to pK^-$ and $Λ_c^+\to Ξ^0K^+$ yields a $6.3σ$ discrepancy under the $\rm KPW$-$\rm SU(3)_F$ ansatz. A comparison of $α(Λ_c^+\to Δ^{++}K^-)$ and $α(Λ_c^+\to Σ^{*}π)$ reveals a pronounced sign-sensitive tension. Accommodating these measurements within the KPW constraint requires anomalously large $\rm SU(3)_F$ breaking effects. Future measurements of $Λ^+_c\toΣ^{(*)0}K^+$, $Σ^{(*)+}K^0_S$, $Δ^+η^{(\prime)}$, $Δ^{++}π^-$, $Δ^+π^0$, $Δ^0π^+$, $Δ^{++}K^-$, and $Δ^{+}K^0_S$ would provide high-precision tests of the KPW theorem.

title: Applicability of the MPCC approach to Zeng reformulations of nonlinear pessimistic bilevel programming
abstract: The vanilla method in bilevel programming is to reformulate it as a single-level mathematical programs with complementarity constraints (MPCC), via the KKT conditions of the lower-level. This method seemed to work only for optimistic formulations. However, in (Zeng, 2020), B. Zeng presented a general method to reduce pessimistic bilevel problems to optimistic ones. In this note, we study how to apply the MPCC approach to the pessimistic counterpart through Zeng's reformulation (Zeng, 2020). While we show that it cannot be applied directly since constraint qualification can be destroyed by the reformulation, it still can be used to solve natural relaxations, in the spirit of (Wiesemann,2013),(Loridan & Morgan,1989), (Loridan & Morgan,1996).

title: Solving the pre-image problem in kernel PCA: The reproducing property is all you need
abstract: Kernel PCA extends PCA to nonlinear dimensionality reduction by implicitly mapping data into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) via the kernel trick, with applications ranging from image denoising to out-of-distribution detection. While its projection map is well understood, appropriately defining the associated reconstruction map is a longstanding challenge since projecting back from the RKHS to the input space is non-trivial. This is known as the pre-image problem. Existing approaches have tackled this problem by either relying on nonlinear optimization, which is prone to numerical instabilities and sensitive to initialization, or by solving a separate supervised learning problem, incurring additional computational overhead. Furthermore, although the projection map of kernel PCA reduces to that of standard PCA when a linear kernel is used, most of these approaches are not guaranteed to recover PCA's reconstruction map in this case, a consistency property that one would naturally expect to hold. In this paper, we leverage the reproducing property of the RKHS to derive a reconstruction map for kernel PCA that is provably consistent. Our derivations rely on the mild assumption that the RKHS either contains linear functions or the kernel is universal, which holds for standard kernels. We further extend the method to the random Fourier features (RFFs) approximation of kernel PCA by introducing a corresponding notion of RFF reproducing property. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed method performs comparably with state-of-the-art methods across kernel choices, while remaining more computationally efficient and maintaining consistent performance in settings where these baseline methods drastically fail.

title: VeilGS: Solving Darkness as a Veil of 2D Basis Maps over Retinex 3DGS
abstract: In a dark capture, the darkness is not uniform. How much light reaches a surface depends on where it lies relative to the few light sources, and the camera compresses what remains with a tone curve. Most low-light 3D reconstruction methods either apply one curve to every pixel of a view, so a dark object beside a lamp and a bright one in an unlit corner receive the same correction, or store the darkness in the 3D representation, where it can absorb scene detail. We present VeilGS, a 3D Gaussian Splatting method for low-light novel view synthesis that treats the degradation as a veil drawn over a clear scene. Each Gaussian carries an albedo and a shading latent instead of spherical harmonics, separating surface colour from illumination. Each view is darkened by a spatially varying gain followed by a global tone curve, and rendering without this veil gives the restored scene. A small network predicts a coarse basis for the gain from the observation, and its coefficients are solved for each view rather than learned. Training through this solve discourages the Gaussians from absorbing what the veil can explain. VeilGS needs no paired normal-light supervision and stores no per-view parameters. On Gaussian-DK, its restored renders score best on no-reference NIQE and CLIP-IQA and are rated highest in a blind user study with 55 participants. On LOM, it achieves results competitive with the state of the art.

title: PAWS: A Parametric Model of Canine Pose and Shape
abstract: We introduce PAWS, a parametric model of canine shape and pose, learned from 3D scans of real dogs. Capturing the full diversity of dogs is challenging, as different breeds vary in size, proportion, and body shape. To capture this range, we scanned 31 dogs across multiple breeds and sizes performing a range of natural movements. From this dataset, we build a parametric model that combines an anatomically faithful skeleton with a linear shape space learned from the 3D scans. Unlike previous models, our model is learned from real dogs in varying poses, allowing for realistic modelling of canine pose and shape. We demonstrate that building on PAWS provides a robust framework for downstream tasks, such as surface reconstruction and image regression. In particular, we show that a limited number of anatomically valid degrees of freedom is sufficient to accurately estimate dog pose and shape.

title: Decision Models for Multilingual Emotion Classification: A Comparative Study Against LLMs and Encoders
abstract: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. We ask whether systems used without training on labelled data (zero-shot) can replace fine-tuning, and what the decision format adds over a general-purpose large language model (LLM). We compare three decision models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, Strands Decider 2B) and two LLMs (GPT-6 Luna, Qwen3.5-2B), given Italian instructions, with two fine-tuned multilingual encoders (tabularisai, XLM-EMO) on four emotions (joy, sadness, anger, fear) in 10 social-media datasets in five languages, with paired difference and equivalence tests. The three best zero-shot systems (two decision models and one LLM) score on average about one macro-F1 point below an encoder fine-tuned on the target dataset; our test sets cannot exclude a gap of 4-5 points, and on single datasets either approach wins by up to 22 points. They beat encoders fine-tuned on another dataset by 8-15 points, though against XLM-EMO this may not extend to new datasets, and instructions in each text's language change their results by under 1 point. Exploratorily, they beat the strongest public emotion model used as is by about 6 points. OpenAI's decision endpoint matches GPT-6 Luna, the LLM it runs on, at a fifth of its median latency, and a 2-billion-parameter decision model beats a same-size general LLM by 10 points, owing to its training, not the decision format. The best zero-shot systems, the LLM included, have an SD of about 1 point across prompts. Without labelled data they are a strong default, and decision models add lower latency and, unlike generative LLM use, per-option probabilities. Fine-tuning won by a wide margin only on the largest dataset, GoEmotions.

title: Beyond Math, Code, and Logic: Do Reasoning Models Transfer to Scientific Argumentation?
abstract: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. While recent advances in reasoning-capable language models have demonstrated strong performance on mathematical, coding, and logical benchmarks, their ability to engage in scientific argumentation remains unclear. We present the first systematic evaluation of language models across seven tasks spanning argument mining, rebuttal generation, and discourse-level reasoning using research papers, peer reviews, and grant proposals. Our study reveals that even frontier models with strong general reasoning skills struggle with domain-specific argumentative tasks, highlighting a fundamental capability gap. To address this, we introduce a training framework that explicitly scaffolds the argumentative reasoning process in language models, substantially improving their competence in scientific discourse. The resulting compact models approach or exceed the performance of much larger proprietary systems and generalize to unseen conversational settings, demonstrating reasoning transfer beyond task-specific supervision. These findings underscore that effective scientific argumentation is not an emergent property of scale, but requires explicit reasoning-aware training, and they point toward practical pathways for building AI systems that can contribute meaningfully to scientific discourse.

title: Projectively Flat Spherically Symmetric Sprays of Constant Curvature
abstract: In this paper, we study projectively flat spherically symmetric sprays of constant curvature. We derive a system of equations that is equivalent to the constant-curvature condition for such sprays and solve it to obtain a complete classification of the projective factor \(p(r,s)\) into four explicit families. We further show that the sprays induced by projectively flat spherically symmetric Finsler metrics of constant flag curvature \(K=0\), \(K=-1\), and \(K=1\) are all special cases of our classification, thereby confirming that the sprays induced by these constant-flag-curvature Finsler metrics are fully contained in our framework.

title: Beyond the Stabilizer Norm: Physicality and Resource Allocation in Pauli-Limited Quantum Certification
abstract: Certification from restricted and uncertain Pauli measurements can be posed as a robust optimization problem: among all physical channels consistent with the data, how small can the fidelity with a target channel be? We first study a linear relaxation that ignores positivity and show that it is exactly characterized by a single scalar, the stabilizer norm of the target Choi state, $s_{\mathrm{wit}}(U)=\|C_U\|_{\mathrm{st}}-1/D$. We then ask whether this scalar continues to determine robustness once the positivity constraint is restored. It does not. We derive a necessary and sufficient KKT condition for the relaxation to remain tight, together with a dual obstruction certifying a strict gap, and give a rigorous computer-assisted proof that two distinct two-qubit targets can have exactly the same stabilizer norm but different physical robustness. The KKT condition depends on structure discarded by the stabilizer norm, including the support and relative signs of the Choi-Pauli coefficients and the algebraic relations among the corresponding Pauli operators. We use this structure to derive simpler sufficient certificates for a strict gap. The dual coefficients also determine how measurement uncertainty enters the finite-data fidelity bound. For a fixed budget, we derive exact shot-allocation rules for a fixed certificate and for compatible observables obtained from shared measurement settings, and we formulate the corresponding joint certificate-design problem. The conjecture that every full-support two-qubit target has positive gain remains open.

title: A Cognitive Agentic AI Framework for Interactive Process Analysis and Optimization
abstract: Complex multivariable process analysis and optimization require coordinated access to simulation, structured data, machine learning (ML), optimization, and scientific literature, often across disconnected software tools. We present a Cognitive Agentic AI Framework (CAAF) that enables interactive, iterative process investigation through natural-language prompts within an established flowsheet. Following harness-engineering principles, CAAF assigns task interpretation, planning, knowledge synthesis, and context management to a large language model while delegating numerical calculations to specialized tools. Dedicated providers connect databases, scientific-document retrieval, ML-assisted Bayesian optimization (BO), and COCO process simulation. The framework is demonstrated on methyl acetate production. Guided by successive prompts, an engineer explored multivariable relationships, conducted 4,000 BO iterations to maximize carbon conversion yield (C-Yield) and minimize specific energy cost (C-SEC), refined operating bounds, and verified selected candidates through process simulation. Re-simulation of 16 candidates within the restricted domain showed close agreement with ML predictions, with a mean absolute C-Yield error of 0.0085 (0.85 percentage points). The highest BO-derived C-Yield, verified by COCO, was 0.921 versus approximately 0.81 in the initial dataset, an improvement of about 11 percentage points. CAAF also detects and reports non-converged simulations, excludes invalid outputs, and continues subsequent evaluations. The results demonstrate how human-guided agentic coordination can combine engineering tools for iterative analysis and optimization with rigorous simulation-based verification under a fixed process topology.

title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids
abstract: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.

title: Calabi-Yau fibrations and orbifold Mordell
abstract: We construct isotrivial projective families of Calabi-Yau varieties with arbitrarily large inf-multiplicities and no divisible fibres over the projective line. As an application, we show that any single instance of Campana's Orbifold Mordell Conjecture for a general-type C-pair of genus at most one (with only finite multiplicities) implies that the Weakly Special Conjecture is false.

title: Quantitative Measurement of Pavement Distress based on Vehicle Camera and Perspective Correction
abstract: Using image data is becoming an important method for highway agencies to automatically evaluate pavement conditions. However, most studies focus on improving detection accuracy rather than obtaining quantitative measurements, such as the length or area of pavement distress. Although field camera calibration can provide such measurements, it is impractical for large volumes of onboard images collected from different vehicles. This study develops a method to quantitatively measure pavement distress directly from in-vehicle camera images without on-site camera calibration. A quadrilateral region of interest is first identified based on lane detection and used to construct a perspective transformation matrix for image correction. Size correction is then performed using the proportions of road markings in the image and a specified scale, which also enables estimation of the actual width of the selected region. The corrected images are subsequently processed using object detection algorithms to obtain quantitative distress measurements. The proposed method can efficiently perform perspective correction for images collected by the same vehicle camera with minimal manual effort. The measured pavement patch lengths show a trend consistent with pavement friction data. By calibrating vehicle cameras using only image information, this study enables quantitative pavement distress detection without additional field experiments. The approach provides a practical solution for processing large volumes of vehicle-camera data, particularly as connected vehicles generate increasing amounts of uncalibrated roadway imagery.

title: Do Alice and Bob Dream of the Oracle? Wishful Cryptanalysis
abstract: For two millennia, offense and defense have forged cryptographic security boundaries. Tools automated calculation and search, while humans drove discovery. Foundation models now mark a shift from automated computation to intelligent scientific discovery. Because cryptanalysis rests on exact mathematical definitions and immediately executable truth, it offers a proving ground for autonomous intelligence to move past security reliant on scarce human attention and explore structures beyond human working memory. Unguided models stall between two opposite traps: authority hallucination, where they surrender whenever prior literature declares a route blocked, and reasoning hallucination, where they produce subtle, unverifiable flaws. Closed platforms and generic agent loops further impede sustained open inquiry. We introduce wishful cryptanalysis, a harness-agnostic methodology that pairs constructive optimism against entrenched assumptions with blinded, zero-import verification against error. Agents first compress reduced-scale theory within provisioned compute so live witnesses certify their mathematics automatically. They then co-adapt primitive, algorithm, and hardware, and climb parameter ladders toward high-round theory. Applied across frontier open-weight and proprietary models with minimal human intervention beyond targets and compute, this paradigm yielded novel attack techniques and thirteen verifiable practical results across Keccak (SHA-3) and AES. These include breaking a fifteen-year-open public challenge and closing longstanding practical gaps, released alongside an early-preview open-source workbench (agent-framework). Extending Kerckhoffs's principle into the AI era, we envision an Open Oracle, an open and auditable public infrastructure that frees cryptographers to legislate security goals, challenge assumptions, distill theory, and co-design resilient standards.

title: Convex Structure-Preserving EDMD: Passive Koopman Matrices as $Q$-Contractions
abstract: Extended dynamic mode decomposition (EDMD) approximates the Koopman operator using a matrix based on a finite set of observables. However, the least-squares matrix of a port-Hamiltonian (pH) system is generally neither passive nor invariant-preserving. We demonstrate that the implicit midpoint discretization of a lifted pH model precisely preserves energy balance, passivity, and all linear Casimirs for every step size. For a fixed storage metric $Q$, the resulting Koopman matrices are the Cayley transforms of $(J-R)Q$, where $J$ is skew-symmetric and $R$ is positive semidefinite. This set does not depend on the step size and is the closure of all Q-contractions. This set is LMI-representable; therefore, structure-preserving EDMD, including ports through a discrete-time Kalman-Yakubovich-Popov condition and Casimirs through affine constraints, is a semidefinite program. The constrained estimate is a projection of the unconstrained estimate in the data-weighted norm and cannot increase estimation error when the population target is pH-compatible. For every $Q$-contraction, a certified bound on the lifted prediction error grows linearly at most in time, whereas it grows geometrically for unconstrained models with Q-gain above one. Benchmarks on a damped pendulum and a damped rigid body demonstrate that constrained models never generate energy and that imposed Casimirs are maintained with solver accuracy (approximately $10^{-8}$). In contrast, EDMD may diverge or lose the Casimir with noisy data. The benchmarks also demonstrate that when $Q$ is the physical energy, the constrained models are less accurate than EDMD and can exhibit significant structural bias.

title: Boundary of the Lagrange and Markov spectra near Hall's ray
abstract: The Lagrange and Markov spectra, denoted by $L$ and $M$, respectively, are closed subsets of the real line with intricate fractal geometry related to Diophantine approximations. In 1975, Freiman proved that both spectra contain the ray $[c_F,\infty)$, where $c_F=4.527829566\dots$, and that this ray is optimal, as both spectra avoid a tiny interval $(ν_F,c_F)$. Using renormalization techniques and the thickness of Cantor sets, we prove that the boundaries $\partial L$ and $\partial M$ have positive Hausdorff dimensions arbitrarily close to $ν_F$. Furthermore, in connection with Berstein's conjecture, which predicts that $[4.1,4.52]\subset L$, we exhibit a gap in $L$ near $4.08$, the first known gap in the region $L\cap[3.945,4.52]$. We also prove that the boundaries of both spectra have positive Hausdorff dimension near $4.5213$ and $4.08$.

title: Distributed Optimization of $M$-Convex Functions Subject to Linear Constraints via Continuous Relaxation and Shapley-Folkman Decomposition
abstract: $M$-convex functions from discrete convex analysis admit tractable minimization and convex extensions that agree with them at integer points. We study the minimization of a separable collection of $N$ $M$-convex functions subject to $m$ linear coupling constraints. Our two-stage algorithm first solves the convex relaxation and then reconstructs an integer solution through local Carathéodory decompositions and an LP purification step. The returned solution has no objective increase relative to the convex-relaxation value and a coupling residual that is $O(m)$ for bounded coupling coefficients, with no explicit dependence on $N$. We prove polynomial value-oracle evaluation of the $M$-convex extension and give both an exact value-oracle-polynomial implementation and a distributed consensus-ADMM implementation under a proximal oracle. We also establish proximity and additive envelope-gap guarantees when Stage~1 uses a strongly convex extension. On an inventory placement problem with up to about $10^6$ products, both guarantees hold on every run, and the method is faster than exact integer-programming benchmarks by a factor that grows with the number of regions.

title: Exponential decay of the quasilinear Maxwell system caused by conductivity on a collar
abstract: We study the anisotropic, quasilinear Maxwell system on a bounded domain $Ω$ with perfectly conducting boundary conditions. It is damped via a conductivity $σ$ which is strictly positive on its support containing a collar of the boundary. We prove that solutions exist globally and decay exponentially to $0$ if there are no magnetic charges on $Ω$, no electric charges off the support of $σ$, and the initial fields are small. Our approach relies on a splitting of the solution via adapted Helmholtz decompositions and an observability-type estimate for a related system without charges, shown by means of Morawetz multipliers. Moreover, one has to control the space derivatives of the solution by its time derivatives, exploiting the structure of the system. The discontinuity of $σ$ introduces an interface which poses significant challenges in all these steps, besides those coming from the quasilinear terms.

title: AutoOntologyBench: A Task-Grounded Benchmark for Agentic Knowledge Engineering
abstract: Foundation-model agents are increasingly extending beyond software engineering (SWE) into autonomous scientific research, where acquiring and integrating domain knowledge remains a critical challenge. Recent industrial advances have increasingly adopted knowledge graphs and ontology-based semantic layers to organize heterogeneous knowledge into reusable representations. We ask: Can autonomous agents construct ontologies that help them solve real tasks, and do they offer measurable benefits over alternative knowledge representations?
