Our central finding is path-dependence: the same tokenizer fails in opposite ways depending on how its output is used. A supervised attack collapses diagnostic accuracy on the reconstruction path, with ROC AUC falling to $\leq 0.013$ at $ε=2/255$ on all four tokenizers, while sparing the token path. An unsupervised, label-free attack does the reverse; its damage concentrates in the multi-codebook tokenizers, worst in MedITok, whose token-path AUC falls from 0.919 to 0.239. The same label-free attack transfers to LLaVA-Med, a frozen medical vision-language model built on MedITok, making it report proliferative diabetic retinopathy in a healthy retina or call a malignant lesion benign, without access to the question, answer, or language-model gradients. Harm is driven by how far the attack moves the tokenizer's internal representation, not by how many tokens change: on the learned-codebook tokenizers, a control attack that changes nearly all tokens but moves the representation less leaves every path and answer intact. Domain-specific pretraining does not provide robustness: MedITok has the best clean accuracy yet is the most fragile, more so than UniTok, its general-domain counterpart. None of six candidate defenses repairs every failure mode, and several fail once the attacker optimizes against the defense directly. Medical tokenizer robustness must therefore be evaluated per downstream path, against an adaptive adversary.

title: Vision-Language Truck Driving Advisories Grounded in Provincial Rules and Forecast Risks
abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can generate context-aware driving advisories, but their outputs may conflict with road conditions or traffic rules, and they typically address a hazard only once it is visible. This matters for long-haul trucking, where heavy trucks need long stopping distances and a single trip may cross several jurisdictions with different traffic regulations. This paper proposes a data generation and distillation framework that integrates structured scene understanding, risk forecasting, and traffic-rule retrieval to generate truck driving decisions and natural-language advisories, with a consistency check on every record. The records, written by an 8B teacher, are then used to distill a 3B-parameter student model for onboard deployment. We also introduce a dashcam dataset covering four Canadian provinces, comprising 11,142 annotated lane-marking frames and 9,494 driving segments. On held-out driving data across all four provinces, the student passes the consistency check in 94.6% of the segments, against 20.2% for the untuned 8B teacher, and announces 26.2% of the risks in the next 10 to 30 seconds before they appear. Of the generated advisories, 97.7% conform to the provincial traffic rules and guidance. These findings suggest that the framework can produce rule-conforming training data for compact driving advisory models.

title: Multimodal Violence Understanding and Temporal Retrieval in Movies with Adaptive Audio-Visual Fusion
abstract: Violence in films and streaming media remains a concern for audience protection and creates substantial workload for manual content classification. Existing violence-detection methods often rely on limited modalities or short video clips, making it difficult to capture complementary evidence and localise violent events in long, untrimmed videos. In this study, we develop a framework for multimodal video understanding that classifies violence severity, predicts multiple violence types, and locates violent events in time. We combine temporally aligned visual and audio features extracted using pretrained encoders through attention-based adaptive fusion, followed by Transformer-based temporal modelling. Our framework supports three complementary tasks: video-level violence-severity classification, multi-label violence-type prediction, and temporal localisation of violent events. We evaluate the framework on the XD-Violence benchmark and examine its cross-domain performance using AIRTLab. On XD-Violence, our multimodal model achieves 93.27\% severity-classification accuracy and a micro-F1 score of 88.60\% for multi-label violence-type prediction, outperforming the corresponding unimodal configurations. We achieve a mean temporal intersection-over-union (tIoU) of 0.5075 for temporal localisation. Our cross-domain experiments reveal performance degradation under different recording conditions, while our movie case studies demonstrate the framework's potential to retrieve potentially violent scenes for further review. Our results highlight the practical value of multimodal intelligent systems in supporting human reviewers with the identification, classification, and temporal retrieval of violent content in films and streaming media.

title: BehaviorICL: Task-Conditioned Decoder States for Visual In-Context Learning
abstract: The usefulness of an in-context demonstration for a vision-language model (VLM) depends on both the query image and the task posed about it. We study whether the frozen target VLM's own decoder states, read before answer generation, can select such demonstrations. BehaviorICL represents each image and task by a task-conditioned processing signature, the hidden states at the final input position across all decoder layers. Its training-free variant, BehaviorICL-Raw, averages cosine similarities between corresponding layer states and passes the retrieved examples with their reference answers to the same VLM. When the same NICO++ images are asked about their object or their context, Raw retrieves largely different demonstrations for the two questions and outperforms an image retriever given task-matched demonstrations on both VLMs. Across two VLMs and eight classification and visual question answering datasets, Raw gives the highest average accuracy among training-free retrievers on both VLMs and exceeds RICES with a CLIP ViT-L/14 encoder by 3.83 points on Qwen and 1.85 on InternVL. A lightweight shared projection, BehaviorICL-Proj, brings further gains on classification. Analyses of extraction text, decoder depth and bank answers help explain these gains, and attention analysis describes how the task text shifts attention at the extraction position toward the classified object. These results support the target VLM's internal states as a practical basis for visual in-context learning.

title: Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework
abstract: Open-weight models advance transparency, research, and innovation, and spread the benefits of AI more widely. They also carry distinct risks. A release cannot be undone, safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning, and no single party can monitor use or withdraw the model. Managing these risks therefore requires an approach tailored to open release. This framework addresses the governance challenge at the heart of that choice. Co-developed by Concordia AI and Z.AI, it adapts the full risk management lifecycle, from risk assessment to mitigation and governance, to the unique properties of open-weight models. This document does not resolve every tension between openness and safety. Rather, it provides the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation for navigating these tensions. As frontier open-weight releases accelerate, risk management best practice and standards are urgently needed. We invite researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society to build on this framework and advance the science and practice of open-weight AI governance.

title: OSLA: Observation-Aware Local Alignment and Cross-Scene Relation Learning for Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification
abstract: Any-Scenario Person Re-Identification (AS-ReID) aims to retrieve identities across spectral modalities and aerial-ground viewpoints using a unified model. However, changes in viewpoint and spectrum can make local correspondences unreliable, while conventional sampling may omit cross-camera positive relations needed for training. To address these challenges, we propose OSLA, an observation-aware framework built on supervised CLIP-ReID that combines Local Identity Alignment (LIA) and Cross-Scene Relation Learning (CSR). Specifically, LIA uses historical identity observations and competing-identity information to select reliable cross-scene local correspondences while allowing unmatched regions. Local-to-global distillation transfers identity knowledge from correctly classified historical local features into the global representation. CSR couples observed-cell sampling with spectrum-grouped ranking to jointly organize and optimize cross-camera relations. Sampling across two cameras and two spectra provides same- and cross-spectrum positives, while ranking constrains positive-negative scores separately by gallery spectrum on the final retrieval descriptor. Both modules operate only during training, preserving the original visual encoder and retrieval descriptor at inference. Experiments on WHU-MARS-1000 and WHU-MARS-2337 demonstrate that OSLA achieves absolute Rank-1 gains of 5.0% and 4.8% over UAD, respectively, under the AS-ReID protocol. The code will be available.

title: ReSUL: Learning Regional Sensor Utility for Robust Multisensor Semantic Segmentation
abstract: A corrupted sensor observation is not necessarily useless: misalignment can place informative scene structure at the wrong location. Robust multisensor segmentation must determine where to retain this evidence, where to exclude it, and where repair can recover its value. We introduce Regional Sensor Utility Learning (ReSUL), which learns these choices through their effect on segmentation risk. ReSUL compares full-sensor predictions, sensor-exclusion paths, and a re-registration path for displaced thermal inputs. A router predicts each path's signed reduction in category-balanced Brier risk relative to a fixed reference, then uses these estimates to allocate spatial mixture weights. This supervision connects spatial allocation to measurable task benefit without requiring fault labels at inference. MFNet experiments compare project-trained models under eleven clean and disturbed input conditions. ReSUL ranks first in 10 of 11 conditions in both ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-22k comparisons. Under severe thermal displacement, it reaches 54.58% and 55.63% mIoU, exceeding the strongest competing method in each group by 7.19 and 5.63 percentage points. Fixed-bank MFNet ablations show that utility supervision improves all eleven condition means over task-only routing. These results support learning how to use disturbed observations through their regional prediction benefit. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/ReSUL.

title: UbiEnlight: User-Perception-Aware Real-Time Low-Light Video Enhancement on Mobile Devices and Smartglasses
abstract: Low-light video capture is now common on smartphones and wearables, yet dynamic illumination coupled with mobile/werable user motion causes noise, blur, and flicker that make videos hard to perceive and use, especially for users with night blindness and near-eye displays. Prior work enhances frames with post-hoc temporal constraints or optimizes videos directly; however,low-light and motion degradations are spatiotemporally coupled, so post-hoc consistency after per-frame restoration often leaves flicker and motion artifacts. We present UbiEnlight, the first diffusion-transformer-based on-device system for real-time, temporally stable low-light video enhancement. UbiEnlight builds on two insights: (1) illumination and structure separate more robustly in the frequency domain, enabling a spectrum-guided diffusion transformer that injects Fourier amplitude/phase priors to correct illumination while anchoring structure without optical flow; and (2) user perceptual tolerance varies by context, motivating a perception-aware controller that adapts sampling depth, attention reuse, and frame caching at runtime. We implement UbiEnlight on smartphones and smartglasses, and evaluate it against state-of-the-art baselines. UbiEnlight improves temporal stability by up to 54.76% under dynamic/extreme conditions while sustaining real-time on-device performance.

title: Algebras Generated by Two Idempotent Matrices: Classification up to Isomorphism and Applications
abstract: This paper is a continuation of the earlier work by the author and Falguni Roy \cite{biswas2025comprehensive} on the algebra \(\operatorname{alg}(P,Q)\) generated by two idempotent matrices \(P,Q\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\). A complete classification of these algebras up to algebra isomorphism is presented, without imposing any additional restrictions on the idempotents. As an application, group invertibility in \(\operatorname{alg}(P,Q)\) is employed to obtain an explicit solution to a particular system of linear equations.

title: Efficient Memory-Constrained Video Object Segmentation via Subspace Optimization
abstract: Memory-based architectures for video object segmentation (VOS) have achieved remarkable performance by maintaining dense feature representations from past frames in a streaming Memory Bank. However, storing these features over time incurs substantial memory overhead and computational cost. In this work, we identify significant temporal redundancy in memory representations, where consecutive frames exhibit highly overlapping low-rank subspaces that remain stable over time. Building on this observation, we propose Memory Subspace Iteration (MSI), a training-free, model-agnostic plugin that exploits temporal subspace stability to efficiently compress streaming memory features. Extensive experiments on standard VOS benchmarks demonstrate that MSI preserves segmentation accuracy across multiple architectures while reducing the memory bank footprint by up to 25%. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/Hai-Anh-LE/MSI_WACV2027.

title: Shallow may be better: Physics-Constrained Lightweight Networks for High-Throughput Particle Image Velocimetry
abstract: Convolutional networks for optical flow typically adopt progressively deeper pyramidal encoders under the assumption that larger receptive fields improve motion estimation. For particle image velocimetry (PIV), however, tracer-particle displacement between frames is bounded by the acquisition geometry, allowing network depth to be derived from the physically admissible displacement rather than inherited from general-purpose architectures. Using a layer-by-layer analysis of spatial-support growth, we derive its explicit upper bound and show that deeper architectures substantially exceed the support required for PIV, compromising training stability, spatial resolution under particle loss, and inference efficiency. Based on this analysis, we develop LIMA3, a lightweight pyramidal displacement estimator with 589,000 trainable parameters. Across synthetic and experimental benchmarks, LIMA3 matches the accuracy of established learned and classical methods with at least an order of magnitude less memory and substantially higher throughput, while retaining the physically expected coarsening of spatial resolution as tracer information is lost. Its linear memory scaling enables megapixel processing within embedded memory budgets, such that LIMA3 can reach over 900 image pairs per second at $640\times480$~pixel on an RTX 5090 and 99 image pairs per second on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The spatial-support analysis provides a transferable design principle for compact optical-flow architectures and bounded-window attention, offering an alternative to compressing oversized general-purpose networks and enabling efficient operation alongside image acquisition.

title: Every IVUS Frame in Its Place: A Zero-Install Browser Tool for Registering Intravascular Ultrasound to the Coronary Angiogram, and a Path to Angiography-Only Plaque Imaging
abstract: Intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) shows plaque composition, calcium and stent apposition that the coronary angiogram cannot, but relating each IVUS cross-section to its position on the angiogram is still largely done in the operator's head. Commercial co-registration is tied to vendor consoles and to set-up at acquisition, so archived angiograms and pullbacks cannot be co-registered, and paired data for training AI models remain scarce. We present a semi-automatic registration tool that runs entirely in a web browser, with no installation and no upload. The clinician picks a contrast-filled reference frame (aided by automatic contrast and cardiac-phase analysis), selects or traces the vessel centerline (aided by Frangi vesselness and minimal paths), and pins the pullback ends and visible landmarks; a monotone piecewise-linear map then places every IVUS frame on the vessel, and each case exports as a frame-level training record. The original Python analysis runs unchanged in WebAssembly and videos are decoded frame-accurately with WebCodecs. On 6 angiographic runs the in-browser analysis was bit-identical to the server pipeline on identical frames; browser decoding differed by at most 2 grey levels, suggested reference frames agreed in all runs and the default automatic centerline in 4 of 6. A 546-frame pullback decoded in 5.3 s. On 36 phantoms with known ground truth, the clinician-guided trace stayed inside the lumen along 87-99% of the vessel, whereas the fully automatic centerline fell from 83% to 0% as noise rose and contrast fell. In a registered Left Main case, one side-branch landmark moved mid-pullback positions by 17.5% of the segment. We map where AI can enter each step, up to predicting a virtual IVUS from the angiogram alone, and make the tool freely available online with a one-click demo.

title: Teacher-Guided Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction for Egocentric Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.

title: A Multimode-Fiber Speckle Sensing Node with a Press-Robust Quantized Network for Liquid-Cooling Thermal Monitoring
abstract: Liquid-cooled AI and HPC racks concentrate heat at cold plates and manifolds, below the granularity of facility sensors. We present a self-contained edge node that turns one multimode fiber into a distributed thermal-event sensor over nine pipe segments, with a 450 nm laser, a camera and a Zynq UltraScale+ device that captures, infers, displays and reports over MQTT. The speckle decorrelates within tens of seconds at constant temperature, and a press can change it as much as a 1 degree Celsius rise. The node averages each 20 s window and feeds two planes, the mean pattern and a 19-dimensional temporal-feature map, to a 61.6k-parameter int8 convolutional neural network (CNN) that treats presses as hard negatives and runs in the programmable logic at 565 microseconds per frame. On a 59-session, 70,148-window dataset, session-held-out validation gives a pooled AUC of 0.961 against 0.876 for decorrelation, no alarm during the hold or the 45 s rebound in 23 press trials against 6 and 16, and a mean per-fold step detection of 83.8% at 0.4 false alarms per hour.

title: When Recognition Meets Discovery: Learning Need Not Be Entangled in One Representation Space
abstract: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) aims to recognize known classes while discovering novel categories from unlabeled data containing both old and novel samples. Existing methods typically optimize recognition and discovery within a shared representation space, implicitly assuming that the same representation geometry can serve both objectives. Through controlled spectral analysis, we uncover a striking asymmetry: old-class discrimination is increasingly concentrated in the dominant singular directions, while novel-class structure is better preserved in the complementary residual space. More importantly, strengthening the former can even degrade the latter, revealing that recognition and discovery compete for representation capacity rather than merely for optimization weight. Motivated by this observation, we propose Dual-Space Spectral Routing, which dynamically decomposes the representation via online SVD and routes supervised recognition and unsupervised discovery to complementary discriminative and general subspaces. We further exploit their distinct responses to old and novel samples to construct a dual-space novelty signal, which guides Subspace Relation Aggregation (SRA) for organizing candidate novel categories. Extensive experiments across multiple GCD baselines, backbones, and benchmarks demonstrate a consistently improved recognition-discovery balance without introducing additional inference parameters. Code will be open source.

title: VTree: Question-Driven Growth of Hierarchical Memory for Agentic Long-Video Understanding
abstract: Long videos spanning tens of minutes to hours far exceed the context window of today's vision-language models, and the standard remedy of sparse uniform frame sampling discards exactly the fine-grained evidence that specific questions depend on. Existing video agents explore on demand but re-explore from scratch for every question and discard their exploration state once an answer is produced, so per-question cost scales with video length. Hierarchical-memory methods instead fix the scope of each depth in advance and deepen along a pre-committed pyramid rather than toward the question. We observe that a video's coarse structure (where its scenes and topics begin and end) is question-independent, whereas which part a question must zoom into, and how deep, is question-dependent. We propose VTree, which builds a coarse hierarchical memory tree over a video once and then, for each question, grows branches only where that question needs depth. The growth is globally routed so any part of the timeline is reachable, sufficiency-gated so drilling stops when the evidence suffices, and query-conditioned so a branch unfolds into the sub-intervals that answer \emph{this} question. Crucially, every expansion is written back into the video memory, allowing later questions to reuse previously discovered structure and evidence without repeating the corresponding expansion process. Across five long-video understanding benchmarks, VTree consistently improves the accuracy of diverse vision-language backbones while substantially reducing the context length and execution time required for each question.

title: LightOnOCR for AMNLT: Reading Chant Notation and Lyrics in One Pass, from Single Staves to Whole Pages
abstract: Aligned music notation and lyrics transcription (AMNLT) asks for the notes of a chant, its sung text and the assignment of syllables to notes in one output. Fuentes-Martínez et al., who defined the task, found that the one vision-language model they tested fell far behind specialised recognisers. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B, a page OCR model with one billion parameters, end to end, vision encoder included, to write a staff as a GABC string whose letters denote staff positions. Trained on the published AMNLT training split alone, it more than halves the best published aligned music and lyrics error rate (AMLER) on Solesmes, the one directly comparable dataset (9.9 against 21.0 %); on Einsiedeln and Salzinnes, measured in a different encoding, its figures are also lower. The benchmark does not measure generalisation to unseen manuscripts: while the pitch error on AMNLT validation stays between 1.7 and 1.9 %, on 200 staves from five unseen manuscripts it falls from 24.9 to 1.3 % as we add chant aligned through CantusDB, Transkribus ground truth and silver staves kept only where two readers agree. Trained also on multi-staff images, it reads whole pages without staff detection (pitch error 3.3 to 3.8 % on validation and test pages, 1.9 % on pages of unseen manuscripts). Remaining errors include Gothic F clefs read as C clefs, notes dropped with abbreviated or illegible text and lower accuracy on pages with small notation. Controlled ablations are needed to explain the gains.

title: Horizon mergers and initial test-charge acceleration in charged black-hole geometries with anisotropic sources
abstract: We study horizon mergers and the initial radial acceleration of charged test particles in static, spherically symmetric black-hole geometries with a string cloud, a Kiselev power-law component, or a logarithmic profile conventionally. After separating the Maxwell contribution, the effective environmental stress tensors are anisotropic and are not identified with homogeneous quintessence or pressureless cold dark matter. Using a common mass-function formulation, we derive the horizon-merger conditions and classify the Kiselev branches. In this family, the inner-event merger charge provides only an upper bound: three distinct positive horizons can additionally require a positive lower charge bound associated with the event-cosmological merger. For a test particle released from rest relative to a static observer, we derive the local charge-to-mass threshold for outward initial acceleration. Writing $λ=q/μ$ and $z=Q/Q_{\rm ext}$, where $Q_{\rm ext}$ is the inner-event merger charge, the subextremal string-cloud threshold has infimum $1/z$, approached only at infinity. For the subextremal logarithmic profile, the threshold exceeds unity throughout the finite exterior and attains a finite global minimum. For $α/M=0.4$ and $Q/M=1.2$, this minimum is $λ_*\simeq1.251125$. In a nondegenerate Kiselev static patch, the neutral balance radius is unique and radially unstable. Density matching supplies conditional profile normalizations, not observational fits. For the logarithmic profile, the integration parameter is distinguished from the mass combination inferred from circular motion. These results characterize geometric horizon bounds and test-particle dynamics; they do not establish a two-black-hole force law or a mechanism for cosmic acceleration, nor do they constitute a test of the Weak Gravity Conjecture.

title: Auditing two-stage MS/MS molecular retrieval on MassSpecGym v1.5: Reranking gains, candidate priors and spectrum dependence
abstract: Two-stage retrieval of molecular structures from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) can benefit from candidate reranking, but benchmark gains may also reflect candidate priors, replicate spectra, precursor mass, and training-set coverage. We audit a two-stage retrieval system on the official MassSpecGym v1.5 split (17,556 test spectra). A data-safe DreaMS encoder and composite molecular fingerprints provide an initial shortlist; a support-gated reranker combines pair scores, candidate-relative peak coverage, and mass-feasibility features. The final system achieves 31.05% Recall@1, a 10.05-point gain over its Stage 1 ensemble, while preserving its 72.62% Recall@20. Replacing the query spectrum with one from a different molecule matched on adduct and precursor mass reduces Recall@1 by 9.0 points (15.3 points under molecule-balanced weighting); nevertheless, a training-mean spectrum retains 13.75% Recall@1, indicating substantial spectrum-independent signal. Mass-feasibility features improve Recall@1 beyond score and coverage controls, while learned peak-fragment similarities do not outperform constant coverage. Errors cluster by molecule, and removing close training neighbours causes a large decline in Stage 1 shortlist recall among initially well-covered molecules. We conclude that candidate-relative mass-feasibility evidence improves front-rank retrieval and spectrum dependence, but does not establish learned structural discrimination or eliminate candidate priors. Evaluation should separately assess shortlist reachability, spectrum dependence, and molecule-level generalization.

title: ORDO: Fine-Grained Motion Understanding in Video LLMs via Order-Dependent Supervision
abstract: Video large language models (video LLMs) answer a wide range of questions about real videos, yet they remain weak at fine-grained motion such as whether an object speeds up or slows down. Existing methods train these models on synthetic motion clips, on order pretext tasks such as reordering shuffled clips, or with rewards that compare ordered and perturbed frames. None of them requires that the label be unrecoverable from the frames once their order is discarded, so a model can fit such data from static cues without learning to use frame order. We propose ORDO, a framework that builds this requirement into the training data. We define order-necessary supervision as data in which the unordered set of frames has the same distribution under competing labels, and we realise it for motion attributes with three constructions, time-reversal pairing, matched spatial extent and uniform interval coverage. A procedural curriculum of six motion primitives instantiates these constructions, and low-rank adapters of the language model are trained on it with an answer-level objective and self-distillation replay on real videos. With 4,000 synthetic clips, ORDO raises the mean accuracy over four motion benchmarks by +7.6, +4.9 and +5.1 points on Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3-VL-8B and Molmo2-8B, while the same training with shuffled frames changes it by less than one point. Code and generator will be made publicly available.

title: Causal Dioramas: Controllable Video Generation, Revision and Editing via Intervention
abstract: Two centuries ago, an early cinema-like theater called the Diorama could already control its scenes at will. Today's video generation models produce videos of near-cinematic quality, yet they still lack this controllability. This limitation stems from the inherent semantic gap between text and pixels, since a prompt can describe a video only coarsely and leaves its details and relations beyond control. We bring this ability to video generation with Causal Dioramas, modules that decompose a video into a concept graph of variables that can be intervened on individually. Each instruction is translated into an intervention on the concept graph, modifying the specified concepts and their dependents. A connector then conveys this intervention to the video generator, which reuses the original noise to produce a counterfactual video while preserving all other content. Building on Causal Dioramas, we develop a unified framework for controllable generation, counterfactual revision of generated videos and editing of real videos. We outperform both open-source and commercial models in controllability on T2V-CompBench, CoVEBench and OpenVE-Bench.

title: VidRouteBench: A Benchmark for Budgeted Video-Generation Routing
abstract: Text-to-video generators differ by two orders of magnitude in price, and a cheap configuration of a strong model is often good enough for a prompt. Routing prompts across such arms (model x sampling configuration) should buy quality at fixed budget, but no dataset supports studying it: public video-preference sets contain only closed models, one configuration each. We release VidRouteBench: 16 arms from 7 open families spanning 121x in measured cost ($0.0025-$0.298 per clip), 27,110 clips (1,421 A800-hours) over 1,625 grouped prompts, a quality score frozen after calibration against human preferences (68.7% CV accuracy vs 66.2% for the best single scorer), per-clip scores on 9 identifiable quality dimensions, repeated seeds, an encrypted test split, and a sealed newest family for cold start. The evaluator compares a router against the best prompt-agnostic mixture of arms, not the best single arm. Per-prompt specialisation here is real and predictable (oracle gap 0.642, 47% reproducible across seeds, prompt-arm interaction F=4.47 at p=1.6e-63), unlike LLM-routing arms, where the same pipeline finds none. We then propose OPMU (one probe, many utilities): label a new arm on K probe prompts, predict its 9 dimensions once, and serve any scenario utility by scalarising afterwards. Over 215 utility directions OPMU Pareto-dominates the prompt-agnostic baseline for 94% of directions versus 90% for per-scenario routers, with no per-scenario retraining. Three baselines fail instructively: bag-of-words features lose almost all routing gain in the low-data regime (0.009 vs 0.168); crediting a new arm with its probe average is harmful (-3.32 recovery) although it is the strong baseline on RewardBench-style arms (0.786); Chebyshev scalarisation does not help, our cost-utility front being convex.

title: You Only Think Once: Rescuing Hybrid Vision-Language Models Lost in Thought
abstract: Thinking at length before answering is expected to strengthen the visual reasoning of vision-language models (VLMs), yet hybrid VLMs often get lost in thought: their thoughts loop or exhaust the budget without an answer, so thinking can score below answering directly. Existing early-exit methods watch a thought for the moment its answer is ready and force the answer out of it, but in a hybrid VLM that moment often never comes. We find that the remedy is not to stop a failing thought earlier, but to stop taking its answer: once a thought is given up, the model's own direct answers decide. Based on this, we propose **YOTO (You Only Think Once)**, a method that answers first and thinks at most once. YOTO draws direct answers until a probe-weighted vote settles; only an unsettled problem receives a single thought, which a failure head on the hidden state monitors and stops as soon as it predicts failure, handing the problem back to direct answers. At a matched 20k-token budget, YOTO is up to 5.9 points more accurate than the strongest early-exit baseline, using one failure-head threshold across model sizes. Keeping the released weights frozen, it adds only two linear probes. On the full MathVision benchmark, YOTO improves Qwen3.5-2B from 40.1% to 57.3% and Qwen3.5-4B from 68.3% to 73.7%, above the 72.8% that Qwen3.5-9B, a model more than twice its size, reaches with thinking. Its gains carry over to five further benchmarks and a second model family. These results suggest that hybrid VLMs reason better by answering first and thinking once than by thinking longer.

title: Scale-Aware Reference Attention for Mannequin-to-Model Gown Generation
abstract: Formal gowns are sold online with photos of models wearing them, and buyers zoom in to inspect sequins, lace and beading. Image editors can turn a photo of a gown on a mannequin into a convincing photo of a person wearing it, but they receive every reference photo without any notion of its magnification, and the fine detail of the gown is lost when the output is viewed up close. We propose scale-aware reference attention (SARA), which tells an open diffusion transformer the zoom level of the output and of every reference photo, biases the attention of the output toward references of a similar zoom level, uses macro photos of the fabric as references, and is trained on a mix of whole-garment and zoomed targets. To train and evaluate it, we introduce Kiss3000, a dataset of 915 high-resolution mannequin photos and 2274 on-model photos of formal gowns with cross-domain pairs and splits by style, and zoom-crop evaluation, which compares garment crops at full, half and local scale without pixel alignment and judges local fidelity with two vision-language models gated on control crops. With this protocol, Nano Banana Pro at 4K, the highest-resolution commercial editor we test, loses or redraws local detail on 14 of 20 test gowns. At 1536x2048 pixels, both judges prefer SARA over a LoRA fine-tuning baseline on 18 test items and the baseline on 6 (p=0.023), and over the base model on 26 against 4 (p=5.9e-5), while SARA keeps the gown design as often as the baseline.

title: VideoGym: An Adaptive RL Environment for Long-Video Agents
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains video agents to locate sparse evidence for long-video question answering through structured memory retrieval and temporal re-observation. This training, however, faces a long-tail modality distribution in the data. In our source pool, text-heavy questions account for 58% of samples, compared with 15% graph-heavy, 17% visual-heavy, and 10% time-range questions. Fixed-distribution RL therefore allocates fewer rollouts to underperforming question types. Reweighting these types could increase their sampling frequency but repeatedly reuses the same finite banks of original questions. To solve this problem, we introduce VideoGym, a curriculum-based RL environment that jointly constructs video-grounded training tasks and allocates rollouts among them. Within the environment, a memory-augmented VideoAgent is trained to coordinate retrieval from text, graph, and visual memories with temporal re-observation. Across episodes, VideoGym adapts VideoAgent's training distribution online: it casts per-period sample selection as an adversarial bandit over (modality, mode) arms and applies the EXP3 update to shift sampling toward arms with low answer accuracy. To supply the augmented-mode arms, a TaskGenerator-Verifier pipeline produces harder variants of existing questions that remain answerable within the same video. Across five long-video benchmarks, VideoGym lifts RL accuracy from 60.4% to 64.8% on average and by up to 10.5 pp on underrepresented graph-heavy questions with 3.3x sample efficiency. Together, these results show that task expansion and adaptive allocation can improve video agent learning from limited, imbalanced training data.

title: ABCoord: An Artificial Bee Colony (ABC)-Based Decentralized Distributed Two-Layer Decision-Making Architecture for the Coordination of AI Agents
abstract: Rapid progress in large language models (LLMs) is turning AI agents into multi-agent systems that jointly solve complex tasks, and the architecture that coordinates the agents toward a common goal is gaining fundamental importance in these systems. Since centralized architectures can become bottlenecks as the number of agents grows, whereas distributed architectures incur increasing communication costs, a decentralized coordination architecture that scales with low communication cost is needed. Recently, the structure of the artificial bee colony (ABC) algorithm has been defined for the first time as a two-layer decentralized information-processing and decision-making architecture. ABCoord is built on this proposed architecture. The results show that ABCoord, used for the coordination of AI agents, performs at a level comparable to existing architectures on the BigCodeBench benchmark in the self-test condition, in which the tests are also written by the language model. In the oracle condition, in which the solutions are evaluated with the official tests, the number of solved problems increases considerably.

title: Intervene or Trust CLIP? Competence-Gated Adaptation for Source-Free Cross-Domain Few-Shot Learning
abstract: Source-free cross-domain few-shot learning (SF-CDFSL) adapts a pre-trained vision-language model such as CLIP to a distant target domain from a handful of labeled images, without access to source data. Recent methods improve the fine-tuning of CLIP with token-level interventions and apply them in the same way to every target domain. In this paper, we find that whether an intervention helps depends on how well frozen CLIP already recognizes the target domain: in 5-way 1-shot tasks, intervening improves accuracy by 0.72 points where frozen CLIP misclassifies most support images, but lowers it by 1.31 points where frozen CLIP already classifies them well, and the support set of a single episode suffices to tell the two cases apart; a bias-variance analysis explains both. Based on this finding, we propose Competence-Gated Adaptation (CoGA), which measures frozen CLIP's accuracy and margin on the labeled support set and decides, before training, whether to intervene on the visual tokens or to trust CLIP by fusing the adapted prediction with the frozen one. CoGA adds no trainable parameters and uses no query labels. On the four BSCD-FSL target domains, CoGA achieves the best average accuracy, 59.56% (1-shot) and 68.96% (5-shot), outperforms ATHA and TIR by at least 2.82 and 1.39 points on the same episodes, and consistently improves three further backbones, three parameter-efficient fine-tuning frameworks and five further target domains.

title: Gradient-Free Few-Shot Adaptation of Vision Models via Agentic Coding
abstract: Adapting a vision model to new classes from a few labeled images usually relies on gradient fine-tuning, which is unstable with so few images. We ask whether a coding agent can replace gradient descent for this task. We propose the Agent edit, a method in which a coding agent writes a program that sets the new class weights in the class head of a frozen COCO-trained detector, with no gradient step. The agent runs the detector on the labeled images a limited number of times and sees how much its edit lowers COCO mAP; the program rebuilds the weights without the agent. In the same head and with the same labels, the Agent edit outperforms full-decoder fine-tuning at five shots on 2 of four fine-grained sets, by 11.2 and 12.3 F1 points, and ties on the rest. At ten shots, fine-tuning ties with or outperforms it. Moreover, when the new classes are scored jointly with the COCO classes, the AP of the COCO class to which they belong falls by up to 33.3 points, and limiting that loss lowers F1 on the new classes. Most of the agent's programs share three parts, which we write as a formula that needs no agent. A classifier on frozen backbone features reaches a higher F1 than every method inside the head on every set. Hence a coding agent can replace gradient descent only in part: inside the head and at five shots.

title: Curvature-history tensor memory in inflationary cosmology: Component closure, ghost-free dynamics, and CMB BipoSH likelihood
abstract: We present a generally covariant inflationary model in which curvature history activates a spatial symmetric-tracefree tensor-memory order parameter and generates a scale-dependent quadrupolar departure from primordial statistical isotropy. The curvature source is the four-dimensional Gauss--Bonnet completion of the Kretschmann invariant. A local $(C,χ)$ representation is used only to implement the retarded theory: fixed retarded Cauchy data remove the homogeneous response modes, so the negative-sign localized combination is not an independent phase-space degree of freedom. The projected tensor sector is described by the dressed field $Q_{μν}=\mathcal E_C\widehat Q_{μν}$ with $\mathcal E_C=\exp[B(C)\Box_{\widehat Q}/2]$. Its raw-field Hessian has the exact congruence form $\mathcal E_C^\dagger(\Box_Q-\mathsf M^2)\mathcal E_C$, so an invertible dressing preserves the solution count and the sign of the physical symplectic norm even when $[B(C),\Box_Q]\ne0$. We derive the full quadratic Hessian, eliminate the ADM constraints and retarded response variables through an exact block Schur complement, and obtain the leading anisotropic curvature action. A nonlinear ADM Legendre analysis shows that the representative inflationary solution remains far from the singular threshold associated with an Ostrogradsky branch. A smooth curvature-dependent phase potential gives an approximately constant activated plateau with subdominant memory energy. Finite activation then produces an infrared-regular oscillatory primordial quadrupole and an exact scale-dependent $T/E$ BipoSH covariance. We also give the corresponding cut-sky Gaussian and quadratic maximum-likelihood estimators.

title: Cyclic Discrete Diffusion: A Novel Multi-Class Segmentation Refinement Technique
abstract: We cast image segmentation refinement as a discrete diffusion process. To solve this task we introduce Cyclic Discrete Diffusion (CDD), a novel forward-reverse formulation with a cyclic label topology that maps a discrete label set to the uniform distribution and back. Instead of injecting Gaussian noise as is done for continuous diffusion, CDD evolves segmentation masks through label jumps: at each step, every pixel either remains in its current class or jumps to the next label with a fixed rate. This jump-or-stay mechanism defines a finite-state Markov process with bounded forward and reverse steps, featuring analytically consistent and tractable reverse dynamics. CDD operates natively in a multi-class label space, enabling joint refinement of all classes in a single pass without requiring class-wise decomposition, as commonly needed in prior binary refinement approaches. The proposed formulation admits a finite and controllable number of refinement steps, for which we analyze the convergence properties through spectral gap analysis. We evaluate CDD across diverse segmentation tasks, including multi-class semantic, instance-level, and binary segmentation refinement. Our method consistently improves both region accuracy and boundary quality across multiple backbones and datasets.

title: Covering hypercubic grids by polygonal trails: capacity bounds and the optimum for $P(4,3)$
abstract: The classical nine-dot puzzle asks for a polygonal trail through a square grid using as few segments as possible. We study its higher-dimensional analogue on $P(n,k):=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}^k$ for integers $n,k\ge2$, allowing arbitrary real vertices and unrestricted segment directions, and denote the minimum number of segments by $h(n,k)$. For $n\ge3$ and $k\ge2$, we give a geometric proof of the previously stated capacity bound: a trail of $r\ge1$ segments meets at most $1+r(n-1)$ grid points. Refinements of this bound, combined with exhaustive finite checks, establish $h(4,3)=23$ and $h(5,3)\ge32$. We also exhibit a $22$-segment trail through $63$ points of $P(4,3)$, the maximum possible, and a $23$-segment covering trail contained in $[0,4]^3$, which settles the corresponding box-constrained problem. The general capacity theorem, a large-grid lower bound refuting a previously proposed formula for $h(n,k)$, and the boxed construction are verified by the Lean 4 kernel, whereas the finite exclusions use native reflection and additionally trust the native compiler and runtime. A companion technical note provides the computational specification and reproducible proof artifacts.

title: Green ACO: An Energy-Aware Ant Colony Optimisation for the MAX-SAT Problem with EI/J Scheduling and Thompson Sampling
abstract: NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems demand heavy computation, and this raises real environmental concerns, especially in regions with carbon-intensive power grids. This paper presents Green ACO, an energy-aware Ant Colony Optimisation algorithm for the MAXIMUM SATISFIABILITY (MAX-SAT) problem. At its core is an Expected Improvement per Joule (EI/J) scheduler. At every iteration, it picks the operator that best balances expected quality gain against expected energy cost. Three operators feed the scheduler: WalkSAT, Focused Variable Neighbourhood Search, and Clause-Restart Greedy, ranging from cheap and surgical to aggressive and costly. An offline dual-regime profiling phase calibrates these operators before the search even begins, and, combined with Thompson sampling, this reduces uninformed early operator choices; online call-count warm-up still occurs. A pre-dispatch guard rejects calls when their estimated energy cost, with a safety multiplier, exceeds the remaining budget. Sparse pheromone updates, pheromone caching across budgets, and stagnation-based early stopping trim energy use further, without hurting solution quality. The framework also incorporates a budget predictor that estimates the energy budget required for unseen instances. On four hard MAX-SAT reference instances, Green ACO reaches an average quality of 98.44%. This beats the standard ACO baselines by close to 3 points, while using only 986 J against 4,171 to 6,610 J for the strongest competitors, a six-and-a-half-fold gain in quality per joule. Under the Algerian grid's carbon intensity, this cuts CO$_2$e emissions by approximately 85% compared with the most energy-hungry baseline.

title: Tangent incompleteness under coupled image transformations: margin reconstruction and decision consequences
abstract: Can accurate responses to individual geometric image transformations recover their combined effect on a classifier's decision? For identity-aligned bilinear resampling, coordinatewise assembly may fail at first order. Projecting the implemented transformation onto a fixed logit-margin gradient, we derive a linear term plus signed absolute-value ridges. An exact even--odd identity and ridge-cancellation conditions characterize the missing information. Under independent parameter laws, a noncancelling off-coordinate ridge obstructs even unrestricted additive fits. The coupled correction has $O(s^2)$ projected error, versus a possible $Θ(s)$ axiswise defect; transfer to realized network margins requires local smoothness. Projected RMS errors fall by 82.96% on CIFAR-10 and 82.38% on ImageNetV2 relative to axiswise assembly; realized fixed-pair margin RMS errors fall by 39.75% and 42.73%. The representation prospectively identifies nine strict nonadditive network-margin sign configurations and permits exact minimization of a three-parameter threat surrogate, with conditional selection-regret guarantees. In an independent CIFAR-10 search, coupled-selected transformations uncover 51 top-1 changes versus 41 for axes. On 256 independent ImageNetV2/ConvNeXt-Tiny images and 16,384 transformed decisions at the prespecified scale $s=.40$, multiclass top-1 flip-prediction errors fall from 11.97% to 10.23% (paired improvement 1.74 percentage points; 95% interval [0.93, 2.61]). Directional finite differences are slightly more accurate (10.00%) at higher measured model-construction cost. These results connect first-order sampling interactions to margin reconstruction, decision prediction, and threat selection, without claiming finite-scale network certification.

title: GC-GS: Optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting with Gradient Conflict as a Geometry Signal
abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is commonly optimized with multiple reconstruction losses, which naturally forms a multi-objective optimization problem. This issue becomes more pronounced when perceptual losses are introduced to improve visual quality, as different objectives may impose competing update directions on Gaussian primitives and make it difficult to simultaneously improve fidelity, perceptual quality, and representation efficiency. Based on this view, we reformulate 3DGS training as a multi-objective optimization problem and derive selective conflict-aware position updates that reduce interference between competing objectives while preserving the contribution of each loss. We further observe that gradient conflicts persist throughout training and are most severe in Gaussian position parameters, indicating that objective conflict is closely tied to geometry optimization. We therefore treat position-gradient conflict as a geometry-aware signal to guide densification and pruning. Experiments show that our method achieves better rendering performance while improving representation compactness and rendering efficiency over existing 3DGS variants.

title: ROSE-SAM3: Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for Open-Vocabulary Remote Sensing Segmentation
abstract: In open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS) of remote-sensing imagery, class-name prompts can miss objects with varied appearances, while richer descriptions can activate competing classes. We propose Response-Oriented Prompt Selection for SAM 3 (ROSE-SAM3), a training-free framework that selects descriptions using frozen SAM 3 responses on unlabeled target-domain images. We screen candidate descriptions for coverage beyond the native prompts while protecting reliable native class responses, retaining candidates that pass these checks on at least four of five image folds. An offline directed acyclic graph (DAG) search then evaluates candidate combinations and builds a compact PromptBank for each class. Each bank retains the native prompts and adds selected descriptions, which we call residual prompts. At inference, the bank is fixed, and Semantic-Instance Cooperative Head (SICH) uses instance evidence to refine semantic responses before assigning pixel labels. We also introduce RS-OVSS-C to evaluate robustness under six image corruption families across eight remote-sensing datasets, preserving their class vocabularies and reference labels. ROSE-SAM3 achieves 57.3% mean mIoU across eight clean benchmarks and 54.7% on RS-OVSS-C, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/YanghuiSong/ROSE-SAM3.

title: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Bone Scaffold Pore Detection: A Comparative Analysis of Few-Shot Performance
abstract: Evaluating the mechanical properties of bone scaffolds conventionally requires destructive testing or costly Finite Element Analysis, while deep learning alternatives are constrained by the scarcity of labeled biomaterial imaging data. This study introduces the first expert-annotated, pixel-dense dataset of biopolymer bone-scaffold SEM images, spanning five magnification series, and uses it to benchmark two state-of-the-art pre-trained foundation models under a 12-shot fine-tuning regime. SAM3, an instance segmenter, and YOLOv26, a bounding-box detector, feed the predicted pore geometry to regression heads that estimate Young's modulus and compressive yield strength. Our central finding is that both models fail by pore density rather than magnification: YOLOv26's predicted pore counts saturate and porosity estimation collapses on the most crowded frames, whereas SAM3 over-fragments sparse pore fields and merges adjacent pores in dense ones, producing eight catastrophic failures against three for YOLOv26. Averaged across the 44-image evaluation set, YOLOv26 achieves lower porosity error (19.9% vs. 23.1% MAE), higher precision, and a higher F1 score, whereas SAM3 offers pixel-level instance segmentation that YOLOv26's bounding boxes cannot reproduce. We conclude that model selection should be driven by pore density rather than SEM magnification alone.

title: Temporal Persistence for Stylized Rendering: Historical Image Storage and Reconstruction
abstract: The overlapping silhouettes and gradual fading in The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask (released April 27, 2000) produce a distinctive depiction of motion blur, in which earlier scene states remain visible as part of the current image. Reproducing this appearance in a modern renderer involves decisions about when historical images are sampled, how their contributions are retained, and how the resulting history can be represented within the available memory and processing budget. In this paper, we investigate these decisions through complete image histories, shared image regions, and selectively retained pixel changes, using Godot engine implementations evaluated against independently composited references. For a ten-image history sampled at 20 Hz on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti, half-float storage halves history allocation and reduces median storage-pass duration by factors of 2.40 at 720p and 1.73 at 1080p, preserving the supplied source precision. The adaptive experiments examine how memory savings depend on reconstruction metadata and allocation, including a sparse representation that reduces allocation by 83.81% at low resolution with 445.25 times the GPU duration.

title: NOVA: Normalization-Aware Output-Guided Attention Acceleration for Video Diffusion Transformers
abstract: Video diffusion transformers (vDiTs) have become the main backbone for video generation. The quadratic cost of self-attention limits their efficiency at high resolutions and long durations. Existing sparse attention methods often rely on preserving high attention weights. However, these criteria do not fully capture the fidelity of the final value-weighted output, whose error depends jointly on changes to the attention numerator and the softmax denominator. We propose NOVA, a coarse-to-fine sparse attention framework that first approximates the full normalized output using size-weighted key/value centroids. Building on this estimate, we construct a residual proxy that accounts for coupled numerator-denominator errors by centering value contributions around the estimated output. This proxy guides the selection of query-key blocks for refinement under a predefined block budget for each query cluster. Selected blocks are evaluated through exact token-level computation, while the remaining blocks contribute through their centroids under a shared softmax normalization. On five vDiTs, NOVA achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS among sparse attention methods, improving PSNR by up to 1.55\,dB over the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 1.82$\times$ end-to-end speedup on an H100 GPU.

title: Is It the Agent or the Retry? Separating Selection from Agency in Text-to-Image Generation
abstract: Agentic text-to-image systems wrap generators in loops of planning, routing, verification and refinement, and report large gains on compositional benchmarks, almost always relative to a single sample. We ask how much of the gain survives against Single-tool Rejection Retry (\ours): the strongest generator already in the system's pool, an off-the-shelf verifier, and retries that stop at the first accepted image under the system's own budget. Auditing four recent systems with official evaluators, we find that on GenEval SRR matches the accuracy of OctoT2I (0.962 vs.\ 0.96), recovers 63 to 90% of the gain of GEMS depending on the verifier, and exceeds GenPilot by 12 points with 2.3 generations per image; the effect persists with generators not tuned to the benchmark and on T2I-CompBench++. A closed-form analysis predicts the accuracy of SRR at every budget and shows that its gain is capped by the verifier's likelihood ratio. The same analysis also exposes genuine agentic gains: on GenEval 2, even the best of five samples chosen by the evaluator stays 15 points below the score GEMS reports (12 at the upper end of its 95% interval). We prove a ceiling on the accuracy that routing across generators can add, bracket it between one and three points on OctoT2I's own pool, and show that what OctoT2I's routing buys is compute (about 2.5 less than SRR at equal accuracy), not accuracy. In our offline distillation experiments selected samples teach the generator no more than random ones, which a short information argument explains. We end with a reporting checklist for agentic generation papers.

title: PhoneQC: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Order-Level Smartphone Trade-in Inspection
abstract: As vision-language models enter remote smartphone trade-in, sellers already upload six views and a diagnostic screen, which makes it easy to treat the human quote as a step a model can take over. A model may mark a crack or read the screen, yet the quote is a staff form: appearance fill stays near 0.25, and the closed models that score a little higher do so only on the orders they answer, so human appraisal remains necessary. Two obstacles stand in the way. (1) Single-view defect sets and attribute benchmarks do not score an order-level form under a fixed input contract, so a box or a leaked field can be mistaken for a finished quote. (2) The unread half of the form is the staff fields, and a model left to emit boxes or captions does not learn them. We present PhoneQC, a 335-order iPhone-heavy cut that ranks systems by a 0 to 100 form score (Score100) only inside matched protocols (images alone; images plus a detector sidecar), with a declared upper bound that is not ranked as a peer. As a case study on that board, field-only LoRA freezes the backbone, adapts attention projections, and supervises staff fields while leaving the defect list empty; the adapter sees the same images as the zero-shot model. On image-only T1 the 3B model rises from 26.6 to 33.3 at coverage 0.928; without the empty-blocker item the open ranking still favors the adapter, while the remaining gap to a person stays large on this cut.

title: StateBind: Exposing the Symbol-to-State Binding Gap in Visual Measurement
abstract: Reliable vision systems should connect numerical claims to visible evidence. In visual measurement, this requires mapping candidate values to image-specific physical states. StateBind-200 augments 200 real images with human-refined local geometry and matched Numeric, Calibrated, and Physicalized interfaces. Across a 128-image held-out evaluation and 6,696 controlled calls, physicalizing identical candidates raises three-model majority accuracy from 75.54% to 91.13%, a source-image-balanced gain of +15.30 points. Calibration and additional reasoning leave most of the gap intact; target localization can succeed despite incorrect value-lattice binding, with a larger burden for two-endpoint ruler spans. An independent 40-image geometry audit yields a 0.08-tick median target discrepancy and preserves the main effect under disagreement sensitivity. We further propose Factorial StateBind, a training-free selective verifier. Two VLMs propose target and lattice components, an independent VLM validates their evidence, and valid combinations are resolved deterministically. A precision mode selected on 69 development images combines component validity, four-way agreement, and state separation. Applied unchanged to held-out evaluation, this high-precision evidence gate reaches 91.67% candidate precision across 36/128 images (28.12%) and 9.68% of ordered cells. The results identify instance-specific symbol-to-state binding as a distinct reliability bottleneck and provide an interpretable evidence gate for numerical visual claims.

title: Seeing Beyond Pixels: Radar Feature Generation from Images and Sparse Returns
abstract: Camera-radar fusion benefits from complementary visual and geometric information but often relies on complete radar representations, leading to substantial computing overhead. However, the extent to which visual information can compensate for limited radar measurements remains insufficiently explored. Therefore, we propose Vision-informed Radar Token Generation (VRTG), which exploits cross-modal information to generate task-relevant radar features from camera images and sparse radar measurements. Specifically, VRTG first leverages image-derived object cues to select a limited number of informative radar points. It then establishes calibrated one-to-one associations between visual objects and radar returns, using matched measurements to refine object ranges while retaining visual estimates for unmatched objects. Finally, the associated object features and visual context are transformed into radar tokens compatible with existing camera-radar fusion networks. Experiments on RADIal demonstrate that VRTG achieves 90.76\% vehicle-detection F1 and 86.68\% free-space mIoU using only four radar points per frame, approaching the performance of the full-radar model.

title: Separating Module Gain From Transport Plan Contribution in Audio-Visual Dynamic Facial Expression Recognition
abstract: A cross-modal routing module can improve over its backbone while its transport plan accounts for no demonstrable part of that improvement. In ABVnet with DFEW, Sinkhorn cross-modal routing (SCR) exceeds the retrained baseline by 0.87 unweighted average recall (UAR) points, a resolved difference, yet sits 0.17 points above an individually trained, parameter-matched pooled variant, an unresolved difference that establishes no equivalence; under the development protocol the comparison with the baseline reverses. Separating the two needs comparisons a module-against-backbone test cannot supply: parameter-matched variants changing only the plan rule, and interventions replacing the plan without retraining. The evaluation covers MMA-DFER and ABVnet on DFEW and MAFW, and MMA-DFER on CREMA-D, with a single training run per configuration and paired fold intervals. ABVnet with DFEW motivated the follow-up after the broader results were available. Replacing the plan everywhere with a uniform one reduces UAR by 0.72, whereas permuting its rows gives an unresolved difference of -0.20 UAR points; permutation is less damaging by 0.51 UAR points, a resolved contrast. Replacing the plan with the product of its own marginals, preserving both marginals and removing only frame-specific mixtures, reduces UAR by 0.70. These reductions concern reliance at inference; attribution of the module gain to the transport plan remains unestablished. Under the 1.5 fold-dependence widening, the baseline gain remains resolved, whereas the replacement reductions and the paired contrast are unresolved.

title: In-pixel lock-in readout for wide-field nitrogen-vacancy radio-frequency spectrum analysis
abstract: The growing use of radio-frequency (RF) technologies requires compact, room-temperature sensors that can analyze a wide RF band in real time. Here we present a quantum RF spectrum analyzer based on the gradient-encoded electron spin resonance of a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) ensemble in diamond and read out with a $512\times542$-pixel lock-in camera that demodulates the signal in each pixel. On/off keying the signal under test at the camera's reference frequency lets every pixel extract the spin-resonant photoluminescence modulation. Before digitization, each pixel suppresses the static background and low-frequency noise that limit conventional camera readout. Translating a single permanent magnet tunes the encoded band continuously from 10~MHz to 32~GHz. The magnet position establishes a trade-off between instantaneous bandwidth (up to 4~GHz) and frequency resolution (7--22~MHz), with a 5~ms readout time. The wide-field readout integrates all spectral channels in parallel in a room-temperature sensor head and requires no phase synchronization to the RF carrier. The SNR remains above 70 at an applied power as low as $-32.5$~dBm. The magnetic-field configuration can be adapted to different RF bands without changing the pixel-parallel readout.

title: RALC: Risk-Controlled Local Adoption of Segmentation Updates with Few Calibration Images
abstract: Fine-tuning a road-scene segmenter for rain and nighttime driving can introduce errors on normal daytime images. With few labeled normal images for calibration, a whole-image risk check may reject changes that would pass if adopted locally. Risk-Controlled Adoption of Label Changes (RALC) selects local changes from a fixed model update, using confidence differences and an image score to form nested candidates. On each normal calibration image, RALC measures how many more errors each candidate makes than the original model, assigning zero loss when errors stay the same or fall. At test time, each replacement can add at most one error, so the replacement count bounds the net increase without test labels. RALC combines this candidate-dependent bound with recorded calibration losses to select the largest set that passes the risk check. If the models and adoption rules are fixed before calibration and normal calibration and test images are exchangeable, the expected per-image loss stays within budget. On held-out BDD100K, we evaluated three weight-interpolated updates with 10 additional normal images per calibration draw. At a common fixed budget, adverse-scene mIoU was 1.89--3.19 percentage points higher with RALC than with whole-image adoption, while measured mean normal loss was also higher. After matching this loss post hoc at 1,000 pixels per image, RALC still led by 1.135--2.428 points. Selecting changes in $8\times8$-pixel cells recovered 93--98% of this advantage. With 250 calibration images at the original budget, both rules adopted all three updates in full.

title: Seeing the Invisible: How Vision-Language Models Read, Predict and Trace Radio Fields
abstract: Operating in the physical world requires reasoning beyond what cameras directly capture. In a city, radio signals are invisible to the lens, yet their strength is governed by the buildings and streets an image does show. Given only these visible structures, can vision-language models (VLMs) infer the invisible radio field they shape? Probing true physical reasoning requires exact fields in real cities, alongside controlled interventions where a single physical factor changes. We build a label-free engine that turns any coordinate on Earth into a ray-traceable city, simulates matched single-factor counterfactuals, and computes every answer exactly. This yields RadioVISTA, a benchmark and training dataset for visual reasoning about invisible fields. Physically, a radio field is the sum of its propagation paths, yet across six continents we uncover a striking field-path dissociation: frontier VLMs accurately judge where a field is strong, but fail to tell whether a single direct or one-wall path exists. Open models fail even earlier at reading the field itself, and are systematically wrong, scoring below random guessing even when credited for any of four attempts. On unseen cities, fine-tuning brings a 9B open model close to frontier proprietary models on fields, yet neither supervised nor reinforcement fine-tuning improves path tracing. Supervising only final answers teaches models to approximate the field, yet leaves single-path geometry out of reach.

title: ReMiC: Representation-Driven Token Pruning for 3D VLMs via Minimax Hierarchical Clustering
abstract: 3D vision-language models (3D VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in 3D scene understanding and spatial reasoning. However, their reliance on multi-view inputs produces long visual token sequences, imposing substantial computational overhead during inference. Existing pruning methods often rely on token salience or feature diversity as proxies for representativeness, without explicitly modeling the representation gap between the original token set and the retained subset, thereby leading to suboptimal representation of the original scene. In this paper, we propose ReMiC, a training-free, representation-driven token pruning framework based on minimax hierarchical clustering. ReMiC treats retained tokens as prototypes for the original observations, formulating pruning as minimizing the maximum representation error under a fixed token budget. Local prototype initialization allocates tokens according to regional representation needs, while global prototype refinement updates the selected prototypes using cross-region information to further reduce the maximum representation error. Extensive experiments conducted on three representative 3D VLMs across five 3D scene understanding benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and generalization of our method. Notably, by retaining only 10% of visual tokens, ReMiC preserves 93.2% of the performance of Video-3D LLM and achieves a $2.04\times$ faster inference speed.

title: Using potential derivatives to reduce the cost of rectangular collocation: a general and versatile approach for computational vibrational spectroscopy without a potential energy surface
abstract: We modify the exact Cartesian kinetic energy operator, rectangular collocation approach of Manzhos and Carrington [J. Chem. Phys. 145 (2016) 224110] by using information contained in potential derivatives to decrease the number of required potential points. We show that this makes it possible to substantially reduce the number of collocation points, which is important, in particular, when energies are computed directly ab initio. Vibrational band intensities are also computed. We first demonstrate the method on Cl2CO and compare to high-accuracy Smolyak collocation calculations on an accurate potential energy surface (PES). Sub-cm-1 accuracy is obtained with a few thousand Gaussian basis functions and potential points. A spectrum computed directly from DFT energies and a comparison to GVPT2 (generalized vibrational perturbation theory) are also presented. We then consider LiCO2 as a more anharmonic case, for which a quartic force field potential is less reliable, and which also serves as a surrogate model for a catalytic system (mimicking CO2 bond weakening by charge donation). The rectangular collocation method is used to compute the spectrum of LiCO2 directly from ab initio energies and to compare to GVPT2. The method is implemented as a Claude Skill and is easily usable by anyone on any molecule. The method is a general and versatile tool for anharmonic computational vibrational spectroscopy. It does not require a PES and no coupling is neglected.

title: Every friend of 10 has at least eleven distinct prime factors
abstract: A friend of $10$ is a positive integer $N\neq 10$ such that $σ(N)/N=σ(10)/10=9/5$. Whether one exists is an open problem. Thackeray proved that a friend of $10$ has at least $10$ distinct prime factors. We describe a computer-assisted proof that it has at least $11$. The proof is an exhaustive search over sets of primes, carried out by a recursive certifier written in PARI/GP, which extends the open-source project caioross/solitary10. The new ingredients are a split of ``almost tight'' nodes that avoids enumerating the smallest unknown prime, a treatment of nodes with three or more unknown primes by a saturation dichotomy, a counting rule for unfactored cofactors of cyclotomic values, and the correction of a soundness gap in the earlier closure rule. The certification run for $ω=10$ visited $157{,}210{,}962$ nodes in $11.4$ hours on $12$ threads. As a consequence, a friend of $10$ would be larger than $10^{38}$.

title: DINO-KNN: Training-Free Multiclass In-Context Segmentation via Nearest Neighbors
abstract: In-context segmentation (ICS) segments a target image given a few annotated reference images. Recent training-free methods built on frozen foundation models segment one class at a time and gain little from additional references. We study the multiclass, multi-reference setting and ask how far a simple joint decision rule can go. We introduce DINO-KNN, which stores every labeled reference patch of a frozen DINOv3 encoder in a single memory and labels each target patch by a distance-weighted vote of its k nearest neighbors. All classes are predicted in a single pass, with one label per pixel, without training or a mask decoder. We evaluate on eight datasets, four natural and four medical, with R=1 to 15 reference images and three reference seeds. DINO-KNN achieves the best average mIoU at every R; it is the best method on six of the eight datasets from R=3 and on seven of the eight from R=7. Its accuracy continues to grow with the number of references, from 37.8 mIoU at R=1 to 56.2 at R=15, while the strongest baseline, INSID3, rises from 36.1 to 42.9. DINO-KNN is also 2.1x faster than INSID3. The code will be made public.

title: Robust Trajectory Prediction Under Sensing and V2X Noise: Evaluation and Mitigation Strategies
abstract: Anticipating the future behavior of surrounding objects is key for the safe and efficient navigation of autonomous vehicles. State-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models are typically trained and evaluated on large-scale, highly curated datasets obtained by filtering any object detection and tracking noise through extensive offline post-processing. However, in real-world deployments, the detected objects' state (position, heading, and speed) estimates are inherently affected by sensing and localization uncertainties. These uncertainties can be even higher for connected and automated vehicles receiving information from other road users through Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communications. In this paper, we first investigate the sensitivity of five state-of-the-art Transformer-based interaction-aware trajectory prediction models to realistic noisy object state estimates. Numerical results show that prediction accuracy degrades by up to a 6x factor as the noise level increases, highlighting the models' sensitivity to the mismatch between the noise conditions encountered during training and those experienced at deployment. We then show that retraining models on a more realistic noise-augmented dataset is a more effective strategy to mitigate the impact of noisy object state estimates on trajectory prediction accuracy than using denoising modules at the input. Retrained models limit the prediction accuracy degradation below a 1.5x factor. The noise-augmented dataset is openly released to support further research.

title: Urban State Representation for Autonomous Mobility: A Survey of Multimodal Perception, Architectures, Datasets, and Benchmarks
abstract: Cities are sensed by many platforms at once: on-board cameras, LiDAR and radar on autonomous vehicles, roadside units at intersections, drones and satellites overhead, and the GNSS traces of millions of trips. Yet most learned representations are built for one platform, one city, and one task. We survey this fragmented landscape through a single lens, the Urban State Representation (USR): a georeferenced, layered, time-varying, uncertainty-aware state that any sensing platform can write to and any downstream task can read from. We (i) formalize USR and five desiderata for it, and relate it to bird's-eye-view (BEV) features, occupancy, vectorized maps, neural fields and 3D Gaussians, scene graphs, road-network graphs, language tokens, and world-model latents; (ii) organize sensing platforms, cross-view (ground-aerial) matching, fusion operators, 3D geometric foundation models, end-to-end and vision-language-action models, and generative world models and data engines in one taxonomy that spans sensors to decisions; (iii) compile 26 urban datasets and simulators across ego, cooperative (V2X), aerial, trajectory, and language settings, with a metric glossary, a cross-benchmark results snapshot, a trend analysis, and a platform-coverage gap analysis; and (iv) review applications and propose, as an outlook, USR-5, a five-test protocol with explicit references and one aggregate score for measuring whether a state is shared, together with a research agenda of six open problems covering cross-city and cross-sensor transfer, uncertainty, efficiency, sim-to-real evaluation, and governance. This survey is an entry point for computer vision, autonomous driving, transportation, and urban computing researchers; the paper list, datasets, and USR-5 code are at https://github.com/binayksingh/Awesome-Urban-State-Representation.

title: Spatially varying modified Chaplygin gas wormhole with minimum violation of energy condition
