These findings suggest participatory governance design must attend to the discursive conditions under which institutional actors enter deliberative spaces, rather than assuming inclusion is inherently consensus-building. HSABM-LLM offers a novel platform for integrating political ecology insights into computational social science.

title: PSC-Gen: Physical Sequence Conditioning for Video Generation via Agentic Visual Planning
abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have enabled the synthesis of high-fidelity, visually compelling videos. However, despite being trained on internet-scale video data, understanding underlying physical laws and generating physically plausible dynamics remain challenging. To mitigate this, conditioning video generators on explicit physical reasoning has emerged as a promising direction. Nevertheless, existing conditioning approaches often fail to incorporate detailed physical guidance into generation, resulting in physically implausible motion or visual artifacts. We propose PSC-Gen, a training-free framework that employs an agentic approach to synthesize visual conditions and inject their core dynamics via low-frequency filtering. By iteratively planning physical states and verifying generated keyframes, our Physics Agent constructs visually and physically consistent keyframe sequences. We then interpolate these keyframes into a continuous physical sequence and inject only its low-frequency components, steering the video model to preserve physical dynamics while synthesizing fine visual details. Qualitative and quantitative evaluations across physics-informed and robotic manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that PSC-Gen faithfully follows instructions and generates physically plausible videos.

title: The Complexity of Oracle-Efficient Realizable Transductive Learning
abstract: In realizable transductive online learning, the learner knows the entire sequence of $T$ instances in advance, and the labels are consistent with one of $N$ hypotheses. With explicit access to the hypothesis class, the halving algorithm makes at most $\log_2 N$ mistakes. Can a comparable guarantee be achieved using only polynomially many empirical risk minimization (ERM) queries? We answer this question negatively, even for a weighted-ERM oracle that optimizes arbitrary real-valued linear objectives and returns a complete maximizing hypothesis. For every fixed $β\in(0,1)$ and every randomized learner making polynomially many oracle queries, there exists a fixed realizable instance with exactly $N=2^{\lfloor T^β\rfloor}$ hypotheses on which the learner makes $Ω_β(\sqrt{T\log N})$ mistakes in expectation. This matches the agnostic-rate upper bound achieved by random playout using $O(T)$ oracle calls. The separation persists for much smaller classes as well: along a sequence with $\log N=Θ((\log T)^2)$, we establish a mistake lower bound of $\exp(Ω(\log T/\log\log T))$. Our main technical contribution is a composition lemma that combines two realizable prediction problems such that their mistake lower bounds add, up to a small loss, while their hypothesis class sizes grow only additively. Iterating this lemma yields a family of hard instances spanning the desired parameter regimes, establishing a sharp separation between information-theoretic and oracle-efficient mistake guarantees.

title: Exactly solvable Brill waves: explicit gravitational-wave initial data with trapped surfaces
abstract: Vacuum initial data for pure gravitational waves on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (Brill waves) have so far been obtained only numerically. Here a one-parameter family is solved exactly: in toroidal coordinates the constraint separates, and a suitable seed function makes every mode equation hypergeometric. The data are real analytic and asymptotically flat and exist precisely for $k<k_c=0.8048\ldots$; their mass is an explicit series with a pole at $k_c$. Near $k_c$ the data provably contain trapped surfaces and an apparent horizon. A scaling symmetry yields further solvable families, one of them elementary.

title: Operating-Condition Normalization in C-MAPSS: Matched Historical Baselines, Multi-Seed Robustness, and Prognostic-Score Trade-offs
abstract: Operating-state changes can obscure turbofan degradation signals, but a reduction in remaining-useful-life (RUL) error after condition-wise standardization may reflect weaknesses of the comparison features instead of a unique benefit of normalization. A controlled retrospective audit examines NASA C-MAPSS FD002 and FD004 with engine-disjoint folds, raw condition identifiers, two constructions of causal history, early-life baselines, and continuous operating-setting correction. Ridge regression, random forests and XGBoost are compared under explicit training-engine-only fitting rules. The previously reported XGBoost FD004 terminal RMSE decreased from 30.38 to 29.08 cycles following six-condition standardization; however, raw sensor values accompanied by condition-matched histories and condition identifiers achieved 28.09 cycles, reversing the naive point estimate ranking, although the paired-engine interval spans zero. For FD002, normalized XGBoost reduced terminal RMSE yet increased the asymmetric NASA score (12,616 to 13,289). Additional model-seed, condition count, RUL-cap, grouped-validation and explanation checks test sensitivity rather than postulating a universally optimal representation. The six clusters reproduce known simulator operating regimes; no new condition discovery algorithm, causal diagnostic method, or field ready prognostic system is claimed. Since the official test endpoints were also used in earlier exploratory comparisons, all newly examined alternatives are reported as retrospective benchmark evidence, not as results from a pristine confirmatory holdout.

title: Analytical Modeling and Optimal GPU Provisioning for Disaggregated LLM Inference
abstract: We present OSplit, an exact analytical method that enables efficient partitioning of a GPU L1 domain into prefill and decode workers, including sharding for classical and advanced GPUs. OSplit takes into consideration model parameters, enabling any inference model to be partitioned into prefill and decode workers with a goal of producing the maximum throughput possible. OSplit is based on a capacity model that takes as inputs the model, the loading scheme (batch size, max sequence length), and models an inference serving framework (vLLM) and computes the efficiency of each GPU. For this, we model H100 and GB300 GPUs, and model a scale-up domain, along with FlashAttention-based kernels. OSplit first computes an optimal collective generation policy, which gives inputs to the capacity model that enables optimal split of prefill and decode GPUs. We evaluate our scheme over H100 (NVL8) and GB300 (NVL72) using vLLM inference serving and show throughput, predicted and measured latency, showing near-perfect theoretical-to-measured values over leading LLMs (Llama and Qwen)

title: An Algebra with straightening laws which is an integral domain and which is not Cohen--Macaulay
abstract: A 4-dimensional algebra with straightening laws which is an integral domain and which is not Cohen--Macaulay over an arbitrary field is constructed. Furthermore, it is shown that every three-dimensional graded ASL domain is Cohen--Macaulay.

title: Frozen by the Mean: Early Temporal Guidance Unfreezes Motion in Video Diffusion Models
abstract: Video diffusion models can render convincing frames while failing to produce the requested action. Increasing classifier-free guidance (CFG) can strengthen motion, but also saturates and shifts colors. Scalar CFG assigns the same coefficient to the averaged and frame-varying components of its prediction difference, limiting independent control of temporal variation. THAW, Temporal Harmonic Amplification during Warm-up, retains stock CFG and adds a separately weighted residual during an initial denoising window. Its dose specifies the added norm relative to the current CFG difference, giving the extra guidance a consistent relative budget across sampling steps. THAW is training-free and reuses CFG's two model predictions with an unchanged network evaluation count. It improves cost-matched motion over scalar and scheduled CFG on five video models, with positive point estimates against existing guidance methods on three of them. On VBench, THAW raises dynamic degree by about 14 to 15 points over stock CFG while increasing total scores on a different set of three models.

title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub
abstract: AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories. We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.

title: Contrastive Gradient Guidance for Test-Time Multi-Preference Alignment of Diffusion Models
abstract: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.

title: Beyond File-Level Splits: Rethinking Symbolic Music Evaluation via Multi-View Alignment
abstract: Symbolic music generation often continues MIDI passages by predicting subsequent notes or events. Held-out prediction loss can overestimate generalization to unseen compositions when training contains another performance or arrangement of a test work. We introduce Multi-View Alignment-Aware Same-Work Identification, combining complementary musical representations with temporal alignment of shared passages to remove test-work versions from training while preserving unrelated material and fixing evaluation files. In a controlled cohort of 100 manually verified pairs selected for high embedding similarity, replacing 3.29% of training windows with test-work versions reduces mean per-group NLL by up to 30.16% relative to matched unrelated content. Across two datasets and two generators, our method brings test losses closest to a reference built from independent work labels. Compared with removing the same number of files at random, it leaves fewer test works exposed and retains more eligible content, including about 99% of eligible tokens on the piano-performance dataset. A separate study on that dataset matches training tokens and updates: no test works remain exposed under the dataset labels, and mean relative test loss is 2.15% higher than an independently selected reference. These findings support keeping all versions of each composition in one split when evaluating generalization to unseen works. The project is available at https://kunbai05-nb.github.io/.

title: JevNavAgent: A Single-Forward Visual Navigation Agent with Trajectory-Level RL for Gigapixel Pathology
abstract: Gigapixel whole-slide images (WSIs) exceed single-pass vision-language model (VLM) capacity at cellular resolution, while multiple instance learning relies on query-agnostic offline patching without interactive reasoning. Multi-step VLM navigation agents inspect regions on demand, yet face two bottlenecks: (1) autoregressive action decoding incurs heavy latency, throttling exploration and online multi-trajectory RL; and (2) offline distillation suffers from an existential-versus-universal stopping asymmetry between positive detection and negative exclusion, inducing thumbnail and kinematic shortcuts while leaving policies prone to passing metastases without stopping. Under the Jev (System One) paradigm, a model predicts distributions over predefined decision spaces in one forward pass (0 generated tokens) while deterministic code executes navigation. We build JevNavAgent, a 2B-parameter agent combining factorized stopping, spatial-candidate, and contextual-bilinear answer heads with overview modality dropout. We pair Stage-1 offline counterfactual trajectory alignment (mitigating depth and panning shortcuts) with Stage-2 online trajectory-level GRPO (Traj-GRPO), using decoding-free rollouts to optimize branch-level lesion discovery, in-polygon stopping, and step-wise confidence gain. On Clean Visual WSI-VQA, JevNavAgent achieves 51.57% multi-scale (50.43% terminal-step) overall and 51.39% focal accuracy, outperforming frontier VLM agents and 4B-11B open-source cascades while running nearly 12x faster than frontier APIs (5.63s vs. 66.64-70.04s). On CAMELYON16 Official Test, Traj-GRPO reaches 22.45% localization (converting 11/12, or 91.7%, of visited tumors into grounded stops) with 93.75% specificity and 69.77% slide accuracy, surpassing Stage-1 SFT under matched stopping rules alongside zero-shot budget scaling.

title: Orthosymplectic $K$-matrices in small dimensions
abstract: Using elementary methods, we describe coideal subalgebras of quantum orthosymplectic algebras of small dimensions, classify the corresponding $K$-matrices and find explicitly the centralizers of these subalgebras in the vector representation. The main attention is paid to generators with a Cartan term. For them, at generic values of the parameters, we find the centralizers and all $K$-matrices and describe the decomposition of the vector representation over the coideal subalgebra. We find all special values of the parameters of two types and, at a generic point of each set of special values, describe the decomposition of the vector representation and all $K$-matrices. At special values of the first type the dimension of the centralizer grows. One hypersurface of such values is related to Cartan terms, and on it one of the generators is given by the same formula as in the quantum electrical algebra. At special values of the second type the dimension of the centralizer is the same, but nonzero nilpotent elements appear in it. The $K$-matrices on the sets of special values of the second type are obtained from those already found by substituting the condition, and there are no others. We describe the classical limit, including the limit of special values. We formulate an observation relating the admissibility of a Cartan term to the first homology of the classical subalgebra.

title: A high-speed and high-resolution 3D velocity map imaging system with a neuromorphic camera
abstract: An improved camera-based 3D-velocity map imaging (VMI) system was demonstrated with a neuromorphic camera. We show a machine vision event-driven camera can achieve an unprecedented latency of 2 microseconds when detecting single ion/electron with a microchannel plate imaging detector, which boosts the speed of the momentum imaging system to more than 100 kHz, while the system with a conventional frame camera is limited to a few kHz. The high spatial resolution of the camera offers additional performance boost while maintaining excellent multi-hit capability and a high time resolution.

title: Exact-Order Mellin Transfer and Prime-Support Filtrations
abstract: We establish a unified exact-order Mellin transfer principle that converts the multiplicity of a critical Mellin pole into arithmetic prime-support depth. For an exact-order Möbius transform in lattice dimension $\ell$, a base pole of order $r$ at $s=\ell/2$ satisfies \[ \ord_{s=\ell/2}\widehat{\mathscr P_{N,\ell}H}=ω(N)-r. \] The complete Jordan--Mellin jet is explicit, and its first surviving coefficient selects the canonical weight $W(N)=\prod_{p\mid N}\log p$. After the corresponding jet normalization, this weight governs a kernel-independent moving-support law and a mod-Poisson regime. With simultaneous splitting marks in finite Galois extensions, the same weight yields a multivariate polynomial whose mixed coefficients are reciprocal compositum degrees; it recovers pairwise intersection degrees and, under a full-rank hypothesis, also governs the coupled saddle and large-deviation geometry. In spectral geometry, a two-variable family attached to any positive self-adjoint elliptic operator has a transverse normal crossing whose parameter jets generate every higher critical pole order; exact-order dilation therefore realizes every positive prime-support depth. An explicit Bernoulli--Barnes/Barnes--Epstein model shows how a pole collision shifts the finite critical layer from one-prime to two-prime support. Thus arithmetic support, Galois compositum data, and spectral pole geometry arise from one exact-order Mellin mechanism.

title: Cure-Fraction Random Survival Forests: Separating Cure from Latency
abstract: In many cancer and clinical studies, the population under study has a positive fraction of long-term survivors, motivating survival models that distinguish probability of long-term survival (cure fraction) from the latency of the subgroup that is susceptible to the event. Existing survival trees and forests partition data using criteria that emphasize differences in the ranks of survival times and therefore need not identify covariates associated with cure probability. We introduce cure-fraction based survival trees (CBST) that recursively partition the covariate space using contrasts in tail survival probability supported by adequate follow-up. The resulting ensemble forest targets long-term survival heterogeneity directly rather than ranking of the survival times. We establish consistency for the induced tail-survival target and derive conditions under which our procedure consistently recovers cure-rate related partitions and cure probabilities. The analysis clarifies the separate roles of follow-up maturity, localization, and residual-tail bias in identifying cure effects and supporting statistical inference. We further develop variance estimation and asymptotic results and uncertainty quantification for predictions from the ensemble forest. Simulations show that the cure-fraction based splitting criterion can improve recovery of cure heterogeneity relative to a log-rank based forest when cure incidence and latency are driven by different covariates. Analyses of temporally held-out cohorts from the Sao Paulo Hospital Cancer Registry demonstrate that our method produces stable long-term survival risk groups while preserving substantial late follow-up support. The proposed framework provides a nonparametric approach to learning and interpreting cure heterogeneity in settings where long-term survival is the primary scientific objective.

title: Normal Homogeneous Counterexamples to Wolf's Homogeneity Conjecture
abstract: We construct free Clifford--Wolf subgroups of order two whose quotients of compact, connected, simply connected normal homogeneous manifolds are not homogeneous. The universal covers are the oriented real flag manifolds $M_{d}=SO(N)/\prod_{i=1}^{q}SO(d_{i})$, equipped with the metric induced by the negative Killing form, where $N\geq4$ and $q\geq3$ is odd. We determine its full connected centralizer, the effective connected isometry group of the quotient, and the corresponding orbit space. These calculations prove nonhomogeneity and give explicit formulas for the cohomogeneity, fundamental group, and Euler characteristic. These examples are found by ChatGPT 6 Astra.

title: MM-Open5x: Practical Conformal Electronics via Multi-Material Multi-Axis Additive Manufacturing
abstract: Multi-axis, multi-material additive manufacturing enables the production of conformal electronic systems that are difficult to realise using planar processes and can offer enhanced performance; however, accessibility and reproducibility remain challenging. This paper presents MM-Open5x, an open and low-cost multi-material, multi-axis additive manufacturing workflow for practical conformal electronics. The workflow spans design, simulation, toolpath generation, fabrication, testing, and assembly, and is released alongside complete design files, toolpaths, and representative G-code. Representative case studies demonstrate both the benefits and limitations of multi-axis deposition in practice, explicitly documenting common failure modes, calibration sensitivities, assembly bottlenecks, and material variability. Rather than prescribing an optimal solution, MM-Open5x is presented as a transparent, reproducible foundation upon which a broader community can iterate, extend, and apply conformal electronics workflows across diverse application domains.

title: Pauli-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo method for bipolar charge transport in graphene
abstract: We develop a Pauli-consistent ensemble Monte Carlo method for bipolar charge transport in graphene, with an explicit treatment of phonon-assisted interband scattering, including electron-hole generation and recombination. The method employs a valence-vacancy representation to describe coupled electron and hole populations without explicitly simulating the highly populated valence band. It preserves the discrete occupation bounds during both free flight and scattering while conserving net charge. The numerical properties of the method are assessed through sensitivity and refinement studies and comparison with an independent deterministic discontinuous Galerkin solution of the same kinetic model. The two approaches show very good agreement for the time evolution, carrier distributions, and steady-state transport observables across the investigated transport regimes. The results also demonstrate the computational practicality of the method for microscopic simulations of bipolar graphene transport.

title: R2WM: Recursive Reasoning Wireless Model for Long-Horizon mmWave Beam Prediction
abstract: Long-horizon beam prediction aims to extend beam-training intervals while supporting beam alignment in mobile millimeter-wave systems. Although pretrained large models can improve prediction over compact recurrent baselines, their large backbones impose substantial storage and computing requirements. To address this limitation, we propose a recursive reasoning wireless model (R2WM). Given a fixed history of beam indices and angles of departure (AoDs), R2WM repeatedly updates coupled latent and prediction states using a shared causal-attention backbone before jointly decoding the future beam indices. Backbone reuse increases computational depth at fixed parameter count. In the standard 10-step DeepMIMO setting, R2WM achieves an average normalized beamforming gain of 0.9597, compared with 0.8629 for the prompt-as-prefix large language model, with 99.1% fewer parameters and 59.1% fewer counted floating-point operations. Transfer experiments show that R2WM retains normalized gain under the tested carrier-frequency and antenna-count changes, while its beam-index-only variant retains gain under the tested base-station change. Component ablations show higher gains with historical AoD conditioning and causal attention. Recursion analysis reveals a gain-computation trade-off across separately trained configurations with the same parameter count. An additional comparison with a nonrecursive Transformer of similar parameter count shows higher gain for R2WM at greater computational cost. These results support accurate long-horizon beam prediction without a large pretrained backbone.

title: AdapToC: A Unified Framework for Multi-Task Visual Token Communication
abstract: Pretrained discrete visual tokenizers supply compact latents for synthesis, recognition, and embodied perception, yet wireless token streaming remains fragile. Under fading and noisy pilots, hard cyclic redundancy check (CRC) erasures turn corrupted blocks into missing tokens while frozen decoders amplify edge errors, which can collapse unequal error protection (UEP) into a binary choice between strong coding and omission under severe fading. Soft bit posteriors break this collapse. We present AdapToC, a single-pass transceiver that restores multi-tier rate-distortion tradeoffs without altering tokenizer weights or differentiating through pixel decoders. We align codebook geometry to the channel via offline frequency-weighted Pseudo-Gray relabeling and Halton dispersion to contract bit and burst errors with zero overhead. Because soft recovery pulls intermediate rates onto the three-tier convex hull, our unit-gated AdaLN sender schedules protection tiers across channel budgets, while our pilot-calibrated receiver feeds factorized codebook posteriors into a ConvNeXt-attention restorer with CRC bypass. We co-train AdapToC solely in latent space via counterfactual utility estimation and codebook cross-entropy regularization. On identical VQGAN-f16 tokens, AdapToC outperforms TONIC and adaptive TokenCom+AMC, cuts multi-SNR Rayleigh LPIPS from 0.6551 to 0.3312 within the frozen-tokenizer PSNR ceiling, and saves 43.8% Rician-K6 symbols at matched quality. Our single-pass restorer runs 8.3x faster than iterative resampling, raises accuracy while accelerating decoder-free recognition 20.6x, and improves fidelity plug-and-play across TiTok, VAR, and zero-shot NuPlan.

title: A Proof of Blackburn's Conjecture on Non-Overlapping Codes
abstract: A code is non-overlapping if no nonempty proper prefix of a codeword is a suffix of a codeword. Let $S_n(q)$ be the largest size of a non-overlapping code of length $n$ over an alphabet of size $q$. Levenshtein proved that $S_n(q)\le c_nq^n$, where $c_n=(1/n)\bigl((n-1)/n\bigr)^{n-1}$. The codes $I^{n-1}J$, where $I$ and $J$ partition the alphabet, attain this bound when $n$ divides $q$, and Blackburn conjectured that for every $n$ and all sufficiently large $q$, the best such code is a maximum non-overlapping code. We prove this conjecture. The proof uses generating functions for the nested partitions that describe maximal non-overlapping codes. We also show that only the codes $I^{n-1}J$ with $|I|=(n-1)q/n$ and their reversals meet Levenshtein's bound.

title: Pretraining Representation Lottery Determines Fine-tuning Generalization
abstract: Large scale pretraining (PT) followed by fine-tuning (FT) is the central paradigm of modern deep learning, yet how PT shapes FT generalization remains poorly understood. We use a synthetic setup in which the ground-truth concept geometry of entities is known, as a controlled testbed to study how representational geometry affects model behavior and how PT representations determine FT generalization. We first show that models differing only in training seed can closely match in PT loss yet vary substantially in FT generalization. We hypothesize that a representational lottery underlies this phenomenon: the random seed dependent geometry formed during PT determines what FT can reach. We confirm this causally. First, injecting the ground-truth concept geometry into the model yields near-ceiling FT generalization, showing that good representations directly drive generalization. Then, distilling a lucky seed's learned representation into an unlucky seed unlocks FT generalization, while distilling the same model's behavior does not. Furthermore, representation distillation can merge entities that never interacted during PT, which FT alone cannot. Finally, we show that regularizing representational drift during FT enables naturalistic learning: only models with good representations learn the task, and they generalize, while models with poor representations fail to fit it. Under plain FT, by contrast, models with poor representations fit the training objective by reshaping their pretrained representations. We reproduce the distillation result in Pythia-160M and Pythia-410M, each pretrained multiple times with different random seeds, and show that the transferable representation lives in the deep layers at both scales. Overall, PT acts as a lottery over representations, and the representation a model draws determines how it adapts during FT in a way that behavior alone does not explain.

title: Multi-Order Passive Macromodeling from Layouts via Nested Port-Hamiltonian Learning
abstract: Compact, passive state-space macromodels of interconnects and power-delivery networks are essential for stable transient signal- and power-integrity simulations. However, conventional flows require costly per-layout full-wave electromagnetic (EM) simulations, while both traditional fitting and prior learning surrogates rely on post-hoc fitting or passivity perturbation that degrades accuracy without guaranteeing convergence. In this work, we propose an end-to-end macromodeling framework that learns directly in the passive space, mapping physical layout graphs to multi-order port-Hamiltonian (pH) macromodels. Specifically, our network encodes each layout graph into unconstrained matrix blocks and assembles them via a complete, prefix-nested pH parameterization that guarantees continuous-frequency passivity and stability by construction, yielding valid $k$-state macromodels via direct state slicing in one forward pass. To train all orders without reference realizations, we supervise the network directly on S-parameters through a progressive order-growth curriculum. Evaluated on 27k unseen test structures from a 270k-structure advanced-packaging dataset, our framework reduces mean S-parameter error by $42\%$ on average (up to $65\%$) over established macromodeling tools fitted to ground-truth EM responses, achieves zero passivity violations across $459{,}000$ exported models, and accelerates macromodel generation by $11{,}000$--$39{,}000\times$ ($36$--$85$~ms per layout).

title: Imagine Smarter, Drive Faster: Efficient World Modeling for Decision-Aware Autonomous Driving
abstract: World models hold great promise for autonomous driving planning, yet their ability to imagine the future often comes at a formidable computational cost. Efficiency efforts, such as knowledge distillation and domain-specific pre-training, often shift this burden to costly teachers or training pipelines, leaving lightweight world modeling an open challenge. We introduce FastWorld, a natively lightweight world-model framework for efficient autonomous driving planning. FastWorld reduces computation through compact scene representations, short-horizon action-conditioned prediction, and selective candidate verification and score refinement. These designs support efficient future-informed planning without teacher distillation or additional domain-specific pre-training. On NAVSIMv1, FastWorld achieves 92.2 PDMS at 132 FPS on a single 4090 GPU. It also achieves 89.4 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2 and an average L2 of 0.40 over 3 seconds at 17 FPS on nuScenes. Code and models can be found at https://github.com/MoyangSensei/FastWorld.

title: Massive Particles in Carrollian Holography
abstract: Understanding how massive particles are encoded in boundary operators is a central problem in Carrollian holography. We construct a three-dimensional Carrollian description of a massive scalar in four-dimensional flat spacetime, together with an explicit bulk-to-boundary integral transform. In this construction, nonzero mass requires infinitely many linearly independent primary states, while the absence of bulk spin imposes relations among their descendants. We show that these relations are equivalent to null-state decoupling and give a local constraint on the boundary fields. The integral transform preserves the full Poincaré symmetry and maps bulk scalar data to fields satisfying this constraint. We also obtain two- and three-point functions and the associated formal operator product expansion coefficients. The integral transform evaluates bulk data at complex momenta, making analytic continuation essential in Lorentzian signature. This construction provides a concrete starting point for relating massive scattering amplitudes to Carrollian correlators and for reconstructing bulk fields from boundary data.

title: Where Does a Weight-Editing Agent Help? Blind Diagnosis and Repair of Deployment Faults in Vision Models
abstract: Language-model agents can read and edit the weights of neural networks without gradients, and this is increasingly presented as a new way of repairing models. We ask what such an agent adds, in a setting with a known answer. A vision model moved into a new system may be broken by a preprocessing, weight-conversion or output-convention fault; an agent restricted to forward passes must decide whether a fault exists, name it, and undo it by editing the weights. Over 183 runs on classification, segmentation and detection, scored against the fault-free model, we find three things. When the kind of fault is known, the agent is not needed: a script written afterwards repairs 30 of 48 faults against the agent's 33. But the agent did not have to be told: on five fault types outside every script it repairs 15 of 15 where that script repairs 4, and it never edits any of 21 fault-free models. And its limits are predictable: it needs a trustworthy per-layer reference for the model's activations and a fault that is an invertible structured transformation; without them, small faults are missed and repairs stay partial. We derive guidance on when to use an agent and when a script.

title: Joint Client Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Optimal Federated Learning over Wireless Networks
abstract: Federated learning often relies on partial client participation because full participation is costly in cross-device wireless systems with limited uplink resources, heterogeneous channel conditions, energy constraints, and strict upload deadlines. However, partial participation introduces sampling variance, causing the sampled update to deviate from the full-participation update. Existing optimal client sampling methods reduce this variance but usually rely on simplified client-count budgets, while wireless-aware scheduling methods account for communication constraints but do not directly optimize sampling variance. This paper proposes resource-aware optimal client sampling (RAOCS), a unified variance-minimizing client scheduling framework under uplink resource-block, round deadline, update-information, and energy constraints. The resulting problem admits a capped water-filling solution that balances client update importance, wireless resource cost, and energy feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that RAOCS achieves accuracy comparable to that of OCS while reducing the average upload time per iteration by more than a factor of 252.

title: 3DCodeFactory: Scaling Training Data for 3D Code Agents
abstract: As code agents evolve, their scope is expanding from generating simple static 3D meshes to constructing structurally complete, complex, interactive 3D scenes. However, existing datasets mainly rely on converting or captioning pre-existing 3D assets, consisting mostly of single-turn code data for static single objects and struggling to scale task diversity and scene complexity, leaving such training data scarce. We present 3DCodeFactory, an automated framework that directly constructs diverse, complex 3D training data from abundant raw text (e.g., diffusion prompts and product descriptions). The framework first leverages an image generator to synthesize 3D reference images from raw text as visual anchors, guiding the generation of concrete modeling specifications and interactive functional requirements; meanwhile, it jointly constructs visual, specification, and functional rubrics from the reference images and requirements to automatically score and filter multi-turn agent rollouts. Based on this framework, we release 3DCodeFactory-Data, comprising 5,045 high-quality task instances and multi-turn interaction trajectories. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.8-27B on 3DCodeFactory-Data significantly improves performance on BlenderWorld, P3D-Bench, and 3DCodeBench, consistently outperforming models trained on existing open-source 3D code datasets, with our 27B model further surpassing the same-series 2.4T flagship Qwen3.8-Max in overall performance.

title: Transient coupling of Marangoni spreading and interfacial waves
abstract: How does an initially non-uniform distribution of surfactant generate waves on a de- formable interface, and how do those waves then govern the redistribution of the surfactant? We answer this question for the linear Cauchy-Poisson problem of an axisymmetric interface between two viscous fluids, released from rest with independently prescribed distributions of surfactant and of interface displacement, by Hankel and Laplace transforms. In Stokes flow the pressure and the viscous normal stress of the Marangoni flow cancel in the nor- mal traction on the interface, for any viscosity ratio, so that the surfactant relaxes without displacing the interface: the coupling between surfactant redistribution and interface de- formation is inertial. With inertia, the Marangoni flow initiates a capillary-gravity wave whose polarity, at leading order for thin boundary layers, is set by the sign of $ρ_l μ_l - ρ_u μ_u $, and the surfactant is then carried by the wave, so that its concentration performs weakly damped oscillations at the wave frequency after the Marangoni relaxation of a flat surface has ended. The amplitude of these oscillations is given in closed form at small viscosity; its maximum does not coincide with that of the familiar resonant damping, and the surfactant and the interface shape decouple exactly only when the two fluids have equal densities and viscosities. A localized displacement radiates a wave packet that the surfactant damps, and a localized surfactant redistribution initiates a wave on an initially flat interface. Direct numerical simulations with sharp geometric surfactant transport verify these predictions.

title: The Seifert--van Kampen Theorem
abstract: The Seifert--van Kampen theorem computes the fundamental group of a space from an open cover by two path-connected subspaces, provided their intersection is path-connected. This article gives a self-contained account of the theorem, explains its universal-property formulation as a pushout in the category of groups, and derives several standard computations. Particular attention is paid to base points, the role of path-connectedness, and the passage from a topological decomposition to a group presentation. The purpose is expository: the results are classical, and no claim of a new theorem is made.

title: Local Pressure Induced Quantum Dot to Ring Transition and Aharonov Bohm Effect in Reconfigurable MoTe2 Bilayers
abstract: We demonstrate that local pressure provides an effective means of engineering reconfigurable quantum confinement in MoTe2 homobilayers. By applying a smooth, spatially varying pressure profile, we show that the confinement geometry can be continuously tuned from a conventional quantum dot to a quantum ring, with the emergence of annular confinement being a distinctive feature of AB-stacked bilayers. This crossover originates from the pressure-induced spatial modulation in the electronic parameters, which produces an off-center minimum in the effective confinement potential, thereby redistributing the ground-state probability density away from the center and giving rise to an annular confinement geometry. In the quantum-ring regime, a perpendicular magnetic field gives rise to a flux-periodic energy spectrum and persistent currents, providing characteristic signatures of the Aharonov-Bohm effect. By coupling the pressure-induced quantum ring to source and drain leads, we further demonstrate pronounced Aharonov-Bohm conductance oscillations, accompanied by real-space current patterns exhibiting constructive and destructive interference at integer and half-integer magnetic flux quanta, respectively. These findings establish locally pressurized MoTe2 bilayers as a lithography-free platform for reconfigurable quantum confinement and realizing pressure-tunable Aharonov-Bohm interferometry in two dimensional materials.

title: DiscernBench: Evaluating Cooperative Discernment of LLM Agents in Institutional Settings
abstract: The deployment of large language models in operational settings demands evaluation of judgment under institutional constraint. We introduce DiscernBench, a benchmark for evaluating cooperative discernment: the ability of an agent to determine whether to comply with, refuse, or escalate a request in an institutional setting. DiscernBench comprises scenarios derived from real-world incident reports across domains such as aviation, law enforcement, and emergency management. We evaluate eight LLMs across three decision-making configurations and analyze both final decisions and the intermediate judgments produced during multi-agent deliberation. Under disagreement, Final Responders exhibit model- and role-dependent aggregation patterns in which a lone specialist recommendation can disproportionately influence the collective decision, a phenomenon we term Minority-Signal Override. Role-specialized multi-agent deliberation raises average over-escalation from 3.79% under direct single-agent judgment to 28.27%, with the direction and magnitude of minority-signal influence varying substantially across models and specialist roles. These results reveal distinct collective decision behaviors that are not captured by final-answer accuracy alone. Trustworthy multi-agent systems therefore require evaluating not only individual specialist reasoning, but also how conflicting judgments are transformed into collective decisions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Disha1001/DiscernBench.

title: Simplified Plotkin-type Bounds for Function-Correcting Codes with b-Symbol and Sum-Rank Distances
abstract: Function-correcting codes (FCCs) are a coding framework that enables reliable communication with minimal redundancy while ensuring the recovery of specific functions of transmitted messages. FCCs have been studied recently under the $b$-symbol distance and the sum-rank distance. Existing general Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under these distances require computing the pairwise distances between vectors that map to different function values. As a result, these bounds are often computationally difficult to determine. In this paper, we derive simplified Plotkin-type bounds on the optimal redundancy of FCCs under the $b$-symbol and sum-rank distances. These bounds depend only on the number of message vectors corresponding to each function value and the sum of pairwise distances among vectors mapped to the same function value. The proposed bounds apply to arbitrary functions and are considerably easier to evaluate than existing Plotkin-type bounds. The known simplified bounds for linear functions under the $b$-symbol and sum-rank distances are subsumed as special cases of the proposed bounds. Furthermore, we obtain a tighter bound for linear functions under the sum-rank distance than the existing bound.

title: Worst case tractability of weighted linear tensor product problems under the absolute error criterion
abstract: This paper studies weighted linear tensor product problems in the worst case setting. We consider algorithms that use finitely many evaluations of arbitrary continuous linear functionals. We investigate algebraic and exponential tractability under the absolute error criterion in the case $λ_1>1$, where $λ_1$ is the square of the univariate maximal singular value. We obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for various notions of algebraic and exponential tractability on weights and univariate singular values. Our approach is to convert algebraic tractability of the problems for the absolute error criterion with $λ_1 > 1$ to exponential tractability of the normalized problems. Specifically, we solve Open Problem 27 as posed by Novak and Woźniakowski (2008).

title: Reporting Differential Privacy Guarantees via Operationally Equivalent $\varepsilon$: What Does $\varepsilon=19.61$ Mean for the 2020 U.S. Census?
abstract: The large value $\varepsilon=19.61$, reported as an approximate differential privacy (ADP) parameter for the 2020 U.S. Census, has prompted doubts about the adequacy of Census privacy protection. It was obtained by converting component zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) guarantees to ADP at $δ=10^{-10}$. A single ADP pair can substantially loosen the original upper bound on the power (true positive rate) of a distinguishing test. At significance level $α$, we express the original bound as the smallest pure differential privacy (DP) parameter giving the same power bound. We call this the $α$-operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$. The full curve represents the original bound exactly on $(0,1)$, even when the bound is nonconcave. For maximum-power curves and bounds derived from trade-off functions, we characterize the extrema of operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ over an interval of significance levels. When finite, they give the parameters of the pure DP bounds that enclose the original power bound on that interval. The mapping preserves the ordering of power bounds at each significance level. For Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with equal noise variance, conversion to single ADP pairs or Gaussian DP envelopes can reverse this ordering. For the P.L. 94-171 redistricting data, we reproduce the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$ as the sum of rounded component ADP values. The published zCDP guarantee yields operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ values of approximately 4.25, 2.94, and 3.18 at significance levels of 1%, 5%, and 10%, respectively. Converting the same guarantee to a single ADP pair at $δ=10^{-10}$ gives power bounds near 1 at all three levels. The pure DP scale thus clarifies constraints on distinguishing attacks that are difficult to discern from the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$.

title: ArrythML-II: An Optimized TinyML Framework for ECG Arrhythmia Detection and Multi-Class Beat Classification on Wearable Devices
abstract: This paper presents ArrythML-II, an optimized TinyML framework for on-device ECG arrhythmia detection and multi-class beat classification on wearable platforms. A systematic hyperparameter optimization framework is developed to identify compact autoencoder architectures for binary ECG arrhythmia detection. A custom scoring mechanism jointly considers detection performance, reconstruction-error thresholds, and model size to guide architecture selection. The framework is further extended to six-class ECG beat classification using a lightweight classifier derived from the optimized autoencoder architecture. Both models are INT8 quantized and deployed using TensorFlow Lite Micro on a custom-developed, battery-operated, single-lead ECG device based on the PSoC~6 microcontroller. The deployed autoencoder and classifier have model sizes of approximately 44~KB and 22~KB, respectively, with end-to-end processing times of 5.1~ms and 4.7~ms per ECG segment. Model inference accounts for 3.95~ms and 1.38~ms of these processing times, respectively. In the refined arrhythmia detection evaluation using the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database, the autoencoder achieved an accuracy of 84.76\%, precision of 82.68\%, and recall of 77.99\%. The multi-class classifier achieved 82.29\% accuracy, weighted precision of 90.18\%, and weighted recall of 82.29\%. Beyond offline model evaluation, the wearable platform is validated using preloaded ECG segments, live ECG signals, and an ESP32-S3-based ECG emulator that replays annotated MIT-BIH recordings as analog waveforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating optimized TinyML models into wearable platforms for real-time ECG analysis.

title: ArgsWorld: Unifying 3DGS Scene Reconstruction, Generation and Extrapolation with Autoregressive Diffusion Transformer
abstract: Autoregressive diffusion world models deliver strong video generation performance, yet they typically output only RGB frames rather than explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene representations, creating a gap between learned visual world dynamics and usable 3D assets for downstream robotics, simulation and rendering. To bridge this gap, we introduce ArgsWorld, an autoregressive diffusion model that also produces an explicit 3DGS scene. For each generation chunk, the diffusion transformer jointly processes clean historical image latents and noisy latents for new views. It keeps the historical image latents fixed and refreshes the scene features so that the Gaussian representation can be revised as new regions come into view. Our 3D Self-Forcing Distillation trains the model on its own generated histories using a mixture of single-view and multi-view data. Distribution matching supervises direct image latents and latents of Gaussian renderings at both generation and additional cameras. ArgsWorld unifies 3D scene reconstruction from posed images, scene generation from image or text prompts, and scene extrapolation across camera segments with disconnected endpoints. Experimental results demonstrate that ArgsWorld achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple 3D scene modeling tasks. Project page: https://m4a1tastegood.github.io/ArgsWorld/

title: STAC++: Plug-and-Play Adaptive Spatio-Temporal Aware Cache Compression for Streaming 3D Reconstruction
abstract: Streaming 3D reconstruction must preserve geometry under limited memory, yet STAC's fixed-resolution spatial key-value (KV) cache grows as scenes expand. We propose STAC++, a plug-and-play, training-free framework that compresses and reuses spatial memory for long-term reconstruction in unbounded scenes. Adaptive Spatial KV Cache (ASKC) organizes KV states into an octree with adaptive resolutions across regions and layers. Response-Aware Cache Compression (RACC) guides KV merging by measuring attention-output changes, balancing storage savings with geometric preservation. Temporal Context Refinement (TCR) reuses cached intermediate features and recomputes only a short backbone suffix to refine historical predictions with later observations. Integrated into four pretrained streaming backbones, STAC++ reduces spatial memory consumption while maintaining competitive reconstruction quality on long sequences and large scenes, with further quality gains from refinement at limited computational overhead. The code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Balancing Causation, Correlation, and User Intent
abstract: Turbulence states vary widely in modeling difficulty, requiring distinct paradigms; thus, no single AI or data-driven approach suits all flows. We propose an operational framework classifying data-driven turbulence modeling by balancing physical causation and statistical correlation via non-equilibrium flow memory and user intent. Using the Mori--Zwanzig projection formalism, we decompose unclosed turbulent stress into a local response ($τ_{ij}^L$) and a spatio-temporally non-local memory integral ($τ_{ij}^{NL}$). Near statistical equilibrium, rapid relaxation suppresses advective memory, letting local correlations capture physical causation via intrusive $τ_{ij}^L$ constitutive relations in Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations. Because the elliptic Poisson equation for fluctuating pressure couples stress evolution to eddy dimensionality beyond single-point velocity-gradient componentiality, local closures are not strictly valid even at equilibrium, yet remain acceptable engineering approximations. In non-equilibrium turbulence, modeling bifurcates by user intent. For predicting unseen geometries, large coherent structures sustain non-local memory ($τ_{ij}^{NL}$), invalidating local total-stress closures and requiring first-principles causal scale resolution guided by Rules-Augmented AI (RAAI), with resolution set by a recent non-equilibrium theory. Conversely, for rapid design in a known, parameterized coherent flow class, a purely correlational strategy suffices: combining Non-Intrusive Reduced-Order Modeling (NIROM) with uncentered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) across multi-realization ensembles yields zero-solver synthesis of stationary statistics and unsteady coherent evolution from governing dimensionless parameters. This framework aligns physical causation, statistical correlation, and user intent across flow regimes.

title: Inference Dynamics: Image Classifiers Keep Using Visual Cues After They Are Removed
abstract: Image classifiers are typically evaluated by their final predictions, treating inference as a static image-to-label mapping. Reliability, however, also depends on whether a model can relinquish evidence after that evidence disappears. We reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon: removing a local visual cue from its original location may not remove its influence on the prediction. Once captured by early layers, the cue can become distributed across later representations, making ``no longer visible'' different from ``no longer relied upon.'' We introduce Inference Dynamics, a process-level framework for tracing how cue influence evolves and remains withdrawable across network depth. Given an image and a matched cue-removed reference, we replace cue-aligned states in the original branch with their reference counterparts at successive layers and measure recovery toward the cue-free prediction. The resulting trajectory separates evidence locality from decision-level withdrawability. Across datasets and architectures, we find locality declines before withdrawability collapses: cue-induced information becomes less concentrated at its original support while its effect remains active, before entering an evidence lock-in stage. Consequently, fixed late-stage correction may alter the final readout without removing accumulated cue dependence. We therefore propose Evidence Reset, which selects an input-dependent layer before lock-in and reconstructs cue-aligned states toward their cue-free counterparts. Our results establish evidence withdrawability as a process-level dimension of classifier reliability and suggest a new intervention principle: correction depth should follow the dynamics of evidence rather than be fixed in advance.

title: NavDecision: Parallel Multi-Step Action Prediction with Persistent Self-Referential Learning for Vision-and-Language Navigation
abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires timely decisions based on instructions and visual observations. However, autoregressive VLN models generate action descriptions token by token, introducing substantial inference overhead. Decision models offer an efficient alternative but face challenges in maintaining short-horizon action coherence and long-horizon goal alignment. To address these challenges, we propose NavDecision, an efficient multi-step VLN decision model. We introduce parallel multi-step action prediction (PMAP) to predict multiple action distributions from a shared vision-language state, and memory-augmented self-referential policy optimization (M-SRPO) to learn from unsuccessful trajectories using successful trajectories as references. A cross-iteration success memory further accumulates historical successful trajectories to provide informative training feedback. NavDecision achieves success rates of 64.60% on R2R-CE and 64.57% on RxR-CE with a 4B backbone. Compared with existing autoregressive VLN methods, it delivers significant inference speedups of up to $22.28\times$ and $18.96\times$ while maintaining comparable navigation performance.

title: Floquet-Induced Valley Polarization and Topological Phases in Twisted Bilayer Graphene Heterostructures
abstract: We theoretically investigate twisted bilayer graphene (tTBG) heterostructures subjected to circularly polarized light. Inversion symmetry is broken through the combined application of an out-of-plane electric field and the incorporation of insulating substrates, enabling precise control of the valley degrees of freedom and associated topological phases. We identify a regime in which the valley degeneracy is lifted: one valley retains a gapless, linear Dirac-like dispersion, whereas the other develops a finite band gap and becomes electronically inactive. The interplay between Floquet driving and inversion-symmetry breaking induces topological phase transitions characterized by Chern numbers C = -2, C = -1, and C = 0, together with the emergence of perfectly valley-polarized domain-wall channels. Furthermore, magnetic asymmetry arising from proximity to adjacent two-dimensional ferromagnetic contacts enables spin-valley filtering. These findings establish the potential of graphene-based heterostructures as highly tunable systems for controlling spin and valley degrees of freedom.

title: Dhaani: A Data-Flow-Driven Tool for Greenfield Construction and Brownfield Modernisation
abstract: Large language models can generate plausible code quickly, but an end-to-end prompt leaves developers with little control over decomposition, interfaces, or the assumptions that must survive later revisions. We present Dhaani, a free desktop application for greenfield program construction and brownfield repository modernisation. It makes an annotated data-flow diagram (ADFD) the inspectable contract between intent and implementation. In the greenfield workflow, Build, a user turns natural-language requirements into a typed graph, reviews process specifications and pre/post-conditions, ratifies generated modules, and proceeds in dependency order for Python or .NET (C#). In the brownfield workflow, Migrate uses source inference to recover an ADFD from a Fortran repository, performs target generation in bounded dependency groups, and exposes source-target alignment, generated code, errors, time, token use, and cost. The tool keeps code and artifacts on the user's machine and supports cloud or locally hosted models. Two scientific synthesis case studies produced executable systems where matched low/no-code baselines failed or were substantially less accurate. On 50 open-source Fortran repositories, the migration workflow made all 382 fixed source-oracle probes runnable and passed 327 (85.6%); two direct translation baselines each passed 83 (21.7% of planned probes). Pre-built installers and usage instructions are freely available. Tool and usage guide: https://shraddhasurana.github.io/dhaani/. Video: https://youtu.be/SShWwOMgJ9c.

title: History-bearing thalamocortical signals reconstruct and redirect later decisions in a circuit model
abstract: Experience can guide an ambiguous choice or bias a choice despite strong current evidence. We asked how a thalamocortical circuit carries historical content forward and regulates its influence across successive decisions. In published data from adult male mice, suppressing posterior parietal cortex (PPC) or pulvinar (PUL) improved current judgments most when sensory history conflicted with the stimulus, reflecting reduced historical weighting. In trained thalamocortical circuit models, replaying recorded PUL input to PPC reconstructed a historical trace after equalizing complete recipient states across histories. Replaying the opposite history redirected the later choice, even after the circuit correctly judged an intervening strong stimulus. This historical message occupied a low-dimensional direction in thalamic output that remained broadly reachable under firing-rate bounds; redistributing the arriving current at matched energy showed that fine spatial organization, beyond total input strength, selectively shapes later history use without disrupting current choices. Strong sensory evidence suppressed historical output while preserving internal state differences, whereas ambiguity recruited neuronal rectification thresholds and readout alignment to express history. Small shifts in the cortical operating point modulated later historical influence, and partial attenuation of recurrent drive reduced it across all circuits while preserving current commitments; correspondingly, recurrent dynamics were essential for predicting post-stimulus trajectories in held-out histories. Together, these findings distinguish three operations in history-guided choice: returning thalamocortical input determines which past is reconstructed, recurrent dynamics carry its influence forward across intervening demands, and current sensory evidence gates how strongly it enters the decision.

title: HighwayVerse: A Chain-of-Inspection Benchmark for Highway Infrastructure Anomaly Understanding
abstract: Practical highway infrastructure inspection entails progressive diagnostic reasoning from visual perception to maintenance decisions, yet existing benchmarks remain confined to isolated tasks, leaving Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) insufficiently evaluated across sequential inspection stages. Meanwhile, current datasets focus primarily on highway pavement defects, falling short of real-world inspection across diverse infrastructure components such as highway pavements, guardrails, glare screens, and drainage systems. To address these gaps, we formulate the Highway Infrastructure Inspection Progression Chain (HIIP-Chain), spanning Anomaly Detection, Anomaly Recognition, Condition Analysis, and Maintenance Resolution, and introduce HighwayVerse. HighwayVerse comprises 14,143 real-world Ground and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) inspection records spanning 100 and 17 anomaly categories, respectively, with 84,858 expert-reviewed question-answer pairs. We evaluate 12 open-source and closed-source MLLMs using the chained metric Final, which credits a correct maintenance decision only when all preceding diagnostic stages are completed correctly. Results show that although models achieve relatively high accuracy when initially judging whether an anomaly is present, their markedly lower Final scores expose struggles across downstream recognition, analysis, and decision-making. This discrepancy indicates that current MLLMs do not fully comprehend specific highway anomaly patterns beyond superficial initial judgments. Furthermore, we propose LaneRAG, a training-free retrieval-augmented framework that provides hierarchical reference guidance achieving consistent performance improvements across diverse MLLMs. Our dataset, evaluation benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.

title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
abstract: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol. We develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, in good agreement with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. We further combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing, finding that squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged. Our results establish quantum limit cycles as a metrological resource and clarify the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.

title: Not All Directions Are Flat: Decomposed-Gradient Flatness for Sparse-View 3D Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Many applications of novel view synthesis, such as augmented reality and robotics, can afford only a few input views, since dense capture is costly. With such sparse views, however, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) overfits the training views and degrades at unseen viewpoints. Among the approaches to this problem, flat-minima optimization treats the Gaussians as trainable parameters and steers training toward flat minima, which generalize better, by perturbing the Gaussians with random noise or along the training gradient. However, these perturbations ignore their direction relative to the other training views. Interestingly, we find that the direction of the perturbation determines whether it improves generalization. Specifically, we decompose the gradient of each training view into a component parallel to the average gradient of all views, on which the views agree, and an orthogonal component, on which they disagree. Perturbing along the orthogonal component improves generalization, whereas perturbing along the parallel component does not. We further find that the flatness correction often opposes the reconstruction gradient, shrinking or even reversing the reconstruction step. Based on these findings, we propose DecoFlat, which perturbs each Gaussian along the orthogonal component together with random noise. Furthermore, we introduce a conflict-aware correction, which removes the part of the flatness correction that opposes the reconstruction gradient, and a rescheduling of the spherical-harmonics color, which suppresses the overfitting of view-dependent appearance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DecoFlat, as a plug-in optimizer, consistently improves vanilla 3DGS and a wide range of sparse-view 3DGS methods.

title: DeRail: Escaping Trajectory Priors via Counterfactual Action Steering for Mid-Execution Instruction Switching
abstract: Robots operating in the real world must often adapt when user instructions change mid-execution, yet current instruction-conditioned robot policies, including Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs), are largely evaluated under fixed-instruction episodes. We study mid-execution instruction switching and identify trajectory hijacking as a key failure mode, where the policy fails to redirect sufficiently toward the switched target, with its post-switch behavior remaining fully or partially drawn toward trajectories associated with non-target tasks. We propose Counterfactual Action Steering (CAS), a training-free, model-agnostic inference-time method that identifies interfering non-target tasks, queries the same policy with corresponding counterfactual instructions, and uses target--counterfactual action differences to steer execution away from interfering trajectory priors. Experiments on LIBERO-Goal-Switch and CALVIN-Custom-Switch across five VLA and WAM policies, together with real-robot evaluation, show that CAS consistently improves switching success; for example, on CALVIN-Custom-Switch in the $[15,21]$ switching range, CAS improves $π_{0.5}$ from 5.8\% to 54.6\%. Successful CAS-guided rollouts further provide higher-quality self-training supervision than vanilla successful rollouts with the same number of trajectories, yielding stronger policies that generalize to unseen later instruction switches. Code will be made publicly available.

title: Synthetic EHR Generators Should Be Audited Like LLMs
abstract: Synthetic electronic health record (EHR) generation is increasingly adopting large autoregressive models, yet privacy evaluation has not kept pace, relying heavily on similarity-based heuristics and aggregate metrics that can obscure patient-specific memorisation. We argue that these models should additionally undergo LLM-style memorisation audits at the level of individual patient records. We support this position by comparing membership-inference evaluations across four prominent autoregressive EHR generators, highlighting inconsistent evaluation practices in patient representations and attack procedures. We evaluate trajectory reconstruction from partial context and introduce randomly assigned patient-level canaries to distinguish memorised associations from clinical generalisation. We examine these methods in a GPT-2-style model deliberately overfit to 1,000 MIMIC-IV patient trajectories, creating a controlled setting in which memorisation should be readily detectable. The model systematically recovers training patients' canaries, and their trajectory reconstruction approaches perfect accuracy with increasing context. Held-out patients show no systematic canary recovery, while reconstruction remains low and improves only marginally with additional context. These experiments establish a positive-control baseline for further evaluation of these methods in realistically trained models.

title: Lagrangian particle simulations of an idealized deep convective squall line: Aggregation, fragmentation, and their polarimetric signatures
abstract: We investigate secondary ice production (SIP) in an idealized deep convective squall line using the Lagrangian particle model McSnow coupled to ICON. The model represents ice particle properties, including habit, riming degree, and mass composition. We introduce a parameterization of collision-induced ice--ice fragmentation linked to apparent density as a measure of particle fragility. We compare rime splintering (RS), freezing fragmentation (FF), and collision-induced fragmentation (CF), including turbulence-enhanced collision rates. Collision-induced fragmentation is the dominant SIP mechanism, strongly increasing ice number concentrations in the dendritic growth zone. Freezing fragmentation contributes little because sufficiently large raindrops are scarce. Rime splintering produces secondary ice at lower altitudes and indirectly promotes large aggregates. Turbulence has little effect on fragmentation but enhances the aggregation of fragments. Fragmentation shifts the particle size distribution toward smaller sizes and reduces precipitation, while turbulence-enhanced aggregation partly restores large particles and precipitation. McRadar forward simulations show that SIP affects radar moments and Doppler spectra. Specific differential phase KDP provides the clearest conventional radar signature of fragmentation. Spectral differential reflectivity identifies secondary ice source regions through enhanced signals at the slow edge of the Doppler spectrum. Our results identify collision-induced fragmentation as a key source of secondary ice in deep convection and show that its impact depends on interactions with aggregation and turbulence. Spectral polarimetric radar observations may help constrain SIP in nature.

title: Ion Backflow Suppression and Absorption Dynamics in Cascaded GEM Structures
abstract: Ion backflow (IBF) is a persistent challenge in Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) detectors: positive ions drifting back into the sensitive volume distort the drift field and degrade both spatial and energy resolution. We investigate the ion-absorption characteristics of single- to quintuple-GEM detectors using ANSYS and Garfield$^{++}$ for an Ar/CO$_2$ (70:30) gas mixture. A layer-resolved formalism is developed that distinguishes conditional foil-level absorption from a detector-level absorption metric that correctly weights ion production at every amplification stage. For the conventional biconical geometry, cascading foils improves the overall ion-absorption fraction only moderately, from 47.83\% for a single GEM to 59.06\% for a quintuple GEM. Replacing the biconical holes with a single-conical profile raises the absorption fraction to 75\%-87\% across the same range of multiplicities and reduces the IBF/Gain ratio by a factor of two to three an improvement that exceeds what is gained by adding four additional biconical foils. As a secondary test under more realistic conditions, the second transfer-gap length of a triple-GEM detector is varied from 1.2 to 3.5~mm. The gain shows a non-monotonic dependence with a maximum near 2.0-2.5~mm, while the IBF/Gain ratio decreases monotonically with increasing gap length; the single-conical geometry retains its factor-of-two advantage throughout. These findings establish that ion suppression in cascaded GEM structures is governed not only by the number of foils but primarily by the local ion-collection properties of each foil, and that single-conical holes represent a promising route to improved performance in high-rate detector applications.

title: Profinite groups with coprime automorphisms whose orbits generate nilpotent subgroups
abstract: Suppose that a profinite group $G$ admits a finite group of coprime automorphisms $A$ such that for any $φ\in A$ every subgroup $\langle x^{\langleφ\rangle}\rangle$ generated by the $\langleφ\rangle$-orbit of an element $x\in G$ is nilpotent. It is proved that $[G,A]$ is pronilpotent, and if $A$ is soluble and the fixed-point subgroup $C_G(A)$ is locally nilpotent, then $G$ is locally nilpotent.

title: When do stored facts become available in looped transformers?
abstract: Looped transformers do not acquire new knowledge during a forward pass. Prior work shows that they store as many bits in their weights as non-looped models. It remains unclear how recurrence makes this knowledge available during inference. We study this question using synthetic factual recall and multi-hop reasoning, measuring depth-resolved readable information in bits with native readouts and tuned lenses. Under final-loop supervision, single-hop facts become readable progressively: heavier memorization loads delay retrieval despite comparable final readable information. Untied baselines of equal unrolled depth concentrate retrieval near the end of their stacks, whereas looped models expose facts earlier. This delay is not intrinsic to the tested recall tasks: training with supervision and depth-specific readouts at every loop makes near-final information readable after the first loop in all tested configurations. Representational analysis shows value-related structure emerging within states organized by the query key. We then study multi-hop chains whose facts are stored in the weights rather than given in the prompt. Intermediate entities become decodable in chain order, and aligned transitions show next-entity structure developing while current-entity structure remains dominant. Interventions in a released six-recurrence model establish a causal role for these representations. Counterfactual replacements of a probe-defined entity component at a single prompt position redirect downstream bridge entities and the final answer. Conversely, replacements from queries that reach the same entity through different preceding relations, preserving the remaining relation suffix, retain the original answer in over 99.5\% of tested cases. These results distinguish a training-dependent schedule for factual recall from the causal role of retrieved-entity representations in subsequent composition.

title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
abstract: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

title: Learning free energy across a differentiable temperature range by deep generative modeling
abstract: Free energy governs the directionality, stability, and temperature sensitivity of physical, chemical, and biological transformations. Conventional free energy calculations, such as thermodynamic integration and free energy perturbation, often have to be performed at individual temperatures and are limited by the high cost of sampling an extensive set of thermodynamic states. Here, we introduce learned temperature-differentiable free energy perturbation (TD-FEP), a deep generative framework that learns a temperature-conditioned, invertible mapping between reference and target systems through data-free, energy-based optimization. TD-FEP thereby unifies one-shot state generation and free energy calculation across a continuous temperature range. We validated TD-FEP across a broad range of applications, including isolated molecules, periodic materials, and chemical reactions.

title: Large Deviations and Critical Scaling in the Finite-Population Granovetter Threshold Model
