title: Efficient numerical computation of the generalized Marcum $Q$-function with applications
abstract: The computation of the generalized Marcum $Q$-function, $Q_ν(a,b)$, is fundamental to radar detection and wireless communications. The state-of-the-art \textbf{Algorithm 939} (Gil et al., ACM TOMS 2014) serves as the current gold standard by employing a hybrid evaluation scheme combining series expansions, asymptotic formulas, numerical integration and recurrence relations. However, it suffers from a computational bottleneck: in the ``large $a$, small $b$'' regime, the algorithm resorts to computationally expensive numerical quadrature, thereby limiting its overall efficiency. To bridge this gap, we utilize a series representation of the generalized Marcum $Q$-function to construct the Series Expansion based on Recurrence Relations (\textbf{SE-RR}) algorithm. Expanded in powers of $b$, this series computes its coefficients via a stable recurrence relation, resulting in a remarkably low computational cost. By analyzing rounding, truncation and cancellation errors, we identify the optimal region for SE-RR as the ``large $a$, small $b$'' regime, which covers the parameter space where Algorithm~939 relies on costly numerical quadrature. Consequently, we integrate SE-RR into Algorithm~939 to develop a hybrid algorithm for evaluating $Q_ν(a,b)$. Benchmarked against $10^7$ log-uniformly sampled parameter triples $(a, b, ν) \in [0.01, 100] \times [0.001, 100] \times [1, 1000]$, the hybrid algorithm achieves an average speedup of 82.2\% overall, while in the region where SE-RR is applied, it delivers an average speedup of 156.6\% and a maximum pointwise speedup of $\mathrm{5.49}\times$. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the hybrid algorithm by computing the cumulative distribution function of the noncentral chi distribution and outage probabilities for 5G/6G ultra-reliable low-latency communications.

title: THETA: Heat Diffusion as a Structural Prior for Cross-Domain Transfer in Graph Foundation Models
abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) aim to learn transferable representations across domains with heterogeneous node attributes and graph structures. However, relations inferred from node attributes can rely on domain-specific feature semantics, limiting their transferability to unseen graphs, particularly in low-label regimes. We propose THETA (Topology-aware HEat-based TrAnsfer), a graph foundation model that leverages Heat Kernel Signatures (HKS) as a topology-based structural prior for cross-domain transfer. By characterizing nodes' heat-return behavior across diffusion scales, HKS provides a common structural descriptor across graphs without requiring aligned attribute semantics, complementing feature-based relations with information about local and multiscale connectivity. THETA incorporates this prior into both pre-training and few-shot adaptation. During pre-training, it combines HKS with node attributes to construct refined graph views and trains a shared encoder via contrastive learning. During adaptation, it uses HKS to guide edge-weight adjustment and prototype refinement while keeping the encoder frozen and retaining the contribution of labeled support nodes. Through HKS, THETA uses structural information from heat diffusion to guide both representation learning and few-shot adaptation with unlabeled target-domain data. Extensive experiments across diverse graph domains demonstrate that THETA consistently outperforms existing baselines on downstream tasks, highlighting the value of heat diffusion as a structural prior for transferable graph representations.

title: Computer-Aided Analysis of Gradient Descent under Generalized Smoothness
abstract: First-order methods constitute a central algorithmic paradigm in high dimensional applications. Under classical assumptions, their performance has been studied quite comprehensively with the developed theoretical apparatus of modern optimization. The development of the Performance Estimation Problems framework led to even deeper understanding and allowed computer-assisted derivation of exact worst-case guarantees. Due to convex nature of PEP programs, the framework is not applicable for systems that involve non-convex constraints. This includes a wide range of non-standard assumptions, some of them are highly relevant for practice such as generalized smoothness. In this paper proposes an approach of utilizing template solutions to derive guarantees in settings that do not admit convex formulation of exact worst-case performance problem. The approach is showcased by studying the performance of the gradient descent method for convex functions that also satisfy generalized smoothness assumption. Despite the inherent conservatism of the approach, this paper improves an existing convergence guarantee in the semi-automated manner.

title: Finite conformal models and the Kac--van de Leur conjecture
abstract: We prove that every simple Lie superalgebra containing the centerless Virasoro algebra, with diagonal $L_0$-action, uniformly bounded weight multiplicities, and support in finitely many cosets of $\Z$, is isomorphic, as a parity-graded Lie superalgebra, to a member of the Witt, special, contact, or Cheng--Kac families. Thus the amended Kac--van de Leur list is exhaustive. Every such algebra admits a finite ordinary conformal model and is a quotient by the full center of a twisted coefficient algebra of a finite simple conformal superalgebra. For Lie superalgebras containing the centerless Virasoro algebra, we also prove that linear commutator growth is equivalent to uniformly bounded weight spaces, provided the grading is diagonal and integral and each weight space is finite-dimensional.

title: PartPO: Part-Level Policy Optimization for Shape-to-Program Generation
abstract: We present PartPO, a reinforcement learning method for generating structured shape programs from 3D point clouds. Existing shape-to-program models are trained with supervised learning on procedurally generated data and generalize poorly to more diverse shapes, while reinforcement learning from execution feedback assigns a single scalar reward to a long program that builds many parts, making credit assignment difficult. PartPO instead builds on a core property of the task: shape programs are self-describing, with each semantically named part produced by its own code block. It segments each generated program by its parts and applies part-level rewards only to the code of the corresponding part, a category reward only to the object name, and a shape-level reward to the whole program. The required part supervision is obtained without manual annotation, by grounding part names on target meshes with an open-vocabulary segmentation model prompt-tuned on the model's own outputs. Applied to MeshCoder, PartPO improves reconstruction accuracy and execution success on ShapeNetCore and ABO over the base model, rejection-sampling fine-tuning and trajectory-level RL, and generalizes to the unseen HSSD dataset. Code will be released at https://github.com/HannuoZ/PartPO.

title: NANO: Unifying Missingness and Input Uncertainty in Tabular Learning
abstract: Missing values are common in tabular data, yet current approaches to handling them often overlook two dimensions. First, an observed value may be uncertain, while a Not-Observed (N.O.) value may still have a reasonable estimate. Inputs should therefore span a continuous spectrum from no evidence to a fully trusted observation. Second, Not-Applicable (N.A.) means that no meaningful value exists for a record, yet this semantic state often lacks explicit representation. To address both dimensions, we introduce NANO, a unified plug-in for input encoding that fits most token-based architectures. Guided by Bayesian evidence weighting, NANO adjusts the influence of a supplied value according to confidence, with all zero-confidence estimates mapped to the same N.O. representation. NANO accepts, but does not require, per-example confidence information during training or inference. For N.A., a separate representation enables models to encode inapplicability and its schema-defined reasons into context. Experiments across eleven datasets and nine backbones show that mixed-confidence training enables a single NANO model to generalize across inference confidence levels, remaining competitive without estimates and improving steadily as estimate reliability and confidence increase. The effectiveness of NANO's handling of N.A. is further demonstrated on three augmented datasets.

title: Linking vascular pathways to organ anatomical structures in the Human Reference Atlas
abstract: As part of the Human Reference Atlas (HRA) initiative, which brings together more than 25 international consortia to map the entire healthy adult body, we developed a multiscale Vasculature Common Coordinate Framework (VCCF). The VCCF uses vascular pathways to describe the location of organs, anatomical structures, and cells throughout the body. Here, we present the VCCF Blood Vasculature Organ Crosswalk, which links blood vessels to anatomical structures they supply or drain, and the Pathways Crosswalk, which lists relationships between blood vessels, lymphatic vessels, and nerves. Blood Vasculature Organ Crosswalk Diagrams support the authoring and review of the crosswalk tables. In machine readable files, we catalog 349 blood vessels from these diagrams, with 663 linkages to 295 anatomical structures across 20 organs/body regions and 28 functional tissue units. The VCCF crosswalk tables and diagrams have been validated algorithmically and by 11 organ experts. They have brought together experts from different domains to document existing knowledge of the human vasculature and identify gaps where future research is needed.

title: Verified parameter estimation for differential-equation models: NIST reference problems and the theophylline flip-flop
abstract: Parameters fitted to differential-equation models carry two kinds of error: statistical error from noisy data, and numerical error from the solver and the optimizer that compute the fit. Standard fitting tools report the first and leave the second unexamined, and they return one optimum without saying whether another parameter set fits the data equally well. We describe SIRPY, a differential-equation solver that checks every solution it returns by substituting it back into the equation, and we test it in two settings. First, on eleven nonlinear-regression reference problems from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), each written as a first-order differential equation and fitted by least squares with every model curve supplied by SIRPY, the estimates agree with NIST's certified values to 7.1 to 8.8 significant digits on ten problems, with all 6{,}281 solves verified; the eleventh problem exposed a limitation of the residual check, which we report and explain. Second, on the classic theophylline pharmacokinetic data, SIRPY found two parameter sets whose predicted curves agree to within $1.7\times10^{-11}$~mg/L and matched the reference fit from the R package \texttt{nlme} to every printed digit; the data alone cannot decide which rate is absorption and which is elimination, and physiology must. We state precisely what the verification certifies, what it does not, and what remains to be done to turn a residual check into a proven bound on estimation error.

title: Persistent Jailbreak Backdoor Attack
abstract: Safety alignment is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) to produce helpful and harmless responses. However, an attacker can plant a jailbreak backdoor in an LLM such that adding a universal trigger word or phrase to a harmful prompt elicits attacker-desired responses. Existing jailbreak backdoor attacks induce distinct behaviors on backdoored inputs and safety samples (harmful prompts paired with refusal responses), making the backdoors susceptible to subsequent safety alignment and advanced defenses. In this paper, we propose a persistent jailbreak backdoor attack that reduces the divergence between clean and trigger-conditioned continuations during LLM decoding, making backdoored samples difficult to distinguish from safety samples. We also introduce a deferred-response mechanism that postpones harmful generations, further disguising the backdoor behavior. We evaluate our attack, PJBack, on eight LLMs from five model families, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. PJBack achieves an average attack success rate of 93.9% and bypasses all seven evaluated defenses while preserving benign utility. In contrast, five existing backdoor attacks either achieve limited attack success or fail to withstand the evaluated defenses.

title: Ego-HMB: Human Motion Bridging from Egocentric Images via A Motion Bridge Diffusion Model
abstract: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.

title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling for Mitigation of Spatially-Variant System Blur in Ultra-High-Resolution CT of Trabecular Bone
abstract: Objective: CT spatial resolution degrades with distance from isocenter. We evaluate diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) deblurring for restoring structural detail and harmonizing texture features (TFs) of off-center trabecular bone to isocenter in ultra-high resolution CT (UHR CT). Methods: DPS pairs a diffusion prior, trained on isocenter UHR CT patches of trabecular bone from four human femora, with a likelihood term enforcing consistency with the observed image. Two variants were tested on a held-out femur at radial shifts of 90, 130 and 160 mm: KnownBlurDPS, with an anisotropic Gaussian kernel derived from modulation transfer function measurements, and BlindDPS, which estimated the kernel jointly with the image. Restored patches were compared with isocenter ground truth by structural similarity (SSIM), gradient magnitude similarity deviation (GMSD), and concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) of 40 gray-level co-occurrence and run-length TFs. Results: Both DPS variants improved SSIM and GMSD by 1-10% and mean TF CCC by 30-130%. The number of reproducible TFs (CCC > 0.80) at 90/130/160 mm rose from 13/2/1 without deblurring to 33/35/29 (KnownBlurDPS) and 40/36/16 (BlindDPS). At 90 mm, the accuracy of a linear classifier predicting the shift from TFs dropped from 79% to chance level with BlindDPS. Conclusion: DPS partly restores trabecular detail and TF reproducibility lost to spatially-variant blur in UHR CT; the blind variant matches the measured-kernel variant up to 130 mm. Significance: DPS deblurring can standardize trabecular bone TFs against patient mis-centering, potentially improving the robustness of TF-based CT radiomics; its blind form needs no CT system characterization.

title: A Parallel APSOR SPIKE Algorithm for Classical and Soft Layer Obstacle Problems
abstract: This paper presents a parallel scheme for classical obstacle problems and for obstacle problems with a soft layer. The adaptive projected SOR method (APSOR) \cite{MS21} finds the contact set on one process. The linear system defined by the frozen contact set is then solved exactly in parallel by the SPIKE algorithm \cite{PS06}, in which the diagonal blocks are factorized independently and the coupling is condensed into a small reduced system. The remaining nonlinearity of the soft-layer problem \cite{CRWX21} is resolved by a Picard iteration in which every pass reuses the factorization, and a Karush--Kuhn--Tucker (KKT) test stops the iteration. The scheme needs no tuned relaxation parameter. Convergence is proved: APSOR decreases the energy, the SPIKE solve is exact and independent of the number of processes, the Picard iteration is a contraction with factor below $0.052$ on the unit square, and under strict complementarity the loop stops at the unique KKT point. Four classical problems \cite{TSFO14} and four soft-layer examples \cite{CRWX21} in one and two dimensions are computed and compared with exact and analytic solutions (maximum errors $1.1\times10^{-8}$, $7.2\times10^{-14}$ and $6.0\times10^{-4}$), and the KKT test is passed in all eight runs. CPU timings with 1 to 16 MPI ranks show that the SPIKE decomposition takes most of the time in two dimensions, so that the part that is distributed over the ranks is the dominant part of the work.

title: Combined quasi-neutral and zero-relaxation limit of Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck system
abstract: In this paper, we consider the combined quasi-neutral and zero-relaxation limit of Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck system. With well-prepared initial, we show that the convergence from Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck system for electron and Vlasov-Poisson-Fokker-Planck system for ion to the incompressible Euler equations and compressible Euler equations, respectively.

title: The Geometry of Banach space operator-valued measures with cyclic dilations
abstract: In this paper, we investigate the geometric properties of operator-valued measures with cyclic dilations. Under a localization condition on the normal part of the bidual, we establish James-type characterizations of shrinking, bounded completeness, and reflexivity for projection-valued measures. These characterizations apply to spaces admitting no continuous Schauder frame, including $L_1[0,1]$. Using vector measure representations and interpolation, we prove that an operator-valued measure admitting a cyclic dilation has a reflexive cyclic dilation if and only if the underlying space is reflexive. Under the same cyclicity assumption, we also characterize the existence of cyclic dilations on spaces containing no $\ell_1$ and on KB-spaces. The dilation spaces can be chosen to be order-continuous Köthe function spaces. Without assuming cyclicity, we give a weak compactness criterion and local variation conditions for reflexive dilations; an example on $\ell_2$ shows that reflexivity alone is insufficient. For a separable space containing no $c_0$, a normalized operator-valued measure is induced by a continuous Schauder frame if and only if it admits a cyclic dilation and has $σ$-finite operator-norm variation. Finally, for measure quotients whose synthesis maps admit bounded linear right inverses, we construct compatible cyclic $L_p$-dilations and represent the quotient spaces as inductive limits, with applications to ReLU Barron spaces.

title: Flag algebras and the exact largest probability of a linear inequality between iid random variables
abstract: How large can $\mathbb P[X_1+X_2+X_3<2X_4]$ be when $X_1,\dots,X_4$ are independent with a common law $μ$ on $[0,\infty)$? Previous work gave lower bounds through explicit constructions and upper bounds through exchangeability. The best lower bound, $0.4006953723\ldots$, was conjectured by \citet{BF} to be the exact value of the supremum. We prove this conjecture and formalize the proof in Lean~4. The improved upper bound uses the fact that independence gives more than exchangeability: two subsamples are conditionally independent given their shared points. As in Razborov's flag algebras, this yields a semidefinite program on the sign patterns of a few sample points. The new ingredient is to record also whether one sample point exceeds a fixed multiple of another, at ratios read off the extremal construction: with three such cutoffs, four sample points give an exact certificate, while additive comparisons alone leave a gap at seven points. We extend this study to the functions \[ S_2(c) = \sup_μ\mathbb P_μ[X_1+X_2<cX_3],\qquad S_3(c) = \sup_μ\mathbb P_μ[X_1+X_2+X_3<cX_4] \] and determine their exact values on several intervals of $c$. On other intervals, we provide lower and upper bounds that certify eighteen discontinuity points of $S_2$ and five of $S_3$, consistent with a nested staircase structure. The certified jumps are explained by new winning patterns becoming feasible in the lower-bound constructions. We answer Problem~5.3 of \cite{BF} by showing that no coefficient $c$ satisfies $S_3(c)=1/2$, and prove the analogous statement for $S_2$. The thresholds $\sup\{c:S_2(c)\le1/2\}$ and $\sup\{c:S_3(c)\le1/2\}$ are respectively the golden ratio $(1+\sqrt5)/2$ and the silver ratio $1+\sqrt2$.

title: Curvature Mismatch and Local Errors in Galaxy Property Estimation
abstract: Linear probes are widely used to evaluate learned representations and infer physical quantities from unlabelled data. The probe's predictions are from an affine function in ambient space restricted to the underlying representation, and consequently, even a representation that has complete information needed to predict a target can produce systematic probe errors when that information is encoded in a form inaccessible to the linear probe. Here we share that some of this probing error is due to the innate geometry of the manifold. Linear probes, when evaluated on a curved manifold, generally have a nonzero intrinsic Hessian (what we colloquially call "probe-facing curvature") given by $\langle w_N,\mathrm{II}\rangle$, the manifold's second fundamental form dotted with the probe's normal component. We fit linear probes to galaxy embeddings from five pretrained encoders and intervene on this curvature term to evaluate its contribution to the probe performance. We find that keeping this inherited curvature improves the local fit where it matches the label's curvature. Removing the curvature component of the probe where it does not match the label curvature also provides improvements, and correcting it in every neighbourhood raises held-out local $R^2$ by 0.006 to 0.010 on galaxies, gaining more where the two curvatures disagree. We isolated these gains to be from the underlying geometry and not an automatic guarantee from least squares training.

title: IteraSong: LLM-Guided Iterative Symbolic Music Creation in a Web DAW
abstract: Music creation is inherently iterative, yet many symbolic generation systems still center on producing or regenerating isolated outputs. We present IteraSong, an interactive web-based Digital Audio Workstation (DAW) for LLM-guided iterative symbolic music creation. Unlike one-shot generation systems, IteraSong supports a generate-audition-edit-refine loop over a persistent multi-track project. Users initialize a fully labeled pop draft, then progressively refine it through natural-language instructions. The LLM maps requests to a hierarchical action space of editing primitives exposed via Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools, spanning global, track, section, and bar/note scopes. The demo enables attendees to edit multi-track compositions in natural language, apply deterministic and generative edits, and undo/redo changes in real time.

title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. We present Tenlai-TTS 2.0, which learns continuous speech representations through end-to-end training to balance acoustic detail with autoregressive predictability. The model comprises a speech encoder with a capacity-controlled Gaussian bottleneck, a large language model (LLM) with an autoregressive diffusion transformer (AR-DiT) head, a flow-matching (FM) mel-spectrogram decoder, and a multi-task recognition model (RM). With energy normalization and fixed-variance Gaussian noise, the bottleneck has a closed-form upper bound on its information rate. Through joint optimization with reconstruction, recognition, and next-patch prediction objectives, we learn continuous speech representations that suit all three tasks and train the LLM and AR-DiT for autoregressive generation. The LLM and AR-DiT are further optimized using differentiable reconstruction and recognition feedback on their predicted latents through the FM decoder and RM. On Seed-TTS-eval, this feedback-based optimization reduces character error rate (CER) from 0.82% to 0.74% on test-zh and from 8.32% to 7.08% on test-hard-zh, and word error rate (WER) from 1.32% to 1.27% on test-en, compared with joint training alone. Subsequent reinforcement learning further reduces CER to 6.29% on test-hard-zh and WER to 1.08% on test-en, with speaker similarity scores of 0.811, 0.766, and 0.784 on test-zh, test-en, and test-hard-zh, respectively.

title: SatMend: LLM Agents for Automated Software Repair in Satellite Constellations with Intermittent Ground Contact
abstract: Satellite constellations rely on onboard software to sustain services across cooperating spacecraft. Maintaining this software requires handling related component versions and different failure causes while delivering repairs through intermittent ground contact. Automated software repair in satellite constellations remains underexplored, particularly the coordination of repairs across related versions with verified onboard recovery under intermittent ground contact. To address this gap, we propose SatMend, a software repair method driven by ground-based large language model (LLM) agents. SatMend organizes related versions into persistent sessions to retain diagnostic context and combines source and runtime evidence to select code repair or state recovery actions. It validates each version separately and submits ready candidates during continued repair, allowing ground preparation to overlap with onboard delivery and verification. Experimental results show that across configurations with 16 to 64 satellites, SatMend restores 192 of 224 faulty applications within 600 s, compared with 40 for SWE-agent, 77 for Agentless, 124 for RepairAgent, and 115 for SWE-Search. These results demonstrate SatMend's effectiveness in restoring applications and supporting service continuity in satellite constellations with intermittent ground contact.

title: Generation and characterization of unsteady inflows in a fan-vane wind tunnel
abstract: Wind-tunnel experiments often require inflows with specific combinations of turbulence intensity and integral length scale because both can influence the measured response. To broaden the range of attainable inflows, this study uses pseudorandom vane excitation to generate large-scale turbulence and examines how both quantities vary with the amplitude and spectral shape of the vane-angle command. In each test, the 15 servo-driven vanes downstream of a 768-fan array received the same angle command, and all fans operated at a common, constant duty cycle. Hot-wire measurements covered twenty heights and selected spanwise and downstream positions. At a fan-control duty cycle of 60%, increasing vane angular amplitude raised profile-mean turbulence intensity from 7.3% to 31.8% under periodic forcing and from 6.2% to 23.0% under pseudorandom forcing. With the normalized pseudorandom command spectrum held fixed, larger angular amplitudes increased the low-frequency share of velocity variance, accompanied by longer correlation times and larger integral scales. At a root-mean-square angular amplitude of 15 degrees, changing the command spectrum yielded profile-mean integral length scales of 0.88-1.67 m at similar turbulence intensities. The principal features of the velocity spectra persisted between 2 and 4 m downstream, while integral scales continued to change. Both forcing types exhibited middle-region minima in turbulence intensity and integral scale. Regional analysis of a representative pseudorandom case linked these minima to weaker low-frequency fluctuations and shorter correlation times. These findings provide a basis for selecting vane inputs according to the turbulence-intensity and integral-scale requirements of the intended test region.

title: Electron Parameters in H2:Ar:CH4 Plasma Maintained by Microwave and Laser Radiation
abstract: Electron parameters in an atmospheric-pressure hybrid plasma in the 95H2:3Ar:2CH4 mixture maintained by pulsed-periodic microwave radiation (2.47 GHz) and CO2 laser radiation (10.6 μm) were studied. The plasma was generated in a quasi-cylindrical reactor, which was a resonator for TM011-mode microwave radiation. It was shown that in the hybrid plasma emission spectra the Hα and H{\betta} lines are strongly broadened and can be approximated by the sum of two Lorentzian contours (dual-Lorentzian approximation). The Stark broadening of the Hα and H{\betta} lines was used to measure the electron density in the plasma, and the ratio of their intensities allowed to estimate the electron temperature. To simplify the description of the hybrid plasma properties the concept of two plasma states caused by the pulsed injection of laser energy into the plasma was introduced. The hybrid plasma state, corresponding to the plasma state during the laser pulse, is characterized by a high electron density of (1-2.5)*10^17 cm-3 and an electron temperature of ~0.5-0.6 eV. The electron density in the state corresponding to the time intervals between laser pulses (1.8*10^14-5*10^15 cm-3) is more than an order of magnitude lower than the electron density in the first state, but it is 2-10 times higher than the electron density in microwave plasma ((1-5)*10^14 cm-3). The electron temperature in this state is 0.16-0.24 eV. The radius of the dense plasma region with an electron density of ~10^17 cm-3 is estimated to be ~0.5-1 mm.

title: InfoField3D: Differentiable Information Field for Embodied Task-Oriented View Planning
abstract: Effective task execution requires embodied agents to select observation positions that provide sufficient task-relevant information. Existing approaches typically predict viewpoints with learned models or score discrete candidates, but they either struggle to incorporate new constraints such as reachability or require extensive candidate evaluation to search. We introduce InfoField3D, which lifts geometry-bound information into a differentiable analytic field, whose value at each 3D observation position represents the task-required information accessible there. It uses low-order spherical harmonics to encode directional information responses and analytic line integrals of Gaussian occupancy functions to model occlusion along lines of sight. This formulation casts task-driven camera placement as a well-studied constrained continuous optimization problem, enabling both flexible incorporation of constraints through the feasible domain and efficient viewpoint search even in the presence of occlusion. Experiments show that InfoField3D compactly preserves the pointwise information landscape with high fidelity and generally recommends higher-quality, more robust viewpoints at lower search cost than the evaluated baselines. Controlled evaluations with a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy further suggest that the recommended views can improve downstream task performance under information-limited initial viewpoints.

title: EVis+: Literature-Grounded Visual Analytics for Hypothesis-Driven Geoscientific Data Exploration
abstract: Scientific researchers often interpret observational data in light of prior findings reported in the scientific literature. However, scientific literature typically remains external to visual analytics environments, requiring researchers to manually connect published findings with the data and hypotheses under investigation. In this paper, we present EVis+, a literature-grounded visual analytics system for condition-event time series analysis in geoscience. EVis+ enhances observational data exploration by retrieving and synthesizing literature-derived insights relevant to the dataset and analytical goals, transforming user-selected insights into testable hypotheses and mapping them to domain-specific visualizations through expert-curated templates, and supporting evidence examination, discrepancy validation, and literature-driven re-exploration to support iterative hypothesis refinement and scientific exploration. Rather than handing scientific analysis to an unconstrained language model, EVis+ uses structured AI-assisted transformations that keep intermediate results visible, allowing researchers to inspect and guide the analysis at each step. We evaluate the system through an evidence-grounding audit, a structured expert assessment of the insights, and case studies with geoscientists and a comparative study with domain experts.

title: Why Adaptive Optimizers Struggle with Large Convolution Kernels
abstract: Large convolution kernels enlarge the receptive fields of ConvNets at a modest computational cost, but they are notoriously difficult to train. Existing large-kernel networks therefore rely on costly training techniques, such as parallel small-kernel branches with batch normalization. In this paper, we trace this difficulty to adaptive optimizers such as Adam, which normalize the update of every weight separately. Since input features rarely average to zero, all weights of a kernel share a common gradient, and these optimizers move the mean of a $k\times k$ kernel $k$ times as far as a single parameter. We find this mean amplification in widely used ConvNets and vision transformers, and show that it can force the maximal learning rate to fall as $1/k^2$. We further prove that the basis of the discrete cosine transform (DCT) isolates the mean and is the only orthonormal basis that diagonalizes every stationary gradient statistic with mirrored boundaries. We therefore train large kernels through their DCT coefficients and convert them back after training. The resulting method, DCT-Rep, requires only a few lines of code and adds no parameters, no inference cost and negligible training overhead. Extensive experiments on image classification, object detection, semantic segmentation and image restoration show that DCT-Rep consistently improves large-kernel ConvNets and vision transformers, by $+0.79\%$ top-1 accuracy for a large-kernel ConvNeXt-T and $+0.43\%$ for ViT-S/16 on ImageNet-1K, $+1.4$ box AP on COCO, $+1.2$ mIoU on ADE20K and up to $+0.4$ dB on image deblurring, where the gain grows with the kernel size.

title: Unknotting number is strictly subadditive for the trefoil
abstract: A trefoil and a certain fourteen-crossing knot take four crossing changes to unknot separately and at most three together. We extend this example to infinitely many prime partners and show that the same partners give a saving for every nontrivial positive braid knot and, up to mirror, every nontrivial torus knot.

title: Möbius Fusion Algebra
abstract: Given a pseudo-unitary modular tensor category $\mathcal{C}$ with an anti-monoidal involution $\mathsf{P}$, we define a generally non-commutative algebra from this data, which we call the Möbius fusion algebra $\mathfrak{M}$ of $(\mathcal{C},\mathsf{P})$, in terms of ribbon graphs drawn on the Möbius band, where the orientation-reversal of the Möbius band acts on the graphs by $\mathsf{P}$. We show that this algebra is semisimple, and give a formula for the dimensions of its simple modules, in terms of the modular $S$-matrix of $\mathcal{C}$ and a certain set of quantities extracted from the action of $\mathsf{P}$. This formula is expected to play the role of a non-orientable analogue of the Verlinde formula, in the context of Reshetikhin-Turaev-type topological quantum field theories on non-orientable manifolds.

title: Optimal isotropic three-material conducting composites with an ideal conductor, in the plane and in space.Bounds and optimal structures
abstract: The paper describes an optimal isotropic three-dimensional, three-material conducting composite. One material is an ideal conductor, the volume fractions are prescribed, and the objective is to minimize the effective conductivity over all admissible layouts. We first derive a lower bound for the effective conductivity as a function of the material properties and volume fractions. The composite energy is bounded below by a constrained polyconvex envelope, where quadratic and cubic null Lagrangians are imposed through Lagrange multipliers. We further assume that the fields in optimal structures are positive semidefinite. Together with the use of the cubic null Lagrangian, this assumption makes the bound exact. The resulting bound determines the extremal conductivity and the set of associated support fields in optimal structures. Depending on the parameters, it has five regions with different analytic expressions. We then prove the bound attainability by constructing optimal structures that realize the bound in every region. They are spherical atoms: a core of the intermediate-conducting material, surrounded by a mantle of wrapped optimal planar structures. In the two extreme regions, a crust is added from the material whose prescribed volume fraction is excessive.

title: Complementary Geometry in Gaussian Splatting
abstract: Gaussian Splatting has achieved high visual quality in novel view synthesis, but the accuracy of its rendered geometry remains a challenge. In particular, the rendered depth is computed as an opacity-weighted average along each ray, which may not correspond to the actual scene surface. In this paper, we observe that depth predictions from different views of the same frozen Gaussian representation exhibit complementary errors, allowing us to improve novel-view geometry using information from other views without modifying the original representation. Based on this observation, we propose REVEAL, a general framework that selectively refines novel-view depth using complementary geometric information. Specifically, we first reproject depth predictions from source views to the target view and combine them using robust multi-view consensus. We then introduce a learned selection mechanism to determine whether the candidate depth is more accurate than the original prediction, based on the expected reduction in depth error. In addition, we introduce RIG, a real-world benchmark captured with synchronized RGB-D cameras, which provides ground-truth depth for evaluating both static and dynamic reconstruction models. Experiments on 6 Gaussian Splatting backbones across 3 benchmarks show that REVEAL consistently improves depth accuracy while maintaining comparable rendering quality.

title: A Local-to-Global Approximation Framework for Covering Disjointness-Compliable Set Families
abstract: Many network design problems can be formulated as covering a family of vertex sets by edges. We develop a local-to-global approximation framework for disjointness-compliable families with polynomial-time membership tests. A class of vertices is deficient if it belongs to the family and feasible otherwise. Our local problem seeks a minimum-cost tree that connects one deficient class to feasible classes so that their union is feasible. If this local problem admits a polynomial-time $α$-approximation, then the covering problem admits a polynomial-time $(1+\varepsilon)(\sqrt{2}+\sqrtα)^2$-approximation for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. Our algorithm first connects deficient vertices that are difficult to separate and then handles regions containing one deficient class at a time. To bound the total local cost, we compare the local trees with a feasible forest. We delete edges of this forest after using them in the bound, so each is counted at most once even when regions overlap. As applications, we obtain polynomial-time $(8+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for generalized point-to-point connection and multiroot quota tree, including multiroot $k$-minimum spanning tree. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-time constant-factor approximations for both problems. We also obtain a randomized approximation for multiroot covering Steiner that has the same asymptotic ratio as the known approximation for its single-root version.

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
abstract: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

title: A fourfold Toda bracket that is not defined, although both threefold subbrackets contain zero
abstract: We give an explicit example, in the stable homotopy groups of spheres, of a fourfold Toda bracket that is not defined although both of its threefold subbrackets contain zero. Namely, $0\in\langleν^2,2,η^2\rangle$ and $0\in\langle 2,η^2,ν\rangle$, but $\langleν^2,2,η^2,ν\rangle$ has no defining system in the sense of Kochman. This answers a question of Isaksen. The computational input consists only of relations from Toda's book, together with an explicit choice of null-homotopies. The same holds, in the sense of Walker, for the unstable quadruple $(ν_n^2,2ι_{n+6},η_{n+6}^2,ν_{n+8})$ for every $n\ge10$. Moreover, for $n\ge10$, even Cohen's fourfold bracket of this quadruple is empty.

title: Tacinf: A Unified Tactile Infrastructure for Robot Manipulation
abstract: Force-aware manipulation requires robots to infer appropriate interaction forces from task context and tactile feedback. We present Tacinf, a low-cost, modular infrastructure that enables policies to predict robot actions and fingertip forces from task language, vision, and touch. Task instructions can optionally specify the desired force level. Tacinf integrates simulation data synthesis and tactile benchmarking (Tabero), vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policy learning, handheld data collection using the same gripper as robot deployment (Tacumi), and task-aligned sim-to-real evaluation (Taco). Together, these components form an integrated workflow connecting data collection from multiple sources, foundation-model training, and hardware deployment. We validate each component, including the simulation data, benchmark, controller, and Tacumi, and are releasing the full stack as open source. A foundation model fine-tuned solely on tactile simulation data transfers zero-shot to different real-robot tasks. Across eight policy variants, mean task success rates are strongly correlated between simulation and the real robot (Pearson r=0.998, mean maximum rank violation MMRV=0.010). For the four policies with reported force measurements, mean grip force is higher under firm instructions than under gentle instructions on all three tasks in both domains. When both object positions and instances are randomized, a mixture of teleoperation, simulation, and Tacumi data raises mean real-robot task success from 20% with teleoperation alone to 60%.

title: Fuzzy e-Means: Fuzzy c-Means on Large Data with Moving-Average Mini-Batch Updates
abstract: Fuzzy c-means (FCM) gives every point a degree of membership in every cluster. Its standard solver, alternating optimization (AO), needs a full pass over the data per iteration and often many iterations, while methods built for large data stop at a worse objective or still need tens of passes. We run FCM with the optimizer of e-means, a recent mini-batch k-means that keeps moving averages of the number and the sum of the points in each cluster and sets its batch size and step size by scaling laws. The optimizer carries over because an FCM centroid is also a weighted sum divided by a total weight, but this direct transfer fails in two ways: the e-means rule that relocates nearly empty clusters also removes the centroids of small, distant groups, and FCM started from random points can settle in poor local minima. Fuzzy e-means (e-FCM) therefore starts with one pass of e-means with hard assignments and then runs fuzzy moving-average passes without relocation. On 28 configurations with up to 109.5 million points and 16,384 clusters, e-FCM reaches the objective of 25 AO iterations in two to four passes when clusters hold several hundred points or more, 11 to 20 times faster than AO on one-million-point embedding sets with 1,024 clusters. It ends within 0.16% of converged AO on these sets and below converged AO where AO from random points lands in poor minima, but it is slower than AO on small low-dimensional problems, where an AO pass takes milliseconds. Finally, the common fuzzifier m=2 makes the centroids collapse or merge on most high-dimensional sets, and e-FCM can choose the fuzzifier by matching a known overlap at about two passes per candidate value.

title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
abstract: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

title: Seeing Is Not Acting: WARD Diagnoses the Evidence-to-State-to-Action Gap in Longitudinal Clinical Agents
abstract: Large language models for longitudinal clinical care must revise their assessments and actions as patient information accumulates. However, benchmarks centered on isolated responses or final task outcomes provide limited insight into intermediate failures in evidence use, state updating, and action selection. We introduce WARD, a benchmark for evaluating how clinical agents translate accumulating evidence into patient-state judgments and timely, safe actions. WARD comprises 4,560 clinical tasks across seven clinical output domains, organized into 240 checkpoints from 40 longitudinal clinical trajectories spanning 95 hospitalizations. Its Longitudinal Track evaluates these tasks under controlled cumulative evidence. Its Interactive Track evaluates end-to-end, tool-mediated clinical management across 271 verifiable evidence items and 141 reference transitions. Across 12 models with scorable checkpoint outputs, evidence recognition consistently outpaces downstream state and action decisions, with linked-evidence nonresponse reaching 74.47--90.90\%. Models also struggle to retain and update information over time, while in the Interactive Track only 11.46\% of executed actions advance a reference transition. These results reveal a persistent evidence-to-state-to-action gap and highlight the need for process-level evaluation of longitudinal clinical agents.Code and data: https://github.com/Dingsuper-creator/WARD.

title: TurboFHE: An Efficient and Scalable Multi-GPU Framework for Homomorphic LLM Inference
abstract: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving large language model inference but remains computationally intensive. Existing multi-GPU FHE inference systems rely on expert-crafted parallelization plans that generalize poorly across hardware platforms and applications. We present \fwName, a framework that automatically compiles CKKS inference programs into efficient multi-GPU executables. Its compiler can split different nodes of the same computation graph at the ciphertext and polynomial level. Guided by a measurement-based performance model, its hardware-aware planner jointly optimizes task partitioning, placement, operand residency, and transfer scheduling. %Critical-path-guided rewrites extract shared computation and restructure homomorphic sums. Its backend then generates optimized GPU kernels and executes plans using CUDA graphs and selective point-to-point transfers. \fwName adapts its plans to diverse hardware configurations and FHE inference algorithms for large-scale models. On a single A100 GPU, \fwName achieves a $24.5\times$ speedup over THOR's reported BERT-Base inference latency. For Cerium's Llama-3-8B workload, \fwName outperforms Cerium's expert-crafted plans by $1.14\times$, $1.16\times$, and $1.24\times$ on 2, 4, and 8 RTX PRO~6000 GPUs, respectively. On A100 GPUs, \fwName achieves $98.0\%$, $91.8\%$, and $79.3\%$ parallel efficiency for the same workload on 2, 4, and 8 GPUs, respectively.

title: Constraining Dehnen-inspired dark matter halo with S2 star's orbit
abstract: We use the orbit of S2 star around Sagittarius A* to constrain three black hole backgrounds motivated by Dehnen profiles with inner slopes $γ=0$, $1$, and $5/2$, which are characterized by the scale radius $r_s$ and density $ρ_s$ of the dark matter halo. An exact turning-point integral gives the pericenter advance at finite eccentricity, and an exterior expansion identifies the leading halo contributions. A fifteen-parameter Bayesian analysis combines astrometric and spectroscopic observations with the measured precession parameter, from which we obtain the marginalized $1σ$ upper limits $r_s/M<0.236$, $0.168$, and $0.030$, and $ρ_sM^2<0.536$, $0.578$, and $0.004$, respectively. The leading halo monopole in the first two metrics is degenerate with the central mass. At fixed dynamical mass, their leading radial profile correction produces retrograde precession. The $γ=5/2$ metric introduces an additional angular deficit contribution, which enhances the precession response and accounts for its smaller parameter limits.

title: Cylindrical Ricci flows and the PDE-ODI principle
abstract: We derive precise asymptotics for ancient asymptotically cylindrical Ricci flows. We establish a dichotomy in which the leading deviation from the cylinder is either linear or quadratic in the axial variables. In the linear case, we show that the flow is exponentially asymptotic to a Bryant soliton times a Euclidean factor. For $κ$-solutions, we further show that the flow is isometric to such a product, up to parabolic rescaling. In the quadratic case, we obtain higher-order asymptotics governed by a finite-dimensional invariant. We also establish propagation of cylindrical regions and uniqueness of cylindrical tangent flows. These results closely parallel those in our earlier work on cylindrical mean curvature flows. Both analyses use the same PDE-ODI principle and yield a unified treatment of cylindrical Ricci flow and mean curvature flow. The essential new ingredient in the Ricci flow setting is a coherent harmonic map heat flow gauge, which allows us to apply this principle without assuming a sign for the curvature. The local analytic tools developed here also form part of a program aimed at constructing Ricci flow with surgery in dimension 4.

title: Global large-data strong solutions to the 2D barotropic compressible Navier-Stokes equations with linear bulk viscosity
abstract: This paper concerns the global well-posedness of the two-dimensional(2D) compressible Navier--Stokes equations with density-dependent bulk viscosity and far-field vacuum. We consider the constitutive laws \(P(ρ)=ρ^γ\), with \(γ>1\), and \(λ(ρ)=ρ\), for which the bulk viscosity degenerates in vacuum. Under suitable regularity and weighted integrability assumptions on the initial data, and assuming only that the total mass is positive, we establish the existence and uniqueness of global strong solutions without any restriction on the size of the initial energy or any radial symmetry assumption. The central difficulty is to derive an upper bound for the density on arbitrary finite time intervals in the absence of enhanced bulk dissipation. To overcome this difficulty, we develop a logarithmic energy method based on successive density levels, which exploits the dissipation accumulated along particle trajectories as the density increases. Combined with weighted estimates, pressure estimates, and the analysis of the effective viscous flux and vorticity, this method yields the density bound required to close the global continuation argument. Our result extends the large-data global strong-solution theory for density-dependent viscosity to the critical linear bulk-viscosity law in the general two-dimensional whole-space setting.

title: AgenticMM: A Material-Centered Multi-Agent Architecture for Scalable First-Principles Materials Modeling
abstract: Multi-agent frameworks are attracting increasing attention as a means of autonomously driving complex, long-running workflows in first-principles materials modeling. However, such frameworks commonly organize AI agents by computational task or scientific role. When scaled across many materials, this organization can require repeated transfers of material-specific context and complicate persistent execution and resource coordination. Here, we introduce AgenticMM, a material-centered multi-agent architecture in which each material has a persistent agent that owns its complete workflow and retains its scientific context, while a persistent coordinator allocates shared resources, mediates communication, and tracks campaign progress. AgenticMM is designed to incorporate reusable, prompt-based skills as modular definitions of these workflows. Using DefectSkills prompts, we demonstrate the feasibility of AgenticMM through a multistage point-defect campaign in which material-specific agents concurrently perform host electronic-structure, phase-stability, and intrinsic-defect calculations for five chemically diverse semiconductors.

title: Tissot indicatrix for location encoders: Characterizing local distortion in learned geographic embeddings
abstract: With the increasing adoption of geographic artificial intelligence, location encoders are widely used to map geographic coordinates to learned embeddings for tasks in Earth observation and geospatial modeling. Similar to map projections, location encoders can distort geographic space, that is, equal-distance displacements in different directions can result in unequal embedding changes. However, such distortion remains largely unexamined, and it can propagate into downstream applications. We adapt Tissot's indicatrix, a cartographic tool for map projection distortion, to characterize this distortion. At each location, we compare encoder outputs at equal distances in 32 directions and fit a tensor, represented by an ellipse, whose elongation (anisotropy) and orientation describe the local distortion. The fit requires only encoder outputs without access to model internals and is validated against references with known geometry. By applying the method to thirteen released checkpoints of five encoder families, we find that distortions vary across space and inherit the input geometry to varying degrees, closely in GeoCLIP with its Equal Earth input (anisotropy correlation of 0.88) and weakly or moderately in the other encoders. The distortion also affects the locations an encoder treats as neighbors. Within 1km of 20 query sites, the 40 nearest neighbors in geographic and embedding space overlap by a median of only 57.5--87.5% across the checkpoints, while the fitted ellipses select exactly the same embedding neighbors in 265 of 299 comparisons. These findings provide a geographic basis for assessing location encoders, and the accompanying eTissot package implements the methods for user-specified encoders.

title: Hyperbolic network embedding via dimensional annealing and Barnes--Hut approximation
abstract: Common features observed in complex networks from various domains can be explained by network geometry in hyperbolic space. Inferring the latent coordinates of nodes enables efficient navigation, link prediction, and geometric renormalization. However, the loss landscape of the hyperbolic model is extremely rugged due to the topological constraints of the low-dimensional embedding space. To overcome this, we introduce the dimensional annealing framework, which bypasses these constraints by introducing an auxiliary dimension. We show that dimensional annealing achieves higher-quality embeddings than existing energy-based embedding methods. Additionally, we incorporate the Barnes--Hut approximation for computational scalability.

title: Persistence and Breakdown of the Initial Gaussian Rate Function for 1D Quasi-Periodic Cubic NLS
abstract: We study rare events for the spatial supremum of the solution amplitude in the 1D cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation with weak nonlinearity and Gaussian quasi-periodic initial data.Under suitable polynomial decay assumptions in Fourier space and a Diophantine condition controlling small divisors arising from spatial quasi-periodicity, we prove that the initial Gaussian rate function persists uniformly on the \emph{critical logarithmic correction time scale} with a \emph{small enough} prefactor. Using the \emph{Akhmediev breather}, we obtain that the same Gaussian rate function \emph{fails} to hold uniformly on this time scale with a \emph{large} prefactor. This also implies that the initial Gaussian rate function cannot, in general, persist uniformly on arbitrarily long polynomial time scales.

title: Zarc: Exact Nearest Neighbors over a Billion Vectors in Seconds
abstract: Exact k-nearest-neighbor vector search lies on the critical path of machine learning systems, from sparse attention in the latest large language models (LLMs) to long-context memories and training-data deduplication. Exhaustive GPU search scans the whole dataset for every query, while approximate indexes return inexact neighbors. Recent methods skip almost every vector with a cheap half-precision proof that it lies too far away, but only on one GPU that holds the whole dataset. Our insight is to keep only the short rows of these proofs in GPU memory and to fetch the few remaining full vectors from host memory. Our system, Zarc, answers Euclidean, cosine, inner-product, and filtered queries exactly under updates. On four H100 GPUs, it answers 10,000 exact queries over one billion vectors in 1.1 seconds instead of five minutes. On eleven open LLMs, it retrieves the exact top-10 attention keys 2.2x to 13.1x faster than exhaustive search. In sparse attention over one million tokens, it runs 3.1x faster than bf16 selection with FlashInfer, which misses the exact top-64 for most queries.

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. We construct a dataset of 501,865 optimized topologies, generated using 51,800 GPU-hours and encompassing structures with up to one million elements and substantially more complex loading and support configurations than any existing structural topology optimization dataset. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset for 3D topology optimization structures. Trained on this dataset, OAT3D generates structures at 512$^3$ resolution and achieves a $44.9\times$ speedup for raw candidate structure generation or $3.65\times$ speedup to reach similar compliance over conventional topology optimization. These contributions expand the scale and diversity of data-driven topology optimization for three-dimensional structural design.

title: MM-DataLoop: Closing the Data-Side Loop for Recursive Self-Improvement in MLLM Post-Training
abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a path toward improving models through repeated evaluation and revision. We study its data side in multimodal language model (MLLM) post-training, where heterogeneous operations and cross-round evidence must be coordinated. MMDataLoop organizes data interventions into five operation families and connects them through an Observe-Diagnose-Plan-Execute-Verify-Reflect cycle with shared rule memory. Across 34 candidate rounds on Qwen3.5-0.8B and five benchmarks, we hold the base initialization, shared training schedule and evaluation protocol fixed while varying data recipes. The five-benchmark mean reaches 63.04 at R33, up 5.32 points from the zero-shot baseline; R29, R32, and R33 form a close top cluster within 0.09 points. In eightcandidate comparisons, guided search reaches the preselected target in six candidates and identifies the top observed candidate, while random arms show higher means and lower dispersion. The selected R29 recipe also scores above two full-pool baselines under the same epoch schedule. Together, these findings establish MM-DataLoop as a traceable workflow and provide an empirical basis for studying how data-side decisions shape outcomes across MLLM post-training recipes.

title: NoeVera: Can Knowledge Guide Experiments and Experiments Refine Knowledge?
abstract: With the growing demand for large language model (LLM) services, optimizing LLM serving systems is becoming increasingly complex, and the bottleneck is no longer predicting how a given configuration will perform. The harder problem is deciding what to investigate: which mechanisms matter for a workload, which configurations are worth testing, and what evidence a decision still needs. In this work, we present NoeVera, an agentic Second Brain that goes beyond just one-shot retrieval by turning papers, code, benchmarks, and experimental results into a persistent, provenance-preserving knowledge base with three planes: source evidence, reusable synthesis, and agent memory. Decision-aware retrieval assembles compact evidence packs, role-specific agents reason over them and invoke a simulator (Vidur or GAUSS) whenever quantitative support is needed, and every finding is written back as a scoped evidence record, so knowledge guides experiments and experiments refine knowledge. In configuration search over four serving scenarios, NoeVera comes within 5% of the optimum in a median of 6-7 simulator calls, versus 9 for Bayesian optimization and 15 for a knowledge-free agent with the same tools; on A100 GPUs, its representative configurations deliver ~1.30x vLLM-default throughput and meet every scenario's latency objective. When reused, provenance-preserving evidence records over-generalize on only 8% of applicability traps, versus 28% for a general-purpose agent memory. On the held-out 48-task split of a 72-task benchmark, NoeVera scores 29% higher than an equally equipped agent and 36% higher than its single-call retrieval counterpart (0.80 vs. 0.62 and 0.59), and even when baselines receive NoeVera's own prompts, a statistically significant part of its evidence-evolution advantage remains.

title: Denoised but Not Improved: What EEG Denoising Does to a Downstream Task
abstract: Scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is routinely denoised before it reaches a downstream model, and the denoising literature scores a method by how closely its output matches a clean reference waveform. That reference does not exist for real scalp recordings: it is synthesized by adding artifact templates to signals merely presumed clean, and even an exact separation would return cortical activity blurred by volume conduction rather than the activity itself. Fidelity to it is therefore an unvalidatable objective, and whether it predicts any downstream benefit has gone largely unexamined. We report an audit that examines it. Holding a seizure-detection pipeline fixed and varying only the preprocessing stage, we find that five standard denoising methods, spanning analytic, cross-channel and supervised deep families, all fail to improve on the unprocessed signal, and most degrade it. To say what such a stage must instead do, we formalize a label-only, classifier-free probe that reads it by the separability geometry it induces on task-relevant features, decomposing any change into a between-class distance and a within-class scatter term. On a transform that does improve the task, the probe attributes the entire gain to a roughly one-quarter reduction of within-class scatter, with class separation statistically unchanged. What a downstream model benefits from is therefore variance suppression on task-relevant structure, which waveform-fidelity metrics neither measure nor reward.

title: CFANet: Learning Conflict-Free Weather Adapters for All-Weather Image Restoration
abstract: All-weather image restoration aims to recover clean images from diverse weather degradations such as rain, haze, and snow. Most existing all-in-one methods handle different weather types with a unified network or rely on single-label weather modeling. However, real-world adverse weather is often compositional, where multiple known weather primitives may coexist in a single image. To this end, we propose Conflict-Free Adapter Network (CFANet) for open-compositional all-weather image restoration. CFANet first employs a Weather Mixture Router (WMR) to predict non-exclusive composition weights for rain, haze, and snow from shallow features. Guided by these weights, a Shared-Private Weather Adapter (SPWA) dynamically composes a common adapter with weather-private adapters inside each Conflict-Free Adapter Block, preserving shared restoration capability while providing weather-specific residual adaptation. Moreover, a lightweight Natural Color Adapter (NCA) performs constrained color calibration to improve color fidelity and visual naturalness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves competitive adverse weather image restoration performance and benefits downstream visual tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/wenchao-tech/CFANet-main

title: Where to Hide the Traps: Robust Placement in Verifiable Blind Quantum Computation
abstract: Trap-based verification of blind quantum computation hides test qubits among the positions of a measurement pattern, and existing protocols choose the trap configuration without regard to the delegated computation. We model trap placement as a zero-sum game between a client, who chooses a trap distribution, and a server, who chooses where to apply a Pauli deviation, with a damage profile $w$ and a per-trap detection constant $c$. Since the client cannot know how damage from several positions combines, we solve the game for all monotone subadditive damage functions consistent with $w$ at once. In a single round, placing traps in proportion to $w$ guarantees soundness error $1-c/\|w\|_1$ and is optimal up to a factor $1+\max_iw_i$, while the optimistic solution can fail completely. Over $T$ test rounds, the error decays exponentially against a server that repeats the same deviation, but a general server can keep it at $Θ(\|w\|_1/(cT))$, and against such servers the damage-weighted placement is exactly optimal. Damage profiles follow from the flow of the pattern: for brickwork patterns with $m=4h+1$ columns, only $(2h+1)^2$ positions can affect a decision qubit, whatever the width. With $k$ traps per round, placing them on this set reduces the number of test rounds by the same factor as for a single trap; with unrestricted trap sets and flat damage we recover the known optimality of fractional coloring. Finally, trap statistics certify the aggregate damage with a number of rounds independent of the number of positions $N$, whereas locating the damage requires $Ω(Nε^{-2}\logδ^{-1})$ rounds.

title: Look Back: Reinforcement Learning with Counterfactual World Models
abstract: Agents in complex, stochastic environments must contend with dynamics that can exceed their world models' predictive capacity and randomness that obscure the consequences of their actions. We hypothesize that, compared to imagining entirely new trajectories in such complex environments, it can be easier to transform observed trajectories with alternative actions. Counterfactual world models condition on observations to predict alternative outcomes under the same underlying environmental randomness, using experience as a reference for predicting action-dependent changes. We present a policy gradient estimator, REINFORCE Look Back (RLB), that uses counterfactual returns as baselines to distinguish action effects from environmental luck, and prove conditions for unbiasedness and variance reduction. In settings where environmental evolution is harder to predict than action-induced changes, we show that counterfactual world models are easier to learn and support better policy learning than ordinary world models. Our findings suggest that counterfactual thinking can help agents learn effective behavior without independently reproducing the full complexity of their worlds.

title: Revealing Semantic Gaps in Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines via Obligation-Targeted Semantic Fuzzing
abstract: Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) prove correct execution of programs and underpin systems securing billions of dollars in digital assets. Their security depends on alignment between the instruction set architecture (ISA) that programs target, such as RISC-V, and the constraint system, polynomial equations that check the prover's record of every intermediate value (the witness). Mismatches, or semantic gaps, come in two kinds: underconstraint bugs let a malicious prover forge a proof of an execution the ISA forbids (a soundness violation), and divergence bugs make the zkVM itself deviate from the ISA or crash, so an honest prover cannot prove a legitimate execution (a completeness violation). Both cluster at corner cases such as division by zero that conventional fuzzing almost never reaches, and underconstraint bugs leave program output unchanged. Our key insight is that these corner cases correspond to constraint obligations derived from the ISA specification and the proof system's algebraic structure. We build Beak, a reinforcement-learning fuzzer in which obligations replace three random decisions: they supply inputs that trigger each obligation, reward executions that trigger new combinations of obligations, and direct witness tampering to the step where an obligation is triggered. Beak flags divergence bugs by comparing registers against a reference RISC-V emulator, and underconstraint bugs by checking whether the constraints accept a tampered witness. On six leading production RISC-V zkVMs, Beak detects 25 of 37 known bugs (67.6%) versus 5 (13.5%) for the prior state of the art, and discovers 14 previously unknown bugs, all responsibly disclosed and patched.

title: Finite-Dimensional Internal Stabilization of Steady States of the Gray-Scott System
abstract: In this article, we establish the local exponential stabilization of every steady state of the Gray-Scott system with homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, other than the trivial state $(0,1)^{\top}$, at any prescribed decay rate by finite-dimensional feedback controls supported in an arbitrary nonempty open subset of the domain and acting only on the first equation of the system. Our approach does not require the steady state to be spatially constant and accommodates non-self-adjoint linearizations with variable coefficients. The proof combines unique continuation, a nonvanishing property of the steady-state coupling, the Fattorini-Hautus condition, and Riccati-based feedback.

title: Neural Agent Compiler: Learning to Schedule Soft Dependencies
abstract: Large language model agents accomplish complex tasks by coordinating multiple reasoning steps and tool operations, which form dependencies among their operations. Existing orchestration methods primarily consider hard dependencies that determine when an operation can legally begin, but overlook soft dependencies, i.e., information that is not required for execution but may improve an already executable operation. We identify soft-dependency scheduling as an important problem in agent execution. To this end, we introduce Neural Agent Compiler (NAC), a learned scheduler that predicts the task-quality and resource consequences of three execution modes and selects the highest-utility legal mode at a scheduling boundary. NAC represents the executable continuation, pending information event, and resource state in a shared memory, and uses a utility function to adapt the consequence predictions to different resource preferences. Across AppWorld, WebShop, and $τ^2$-bench, NAC achieves 276/417 AppWorld task completions, a 74.69 WebShop Task Score, and 59/100 $τ^2$-bench successes. Additional studies show that the learned scheduler reduces execution work, establishing soft-dependency scheduling as a promising solution for orchestrating tool-using agents.

title: Giant thermal transduction via feedback-phase engineering in a thin-film lithium-niobate opto-electro-mechanical oscillator
abstract: Conventional resonant MEMS thermometry typically relies on the intrinsic temperature coefficient of frequency (TCF) of mechanical resonances. Here we show that embedding a suspended thin-film lithium-niobate mechanical resonator in an opto-electro-mechanical (OEM) feedback loop enhances the intrinsic coefficient by two orders of magnitude. By using laser--cavity detuning to control the loop's round-trip phase, and thus the Barkhausen-selected oscillation frequency, we engineer an effective TCF of $+1.24\times10^{4}$~ppm/K: a 100-fold enhancement and a sign reversal relative to its intrinsic TCF of $-124$~ppm/K. Temperature-dependent and open-loop phase measurements confirm that this giant response originates from feedback phase selection rather than from the passive resonator itself. This interpretation is further supported by the independently measured closed-loop oscillation frequencies and a detuning-dependent delay model. The same architecture also supports 2:1 subharmonic injection locking, yielding sub-6~Hz linewidths, reference-limited frequency stability, and tunable operation from $76.71$ to $76.82$~MHz. These results establish feedback-phase engineering as a general, post-fabrication route to both giant thermal transduction and low-noise yet tunable mechanical oscillation.

title: An explicit BGG-type resolution of the spin/oscillator module for osp(2m+1|2n)
abstract: We construct an explicit resolution of the spin/oscillator representation of the Lie superalgebra osp(2m+1|2n) by parabolic Verma modules. The resolution appears as the Chevalley-Eilenberg chain complex of the Lie algebra of quadratic operators in the universal Heisenberg algebra of the vector superspace C^{m|n}. In particular, its differentials are given by unified linear algebra formulas and all have degree 2 with respect to the standard grading of Verma modules.

title: On the Interplay between Backtracking and Latent Confidence Directions in Reasoning Models
abstract: Reasoning models deliberate over multiple answer proposals, often resulting in excessively long traces due to backtracking, even when the correct answer has already been reached (Across three 32B models, ~87% of rollouts contain 1 unique answer yet still make ~8 answer proposals on average). Given this potentially "decorative" chain of thought (CoT) reasoning, can we look to the model internals to determine if the model will backtrack or commit to an answer proposal? Operating under the hypothesis that models maintain an internal representation of their uncertainty, we seek to extract this representation and characterize its relationship with backtracking behavior at answer proposals.
