abstract: We study normalized two-term Rogers dilogarithm relations in cubic fields. For integral, nonunimodular rank-two monomial configurations whose base argument generates a totally real cubic field, finite-prime valuations force the arguments and their complements to be units. Normalization preserves the generated order and reduces the problem to two cubic families without a maximal-order assumption. In the simplest cubic family, an existing unit-equation classification yields exactly ten relations up to simultaneous reflection, with distinct coefficients 2, 3, 7, 13, 19, 31 and 97. Explicit five-term certificates prove all ten evaluations. In the second family, a sharpened lower bound for the height of a solution, together with the two-logarithm theorem of Laurent, Mignotte and Nesterenko, reduces the unit equation to a short certified computation, and the family contributes no relation in this class. A unit-index argument restricts, independently, wedge relations between arbitrary exceptional units of non-Galois totally real cubic fields: any such relation would have a coefficient with no prime factor below 23 and would contradict Ennola's conjecture on fundamental units. In cubic fields with one real embedding, the only five-term certified relation between exceptional units with coefficient greater than one is Lewin's identity. Together, these results give exactly eleven identities in the two classes considered, up to the stated reflections.

title: MISeg-Agent: A Human-in-the-Loop Agentic Framework for Error Diagnosis and Executable Prompt Review in 3D Medical Image Segmentation
abstract: Despite the strong performance of modern medical image segmentation models, their predictions can still contain localized errors that compromise segmentation quality. Identifying and correcting these errors is therefore essential for improving the reliability of existing segmentation results. While interactive segmentation models enable targeted corrections, identifying potential errors, determining where to intervene, and evaluating corrective actions remain challenging. Moreover, each correction changes the current mask, requiring subsequent error diagnosis and recommendations to adapt accordingly. To address these challenges, we propose MISeg-Agent, a human-in-the-loop agentic framework that diagnoses segmentation errors and provides evidence-based correction recommendations. MISeg-Agent first selects a suitable pretrained segmentation model based on benchmark performance and computational requirements. Given its predicted mask, the framework identifies potential missing and excess foreground regions and recommends suspicious slices and corrective points for review. The framework then evaluates candidate point prompts using an interactive segmentation model and presents the resulting corrections for human verification before applying them. By operating directly on images and predicted masks, the error diagnosis process remains independent of the underlying segmentation model architecture. Evaluations on CT datasets demonstrate that MISeg-Agent improves initial segmentation results and produces final masks closely aligned with reference annotations. By integrating adaptive error diagnosis with validated correction recommendations, MISeg-Agent provides an interpretable approach to identifying and reducing residual errors in existing medical image segmentations.

title: Giant magnetic anisotropy in layered polar metal Sr$_3$Co$_2$O$_7$ from Charge-disproportionation orbital unquenching
abstract: Crystal-field quenching usually suppresses orbital angular momentum and limits magnetic anisotropy in transition-metal oxides. Here we identify charge disproportionation as a route to giant magnetocrystalline anisotropy in the layered polar metal Sr$_3$Co$_2$O$_7$. First-principles calculations reveal an energy preference of 234.0 meV per cell for in-plane [110] magnetization over [001]. Charge disproportionation and the associated polar displacement reconstruct the local cobalt crystal fields, creating inequivalent sites with distinct orbital hierarchies. This reconstruction enables a strongly directional orbital response, particularly at the displaced cobalt site, where orbital angular momentum is recovered for in-plane magnetization. Spin--orbit coupling converts this response into a large magnetic anisotropic energy. In the centrosymmetric reference, the orbital moments remain nearly quenched and the anisotropy is strongly reduced. A local Green-function and orbital-moment analysis connects the large energy scale to orbital unquenching, while the conventional second-order contribution is small within the adopted approximation. These results identify charge-disproportionation-driven orbital reconstruction as a design principle for large anisotropy and motivate layered perovskites and magnetic polar metals as platforms in the search for rare-earth-free permanent magnets.

title: On the linear stability of elliptic relative equilibrium in planar restricted $(n+1)$-body problem
abstract: In this paper, we consider the restricted $(n+1)$-body problems, where the $n$ primaries forming an a homographic motion generated by the planar central configuration, and the massless particle is attracted by this $n$ primaries. We are interested in the linear stability of the elliptic relative equilibria of the massless particle under the pulsating coordinates. The main contribution of this paper first lies in the investigation of a general $(α,β)$-system (1.7). We obtain large-range spectral instability and small-range stability results valid for arbitrary eccentricity. The restricted $(n+1)$-body problem arises as a special case of this system. Accordingly, we derive several criteria for spectral instability and linear stability for this problem. As a final application, we establish some stability results of elliptic relative equilibria for massless particle under some special central configurations.

title: Who Sent It or How It Moved? Sender Shortcuts in Cryptocurrency Anti-Money-Laundering Benchmarks, Audited on Elliptic2 and Elliptic++
abstract: Two public benchmarks dominate graph-based anti-money-laundering (AML) research on Bitcoin: the transaction-level Elliptic dataset, extended as Elliptic++, and the subgraph-level Elliptic2. In both, a label is assigned according to the entity that sends the funds. We ask whether models trained on these benchmarks learn how laundering moves or merely who sent the money, and we propose a diagnostic protocol to tell the two apart: a sender lookup baseline, a novelty baseline, a sender-disjoint split with a leakage check, and a decomposition of performance into sender, receiver and intrinsic signal. On Elliptic2 the task largely reduces to classifying the sender. Under the standard random split, a no-learning lookup of sender history reaches a PR-AUC of 0.954, against 0.975 for gradient boosting on 456 features; our reimplementation of RevClassify reproduces its reported 0.97 and falls to 0.126 without sender information. When senders are held out, performance drops to 0.746, and the subgraph's own structure, transactions and receivers fall from 0.619 to 0.186. On Elliptic++ the same protocol finds the shortcut negligible: sender history reaches only 0.340 against 0.986 for the full model (3.5 against 10.1 times the test prevalence), adding it to the full model raises PR-AUC by less than 0.004 in every seed, and the transaction's own features keep 0.883 when sending addresses are held out. We trace the difference to the unit of sender identity: Elliptic2 senders are entity clusters that recur across many labeled subgraphs, whereas Elliptic++ senders are individual addresses, and fewer than half of test transactions have a sending address seen in training. A shared sender-based label rule thus produces a severe shortcut in one benchmark and a negligible one in the other, so the diagnostic must be run on each benchmark.

title: Agentic Root Cause Reasoning and Localization of Unsoundness in Static Call Graph Analysis
abstract: Static call graph tools cannot soundly model every dynamic language feature, yet rarely reveal when, where, or why their results are unsound. We present CGRizz, an agentic framework that diagnoses unsoundness for developers and warns users about it. During training, CGRizz compares static and dynamic call graphs to identify boundary edges: calls observed at runtime but missing from the static graph. For each edge, an LLM agent proposes a root cause, including the unmodeled program pattern and responsible tool location. CGRizz validates each proposal using three independent forms of evidence: runtime instrumentation detecting the pattern, a test case reproducing the missing edge, and a warning inserted at the implicated tool location. Validated reports help developers diagnose limitations, while the warnings form an instrumented build that flags potential unsoundness in new programs without dynamic analysis. We evaluate CGRizz on three benchmark suites using WALA, OPAL, and Soot. Of 1,459 boundary edges, CGRizz reasons about 10.3% directly, all confirmed by manual audit, and resolves another 84.1% by grouping edges with validated root causes. Tool maintainers confirmed several limitations, some of which have been fixed. The warnings flag 74%-92% of unsoundness in held-out programs. Guided by CGRizz reports, a coding agent refactored programs to remove 64% of targeted root-cause patterns while preserving functionality.

title: The probability that two random generalized derangements have the same number of cycles
abstract: Using singularity analysis, we show that the probability that two independently and uniformly selected generalized derangements of size $n$ have the same number of cycles is asymptotically the same as the corresponding probability for unrestricted permutations, namely, $\sim \frac{1}{2\sqrt{π\log n}}\;.$

title: Sharpe Ratio Inference after Machine Learning
abstract: The economic value of return signals is often assessed using the Sharpe ratios of portfolios based on those signals. In modern asset pricing, return signals often depend on many features, including state variables and firm-specific characteristics, and machine-learning methods are increasingly used to estimate them. But how much confidence can we place in the estimated Sharpe ratios? We find that signal-estimation error can remain consequential for inference even in large asset panels. Moreover, pooling observations across assets does not necessarily make this uncertainty negligible when predictors contain common features or exhibit substantial cross-sectional dependence. As a remedy, we develop a debiased Sharpe-ratio estimator that accounts for signal-estimation error and provides valid confidence intervals and tests against benchmarks. Our target is the population Sharpe ratio of a specified portfolio rule evaluated at the true conditional expected returns given the features. The framework covers market-timing, long-short, and other signal-based portfolios, allowing the number of assets to grow with and greatly exceed the time-series sample size. The method combines orthogonal portfolio moments with time-series cross-fitting and remains valid under suitable estimation-error bounds for machine-learning forecasts. Empirically, we revisit the setting of Gu et al. (2020) using machine-learning estimators of the return signals. The strongest long-short Sharpe-ratio gains relative to market benchmarks remain significant after debiasing, providing statistical evidence of the economic value of their feature set. Conventional and debiased Sharpe-ratio estimates are generally similar, while the associated confidence intervals and tests can differ substantially. These differences vary across signal estimators and portfolio rules and do not uniformly weaken the evidence of portfolio performance.

title: Performance Evaluation of Nonlinear Model Predictive and Sliding Mode Controllers on a 4-Cable Spatial CSPR in Simscape
abstract: This paper offers a comprehensive comparative study between Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) and Sliding Mode Control (SMC) applied to a spatial Cable-Suspended Parallel Robot (CSPR) actuated by four cables. The robot is modeled in two parallel ways: (i) via an analytical dynamic model with included cable elasticity and frictional losses, and (ii) in MATLAB Simscape Multibody, capturing realistic physical effects. Both controllers are implemented under identical reference trajectories, system constraints, and tuning strategies. Our results show that NMPC achieves superior tracking accuracy and stronger disturbance rejection compared to SMC, but at the cost of higher computational demand. Moreover, both controllers were tested on an analytical model of the robot and a Simscape model. The close agreement between the two, for both control schemes, confirms the accuracy of the analytical formulation and its consistency with the physics-based simulation. The study highlights the value of physics-based simulation as a complementary tool for validating advanced controllers under realistic conditions, and demonstrates that NMPC offers superior performance for the studied high-precision, constrained CSPR.

title: CarlHOI: Counterfactual Predictive Imagination for Generalizable Multi-Humanoid Object Interaction under Constrained Environments
abstract: Recent advances in physics-based humanoid control enable teams of varying sizes to coordinate their movements and cooperatively transport shared objects. However, adapting learned cooperative behaviors to unseen environmental constraints remains challenging, particularly when obstacles require coordinated detours and changes in team configuration. We propose CarlHOI, a counterfactual predictive imagination framework built upon a counterfactual-anchored relational latent world model (CarlWM) for human-object interaction (HOI), enabling multi-humanoid teams to adapt to unseen environmental constraints without retraining their underlying cooperative control policies. CarlHOI explicitly represents the shared object, individual humanoids, and environmental obstacles as interacting entities. Trained offline using counterfactual simulator rollouts, the model imagines alternative collective futures under different shared waypoint commands, predicting how the coupled humanoid team and object would respond. By evaluating these imagined outcomes through predicted progress, failure, and contact risks, and long-horizon value estimates, CarlHOI selects adaptive guidance commands while preserving the pretrained cooperative controller. We introduce a benchmark comprising three challenging obstacle-constrained transport tasks to evaluate adaptation and generalization. Despite being trained exclusively with four humanoids, our model generalizes without retraining to teams of two to ten humanoids, unseen obstacle geometries and placements, unseen objects, and novel combinations of environmental constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate improved cooperative transport success over evaluated baselines across diverse configurations. Results highlight the potential of counterfactual predictive imagination to extend pretrained multi-humanoid cooperative skills beyond their original training conditions.

title: Refine, Don't Reinvent: RASA-Bench for Source-Grounded Hindi Prose Refinement
abstract: For a producer of Hindi creative prose, drafting is cheap and editing is not: a machine-written episode, story, or essay reads as under-written and flat, laced with translationese, and it sometimes quietly alters what the source says. RASA-Bench targets that editing task across three Hindi prose forms, measuring how well a model refines an under-written AI draft, a task distinct from writing from scratch. Across 2,050 drafts and eight refiners (16,400 rewrites), a four-layer protocol credits a rewrite only after it passes a faithfulness check against its own source, then ranks the survivors by holistic editorial preference through per-form Bradley-Terry fits whose centered coefficients are standardized before equal-weight averaging. Staying faithful proves to be a decisive test that behaves differently by form: gate-failure rates range from 9.1% on short stories to 29.5% on audio fiction, and the drift that disqualifies a rewrite shifts from events and identity in narrative to claims and evidence in essays. A 600-case human audit puts gate agreement at 0.925 (0.91 to 0.94 across forms), whereas subjective preference is form-sensitive and least settled for essays, among human readers no less than the model judge. The benchmark, evaluation protocol, and Hindi prose diagnostics are available at https://abdur75648.github.io/rasa-bench.

title: A compact nonformal manifold with holonomy Spin(7)
abstract: We construct a compact simply connected eight-manifold with holonomy Spin(7) and a triple Massey product of degrees $(3,2,2)$ that does not contain zero. The manifold is a resolution of a flat orbifold. Joyce's gluing theorem gives it a torsion-free Spin(7) structure. The resolution map factors through a quotient of $Y\times S^1$, where $Y$ is Martín-Merchán's nonformal $G_2$ manifold. The map to this quotient has degree one, so pullback preserves a nonzero Massey pairing. On the resolution the detecting degree-two class annihilates the full indeterminacy. Simple connectivity and nonformality imply full Spin(7) holonomy. The manifold has $(b_2,b_3,b_4^+,b_4^-)=(22,10,91,27)$.

title: Why Units Die in the Layer After a Frozen Random Encoder, and What the Number of Live Units Measures
abstract: Reinforcement-learning agents can learn Atari games through a convolutional encoder whose random weights are never trained. They reach expert play in Pong and, without random action repeats, in Breakout, but training takes far longer and few ReLU units in the layer after the encoder stay alive. A dead unit outputs zero for every input and cannot learn. In earlier work we took the number of live units to measure the game's complexity. Here we ask why units die and correct that conclusion. We find that more units die as the layer's inputs lie farther from zero relative to how much they vary. We call this ratio the offset. Earlier work showed this in sparse autoencoders at the start of training. We saw it after training in agents, image classifiers, a reservoir computer and sparse autoencoders on GPT-2. A random encoder leaves the offset of its input roughly unchanged, and a formula predicted its median offset within 25 percent in all 44 cases. So a game with a bright, mostly unchanging screen gives the next layer a large offset. In Pong, subtracting the average screen raised the number of live units from between 3 and 6 of 64 to between 59 and 63, so the number alone cannot show a game's complexity. On unaltered screens none of the agents reached a training score of 18 in 50 million steps. With the subtraction all did within 5 million, about as fast as a trained encoder on unaltered screens. In Breakout the subtraction left more units alive, but average training scores did not clearly improve, and a large gap to a trained encoder remained. So we do not treat their number as something to raise for its own sake. The evidence is from small networks and three games, and in agents and image classifiers changing the offset also changed the size of the inputs. We suggest measuring the offset before training a layer on a fixed front end and, if it is large, trying to subtract the mean input.

title: DREAM: Dual-Memory Reasoning for Anticipatory 3D Perception in Autonomous Driving
abstract: Autonomous driving systems must not only interpret the current scene but also anticipate perceptual challenges such as occlusions, sparse observations, and recurring failure patterns. However, most existing LiDAR semantic segmentation methods operate in a frame-centric manner, processing each scan independently and discarding past contextual experience, which limits robustness under dynamic scene changes. We propose DREAM, a Dual-memory REAsoning framework for continual LiDAR seMantic segmentation that reframes perception as an experience-driven and anticipatory process. DREAM maintains two complementary memory banks in a strictly online setting: a latent memory that stores compact semantic abstractions of previously observed scenes, and an error memory that records representations associated with uncertain predictions. At each timestep, relevant memory entries are retrieved via cosine similarity and integrated into the feature space through a lightweight modulation mechanism, enabling the model to reinforce consistent semantic patterns while suppressing recurring failure modes. The backbone remains frozen and no past scans are replayed, ensuring computational efficiency and bounded memory growth. Extensive experiments on multiple large-scale LiDAR benchmarks demonstrate that DREAM achieves state-of-the-art performance, with consistent improvements on dynamic and small-scale objects, highlighting the effectiveness of persistent and error-aware memory for robust long-horizon perception.

title: Exact many-body scars of generic spin models from singlet covers
abstract: The square-lattice transverse-field Ising model has exact zero-energy eigenstates at any field: products of singlets on alternate plaquette diagonals. A longitudinal field isolates them from a symmetry-protected degeneracy. The mechanism is that a site coupled equally to both ends of a singlet annihilates it. The result thus holds for any spin $s$, anisotropic exchange, a large class of bond disorder and certain three-spin terms. This mechanism decides which lattices host such states: two of the 11 Archimedean lattices (four at $s=1/2$), bcc and quasicrystals with spins on the edges. Singlet pumping cools any state into them.

title: Stopping-Time Leakage in Blind Quantum Delegation
abstract: Blind quantum computation lets a client delegate a computation while hiding it from the server, up to a declared leakage. Its security definitions cover a single round. A variational quantum algorithm, however, delegates many rounds, and its classical optimizer decides from private data when to stop. We study what the resulting round count tells an honest-but-curious server. For protocols with one-time-padded transcripts and fresh randomness in every round, we prove that the server's best distinguishing advantage over the whole sequence equals the total-variation distance between the stopping-time distributions, so the round count is the only residual channel in this model. We also show that soundness composes as $δ\,\mathbb{E}[T]$ under adaptive stopping, given a conditional per-round soundness property that composably secure verifiable protocols provide. In simulated delegated eigensolvers for the transverse-field Ising chain, the local Polyak-Lojasiewicz ratio measured in iterations 5 to 15 predicts the noiseless stopping round with a leave-one-out error of 1.7 iterations, compared with 10.3 for a constant predictor. Across 14 configurations that differ in optimizer, stopping rule, initialization, system size, shot budget and problem family, the leakage is significant in 12 and ranges from 0.14 to 1.68 bits, and a maximum-entropy bound estimated on held-out sessions lies above it in all of them. For defense, we show that any mechanism acting after the stopping decision can only add rounds, and that differentially private padding costs the full adjacency radius. A fixed public iteration budget removes the channel completely; set at the median run length, it costs 10% of the remaining energy gap. A differentially private stopping rule based on AboveThreshold protects every pair of instances, but it must often stop too early, which makes it costly.

title: Mitigating Nested GTP Attacks: A Closed-Loop eBPF Defense for 5G and Beyond Networks
abstract: The evolving cellular networks continue to rely on the legacy GPRS Tunneling Protocol-User Plane (GTP-U) to encapsulate and route user data traffic across the data plane. Recent security research demonstrated that nested GTP-U (GTP-in-GTP) payload vulnerabilities enable a diverse range of attacks on victim users. To address this vulnerability, in this paper, we propose a closed-loop extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and eXpress Data Path (XDP) defense to detect and mitigate nested GTP-U attacks in 5G and beyond networks. The proposed framework contains three components: an in-kernel XDP Detection and Drop Module (XDP-DDM), a user-space User-Plane Telemetry Agent (UP-TA), and a multi-threaded Control-Plane Mitigation Orchestrator (CP-MO). We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. We also show that the proposed solution has minimal impact on the user's throughput and round-trip time.

title: Monogenic signal analysis for wavefield characterisation in distributed acoustic sensing
abstract: The spatio-temporal wavefield sampled by distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) contains intertwined information about signal strength, oscillatory structure and propagation. We introduce a methodology to disentangle these properties, with applications to the analysis of weak arrivals obscured by noise or stronger wave trains. The method is based on the monogenic signal, a two-dimensional extension of the analytic signal defined via the Riesz transform. In DAS, the monogenic signal decomposes locally dominant arrivals into their amplitude, phase and apparent slowness along the fibre. Moreover, the consistency of the wavefield orientation, quantified using the notion of directional coherency, allows coherent arrivals to be identified and enhanced. In this work, we apply the monogenic signal to analyse submarine T-wave recordings following the magnitude 3.5 earthquake of 5 October 2023 in the western Alboran Sea, acquired along approximately 60 km of the Estepona-Tetouan fibre-optic cable. Directional coherency allows us to enhance coherent wave trains, attenuating the incoherent background while preserving their oscillatory structure. Combining the monogenic attributes, we track individual oscillations across the fibre, obtaining spatially consistent apparent-slowness estimates. Together with varying cable geometry, these estimates allow us to infer the incoming directions of two wave trains, revealing distinct backazimuths. We extend the methodology to direction-selective enhancement, revealing a weaker third wave train with opposite moveout that is obscured by stronger arrivals. Beyond these examples, we show that monogenic analysis offers new possibilites for wavefield comparison, with promising applications to lossy data compression and inversion. Our results highlight the versatility of monogenic analysis and its potential to become a central tool for interpreting DAS recordings.

title: Blind Channel and Noise-Variance Estimation for MIMO Thermal Noise Modulation Systems via Generalized Expectation-Maximization
abstract: Thermal Noise Modulation (TNM) is a communication paradigm in which information is conveyed through different thermal-noise variance levels rather than deterministic signal waveforms. Its stochastic nature makes conventional pilot-based channel estimation challenging, while pilot transmission introduces additional overhead and reduces spectral efficiency. This paper proposes a pilot-free blind receiver for M-ary TNM systems based on the Generalized Expectation-Maximization (GEM) framework. The proposed receiver jointly estimates the channel matrix, latent transmitted symbols, mixture probabilities, and unknown transmit-noise variance levels directly from received observations, without requiring pilot symbols or prior knowledge of the variance constellation. The modulation order M and receiver-noise variance are assumed to be known. Since the maximization step has no closed-form solution, a gradient-ascent procedure is incorporated into the GEM framework to iteratively update the unknown parameters. The proposed approach enables simultaneous channel estimation, symbol detection, and variance learning within a unified blind-receiver framework. Simulation results demonstrate accurate channel Gram matrix estimation and effective symbol detection without pilot overhead. Moreover, the proposed variance learning scheme achieves performance close to that obtained with perfectly known transmit variance levels, with only moderate BER degradation, demonstrating its potential for practical MIMO TNM systems.

title: What Should World Models Plan Over? Learning Geometry-Aligned Representations of Body Motion
abstract: We introduce MotionPort, which learns low-dimensional latent representations of body motion for accurate dynamics prediction and effective long-horizon planning. Existing world-model planners often search over action representations learned for prediction, yet we show that predictive accuracy alone does not ensure that optimization can discover successful trajectories. MotionPort addresses this mismatch by representing body trajectories rather than action chunks and organizing the search space by motion similarity, helping predicted improvements translate into successful execution. Without fine-tuning state encoders, MotionPort raises average goal-reaching success from 37.9% to 87.8% across three backbones and seven settings in four domains. On the evaluated AntMaze-OGBench tasks, it achieves 72% success, compared with 4% for the strongest baseline.

title: DictaRashi: A State-of-the-Art OCR Model For Rashi Script
abstract: We release DictaRashi, a Tesseract OCR model for scanned Hebrew books printed in the so-called "Rashi" font. We trained DictaRashi on over one million manually corrected lines of text from over 100 different books of Rabbinic and post-Rabbinic literature. On a held-out set of 1,120 manually transcribed lines from scanned Rashi-script pages, DictaRashi reaches a character error rate (CER) of 0.86% and a word error rate (WER) of 3.38%, setting a new state-of-the-art for publicly-available Tesseract models. We provide a full comparison of our results to those of the 31 other publicly available Hebrew Tesseract models; the best of those models achieves a 2.98% CER and 11.86% WER. We further demonstrate that DictaRashi outperforms the current frontier LLMs on this OCR task. We release the test set of Rashi-script documents so that it may be used as a benchmark for future work in this area. We are pleased to release the model and test set to the community under a CC BY NC 4.0 license.

title: The Kaplansky-Aupetit conjecture for C*-algebras
abstract: We settle the Kaplansky--Aupetit conjecture when either algebra is a $C^*$-algebra. More precisely, if $A$ is a unital Banach algebra and $B$ is a unital $C^*$-algebra, or if $A$ is a unital $C^*$-algebra and $B$ is a unital semisimple Banach algebra, then every unital invertibility-preserving linear surjection $ϕ: A\to B$ is a Jordan homomorphism. In fact, it suffices to assume that $ϕ$ preserves the invertibility of products of two exponentials, or of individual exponentials when both algebras are $C^*$-algebras. Claude Opus 5.5 found the original proof when both $A$ and $B$ are $C^*$-algebras by adapting a resolvent estimate from a recent preprint of Colbrook and Stepaniants, while OpenAI's GPT-6.1 further generalized this to the case where only one algebra is a $C^*$-algebra.

title: probly: Uncertainty-Aware Machine Learning
abstract: As machine learning systems are increasingly deployed in real-world applications, the question of how to represent and quantify uncertainty has moved from a methodological side issue to a central concern. In practice, however, making a model uncertainty-aware is still surprisingly difficult: relevant tools tend to be scattered across libraries, each tied to a particular framework and a particular approach to modeling uncertainty, and the choice of representation, quantification, and evaluation is typically left to the user without much guidance. In this paper, we present probly, a Python package that addresses these issues in a single, modular framework. probly offers (i) lightweight transformations that turn existing models into uncertainty-aware ones, currently supporting PyTorch, scikit-learn, and Flax, (ii) several representations, including second-order distributions, credal sets, and conformal prediction, (iii) the corresponding quantification measures, and (iv) a number of evaluation protocols, which can be combined more or less arbitrarily. Using probly, we conduct a benchmark study on three standard tasks --- selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. In addition, and unlike existing benchmarks, we evaluate suitable methods on first-order data, i.e., datasets for which the target itself is a distribution over outcomes. We further illustrate the flexibility of the package on a number of less standard case studies, including large language models, graph neural networks, and data streams. The package is publicly available at https://github.com/pwhofman/probly.

title: Hodge cycles of Klein hypersurfaces
abstract: We study the space of Hodge cycles on Klein varieties. Relating it to the Hodge characters in a covering Fermat variety, we decompose the space of Hodge characters into a part generated by classes of rational subvarieties, and a non-trivial part which we call exceptional. Using Dirichlet characters we show that the exceptional part is always finite. Furthermore, we give sufficient conditions under which there are no exceptional characters, providing infinitely many new cases of the Hodge conjecture for Klein varieties. Finally, we describe the set of exceptional characters of Klein varieties for small dimensions.

title: Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
abstract: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $β_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $λ$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}β_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $λ=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $λ\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $λ=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $λ=1/B$ perform better empirically.

title: Sánchez, Feijóo, or Abascal? Speaker Attribution and Ideological Congruence in LLM Personas Reading Posts on X of the Leaders of the Three Main Parties of the 29N General Election in Spain
abstract: Source cues are central to political communication, yet reception studies with large language model (LLM) personas as synthetic audiences have not tested whether personas respond to who speaks and not only to what is said. With Spain's general election of 29 November 2026 in mind, we run a speaker-attribution experiment using 1,075 anonymised X posts by the leaders of PSOE, PP and VOX on four topics (the economy and employment, household costs, immigration and corruption) and 791 distinct value-grounded, LLM-generated personas. Each post was assigned to 300 topic-selected persona profiles, 150 grounded in the Inglehart-Welzel cultural map and 150 in Moral Foundations Theory, under four conditions: no author, Sánchez, Feijóo or Abascal, yielding 322,470 complete persona-post quartets. Naming any leader lowered support for identical text, with the penalty for Abascal nearly twice as large as those for Sánchez and Feijóo. The penalty follows the persona's elicited left-right self-placement (ideological congruence): left personas spare Sánchez and right personas spare Feijóo, although ideology was never in the message-evaluation prompt. Corruption posts were penalised under every name, whereas on other topics the ideologically closest leader generally produced little or no penalty. The leader order matches public opinion in 48 CIS barometers (2022-2026) in all three groups and the sign of all twelve differences, but fits barometers before the model's 2024 knowledge cutoff better than recent ones. Our findings demonstrate that LLM personas evaluate political speakers through systematic, value-congruent priors: however, while they replicate human candidate rank-orders across survey barometers, this alignment is ordinal rather than quantitative, highlighting their utility for controlled source-effect experiments though not as substitutes for empirical public opinion surveys.

title: CivicBench: Robust Detection of AI-Generated Political Video
abstract: AI-generated video of politicians can pass for real footage, and once such fakes are common, real footage can be dismissed as fake. Platforms address both problems with detectors, but whoever uploads a clip controls its pixels. Existing datasets of political video are small, show real politicians, and test no attacks. We introduce CivicBench, with 10,800 generated clips of invented politicians from eight open generators and 2,632 public-domain or openly licensed real clips. Each clip can be attacked, to hide a fake or to frame real footage. Published detectors trained on a general benchmark reach at most .781 AUC on CivicBench. Adversarial changes of 1 gray level per pixel hide nearly every generated clip from the detectors not built to resist attacks. An attack's reach is how far it can move a clip's score. A clip keeps its label when its margin from the threshold exceeds this reach, and we find that the reach grows almost linearly with the budget. On this basis, we propose Tau-Anchor, which fine-tunes an encoder pretrained on attacked images. It attacks real and generated clips during training and adds a margin term at its deployed threshold. It reaches .941 AUC on CivicBench. It also keeps .668 of generated clips flagged at 2 gray levels, against at most .289 for published detectors. When real clips are framed at the same 2 gray levels, Tau-Anchor's false alarms rise only from 8% to 14%, whereas four published detectors flag nearly every framed real clip at just 1 gray level. External political footage and two general benchmarks show the same pattern under attack. Code and data are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/CivicBench.

title: From Distributional to Temporal Interactions in McKean--Vlasov Games and Control
abstract: The paper examines the relation between time and population in stochastic games and control. The idea is to substitute the interaction described via the population law with the interaction described via the occupation measure of a single self-interacting trajectory. Thus we study how McKean--Vlasov fixed point games and Mean Field Control problems compare with their resulting self-interacting counterparts. Assuming appropriate dissipativity and regularity conditions, we find that the ergodic costs, value functions and optimal feedback sets are identical, and the fixed point equilibria are equivalent. In addition, we obtain uniform bounds on both trajectories and costs for finite horizon problems. These bounds allow proving asymptotic equivalence of the normalized value functions, and enable the transfer of equilibrium strategies and optimal feedbacks from one representation to another, with approximation errors that vanish as the horizon length increases.

title: Estimating a Transition Point from Gibbs and Ground States
abstract: We study how observed many-body system size affects the number of state copies needed to estimate a zero-temperature first-order transition point. The unknown Hamiltonian has bounded, translation-invariant on-site and nearest-neighbour interactions on a 3D cubic lattice with local dimension three. The field coupling is known, and all models share a known boundary field penalizing one local level. The limiting order parameter is uniformly separated across the transition. Each query returns an independently prepared Gibbs or ground state at an adaptive field and system size. For error $ε$ and fixed confidence, we prove an exponential separation between two size caps at the same temperature. There are absolute constants $0<c_0<C$ and $c_1>0$ such that, at inverse temperature $β=c_1/ε$, restricting side lengths to $L\le c_0/ε$ requires $\exp(Ω(1/ε))$ copies in worst-case expectation, even with collective measurements. Allowing $L\le C/ε$ permits $O(\log^2(1/ε))$ copies and $O(ε^{-3})$ total spins, using local measurements and polynomial classical postprocessing. The minimax expected total spin count is $Θ(ε^{-3})$ uniformly for $β\ge c_1/ε$. At fixed positive temperature it is $Θ_β(ε^{-2})$, attained from one- and eight-site Gibbs states followed by exponential classical computation. For ground-state copies it is $Θ(ε^{-3})$. The lower bound uses a three-state ferromagnet whose boundary suppresses the sector carrying transition information. A spanning-forest argument and edge-boundary counting control its Gibbs weight uniformly over fields and allowed sizes, and a trace-distance hybrid argument handles adaptive learners with quantum memory. The upper bound combines finite-volume free-energy estimates, concavity and local order-parameter measurements.

title: When Simpler Beats Learned: Dual-Weighted Sampling vs. Machine Learning for the Pricing Subproblem in Graph Coloring
abstract: The graph coloring problem can be solved to optimality by branch-and-price (B&P), but its performance hinges on the column generation (CG) step, where each iteration requires solving a maximum weight independent set (MWIS) pricing problem. The state-of-the-art machine-learning (ML) pricing heuristic follows a prediction-sampling paradigm: a learned model scores each vertex of a graph, and independent sets are sampled from the induced distribution. We observe, however, that the scoring procedure does not need to be learned, and critically assess the role of ML by replacing the learned scores with the dual solution of the restricted master problem, resulting in Dual-Weighted Sampling, a proposed lightweight alternative that requires no feature engineering or training. Within a unified CG and B&P framework that varies only the pricing oracle, Dual-Weighted Sampling outperforms MLPH, hand-crafted heuristics, and exact solvers on the established graph coloring benchmark in both runtime and solution quality. In particular, it remains competitive on the DIMACS random family, where MLPH was shown strongest in the original evaluation, while achieving more than a two-fold speedup in CG runtime on recursive-sparse and real-world graph families.

title: Classes de Steinitz d'extensions galoisiennes non ramifiées
abstract: Let $K$ be a number field and $Cl_{K}$ its class group. Let $Γ$ be a finite group. We denote by $ R_{nr}(K,Γ)$ the subset of $Cl_{K}$ formed by the classes which are realizable as Steinitz classes of Galois extensions of $K$, unramified at the finite places of $K$ and having a Galois group isomorphic to $Γ$. If $Γ$ is abelian and the narrow class number of $K$ is prime to the order of $Γ$, then $R_{nr}(K,Γ)=\emptyset$. In the present article, for any $Γ$ we consider the set $R'_{nr}(K,Γ):=\lbrace 1 \rbrace \cup R_{nr}(K,Γ)$. We prove that $R'_{nr}(K, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ is a subgroup of $Cl_{K,2}:=\lbrace c\in Cl_{K}\vert c^{2}=1\rbrace$ ; furthermore, it is equal to $Cl_{K,2}$ under a certain assumption on $K$. Using this result we show that $R'_{nr}(K,Γ)$ is a subgroup of $R'_{nr}(K, \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z})$ if $Γ$ either has odd order, or has a noncyclic $2$-Sylow subgroup (for instance $Γ$ a nonabelian $2$-group, $Γ=S_n$ or $A_n$, with $n\geq 4$), or has a normal cyclic $2$-Sylow subgroup (for instance $Γ$ nilpotent having even order).

title: Into My Arms: Structured reinforcement learning for autonomous transport of objects and humans
abstract: Whole-body humanoid manipulation remains bottlenecked by high-dimensional state-action spaces, contact-rich environments, and long task horizons. This trilemma is a challenge that state-of-the-art reinforcement learning (RL) methods are yet to resolve reliably. We address it with three contributions that add just enough structure to guide exploration: Sparse Interaction Edges (SIE) for whole-body manipulation, Interaction Gated Transport (IGT) for sustained transport over long horizons, and a Hinted Object Path (HOP) that resolves collision and search complexity bottlenecks. Across all three, the policy remains free to discover its own manipulation strategy. The method generalises from rigid object to human transport. As a flagship demonstration, we show, to our knowledge, the first bed-to-wheelchair transfer of a medical mannequin by a humanoid robot completed with no human intervention during execution. In the domain of human transfer, we show that a single policy can adapt across substantial variations in body mass, size, and random force perturbations, all while training on a single GPU in under an hour. Our approach offers a pathway to fully RL-driven humanoid manipulation, enabling assistive robots that can help humans. Website: https://elle-miller.github.io/into_my_arms

title: py4radiation: a framework for generating heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom radiation fields for astrophysical simulations
abstract: Modelling multiphase gas in and around galaxies is key to understanding the baryon cycle in galaxy evolution. Modern simulation codes rely on heating/cooling functions and ion fractions to capture the thermodynamics and chemistry of such gases, but coupling all physical factors remains challenging. We present a new Python-based, parallelised package that acts as an integration framework, connecting well-established astrophysical codes and models to produce self-consistent heating/cooling functions and ion fractions from custom ionising UV/X-ray backgrounds. The package returns multi-dimensional tables that can be readily coupled to hydrodynamic and post-processing codes to study radiative processes and extract observables, as we demonstrate with static cloud simulations. Our simulation suite studies the thermodynamic history of a static circumgalactic cloud with smoothed edges subjected to meta-galactic and starburst heating. We find that the clouds experience damped pulsations regulated by strong cooling-driven inflows and heating-driven outflows that constantly overshoot pressure equilibrium. Meta-galactic heating is weak and produces a confined and dense cloud, while starburst heating is strong and sustains large clouds only a little smaller than those obtained with the standard $10^4\,\rm K$ cooling floor. Starburst radiative heating acts as a damping agent, thereby reducing mixing. py4radiation comes with extensive documentation and a sample catalogue of heating/cooling functions and ion tables for a selected set of input meta-galactic and starburst spectral energy distributions. The code is publicly available and can be easily expanded.

title: S1Arena-MM: Which Multimodal Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
abstract: Perception systems often make discrete decisions: flag a hateful meme, predict whether a pedestrian will cross, detect a spoofed voice, or select the next move in a game. System-1 models, such as OneJev and Jev-Omni, read the media and return probabilities over the options in a single forward pass, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) generate text. Which multimodal decisions can System-1 models handle, and where do MLLMs perform better? We introduce S1Arena-MM, a benchmark that gives every model the same decision requests and scores the probabilities it returns. It contains 51,060 questions across 94 tasks with image, video, and audio input, drawn from 94 public datasets and three program-generated ones. It also includes 102 closed-loop game environments that a model plays from screenshots; in real-time mode, the game continues while the model decides. We evaluate 33 open models: 12 System-1 models and 21 MLLMs read at the answer token. On static decisions, the best System-1 model leads the best MLLM by 4.9 percentage points on images and is within one point of it on video and audio. Post-training for decisions mainly improves the probabilities: on video, a System-1 model has a lower Brier score than the MLLM that it is post-trained from in 10 of 12 pairs. With up to 2,048 thought tokens per question, the most accurate MLLMs pass the best System-1 models only slightly, and thinking raises the Brier score of most MLLMs. Closed loops separate the models: three System-1 models built on a 27B MLLM reach 22.0-33.3% progression in BALROG, and no other model exceeds 9.7% with thinking off. In real-time GameWorld, latencies of up to 1.1 s per decision cause no measurable loss of progress for System-1 models. Code and data: https://github.com/zhaoyang02/S1Arena-MM.

title: Principles of Material Memory
abstract: Materials keep traces of how they were driven: a field leaves a magnetization behind, and a sequence of forces can leave a pattern that records the order in which they acted. It remains open what such a history records, which interactions create the record and which dynamics preserve it. This review relates the three. Forces applied in different orders can leave different states after the drive is removed, and in a spatial network the preferred local arrangements may not be reconcilable around a closed loop. Both effects compare two paths, one in time and one around a loop in space, and both are described by commutators, curvature and holonomy. Restoring forces and fluctuations then set how long the trace survives: a displacement relaxes, a phase diffuses, and barriers protect a pattern against rare thermal transitions. Near an instability, a weak writing bias is amplified while the coordinate that carries the state has no restoring force, and the barriers that retain the chosen state form only afterwards. The choice is therefore as accurate as the detection of the bias against the noise during the time for which the coordinate is free. Once a state is stored behind a barrier, a static bias replaces it through the same thermal channel by which it would be lost. The ratio of the mean retention time to the mean rewriting time is then bounded, up to a prefactor close to one, by the Boltzmann factor of an effective energy bias, whatever the height of the barrier. Calculations for capillary rotors and point-dipole arrays show how the geometry of the interactions constrains the patterns that a material can store. In a model of three coupled amplitudes, a weak bias makes two mirror-image patterns lose stability at slightly different coupling strengths, so that a coupling pulse between the two thresholds erases one pattern and preserves the other.

title: ComplexIF: A Challenging Multi-Turn, Multi-Constraint Instruction-Following Benchmark
abstract: As frontier LLMs saturate existing instruction-following benchmarks, measuring further progress requires harder tests that remain faithful to real use. In practice, users often combine several constraints, add them at different turns of a conversation, and expect all of them to hold in the assistant's response. We introduce ComplexIF, a challenging benchmark for this setting, together with the automatic pipeline that generates it. The pipeline expands seed requests into multi-turn conversations, weaves constraints into their turns, and keeps only tasks that a strong model can solve, so difficulty can be raised by adding constraints or turns while every task stays solvable. ComplexIF's two splits test complementary sides of instruction following: a verifiable split of format constraints, checked by programs, and a rubric split of semantic instructions, such as a tone or an audience, checked with an LLM judge. Across 14 proprietary and open-weight models, even the strongest satisfies every constraint on fewer than half of the verifiable tasks, and no model leads on both splits.

title: $w_0$ Is All You Need: Field-Level Matching of General Dark Energy Models to $w_0$CDM Simulations
abstract: We show that clustering in general dynamical dark energy models $w(z)$ can be predicted with constant dark energy $w_0\text{CDM}$ models at the field level via spectral equivalence. The prescription of this method requires equating comoving distances to the last scattering surface between predictor and target models, which is equivalent to requiring equal recent background expansion history averages. Dark energy models with the same distance thus form approximate equivalence classes, with nearly identical matter fields. To test the precision of spectral equivalence beyond the CPL parametrization, we run $N$-body simulations with various dynamical dark energy models, including spline-based $w(z)$, all matched to a single $w_0\text{CDM}$ run. Our measurements show that the power spectra of all matched dark energies agree with the predictor within $0.2\%$ up to $k = 0.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ and within $0.6\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We also compare the non-Gaussian information contained in the simulated fields. Bispectra differ by at most $0.26\%$ across all runs up to $k = 0.5\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$ and $1.75\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$, while wavelet scattering transform coefficients are all within $0.05\%$. The decorrelation, $1 - r^2$, between each matched field and the predictor stays below $0.006\%$ up to $k = 1\,h\,{\rm Mpc}^{-1}$. We run a toy power spectrum analysis in the CPL parametrization demonstrating that a $w_0$-only emulator could produce the same posterior without any knowledge of the full $w_0w_a$ model. This matching prescription thus offers a new tool to constrain dynamical dark energy models with arbitrary equations of state at the field level, without running additional simulation suites.

title: Few-gluon interactions in high-energy collisions
abstract: A conventional narrative developed for high energy heavy ion collisions prior to the RHIC program assumed hadron production dominated by hot and dense QGP formation, expansion and freezeout. Proposed diagnostics included detection of elliptic and radial flows via correlation and spectrum analysis and jet quenching in a dense medium via rescaled spectrum ratios. The validity of that narrative has come into question in recent years with detection of similar features in data from small collision systems. In response, several recent observations hint at a strongly modified narrative. Study of p-Pb spectra has revealed that the Glauber Monte Carlo estimation of A-B collision geometry is quite misleading. Collision geometry should instead be inferred by inverting ensemble-mean $\bar p_t$ data. A method has been developed to transform $v_2(p_t)$ data to quadrupole spectra $\bar ρ_2(p_t)$ that provide new insights into the true correlation mechanism. Accurate $p_t$-integrated $v_2$ vs $n_{ch}$ measurements for p-p collisions reveal a cubic trend suggesting a three-gluon interaction as the true mechanism. The p-p $v_2(n_{ch})$ trend has been generalized to describe all A-B collision systems in common in terms of an extensive measure $V_2^2 \equiv \bar ρ_0^2 v_2^2$ (number of correlated pairs). A similar program has been applied to jet-related contributions to spectra and angular correlations with a comparable result, a quadratic trend on $n_{ch}$ as expected for two-gluon interactions. Those new results suggest that the relevant data features actually represent multipole (color dipole and quadrupole) radiation from few-gluon interactions within a low-density system.

title: Characterizing Ultrafast Processes via Work
abstract: Consider the following cycle for a mean-field system initially in thermodynamic equilibrium: an instantaneous parameter jump, relaxation to the new equilibrium, and a reverse jump. For certain systems and parameter values, the two equilibrium macrostates coincide in the thermodynamic limit. We characterize this matching phenomenon through the work required to perform the cycle. Our main result concerns scalar many-particle mean-field systems under suitable assumptions. In the matching regime, the total work has a non-Gaussian limiting distribution, and the average work per particle tends to zero. Away from matching, the properly rescaled fluctuations of the total work have a Gaussian limiting distribution, and the average work per particle converges to a strictly positive constant. Further motivation arises from a contact-geometric model of thermodynamics, in which matching corresponds to a Reeb chord between two equilibrium Legendrian submanifolds.

title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
abstract: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

title: Gorenstein homological algebra over comma categories
abstract: Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ be abelian categories with enough projective objects. In this paper, we characterize those functors $F:\mathcal{A}\to \mathcal{B}$ for which the Gorenstein projective objects in the comma category $(F\downarrow \mathcal{B})$ admit an explicit description in terms of the Gorenstein projective objects of $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$. As a main application, we obtain estimates for the global Gorenstein projective dimension of $(F\downarrow \mathcal{B})$ in terms of those of $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{B}$ and the functor $F$, and derive exact formulas in several important cases. Our categorical approach also yields dual results concerning Gorenstein injective objects and dimension. Special attention is devoted to the module category over a triangular matrix ring $ \begin{pmatrix} A & 0\\ U & B \end{pmatrix}$, the product category $\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}$, and the $n$-morphism category $Mor_n(\mathcal{C})$ associated with an abelian category $\mathcal{C}$ and an integer $n\geq 2$.

title: Model-Averaged Shrinkage Estimation of the Spectral Density Using Welch's Method
abstract: We propose a shrinkage estimator of the spectral density based on a three-level hierarchical model. At the first level, we smooth Welch's spectral density estimator and model it as arriving from a Gaussian distribution centered at the true spectral density. In the second level, we place a normal prior on the true spectral density. We center this prior at a spectral density estimated assuming the data from an ARMA($p$,$q$) process. From these two levels, we create a conditionally specified shrinkage estimator. The conditional specification, of course, is the order of the ARMA process, i.e., the values of $p$ and $q$. We avoid selecting a particular order by creating a third level in which priors are placed on $p$ and $q$. Our final estimator is then a weighted average of shrinkage estimators. The average is taken over a set of ARMA($p$, $q$) models, and the weights are governed by the posteriors of $p$ and $q$. The methods introduced in this paper are similar to those presented in Botts and Daniels, but distinct from them in one critical way: the first level of the hierarchy. In the first level of our model, we borrow from recently developed theoretical results of Welch's spectral density estimator. Our estimator is consistent, computationally simple, and has performance comparable (and often superior) to other estimators.

title: Commutative bishuffle algebras and Pattern Avoidance
abstract: This paper introduces the notion of a commutative bishuffle algebra, that linearizes classical pattern avoidance. The free commutative bishuffle algebra on one generator has a basis of permutations, divisibility of monomials is pattern containment, and the classes of permutations avoiding given patterns are the monomial bases of its quotients by monomial ideals. This free algebra is not Noetherian, but we show that its quotient by the antisymmetrizer $e_k$ is Noetherian for every $k$, and we conjecture that the same holds for its quotient by any nonzero ideal stable under the symmetric groups, in analogy with the Specht problem. We develop Gröbner bases for ideals of the free algebra and prove that the elements $e_k\oplusτ$, with $τ$ ranging over any set of permutations, form a Gröbner basis for the lexicographic ordering and for its opposite. This gives an algebraic form of the theorem of Backelin, West and Xin: the permutations avoiding all $k\cdots21\oplusτ$ and those avoiding all $12\cdots k\oplusτ$ are two monomial bases of one and the same quotient.

title: Beyond Language Optimization: Enhancing Visual Representations for Radiology Report Generation
abstract: Accurate chest X-ray radiology report generation (RRG) requires recognizing clinically relevant abnormalities and accurately describing them. Although Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves the clinical accuracy of generated reports, our analyses suggest limited improvements in visual representations for abnormality recognition. To address this limitation, we propose a selective regional visual distillation framework that enhances visual representations of challenging abnormalities while preserving existing visual capabilities. Specifically, we train a region-aware teacher with targeted supervision on challenging anatomical regions to acquire complementary visual knowledge. Rather than transferring all teacher features, we verify their utility through regional feature replacement and select only those that improve the original student's performance. We further introduce a Spatially Gated Residual Adapter (SGRA) to distill these verified features while minimizing interference with the student's existing visual representations. Experiments on MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray demonstrate improved clinical report accuracy and region-level abnormality recognition across different multimodal large language model backbones, while largely preserving performance on non-target findings.

title: A surprising bound for the $2\times2$ matrix weighted martingale multiplier
abstract: For real $2\times2$ matrix weights, we prove that a scalar martingale multiplier on a dyadic root has $L^2(W)$ norm at most $CQ\sqrt{1+\log(Q)}$, where $Q$ is the dyadic matrix $A_2$ characteristic. A single multiplier, with signs alternating by generation, attains this order for every sufficiently large characteristic scale. We show that the restriction on the matrix size is essential: these estimates jump to the order $Q^{3/2}$ from the matrix size $3\times 3$ onward.

title: Low Vibration Closed-Cycle Flow Cryostat for Ion-Cavity Experiments
abstract: Cryogenic operation below 10 K suppresses trap-electrode and dielectric heating of trapped ions while cryopumping residual gases to ultra-high vacuum (UHV) without requiring a bakeout. These advantages are particularly important for cavity-integrated ion traps, where nearby dielectric surfaces can increase motional heating and rapid design-build-test iterations benefit from eliminating bakeout cycles. We have developed a custom 4 K cryostat cooled by a ColdEdge Technologies (CET) Stinger closed-cycle $^{4}\text{He}$ flow cryogenic system to study various ion trap optical cavity structures designed to serve as a photonic interconnect between remote, compute-capable trapped $^{171}\text{Yb}^{+}$ ion quantum processors, enabling long baseline entanglement distribution $(>10\text{ km})$. We integrate an Alpine Quantum Technologies (AQT) Paul trap and Fabry-Pérot optical cavity at the 4 K stage. The cooling capacities of the cryostat 40 K and 4 K stages were measured to be 5 W at 45 K and 0.5 W at 6.1 K. Vibrations of the 4 K stage relative to the optical table are less than $12\text{ nm}_{\text{RMS}}$ in three dimensions, as measured using a Michelson interferometer. An ultra-high vacuum (UHV) is inferred by studying the rate of hydrogen-$\mathrm{Yb}^{+}$ ion collisions. Ion storage times exceeding 5 days without laser cooling have been reported and the position of the trapped ions are reproducible within $\sim10\text{ }μ\text{m}$ following repeated thermal cycles to room temperature. The uptime of this system is 72 days and offers convenient access to the 4 K stage for in-vacuum maintenance and system modifications. Using this platform, we demonstrate spatial overlap and interaction between a trapped $^{174}\text{Yb}^{+}$ ion and the optical cavity mode on the 1345 nm transition, establishing preliminary experimental validation of the integrated cryogenic ion-cavity structure.

title: Parity-safe digraphs with countably many ends are kernel-perfect
abstract: A kernel of a digraph is an independent set that every other vertex points into, and a digraph is kernel-perfect if every induced subgraph has a kernel. A digraph without odd cycles in which no ray contains infinitely many vertices that each send an infinite fan of disjoint paths to that ray is safe. The conjecture that every safe digraph is kernel-perfect was proved earlier for digraphs with finitely many ends. We prove a stronger statement for at most countably many ends. Number the vertices of a ray, and let the type of a path that ends on the ray be the parity of the sum of its length and the number of its last vertex. A fan is mixed if it has infinitely many paths of each type, and a digraph is parity-safe if it has no odd cycle and no ray containing infinitely many vertices with a mixed fan to it. Yablo's graph (omega,<) is not parity-safe. Its variant with edges only between vertices of different parity has a kernel - it is parity-safe but not safe. Our main result is that a parity-safe digraph with at most countably many ends is kernel-perfect, and the claim for safe digraphs follows since safety implies parity-safety. The digraph may have any cardinality, and nothing is assumed about the structure of the ends, but the case of uncountably many ends remains open.

title: Joint Dynamics of Spins and Frequency-Resolved Bosonic Occupations: A Projection-Operator Approach
abstract: We derive weak-coupling kinetic equations for frequency-resolved bosonic mode occupations in the spin--boson model. Rather than integrating out the bath completely, we retain these mode occupations as independent dynamical variables whose equations are coupled to those for the spin observables. A projection-operator construction closes the dynamics on a product-spin ansatz and an undisplaced Gaussian environment with a diagonal covariance matrix. The equations are obtained to second order in the interaction parameter $λ$ for an arbitrary number of spins within this factorized closure, and are solved numerically for a single spin. A fixed-truncation calculation using the hierarchical equations of motion provides a benchmark for the spin dynamics with the Drude--Lorentz spectral density. The numerical results reveal a redistribution of bosonic mode occupations concentrated near the spin transition frequency $Ω=\sqrt{Δ^2+h^2}$. We also examine the response of the coupled spin--boson system to structured spectra, nonthermal initial occupations, and slow modulation of the coupling. The calculated mode occupations also allow changes in the bath-side occupation and energy densities $p(ω)δ\langle N_ω\rangle(t)$ and $ωp(ω)δ\langle N_ω\rangle(t)$ to be obtained without requiring an exponential decomposition of the bath correlation function. Its scope is restricted to weak coupling, diagonal Gaussian bath states, and, for time-dependent couplings, the adiabatic regime.

title: One machine, three drawings: a didactic analysis of a teaching progression for the function concept from Grade 4 to Grade 10
abstract: The function concept can be entered through a correspondence between sets, a relation that is single-valued, or through a process that turns an input into an output. This paper presents the design rationale and a critical analysis of a source progression for functions (Grades 4-10, nominal ages 9-16, with two levels on relations between quantities), from which French-curriculum and International Baccalaureate chapters published at https://commeunjeu.org are assembled. One schema is presented first and kept throughout: a function is a machine that takes an input, applies a rule and gives exactly one output. Its drawing changes with age (a robot, then a box, then the arrow $f : x \mapsto f(x)$), and each change is shown once, the two drawings side by side; after 15 the box returns only in the lessons, to explain composition and the inverse. The properties that research identifies as difficult (the uniqueness of the output, the constant function, the function without a formula, two rules for one function, preimages) are posed on the machine from Grade 4; the word relation is kept for the link between two quantities, where covariation is taught; the set of ordered pairs comes back as the graph. The choices are related to the function machine as a cognitive root and to its authors' own warnings, to process-object accounts, to studies of concept images and of covariation, and to the French and IB curricula. A block-level audit of the dated source documents found the machine in only 2 of the 177 exercise blocks of Grades 7 to 10, no exercise asking pupils to draw a machine, and public chapters that opened on the relation; the revisions made after the audit are recorded with their counts before and after. No empirical evaluation is reported; hypotheses for one are stated.

title: Tabular Foundation Models for Weighted Regression and Classification
abstract: Weighted regression and classification have applications ranging from missing-data analysis and causal inference to insurance pricing and particle physics. Existing weighted methods must be fitted and tuned on each dataset, which is costly for flexible nonlinear learners. Tabular foundation models avoid this cost. A Transformer is pretrained once on many simulated datasets and then predicts on a new dataset by in-context learning, using its observations as context without further fitting. Recent models such as TabPFN-3.5 surpass tuned conventional methods, but they cannot use sample weights. We develop a general pipeline that adapts such models to weighted prediction through weighted attention, a normalized weighted loss, and pretraining on synthetic weighted prediction tasks from missing-data problems. Applied to TabPFN-3.5, it yields WeightedPFN, which performs strongly on real datasets, both in missing-data problems and in out-of-distribution causal tasks, while running about as fast as linear baselines. We also establish a statistical theory showing that a suitably pretrained weighted Transformer attains the nonparametric minimax rate for weighted regression on new datasets without further fitting.

title: Interpolation of nonlocal Sobolev spaces for general gradients
abstract: We study the interpolation structure of nonlocal Sobolev spaces associated with general radial gradients. For compactly supported kernels satisfying suitable regularity and two-sided growth assumptions of fractional order, we characterize the spaces $H^{ρ,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$, $1<p<\infty$, by the Gustavsson--Peetre interpolation method between $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and $W^{1,p}(\mathbb{R}^n)$. The function parameter is determined, up to equivalence, by the behavior of the kernel near the origin. We also establish a complex interpolation formula between spaces associated with different kernels and integrability exponents, in which the interpolated kernel is their geometric mean. For the corresponding nonlocal Gagliardo spaces $W^{ρ,p}(\R^n)$, defined through an integral seminorm of first differences, we prove an identification with generalized Besov spaces and a real interpolation characterization involving the same function parameter. These results extend the classical relation between Bessel potential and Gagliardo spaces beyond power-type kernels, yielding continuous embeddings between the two families and their coincidence in the Hilbertian case. We further discuss logarithmic kernels and restriction spaces on Lipschitz domains, and obtain extension and compact embedding results for the Gagliardo spaces under weaker assumptions on the kernel.

title: A phenomenological decomposition of SRC-inspired occupation effects in imbalanced Fermi superfluids
abstract: Imbalanced two-component Fermi superfluids are usually formulated with sharp Fermi-step occupations, although interacting systems exhibit depletion below the Fermi surface and a high-momentum tail. We introduce a sector-resolved phenomenological framework in which one prescribed short-range-correlation (SRC)-inspired momentum distribution modifies either the anomalous pairing contribution (model P), the imbalance-induced blocking term (model B), or both (model P+B). The four realizations---ideal, P, B, and P+B---are compared through the grand-potential landscape and through a fixed-density reconstruction of the paired/phase-separated to polarized-normal boundary in three and two dimensions. In both dimensionalities, the pairing-sector modification accounts for nearly all of the reduction in the critical polarization, whereas the blocking-sector correction remains subdominant. Consequently, the phase boundaries form two nearly degenerate pairs, ideal $\simeq$ B and P $\simeq$ P+B. These results quantify, within the stated phenomenological construction, how a prescribed SRC-inspired occupation propagates separately through the pairing and blocking sectors of an imbalanced superfluid.

title: A Cascaded Framework with a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN Model for Pre- and Post-Treatment Glioma Segmentation
abstract: Accurate glioma segmentation is vital for diagnosis and follow-up, but manual segmentation is time-consuming, subjective, and variable across interpreters. Gliomas are heterogeneous in size, shape, and location. Deep learning has therefore emerged as a potential solution. CNNs excel at local features but may struggle with long-range dependencies, whereas Vision Transformers capture global context efficiently but incur higher computational complexity. Most previous studies focused on pre-treatment gliomas; post-treatment cases with resection cavities (RCs) remain less explored. This study proposes a Cross-Attention-Guided Mamba-CNN (CMC-Seg) model within a cascaded framework for pre- and post-treatment diffuse glioma segmentation, aiming to balance accuracy and computational cost. Experiments used BraTS 2025 mpMRI of diffuse glioma patients. After preprocessing, a coarse segmentation model extracted tumor-centered patches, which were fed to CMC-Seg for fine-grained segmentation. CMC-Seg was compared with 3D U-Net, SegResNet, SwinUNETR, UNETR, nnFormer, and SegMamba. On the test set, CMC-Seg achieved the highest mean Dice (81.20%) and non-enhancing tumor core (NETC) Dice (77.09%). It also achieved an RC Dice of 78.63% and the lowest 95% Hausdorff distance (HD95; 4.39 mm). Results were comparable to CNN and Mamba baselines and significantly better than Transformer-based baselines (P < 0.05). CMC-Seg required the fewest inference GFLOPs (381.49). Ablation experiments indicated that multi-direction scanning and cross-attention improved performance, particularly for RC (P < 0.05). Grad-CAM explainability experiments showed that CMC-Seg focuses on diagnostically relevant tumor regions.

title: When Does Fine-Tuning Beat Prompting for Qiskit-to-CUDA-Q Translation? An Execution-Verified Study
abstract: Moving quantum code from Qiskit to NVIDIA CUDA-Q is a practical adoption cost that language models are starting to automate. We ask whether a small open model can learn this translation, and how to measure it so that the result can be trusted. Both programs can be executed and their state vectors compared, so a kernel counts as correct only if it prepares the same state as the Qiskit reference (fidelity >= 0.999), with no text matching and no LLM judge. We build a 640-task benchmark with three test sets (larger circuits, an unseen circuit family, an unseen Qiskit coding style) and a QuantumKatas regression probe, and we test the evaluator before training. Measurement counts miss every phase-only error; a surface rule-based translator solves two of three original splits (text substitution); a converter that executes the Qiskit input and maps the circuit solves all 640 tasks -- so the benchmark measures source-level translation, not whether a circuit can be ported after running it. No base model emits a valid CUDA-Q kernel zero-shot.
